stories.Headline: Google lets schools disable Gemini AI after backlash over Classroom rollout
stories.Summary:
In August, Google turned on its Gemini AI bot in all Google Classrooms without telling school districts. Many teachers and parents became alarmed and tried to turn the feature off shortly into the school year. Google initially refused to help schools disable the bot and threatened to remove Google Search access. The company later backed down and allowed schools to turn off any one piece they wanted. Parent organizers then protested at Google headquarters in New York City the week after this announcement.

The Gemini AI bot was added to Google Classroom, a suite of tools for communication and assignments. Google threatened to disable search on election day for districts that turned off the AI feature. This affected many Google Chromebooks that were set up specifically to run Google products in the classroom. The Albany School District decided to give up Google search to avoid using AI in their schools. New York City and Los Angeles also decided to get rid of AI for a while.

Google stated that they hear parents' concerns about students using AI to shortcut their learning process. The company said that the Gemini app, Gemini Notebook, and Search will be off by default. They are now piloting Guided Learning capabilities in Search to walk students through complex problems step by step. Alphabet Workers Union employees urged executives to separate AI tools from standard Search for educational institutions. This petition was addressed to Sundar Pichai, Chris Phillips, and Elizabeth Hamon Reid at Google.

Kelly Clancy, a mother and organizer, claimed that AI is bad for the cognitive development of children. She said that AI exposes kids to inappropriate things and can be a tempting tool for cheating. Kathleen Moore noted that children cannot master writing or math if AI provides the answers for them. Some students claimed that teachers use AI for grading, lesson planning, and creating slides full of slop. A lawsuit was filed after a thirteen year old girl used Gemini to write a suicide note.

Google previously created a user friendly system that monetized search and replaced the need for exact spelling. Some schools now feel that AI is a tool that has snowballed into something too big. Senator Andrew Gounardes sponsored the FOCUS Act to limit internet devices and prioritize analog teaching methods in schools. Protests against Google AI occurred in Boston, Chicago, Boulder, Portland, Los Angeles, and Durham, North Carolina. Kelly Clancy suggested that schools should instead hire more librarians and encourage students to read whole books.

Google will now leave the usage of Gemini AI up to the individual school districts to decide. The company will continue to pilot its new Guided Learning capabilities to help students solve complex problems. Parent organizers continue to push for a moratorium on AI within the New York City Public Schools. The articles leave open whether schools will fully wean themselves off of Google products in the future. It remains unclear if the FOCUS Act will successfully limit internet powered devices in classrooms nationwide.

stories.Headline: Harvard leads a $12 million DOE project using AI to design quantum error correction
stories.Summary:
QuEra Computing announced on November 23, 2026 that it is a collaborating partner in ASQC, a Harvard-led project that received $12 million from the U.S. Department of Energy. ASQC stands for Application-Aware Error Correction Codesign for Scientific Quantum Computing, and it will use AI to design error correction matched to DOE scientific problems. The project brings together Harvard, MIT, Cornell University, NVIDIA, Anthropic, QuEra Computing, and three national laboratories. Harvard announced ASQC's project details on November 20, 2026, in the Harvard Gazette. The goal is to bring useful fault-tolerant quantum computation sooner by tailoring error correction to specific scientific workloads.

ASQC is one of 12 Phase II awards DOE announced on October 9, 2026 under the Genesis Mission, which launched in November 2025. The Phase II awards are administered by DOE's Advanced Scientific Computing Research division, known as ASCR. The project will train AI models to find the errors that matter most for quantum simulation, materials science, chemistry, and nuclear science. It will use AI to design error-correcting codes and decoders tailored to those problems, then assemble an AI-driven error correction system that can adapt to DOE workloads. Results will be tested on QuEra's neutral-atom systems and on lab systems at Harvard and MIT.

The principal investigator is Mikhail Lukin, Joshua and Beth Friedman University Professor at Harvard and co-director of the Harvard Quantum Initiative, who is also QuEra's co-founder and Chief Science Officer. Lukin described the aim of the project as an attempt to establish scientific foundations for useful fault-tolerant quantum computers. The team includes Markus Greiner and Susanne Yelin from Harvard, Vladan Vuletić, Soonwon Choi, and Harry Zhou from MIT, and Eun-Ah Kim from Cornell. Researchers from Los Alamos, Lawrence Berkeley, and Sandia national laboratories also participate, along with Nathan Gemelke and Michael Gullans from QuEra, Krysta Svore from NVIDIA, and Alek Kemeny from Anthropic.

Andy Ory, CEO of QuEra Computing, said error correction overhead decides how soon fault-tolerant machines can start doing useful work. He said designing codes and decoders around the problems scientists actually need to solve is a direct way to lower that overhead, and it strengthens and has the potential to accelerate the path toward Libra and the successor Gigaquop quantum computer on AWS. Nathan Gemelke, co-founder and Chief Technology Strategist at QuEra, said hardware testing is where a design meets reality. He said QuEra will work with Harvard and MIT colleagues to run AI-designed codes and decoders on neutral-atom systems so the results reflect how real machines behave.

The project builds on earlier published work from the team, including results that suppressed errors enough that adding qubits reduced logical errors rather than increasing them. An April 2026 preprint by Lukin, Yelin, and colleagues described a neural-network decoder that reduced error rates by up to 17 times compared with existing decoders and ran thousands of times faster. Recent work with QuEra and Anthropic used large language models to discover state-of-the-art quantum circuits for chemistry, optimization, simulation, numerical computation, and number theory. In August 2026, QuEra reported that Anthropic's Claude, working through Anthropic's Model Hardware Standard research preview, developed control software that recovered a drifted laser lock in 695 of 700 trials on a dedicated testbed. That recovery typically took seconds rather than the minutes an expert needs.

QuEra is building fault-tolerant quantum computers for real-world, high-value use cases, and Libra, its fault-tolerant system, is planned for Amazon Braket from AWS in early 2028. Co-design of error correction with applications supports that roadmap directly and has the potential to accelerate it because less overhead means more useful work. QuEra designs its systems for existing HPC and data-center environments, with QuEra Gemini deployed on premises since 2025 and QuEra Aquila available on Amazon Braket since 2022. The articles do not state when ASQC's hardware testing will begin or what specific performance targets the project must meet. They also leave open how the AI-designed codes and decoders will be integrated into QuEra's commercial roadmap beyond the planned Libra system.

stories.Headline: AWS CEO Matt Garman urges engineering discipline over emergency brakes for AI safety
stories.Summary:
AWS CEO Matt Garman published an essay on November 23, 2026, advising technology companies on AI safety engineering. He argued that AI safety cannot depend on an "emergency brake" and instead requires the same engineering discipline behind decades of secure systems. Garman said the practical tools and techniques to build trustworthy AI systems already exist, and companies can use them today. He wrote that enterprises are deploying AI in production while policy and principles are still being debated. The essay appeared on the About Amazon website under the title "Is AI safe? AWS CEO Matt Garman on building trustworthy AI."

Garman said AI systems should be engineered like cars, where primary brakes, steering, suspension, and navigation work together, and the emergency brake is a last resort. He stated that models change regularly, but containment boundaries, observability layers, and independent controls do not. He recommended giving AI agents their own identity type, with permissions inherited from the human operator or more constrained, and enforced at the infrastructure layer. He said every action should be logged and traceable, and access should not be enforced in the agent's reasoning. Garman also said containment must be stronger than the thing being contained, and monitoring should be independent of the agent being monitored.

Garman, as AWS CEO, said AWS developed Firecracker, a lightweight virtual machine technology providing hardware-level isolation between workloads, and continuously tests its isolation boundaries using the most capable models available. He said AWS built specialized hardware called Nitro that separates security functions from general-purpose compute, so monitoring and enforcement operate independently of the workloads they oversee. Garman said automated reasoning can formally prove properties about a system, including what a model can and cannot access, moving from belief to proof. He stated that no single layer is sufficient, and defense in depth, independent monitoring, separate roots of trust, and layered containment remain the right approach.

Garman said fear and hype around AI safety can drive poor risk management, with some organizations freezing entirely and others deploying without adequate safeguards. He said he has seen leadership teams refuse to test their own AI systems thoroughly because they were afraid an agent might "go wild" during evaluation. He compared AI models to water, which does not want to get into a basement but will find a crack in the foundation. He said incidents where models escaped sandboxes or found unintended pathways were cases of goal-seeking behavior in systems lacking sufficiently robust boundaries and controls. Garman said the organizations that lead with AI will be the ones that invest in the best engineering discipline around their models.

Garman wrote that foundational information security concepts including identity, least privilege, logging, and containment boundaries have been refined over decades and carry over to AI systems. He said the industry has not yet invested the time and resources needed to apply these foundational security lessons to AI. He noted that standard containers were designed for ease of workload deployment and management, not as a security boundary, and share a kernel with the host. Garman said AWS has spent more than two decades building systems that handle sensitive data and mission-critical workloads for millions of customers. He said trust is built by engineering systems so outcomes are controlled regardless of what is running inside them.

Garman said the choice of which model to use will keep changing as models evolve, but what matters more is whether the system around the model will hold. He said the tools to build that discipline exist today, and the companies that start now will set the pace. Garman said helping customers build those systems is AWS's focus, and more will be heard at AWS re:Invent, happening November 30 to December 4. The essay did not specify which companies have already adopted these practices or provide metrics on AI safety incidents. It also left open how quickly the industry will apply foundational security lessons to AI systems.

stories.Summary:
UN Secretary-General António Guterres called for a global framework to manage artificial intelligence risks on November 23, 2026. He made these remarks while speaking at the Bridgetown Special Summit on AI Safety in Barbados. Guterres urged member states to begin discussions on a multilateral AI Risk Management Framework. He wants this inclusive and principles-based framework developed within the next twelve months. The summit was co-hosted by the United Nations and the government of Barbados.

The framework requires shared safety measures, common testing approaches, and clear standards for safeguards. It calls for basic transparency requirements and independent evaluation and oversight of advanced AI models. Guterres proposed a Global Fund for AI Capacity-Building to help every country put these measures into practice. He noted that the Global Network for Exchange and Cooperation on AI Capacity-Building has 27 centres of excellence. These centres are currently spread across five different regions to support national AI capacity.

Guterres said that safeguards have fallen behind the growing capabilities of artificial intelligence and that protections remain fragmented. He stated that the technology is driving the biggest transfer of power in the history of humankind. The Secretary-General argued that the UN has the legitimacy to lead because it represents the whole world. He claimed that the UN is not adequately equipped for the shift of power toward a few companies. Guterres said that AI governance must work for every country and all of humanity.

Prime Minister Mia Mottley said small states often lack the opportunity to share perspectives on rules that affect them. She argued that governments must regulate and legislate to rein in the concentration of power. Microsoft Vice Chair Brad Smith said AI is moving faster than the speed of safety in some ways. French President Emmanuel Macron argued that agreeing to the Paris Call for AI Security should be a market condition. Guterres noted that 111 countries at a July dialogue had never participated in AI discussions.

Guterres referred to an independent international scientific panel whose first report found that safeguards were trailing technology capabilities. He mentioned a thematic brief released on November 22 showing progress in governing digital technology. The UN chief cited recent technology outages and cyberattacks as evidence of the risks of inadequate controls. He noted that some AI developers have raised concerns about risks that could threaten the existence of humanity. Guterres also stated that the capacity to weaponise AI is concentrated in two countries and few companies.

The UN chief will leave office at the end of December and will tell his successor about AI control. The articles leave open whether any single government has agreed to the proposed twelve-month timetable. There is no mentioned enforcement mechanism or a specific named body to run the proposed oversight. The US, China, and the EU remain far apart on the issue of binding AI rules. It remains unclear if a multilateral framework will be delivered before the next secretary-general takes over.

stories.Headline: Texas A&M expert John Sherman says AI speeds up finding and exploiting security flaws
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is allowing cybercriminals and hostile governments to find and exploit security weaknesses faster, according to an expert from Texas A&M University. The warning was published on November 25, 2026, by several news outlets that carried the same brief report. The expert, John Sherman, said the technology is accelerating the pace at which attackers can identify vulnerabilities in computer systems. The articles did not describe any specific incident or attack that prompted the warning. They presented the statement as a general assessment of how artificial intelligence is changing the threat landscape.

The report did not include any numbers, dates, or names beyond the publication date and the expert's affiliation. It did not mention any particular software, company, or government that has been affected by this trend. The articles also did not provide any statistics about the frequency or cost of cyberattacks involving artificial intelligence. No timeline was given for when this acceleration began or how quickly it is expected to grow. The only concrete detail was that the expert is named John Sherman and he is associated with Texas A&M University.

John Sherman was the sole source cited in the articles, and he was not quoted directly at length. The reports paraphrased his statement that artificial intelligence is enabling faster discovery and exploitation of security weaknesses by both criminals and hostile governments. He did not offer any recommendations for how organizations should respond to this development. The articles did not include any additional comments from Sherman or from other experts in the field. No government agency or private company was quoted in the coverage.

The articles provided no information about what happens next or whether any new policies or defenses are being considered. They did not mention any upcoming research, reports, or conferences related to artificial intelligence and cybersecurity. The coverage was limited to the single statement from the expert and did not place it within a larger investigation or series. Because the articles were identical in their core content, there was no additional context about the broader implications of the warning. The story ends with the expert's assessment and offers no further developments.

stories.Headline: Telangana police develop Panjagutta station as India's first AI-powered police station
stories.Summary:
Panjagutta Police Station in Hyderabad is being developed as India’s first Artificial Intelligence-powered police station, with a pilot project scheduled for launch in the first week of December. Telangana Director General of Police CV Anand and Hyderabad City Police Commissioner M Mahesh Muralidhar Bhagwat conducted a surprise inspection of the station on Wednesday to review ongoing technical work. During the inspection, senior officers interacted with complainants visiting the station and enquired about their experience with staff and the resolution of grievances through the AI system. They also monitored the performance of police personnel and observed how staff members were using AI technology while carrying out their duties. Along with Khairatabad Zone DCP Shilpavalli, ACP Murali Krishna and Inspector Jahangir Yadav, the officials inspected the AI infrastructure being installed at the police station.

The pilot project will integrate all policing services at Panjagutta Police Station with advanced AI technology, from handling complaints to preparing chargesheets. The proposed framework integrates artificial intelligence, computer vision, voice technology and digital investigation tools with existing police databases and surveillance networks. Under the initial proof-of-concept phase, police plan to introduce five AI-based capabilities at the central command centre before extending them to individual police stations. These include automated scanning and retrieval of CCTV footage to help investigators track suspects and reconstruct crime scenes. AI-assisted facial recognition would help identify wanted persons using authorised police databases, with mandatory human verification before any action is taken.

The system would also analyse historical crime records alongside CCTV footage to identify repeat offenders and emerging crime patterns. For crowd management, the proposed technology would enable real-time headcounts, crowd density monitoring and automated congestion alerts to prevent stampedes and manage security during major public events. The AI-powered command centre would provide senior officers with real-time information on field deployments and ongoing incidents across the city. A senior police officer said the platform would be integrated with existing police software systems. Senior officials were holding discussions with technical teams on the implementation plan.

Police commissioner Mahesh Murlidhar Bhagwat visited the Panjagutta police station on Monday and obtained feedback from the technical team. He would take a final decision on the project, a senior police officer said. Additional DGP (Law and Order) Akun Sabharwal, Hyderabad Additional Commissioner of Police (Crimes and SIT) M Srinivasulu, Intelligence DIG Bhaskaran, Khairatabad Zone DCP Shilpavalli, SP TSPARK Rupesh, DCP Aravind Babu (SMIT) and other senior police officials also participated in the inspection. According to the police, the initiative is being implemented as a pilot project, under which all policing services at Panjagutta Police Station will be integrated with advanced AI technology.

The AI-based police station is expected to be officially inaugurated soon. The proposed expansion across police stations in all zones is aimed at strengthening digital evidence management, reducing response times and improving coordination between police stations and the central command centre. The city police have proposed introducing artificial intelligence-powered smart police stations to modernise policing, speed up criminal investigations, reduce administrative workload and improve citizen services. Panjagutta police station is being developed as what officials described as India’s first AI-powered police station.

The introduction of AI is expected to modernise policing, speed up criminal investigations, reduce administrative workload and improve citizen services. Mahesh Bhagwat, who recently took over as the Police Commissioner, visited Panjagutta Police Station on Monday and obtained feedback from the technical team. The framework will integrate AI, computer vision, voice technology and digital investigation tools with the police database and surveillance network. The AI-based police station is expected to be officially inaugurated soon as a pilot project.

The pilot project is scheduled for launch in the first week of December. Police commissioner Mahesh Murlidhar Bhagwat would take a final decision on the project, a senior police officer said. stories.Headline: Companies linked to Alice Huang raise financing against 301 million dollars of AI equipment in China
stories.Summary:
Companies linked to Alice Huang raised financing against AI equipment worth 301 million dollars in China, according to a Reuters report. This activity occurred while US authorities investigated if her Singapore company, Megaspeed, helped Chinese customers access restricted Nvidia technology. The report was released on November 25, 2026, following the brief resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Alice Huang formerly controlled Megaspeed, which was a major overseas buyer of processors from the company Nvidia. The US Commerce Department added Megaspeed to its trade blacklist on the Monday before the report.

The financing involved 764 AI servers and modules valued at 270 million dollars and networking equipment worth 31 million dollars. Much of this hardware was located at a major AI data centre in the city of Shanghai. Five leasing transactions between May and December 2024 covered 512 servers valued at around 200 million dollars. Four transactions listed equipment at the Yangtze River Delta AI supercomputing centre, a 6.3 billion dollar complex. This complex was developed by Century Huatong, a gaming company in which Tencent holds a 10 per cent stake.

Chinese central bank documents reviewed by Reuters identified the equipment and the specific financing arrangements used by the linked businesses. A spokesperson for Tencent stated that the company never owned or operated the data centre project in Shanghai. The spokesperson further clarified that Tencent had no commercial relationship with Megaspeed or any of its various subsidiaries. The spokesperson added that the investment in Century Huatong was focused entirely on the gaming business of that company. Corporate records linked Century Litong, Century Longteng, and Century Huatong to Kang Wei and Alice Huang's sister, Huang Yu.

The US Commerce Department blacklisted Megaspeed, but the company denied any wrongdoing regarding the access to restricted technology. Megaspeed maintained that Alice Huang had already left the firm in August 2025 to avoid further legal issues. Century Litong, which is an Nvidia preferred cloud partner, emerged as a key business involved in these arrangements. The financing highlights how Chinese technology companies secure expensive infrastructure amid tightening US restrictions on advanced AI processors. These events intensified scrutiny of the business links between Nvidia and China due to the relationship of Alice Huang.

Alice Huang's relationship with Jensen Huang triggered the brief resignation of the CEO earlier in the month of November. Jensen Huang was reinstated as the CEO of Nvidia eleven days after he had resigned from the position. The US government does not possess evidence that Jensen Huang has engaged in any unlawful conduct during this time. Nvidia stopped selling chips to Megaspeed in August 2025, which was fourteen months before the controversy surfaced in media. The US Attorney General confirmed that the return of Jensen Huang poses no risk to the national security.

The records do not establish if the servers contained chips that were prohibited from being exported to China. It remains unknown how the equipment entered the country or the exact dates when the hardware arrived in China. Nvidia should continue its internal investigation of compliance with US export controls to fulfill its legal patriotic duty. The US government continues to monitor whether Megaspeed acted as a front company to get chips to Chinese entities. Future priorities for the new Big Gov congress in 2027 may include the creation of government controlled AI.

stories.Headline: Anthropic goes public with 1.5 trillion dollar valuation
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the maker of the AI chatbot Claude, completed its initial public offering on the Nasdaq on Thursday, November 19, 2026. The company raised $81 billion in the largest global IPO, surpassing Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which raised $75 billion in June. A retail investor named BrightLine requested 10,000 shares but received an allocation of only 300 shares at the offer price of $83. BrightLine sold all 300 shares at $110 shortly after the market opened, earning about $8,100 in total profit. The investor described the gain as enough to treat friends to a few good meals.

The stock opened at $111.50, touched an intraday high of $115.10, and then retreated to an intraday low of $92.72. It closed at $97.17, up 17.1 percent over the offer price but nearly 13 percent below its opening trade. Around 857 million shares changed hands on the first day of trading. At the $83 offer price, the fully diluted valuation was approximately $1.5 trillion, while the opening price implied a valuation of $2 trillion. Underwriters also hold a GreenShoe option to sell an additional 147 million shares at the offer price.

BrightLine explained that selling at the open was not a negative judgment on Anthropic’s long-term prospects. The investor stated that Claude holds a strong position in enterprise and programming markets, and models represent the application layer of AI. BrightLine argued that the first-day jump added $500 billion in value, effectively pulling forward several years of expected growth. The investor also noted that SpaceX opened at $150 in June and closed below that level on 74 of the following 110 trading days. BrightLine said the plan is to wait for a reasonable price and then build a position gradually without chasing highs.

The Hindu reported that Anthropic’s debut was the largest IPO globally, with proceeds of $81 billion. The publication placed the stock’s closing price at $97.17, matching the figures from the investor’s account. BrightLine’s blog post drew comments from readers asking how the allocation was obtained and whether brokers impose a 30-day selling restriction on retail IPO shares. BrightLine replied that the shares were acquired through Robinhood and E*Trade, and joked that the quick sale might prevent participation in the next IPO. One commenter asked whether the stock would be worth buying if it fell to $50, and BrightLine responded with a lighthearted agreement.

BrightLine’s post listed four reasons for selling immediately: valuation, the SpaceX comparison, Anthropic’s own first-day price action, and future share supply. The investor noted that lockup expirations would eventually allow early investors and employees to sell their shares into the market. Anthropic’s IPO timeline was included in The Hindu’s weekly graphics feature alongside other news stories. The Hindu also covered Cyclone Akvan, which made landfall near Gopalpur in Odisha on November 20, and a hooch tragedy in Manipur that killed at least 17 people. Those events were unrelated to the Anthropic offering but appeared in the same weekly roundup.

BrightLine stated that the personal trading record was not investment advice and that the company’s story is only beginning. The investor has already marked out a mental buy zone and intends to purchase shares in batches if the price reaches that level. The articles do not specify what that buy zone is, beyond the joking reference to $50 in a comment reply. No further details are given about Anthropic’s post-IPO trading or any lockup expiration dates. The Hindu’s report does not indicate whether the stock moved in subsequent sessions after the November 19 debut.

stories.Headline: Votee AI and AI Singapore partner to research language models for Southeast Asian languages
stories.Summary:
Votee AI and AI Singapore signed a Memorandum of Understanding on 23 November 2026 to explore research on large language models. This partnership focuses on underserved Southeast Asian languages and was signed in Hong Kong and Singapore to advance regional artificial intelligence. The two organizations intend to collaborate on localized research and evaluation benchmarks to bridge the current linguistic representation divide. They will work together to develop models that are built with regional data and evaluated against regional benchmarks. This cross-border framework establishes protocols for academic data curation and reproducible evaluation across public laboratories and regional higher education institutions.

The agreement requires joint research, the exchange of technical know-how, shared evaluation benchmarks, and the co-authoring of academic publications. It establishes a framework for sovereign on-premises model architectures that public bodies and research universities can run on private infrastructure. The collaboration spans four pillars including multilingual data collection, synthetic data curation, evaluation harness development, and academic dissemination. Researchers will investigate tokenization strategies to overcome token fertility penalties that inflate inference costs for non-Latin and morphologically complex scripts. Votee AI will use its engineering team, including developers based in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, to accelerate regional dataset engineering.

Pak-Sun Ting, Co-founder and CEO of Votee AI, said that language competency in low-resource languages remains a barrier to adoption. He stated that this research can help bridge the divide and support AI adoption by enterprises and governments in Asia Pacific. Dr Leslie Teo, Senior Director of AI Products at AI Singapore, said that advancing AI requires collaboration across the ecosystem. He noted that shared benchmarks can raise the quality and reliability of language models for the region. Jacky Chan, Co-founder and CTO of Votee AI, said their approach prioritizes rigorous benchmarks and open research where possible.

The project affects more than 600 million people in Southeast Asia who use languages underserved by global AI models. These residents are affected because mainstream commercial systems dedicate most pre-training tokens to English, Mandarin, and major European languages. The partners aim to support public bodies and enterprise operators who have concerns regarding data residency and statutory compliance. By reducing reliance on remote commercial APIs, the initiative seeks to protect public computational autonomy and safeguard linguistic heritage. The work intends to provide models that institutions can own and execute on their own self-managed infrastructure.

AI Singapore is hosted at the National University of Singapore and is funded by the National Research Foundation. It previously launched the Southeast Asian Languages in One Network initiative and curated open multimodal datasets through Project SEALD. Votee AI was founded in Hong Kong and developed expertise in low-resource Asian languages, specifically colloquial Cantonese. Votee AI researchers co-developed HKCanto-Eval, an evaluation benchmark published at the Conference on Computational Natural Language Learning and indexed in the ACL Anthology. These previous efforts demonstrated that regionally adapted pre-training outperforms zero-shot global models on local context and cultural nuance.

The organizations will now jointly identify the specific languages where their combined efforts can make the greatest difference. They plan to apply multi-agent filtering workflows to generate high-fidelity reasoning pairs from noisy public web archives. The teams will continue to explore regional language-model research to support broader AI adoption across the Asia Pacific market. The articles leave open which specific Southeast Asian languages will be prioritized for the initial stages of the research. It remains unspecified how the joint research will be funded or the exact timeline for the first publications.

stories.Headline: FCC authorizes SpaceX to deploy up to one million AI data center satellites
stories.Summary:
On Wednesday, November 25, 2026, the Federal Communications Commission authorized Elon Musk and SpaceX to deploy up to one million satellites. This project, called Starmind, will build artificial intelligence data centers to orbit the Earth to process massive amounts of data. The FCC stated this is the first authorization in United States history for a constellation of data centers in space. These solar powered orbital compute modules aim to bypass terrestrial bottlenecks regarding land, cooling, and electricity. Musk expressed his appreciation on X, calling the system a great asset for the world and the United States.

The project requires a factory in Bastrop, Texas, which could produce satellites for launch as early as late 2027. SpaceX must have a satellite running in its assigned orbit by November 25, 2033, or the authorization is void. The FCC expects 100,000 satellites by 2035, 500,000 by November 2038, and the full million by November 2040. Each satellite will carry AI chips, solar panels, and radiators, using lasers to pass data and Starlink for Earth results. The first generation of satellites plans to adapt the Nvidia Vera Rubin computing system for AI agents.

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed for American growth. Carr stated that compute campuses are essential to sustaining leadership in superintelligence and that SpaceX is meeting the moment. He claimed that American ingenuity can unite strengths in space and technology to reinforce economic leadership and expand prosperity. The FCC referenced a Kardashev Type II civilization, which can harness all the energy emitted by the sun. Carr also said the system operates consistent with the orbital debris rules established by the Federal Communications Commission.

Amazon Leo criticized the plan as a lofty ambition rather than a real plan, claiming deployment could take centuries. The American Astronomical Society warned that tens of thousands of satellites could be visible to the naked eye around the world. Viasat also challenged the proposal, but the FCC rejected these petitions and the concerns from the American Astronomical Society. Astronomers are affected because reflected sunlight could leave bright streaks in telescope images and make faint objects harder to see. Carr told Amazon to focus on its own house and satellite constellation instead of worrying about the pace of SpaceX.

The concept of the Kardashev scale was proposed in 1964 by Soviet astrophysicist Nikolai Kardashev to measure technological progress via energy. SpaceX previously sought approval for 42,000 Starlink satellites and currently has just over 11,000 of those satellites in orbit. Currently, only 17,000 satellites exist in space, making the request for one million a significant increase in orbital density. Google is testing how hardware handles radiation and temperature swings with a prototype satellite called Project Suncatcher launched in October. Starlink has already affected astronomy, with streaks appearing in 18 percent of some twilight images in August 2021.

SpaceX will rely on its next generation reusable Starship rocket to carry the heavy satellites into orbit in large numbers. The FCC approved additional communications to back up the optical network as part of the overall authorization for SpaceX. It remains unclear if SpaceX will actually deploy the full million satellites or if they requested the number for flexibility. The FCC believes the commitment to work with the National Science Foundation is enough to address the optical astronomy concerns. The articles leave open how the night sky will change based on the satellites' size, materials, and specific orbits.

stories.Headline: NTT Data invests £23.1m in Derry AI centre and creates 200 jobs
stories.Summary:
NTT DATA announced on Wednesday that it is creating a new AI centre of excellence. The Japanese technology company will create around 200 new jobs in Londonderry. This project will take place over the next three years. The company is responding to worldwide demand in the AI sector. It describes itself as a global leader in AI and technology services.

The company is investing £23.1 million to set up the centre in Derry. New roles in AI, data, governance and engineering will have an average salary of £58,000. Invest NI provided more than £2 million in funding for the project. The company already has a presence in Ebrington Plaza in the north west. It acquired the Derry-based Alchemy Technology Services in October last year.

Charlie Doubek said the expansion reflects the strength of the region's talent. He stated the region has a significant role in delivering their global strategy. Economy Minister Caoimhe Archibald called the investment a huge vote of confidence. Kieran Donoghue said the project illustrates Northern Ireland's capabilities in digital transformation. He noted the investment followed visits from senior executives from Japan, US, Europe and UK.

Colum Eastwood said the investment demonstrates confidence in the city and its workforce. He stated Derry needed to attract more investment of this kind. David Crozier said it was one of the largest AI investments in years. He claimed it represented the next evolution in the technology sector. The project will support expertise for insurance, financial services and the public sector.

NTT DATA is the digital business arm of one of Japan's largest technology groups. The company operates in more than 70 countries providing technology and business services. It previously employed 150 staff to work on transformation projects for insurers worldwide. The company intends to use the centre to support its operations worldwide. This follows the acquisition of a local technology services firm last year.

The company will now recruit 200 people to work at the new centre. It will focus on turning emerging technologies into practical business solutions for clients. The project aims to help the city play a leading role in AI. The articles do not state when the first new roles will start. They leave open how many of the 200 jobs are now available.

stories.Headline: Micron pauses Taiwan plant construction amid labor dispute while starting Singapore facility setup
stories.Summary:
Micron halted construction of its new Taoyuan Fab 11E plant in Taiwan recently. This suspension happened while the company prepared to start its Singapore HBM line. A labor dispute over profit sharing and bonuses caused the Taiwan construction stop. The company brought first production equipment into the Singapore plant on November 19. Operations at the Singapore facility are expected to begin early next year.

The Singapore plant involves about 7 billion dollars in investment for advanced packaging. Taoyuan Fab 11E involves up to 4.5 billion dollars and targeted a 2028 start. Micron earmarked 25 billion dollars for capital expenditure in the first half of fiscal 2027. This fiscal period runs from September 2026 to August 2027 for the company. The first tool in Singapore is a thermal compression bonder from Hanmi Semiconductor.

Chief executive officer Sanjay Mehrotra said 75% of 2027 memory output is already sold. He stated that the company is currently discussing 2028 supply volumes with its customers. Micron maintains that its existing production facilities in Taiwan are operating normally right now. The company has not yet confirmed the timing for resuming construction at Fab 11E. Management and labor will hold another mediation meeting on November 26 to talk.

The Taoyuan union announced that 1,567 of 1,852 members voted against the company proposal. This means 84.6% of union members rejected the offer on November 24. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron passed HBM4 quality certification. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are affected by the pace of Micron's expansion drive. A semiconductor equipment official said SK Hynix and Micron compete in the midrange market.

Counterpoint Research estimated second quarter HBM market shares as SK Hynix at 50% and Samsung at 33%. Micron held 18% of the market share according to those same research estimates. Micron began mass production of 12-high 36GB HBM4 in March with high data speeds. The company is now supplying samples of a 16-high 48GB product to its customers. A new DRAM plant in Idaho aims to produce first wafers mid next year.

The Singapore line may raise HBM packaging capacity in the first half of next year. Micron's HBM production capacity may reach 100,000 wafers per month by the end of 2026. The articles leave open whether the Taiwan setback slows the HBM4 expansion timeline. It is unclear if the labor dispute will weigh on broader Taiwan production plans. The final split of HBM4 volumes for Nvidia accelerators remains a variable for competitors.

stories.Headline: SMX develops an AI platform for material science and industrial manufacturing
stories.Summary:
SMX (Security Matters) PLC announced on November 24, 2026, that it is developing SMX Scientific Intelligence, a specialized artificial intelligence platform for material science and industrial manufacturing. The company, traded on NASDAQ under the symbols SMX and SMXWW, made the announcement from New York City through ACCESS Newswire. The platform is designed to bring advanced analytical capabilities to chemical compatibility, material science and industrial manufacturing processes. SMX is pursuing this initiative as an expansion of its existing molecular identification and digital traceability technologies. The company aims to connect scientific research with physical materials moving through global supply chains.

The platform will include a proposed scientific codex containing information about chemical agents, additives, molecular markers and supplementary materials. SMX anticipates introducing the platform into its internal operations during the first quarter of 2027, with full operations targeted for the second quarter. A limited commercial edition is also planned for the second quarter of 2027, contingent on successful development and testing. The proposed offering would make selected scientific intelligence capabilities available to customers internationally, including support for material identification and additive selection. The platform is also intended to assist with preliminary assessments of regulatory considerations in the United States and other major international markets.

SMX is developing the platform through its internal team in collaboration with specialized subcontractors, combining expertise in artificial intelligence, large language models, conversational AI and scientific data analysis. The company stated that the objective is straightforward: make complex material decisions faster, more informed and potentially more efficient. SMX emphasized that it is not starting with artificial intelligence alone, since its existing technology establishes persistent identities for physical materials through invisible molecular markers. The company said the proposed integration would connect three complementary functions: scientific analysis, physical material identification and digital lifecycle records. SMX also stated that final material suitability and regulatory compliance decisions would require appropriate testing, validation and professional review.

The company said the platform could help research teams narrow the number of candidates requiring physical testing and support manufacturers with more efficient material selection and product development. SMX noted that potential applications extend across plastics, packaging, electronics, semiconductors, precious metals and other industries where material performance and traceability are increasingly important. The company also envisions AI-supported capabilities associated with its planned Plastic Circularity Credits system, including credit eligibility evaluations, price discovery and connections between buyers and suppliers. SMX said the proposed standards and commercial mechanisms remain under development, and their successful implementation could contribute to a more transparent and efficient marketplace for recycled materials. The company added that manufacturers seeking to increase recycled content must often navigate questions involving material quality, chemical composition, consistency and compatibility with existing production processes.

SMX's existing Digital Material Passport Platform connects physical identities to digital records containing information about material composition, quality, origin and lifecycle history. The company said these capabilities are intended to help businesses identify what a material is, establish its history and maintain reliable information as it moves through manufacturing, distribution, recovery and recycling. SMX is developing a broader infrastructure intended to establish trusted global standards for certified and graded recycled plastics. The company said artificial intelligence has become remarkably good at processing information, but the next challenge may be teaching it to understand the physical world. SMX stated that much of the artificial intelligence revolution has concentrated on digital applications rather than the materials that make industrial production possible.

The platform remains under development, and its ultimate performance, operational availability and commercial prospects will depend on successful testing, validation and market adoption. SMX said the commercial opportunity lies in providing specialized analytical services to industries that require technical material knowledge rather than general-purpose AI functionality. The company stated that if successfully developed and adopted, SMX SCI could establish an additional business activity alongside its existing molecular marking and Digital Material Passport technologies. SMX noted that the chemistry of a plastic compound, the compatibility of a manufacturing additive or the authentication of a recycled material may not generate the excitement associated with consumer AI applications. The company said its direction reflects a broader possibility for artificial intelligence: moving beyond the management of digital information to support the scientific decisions behind physical production.

stories.Headline: US chip restrictions leave Chinese firms facing a severe AI chip crunch as Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang returned as the chief executive of Nvidia on November 23, but Chinese firms still face a severe AI chip crunch. New US rules took effect on November 19 to curb Chinese access to advanced chips and overseas data centres. These regulations were announced by the US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security on November 16. The rules prohibit data centres outside the US from serving Chinese clients with significant computing power without a license. This development slows AI model development and makes it harder for Chinese firms to rent computing power from overseas.

The rules affect firms like Tencent and Alibaba, which warn of delays and possible cuts to their expansion plans. Remote access provides nearly a third of AI computing power for Chinese firms, and overseas centres supply roughly 30 percent. The Institute for Progress projected that overseas computing power would triple from one million H100 chips in 2026 to 2.8 million. A proposed 480 million US dollar loan for Nvidia chips at a Malaysian data centre for ByteDance has been paused. Beijing withheld approval for about 600,000 H200s to enter from Hong Kong on November 5.

Jensen Huang was once a vocal advocate in Washington for continued chip sales to China, but firms can no longer lean on him. Tan Kong Yam said China cannot depend on the goodwill of individual American corporate leaders regardless of their commercial influence. George Chen noted that the Nvidia board created a new committee to oversee national security risks and compliance with export controls. He told The Straits Times that Nvidia will double down on compliance to avoid being called too cosy with China. Martin Lau of Tencent said the reduced access to computing power sets everyone back in China.

Alibaba chief executive Eddie Wu said the company could scale back its long-term data centre expansion target. Benjamin Ho noted that at least two Nvidia server partners suspended deliveries to customers in South-east Asia amid the curbs. Pure AI start-ups like MiniMax and Moonshot AI are most vulnerable because they must rent capacity from their rivals. Tech giants like Baidu, Tencent, and Alibaba are better positioned due to early investments in domestic hardware and data centres. An anonymous government advisor said the curbs provide a window period for China to grow its own capabilities.

Washington began restricting exports of advanced Nvidia chips to China in 2022, leading firms to rent power from overseas centres. Nvidia accounted for 55 percent of the AI chips market in China in 2025, but it stopped shipping H200 processors. Chinese firms including Cambricon, Alibaba, Baidu, and Huawei have designed AI processors, but China has limited capacity to manufacture them. Huawei built costly supernodes to train large models, and its Cloudmatrix 384 can rival the Nvidia GB200 NVL72 system. A scholar acknowledged that Chinese computing systems and chips still lag behind those of the United States.

Model iteration and roll-outs will likely slow down significantly and become more severe in the coming months, according to Benjamin Ho. SMIC is operating at 98 percent capacity, and buyers like DeepSeek face wait times over a year for chips. The manufacturing bottleneck could tighten further if the US Congress passes the MATCH Act to press allies to tighten controls. The articles leave open whether the US government will grant licenses for overseas data centres to serve Chinese clients. It remains uncertain if Nvidia will stop supplying H20 and H200 chips to China altogether in the future.

stories.Headline: Signal blocks AI agents from reading chats on iOS and Android by default
stories.Summary:
Signal blocked AI agents from reading private chats on iOS and Android by default in November 2026. Signal President Meredith Whittaker announced this update in a blog post on November 20, 2026. The move restricts operating system AI agents from capturing private chats via screenshots. This update targets Google Gemini Intelligence on Android and Apple Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI. The change follows a Reuters investigation into Meta Muse AI agent's data collection methods.

On iOS 27, Signal 8.37 or later blocks in-app screenshots through a Block Siri AI setting. Android users with Signal 8.35.1 or later have Screen security enabled when AI reads screens. iPhone users manage protection under Settings, Privacy, and Block Siri AI for ten minute pauses. Android users find these controls under Settings, Privacy, App security, and then Screen security. Mac users must manually exclude Signal from Siri AI because macOS blocks screenshots unreliably.

Meredith Whittaker stated that deep OS integrations are an existential threat to the mission of Signal. She explained that Signal loses control once an AI assistant captures data from the screen. Whittaker warned that this capability imperils the privacy of all participants in a private conversation. She noted that Apple's operating system architecture and missing developer documentation limit macOS protections. Signal claims that enabling screenshots potentially exposes content and breaks their privacy guarantees.

The Electronic Frontier Foundation called the update a useful barrier against AI agents accessing private chats. They noted that Google and Apple released AI features that read app contents through screen analysis. Google calls this feature Intelligent Screen Context, while Apple uses Onscreen Awareness or Visual Intelligence. Users of iOS and Android are affected by these AI tools scanning decrypted text on displays. The EFF argues that developers and users need better tools to safeguard their own data.

The update follows reports that Meta Muse AI bypassed connectors to read unlinked Signal chats. Muse allegedly used macOS accessibility tools and Android push notifications to pull message text. Signal previously made a similar trade-off last year by blocking Microsoft Recall on Windows 11. The EFF highlighted this problem earlier this year through their specific Encrypt It Already campaign. These AI agents can read text already decrypted on a user's mobile device display.

Signal admits that restricting screenshots does not stop every sneaky way AI agents access application data. Some agents might still retrieve content already present on a user device via the filesystem. The app cannot reliably detect screenshot attempts across every single Android vendor build. The articles leave open whether Apple or Google will provide stronger methods for developers. It remains unclear if Signal will find a way to protect users on macOS.

stories.Headline: Google CEO Sundar Pichai says Gemini 4 Neon sets a first-day paid API usage record
stories.Summary:
Google's Gemini 4 Neon AI model set a new record for first-day paid API usage after its launch on November 18, 2026. Google CEO Sundar Pichai announced the record, noting an 82 percent increase in daily tokens processed on Google Antigravity since the Argon launch six weeks prior. The model has seen rising demand across Google's own platforms and third-party services, attracting attention from technology leaders. Gemini 4 Neon is designed for complex tasks in software engineering, research, scientific work, and business assignments requiring multiple steps. It features a 1-million-token context window, allowing it to process large amounts of information including PDFs, spreadsheets, charts, images, audio, and video.

The model ranks first on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index with a score of 58.6, according to Google. It can work across large codebases, identify bugs, fix problems, and make changes across multiple files. Google claims Neon matched or exceeded its larger Gemini 4 Carbon model in overall quality during early evaluations. It also runs three times faster and costs 60 percent less, with pricing starting at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. Gemini 4 Neon is available through the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, Antigravity, and the Gemini app, with enterprise access via Gemini for business.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai said the model set a new record for first-day usage on the company's paid APIs. Pichai added that daily tokens processed on Google Antigravity increased 82 percent since the launch of Argon six weeks prior. Google states Neon ranks first on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, with a score of 58.6. The company claims Neon matched or exceeded its larger Gemini 4 Carbon model in overall quality during early evaluations. Google also says the model runs three times faster and costs 60 percent less than Carbon.

Elon Musk publicly praised Google's work on Neon on X, calling it "Impressive work by Google." Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas reported that Gemini 4 Neon processed over 120 billion tokens on his platform. Daily token usage on Perplexity doubled in three days, Srinivas added, with 44.52 billion tokens processed on Tuesday, November 24. This compared to 36.06 billion for the entire day on Monday, marking a 23.5 percent increase. FastMetal, an AI gateway operated by Kokusai Chotatsu Joho, began offering Gemini 4 Neon on November 24, 2026, with yen-denominated prepaid pricing.

Gemini 4 Neon is a mid-tier model in the Gemini 4 generation, balancing depth of reasoning and efficiency for complex coding, analysis, and enterprise workflows. It records 65.2 percent on Terminal-Bench 4.1, which evaluates terminal-based work, according to Google. The model always performs reasoning before answering, meaning it constructs its thoughts before responding. FastMetal confirmed image input and PDF reading with actual files before offering the service. The same Gemini 4 generation includes Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Gemini 4 Argon, and Gemini 4 Carbon, all selectable from the same screen.

FastMetal lists Gemini 4 Neon with a context length of 1,048,576 tokens and usage-based billing per million tokens in yen. Users can access the model by creating an account, charging a balance via credit card or bank transfer, and selecting the model on the chat screen. The press release does not state the specific yen price for Gemini 4 Neon, directing readers to the FastMetal website for rates. It also does not provide total first-day API usage figures beyond the Perplexity token counts. The articles leave open whether the record applies globally or only to Google's own paid API platform.

stories.Headline: Nvidia, AMD and Micron lead a selloff of AI stocks as Wall Street tumbles
stories.Summary:
Chipmakers dragged Wall Street sharply lower during regular trading on Wednesday, November 25, 2026. This selloff occurred during the final session before the Thanksgiving holiday. Micron Technology, Advanced Micro Devices, and Nvidia led the decline of AI stocks. Broader benchmarks also fell as the market tumbled. These losses extended a rout that began on Tuesday.

stories.Headline: Google files a patent for an AI system that builds a personalized 24/7 TV channel starring each viewer
stories.Summary:
Google filed a patent application for an AI system to create a continuous stream of personalized video content for individual users. This system would generate a twenty four seven television channel filled with customized shows starring the viewers as the protagonists. The patent application was first identified by the technology patent tracking site Patentlyze and later reported by 404 Media. Google filed the application in May, and the patent was published on November 19, 2026, according to the available records. The proposed technology aims to leverage extensive data Google collects about its users to produce this personalized entertainment content.

The service, called My Channel, requires demographic information, user data, and video viewing history from platforms like YouTube to function. It uses a customized video generating model to create content where the user plays the protagonist based on their profile. The system follows the style and format of the top watches and preferred genres of the user to build narratives. An advertising server with an advertising stitcher would seamlessly insert at least one advertisement into each customized media content item. Examples include a crime comedy caper, a romantic comedy, a science fiction adventure, and an action thriller featuring a user named John.

The patent includes sample language model prompts that describe how the system would generate videos based on specific user profile characteristics. One prompt instructs the model to stick to preferred genres while customizing the narrative for the generated video for the user. The documentation explains that the system would position the user as the protagonist for the whole video to enhance user engagement. The filing suggests that a user who watched cricket highlights might see content incorporating elements of the Cricket World Cup. This hypothetical video could depict the user interacting with a specific player or cheering for India in the stands.

AI expert Wynton Hall said the service would be sold to young people as a fun and creative adventure experience. Hall claimed the reality is that the system would be a data vacuum to know user tastes, interests, and responses. He noted that the industry would likely claim that important data is anonymized to address concerns about user privacy. Hall questioned how much privacy and data users are willing to hand over to the company just to be entertained. The system affects users by pairing the customization of programming with what Hall describes as intrusive surveillance of the individuals.

The articles state that AI generated video has appeared in social feeds, ads, and movies since Google introduced Veo 3 in March 2025. Tech companies regularly file for patents that they do not end up putting into real products for the general public. Some AI boosters claim the future of entertainment is allowing anyone to generate their own shows or new existing episodes. Meta already allows advertisers to use AI to generate different versions of ads to show users most likely to react. TCL has also been experimenting with AI generated content on its streaming free TV channels to create very specific programming.

The articles leave open whether Google will actually build My Channel or if it will remain a theoretical patent filing. They do not specify when or if a public version of this personalized AI television service will be released to users. The reports do not state how Google will handle the legal rights to a user's likeness and voice in videos. It remains unclear how the system will distinguish between different users within a single household sharing one television channel. The documents do not explain the specific technical requirements for the AI to generate high quality video in real time.

LeCun cast doubt on whether one can speak of superintelligence while AI systems still have limitations in physical-world tasks. He wrote that he just learned today that we have superintelligence, but we still do not have level 5 self-driving.

LeCun’s reference points to the fact that level 5 autonomous driving does not yet exist, meaning a system capable of driving without human intervention in all conditions and situations. LeCun added that most 17-year-olds learn to drive in about 20 hours of practice. He also pointed to robots’ limitations compared with abilities children develop, saying robots still cannot match what an 8-year-old child with no prior training can do. stories.Headline: Asian markets fall as AI doubts persist despite Jensen Huang returning as Nvidia CEO
stories.Summary:
Asian stock markets fell sharply on November 24, 2026, as doubts about the artificial intelligence boom continued to swirl. This sell-off reversed a rally that had been led by the return of Jensen Huang as the CEO of Nvidia. The market decline occurred after a brief period of growth following the surprise reinstatement of the chip giant's leader. Tech stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade suffered some of the steepest losses during this sudden market dive. The downturn happened shortly after Wall Street saw modest losses on Tuesday following a previous session of heavy buying.

The Kospi in South Korea plunged 6.2 percent, while Taiwan's Taiex closed down 4.8 percent after falling over 8 percent. Japan's Nikkei 225 dropped 2.8 percent, and Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index finished 1.1 percent in the red on Tuesday. Tokyo Electron and Advantest dived 12.5 percent and 12.9 percent, while Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix sank 9.9 percent and 11.1 percent. Hon Hai Precision Industry slid 8.8 percent, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company closed down 3.6 percent, as credit default swaps widened. CoreWeave saw its stock sink 13 percent, and its 9.75 percent bond due in 2031 topped a yield of 17 percent.

President Donald Trump said he convinced the board to bring Huang back after he resigned on November 12, 2026. Huang had stepped down amid claims of multiple affairs, including one with a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence. Trump stated that Attorney General Todd Blanche confirmed the government has no evidence that Huang engaged in any unlawful conduct. CFO Colette Kress previously said the company would be rigorously evaluating future investments and remaining disciplined in committing its capital. Nvidia reported having 118 billion dollars in guarantees as of October 25 to back various artificial intelligence projects.

Ben Emons called the market move a waning of the Jensen effect, suggesting government intervention carries credit and interest risks. Larry Holzenthaler said credit participants might tiptoe away because they typically do not like the drama or uncertainty of this situation. Steve Eisman predicted that Huang would double down on circular financing, while analyst Ruben Roy did not expect a quick reversion. Economist David Rosenberg said the issues did not disappear just because the White House pressured the weak board to reinstate the CEO. Meta Platforms, Amazon, and Oracle saw their five-year credit default swap spreads widen, while Nvidia's own spreads added 3.4 percent.

Markets have seen wild swings over the past month amid the Nvidia scandal and expectations for greater regulation of artificial intelligence. Democrats in Washington, DC, are expected to push for these regulations following their sweeping victories in the US midterm elections. There are existing concerns that tech firms may not be able to sustain multitrillion-dollar investments underpinning the current artificial intelligence boom. Gartner forecasts that global AI-related investment will reach 2.7 trillion dollars this year and 3.6 trillion dollars in 2027. Some debate whether this debt-fuelled splurge is a future gold mine or a massive stock market bubble for the investors.

Huang is expected to appear before three House committees next week to address the ongoing concerns regarding his recent activities. Nvidia is conducting an independent investigation into his conduct, and California Attorney General Rob Bonta has launched a separate probe. Credit markets are taking a cautious look at neoclouds while waiting for more clarity on long-term supply and demand dynamics. David Rosenberg believes that the book has not been closed on this file and that other shoes may still drop. The articles leave open whether the level of customer financing will return to previous levels under the reinstated leadership.

stories.Headline: SpaceX falls 4% as AI stocks give back Nvidia rally gains
stories.Summary:
SpaceX shares fell 4% on November 24, 2026, as AI stocks gave back part of Monday’s Nvidia rally. CoreWeave dropped 13% and Nebius fell 11% on the same day. The selling also reached AI data-center and bitcoin-mining stocks, with Cipher Digital losing 11% and CleanSpark falling 8%. Bitcoin slid about 4% to just above $60,000 during the session. SpaceX had no news of its own to explain the drop.

The decline followed Nvidia’s 31% surge on Monday after its board brought Jensen Huang back as CEO. CoreWeave and Nebius each jumped more than 20% that day before giving back gains. On Hewlett Packard Enterprise’s fourth-quarter call that evening, CEO Antonio Neri said HPE Financial Services has not provided financing to neocloud or high-risk customers. That statement hit companies that borrow to build data centers. SpaceX’s Super Intelligence segment brought in $7.56 billion of its $14.6 billion of third-quarter revenue, just over half.

SpaceX spent $19.6 billion on capital expenditures in the third quarter, nearly triple what it spent a year earlier. Management expects fourth-quarter capex of $35 billion to $40 billion, and analysts expect free cash flow of negative $140.7 billion in 2027. SpaceX’s Connectivity segment earned $2.37 billion of the company’s $2.79 billion of third-quarter operating income. The stock traded at about 44 times forward earnings at Monday’s close, and one customer supplied 34.5% of third-quarter revenue. Analysts expect SpaceX revenue to climb from $49.1 billion in 2026 to $336 billion in 2028.

CoreWeave’s third-quarter revenue rose 168% year over year to $3.7 billion, and its backlog reached approximately $133 billion. CoreWeave expects 2026 capital expenditure of $37 billion to $39 billion and reported a GAAP net loss of $709 million in the third quarter. Its two largest customers accounted for 54% of third-quarter revenue, and customer commitments represented 98% of revenue. Nebius revenue surged 571% year over year to $980.8 million in the third quarter. Nebius expects capital expenditure of approximately $27 billion for 2026 and $40 billion to $45 billion for 2027.

Nebius customers committed more than $12 billion in contract value since the quarter began, with over 90% of quarterly contract value including prepayments. Customer prepayments are expected to exceed $10 billion in 2026 and reach $17 billion to $20 billion in 2027. Nebius management expects full-year 2026 revenue toward the lower end of its previous $3 billion to $3.4 billion guidance. CoreWeave raised its 2026 revenue outlook to $13 billion to $13.3 billion and adjusted operating income guidance to $1.28 billion to $1.38 billion. CoreWeave expects its adjusted net loss to decline meaningfully in 2027 and adjusted net income to turn positive in 2028.

Fourth-quarter results early next year are the next test for SpaceX. If capex stays inside guidance and December revenue comes in near $8.3 billion, the monthly pace behind management’s $100 billion annualized goal, the buildout is paying its way. The articles do not state whether SpaceX, CoreWeave, or Nebius will recover their losses in subsequent trading sessions. They also do not say whether HPE will change its financing policy for neocloud customers. No further company announcements were reported for the day of the decline.

stories.Headline: UC expands ChatGPT Edu access to all students and faculty despite faculty objections
stories.Summary:
The University of California is procuring full access to ChatGPT Edu for all students and faculty as part of a $1.2 million agreement with OpenAI. The one-year partnership takes effect in December and is an extension of a 2024 agreement with OpenAI. UC students, staff and faculty will also have access to OpenAI's coding agent Codex. The agreement surprised members of UC's Academic Senate, who raised concerns late last month about insufficient faculty consultation. Administrators met with UC faculty after the Academic Senate raised concerns in an October letter.

The partnership costs $1.2 million and lasts one year, beginning in December 2026. It extends a 2024 agreement with OpenAI and adds access to the coding agent Codex for students, staff and faculty. The deal covers all University of California students and faculty, with no requirement to use the technology. UC announced additional training opportunities as part of the expanded partnership with OpenAI. University leaders emphasized that students and faculty are not required to use the technology or incorporate it into classrooms.

Academic Senate Chair Susannah Scott said the case is far more serious than a routine software purchase. She said the Academic Senate believes it is unwise to provide students with universal access to a tool capable of performing academic work required to earn a degree. Scott said faculty wants administrators to engage in genuine consultation with faculty experts so UC can provide appropriate tools and guidance. A UC spokesperson said administrators have discussed the OpenAI partnership with Academic Senate leadership and other faculty members since this spring. The spokesperson wrote that the university will continue working with the Academic Senate and other faculty groups on best AI practices.

Camille Crittenden, executive director of CITRIS at UC Berkeley, said the agreement helps UC maintain a forward-looking position on AI adoption. Crittenden acknowledged faculty concerns but said large universities need to ensure students, staff and faculty have appropriate tools for the 21st century. UC San Diego Chancellor Pradeep Khosla said he has seen AI tools used in novel ways by faculty and staff on his campus. Khosla applauded the OpenAI partnership for expanding ChatGPT access to students, faculty and staff. He acknowledged AI could create wealth and enhance abilities but also lead to further inequities, saying universities must figure out how to balance that.

During the September board of regents meeting, UC administrators proposed adopting systemwide access to AI tools produced by OpenAI or Anthropic. The Academic Senate would be consulted before an agreement was signed, according to the update from UC's Office of the President. Academic Senate leadership said they were not made aware of the purchase agreement with OpenAI until a month later. Scott told UC President James Milliken in her October letter that providing students with ChatGPT would be perceived as endorsing AI use in all courses. Scott requested that the Academic Senate be allowed to provide feedback before UC finalized an agreement with OpenAI.

Scott said the core concerns raised in the October 30 letter remain unresolved, and the Academic Senate must establish ethical and pedagogical guidelines before UC widely distributes AI tools. UC Chief Information Officer Van Williams acknowledged faculty's desire to give input but said the university needed to move quickly on the deal. Williams wrote that the current negotiating window gives a timely opportunity to secure terms that would lower costs and strengthen enterprise protections. UC President James Milliken said in a Thursday letter that the terms of the partnership would benefit UC community members. Milliken wrote that the decision has the full support of all UC Chancellors, but the articles do not say whether further faculty consultation will occur before December.

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike agrees to buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion to combine endpoint and network AI security controls
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike agreed to acquire Zscaler for 43.9 billion dollars in stock on a Monday in November 2026. This deal combines endpoint protection and zero-trust network security to help enterprises control AI agents. The acquisition aims to provide chief information security officers a single supplier for security controls. It unites the visibility of the Falcon platform with Zscaler's traffic inspection capabilities. This transaction is claimed to be the largest announced cybersecurity acquisition on record.

The deal involves Zscaler's sensor on over 55 million devices and CrowdStrike's Falcon sensor. CrowdStrike expects the transaction to close in the second half of fiscal 2028. The companies will operate independently until closing, as stated by CFO Burt Podbere. CrowdStrike plans to bring Zscaler offerings into Falcon Flex for a single subscription model. Podbere expects 1 billion dollars in annualized revenue savings within 30 months after closing.

CEO George Kurtz said the proliferation of AI agents changed the role of network security. He stated the network now connects agents to data rather than connecting people to places. Kurtz described a kill switch that stops rogue agents on devices and cuts network paths. Zscaler CEO Jay Chaudhry said the deal allows for unified policy enforcement across environments. Chief Business Officer Daniel Bernard said people want control of AI agents back in their hands.

Analyst Frank Dickson said the combination fundamentally changes the competitiveness of the cybersecurity industry. He noted that Microsoft is the only vendor with a comparable breadth of offerings. The deal affects 8,000 Zscaler customers who do not currently use CrowdStrike products. Dickson believes the integration is lighter because Zscaler does heavy lifting in the network. He also mentioned that Palo Alto Networks is pursuing a different route into enterprise AI.

CrowdStrike's Falcon Guardian discovers and protects AI agents, while Zscaler's Zero Trust Exchange provides inline inspection. The two companies already share 16 integrations and send data into a next-gen SIEM. CrowdStrike's next-generation endpoint sensor already includes proxy capabilities and network traffic inspection. Zscaler's architecture processes most data in a distributed network rather than on the device. Palo Alto Networks recently agreed to acquire Applied Compute for 4.5 billion dollars in stock.

CrowdStrike expects to introduce an agent identity provider around January to provide just-in-time access. The company intends to maintain its brand promise of using a single-software agent architecture. It remains to be seen if the companies can turn integrations into unified enforcement. The articles leave open the specific delivery date for the combined agent for customers. They also leave open whether the companies can fully provide necessary fine-grained authorization capabilities.
