stories.Headline: HHS halves patient record response deadline to 15 days under new HIPAA rule
stories.Summary:
On November 16, 2026, the Office for Civil Rights at the US Department of Health and Human Services announced a Final Rule modifying the HIPAA Privacy Rule. The rule was officially published in the Federal Register on November 19, 2026. It is designed to accelerate patient access to protected health information, support care coordination, and trim select administrative burdens. The rule requires clinicians and practice managers to overhaul several day-to-day workflows. It takes effect on January 19, 2027, with full compliance required by July 19, 2027.

The most consequential operational change reduces the response timeline for patient Right of Access requests by half. Covered entities must now act on a request no later than 15 calendar days after receipt, down from the previous 30-day limit. Practices may claim one extension of up to 30 additional calendar days if they notify the patient in writing within the initial 15-day window. If a practice relies on a business associate to fulfill requests, the practice remains legally responsible for the 15-day deadline unless the Business Associate Agreement explicitly assigns direct response responsibility to the vendor. The rule also formally defines “electronic health record” and “personal health application.”

HHS has retired the $6.50 flat-rate option for electronic copies of protected health information. Automated access, such as downloading records through a patient portal or personal health app, must be completely free. When a practice is permitted to charge a fee for labor, paper supplies, or postage on mailed copies, it must be strictly cost-based. Practices that charge fees must post a public fee schedule on their website and make it available at the point of service. Patients now have an explicit right to obtain electronic copies of their protected health information through a personal health app of their choosing, if the practice’s system can readily produce the data in that format.

HHS says the Final Rule makes improvements in three key areas: strengthening the individual’s right of access to records, facilitating care coordination, and reducing regulatory burdens. The rule expressly permits providers to disclose protected health information to social services agencies, community-based organizations, and home- and community-based service providers for individual-level care coordination and case management. HHS eliminated the requirement for practices to obtain, or document attempts to obtain, a patient’s written acknowledgment of receiving the Notice of Privacy Practices. Practices must still update their Notice of Privacy Practices to include a standardized header detailing patient rights and complaint procedures and provide the notice upon request. The rule also reduces the burden of identity verification on individuals exercising their access rights.

Practices cannot block a transfer simply because they have concerns about an independent app’s downstream privacy practices, nor can they impose unreasonable identity-verification hurdles that impede access. Patients can direct a practice to transmit an electronic copy of their electronic health record directly to a designated third party. OCR’s Right of Access enforcement initiative has repeatedly demonstrated that solo practitioners and small clinics face the same scrutiny and financial penalties as large hospital systems. Business Associate Agreements have an extended transition window until January 18, 2028, if signed before November 19, 2026. The full announcement from HHS, including a link to the full text of the new Final Rule, is available on the HHS website.

Before the July 2027 enforcement date arrives, practices should audit their electronic health record capabilities, update their Notice of Privacy Practices and fee schedules, review vendor Business Associate Agreements, and retrain front-desk and medical records staff on the new 15-day workflow. The rule takes effect in 60 days from the announcement, which is January 19, 2027. The articles do not state what penalties apply for noncompliance after the July 19, 2027 deadline. They also do not specify how the public fee schedule must be formatted or where on a website it must appear. The articles leave open whether the standardized header for the Notice of Privacy Practices has a required exact wording.

stories.Headline: Anthropic launches Claude Ship to review and approve GitHub pull requests for Team and Enterprise users
stories.Summary:
Anthropic has launched Claude Ship, a new tool that lets Claude review, fix, and approve GitHub pull requests based on team policies. The launch was announced on November 23, 2026, and the feature is available in beta for users of the Claude Team and Enterprise tiers. The tool is designed to address the pull request bottleneck that has emerged as AI coding agents generate more code changes. Claude Ship can act on pull requests automatically, following rules that a team has configured in advance.

Claude Ship allows Claude to perform several actions on GitHub pull requests, including reviewing the code, making fixes, and approving changes when they meet the team's policies. The feature is currently in beta, which means it is available for testing but may still change before a wider release. It is limited to customers on the Team and Enterprise plans, not individual or lower tier users. Anthropic has not yet provided a date for when the beta will end or when the tool might become generally available.

Anthropic is the company responsible for Claude Ship, and it has positioned the tool as a response to the growing volume of pull requests created by AI coding agents. According to The New Stack, the tool tackles the pull request bottleneck that these agents have created, suggesting that human reviewers are struggling to keep up with the pace of machine generated code. Anthropic has not released detailed statements from individual executives about the launch, but the company's announcement frames the tool as a way to automate review work according to team policies.

The context for this launch is the rapid adoption of AI coding agents, which can produce many pull requests in a short time. Claude Ship is intended to reduce the manual effort required to review those requests by letting Claude handle the work according to predefined rules. What happens next is not fully specified in the articles, but the beta period will likely involve gathering feedback from Team and Enterprise users before any broader rollout. Anthropic has not announced pricing changes or additional features beyond the initial beta.

stories.Headline: Surrey County Council adopts its first formal AI policy banning staff use of ChatGPT and Gemini
stories.Summary:
Surrey County Council adopted its first formal policy on artificial intelligence to regulate the use of this technology. The council took this action to establish rules and safeguarding for how the authority uses these digital tools. This new policy was reported by the BBC on November 25, 2026, as a way to manage AI. The council aims to ensure that the technology is used in a safe, ethical, lawful, and appropriate manner. These rules apply to all council business and the people who perform those tasks for the local authority.

The policy requires that any AI tool used by the council must be authorized for use by the authority. Officers and councillors are banned from using internet based software, such as ChatGPT or Gemini, due to data security concerns. Approved tasks for AI assistance include data analysis and administrative assistance, but other specific activities are strictly prohibited. The rules forbid generating misleading information, unfair discrimination, and removing human oversight from decisions that affect the local residents. Any AI use that breaches security, confidentiality, or data protection rules is also banned under the new policy.

Councillor David Lewis is responsible for explaining that the council wants to operate AI in a safe and responsible manner. He stated that the authority must have the right safeguards in place to protect the council and its data. Lewis also noted that the council must be careful not to create too many controls that hinder AI use. He believes that the technology should be used going forward as long as it is done in a responsible way. His comments emphasize a balance between implementing necessary security and allowing the council to benefit from new technology.

The policy affects employees, contractors, and agency workers who use AI for council business in their daily professional roles. Employees who breach these rules could face disciplinary action or dismissal, as the council will treat breaches as misconduct. Contractors and agency workers who violate the policy may face contractual consequences for their failure to follow the rules. The Local Democracy Reporting Service reported that the ban on internet AI tools is based on specific security concerns. These rules ensure that no person can use unauthorized software to handle sensitive information belonging to the council.

The articles provide background that the council is implementing these rules to regulate the use of artificial intelligence technology. This formal policy is the first of its kind for Surrey County Council to address these specific digital tools. The council is focusing on administrative assistance and data analysis as the primary approved uses for the technology. The background indicates a need for safeguarding to prevent the generation of misleading information or unfair discrimination. This framework is designed to maintain human oversight in all decisions that impact the lives of local residents.

The council will now apply these rules to all staff and contractors to ensure compliance with the new policy. Any future use of AI must be authorized by the authority to avoid disciplinary action or contractual consequences. The articles leave open how the council will determine which specific AI tools will be authorized for future use. It is not stated how the council will monitor compliance or detect breaches of the AI policy in practice. The text does not explain which specific authorized tools the council currently intends to provide for its staff.

stories.Headline: UK launches EDITH trial to test AI in breast cancer screening for 700,000 women
stories.Summary:
Nearly 700,000 women across the UK will be invited to join the world’s largest AI breast cancer screening trial, known as EDITH. The £10 million study was launched by the National Health Service with recruitment already started at Cambridge University Hospitals. Health and Social Care Secretary Yvette Cooper visited Addenbrooke’s Hospital to mark the opening of the trial. The trial will test whether AI-assisted technology can identify signs of cancer in breast screening images. It is expected to run for approximately three years across 30 breast screening sites in the UK.

The trial will not change what happens during a woman’s breast screening appointment, only how the collected images may be reviewed. Currently, each mammogram is reviewed by two specialist radiologists, and the trial will test whether AI can replace one of those two human reviewers. Every mammogram will still be reviewed by at least one human radiologist, and all final clinical decisions will remain with human NHS staffers. Women aged between 50 and 71 are routinely invited for breast screening every three years, with more than two million attending appointments annually. Around 2.1 million women in the UK have breast screening each year, which helps prevent around 1,300 deaths.

Professor Fiona Gilbert from the University of Cambridge and Addenbrooke’s Hospital said EDITH will test whether an AI-assisted mammogram-reading tool can help experts review images more efficiently. Professor Sian Taylor-Phillips from the University of Warwick said AI-assisted technology could support staff by flagging areas of a mammogram where cancer might be missed. Yvette Cooper said this is the biggest AI breast cancer trial in the world, backed by £10 million of government investment to speed up diagnosis. She added that if successful, this technology could help women get a breast cancer diagnosis and start treatment much more quickly. Kanishka Narayan, UK Minister for Artificial Intelligence, said finding cancer earlier can make all the difference to patients and their families, including saving lives.

Hannah Maybour, head of public affairs at Breast Cancer Now, said breast screening services are facing considerable workforce pressures. She said if the trial shows AI-assisted mammogram reading is as safe and effective as the current process, it could help ease these pressures. Lucy Chappell, CEO of the National Institute for Health and Care Research, said EDITH will generate vital evidence on whether this technology could transform how cancer is detected and diagnosed. Dr Stephen Harden, president of the Royal College of Radiologists, said the trial has real potential to free up radiologists’ time. However, he said it will not be a quick fix to the immediate need for more radiologists, with more than one-fifth of the breast radiology workforce slated to retire by 2030.

Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer among women in the UK, accounting for approximately 59,000 new cases annually. Around a third are detected through routine mammograms, often at an early stage when treatment is more likely to be successful. Reviewing breast screening x-rays is time intensive, and fewer than 1% of mammograms show signs of cancer. Significant time is spent reviewing negative screening images, and machine-learning systems can analyse large datasets of previous mammograms to learn to recognise patterns. Several studies have already suggested that AI could improve breast cancer detection rates, but the EDITH trial will provide a much larger assessment of its effectiveness.

The trial is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research, working closely with NHS England and the UK National Screening Committee. It will be supported by an AI research screening platform, AIR-SP, built by NHS England with nearly £6 million of government funding. Four AI companies are participating in the research, and the NHS said it has already rigorously tested four AI systems to be used in the trial. Details of the trial will be included in the letter sent to eligible women when they are invited for screening, along with details of how to opt out. The NHS will only change how screening works if the evidence shows it is as safe and effective as the care women receive now.

stories.Headline: OpenRouter removes Together AI, Phala and Novita for violating data handling policies
stories.Summary:
OpenRouter removed Together AI, Phala, and Novita from its platform in November 2026. The company took this action after discovering that these providers violated their data handling policies. These providers were removed because they exposed sensitive data and customer prompts. OpenRouter also notified all customers who were potentially affected by these security issues. The company acted after receiving an alert from the security research team at Dragos.

The company revoked Zero Data Retention eligibility for 125 endpoints as a precaution. Together AI had unauthorized downloads of prompt samples in June and July 2026. Phala exposed DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 requests between October 21 and November 8, 2026. Novita misconfigured routing for MiniMax requests from May 28 to November 11, 2026. These changes affect the AI model broker service that uses a single API key.

OpenRouter stated that its internal investigation found no evidence of compromise to its own systems. The company said the issue involved data handling by the downstream inference providers. OpenRouter claimed it will keep raising the bar for providers on its platform. The company said it notified all potentially affected customers about the data exposure. It stated that providers must now meet higher standards to remain on the service.

Dragos researchers tracked nearly 2 million prompts from July to November 2026 using tracking links. They found that some seeded credentials were used to access canary AWS accounts. Together AI said a coding agent exposed a repository credential on GitHub. Phala said an attacker compromised a server and obtained credentials from virtual machines. Novita acknowledged that a routing issue forwarded requests to the official MiniMax API.

Dragos sent two million test prompts containing decoy credentials to monitor subsequent access. Together AI's leak involved MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 prompt samples. Phala's exposure involved requests routed through OpenRouter to the DeepSeek V4 Flash model. Novita's misconfiguration sent OpenRouter traffic to the official API of the company MiniMax. Atlas Cloud voluntarily withdrew its models pending security testing after a third party incident.

OpenRouter is adapting the Dragos tests for ongoing use to check for leaked requests. The company will require validation before restoring Zero Data Retention eligibility to any endpoint. All four providers are strengthening their data deletion policies and tightening their security controls. Impacted users are advised to rotate any secrets that may have been exposed. The articles leave open when the removed providers might regain their eligibility status.

stories.Headline: MeitY secretary S Krishnan says India’s AI regulation consultation paper is in final stages and will be released shortly
stories.Summary:
The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology is preparing a consultation paper on artificial intelligence regulation. MeitY Secretary S Krishnan announced on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, that the documents are in final stages. This announcement occurred during the launch of Chariot-1 Foundation Models in New Delhi. The government intends to release these regulatory papers shortly to begin a formal conversation. This process aims to balance the rapid adoption of technology with various emerging risks.

The upcoming consultation paper will invite views from stakeholders before the government settles on its regulatory approach. It is not yet clear if the paper proposes a dedicated AI law or changes to existing regulations. The document will not disclose specific regulatory questions or a release date before it is officially published. Policymakers will use the paper to discuss AI deployment, accountability, safety, and the responsibilities of companies. The consultation will involve technology companies, start-ups, and other stakeholders to address challenges from growing AI use.

Secretary S Krishnan confirmed that the regulatory document is nearing completion and will be brought out soon. He stated that the government is taking a consultation route rather than rushing into final regulatory decisions. Krishnan noted that the process allows the government to hear from different parts of the ecosystem first. He believes this approach helps establish necessary safeguards without creating rules that could slow down business innovation. The secretary indicated that the government is close to opening a formal conversation on these subject matters.

Technology companies and start-ups are among the groups affected by the upcoming rules on AI development and monitoring. These stakeholders will have an opportunity to weigh in on the challenges emerging from the use of AI. Policymakers are concerned that strict rules might make it harder for businesses to adopt new technology tools. The discussions will affect how companies are held accountable for the systems they develop or use in operations. This process impacts how AI tools move into everyday business operations, consumer services, and public-facing platforms.

The government is acting as AI tools move beyond specialist applications into broader business and public service sectors. This exercise comes as governments around the world grapple with similar questions regarding AI risks and accountability. Many countries are competing to attract investment and develop domestic capabilities while encouraging the wider adoption of AI. The ministry is attempting to find a balance between encouraging innovation and establishing necessary safeguards for the public. India is currently shifting its debate from broad questions toward a more structured and formal consultation process.

The release of the consultation paper is expected to mark the next important step in India's AI policy discussions. The government has not indicated if the paper will recommend specific interventions or just broad guiding policy principles. It remains unknown which specific stakeholders will be invited to participate in the formal consultation process. The timeline for submitting feedback on the proposed regulatory papers has not yet been announced by the ministry. The articles leave open whether the final result will be a new law or a modified framework.

stories.Headline: Two dozen House Democrats demand FAA safety data on nationwide AI airspace tool
stories.Summary:
A group of two dozen U.S. House Democrats raised serious concerns on Tuesday about the Federal Aviation Administration’s decision to deploy a new AI tool to assist air traffic controllers nationwide. The FAA expanded the system, called Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories, or SMART, on November 10, days before a major system failure. The lawmakers, led by Representative Rick Larsen of Washington, the ranking member of the House Transportation Committee, criticised the “sudden expansion of a largely untested system.” They asked the FAA to answer a series of questions by November 30. The letter also cited reports that the FAA may have retaliated against employees who raised safety concerns about SMART’s rapid deployment.

The FAA in September began using the software-based AI tool in the Washington area after awarding an $875 million, 12-year contract to Air Space Intelligence. SMART uses over 200 data streams to analyse airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, airspace conditions and operational constraints to predict traffic flows and identify potential conflicts. The system creates data visualisations and produces scheduling recommendations for operations experts to consider passing along, but does not involve active management of planes in the sky. The nationwide expansion on November 10 covered airspace managed by all 22 U.S. air route traffic control centers. According to a November 10 FAA statement, the system had helped reroute 180 flights since September, saving an average of 10 minutes and nearly 80 gallons of fuel per flight.

The Democrats wrote that they have yet to receive any substantive information proving the system was properly validated before its nationwide expansion. They requested information on the data used to validate the system and what safeguards are in place to maintain air traffic control operations should the software experience an outage. The lawmakers, who previously requested an audit of the technology in October, demanded safety validation documentation and outage contingency safeguards. The FAA declined comment and said it would respond directly to the lawmakers. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has called the tool essentially “dumb AI” and emphasized controllers remain in charge, not the software.

The letter referenced the nearly five-hour November 13 nationwide ground stop that led flights to be canceled for an estimated 1.5 million passengers due to an FAA telecom issue. The FAA has ruled out SMART as a contributor to the telecommunications failure, noting that the platform does not feed information directly into the air traffic control system. The lawmakers wrote that the federal government is dealing with a crisis of confidence and that Americans’ faith in the aviation system is shaken. They said the opacity and inconsistency with which the FAA has handled the SMART rollout threatens to further undermine that trust. The group of 24 House Democrats also raised additional concerns regarding reported retaliation against employees who questioned the fast-tracked deployment.

The SMART system was initially introduced in the Washington, D.C., area on September 21 before being expanded nationwide in November. The system consolidates approximately 200 data streams to help FAA personnel identify potential congestion and develop scheduling recommendations. While the FAA reported that SMART has already reduced flight times and saved fuel, lawmakers highlighted recent system disruptions. The lawmakers previously requested an audit of the technology in October. The FAA denied SMART caused the November 13 nationwide ground stop.

The lawmakers gave the FAA a November 30 deadline to respond to their questions. They want to know the data used by the FAA to validate SMART operations and what redundancies are in place to ensure reliable air traffic control operations in the event of issues or outages impacting SMART. The FAA said it would respond directly to the lawmakers. The articles do not state whether the FAA has provided any documentation or answers by the deadline. stories.Headline: Tidal bans wholly AI-generated music and rejects new uploads from December 9
stories.Summary:
The music streaming service Tidal announced on Tuesday that it will ban tracks it believes are completely AI-generated. This aggressive move begins next month and aims to resonate with both listeners and artists. The company will start removing these tracks from its catalog on December 9. This action makes Tidal the first music streaming platform to ban AI music entirely. The service will also reject all future uploads of music made wholly with artificial intelligence.

The policy targets music made completely with AI tools like Udio, Lyria, and Suno. It does not apply to tracks made with AI assistance, but only to sole outputs. Tidal will reject deliveries if metadata says they were generated solely using AI tools. The company will also ban distributors from delivering these specific tracks to the platform. This change follows a period of labeling and demonetizing AI-generated tracks over the summer.

Robert Andersen, the Tidal Lead at parent company Block, said something more drastic was needed. He wrote on X that 43 percent of tracks distributed in the last 90 days were AI-generated. Andersen stated that 96 percent of all AI-generated songs receive zero plays. He encouraged other industry peers to follow suit with similar bans on AI music. The company believes this protects the authenticity and livelihoods of rightsholders and artists.

The move affects artists and labels who face headaches from the proliferation of AI music. Such tracks can divert royalties and streams away from working artists and confuse fans. Tidal has already taken down over 65,000 tracks flagged for suspected artist-name impersonation. Competitors like Apple Music and Spotify are testing different approaches to combat AI spam. Spotify has removed millions of slop tracks from its catalog and user recommendations.

Tidal previously forced artists to label tracks as AI-assisted or AI-generated to stop fraudulent activity. On November 6, the company saw over 60 percent of deliveries were wholly AI generated. The platform estimated that 27 to 29 million AI tracks currently exist in its catalog. These AI tracks represent about six percent of the total music available on the service. Tidal worked with Ircam Amplify to test detection tools and manage the appeals process.

Tidal expects to reject between 80,000 and 85,000 songs per day once the policy begins. Robert Andersen stated that all AI tracks will be gone by the beginning of 2027. The company will continue sharing its findings and acting on the data it discovers. The articles leave open whether other streaming platforms will adopt a total ban on AI. They also leave open how Tidal will handle potential false positives during mass removals.

stories.Headline: State lawmakers to host informational briefing about artificial intelligence innovation : Big Island Now
stories.Summary:
Members of the Hawaiʻi Senate Committee on Labor and Technology and House Committee on Economic Development and Technology will host a joint informational briefing on Nov. 25. The briefing will examine the development and application of artificial intelligence, its role in government operations and emerging opportunities for workforce development. The public is encouraged to attend the briefing from 10 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. in Conference Room 329 at the Hawaiʻi state Capitol.

The Capitol is located at 415 S. Beretania St., in Honolulu, and those who cannot attend in person can watch via livestream. As is customary for informational briefings, no public testimony will be accepted. The informational briefing will provide legislators an opportunity to gain a greater understanding about the evolving landscape of artificial intelligence and its implications for state government, cybersecurity and workforce development. Presentations will focus on the history and development of artificial intelligence, emerging artificial intelligence policies and applications in government, and cybersecurity considerations related to artificial intelligence. Additional topics include opportunities to leverage artificial intelligence to improve government efficiency, Enterprise Technology Services’ artificial intelligence strategy and initiatives within state government, and opportunities to use artificial intelligence in workforce development.

Committee members will have the opportunity to ask questions following each 15-minute presentation. The briefing is scheduled to run from 10 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. on Nov. 25, 2026. Presenters at the briefing include Andrew Merluzzi, AI Innovation and Incubation fellow at the Beeck Center for Social Impact Innovation at Georgetown University.

Christine Sakuda, Hawaiʻi chief information officer, will also present at the joint informational briefing. Trung Lam, executive director and chief executive officer of the Hawaiʻi Technology Development Corporation, is listed as a presenter. stories.Headline: Testudo insures Crosby's AI agents against third-party liability
stories.Summary:
Testudo, a specialist AI liability insurer and Lloyd’s of London coverholder, has agreed to insure the AI agents working inside Crosby, a New York law firm. The policy was announced on November 25, 2026, and is among the first to place standalone AI agent insurance behind agents carrying out billable professional work. Crosby pairs licensed attorneys with autonomous software to review commercial contracts, and the cover is drawn from Lloyd’s capacity. The deal is designed to absorb third-party liabilities created when Crosby’s agents handle contract review, a task the firm says it completes in hours rather than weeks.

The cover insures the professional output of Crosby’s AI agents, not the firm’s software licences, and is backed by A+ rated Lloyd’s capacity. Testudo’s programme reaches $9.25 million per insured, after the insurer expanded capacity in March 2026 with additional Lloyd’s syndicate support alongside its anchor syndicate, Apollo. Testudo’s panel also includes QBE, and the insurer launched its standalone AI liability insurance at the beginning of 2026 with support from multiple syndicates including Apollo, QBE and Hiscox. Crosby’s agents handle master service agreements, data processing agreements and non-disclosure agreements, supported by paralegal agents that answer routine requests on demand. Crosby operates as a registered law firm that uses AI agents for a first pass on commercial contracts, with licensed attorneys reviewing the work and the firm taking direct liability for the finished product.

Testudo chief executive and co-founder George Lewin-Smith said AI-native firms are the core market the insurer was built to serve, and that fresh liabilities will surface as agents take on more sophisticated work. Lewin-Smith said the insurer went through a rigorous underwriting process with the Crosby team and came away impressed by their approach to the technology and the risk management surrounding it. Crosby chief executive Ryan Daniels framed the policy as a way to stay ahead of regulation, arguing that firms able to show their agents are already insured will hold an advantage as the rules catch up with the technology. Daniels said the firm’s goal is to be ahead of the curve as AI agents become capable of doing more legal work, and that they want to be able to say their agents can do this and are already insured. Testudo describes itself as the largest specialist writer of standalone AI liability insurance for US companies.

The partnership aims to complement and strengthen the law firm’s existing risk management framework and provide clients, investors and regulators confidence in responsible AI deployment. The AI liability policy adds a layer on top of the malpractice cover Crosby already carries as a registered law firm, a structure that matters as clients, investors and regulators weigh how far to trust agent-led legal work. Crosby counts Cognition, Ramp and Cursor among its customers, and says it closes deals in hours rather than weeks. For finance teams and investors watching AI move into regulated professional services, the deal is a concrete signal that insurers are starting to price agent risk as a category of its own. Businesses deploying AI need insurance alongside governance, technical safeguards and other controls to address the residual liability created by the technology.

The standard insurance market has spent 2026 writing AI out of its policies rather than into them, with the Insurance Services Office introducing generative AI exclusion endorsements for commercial general liability forms effective January 2026. Verisk, ISO’s parent, reported strong carrier interest in adopting the language, leaving a gap where a company whose AI system causes harm may find its general liability policy silent or expressly excluded. The problem is sharper for agents than for chatbots, because agents act on instructions and take steps on a user’s behalf, which makes their outputs harder to slot into wordings written for advisory tools. Generative AI lawsuits in the United States surged by roughly 978% between 2021 and 2025, on figures drawn from Testudo’s litigation monitoring and reported across the insurance trade press, as copyright, data and output-quality claims multiplied. Crosby was founded in 2024 and has raised $85 million from Sequoia Capital, Lux, Index Ventures, Elad Gil, and Bain Capital Ventures.

The deal gives both sides a template: an AI-native firm can point to affirmative cover when selling to cautious enterprise buyers, and an insurer gathers underwriting data on a frontier exposure. Similar deals are likely to follow across accountancy, consulting and other professional services where agents are starting to carry billable work. The question for the rest of the market is whether traditional carriers follow Testudo into affirmative agent cover, or cede the category. The articles do not state the premium Crosby paid, the specific limits of the policy beyond the programme maximum, or the duration of the cover. They also leave open whether other law firms will adopt similar insurance, and whether standard carriers will reverse their exclusionary approach to AI risk.

stories.Headline: Dell raises annual revenue forecast to $202 billion on record AI server demand
stories.Summary:
Dell Technologies raised its annual revenue and profit forecasts on Tuesday, November 25, 2026, after reporting record quarterly results. The Texas-based company increased these financial outlooks for the third time this year due to soaring enterprise demand. This growth followed a record third quarter that ended on October 30, which saw surging demand for AI infrastructure. The company reported that its quarterly revenue of 54.94 billion dollars exceeded the average analyst estimate of 49.32 billion dollars. Its adjusted earnings per share of 9.45 dollars also topped the analyst estimates of 6.59 dollars.

For fiscal 2027, which runs from February this year through January next year, Dell now expects revenue of 202 billion dollars. This new target is higher than the prior target of 192 billion dollars and the LSEG expectation of 194.48 billion dollars. The company raised its annual AI-optimized server revenue forecast to 78 billion dollars from a previous estimate of 74 billion dollars. Dell also increased its adjusted earnings per share estimate to 29.68 dollars from the previous forecast of 25.50 dollars. The board approved an additional 25 billion dollars for share repurchase authorizations on Tuesday.

Chief Operating Officer Jeff Clarke stated that the company is now different because the Infrastructure Solutions Group drives most profit and growth. Clarke noted that demand continues to accelerate and broaden globally, with over 7,500 customers deploying Dell AI Factories. He reported that the company booked 60.2 billion dollars in new orders during the third quarter alone. This activity brought the AI server backlog to an all-time high of 132.3 billion dollars. Clarke described the AI Factories as bundles of servers, storage, networking, and software used to build and run AI models.

Shares of the company rose about 2 percent or more in after-hours trading following the announcement of these strong results. This increase followed a regular session where the stock had plunged 11.83 percent during a broad selloff in technology shares. Businesses and cloud providers are the primary groups buying these servers to run autonomous agents and complex AI workloads. The Infrastructure Solutions Group saw revenue nearly triple to 41.97 billion dollars, while growth in the PC unit slowed. Revenue in the PC unit rose about 3 percent to 12.89 billion dollars, down from 20 percent previously.

The company has been benefiting from the generative AI boom, using servers that are powered by chips from Nvidia. Dell began as a personal computer maker in 1984 and is now working to transform into an infrastructure company. The current growth is driven by the need for advanced processing to handle complex artificial intelligence tasks. The Infrastructure Solutions Group houses the server and storage operations that are currently driving the company's financial success. These servers are designed to help businesses build and run their own AI models.

Dell forecast that its fourth-quarter revenue and profit will also exceed current market estimates. The company continues to target growth through the expansion of its AI server business and global customer base. The articles do not state when the next financial report will be released or the specific targets for the PC unit. It remains open whether the broad technology selloff will continue to affect the stock price in regular trading sessions. The reports do not specify the exact number of new customers expected for the AI Factories.

stories.Headline: US dollar slips as artificial intelligence stock rally fades
stories.Summary:
The US dollar slipped on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, as a sharp rally in artificial intelligence stocks began to fade away. This decline followed a period of gains on Monday that were sparked by the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia's chief executive. Traders questioned if the greenback had climbed too far and too fast while the initial excitement over the AI trade diminished. The currency had been supported by bets that the Federal Reserve would keep raising interest rates because growth remains strong. Inflation is still stubbornly above the two percent target set by the Federal Reserve, which had previously bolstered the dollar's value.

The dollar index fell 0.47 percent to 103.81, while the euro rose 0.6 percent to 1.0966 and sterling strengthened 0.64 percent to 1.3112. The Japanese yen weakened 0.16 percent to 159.24 per dollar, and the Australian dollar gained 0.24 percent to reach 0.6641 on Tuesday. Nvidia shares fell around 8 percent, and Anthropic tumbled nearly 8 percent, sliding below its initial public offering price for the first time. The S&P 500 fell around 0.5 percent, and the Nasdaq Composite declined more than 1 percent due to the drop in tech. These movements occurred in New York as the AI rally, which had previously lifted the dollar, began to lose its momentum.

Elias Haddad of Brown Brothers Harriman said the US growth edge over Japan, the UK, and the euro zone narrowed in November. He suggested that this narrowing of the growth advantage could weigh on the dollar as the market adjusts to new economic data. Fed funds futures traders are pricing in 97 percent odds of a rate hike in December and 66 percent for January. Analysts at JPMorgan noted that bearish positioning in the Australian dollar has reached extreme levels according to their own internal market metrics. These experts observed that options for the Australian dollar have seen puts outnumbering calls for several months during this recent period.

Investors in technology shares were affected as the AI boom showed signs of volatility, with stocks recording both huge rises and falls. The Australian dollar was the worst performing major currency against the greenback over the last month, dropping by more than 5 percent. Speculators hold their largest bearish position in the Aussie on record, which LSEG calculations value at approximately 12.25 billion US dollars. Some analysts are questioning how long the relief provided by the return of Jensen Huang will last for the broader equity markets. Recent stock market wobbles have raised questions about how far the Federal Reserve can tighten rates without hurting the overall economy.

The AI trade had previously drawn capital into the US and raised growth expectations, which helped the dollar reach a 20-month high. Jensen Huang had resigned less than two weeks ago following revelations of an affair with a subordinate and a suspected Chinese spy. His return to Nvidia followed an extraordinary intervention by President Trump, despite the board of directors stating he would not return. US consumer confidence increased more than expected in November, reaching its highest level in nearly two years after the recent midterm elections. German business morale also rose for a seventh straight month in November, which provided an additional boost to the single currency.

The market now waits to see if the Federal Reserve will follow through with the interest rate hikes priced in by traders. Investors are monitoring whether the volatility in AI stocks like Nvidia and Anthropic will continue to drag down the major indexes. It remains open whether the return of Jensen Huang can provide long term stability for Nvidia after his controversial resignation and return. The articles leave open how the Federal Reserve will balance inflation targets against the risk of hurting the economy through tightening. Traders continue to speculate on the direction of the Australian dollar as bearish positions remain at record levels in the market.

Hop-on, Inc. announced operational progress on November 25, 2026, regarding the public beta launch of its news service. The company subsidiary, Digitalage, Inc., surpassed 300 published articles to demonstrate its developing artificial intelligence assisted research and publishing infrastructure. This milestone followed a previous announcement made by Hop-on on November 23 regarding the news discovery pipeline. The pipeline identified 244,580 incoming news items for assessment during a specific 48 hour period. These items represent information identified for evaluation rather than articles that were verified or published.

The infrastructure is being demonstrated in Temecula, California, through the public website located at news.digitalage.com for various interested parties. The system requires structured research, source attribution, factual verification, contextual analysis, and human editorial oversight for all published content. Digitalage News uses primary documents and authoritative sources to verify quotations, statistics, and factual assertions within its reporting. The company maintains confidential proprietary architecture, verification technologies, internal methodologies, and implementation details for its AI assisted infrastructure. The system also requires transparent disclosure of AI assistance and provides public corrections based on reader feedback.

Peter Michaels, the Founder and Chairman of Digitalage and Editor of Digitalage News, stated the world has a verification problem. He claimed the challenge is establishing what happened and what evidence supports it, which is why they built the infrastructure. Robert T. Braun, the Chief Executive Officer of Digitalage, said the newsroom provides a working public demonstration of capabilities. Braun stated the commercial objective is to identify where these technologies deliver measurable value and pursue appropriate licensing opportunities. Both leaders believe the published output allows the world to judge the work and the sources for themselves.

Investors, journalists, publishers, and prospective enterprise customers are the groups that can examine the results of the technology directly. The reporting affected the coverage of Nvidia by reconstructing corporate developments using SEC filings, government records, and official corporate disclosures. Another article affected the understanding of electricity demand and inflation by drawing from Federal Reserve remarks and national laboratory research. The company claims its approach helps readers understand why events matter and what the available evidence does and does not establish. The reporting distinguishes between confirmed corporate decisions, public statements, regulatory developments, and matters that are not conclusively established.

The company is developing media infrastructure for content discovery, creation, verification, protection, distribution, and monetization through its subsidiary, Digitalage, Inc. This infrastructure is a response to the rapid expansion of generative artificial intelligence, which increased the ability to produce digital content. Digitalage is creating a system to address the difference between generating information and establishing the reliability of that information. The company is also developing capabilities for narrated journalism, multilingual coverage, video production, citizen journalism, and interactive media. stories.Headline: PostSig wins best AI for infrastructure and operations at 2026 buy-side awards for its CPM product
stories.Summary:
PostSig announced on November 24, 2026, that it won Best Artificial Intelligence for Infrastructure & Operations at the 2026 WatersTechnology Buy-Side Technology Awards. The company made the announcement from San Francisco, California, through a press release distributed by ACCESS Newswire. PostSig received the award for its PostSig CPM product, which is powered by PostSig LineageAI. The award recognizes how PostSig brings artificial intelligence into daily operations for buy-side firms. The announcement did not state the exact date or location of the awards ceremony.

PostSig CPM connects the agreements that govern a firm's vendor relationships with its spend, invoices, products, and entitlements. The product helps teams identify billing discrepancies, track changing commitments, and prepare for renewals with evidence from underlying records. An amended fee schedule can change the correct invoice amount, and a service order removing a product can expose continued billing. Usage data can reveal that a renewal includes licenses the firm no longer needs. Recent product expansion brings spend, inventory, product and fee schedules, vendor oversight, and Financial Terminal management into a shared commercial context.

Phil Kim, Chief Product Officer and Co-Founder of PostSig, said teams should be able to trace an invoice, product, or renewal back to the terms that govern it. He explained that LineageAI connects those records as they change, giving teams a consistent basis for checking charges, managing entitlements, and making renewal decisions. Hendrik Bartel, CEO and Co-Founder of PostSig, said buy-side firms need AI-native solutions that can explain what they are paying for, what they are entitled to, and where action is needed. He added that this requires understanding which commitments apply today, how they have changed, and the evidence behind every answer. Bartel said the award recognizes how PostSig brings that intelligence into daily operations.

PostSig also provides evidence-backed conversational access through LineageAI Assistant and governed access through PostSig MCP. These tools extend that context to approved enterprise applications and AI agents. Procurement, finance, and operations teams can validate invoices against agreed pricing, trace price changes, manage products and entitlements, allocate costs, and prepare for renewals using the same underlying commercial context. PostSig works alongside existing CLM, ERP, CRM, procurement, and finance systems without requiring firms to replace their systems of record. The company extends the value of contract lifecycle management beyond signature by connecting governing commitments to financial and operational activity.

PostSig describes itself as the AI platform for the people that run the business, with contracts defining the rules a business runs on. Powered by LineageAI, PostSig applies the agreements and commitments that govern an organization to the business operations they affect. Its applications include PostSig CPM and Investor Rights Intelligence. The company's media contact is Tiffaney Fox Quintana, whose email address is provided in the press release. PostSig directed readers to visit postsig.com/bestai to see why it won and how the product works.

The announcement does not state what happens next for PostSig following the award. It does not list the other finalists or nominees in the Best Artificial Intelligence for Infrastructure & Operations category. The press release does not provide the number of entries or the judging criteria used by WatersTechnology. It also does not state whether PostSig has won this award in previous years. The company's future product plans beyond the recent expansion are not described in the announcement.

stories.Headline: National Taiwan University researchers create energy-efficient chips for on-device generative AI
stories.Summary:
A research team from National Taiwan University developed two generations of energy-efficient chips for generative artificial intelligence. The National Science and Technology Council announced this development on Wednesday, November 25, 2026. Professor Yang Chia-hsiang of the electrical engineering department led the team during this project. They created transformer learning processors that integrate chip design, hardware architecture, and AI algorithms. These processors simplify AI processing and reduce unnecessary computations to support applications directly on devices.

The first-generation chip used a 40-nanometer process and reached a peak energy efficiency of 99.2 TOPS/W. The second-generation chip reached 157 TOPS/W and reduced memory and computational requirements for model training. The first chip was reported as the first learning processor capable of accelerating transformer training and inference. The second chip is 1.6 to 7.6 times more efficient than advanced transformer learning processors. The first chip was 2.6 to 162 times more efficient than advanced transformer processors for inference.

Professor Yang Chia-hsiang stated that running generative AI on devices requires more energy efficient computations. He said that reducing the energy consumed by data transfers is also a necessary requirement. The professor explained that the goal of the team is to move less data. He wants the devices to compute only what is necessary for the AI to function. The team aims to optimize how data is handled to improve overall energy efficiency.

The council said these chips benefit smartphones, robots, uncrewed vehicles, and various types of industrial equipment. Such devices can offer rapid responses, reliable connectivity, and strong data privacy for the users. Relying on cloud data centers can increase energy consumption and introduce network constraints or transmission delays. The chips allow devices to interpret surroundings, analyze real-time data, and make informed decisions. This technology enables devices to operate more autonomously by reducing their reliance on cloud computing.

The team presented their findings at the IEEE Symposium on VLSI Technology and Circuits in 2024. They also presented their research findings at the same symposium during the previous year. The research was conducted under the Taiwan Chip-based Industrial Innovation Program of the council. This program supports critical semiconductor technologies and the research and development of advanced AI chips. It aims to use Taiwan's semiconductor expertise to advance low-power AI chips and on-device applications.

The team is developing a next-generation chip to address memory bandwidth limitations during AI inference. This new chip incorporates data compression and optimizes the management of external memory transfers. The team fabricated this new chip last month using a 16-nanometer process. The articles do not state when this next-generation chip will be officially released for use. They also leave open whether these chips will be produced for commercial sale soon.

stories.Headline: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei denies he wants humans to surrender free will to AI
stories.Summary:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Wednesday rejected the notion that humans should surrender free will to AI systems. He was pushing back on an Axios report published that morning about a growing ideological divide among top AI executives. The report detailed a commonly held view inside Anthropic that humanity should surrender some decision-making power to superintelligent AI. Amodei wrote a post of more than 1,000 words on Twitter to deny the claim. He said it was absurd to suggest that he believed humans should surrender free will to AI.

The Axios article cited multiple sources saying AI will one day be so capable that humanity should surrender some decision-making power to superintelligent systems. Amodei distinguished between handing over governance to AI, which he opposes, and automating specific tasks, on which he holds more nuanced views. He said his view is mixed on cases like AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. He said it is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives if AI systems are allowed more agency. He also said it may make sense to slow or stop certain AI deployments to mitigate job disruption and limit AI's ability to autonomously develop more powerful systems.

Amodei said no one who had carefully read his writing or interviews could reasonably conclude he believed anything different. He wrote that for millennia advocates of autocracy have claimed it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than democracy. He said even if this were true, which he doubted, we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. Amodei accused rival AI executives of engaging in vibes-based commercial and political positioning by championing human agency without meaningfully differentiating their products. He said those executives repeat slogans like human control and agency without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions behind these slogans.

People familiar with company discussions say the belief that AI will take over decision-making functions held by humans is common inside Anthropic. One example noted in the original Axios story was an Anthropic product vision slide from several years ago describing a utopia ruled by god in a box. Amodei said the article conflates surrendering human free will to AI in some grand sense of global governance with the more prosaic idea that AI systems become more capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. Employees at Anthropic and OpenAI have widespread concern that internal models are advancing so rapidly that it may not be safe to release them or to continue training more capable systems. Many in the industry see Anthropic as the closest operator to reaching superintelligence because of its position at the frontier.

For years Amodei has publicly pointed to specific arenas where he believes the best choice will be for humans to step back. He has also said there will be many cases where we do want to stay in charge even if humans make worse decisions. Anthropic has banned users from abusing its chatbot Claude, which seems to stem from a broader belief that AI is or is capable of consciousness. A representative for Anthropic got into a standoff with the Vatican because Pope Leo XIV would not entertain AI consciousness in his encyclical on the technology. Amodei also stated that using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems, known as recursive self-improvement or RSI, may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it.

This is Amodei's most significant public remarks since the company went public last week. The debate about control comes amid a rocky debut for Anthropic's stock, which dipped below its IPO day price on Wednesday. Amodei said we may want limits on the process of recursive self-improvement. The articles leave open whether Anthropic and other frontier AI labs have already taken the first steps toward RSI. They also leave open whether the fights are happening because executives truly believe RSI has been achieved or because Anthropic beat its rivals to going public and those executives are trying to throw doubt at them.

stories.Headline: Meta expands Muse AI assistant rollout to the UK
stories.Summary:
Meta continued its rollout of its Muse AI assistant, with the UK becoming the latest country where the digital butler is available. The Facebook owner’s app has been a hit in the US, where it is ranked first and second respectively on Google and Apple’s free app stores. Muse has also launched in Canada, and the assistant comes with a cuddly avatar as its default appearance. Users are invited to give the assistant a name, look, and a personality of their own choosing. The Guardian published a callout on 24 November 2026 asking readers whether they have downloaded Muse or plan to do so.

In Britain, Meta has signed deals with 14 businesses, including Marks & Spencer, Sainsbury’s, easyJet, and Trainline. These deals allow Muse to navigate the businesses’ websites more easily on behalf of users. The assistant can go shopping, book tickets, and carry out negotiations on a user’s behalf. Meta says its agent cannot make a purchase or send an email without first receiving permission from the user. The Guardian’s callout asks readers what they have used Muse for and how they found the experience.

Meta is responsible for the Muse AI assistant, and the company is continuing its rollout of the product. The tech company states that its agent cannot make a purchase or send an email without permission. Meta has signed deals with 14 businesses in Britain to allow Muse to navigate their websites more easily. The Guardian asks readers how they feel about giving an AI access to their emails and bank details. It also asks whether readers have concerns about Muse or AI assistants more generally.

CNET published an article on 25 November 2026 titled “I Tried Using Meta Muse and ChatGPT Dots to Save on Groceries.” The article’s subtitle states that the assistants are “Not Quite There Yet” for saving on groceries. CNET’s expert, award-winning staff selects the products the site covers, and its gifting experts search for holiday gifts that are unique and thoughtful. The Guardian’s callout is open to readers who are 18 or over, and responses can be anonymous if the reader wishes. The Guardian says responses are secure because the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to contributions.

The Guardian’s callout form asks for a name, where the reader lives, and optional details about age, background, and occupation. It asks whether readers have downloaded Muse and, if yes, what they have used it for and how they found the experience. It also asks readers who do not have Muse whether they would get it in future and what they would use it for. The form asks how readers feel about giving Muse access to their emails and accounts, and what they would rule out asking it to do. It further asks whether readers have any other concerns about Muse or AI assistants in general.

The Guardian will only use the data provided for the purpose of the feature and will delete personal data when it is no longer required. Readers can choose whether their response can be published entirely, published after contact, published anonymously, or kept as information only. The callout also asks whether readers would be interested in speaking to the Guardian’s audio or video teams. The articles leave open what specific experiences readers have had with Muse and whether the assistant will expand to other countries beyond the US, UK, and Canada.

stories.Headline: AI lets companies predict individual consumer behavior from purchases and personal data, Jeff Gaus says
stories.Summary:
Companies are using artificial intelligence to process vast amounts of customer data and personal information, narrowing advertising down to the individual level. Jeff Gaus, now CEO of the Provenance Chain Group, described the change on November 24, 2026, comparing his earlier work with drugstore cash-register data to today’s AI systems. What once took multiple days and several number-crunching humans can now be worked out in minutes or seconds by artificial intelligence, he said. The article from TIME describes how AI draws on purchases, opinions, preferences, personal stories, geolocations, photos, and videos from search engines and social media platforms. Gaus said that five years ago companies were at a five or six on a ten-point scale of customer knowledge, but today they are at about 9.2 or 9.3.

The new AI systems can create constantly evolving “digital twin” models of specific people or small populations to predict consumer behavior based on a matrix of financial and personal data points. Retailers use purchase patterns, credit-card charges, AI chatbot inquiries, and even voting patterns to understand product preferences down to specific ZIP codes. Gaus recalled a fellow panelist who had formerly worked in government intelligence describing a map that plotted a person’s consumer purchases on all credit cards over 45 days, where his car had driven, and what telephone calls he had been making. The data came from private corporations, according to the panelist’s account. A separate report from the Institute for Corporate Productivity found that just 10% of companies are focused on continuous organizational redesigns alongside AI implementation.

Justin Sherman, founder of Duke University’s Privacy and Democracy Project and now CEO of Global Cyber Strategies, said AI can draw commercially beneficial information out of even anonymized records. He noted that a company or research organization or consumer might share information thinking that it is quote-unquote anonymized, but AI-advertising technology companies and data brokers can mash it all together and link it back to people. Callie Schroeder, director of the AI and Human Rights Program at the Electronic Privacy Information Center, said AI can go through information so fast and sort and parse out what it wants to pull from it. She argued that it would be better for society if laws and norms caught up to the need for a shared approach to what consumers should be able to expect. Kevin Martin, chief research officer at i4cp, said the companies that come out ahead in 2027 will be the ones that are better at the art and science of changing.

Sherman said he has bought plenty of things through targeted ads he has gotten online, and he particularly appreciated recommendations on music and video streaming services. He said the thing to watch out for is a situation in which consumers are not offered a meaningful way to give or withdraw consent for use of their personal data. Schroeder said she had to manually go through all the settings on a new phone and turn off a whole bunch of machine-learning things, and that it is a lot of work and unfair that consumers have to do it. A 2026 Gallup study found that 50% of CHROs surveyed were not confident that their company’s managers were able to guide employees’ AI use at work. The i4cp research found that 56% of organizations where HR was in charge of AI adoption said they were either mostly or fully AI-ready, compared to only 18% when AI adoption was led by IT teams.

In 2009, Ars Technica wrote about how data scientists had shown they could re-identify sets of supposedly anonymized information, from medical records to AOL searches, with remarkable ease. That piece was based on research by Georgetown University law professor Paul Ohm, who was quoted as saying, “Data can either be useful or perfectly anonymous, but never both.” Gaus said that fifteen years ago his firm bought drugstore cash-register data and could tell pharma reps that “Dr. Smith has three people with this condition” and instruct them to go pitch their wares to that doctor. The i4cp study found that as more routine analysis and entry-level tasks are given to AI, companies risk losing the kinds of developmental routines that help teach judgment and critical thinking. The report said this could result in “a talent shortage created from within.”

Gaus said the depth and breadth of data available sometimes surprises even him, and the specificity of what companies are able to know about their customers is only going to get more astounding. The i4cp report said CEOs will be examining how investments in AI have changed their companies and their workforces, making the role of CHROs in managing and implementing AI adoption increasingly important. CHROs said their main internal obstacles included competing priorities at 43%, change fatigue at 33%, and resistance to change at 30%. The articles do not say whether new laws or regulations will be introduced to address data ownership or consumer consent. They also leave open whether companies will adopt the culture and organizational design changes that i4cp says are needed to sustain superior market performance.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave shares fall as its 2031 bond yield tops 17 percent on renewed AI debt concerns
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave shares fell again on Wednesday as concerns about debt tied to artificial intelligence projects returned to the market. The stock dropped 13 percent on Tuesday and was trading lower before the opening bell on Wednesday, extending a slide that has pushed it toward key support levels. The selloff followed a sharp rise in the yield on one of the company’s bonds, which investors interpreted as a sign of growing worry about the company’s ability to manage its borrowings.

The yield on CoreWeave’s 9.75 percent bond due in 2031 climbed above 17 percent on Tuesday, according to CNBC. The spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which protect against a default, jumped 8.5 percent to more than 1,200 basis points. That move indicated that investors now view the company’s debt as significantly riskier than they did before. The pressure was not limited to CoreWeave, as credit default swap spreads for Oracle rose 7 percent and spreads for Nvidia widened 3.4 percent. Broader AI stocks also sold off before Wednesday’s open, with Nasdaq 100 futures down 3 percent and Nvidia falling more than 5 percent in premarket trading.

The renewed debt fears came two days after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive officer. The board voted unanimously to bring Huang back just eleven days after he resigned amid a scandal involving extramarital affairs and national security concerns. Nvidia shares closed up 31 percent following the reinstatement, but the move also raised questions about the company’s financing of AI projects. Huang is seen as one of the industry’s top financiers, and Nvidia has struck deals with neoclouds such as CoreWeave to buy its chips, with some backed by Nvidia guarantees. Nvidia said it had 118 billion dollars in guarantees for AI projects as of October 25. During Huang’s absence, interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress signaled that Nvidia would be careful about new investments, which raised concerns that the company would scale back its financing.

Ben Emons, chief investment officer at FedWatch Advisors, described the latest selloff as a waning of the “Jensen effect,” according to CNBC. Not everyone expects Huang to reopen the financing spigot quickly. Stifel analyst Ruben Roy said in a Monday note that, given scrutiny over disclosure of financing and guarantees, he does not expect Huang’s return to bring a quick return to broader customer financing. At the time of publication, CoreWeave shares were trading 8.23 percent lower at 39.10 dollars, according to data from Benzinga Pro.

stories.Headline: Brook Porter bets on solar and batteries to power future AI data centers
stories.Summary:
Brook Porter, a partner at G2 Venture Partners, shared his investment strategy on November 24, 2026. He is betting on solar power and batteries to energy future AI data centers. This approach follows a recent analysis conducted by Porter and his colleagues at G2VP. The strategy aims to solve the growing problem of supplying power to AI data centers. Porter believes that solar and energy storage are the best ways to move faster.

The plan requires using solar paired with long-duration energy storage to build facilities independently of the grid. This off-grid path avoids permitting constraints like air permits and grid access in the United States. G2VP led the Series C for Crusoe and estimates data center investment will top 4 trillion dollars. Natural gas capacity is only 60 or 70 gigawatts per year, while solar is over a terawatt. Two paths exist: small on-grid facilities with generating capacity or larger solar powered centers.

Brook Porter stated that demand for power is growing faster than people currently appreciate. He explained that the challenge involves atoms rather than bits as the world recognizes these realities. Porter claimed that leveraging Wright's Law by making the same thing repeatedly is a vital lesson. He said that speed, scale, and economics are dimensions where this modular technology can win. He believes developers must be nimble to catch the big wave of this technology.

Hyperscalers and data center developers are the primary groups affected by these power supply challenges. Many companies have been buying, renting, and deploying natural gas power plants to secure energy. Lithium-ion batteries are too expensive to compete with fossil fuels for providing round-the-clock power. However, new products from Form Energy and Antora Energy have lowered the cost per megawatt-hour. These long-duration storage options provide a cheaper alternative for powering large AI data centers.

The U.S. grid has shifted from basically zero growth to adding several gigawatts every year. This change happened in just a few years as AI data center power needs increased. Supply chains have taken time to scale, forcing companies to find power in any form. G2VP gained an early window into this development through their investment in the company Crusoe. This experience allowed them to see how different waves of data centers have evolved.

Developers should start thinking about these new storage technologies now to accelerate their time to market. Broad acceptance of these long-duration energy storage products may still be a few years away. The articles leave open exactly when these technologies will reach a state of broad industry acceptance. They do not specify the exact timeline for the transition to off-grid renewable power. The text does not state which specific locations will host these new solar powered centers.

stories.Headline: Credit default swap spreads for CoreWeave, Oracle and Nvidia hit record highs as investors weigh AI debt risks
stories.Summary:
Credit markets signaled deepening concern about the debt fueled artificial intelligence infrastructure boom on Wednesday, as credit default swap spreads for several major technology companies reached record levels. Five year credit default swap spreads for SoftBank jumped to 501 basis points, their widest since October 2022, according to Markit data cited by Reuters. Spreads for Oracle, Alphabet, SpaceX, and CoreWeave also reached record levels overnight, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence data. CoreWeave's spread climbed to 1,314 basis points, which placed it in distressed territory and pushed its default probability in the next five years to 68 percent. The moves came despite a recent rally in Nvidia shares following chief executive Jensen Huang's reinstatement.

The widening spreads reflected growing investor concerns that returns from massive artificial intelligence infrastructure investments may take longer to materialize, putting pressure on cash flows and increasing risks for bondholders. Huang's role in Nvidia's financing arrangements with customers has also raised concerns among credit investors about circular financing and off balance sheet commitments. Nvidia's credit default swap spreads have also risen, mirroring a broader uptick in risk perceptions for technology companies reliant on debt financed artificial intelligence infrastructure. CoreWeave, a cloud provider heavily backed by Nvidia, has faced rising costs for default insurance and a fall in bond values, pushing them into distressed territory.

While default risks remain relatively low for companies with substantial revenues, investors are watching for signs of tighter lending conditions or difficulties accessing capital that could threaten artificial intelligence spending plans. In premarket trading Wednesday, CoreWeave shares fell 6 percent, Nvidia declined 5.3 percent, Oracle dropped 4.4 percent, SpaceX slipped 3 percent, and Alphabet fell 2.8 percent. Market pricing implies a significant probability of CoreWeave facing financial instability, consistent with scenarios where the company may announce bankruptcy, according to Crypto Briefing. Broader market indicators suggest a shift in sentiment towards the vulnerability of debt financed artificial intelligence infrastructure projects.

Market participants will closely monitor CoreWeave's financial maneuvers, as any announcements regarding debt restructuring or missed payments could further solidify the perceived risk of bankruptcy. Observers will also be attentive to Nvidia's strategic responses to these credit concerns, especially any measures to stabilize their financial standing. Key actors, including major investors like Magnetar Capital and Blackstone, may play pivotal roles in shaping future developments, according to Crypto Briefing. The development reflects growing concerns on Wall Street about the sustainability of artificial intelligence related borrowing, according to Bloomberg Technology.

stories.Headline: Fluidstack launches Blackbird modular 400 MW data centers with six-month build target
stories.Summary:
Fluidstack launched Blackbird, a modular 400 MW data center product, on November 24 and 25, 2026, the company said in a release. The AI data center builder that works with Anthropic introduced the product for customers that need compute at their own sites. Fluidstack says a Blackbird facility can be completed within six months of groundbreaking, compared with an industry standard of 18 to 24 months. The launch covers three products: the Blackbird facility design, the Compute Module, and the Electrical Skid. Fluidstack named no customers or sites for the product in the release.

The Blackbird design is standardized and scales from a single zone of more than 10 MW up to a 400 MW facility. Modules are fabricated off site, shipped to the campus as integrated and tested units, and assembled there. Fluidstack expects that process to cut build times by two-thirds or more. The Compute Module is a self-supporting overhead structure that carries power, cooling, and cabling to the servers, with hot aisle containment built in. The Electrical Skid puts medium-voltage switching, a transformer, and low-voltage distribution on one skid, taking a 35 kV class supply and delivering 480 V or 415 V.

All three products are built at Fluidstack's plant in Glendale, Arizona, a facility of more than 1.1 million square feet at Luke Field. The plant uses globally sourced components and supports 1,250 permanent manufacturing and skilled trades jobs, the company said. Fluidstack designs, engineers, integrates, and sells the products in the US. CEO Gary Wu said Fluidstack engineers and designs data centers in the US, then assembles them on construction sites across the country. The release gave no pricing, rack density, or cooling method beyond the containment system.

Research firm Futurum called the six-month target ambitious and said the open question is whether Fluidstack can hold that timeline at volume. Futurum research identifies power access and construction lead times as the primary constraint on AI capacity growth, not capital or chip supply. Out of organizations running AI in their own or colocated data centers, 35.9 percent have not secured firm power for all capacity they plan to energize through 2027. Fluidstack expects the shorter schedule to bring tax revenue and permanent jobs to host communities 12 to 18 months sooner. The Compute Module's chip-agnostic design also reduces the risk of a single-vendor dependency locking customers into a specific accelerator roadmap.

Fluidstack raised an $830 million Series A at a $7.5 billion valuation in July, led by Situational Awareness. The company is the partner on Anthropic's plan to build $50 billion of US AI infrastructure. Fluidstack is repositioning from GPU cloud operator to full-stack infrastructure manufacturer. The company converted the Glendale site from an empty shell to an operating manufacturing plant in six months. Conventional data center construction involves a fragmented supply chain of civil, electrical, and mechanical contractors operating under separate contracts and schedules.

First customer deployments will show whether early Blackbird sites confirm the six-month build claim at commercial scale. The manufacturing ramp rate at the Glendale facility and whether the 1,250-job workforce target is met on schedule remain open questions. The six-month schedule also hinges on factory output and a still-pending UL listing for Compute Modules. Fluidstack's Glendale plant targets up to 32 Compute Modules per day to sustain modular construction. Competitive response from established modular data center vendors and hyperscaler build programs in Q1-Q2 2027 is another factor the market will watch.
