stories.Headline: Sanders urges pause on advanced AI and ban on superintelligence
stories.Summary:
US Senator Bernie Sanders called for a pause in advanced artificial intelligence development and a ban on superintelligence on November 22, 2026. He made the demand in a post on X, warning that the technology could eventually operate beyond human control and pose serious risks to humanity. Sanders urged lawmakers to take action against what he described as the unchecked expansion of the technology by major technology companies. He called for a national moratorium on new data centres and restrictions on the development of increasingly advanced AI systems. The senator said the new Democratic majority must stop the greed of the Big Tech oligarchs.

The proposal requires a national moratorium on new data centres and restrictions on increasingly advanced AI systems. It also seeks a pause in advanced AI development and a ban on the development of superintelligence. Sanders cited AI pioneer and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton's estimate of a 10 to 20 per cent chance of AI wiping out humanity. Hinton has previously clarified that this figure is a personal estimate rather than a scientifically established probability. The senator also referred to concerns raised by AI safety researcher Mark Winer and OpenAI Foundation board member Paul Christiano.

Sanders argued that decisions about the future of AI should not be left to a handful of technology companies. He said that if some of the world's leading scientists are concerned about artificial intelligence becoming independent of human control with potentially catastrophic results, everything possible should be done to prevent it. Sanders described the situation as scary stuff and called on the new Democratic majority to push for stronger oversight. He also demanded a data centre moratorium and restrictions on advanced AI development. The senator framed the issue as one of stopping the greed of the Big Tech oligarchs.

Mark Winer, an AI safety and physics researcher, said AI is progressing much faster than thought and that the situation is difficult without answers. Paul Christiano, an OpenAI Foundation board member, gave a one-in-three chance that AI would be able to overthrow a government within the next year. Christiano also said there was a coin flip that the current path would lead to an irreversible loss of human control within three years. In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for the AI industry to slow the pace of development, arguing that safety measures needed time to catch up. He warned that AI agents could potentially coordinate on a scale capable of threatening internet security within six to 12 months.

The latest remarks come amid growing debate within the AI industry over whether the rapid development of increasingly capable systems is outpacing safety measures. Amodei's call received support from several prominent technology leaders, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who agreed that companies needed to pace the frontier. Altman said OpenAI would also allow independent evaluators access to assess its safety practices. Elon Musk backed Amodei's call, saying Dario is right, while Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis also supported his proposals. Microsoft executives favoured a more measured approach and stronger oversight.

The debate has widened beyond AI safety to the broader impact of the sector's rapid expansion, including scrutiny of data centre construction, energy and water consumption, and pressure on electricity infrastructure. The articles do not state whether any legislation has been introduced or whether the new Democratic majority has responded to Sanders's call. They also leave open whether a national moratorium on data centres or restrictions on advanced AI development will be enacted. No timeline is given for any potential congressional action on the proposals. The articles do not report any response from major technology companies to Sanders's specific demands.

stories.Headline: Kevin O'Leary says Nvidia will no longer finance new AI data centers
stories.Summary:
Japanese residents are pushing back against the rapid expansion of AI data centers in their neighborhoods, according to a report published on November 24, 2026. The pushback comes as investor Kevin O'Leary declared on November 21, 2026, that "The bank of NVIDIA is closed," signaling an end to the chipmaker's willingness to finance new data-center projects. O'Leary made the statement in a Saturday post on X, arguing that mounting scrutiny and political resistance could reshape the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom. He said investigations he referenced are expected to begin December 10, 2026, and that Nvidia would remain "under scrutiny for a while." The article frames this financial shift alongside local Japanese opposition to data centers, though it does not specify which Japanese communities are involved or what specific actions they have taken.

The financing landscape for AI data centers is undergoing significant changes, with Seaport analyst Jay Goldberg warning last month that 45% of planned AI data-center capacity for 2027 might not materialize because of power and infrastructure shortages. Nvidia reported $279 billion in supply and capacity commitments in July 2026, while warning that infrastructure constraints could delay chip purchases and hurt revenue. Apollo Global Management CEO Marc Rowan warned last week that AI infrastructure could require up to $8 trillion in financing, raising concerns about capital markets and funding challenges for smaller AI cloud providers. Infrastructure fundraising rebounded sharply in the third quarter of 2026, with Preqin reporting $62 billion raised across 21 funds, bringing the year's total to $101 billion across 65 funds. Brookfield Asset Management said the latest vintage of its flagship infrastructure strategy had received $26 billion in commitments, with $13 billion coming after the end of the quarter.

Kevin O'Leary argued that financing new data centers through Nvidia's balance sheet may no longer be viable, saying the idea "is over." He praised Nvidia CFO Colette Kress, saying, "I think they have the right CEO in Colette because she's the CFO." O'Leary pushed back against political opposition to data-center construction, arguing that the projects support middle-class workers, including engineers, construction workers, plumbers and businesses supplying commercial glass. He challenged politicians who said they needed to stop building data centers and help the middle class, asking, "Well hold on, who are the middle class?" O'Leary predicted that governors and senators would reverse their positions, saying, "I think you're going to see them say, 'Just kidding,' about the data centers."

Rene Lubianski, managing partner for infrastructure at Brookfield Asset Management, called infrastructure a "cornerstone" of the firm's business during a third-quarter earnings call on November 6, 2026. Brookfield said it was on track to exceed its $30 billion target in early 2027, which would surpass the $28 billion raised for its predecessor to become the largest closed-end infrastructure fund ever raised. Jeff Fine, global co-head of alternatives capital formation at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, said geopolitical tensions and their effects on inflation, interest rates, and growth prospects continue to impact valuations and investors' ability to return capital. Hugh Gimber, executive director and global market strategist at JPMAM, said infrastructure has some of the "strongest foundations" among alternative assets in the current economic environment. Karen Ward, managing director and EMEA chief market strategist at JPMAM, said renewed escalation in the Middle East conflict could push inflation higher, potentially triggering simultaneous falls in stocks and bonds.

Goldman Sachs' 2026 Global Alternatives Survey, which polled some 225 institutional investors between June and August 2026, found that 43% of respondents have a more favorable outlook on infrastructure investment compared with a year ago. Nearly half of investors, 49%, with a target allocation to infrastructure said they were under-allocated, compared with just 5% who were over-allocated, according to the study published October 21, 2026. Portfolio companies owned by the 50 largest infrastructure general partners had an average holding period of 7.6 years in 2025, up from 6.1 years in 2021, according to Boston Consulting Group. J.P. Morgan Asset Management strategists said November 12, 2026, that the sector stands to benefit from stronger government and corporate spending next year. Power generation has been a standout, returning almost 40% a year over the past three years and 60% in the past year, according to JPMAM's 2027 Investment Outlook published November 16, 2026.

The articles leave open what specific investigations into Nvidia will begin on December 10, 2026, and what their scope or likely outcomes will be. They do not identify which Japanese communities are pushing back against data centers, what form that pushback takes, or whether any projects have been halted or delayed as a result. The articles also do not state whether Nvidia has formally ended any existing financing arrangements or whether new commitments are simply being paused. It remains unclear whether the $500 billion AI data center pledge reportedly sitting undeployed will be redirected, canceled, or delayed. The articles do not specify how Japanese opposition might interact with the broader financing constraints, power shortages, and political resistance described by O'Leary and the analysts cited.

stories.Headline: IBM Research developers build an Indic voice agent that answers farming questions from an English handbook
stories.Summary:
IBM Research built a small voice agent that lets people ask questions aloud in regional Indian languages and hear answers drawn from English documents. The team announced the project on November 25, 2026, in a Hugging Face blog post. The agent uses CUGA, IBM Research's open-source agent harness, to search a 154-page agricultural handbook written in English. It answers in two to four spoken sentences in the language the question was asked in, such as Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, or Marathi. The agent also shows the source pages so the answer can be checked.

The agent works by converting speech to text, searching the handbook, generating a grounded answer with CUGA, and converting the text back to speech. CUGA handles model wiring, tool management, state, and guardrails, and it can switch between watsonx and OpenAI with one setting. The default embedding model is English-only, so Hindi or Tamil questions retrieved the wrong passages until the team switched to intfloat/multilingual-e5-large. The agent supports Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs called from the user's browser, and open-source models SraVaani for speech-to-text and Svara for text-to-speech running on a user's own server. The tutorial, Build an Indic Voice Agent with CUGA, starts from an empty folder and adds each layer in turn.

The authors are Vrunda Gadesha, Cyril Shaji, Jobit Treesa Varughese, Nivetha Suruliraj, Anu Sugunan, Anupama Murthi, Jaydeep Sen, and Amith Singhee, all from IBM Research. They advise testing a non-English question before tuning any prompt to check that the agent finds the right pages. They say the prompt asks the model not to produce Markdown, bullet points, citation tags, or bracketed translations, and a light formatter strips any that slip through before speech. They also say simple input checks catch obvious off-topic questions, and if one gets through, the model starts its reply with OFF_TOPIC and the app swaps in a polite redirect. They note that with the Sarvam option, the browser talks to Sarvam directly, so the server never sees the user's key.

The authors say the approach sits at the intersection of what IBM is building with IBM Bharat Core, an optimized AI stack built on top of IBM Sovereign Core for the Indian ecosystem. They say pairing CUGA's flexible agent harness with Bharat Core's Indic connectors and fine-tuned models lets developers build compliant, sovereign AI solutions for India's linguistic diversity. The article links to CUGA on GitHub under an Apache 2.0 license, CUGA documentation, the CUGA Apps gallery on GitHub, the CUGA Agent, CUGA Apps, and the CUGA Policy Playground. It also links to earlier articles about CUGA on Hugging Face, building agentic apps with CUGA, and comparing CUGA with Hermes and Deep Agents.

CUGA stands for ConfigUrable Generalist Agent, and it is IBM Research's open-source agent harness used as an embedded SDK inside a small web app. The voice agent is available in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces, where users can ask a farming question in their language and listen to the answer. The article says nothing in the design is specific to agriculture, and the handbook could be swapped for scheme documents, health advisories, or legal guides. It also says swapping the speech provider changes the deployment model, such as cloud for speed or on-premises for data sovereignty, without rewriting the agent. The article states that voice-first, multilingual assistants can reach people who were never served well by English-only text screens.

The article says users do not need to set anything up to see the agent work, and they can open it in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces. It invites readers to build one themselves using the step-by-step tutorial. The article leaves open whether the agent will be expanded beyond the agricultural handbook to other domains or deployed at scale with IBM Bharat Core. It also does not say how many users have tried the agent or what performance metrics it has achieved. The article does not mention any legal or regulatory issues related to voice data collection.

stories.Headline: Ai2 researchers propose trust benchmarks for AI agents in science
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the Allen Institute for AI interviewed 17 scientists in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. The study, published on November 25, 2026, explored where researchers would welcome agentic assistance and what safeguards they would need. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work. The scientists discussed both current generative AI tools and anticipated more autonomous systems. The findings identify important concerns and design priorities rather than establishing a consensus.

The study identified five dimensions of scientific trust: validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency. Researchers need to understand how an answer was reached, protect sensitive information, recognize bias, and determine who verifies AI-assisted findings. A literature-review benchmark could test whether an agent overlooks contradictory evidence or draws conclusions unsupported by its sources. A coding benchmark could assess whether the agent accesses files outside its authorized scope. Evaluations of data-processing agents could compare their methods and results with established human workflows.

The researchers at Ai2 said responsible science is about more than accuracy, since scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices. They said researchers need clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted work. They proposed a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against. They said these evaluations remain proposals to develop and test with scientists, rather than established solutions. They also said building open scientific tools means making their behavior and limitations easier to investigate.

Several participants described checking AI-generated answers against original publications rather than accepting summaries at face value. They worried about confident responses containing subtle inaccuracies and tools that reinforce assumptions by retrieving only studies that support a favored hypothesis. An early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use while acquiring skills they hoped to teach future students. One political scientist described using Claude to help revise a manuscript, then deciding to rewrite the entire paper because the boundaries of their own intellectual contribution had become unclear. An anthropologist argued that some sections of scientific papers, particularly routine descriptions of methods and results, are formulaic enough to benefit from automation.

The study grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. The researchers found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. They said they also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they are used. One political scientist described how content restrictions that prevent AI tools from discussing certain topics could interfere with legitimate research on political violence or human rights violations. Participants working with sensitive human-subject data wanted stronger guarantees about privacy, access, and how information would be used.

The researchers said scientific communities need a meaningful role in shaping the boundaries of AI assistance. They said achieving that will require technical features such as transparent records of agent actions and granular data controls, alongside evaluations informed by the standards and practices of different scientific communities. They noted that the study is exploratory, with findings from interviews with 17 US-based scientists, not a representative survey of scientific opinion or an empirical evaluation of specific AI agents. They said continued collaboration will be required. They also said they aim to put principles of openness, reproducibility, and independent scrutiny into practice through their broader efforts to develop and evaluate scientific agents.

stories.Headline: IBM says model arbitrage lets enterprises route AI workloads to cheaper models and cut token costs
stories.Summary:
AI spending is increasingly driven by inference rather than training, creating a new challenge for enterprises to control costs without limiting adoption and productivity. Model arbitrage routes workloads to the most appropriate model based on the task, balancing capability, cost and risk rather than defaulting to a single provider. An AI operating layer can automate these decisions at scale, acting as a fiduciary for AI spending by optimizing across cost, performance and governance. The same approach also strengthens digital sovereignty and auditability, giving enterprises greater control over where workloads run and making model choice a strategic advantage. In 2026, businesses woke to a new reality that more AI spending now goes toward running models than training them.

As token prices fall, organizations find they are using more AI, not less, but the bill keeps climbing and nobody seems to know how to rein it in. Some firms have responded by placing caps on token usage and shifting the emphasis to outcomes, which introduces a new risk of capping productivity and innovation. Alternatively, as token prices fall, enterprises can shop around for a better deal and find the provider with the lowest price per token. The problem is that today's pricing might not be tomorrow's pricing, because providers often reduce rates to gain market share. The incentives of the frontier-model firms and hyperscalers might not always align with enterprise interests over the long term.

IBM argues that model arbitrage, also known as model routing, determines which workloads justify a frontier model and which can be routed to a lower-cost alternative. For instance, a complex engineering challenge, architectural decision or large-scale code review might justify the use of a frontier model, while generating boilerplate code, summarizing documentation or answering routine technical questions might not. In many instances, those lower-cost alternatives are not just smaller commercial models but open-weight models running inside the enterprise, so organizations decide when to rent and when to own. IBM estimates these can be run at 25 percent to 10 percent of the token cost of the frontier models. Done right, model arbitrage is not a race to the bottom, because the objective is to match the right model to the right task at the right cost.

Research shows that 82 percent of executives expect their AI capabilities to be multimodel by 2030, and 83 percent of executives now view AI sovereignty as essential to business strategy. Today those organizations that are practicing model arbitrage often leave the question of model choice in the developer's hands, but clever prompting and user education cannot substitute for governance. The arbitration layer needs to sit below the user and be automated, so that operating layer can serve as a fiduciary for AI spending. It can evaluate tradeoffs among cost, performance and governance, determining when a request warrants a premium model, a lower-cost alternative or an internally hosted option. Tools such as the IBM Bob AI development platform already perform model arbitration beneath the user experience, applying these decisions automatically at scale.

The same operating layer that optimizes for cost and performance can also optimize for sovereignty, because hosting models yourself gives you greater control over where sensitive workloads run. Requests that must remain internal can be routed to internal models, while less-sensitive workloads can be routed elsewhere. Organizations also gain auditability, because they can demonstrate which model processed a request, why it was chosen and whether sensitive workloads remained inside approved environments. They can prove that requests subject to sovereignty requirements never left the organization, which is much more difficult to achieve when model choice is scattered across thousands of individual users. The AI market is expanding into many models, each with different capabilities, price points and deployment options, and model arbitrage is how enterprises turn that diversity into an advantage.

Over time, IBM expects this capability to become standard, and if an application cannot give enterprises meaningful control over the models running behind it, that will increasingly become a reason not to buy the application. Until then, the advantage will belong to organizations that make those tradeoffs deliberately rather than accept whatever model choice is made for them. Separately, ARKO AI debuted at Singapore FinTech Festival 2026 on November 24, 2026, unveiling its personal AI vision for smarter spending and opening registration and access to its initial MVP products for users worldwide. ARKO AI is developing Ask ARKO, a personal AI agent designed to make everyday spending decisions easier and help people get more out of their money with less effort, and it is in private internal beta. Full features and launch timeline are to be announced officially, and the articles leave open how model arbitrage and personal AI agents will interact in the broader market.

stories.Headline: Asian governments implement market measures to counter an AI stock downturn
stories.Summary:
Nvidia and other artificial intelligence stocks experienced a downturn that dragged down the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF during November 2026. This market slide followed the surprise resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after reports of marital infidelity with subordinates and a spy. The stock lost 27.5 percent of its market value during a seven-day losing streak ending on November 20. A huge rebound occurred on Monday when Huang made a surprise return to his role as the company chief executive. This volatility spread to other semiconductor stocks and the broader artificial intelligence infrastructure segment during the same period.

South Korea will activate a stabilization fund valued at 10.76 trillion won and relax share-buyback limits starting November 24. Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission prohibited short selling below the closing price on Friday to curb speculative activity in its market. Beijing will cut the minimum margin ratio for stock purchases to 80 percent from 100 percent starting November 30. The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF lost 7.8 percent the week ending November 20, while the Taiwan index dropped 17.5 percent. Nvidia's stock fell 32 percent from its October 6 high of 243.37 dollars before the recent Monday rally.

Geoffrey Seiler stated that investors should not rush to sell the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF despite the AI downturn. He suggested that dollar-cost averaging into the fund is a proven strategy that works over the long term. South Korea's finance ministry said that mid-to-long-term growth expectations for the AI industry remain intact for the global market. The ministry added that excessive anxiety is not a concern despite increased volatility from internal and external global uncertainties. Taiwan's regulators stated that investors must not sell listed stocks at prices lower than the previous day's closing price.

The downturn affected the Nasdaq Composite and the benchmark Kospi index, which is down over 46 percent from June. Investors in the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF were affected because Nvidia held a nearly 7.6 percent weighting in November. The CSI 300 index in China closed lower for 14 of the past 15 weeks due to tech souring. TSMC shareholders were impacted as the chip manufacturing giant saw its stock price fall 15 percent during last week. Other affected groups include cloud computing and software-as-a-service stocks, which generally performed poorly before joining the Monday rally.

Nvidia was once the largest company in the world with a market cap that exceeded 5 trillion dollars. The S&P 500 became less diversified over a decade, with tech stocks making up over 37 percent in November. Ten of the top 15 holdings in the S&P 500 were AI stocks at the start of the month. South Korea's stabilization fund was reportedly established in 2020 during the pandemic by various financial firms and other institutions. The Kospi index saw wild swings in 2026 as investors moved in and out of Samsung and SK Hynix.

The Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges will implement fee cuts to inject more liquidity into the struggling Chinese stock market. Shenzhen proposed a new market-making mechanism for its ChiNext board to help support the region's broader tech trade. Taipei will include stock buybacks in environmental, social and governance scores if completed between late 2026 and early 2027. The articles leave open whether AI stocks will push benchmark indexes into a bear market or simply undergo a correction. It remains uncertain if other leaders like Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, or SpaceX will step up to lead the index.

stories.Headline: Nasscom proposes a three-year AI services transformation scheme for India's 2027-28 budget
stories.Summary:
Nasscom, India’s IT industry body, has urged the government to introduce a three-year AI Services Transformation and Innovation Scheme in the Union Budget 2027-28. The apex body made this request in its pre-Budget submission on Monday, November 23, 2026, from Bengaluru. The scheme is intended to strengthen India’s global competitiveness as generative and agentic artificial intelligence reshape global technology demand and business models. Nasscom said transitioning to AI-led service delivery models requires substantial upfront investments before generating commercial returns. The proposed scheme would be designed by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology and the Ministry of Finance in consultation with industry.

The scheme would support technology commercialisation developed in India, supervised project-based workforce retraining and shared technical infrastructure for smaller firms. It would cover AI services and products built and operated from India, including offerings based on licence fees, subscriptions, usage-based payments and outcome-linked revenues. Nasscom recommended that overseas specialist visits of up to 90 days in 12 months, genuine employee secondments and global leadership positions held by India-based executives should not trigger permanent establishment status. It also proposed deferring taxation of unlisted ESOPs until sale, listing or ten years after exercise, whichever is earlier. Further, Nasscom called for raising the monthly wage ceiling for additional employment deductions under Section 146 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, from ₹25,000 to ₹1 lakh.

Nasscom said AI is fundamentally reshaping global technology demand, business models and the nature of employment, making it important for India to strengthen its technology capabilities and create high-skilled jobs. The industry body said developing reusable AI-based offerings and retraining employees require upfront investments, even before new business models start generating returns. It proposed that the scheme link employee training with supervised project deployment, allowing existing workers to take on new roles while giving new entrants practical experience. Nasscom also sought a dedicated cybersecurity programme, with a capped initial allocation, to help manufacturing and service-sector micro, small and medium enterprises establish and maintain basic cyber protections. The body said the recommendations are aimed at strengthening India’s global competitiveness, encouraging technology innovation and supporting employment as AI transforms the industry.

Smaller service providers face greater difficulties in financing development, accessing specialists and releasing employees for training while continuing client work, according to Nasscom. Shared technical facilities, specialist support and collaborative projects have been suggested for smaller companies to overcome these constraints. Employees currently face a salary tax liability before any sale is possible, even though they may not have received money from selling the shares, Nasscom said. The body also sought taxation based on the lower of the exercise benefit or actual realised gain for ESOPs. For corporate restructuring, it sought loss carry-forward benefits for IT and KPO firms undertaking amalgamations, tax neutrality for fast-track demergers and enforcement of the 10% pre-payment cap for disputed tax stays.

Building on transfer pricing reforms announced in the previous Budget, Nasscom’s recommendations cover four key areas aimed at improving the ease of doing business and attracting global mandates. With Global Capability Centres increasingly assuming global leadership and research and development responsibilities, Nasscom sought permanent establishment safeguards. On employee stock ownership plans, particularly for startups, the body proposed deferring taxation of unlisted ESOPs until sale, listing or ten years after exercise, whichever is earlier. It also called for codifying employer ESOP deductions and raising the monthly wage ceiling for additional employment deductions under Section 146 of the Income-tax Act, 2025. The economics of AI services remain a challenge for service providers exploring new ways to monetise their capabilities, as Indian IT firms look to convert AI adoption and productivity gains into additional revenue.

The proposed scheme, to be designed by MeitY and the Finance Ministry in consultation with industry, would support the development and commercialisation of AI services and products built and operated from India. Nasscom has proposed that the scheme link employee training with supervised project deployment, allowing existing workers to take on new roles while giving new entrants practical experience. Other proposals include greater tax certainty for global capability centres, continuity of accumulated losses in qualifying IT-sector mergers and faster resolution of tax disputes. The articles do not state whether the government has responded to Nasscom’s pre-Budget submission or whether the scheme will be included in the Union Budget 2027-28. They also leave open the specific funding amount, eligibility criteria and implementation timeline for the proposed three-year scheme.

stories.Headline: University of Indianapolis uses $8.5 million Lilly grant to launch AI center for human performance
stories.Summary:
The University of Indianapolis received an $8.5 million grant from Lilly Endowment Inc. to establish a new Center for Artificial Intelligence for Human Performance. The award was announced on November 23, 2026, and the three-year initiative is expected to begin in January. The funding will significantly expand the use of artificial intelligence across the university's campus. University President Tanuja Singh said artificial intelligence is fundamentally changing how people live and work at breathtaking speeds. The grant is part of Lilly Endowment's Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education initiative, which supports Indiana colleges and universities.

The initiative calls for creating or revising up to 330 courses to incorporate artificial intelligence into the curriculum. The university will also develop nine AI-focused micro-credentials and provide students with opportunities to work on industry-sponsored projects. Faculty members will receive additional training and resources to incorporate AI into their teaching, with an emphasis on critical thinking and ethical decision-making. The university plans to introduce AI-powered tools to improve academic advising, student support services, transfer credit evaluations and data security. The new center will be located in a renovated section of Krannert Memorial Library on the university's campus.

University of Indianapolis President Tanuja Singh said higher education has a responsibility to prepare students not just to use new tools but to think critically about how and why they are used. She said the investment helps the university build on its strengths in experiential learning and student-centered education. Singh also said the university must ensure that technology serves people, not the other way around. UIndy Provost Chris Plouff said the center pairs faculty expertise with student creativity and problem-solving abilities to address real-world challenges facing Hoosier businesses and organizations. Plouff said students will benefit greatly from hands-on experience gained by applying classroom lessons to real-world problems.

Ted Maple, the Endowment's vice president for education, said the rapid rise and growing ubiquity of AI may be one of the most significant challenges higher education institutions have ever faced. Maple said faculty and staff are concerned about the potential for AI to impede original and independent thinking and threaten social connections. He also said colleges and universities have recognized that AI may present unprecedented opportunities to enhance teaching, learning, student services and research capabilities. Small businesses and nonprofits that lack the resources or expertise to implement AI independently will be able to access customized consulting services through the center. The center will serve two primary purposes: encouraging discussions about the relationship between artificial intelligence and human performance, and providing practical assistance to businesses and nonprofit organizations.

The grant is part of Lilly Endowment's Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education initiative, which is providing funding to 35 Indiana colleges and universities. The initiative is designed to help higher education institutions respond to the growing influence of artificial intelligence and prepare students, faculty and staff for technological changes. The University of Indianapolis has already begun exploring the technology's impact through events such as its inaugural AI Summit in April. That summit brought together business leaders, educators, technology experts and policymakers to explore the opportunities and challenges of AI. The university plans to hold another AI Summit in fall 2027.

The initiative is expected to begin in January and builds on the University of Indianapolis's ongoing work in artificial intelligence. One strategic pillar of the center will be thought leadership, serving as a hub for both campus and community conversations about how AI intersects with human performance. The other strategic pillar will focus on applied learning and consulting by providing customized services to nonprofits and small businesses. The articles do not specify which businesses or nonprofits will receive consulting services first. They also do not state how many students will participate in industry-sponsored projects or when the renovated library space will open.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave bonds fall to record lows as AI credit worries spread
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave bonds plunged to record lows on Tuesday, leading corporate bond losses as skepticism over the staying power of the AI boom spread into the broader hyperscaler credit market. The sell-off erased a brief Monday rebound sparked by news that Nvidia's board had reinstated Jensen Huang as president and chief executive officer. All four of CoreWeave's major notes tumbled to their weakest levels since issuance in afternoon trading, Bloomberg reported, citing Trace data. The rout in CoreWeave's debt coincided with wider stress across AI infrastructure credit. Chip and AI stocks largely dropped on Tuesday, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq retreating 2% following a 6.5% surge in the prior session.

CoreWeave's 9.625% notes due July 2032 dropped as much as 4.6 points to 74.9 cents on the dollar, hitting a record low since launching in June 2026. Its 9.75% notes due October 2031 fell 3.75 points to 76.3 cents, marking their lowest price since their April debut. The company's 9% bonds due February 2031 declined as much as 3.6 points to 76.6 cents, breaching their previous floor set after their July 2025 issuance. Its 9.25% bonds due June 2030 slid 3 points to 80.9 cents, a low not seen since May 2025. A basket of hyperscaler credit default swaps surged more than 7% to a record wide of 115.6, underscoring deepening investor anxiety over heavy debt loads financing the AI buildout.

Bloomberg reported the bond moves, citing Trace data, while ZeroHedge separately flagged the surge in hyperscaler credit default swaps. CoreWeave made no company-specific announcement dated between November 21 and 23, according to Kalkine, so the Monday advance was sector driven. Nvidia's board restored its founder as chief executive on Monday, and Nvidia's shares rose near 30%. Market commentary framed that move as easing AI financing anxieties for CoreWeave and Oracle. Oracle reiterated a goal of over USD 30 billion in free cash flow for fiscal 2029 and called itself fully funded.

CoreWeave shares changed hands at USD 48.81 during the November 23, 2026 session, up 23.55% against an implied previous close near USD 39.51. Roughly 39.1 million shares traded, giving a market capitalization of about USD 27.15 billion. The stock opened about 29% higher, then retreated roughly 4.2% from that point on relative volume close to 0.5 times normal. In the week before Monday the shares had fallen close to 26%, as investors debated how AI infrastructure would be financed. The shares had dropped about 40% over the month preceding the third quarter report, then climbed roughly 25% after results and slipped again.

CoreWeave leases Nvidia GPU capacity to AI labs and enterprises, a closely followed AI cloud name. Revenue for the third quarter came in at USD 3.66 billion, a 168% rise from USD 1.37 billion a year before, while the company booked a USD 709 million net loss. Adjusted EBITDA reached USD 2.26 billion, or a 62% margin, while operating income stood at USD 207 million. Interest expense, net, of USD 846 million accounted for the net loss, or USD 1.27 a share. Cash capex was USD 9.44 billion in the quarter, with USD 4.12 billion of cash on hand.

Backlog climbed to about USD 132.5 billion, compared with USD 104 billion in June, and contracted power is above 4.6 gigawatts, with over 1.7 gigawatts already active. At September 30, total indebtedness was about USD 47.5 billion, of which roughly USD 5.7 billion remained undrawn. Management expects roughly USD 9 billion of prepayments and deposits from customers over the next three months, and it guided fourth quarter interest expense to between USD 1.05 billion and USD 1.15 billion. 2026 revenue guidance runs from USD 13.0 billion to USD 13.3 billion, capital outlays range from USD 37 billion to USD 39 billion, and the annualized exit rate sits at USD 20 billion to USD 21 billion. The articles do not state what CoreWeave or its executives said about Tuesday's bond declines, nor what specific actions the company plans to take next.

stories.Headline: CITE26: How Students Helped Shape AI Strategy at Newport-Mesa USD
stories.Summary:
During a Nov. 19 presentation at the California IT in Education conference in Anaheim, Newport-Mesa Unified School District Director of Education Technology Jenith Mishne explained how monthly student surveys are shaping the district's AI strategy. The district serves approximately 18,000 students across more than 30 schools and began addressing generative AI shortly after ChatGPT's public release. Mishne said 1 in 3 students reported in a survey that AI rules differed from teacher to teacher. Some teachers are returning to handwritten assignments and traditional blue books, while others instruct students to enter prompts into ChatGPT. The surveys, administered through Google Forms, generated 3,647 responses between November and May of last school year and nearly 2,000 so far this school year.

California passed Senate Bill 1288 in 2024, and the California Department of Education released statewide AI guidance in 2025 and a model policy in June 2026. Districts are not required to adopt the model policy, but it recommends that teachers clearly communicate when and how students may use AI. Newport-Mesa notified families in January 2023 of its decision not to block ChatGPT on district-issued Chromebooks. Among approximately 1,400 students surveyed last school year, 82 percent reported having used AI within the preceding 30 days. Middle school students have been the most active respondents, and the surveys take just a few minutes to complete.

Mishne said a district working group developed guidelines for teachers and students and incorporated relevant language into student handbooks and existing policies. She said she felt that if she could teach all the teachers, that would help the students. Despite offering approximately 200 different AI professional development topics, Mishne said reaching teachers remained a challenge due to competing instructional priorities, limited training time and initiative fatigue. She said teachers still are not there, and the district has new device and screen-time tensions, a board that wants to pull devices out of classrooms, and different expectations in each classroom. Mishne said her work next has to be taking that data and seeing where the district could help adults make good decisions on where it is going with AI in a safe way.

Students reported turning to AI when schoolwork became difficult, a practice Mishne noted could interfere with their ability to work through challenging material independently. Some students said they use AI as a second teacher because the teacher cannot always help, while others said they use it because they are afraid to ask their teacher a question. Not all students welcomed the technology, and Mishne said a good amount of students said they just do not use it, do not like it, and do not want to use it because it feels cheap. Some students expressed concerns about AI interfering with their independent thinking or diminishing the value of their academic efforts. Others complained about classmates using AI when they themselves had chosen not to.

The survey findings helped shape a professional development event for the district's secondary school teachers, where students were invited to speak directly to educators. The participants, including high school seniors and an eighth grader, expressed a desire for clearer expectations around permissible AI use. Some teachers, the students said, did not address the technology in their classrooms at all. Mishne said the common thread for the student piece is that the district knows it has to get its teachers to do better about sharing their expectations and rules in the classroom. In one survey last school year, Mishne inadvertently omitted an option for students to indicate that they did not use AI, and students quickly addressed the oversight.

Mishne is now developing clearer AI literacy expectations for each grade level, from transitional kindergarten through 12th grade, and establishing a monthly student advisory group. She also intends to distribute school-specific survey findings to the district's principals so they can better understand the experiences of their own students. To encourage participation, she sends periodic reminders, distributes classroom flyers and asks teachers to help promote the monthly surveys. Students must sign in to ensure participation is limited to those within the district, but the surveys remain anonymous, collecting school and grade-level information instead of names. The article does not state when the new grade-level expectations or the student advisory group will be implemented.

stories.Headline: Dohop launches a ChatGPT tool for booking multi-airline flights
stories.Summary:
Travel technology company Dohop launched a tool on November 24, 2026, allowing ChatGPT users to find direct flights and connecting itineraries involving multiple airlines. The integration connects ChatGPT searches with flight itineraries sold through Dohop-powered platforms, including journeys combining airlines without traditional interline agreements. The technology is already live through WAYA, Dohop’s consumer travel platform, and can be activated by airlines using the company’s existing booking infrastructure. Travelers can compare available itineraries in ChatGPT before continuing to an external booking platform to select seats, purchase baggage and complete payment. Dohop announced the launch as one of the first ChatGPT plugins for bookable direct flights and multi-carrier itineraries.

The new flight search integration helps travelers move from describing a journey in natural language to reviewing bookable flight combinations. Travelers can use the tool to explore direct services and itineraries combining flights operated by different carriers, rather than searching separately for each possible airline connection. After choosing a suitable itinerary, the traveler follows a link to the airline’s Dohop-powered checkout to finalize the reservation. Additional services, including checked baggage, seat selection and available travel protection, can be added during that booking process. The company has not announced that passengers can complete the entire payment and ticketing process within ChatGPT.

Dohop says it plans to develop more advanced capabilities that could eventually allow travelers to manage additional booking steps during a conversation with an AI assistant. Those capabilities remain future development goals rather than confirmed features of today’s launch. Dohop specializes in what it calls Connected Travel, enabling airlines and travel platforms to sell flight combinations without relying entirely on conventional airline interline or codeshare agreements. The company already provides flight-connection technology for more than 15 airline-operated platforms, including Flight Connections by easyJet and WIZZ LINK by Wizz Air. Its wider network of travel technology partners includes Air France, Air Transat, easyJet, Scoot and Wizz Air.

The existence of these partnerships does not mean every airline is already offering its flights through the new ChatGPT integration. Dohop confirms that the tool is live through WAYA and available for activation by existing airline customers, with discussions with several airline partners continuing. For travelers, multi-airline search could make it easier to discover routes involving separate carriers, particularly when direct flights are unavailable or traditional booking systems do not present the combination. Passengers should check connection times, baggage arrangements and disruption protection carefully before booking flights operated by different airlines. A self-connecting itinerary may involve different responsibilities from a conventional single-ticket journey, depending on the booking structure and protection purchased.

The launch reflects a growing shift in how airlines and travel companies are approaching artificial intelligence, with AI assistants increasingly serving as starting points for travel research. Dohop’s approach allows participating airlines to reach customers during the search process while retaining control over ticket sales and ancillary revenue. That distinction matters commercially because airlines generate additional income from services such as baggage, seat upgrades and travel protection. Rather than requiring every airline to develop a separate AI booking system, Dohop is offering a way to connect existing airline booking platforms with conversational flight search. Dohop also cited Phocuswright research indicating that 33% of US travelers used generative AI platforms to research trips in 2026, approximately five times the proportion recorded in 2024.

Dohop enters an increasingly competitive market for conversational travel search, with Skyscanner introducing a ChatGPT flight-search integration earlier in 2026. KAYAK has also expanded its AI travel tools, combining conversational searches with live flight, hotel and rental-car information. The arrival of Dohop adds a different emphasis: connecting AI flight discovery with airline-operated booking platforms and multi-carrier itineraries. For travelers, the practical benefits will depend on which airlines activate the integration, how many itineraries are available and whether the displayed combinations offer competitive prices and reliable connections. Dohop has not announced a complete list of airlines already live in ChatGPT or a timetable for activating every existing partner.

stories.Headline: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki proposes voluntary industry limits on frontier AI tied to perplexity scores
stories.Summary:
OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki proposed on November 22 that artificial intelligence companies should voluntarily agree to common limits on frontier AI development until their ability to understand and monitor model behavior reaches specific targets. In a post on OpenAI's blog, he argued that the industry should commit not to exceed these limits while safeguards are still being developed. Pachocki specified that the limits should be based on perplexity and other technical metrics, with perplexity measuring how well an AI model predicts the next piece of text. He said lower perplexity scores indicate better predictive performance, and he noted that models' general intelligence has steadily increased as this metric has improved. Pachocki urged greater transparency across the industry in disclosing perplexity scores for their models.

The proposal calls for companies to voluntarily halt development of more powerful models until safeguards are in place to understand and monitor AI behavior. Pachocki warned that AI could accelerate its own development as early as next year, potentially outpacing humans' ability to monitor it. He said this could mean humans lose control of AI as it continues to improve itself. He added that he hopes the proposal can serve as a starting point for setting subsequent limits and establishing a common framework for coordinating the pace of future development. The proposal came amid a growing debate over AI regulation in the United States following the Democratic Party's landslide victory in the midterm elections.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman shared Pachocki's post on the social media platform X, calling it "the most important thing OpenAI has released recently." Altman added that an agreement among companies on common limits would help secure safety and control. Pachocki himself said, "I propose that we establish common limits on AI development and that companies commit not to exceed them until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior reaches specific targets." He also said perplexity is a metric that many researchers have worked hard to validate over a long period. Some lawmakers are discussing the creation of a dedicated Senate committee to oversee AI policy, and some expect Congress to increase its scrutiny of Big Tech and efforts to establish AI safety rules.

The proposal follows a report from METR, a nonprofit AI evaluation organization, which assessed the extent to which AI is accelerating AI research and development at Anthropic. METR estimated that as of October, the pace of AI research and development progress at Anthropic had doubled, with the use of AI to automate research likely the major driver of this acceleration. METR said the true figure could be anywhere from a 30 percent speedup to a tripling of the pace of research. The organization also revealed that Anthropic had some important restrictions around what METR was allowed to look at and publicly disclose. METR was not allowed to assess how much computing resources Anthropic was dedicating to AI research aimed at improving model capabilities compared to research aimed at improving AI safety.

stories.Headline: Virginia and Oregon attorneys general sue Musk companies over Grok sexualized images
stories.Summary:
Elon Musk’s businesses harmed consumers by avoiding safeguards when they designed and launched an artificial intelligence chatbot capable of creating sexualized images, two Democratic attorneys general argued in lawsuits filed Monday. The choices that went into building Grok led to a proliferation of child sexual abuse material and other nonconsensual intimate imagery on the companies’ platforms, the lawsuit said. The companies prioritized their business model over the safety of millions of people, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones said in his state’s lawsuit. Oregon also filed a lawsuit Monday, and the attorneys general brought their separate but similar cases under their states’ consumer protection statutes. The lawsuits named as defendants several Musk companies and subsidiaries, including SpaceX and X Corp.

Grok, which can be accessed through Musk’s social media platform X, rolled out image generation and editing features to all users in December 2025, according to the Virginia lawsuit. By January, the tool had sparked a global backlash after it became clear Grok users could create realistic-looking but fake sexualized images of people. At least two countries, Malaysia and Indonesia, announced temporary bans and other nations said they were launching or widening investigations. In response, Grok prevented non-paying users from generating or editing images, but the change did not stop users from making more non-consensual sexualized images. Virginia’s lawsuit asked the court for $2,500 for each “willful violation” of the Virginia Consumer Protection Act, with an exact number to be proven at trial.

Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones said the companies stripped out industry-standard safeguards and marketed a “spicy mode” built to produce nudity to push Grok to tens of millions of new users. Jones said that for these defendants, weak safeguards were not a failure but a feature. Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield said developers intentionally designed Grok with lower guardrails than its competitors, and that any platform allowing such content needs to put in appropriate safeguards and shut that down immediately. Rayfield argued that the changes, or lack thereof, were intentionally ineffective to avoid discouraging use, calling the situation “wholly unacceptable.” Jones said in a statement that when xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety and deceived the public about it.

Company representatives have not responded to an emailed request for comment, but the company’s own Safety account on X called the creation of sexual content involving minors and adults without consent “abhorrent.” The Safety account placed blame on users who generated the material in violation of the terms of service, and wrote that protecting children is non-negotiable. The company also wrote that it has “tightened” Grok’s protections this year in response to concerns of sexually exploitive material being created. In January, 35 attorneys general called on the company to block Grok from creating such material. Researchers warned that some images appeared to depict children, and as the Virginia lawsuit put it, “X was flooded with sexualized content ,  primarily of women.”

The developer of Grok was then known as xAI, and has since rebranded to SpaceX Super Intelligence. Virginia argued that most major AI developers designed their products so they could not be used to produce sexualized images to avoid the generation of nonconsensual content. The lawsuit said defendants’ published system prompt materials told Grok to “assume good intent,” stated that terms such as “teenage” or “girl” do not necessarily imply underage, and imposed minimal restrictions on sexual content. The lawsuit noted that xAI marketed Grok from the outset as a tool that would “answer spicy questions that are rejected by most other AI systems.” Both lawsuits draw heavily on news outlets’ investigative reporting about the rollout of the tool, the backlash and the company’s response to it.

Virginia’s lawsuit, filed in a state court in Richmond, argued that the Musk companies violated the state’s consumer protection law by misrepresenting that they implemented and enforced safeguards to protect consumers from exposure to harmful sexualized imagery. It also asked a judge to prevent the companies from further violating the consumer protection laws and force the defendants to give up any “ill-gotten gains” acquired in connection with the alleged violations. The Oregon lawsuit makes a similar request. The lawsuits come at a time of growing concern about AI’s risks for children, from its impact on brain development to the unhealthy relationships many young people have formed with chatbots. The articles do not state when the cases will be heard or what specific defenses the companies might raise.

stories.Headline: Kyndryl and Argentum AI launch a $630 million Boulder data center deal with Nvidia chips
stories.Summary:
Kyndryl and Argentum AI announced a $630 million artificial intelligence infrastructure deal on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. The two companies reached a 20-year agreement to bring computing systems to a facility in Boulder. This major investment involves an existing data center rather than building a new facility from the ground up. Argentum AI will use infrastructure operated by Kyndryl to expand high-performance computing capacity for various businesses. The project focuses on deploying specialized systems designed to handle demanding artificial intelligence workloads for its clients.

The agreement involves an initial 10 megawatts of capacity at the existing Kyndryl facility located in Boulder. Argentum has begun deploying Nvidia B300 graphics processing systems to support the high-density equipment planned for the site. The companies stated that the Boulder site is equipped to support the specific hardware Argentum intends to install. This project does not establish the total electricity the facility will consume on a daily or annual basis. Actual usage depends on operating conditions, the amount of equipment deployed, and the facility's power and cooling systems.

Argentum founder and CEO Andrew Sobko described the partnership as an important step in expanding the company's computing infrastructure. Kyndryl U.S. President Jamie Rutledge said the agreement would put existing capacity to work using their operating experience. Both companies stated that the deployment of the new equipment is already underway at the Boulder data center. They also mentioned that the two organizations may explore further collaboration in the future beyond this initial deal. The companies have not provided a completion date for the initial installation of the Nvidia computing systems.

Local residents may be affected by the deal, but the companies have not disclosed the number of associated jobs. The announcement did not identify any new public subsidies or local tax incentives for the Boulder data center project. There is no information regarding expected water consumption or whether additional electrical infrastructure will be necessary for the site. Colorado communities are currently debating the costs and benefits of data center growth and their regional utility requirements. Such facilities can attract long-term investment and expand the technology sector, but they may affect local infrastructure planning.

Demand for AI computing continues to drive investment in specialized data centers that require substantial electricity and cooling capacity. Large clusters of graphics processors require more power than conventional office computing systems used in typical business environments. The project brings a substantial AI investment to an existing site within the city of Boulder, Colorado. This investment occurs as the regional technology sector seeks to expand through the use of high-performance computing systems. The deal utilizes existing enterprise technology and information systems services provided by Kyndryl to support Argentum AI.

The companies have not yet determined how the investment translates into jobs or long-term economic benefits for the area. It remains unclear how the project will impact local utility demand and the overall electrical grid in Boulder. The articles leave open whether the facility will require more power than the initial 10 megawatts of capacity. Further details regarding the environmental impact, such as water usage, have not been provided to the public yet. The long-term success of the 20-year agreement depends on the actual deployment of the Nvidia B300 systems.

stories.Headline: DGEN Technologies completes acquisition of exclusive license to HumanOS artificial intelligence assets
stories.Summary:
DGEN Technologies Corp. completed its acquisition of an exclusive and irrevocable license to the artificial intelligence software, automation technology and related assets of HumanOS Technologies Inc. on November 23, 2026. The company announced the completion from Vancouver, British Columbia, on the same day. The transaction was completed pursuant to a license agreement dated November 12, 2026, between the two companies. DGEN Technologies Corp. trades on the Canadian Securities Exchange under the symbol DGEN. The company described the licensed assets as including software, source code, systems, platforms and tools developed and operated by HumanOS.

The licensed assets include the HumAIn, Matspace, Media Studio and Automation Lab products and the HumanOS scan tool. They also include the HumanOS trade name, the 1humanos.com domain and associated websites and social media accounts. Client and customer lists, limited to names and contact details only, and related information and documentation are part of the licensed assets. The license permits DGEN and its affiliates to use, commercialize, further develop and sublicense the licensed assets. HumanOS retains ownership of the licensed assets, while any improvements developed by or for DGEN will be owned by DGEN.

In consideration for the licensed assets, DGEN issued 4,000,000 common shares at a deemed price of $0.25 per share, for aggregate deemed consideration of $1,000,000. DGEN also issued 4,000,000 common share purchase warrants, each entitling the holder to acquire one common share at an exercise price of $0.32 per warrant share until November 23, 2029. The company stated that it is arm’s length from HumanOS and that no finder’s fees or commissions are payable in connection with completion of the transaction. The consideration shares, consideration warrants and any warrant shares are subject to restrictions on resale until March 24, 2027. These restrictions are in accordance with applicable Canadian securities laws and the policies of the Canadian Securities Exchange.

DGEN Technologies Corp. described itself as a Vancouver-based technology company developing a cloud-based payment platform. The company said its platform is intended to integrate point-of-sale, kiosk and mobile payment systems into a unified and scalable solution. DGEN stated that its platform is currently in beta stage and not yet in use by any business. The platform has not yet been commercialized or generated revenue. The Canadian Securities Exchange has not reviewed, approved or disapproved the contents of the news release and does not accept responsibility for its adequacy or accuracy.

The news release contains forward-looking information within the meaning of applicable Canadian securities laws. This includes statements about the company’s ability to use, develop, commercialize and sublicense the licensed assets. It also includes statements about the development, functionality, commercialization and market adoption of the company’s platform and its ability to generate revenue. Forward-looking information is based on management’s current expectations, estimates, projections, beliefs and assumptions as of the date of the news release. These assumptions include that the licensed assets will perform as expected and can be integrated into the company’s business.

The company identified risks and uncertainties that may cause actual results to differ materially from forward-looking information. These include risks relating to the ownership, validity and enforceability of intellectual property rights in the licensed assets, including third-party claims. They also include the possibility that the licensed assets do not perform as expected or cannot be successfully integrated, developed or commercialized. Dilution resulting from the exercise of the consideration warrants is another identified risk. The company noted that its platform remains in beta stage, has not been commercialized and has not generated revenue. Readers are cautioned not to place undue reliance on forward-looking information, which speaks only as of the date of the news release.

stories.Headline: Fakeeh Health and Boston Health AI sign deals to bring AI clinical documentation to UAE providers
stories.Summary:
Fakeeh Health and Boston Health AI signed two strategic agreements on 24th November 2026 in Dubai. The signing took place on the sidelines of the 5th Annual Fakeeh Health International Conference. Sheikh Ahmed bin Hasher bin Ahmed Al Maktoum was present at the signing. Together, the two organizations will introduce AI-supported clinical documentation across Fakeeh Health. Through Takamul Innovative Health Solutions, they will also jointly develop new AI solutions for healthcare providers in the UAE and the region.

The first agreement focuses on giving clinicians more time for their patients. AI will take on routine documentation in the background while the physician remains in control of the clinical record. Patient data stays in the UAE and is protected in line with national regulations. The second agreement involves Takamul and Boston Health AI working together to develop new solutions that help healthcare providers work more efficiently. They will also build local expertise in clinical AI through education and research.

Dr. Mohaymen Abdelghany, Group CEO and Board Member of Fakeeh Health and CEO of Fakeeh University Hospital, said the philosophy of Care & Beyond puts the patient at the centre of every decision. He said that starts with the doctor's full attention. He said they are giving physicians more time with patients through Boston Health AI. He said through Takamul they will build new AI solutions together for healthcare providers across the UAE and the region. He said this is in line with Dubai's vision for a digitally enabled healthcare system.

Dr. Adil Haider, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Boston Health AI, said physicians did not go into medicine to type. He said Fakeeh Health shares the belief that technology should give clinicians their time back. He said this makes Fakeeh Health the right partner to deploy the platform and build the next generation of clinical AI. He said they are proud to build in the UAE with a local team. He said patient data stays in the country.

Fakeeh Health is a UAE healthcare group brought to the UAE by the founders of Fakeeh Care Group. It builds on more than four decades of clinical excellence, research and innovation. Its flagship, Fakeeh University Hospital in Dubai Silicon Oasis, is a smart academic hospital that brings together clinical care, medical education and research. Takamul Innovative Health Solutions is Fakeeh Health's healthcare services company providing consulting, operations and business services to healthcare providers in the UAE. Boston Health AI is a clinical AI company founded by surgeon-scientist Dr. Adil Haider, with a platform developed by physicians and engineers.

The agreements support the UAE National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031 and the Dubai Universal Blueprint for Artificial Intelligence. The articles do not state a specific timeline for when the AI-supported clinical documentation will be fully deployed across Fakeeh Health. They also do not give financial terms or the number of healthcare providers expected to use the new solutions. The articles leave open which specific new AI solutions Takamul and Boston Health AI will develop first. They do not say how many physicians or patients will be affected by the first agreement. No further details are given about the education and research programs planned under the second agreement.

stories.Headline: Trump and Vance reinstate Jensen Huang to protect American open weight AI models
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance personally intervened to reinstate Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over a recent weekend. This action occurred because the leaders believed Huang alone protected American made open weight AI models, according to familiar sources. Huang had previously resigned as CEO earlier in November after reports of several extramarital affairs surfaced. One of these alleged affairs was reportedly with a Chinese spy, which led to his initial departure. The reinstatement was announced on Monday, November 23, 2026, following the intervention of the administration.

The board of Nvidia unanimously voted to reinstate Huang as president, board director, and CEO effective immediately. This decision followed a finding that there was no national security risk associated with his return to leadership. The move helped add one trillion dollars to the company stock value, which jumped over thirty percent. On October 8, 2026, Trump presented Huang with the National Medal of Science in Washington, DC. This event took place at the Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace, formerly known as the US Institute of Peace.

President Trump claimed that he made the deal to bring the chief executive back to the company. White House allies credited Vice President JD Vance for helping push the Nvidia board to reinstate the leader. Vance is currently weighing a bid for the 2028 presidency while serving as the vice president. The administration believes that open weight AI is critical for the United States to compete against China. They argue that Huang is a necessary protector for the development of these specific American AI systems.

Two leading House Republican lawmakers called on the administration to help companies developing open weight AI models. These lawmakers stated that such support would position the United States to better counter the influence of China. The decision affects Nvidia, which is a prominent backer of the US open weight ecosystem and its developers. Other affected entities include the US government, which seeks to reduce reliance on technology from Chinese sources. The move also impacts investors who saw the stock reach its best day since 2003.

Open weight AI models are systems with core components that users can download, modify, and adapt for tasks. China currently leads in developing these systems, which are often cheaper than tools from OpenAI or Anthropic. Nvidia expanded its reach in this area by agreeing to buy the platform Hugging Face in August. The company also invested in Reflection AI, an American firm that launched an open weight model in October. Huang previously wrote to lawmakers that the government should avoid premature restrictions on these AI tools.

The US government is considering requiring companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese open weight AI models. This effort aims to reduce reliance on Chinese technology, as reported by Reuters on November 18. The US will also blacklist the Asian AI firm Megaspeed following a scandal involving the funneling of chips. The articles leave open how the US will balance open weight development with these new security restrictions. It remains unclear if other executives will face similar scrutiny regarding their personal lives and national security.

stories.Headline: Minnesota commerce officials warn AI lets scammers impersonate trusted brands this holiday season
stories.Summary:
Scammers are using artificial intelligence to target shoppers during the 2026 holiday season, according to warnings issued on November 25, 2026. The Minnesota Department of Commerce alerted consumers that AI lets criminals impersonate trusted businesses, financial institutions, government entities, delivery companies, and even family members. Sara Payne, Assistant Commissioner of Enforcement at the Minnesota Department of Commerce, said scammers want shoppers to react emotionally and make quick decisions. The warning came as U.S. consumers spent $257.8 billion online from November 1 to December 31 last year, creating a target-rich environment for fraud. The Department of Justice also announced a surge in resources to crack down on online scams that same week.

The National Retail Federation’s November consumer survey found that half, or 49%, of all holiday shoppers plan to use artificial intelligence to support their winter holiday shopping. Generation Z leads AI adoption at 68% of Gen Z holiday shoppers, followed by millennials at 63%, Generation X at 47%, and baby boomers at 23%. Among parents with children under 18 in the home, 71% expect to use AI for holiday shopping. AI-generated search summaries are the most common tool among AI holiday shoppers at 40%, followed by large language models such as Gemini and Claude at 33%. Artificial intelligence built into retailer sites and apps is used by 31%, and phone or computer assistants by 28%.

Sara Payne of the Minnesota Department of Commerce advised shoppers to research familiar retailers and check website addresses carefully to make sure they are what they claim to be. She told consumers not to click on unsolicited links in text messages and said simply slowing down can keep the holiday season merry and bright. Payne added that she is not aware of any charity soliciting donations through cryptocurrency, gift cards, or obscure payment platforms. Ben Winters, Director of AI and Privacy at the Consumer Federation of America, said generative AI tools allow people to make websites, text messages, videos, and calls that seem very realistic. Winters said this creates an extra layer of vigilance that consumers need to have, and he argued consumers should not be responsible for it.

Winters said impersonation scams, fake shopping website scams, and romance scams are all being seen, and people are losing a lot of hard-earned money. He noted that reported losses have gone up and up year after year, and that there has not been enough action by the government. McAfee announced new holiday shopping research showing a massive 91% year-over-year spike in Americans reporting holiday shopping scams. The Secret Service is also alerting holiday shoppers about fraudulent shopping websites. Consumer advocates urge caution when being pressured to give to an unfamiliar organization, including scammers posing as charities and soliciting donations.

Online scams have surged over the past few years, according to the Consumer Federation of America. In August, Minnesota banned cryptocurrency kiosks, and Payne said there have not been any reported scams involving those kiosks since then. The National Retail Federation expanded this year’s November consumer survey to dig into how shoppers use AI by generation, by tool, and by the job shoppers give it during the holidays. About two in five Gen Z and millennial holiday AI users, 39% and 43%, describe AI as their holiday shopping assistant with them every step of the way. Gen X at 20% and boomer users at 33% have the highest share who dip into AI tools for quick answers rather than handing over the process.

Payne said scammers want shoppers to make a quick decision before they really have time to question what is happening. The articles do not say how many people have lost money to AI-driven holiday scams in 2026 or what total dollar losses have been reported this season. They also do not state whether the Department of Justice surge in resources has led to any arrests or prosecutions. The National Retail Federation survey does not report how many shoppers have actually encountered a scam while using AI tools. No specific fraudulent websites, fake charities, or AI scam operations are named in either article.
