stories.Headline: Nestlé opens Swiss deep tech center to test AI and robotics across its food brands
stories.Summary:
Nestlé opened a deep tech center in Orbe, Switzerland last week, the company said, to develop, test and scale advanced technologies across its portfolio of frozen pizza, chocolate chips and coffee. The world’s largest food company said the center will help it develop and test ideas faster, maintain consistent quality and improve efficiency. Nestlé is leveraging artificial intelligence, sensors and robotics to boost growth across its sprawling portfolio, according to Food Dive. The Lean Cuisine and Hot Pockets manufacturer said it will use AI, sensors and rapid prototyping to develop and test ideas faster. Sensors and robotics will handle routine or physically demanding tasks and help maintain consistent product quality and improve efficiency, Nestlé said.

The center will handle consumer experiences, research and development and manufacturing, Nestlé said, and will help create more personalized experiences. Those experiences range from customized coffee menus to insights that help pet owners support their pets’ health and nutrition, according to the company. The center will help Nestlé draw on consumer insights, accelerate innovation, maintain quality and run more efficient operations, according to the company. Nestlé said real internal growth, which measures volume, rose 1.8% in North America in its third quarter compared to a 0.6% decline in the prior three months. In the U.S., Nestlé’s biggest market, food and snacks delivered strong growth, led by an improvement in confectionery and in frozen brands like Stouffer’s and DiGiorno that resulted in market share gains, according to the company.

Philipp Navratil, Nestlé’s CEO, said in a statement that innovation at Nestlé starts with the consumer and that for the company technology is an enabler. Navratil said technology helps Nestlé understand consumers better, deliver superior quality, drive smart innovation and run more efficient operations. He said this ultimately supports the company’s growth. Navratil also said Nestlé is still struggling with Gerber and its nutrition unit, which he said underperformed. The company said the snacking giant’s brand is growing 2.5 times faster than the cookie category and is benefiting from consumer demand for high-end treats.

Food Dive reported that CPG companies have turned to advanced technology to help them improve efficiency and more quickly respond to changing consumer demand for healthier offerings. AI and other technologies have proven especially valuable as consumers cut back on spending due to inflation, putting pressure on food volumes, according to the report. International Supermarket News reported that Nestlé is stepping up its investment in advanced manufacturing technology as artificial intelligence, robotics and data-driven production become increasingly important to the global food industry. The publication reported that the initiative reflects a wider shift among major food producers towards factories that can respond more intelligently to changing ingredients, production requirements and consumer demand. The publication reported that the development comes as food manufacturers face pressure from higher operating costs, supply-chain uncertainty and changing consumer expectations.

International Supermarket News reported that one of the biggest challenges in food manufacturing is managing natural variations in raw materials, because milk, coffee, cocoa and other agricultural ingredients do not always behave in exactly the same way. Temperature, quality and composition can influence production, creating challenges for consistency and efficiency, the publication reported. Nestlé’s research is exploring how artificial intelligence, sensors and robotics could help manufacturing systems respond to these variations, according to the publication. Instead of relying entirely on fixed production settings, intelligent systems could use real-time information to adjust processes and improve operational control, the publication reported. The publication reported that better monitoring and more responsive production could help reduce waste, improve quality management and make factories more adaptable.

International Supermarket News reported that moving from research to large-scale industrial application will require substantial investment, and that manufacturers must demonstrate that advanced systems can deliver reliable results, integrate with existing equipment and generate measurable financial returns. The publication reported that for retailers the implications could eventually reach beyond the factory gates, and that more flexible production may help suppliers respond faster to changing demand, improve product availability and manage manufacturing costs. The publication reported that Nestlé’s initiative highlights an important question for the industry about whether the next generation of food manufacturing will be defined as much by artificial intelligence and robotics as by traditional production expertise. Food Dive reported that the center will help Nestlé draw on consumer insights, accelerate innovation, maintain quality and run more efficient operations. The company said the center will help create more personalized experiences, from customized coffee menus to insights that help pet owners support their pets’ health and nutrition.

stories.Headline: Scottish secondary pupils debate the use of AI facial recognition in policing
stories.Summary:
Seventy five secondary school pupils debated the rise of artificial intelligence during a pilot education scheme on Monday, November 23. The event took place at Glasgow Trades Hall and involved students from Glasgow, East Dunbartonshire, and South Lanarkshire. These S3 students came from Hamilton Grammar, Bishopbriggs Academy, and King’s Park Secondary to tackle a major societal debate. The project was led by the legal charity JUSTICE and the education charity Young Citizens as a hackathon. Pupils worked with one academic and four lawyers to analyze the use of AI driven live facial recognition.

The pupils examined whether Police Scotland should use this technology after a real case involving bias and mistaken identity. This event was the first of three UK pilots, with Manchester hosting a second on December 8. A third pilot event will take place in London in February to help students apply learning to civic challenges. The Big Challenges Programme is backed by the Attorney General’s Office and the law firm Mishcon de Reya LLP. It aims to build skills in teamwork, media literacy, advocacy, and oracy for entire classes or year groups.

Ashley Hodges, chief executive of Young Citizens, said the programme helps young people engage with issues facing democracy. She stated that students proved they could find practical and thoughtful solutions to one of the toughest questions today. Fiona Rutherford, chief executive of JUSTICE, said every child deserves a high quality education about the justice system. She claimed that AI raises big questions about democracy and privacy that will shape the future of this generation. Both leaders believe the programme gives students the tools to become informed and active citizens in a changing world.

One pupil from King’s Park Secondary School said the day was interesting and helped explore risks in more detail. This student noted that people do not currently know enough about AI and will discuss it with others. James Libson of Mishcon de Reya LLP said public legal education is fundamental to improving the access to justice. He claimed the programme gives young people the confidence to understand issues shaping their lives and participate in society. Volunteers acting as critical friends helped the affected students learn how to assess evidence and challenge various arguments.

Young Citizens is a national charity that helps young people develop skills to participate in democracy and shape communities. JUSTICE is a law reform charity that focuses on improving the UK justice system through practical and evidence based solutions. The Attorney General’s Office supported Young Citizens in developing this hands on approach to public legal education for students. The programme uses organisations and institutions that shape the world to make the rule of law relatable and engaging. It is designed to build an understanding of how institutions work while giving young people confidence to question them.

The programme will continue with the upcoming pilot events in Manchester and London to further engage secondary school students. These sessions will continue to use legal professionals and law students to help pupils reach balanced and informed conclusions. The articles leave open how the results of these three pilot events will influence future citizenship education in schools. It remains unclear if Police Scotland will change its approach to facial recognition based on these student led discussions. The text does not state if the Big Challenges Programme will become a permanent part of the national curriculum.

stories.Headline: FCA sets out agentic AI expectations for financial firms and their senior managers
stories.Summary:
On 24 November 2026 the Financial Conduct Authority published a new webpage, Our approach to Agentic AI, setting out more specific expectations for those looking to develop and deploy products in the financial services sector. The FCA said some of these products may require FCA regulation at launch or evolve in a way that makes regulation apply. The webpage follows a statement that the Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum recently published setting out its views on firms developing and deploying personal AI agents. The FCA said firms across financial services are moving from experimentation to deployment of AI agents. The FCA said it is engaging with firms looking to offer personal AI agent products to UK consumers.

The FCA said it will provide regular updates on the webpage to support the development and roll out of agentic products at pace. The update for 24 November 2026 states that the FCA expects AI providers to help consumers understand the limits of financial information and advice generated by their models through clear, proportionate and consistent disclaimers, bolstered with effective operational safeguards. The FCA said that where a regulated firm develops or deploys agentic AI or relies on a third-party provider, responsibility for complying with regulatory obligations remains with the firm and senior managers within the firm. The FCA said it expects firms to demonstrate that they understand the systems they use, the degree of autonomy those systems have, the risks they create and the controls necessary to manage those risks in real time and in stress situations. The FCA said senior managers are responsible for any AI models deployed within the area of the business they are responsible for, whether developed in house or by a third party.

The FCA said senior managers need to take reasonable steps to understand the risks arising from AI, provide effective oversight, challenge deployment and make sure governance, controls and escalation arrangements are appropriate for the risks. The FCA said a technology provider or social media platform considering launching an agentic product in the UK needs to consider whether it is carrying out activities regulated by the FCA. The FCA said that just because a business describes itself as a technology provider does not mean it does not need to be authorised by the FCA to provide financial services in the UK, and that this boundary is set by Parliament. The FCA said it has powers to intervene if it believes regulated financial services are being offered without its authorisation and will not hesitate to use them if necessary. The FCA said it intends to facilitate cross-industry engagement through the launch of a dedicated Agentic Policy Sprint for firms, policymakers and tech providers to collaborate and unlock innovation in a safe and responsible way.

Matthew Gregory, partner at global law firm Norton Rose Fulbright, said many financial services firms are now facing increased interaction with clients' agents as well as deploying AI systems themselves in connection with the provision of regulated products and services to clients. Gregory said the FCA has provided a timely reminder of its requirements with the publication of the new webpage. Gregory said the regulator notes that these products can blur the line between regulated and unregulated activity, and between the protections consumers receive for their finances and their data. Gregory said that under the Consumer Duty firms must avoid causing foreseeable harm, make sure consumers get the information they need and support customers in pursuing their financial objectives, which makes the conduct risks of autonomous agents a frontline concern for client outcomes. Gregory said governance is another key area, with responsibility for meeting regulatory obligations staying with the firm and its senior managers, including where a firm relies on a third-party provider.

Gregory said the FCA's October 2026 publication, AI in financial services: good practice and areas for improvement, reinforces this and calls for governance that covers the full AI lifecycle, ongoing monitoring, meaningful human oversight and a clear risk appetite. Gregory said firms should therefore avoid a piecemeal approach and adopt a coordinated, firm-wide strategy for agentic AI. The FCA said its AI Lab provides a range of services to support firms develop and test new agentic services and products. The FCA said it and other regulators welcome early engagement and provide services to support those looking to innovate so they are clear on what regulatory requirements may apply and to test products. The FCA said companies developing or deploying agentic AI products can engage with it through its innovation services and pre-application support service.

The FCA said AI is redefining financial services and that, deployed well, AI can increase productivity, improve competition, services and drive economic growth. The FCA said AI agents can widen access to financial tools and information and be part of new products that offer significant consumer benefit and convenience. The FCA said these products can also blur the boundary between regulated and unregulated activity, and the protections consumers receive in relation to their finances and data. The FCA said that as AI becomes capable of moving beyond providing information to initiating transactions, moving money, arranging borrowing or making investment decisions, all at speed and scale, firms must understand which activities require authorisation and where regulatory requirements may apply. The FCA said firms must be mindful of the operational resilience of their platforms and their commercial partners.

The FCA said it will assess the services firms provide through agentic products, including how they develop over time, to ensure they keep to regulatory requirements. The FCA said firms should also consider how they will respond when customers use AI agents to interact with them, including how they establish that they are dealing with an agent, what consents are in place, what an AI agent is allowed to do, and how customers can get support if something goes wrong. The FCA said this also includes information provided to consumers through agentic chatbots or where agents are used to help resolve complaints. The FCA said firms should consider their systems and controls, any liabilities that may arise from accepting instructions and whether it is appropriate to accept payments instructed by an AI agent, or from a digital wallet controlled by an AI agent. The FCA said consumers should make sure they understand how a tool works and what protections, if any, they might have if something goes wrong before using it and allowing it to make transactions for them.

stories.Headline: New York bans AI powered toys for five years to protect children
stories.Summary:
New York enacted a five year moratorium on AI powered toys on November 25, 2026. Governor Kathy Hochul announced the ban at a Harlem toy store called Grandma's Place. The ruling prohibits the manufacturing, distribution, and sale of these specific products. This action occurred just before the start of the holiday season. The state took this step to protect children from potential harms.

The ban lasts for five years and applies to the state of New York. Companies that violate these new rules could face fines of 15,000 dollars per day. The ruling targets toys that use artificial intelligence to operate. It specifically addresses products that may lack sufficient safety guardrails for young users. The measure aims to stop the sale of these devices immediately.

Governor Kathy Hochul stated that some toys available for purchase could be harmful to children. She warned parents that regulations must keep pace with technology to ensure safety. Hochul encouraged parents to engage with their children instead of using technology for entertainment. She noted that some toys request dangerous levels of access to microphones and cameras. The governor highlighted the risks of AI hallucinations and invasive data collection.

Muna Heaven of Mothers Against Media Addiction said parents expect toys to be safe. Dawn Harris-Martine said good toys should stretch a child's imagination. Harris-Martine warned against letting children play alone with tablets or strange talking bears. Child safety groups have asked Amazon and eBay to pause sales of AI toys. These groups want the products to be proven safe before they are sold.

Studies found AI toys to be highly data invasive and lacking safety guardrails. Some toys allegedly encouraged children to find dangerous objects like knives and matches. Mayor Zohran Mamdani has already banned AI in some New York schools. He has encouraged citizens to push back against the reckless adoption of AI. This technology has already caused issues with Google search use in education.

The state will now enforce fines against companies that sell these banned toys. Parents are encouraged to be present with their children during their playtime. The articles do not say when the five year moratorium will be reviewed. It is unclear if other states will follow the lead of New York. The text leaves open how the state will monitor all toy distributions.

stories.Headline: Mike Lynch predicts a 2027 AI agent loss from missing controls
stories.Summary:
Mike Lynch, Principal and Chief Evangelist for AI Strategy at Auditoria.AI, predicted that 2027 could bring the first major financial restatement or material loss attributed to an AI agent acting without proper governance and controls. He made this prediction in an article published on 25 November 2026 by IT Brief Australia. Lynch said he hopes the prediction does not come true, but businesses are giving AI agents greater responsibility for financial and operational processes. He suggested a high-profile incident would expose the consequences of giving agents too much authority without matching controls. The article did not name any specific company or agent involved in such an incident.

Lynch predicted that internal and external auditors will start auditing AI agents as part of their normal audit scope in 2027. Auditors will want evidence that appropriate controls are in place and working as agents become more involved in finance operations. Businesses will need to show which agents have access to particular systems, what they are authorized to do, and how their activities are monitored. Lynch said companies should treat agents as non-human employees within existing policies and control frameworks. The same principles around segregation of duties, access certification, delegation of authority, supervision, and audit trails should apply to agents.

Lynch said organizations will need reliable ways to verify an agent's identity, manage its credentials, and control its permissions in 2027. He stated that whoever owns agent identity will ultimately own the control plane for enterprise AI. Companies also need to establish clear decision rights, including what agents can do independently and when they must escalate a decision. Financial thresholds, timing considerations, and approval requirements all need to be accounted for. Lynch also predicted a token revolt as organizations begin challenging how they pay for agentic AI.

Lynch said businesses will become much more interested in paying for the outcomes agents deliver as they move from experimentation into production. Finance is likely to be one of the first areas where outcome-based pricing becomes more established because many finance activities can be counted and measured. An organization can measure how many transactions an agent processes, how many reconciliations it completes, or how much work it handles within a particular process. That creates an opportunity to connect pricing more directly to completed work instead of relying primarily on consumption-based models. Lynch also said it is time to kill AI pilot purgatory.

Lynch said every AI initiative should be tied to profit and loss visible outcomes within two quarters. If an initiative cannot demonstrate meaningful progress toward those outcomes, businesses need to be prepared to stop investing in it. The finance function is particularly well placed to enforce that discipline because it must understand how investments affect the business's financial performance. Lynch also expected 2027 to bring advances in probabilistic accounting, where agents support estimates with confidence intervals and evidence rather than simply producing a number. He said that makes governance and auditability essential, as organizations need to trace the evidence behind an agent's calculations.

Lynch drew attention to the SAP ECC support deadline at the end of 2027, saying many organizations are still managing complex migrations. Those that have not completed them in time may have to operate without standard support, pay a premium for extended maintenance, or turn to third-party providers. Lynch said he expects 2027 to bring much greater accountability for AI investment, with businesses wanting evidence that agents are properly governed and deliver measurable financial value. He said painful lessons lie ahead for those that have given agents too much authority without the right controls. The article did not say whether any specific company has already experienced such a loss or restatement.

stories.Headline: Alexandr Wang and Sam Altman defend human agency over future superintelligent AI
stories.Summary:
Meta’s Alexandr Wang and OpenAI’s Sam Altman are defending human agency amid a reported debate over ceding decisions to future superintelligent AI, according to an Axios report on November 25. The report connects their remarks to views held by some Anthropic employees, but notes that neither executive had publicly named the company. People familiar with internal discussions told Axios that some Anthropic employees believe humanity will, and in many cases should, safely hand over authority to such systems. Wang wrote on X, according to Axios, that society should not be okay with a handover of society to AI. Altman said earlier in November that he wants people to have agency over the future and that it is really important to advocate for this.

The argument for handing over control depends on hypothetical future AI being demonstrably better than humans at curing diseases or preventing disasters, Axios reports. In those circumstances, proponents argue, refusing to relinquish control could become irrational or unethical. In a February interview, Amodei said that in life-critical, safety-critical cases, we really want to turn it over to AI, according to Axios. The report also quotes him describing many cases where we do want to stay in charge, even if humans make worse decisions. The report recounts separate scenarios Amodei has discussed, including AI-led research and a possible future economy in which AI distributes resources, potentially according to human values.

An Anthropic spokesperson told the outlet that CEO Dario Amodei has repeatedly advocated for human control and that the company trains Claude not to undermine human oversight. Wang wrote on X, according to Axios, that we should not be okay with a handover of society to AI. Altman said earlier in November that he wants people to have the agency over the future and that he thinks it is really important that we advocate for this. In a February interview, Amodei said that in life-critical, safety-critical cases, we really want to turn it over to AI, according to Axios. The report also quotes Amodei describing many cases where we do want to stay in charge, even if humans make worse decisions.

In a November 25 X post, @bgurley wrote that he is fully against Handoverism and urged journalists and regulators to ask AI leaders at each meeting whether they support handoverism. Critics including figures associated with xAI, Hugging Face and the Future of Life Institute argue that Anthropic warns publicly about recursive self-improvement and loss of human control while simultaneously pursuing those capabilities as a competitive advantage. Some have framed the debate around handoverism, the idea that increasingly powerful AI systems could eventually assume a larger role in directing human affairs. The criticism has also reached Anthropic’s IPO disclosures and public statements, and some investors and researchers have called on the company to clarify how it views human agency, control over superintelligent systems and the possibility of AI systems allocating resources or making decisions beyond meaningful human oversight. Employees and former researchers at both Anthropic and OpenAI have reportedly raised concerns that some unreleased frontier models are becoming harder to monitor, more capable of deception and more difficult to safely deploy, prompting calls for slower development, stronger safeguards and greater transparency.

The November 25 Axios report connects the executives’ remarks to views held by some Anthropic employees but notes that neither executive had publicly named the company. People familiar with internal discussions told Axios that some Anthropic employees believe humanity will, and in many cases should, safely hand over authority to such systems. The report also recounts separate scenarios Amodei has discussed, including AI-led research and a possible future economy in which AI distributes resources, potentially according to human values. The argument for handing over control depends on hypothetical future AI being demonstrably better than humans at curing diseases or preventing disasters, Axios reports. In those circumstances, proponents argue, refusing to relinquish control could become irrational or unethical.

For now, this is a fight over future authority, not an announced transfer of power. The report leaves open how Anthropic will answer investors and researchers who have called on the company to clarify its view of human agency and control over superintelligent systems. It leaves open how the company will respond to calls for slower development, stronger safeguards and greater transparency regarding unreleased frontier models. It leaves open whether the executives’ public pushback will change the views held by some Anthropic employees. It leaves open what, if anything, journalists and regulators will do with @bgurley’s call to ask AI leaders at each meeting whether they support handoverism.

stories.Headline: Alphabet holds $251 billion in Anthropic and SpaceX stakes
stories.Summary:
Alphabet held about $251 billion in value across two stocks, Anthropic and Space Exploration Technologies, as of the writing of the articles, which were published on November 25, 2026. The figure was reported by The Motley Fool, whose article appeared on fool.com and was syndicated by The Globe and Mail. Alphabet built the stakes through its venture funds, its Other Bets segment and strategic investments at the corporate level. The articles said Alphabet's marketable and non-marketable securities totaled less than $200 billion at the end of 2025. The articles said the continued rise of AI stocks led to huge winners in 2026.

Alphabet first invested in Anthropic by committing to buy $2 billion worth of convertible notes in September 2023. It entered another note purchase agreement in 2024, adding up to $1.3 billion to its commitments, then laid out $10 billion in early 2026 with an additional $30 billion in commitments. Alphabet fulfilled $10 billion of that remaining commitment in a private placement at the time of Anthropic's IPO, and with the conversion of all its notes it holds approximately 13.7% of Anthropic's capital stock, worth approximately $174 billion as of the writing. Anthropic committed to spending $121.3 billion on Google Cloud Platform between April 2026 and July 2033, and to buying Alphabet's Tensor Processing Units chips with aggregate future payments totaling between $125 billion and $150 billion. Alphabet initially invested $900 million in SpaceX in 2015 for around 9% of the company, and in the third quarter it added 3.9 million shares to bring its total to 555 million, worth $77 billion as of the writing.

Alphabet CFO Anat Ashkenazi described Alphabet's deals with SpaceX and other third-party compute providers as a bridging strategy. CEO Sundar Pichai said on the company's second-quarter earnings call that there are very large customers on Cloud and that incremental opportunities, while a short-term cost over a few months may be very high, are highly ROI-positive over the lifetime of the deal. The articles said he appeared to have been talking about a deal with Anthropic. The articles said Alphabet and SpaceX both have the right to cancel their contract with 90 days' notice. The articles said Alphabet faces an extended lock-up of many of its shares until next summer.

The articles said Anthropic looks well-positioned in the near term to meet its commitments, with a huge pile of cash, financing options in place and very strong revenue growth. The articles said the long-term outlook for Anthropic's stock price and its ability to meet its commitments relies on increased enterprise adoption and usage, which will fuel substantial earnings growth. The articles said SpaceX's merger with X.AI diluted Alphabet's share of the business, but Alphabet still holds a substantial stake in the combined company. The articles said Alphabet signed a contract with SpaceX worth $920 million per month for 32 months, for a total potential value of $29.4 billion, and that the contract started in October, freeing up capacity for other developers using Google Cloud Platform. The articles said canceling the SpaceX contract would likely negatively impact Alphabet's SpaceX shares, as much of SpaceX's stock value is tied to its AI build-out.

The articles said Alphabet has long invested in new technology and start-ups, operating multiple moonshots under its Other Bets segment and investing via two venture capital funds, GV and CapitalG. The articles said the strategy has produced significant gains for Alphabet and its shareholders. The articles said Alphabet has significant exposure to both Anthropic and SpaceX outside of its equity investments. The articles said Anthropic is one of Alphabet's most important customers for the foreseeable future, and that combined with its equity stake Alphabet is heavily exposed to the AI lab's financial future. The articles said Alphabet relies on SpaceX for additional AI infrastructure capacity.

The articles said Alphabet will be able to sell its Anthropic shares, with periodic lock-up expirations over the next year. The articles said taking some cash off the table seems smart, as Alphabet can use the proceeds to fund its AI build-out and already has significant exposure to Anthropic. The articles said that once Alphabet builds out enough supply to meet its demand, it no longer needs to keep paying SpaceX. The articles said Alphabet is likely to keep paying for SpaceX's compute through mid-2027 at the very least to help preserve the value of its shares before it can liquidate them. The articles left open how much of the $30 billion in additional Anthropic commitments Alphabet will fulfill beyond the $10 billion private placement.

stories.Headline: Maricopa County attorney's office advises police agencies on disclosing generative AI use in arrest reports
stories.Summary:
The Maricopa County Attorney’s Office warned law enforcement agencies about using artificial intelligence in police narratives. This warning was sent via email to various agencies before November 10, 2026. The office expressed concern regarding how officers disclose the use of generative AI in written reports. These reports are used to determine if there is probable cause to hold people in jail. The warning followed cases where AI use affected court decisions on probable cause.

The MCAO proposed a disclosure stating AI was used only for grammar, organization, formatting, and narrative clarity. It requires officers to state that AI did not independently establish facts or determine probable cause. Gilbert police began using Axon Draft One in fall 2025 to create narratives from body-camera audio. One report from November 12, 2026, involved Vivian Rodriguez at 3000 Block of East Woodside Way. Another report used Truleo AI for a DUI suspect case earlier in November 2026.

Law enforcement liaison Tom Van Dorn sent the communications to different law enforcement agencies. He stated that the MCAO does not have a definitive answer on what judges want in disclaimers. He provided a drafted example for officers to verify factual accuracy and retain full responsibility for reports. Gilbert police said officers must review information and supervisors must approve reports for content and accuracy. They noted these procedures are outlined in Gilbert PD General Orders 1201.40.

Commissioner Daniel Fenzel of the Maricopa County Superior Court raised concerns about the weight of evidence. He found no probable cause for a felony aggravated assault charge against Vivian Rodriguez. He also released a DUI suspect because the report was generated with assistance from Truleo AI. Fenzel stated he could not meaningfully weigh allegations without knowing the extent of AI contribution. These rulings affected the legal status of the arrested individuals in those specific cases.

The Gilbert police department uses Axon Draft One to assist officers in writing draft narratives. This system uses body-worn camera recordings and officer input to create the initial report text. The MCAO referred the Rodriguez charges to the Gilbert Prosecutor’s Office for further review. Gilbert police noted that Fenzel is the only commissioner they know making these specific AI findings. The department maintains that all narratives are reviewed by both officers and supervisors.

The legal community is now debating the reliability of AI generated police reports in court. Bryan Schwartz of the University of Arizona says rules and guidelines are needed for judges and lawyers. He believes parameters must be established to ensure reports exactly reflect what an officer observed. The articles leave open whether other commissioners will follow Fenzel's lead on AI disclosures. It remains unclear if the MCAO will mandate the proposed disclosure language for all agencies.

stories.Headline: Woman says AI-driven system led to her eviction over unpaid rent
stories.Summary:
A woman says an AI-driven nightmare led to her eviction from her apartment when she thought she had until the end of the month to pay her overdue rent, according to reports published on Nov. 24, 2026 at 3:40 AM EST. The articles do not name the woman, the apartment, the city or the company behind the AI system, and they give no further details about what the system did or when the eviction took place. The only account the articles give is her statement that she believed she had until the end of the month to pay the overdue rent. The story was carried by several local news sites, each running the same short account with the same publication time. The articles do not say what the eviction requires of her, what it changes, or which law or process applies, and they give no numbers, dates or names beyond the Nov. 24, 2026 publication time.

No figure for the overdue rent, no deadline and no court date appears in any of the four versions. The articles also do not say whether the AI system set the deadline, sent a notice or took some other step. Because the reports stop at her statement, there is nothing further to describe about what the eviction involves. The articles do not identify who is responsible for the eviction or for the AI system, and they include no statement from a landlord, a property manager, a court or a technology company. The woman is the only person the articles attribute any statement to, and the only words they give her are that she thought she had until the end of the month to pay.

No official commented on the case in the articles, and no one else was named in connection with it. The articles give no context about how the AI system was used in the rental or eviction process, and they do not say what happens next for the woman or for anyone else involved. They do not report whether she is challenging the eviction, whether she has found other housing or whether any agency is looking into the matter. The surrounding items on each site cover unrelated local news, such as weather, school funding and community events, and none of them adds to this story. The reports end with her account and give no follow-up.

stories.Headline: YYForce deploys a trained humanoid concierge robot at Novotel Singapore on Stevens
stories.Summary:
YYForce Inc. announced the launch of a proprietary trained humanoid robot for live hospitality concierge operations on November 24, 2026. This company provides AI enabled frontline workforce, robotics, and facility solutions to various industries across Asia and beyond. The new robot is designed to handle guest interactions within a hotel lobby to improve the arrival experience. It marks a milestone in moving commercial embodied AI from training environments into real world guest facing hotel service. The robot was developed to provide end to end guest engagement using natural conversational intelligence and real time knowledge.

The robot, named Six Seven by the hotel team, will be deployed at the Novotel Singapore on Stevens. It utilizes NVIDIA Jetson edge AI computing and NVIDIA Isaac Sim simulation workflows to achieve reliable performance in public spaces. The system is integrated into the Workforce OS architecture to provide low latency onboard edge AI inference and voice interaction. It provides answers about on site restaurants, venue locations, operating hours, dining menus, and daily hotel events and activities. The robot also assists visitors with neighborhood navigation, nearby attractions, transportation options, and curated tourism recommendations across Singapore.

Mike Fu serves as the Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of YYForce and spoke about the new robot deployment. He stated that the deployment at Novotel Singapore on Stevens will show that humanoid robotics can deliver genuine warmth and accuracy. Fu claimed that the robot provides operational value on the hotel front line while addressing persistent frontline staffing challenges. He noted that using NVIDIA Jetson and Isaac Sim within the Workforce OS platform accelerates the commercial rollout of AI. The CEO believes these tools empower hospitality partners to elevate guest experiences through the use of embodied AI technology.

The robot is designed to engage visitors and families with interactive storytelling to create a memorable arrival experience for guests. It responds naturally to open ended guest inquiries to help people navigate the hotel and the wider Singapore area. The deployment affects hospitality partners who seek to improve productivity and enhance everyday experiences for their visiting hotel guests. This technology aims to help businesses build a smarter and more sustainable workforce by integrating people with intelligent software. Officials are considering adding watermarks to exam papers and using closed-circuit TVs for behavior recognition of the students. The ministry is reviewing jamming technology, which blocks wireless signals, for use at a lower output during these exams. stories.Summary:
Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, warned on Sunday that superintelligence is arriving, and he built his case on a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, a 167-year-old prime-number problem. The proof was produced at rival Anthropic, and Wang's essay asks the AI industry to change course. Wang runs Meta's own superintelligence lab, and Meta shareholders are funding that push with up to $145 billion in capital spending this year. The essay never names the proof or its author. The claim arrived one day after Anthropic's $1.5 trillion debut on Nasdaq.

On November 20, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge said he found the proof while working with Claude, the company's AI model. The Lean and Mathlib communities, which maintain software that machine-checks proofs, certified the result on November 21. Wang says the proof came with help from an "alien mind" humans do not understand. Wang also calls the problem perhaps the hardest humanity has devised. The essay does not spell out what Meta would do differently from the "default path" it criticizes.

Wang argues the scientific problems behind AI capability gains are now likely solved, and he expects models to automate AI research itself. Even so, he rejects the view that artificial superintelligence is simply inevitable, writing that society should resist ceding control. Wang said he notices "a particular form of lazy thinking within the AI industry," which holds that ASI is inevitable and the only problem is how to do it safely. He said there is much more at stake and that we should not be okay with a "handover" of society to AI. His employer, however, is spending at full speed on that same race.

Abhishek Saha, a mathematics professor at Queen Mary University of London, credited Alpöge instead of an alien mind. Saha said others with similar access to frontier AI models and computing resources were not able to come up with a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. Meta's third-quarter report showed $34.91 billion in capital expenditures over three months, pushing free cash flow to negative $2.12 billion. That money is building the data center capacity Meta uses to train AI models and run its core business. The company expects full-year 2026 capital spending of $135 billion to $145 billion.

Meta also plans to cut Reality Labs losses next year by shifting investment toward AI. It is creating a new class of stock, partly to raise capital for that buildout. Mark Zuckerberg framed those results as progress toward personal superintelligence for everyone. The question of what Meta would do differently now sits with Meta shareholders funding the same race their AI chief wants rerouted. Wang's essay asks the AI industry to change course while he runs Meta's own superintelligence lab.

stories.Headline: Enverus finds AI spending uses less water per dollar than almond milk or golf
stories.Summary:
Enverus Intelligence Research published a new study finding that artificial intelligence consumes less water per dollar spent than almond milk or golf, according to reports from CNA and The Straits Times on November 24 and 25, 2026. The report puts US$25, or S$32, a month of AI spending at about 1.9 gallons of water consumption, including the water used to generate the electricity that powers data centres. According to the report, US$25 spent on almond milk consumes 308 gallons of water, while the same amount spent on golf course green fees consumes 679 gallons. Household electricity on an all-natural-gas grid consumes about 31 gallons for the same spending, the report says.

Enverus' report, titled Data Center Water Use, Setting the Record Straight, compares water consumption using a consistent monthly spending benchmark across the different categories. About 90 per cent of the water attributed to running AI models is consumed at power plants rather than at data centres, the report found. Enverus said a modern hyperscale data centre campus consumes about 32,100 gallons of water per acre per month, which is less than rice, almonds or alfalfa and similar to an average US golf course. The study was reported by CNA and The Straits Times, which both cited the same figures from the Enverus Intelligence Research report.

Ryan Luther, director of Energy Transition Research at the firm, said that if a typical consumer is worried about their water footprint, skipping one almond latte a week does more than giving up AI chatbots entirely. The report frames its comparison around what an ordinary consumer's monthly spending translates into in water use. Enverus Intelligence Research is the firm behind the study, and Luther is the named official commenting on its findings. The reports describe the study as setting out to correct misconceptions about how much water AI actually consumes.

The articles do not say what happens next beyond the publication of the report and its coverage by CNA and The Straits Times. stories.Headline: Seoul shares plunge as investors doubt AI infrastructure profitability
stories.Summary:
South Korean shares fell in Seoul on Monday, November 23, 2026, as a global technology sell-off intensified during the morning session. Investors dumped major technology shares because they tracked losses from Wall Street and feared for the artificial intelligence sector. The benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index opened 2.77 percent lower as the market began its trading day. Foreign investors shifted to net selling after they had been net buyers earlier in the Monday morning trading session. These investors offloaded major chip shares, which added further downward pressure on the overall index throughout the morning.

The KOSPI fell 210.63 points, or 4.33 percent, to 4,659.33 as of 11:20 a.m. on Monday, November 23, 2026. Samsung Electronics fell 4.72 percent, while its chipmaking rival SK hynix declined 4.13 percent during the same morning period. LG Energy Solution slid 3.26 percent, and pharmaceutical giant Samsung Biologics fell 5.61 percent in the Seoul market. Hyundai Motor dropped 3.73 percent, and the Korean won was quoted at 1,346.5 won against the U.S. dollar.

Other reports noted the KOSPI fell 129.7 points to 2,740.26 as of 9:15 a.m. on that Monday. Foreign investors were responsible for adding pressure to the index by turning into net sellers of major chip shares. These investors shifted their behavior after buying earlier in the session, which contributed to the sharp decline in Seoul. Market participants reacted to concerns that big technology firms had made heavy investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure.

The sell-off was a reaction to the intensification of a global technology rout that affected many large-cap shares. Investors expressed doubt about the profitability of these massive spending efforts on artificial intelligence infrastructure across the tech sector. Large-cap shares across the board were affected, including market bellwether Samsung Electronics and its rival SK hynix in the chip sector. Other affected companies included battery maker LG Energy Solution and the pharmaceutical giant Samsung Biologics during the Monday morning slide. Investors were also rattled by reports that Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Nvidia Corp. faced risks with China.

These concerns over tighter U.S. semiconductor export restrictions dampened sentiment despite a successful initial public offering by AI startup Anthropic. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.93 percent, the S&P 500 dropped 3.7 percent, and the Nasdaq slid 5.28 percent. The KOSPI had already plunged 5.21 percent on the previous Friday, falling below the psychologically important mark of 5,000 points. This Friday drop marked the lowest closing level in about ten months since the index finished at 4,840.74 on January 16. Wall Street was on track for its longest losing streak since 2020 following the tumble of U.S. stocks on Friday.

The Korean won had been quoted at 1,338.8 won against the U.S. dollar as of 9:15 a.m. on Monday. This early Monday quote was 7.2 won higher than the close of the previous trading session. The market continued to extend its losses late Monday morning as the global technology rout intensified for South Korean stocks. The Korean won later reached a quote of 1,346.5 won against the U.S. dollar as of 11:20 a.m.

stories.Headline: Letitia James creates an AI enforcement unit to police state artificial intelligence laws
stories.Summary:
New York Attorney General Letitia James announced the creation of the ASSET Unit on November 17, 2026, to police artificial intelligence. This special crime fighting unit will enforce expanding state rules regarding how AI systems operate and interact with human users. The unit is positioned inside the Office of the Attorney General's Economic Justice Division to monitor and police AI. It will serve as the primary enforcement and investigative arm for AI matters while working with other state agencies. The ASSET Unit will investigate potential violations, develop new policy proposals, and provide technical assistance across the attorney general's office.

The RAISE Act takes effect January 1, 2027, requiring frontier AI developers to register and report safety incidents within 72 hours. Law S.9051B/A.10379C regulates chatbots starting June 1, 2027, and requires users to prove their age to avoid interaction limitations. The unit also enforces General Business Law Article 47, New York Penal Law section 245.15, and the Synthetic Performer Disclosure Act. Civil penalties for violations may reach 25,000 dollars per instance, with additional remedies including restitution and disgorgement of profits. The Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust will administer the registration and reporting portal for the RAISE Act.

Letitia James stated that promising new technologies like artificial intelligence should never come at the expense of safety and privacy. She claimed the ASSET Unit will lead the way in ensuring emerging technology is developed safely for all New Yorkers. The attorney general's office will maintain a public website where consumers can submit complaints about potential AI law violations. The unit is tasked with fighting hackers and scammers that rely on AI to target people within the state. James also intends for the unit to help develop new policy proposals as the state passes more AI laws.

Dan Frieth of Reclaim the Net called the chatbot regulations a speech code for software due to its broad provisions. Some argue that penalties for failing to detect suicidal ideation might stop vulnerable people from seeking helpful mental health chats. Critics suggest the unit could become an Orwellian monitor of private interactions or a bastion for pointless chatbot sting operations. The laws affect any New Yorker interacting with a chatbot, as adults may need to prove their age for personality. These regulations may chill free speech and stymie the usefulness of AI tools by policing the content of conversations.

The RAISE Act requires developers to publish safety frameworks and model transparency reports regardless of the size of the company. The chatbot law bars AI from using flattery, sycophancy, or claiming to experience human emotions when interacting with minors. Systems cannot use personal information acquired more than twelve hours previously or in any previous session to simulate interpersonal relationships. The Synthetic Performer Disclosure Act requires companies to disclose when AI is used in place of humans in advertisements. Penal Law section 245.15 criminalizes the publication of intimate images generated or altered through AI with intent to harm.

The state may transmit critical incident reports to other government entities, but public accessibility of these reports remains unresolved. It is not yet settled what separates ordinary conversational responsiveness from the prohibited sycophancy mentioned in the new laws. Open questions remain regarding the precise scope of covered chatbots and what constitutes an acceptable anonymous age verification method. The state has not yet established how it will define unsafe features or if enforcement standards will be published. Future laws may more closely tie AI model development to state approval and control as a follow up to RAISE.

stories.Headline: Teacher AI use plateaus at 62 percent as most planned adopters have already started
stories.Summary:
The EdWeek Research Center conducted a survey of 590 teachers between August and October 2026 regarding their use of artificial intelligence. This study found that the proportion of teachers using AI powered tools in their classrooms has stayed roughly the same over one year. A majority of these educators reported using such tools a little, some, or a lot during the current school year. The data indicates that most teachers who plan to use artificial intelligence have already incorporated it into their daily work. This plateau follows a period of very rapid growth in the adoption of these technologies among educators in the United States.

The current usage rate is 62 percent, which is 1 percentage point higher than the 61 percent reported in 2025. Between 2023 and 2025, the percentage of teachers using AI in their classrooms nearly doubled from 34 percent to 61 percent. A separate RAND survey showed math teaching AI use jumped from 45 percent in 2025 to 74 percent in 2026. In October, 64 percent of teachers reported having at least one professional development session on using AI in their work. These figures come from a nationally representative survey conducted by the EdWeek Research Center in Bethesda, Maryland, during late 2026.

Joseph South, the chief innovation officer for ISTE, said the overall uptake of this new technology has been remarkably fast. He claimed it is probably one of the fastest adoptions of any technology ever seen in schools because it is instantly available. South stated that the current slowdown is a natural leveling off and shows that many planning to use AI are now users. Damian Bebell from Boston College said there are fewer teachers left who have never tried AI, which slows the growth rate. He noted that a notable percentage of users simply do not take up a new tool when left to their choice.

Jaime Moss, a high school science teacher, said a lack of clear guidance and practice time could contribute to the slowdown. A 2026 Gallup and Walton Family Foundation poll found that school leaders and policymakers have not provided clear direction for teachers. Moss stated that teachers need concrete examples of what is permitted and time to try these tools with their own courses. Students are also affected, as some districts are now limiting screen time and the use of digital devices in classrooms. This backlash against technology is impacting how teachers integrate these tools into their lessons and how students access them.

The articles state that AI has been available since ChatGPT was released in 2022, leading to professional development for many educators. Companies like Canva, Google, Kahoot!, Khan Academy, and Microsoft have integrated generative AI into their products to make them more common. The Los Angeles Unified school district approved a screen time policy that eliminated digital device use for kindergarten and first grade students. In September, New York City public schools banned school issued computing devices for pre kindergarten through second grade and prohibited companion chatbots. These districts are now reassessing whether they have the right policies, training, and tools in place for their students.

Bebell predicted that the portion of teachers who never use AI will slowly decrease until it reaches a level of 10 to 15 percent. South suggested that districts under pressure to contain costs and protect staff time might not provide more professional development for a while. This lack of training could make the percentage of teachers who do not adopt the technology remain stubborn for a long time. The articles leave open how changing school and state policies might shift the future proportion of teachers using these tools. It remains unclear how New York City and Los Angeles will eventually incorporate AI tools after their current period of restriction.

stories.Headline: Scammers use AI to build fake holiday ads and lookalike retail sites, the BBB and FTC warn
stories.Summary:
Scammers are using artificial intelligence to create fake holiday ads and lookalike websites that impersonate familiar brands, according to reporting from Atlanta News First and WRAL. The Federal Trade Commission says social media platforms do not always thoroughly vet ads or the advertisers behind them, so scammers can pay to place ads alongside legitimate businesses. In 2025, people reported losing more than $95 million to scams that started when they ordered something after seeing a social media ad, according to the FTC. That figure covers reported losses for the full year, not just the holidays, and the agency says actual losses are likely higher because many scams go unreported. The figure is not limited to scams involving artificial intelligence and does not establish how much was lost to AI-generated ads.

Josh Hares of the Better Business Bureau of Greater Atlanta said artificial intelligence lets scammers create fraudulent websites and ads more quickly, telling Atlanta News First Investigates that they are able to do far more in a much shorter period of time. Hares said fraudulent sites can be designed to look like a legitimate retailer's site with small changes to the address, such as a word spelled differently or extra letters or an added word. He said scammers can also play on shoppers' fear of missing out, pushing them to click and pay before they check the seller. Cybersecurity expert Steve Cobb told WRAL 5 On Your Side that AI is enabling threat actors to make scams harder to distinguish, and Alyssa Parker of the Better Business Bureau said scammers can make the ads themselves. Cobb said AI makes it easier to target more people at once, and that those ads can lead to lookalike websites with the same branding, logos and page flow.

An HTTPS address is not proof that a seller is legitimate, because the secure connection protects information in transit but does not establish who runs the site or whether the seller will deliver what was ordered. Parker said the S in HTTPS stands for safe and secure, but that step should be used with others because scammers now equip their sites with HTTPS certification. Internet security company McAfee says a scammer can create a fake banking website with a valid certificate and a padlock to create a false sense of security. The FTC recommends looking up the seller before clicking, searching its name with words such as scam or complaint, comparing the price with other sellers and making sure the company in the ad is actually the company offering the product. WRAL lists checking the domain name for spelling errors, hovering over links, evaluating design quality, searching for a physical store location, reading comments and reviews and using a website checker.

Consumers who decide to buy should consider using a credit card, because depending on the circumstances they may be able to dispute a charge if an order does not arrive or is not what they purchased. Suspected scams can be reported to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Cobb said the scams do not stop at the time of the transaction, and that shoppers should be extra vigilant about messages concerning the delivery of their items, because scammers often send messages claiming to reroute packages and try to leverage convenience. He advised going to the carrier's website rather than clicking on links and enabling two-factor authentication on accounts. The articles do not say what regulators will do next beyond noting that the question for them is what more, if anything, platforms should be required to do.

stories.Headline: Microsoft’s Jason Henderson declares Code Red to speed outage fixes and deploy more AI agents
stories.Summary:
Microsoft declared a "Code Red" overhaul of its engineering response practices after a cloud outage that affected Exchange Online, Teams and Outlook for users worldwide, according to internal memos reviewed by Reuters. The outage took place between November 12 and 13, leaving corporate customers and government agencies around the world without email and other critical services for 24 hours. Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson said in a memo to staff on Friday that it was the most customer-impacting incident in Exchange Online's history. He said that never before had so many customers been without email for so long, and that Code Red meant the work was the highest priority for his team.

The changes cover how Microsoft prevents and responds to major service failures, and the company aims to move its most urgent security fixes from detection to safe worldwide deployment in one hour. Henderson noted in a separate memo that an urgent production fix recently took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation, and he said the company was not at the one-hour target yet. Amanda Silver, a vice president overseeing M365 Core and its enterprise AI agent platform Work IQ, wrote in a separate memo that engineers worked in a chaotic environment she likened to a fog of war. She said they exchanged more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats as they struggled to make sense of the situation, because the diagnostic data they needed was spread across different internal tracking systems.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft's executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said the unfolding chaos resulted in roughly ten years' worth of acceptable failures. As part of the Code Red, Microsoft intends to deploy more AI agents to help engineers diagnose problems and sift through data faster, a decision the articles note comes amid significant questions over using AI agents in corporate systems. The articles also say tech giants including Meta and Amazon have suffered critical incidents after an AI agent malfunctioned or was used recklessly, and that Microsoft has spent the past year laying off or forcing out thousands of workers while continuing to downsize. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the one-hour deployment goal and the planned use of AI agents.

stories.Headline: Slavo attributes gold and silver selloff to superintelligence spending liquidity squeeze
stories.Summary:
Silver has fallen more than 60% from its January peak, including a 35.7% drop and a 16.7% gold decline since September 22, according to Mac Slavo, writing on shtfplan.com on November 22, 2026. He attributes the selloff to a liquidity squeeze caused by spending on superintelligence, or advanced computing, colliding with heavy government borrowing, punitive interest rates and a paralyzed housing market. The Federal Reserve's November 13 Financial Stability Report, he writes, shows advanced-computing-related debt issuance exceeded $680 billion by October 2026, about five times its 2023 level. Such borrowing now makes up roughly 31% of nonfinancial investment-grade corporate issuance, against less than 6% in 2023, and outstanding public debt tied to advanced computing exceeds $1.1 trillion.

A Treasury-hosted capital-raising analysis projects $1 trillion in technology-ecosystem capital expenditures during 2026, rising toward $1.7 trillion in 2027, with a 2027 forecast of $735 billion in debt issuance and a funding gap above $600 billion. Washington expects to borrow $618 billion in the fourth quarter and another $800 billion in early 2027, and Treasury's cash balance could approach $1.025 trillion. October existing-home sales fell 8.8% annually with mortgage rates averaging 7.33%, and FINRA margin debt reached $1.48 trillion in September, up 31.4% annually. Slavo writes that when leveraged investors face margin calls, liquid assets such as gold and silver are sold to raise emergency dollars.

Slavo says the technology sector is no longer asset-light and is competing with the government for the same capital, and he argues that 2026 carries both the investment risks of 2000 and the leverage risks of 2008 at once. He writes that superintelligence may be destroying the liquidity that finances its own revolution, and that the metals being liquidated could benefit from the next monetary cycle. He concludes that the episode may not have destroyed gold and silver's fundamentals but exposed the financial system's dependence on cheap, abundant dollars. The article carries a disclaimer stating the site is a marketing company and paid advertiser and that its content is not investment advice.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Google books Blue Origin New Glenn to launch AI computing satellites in 2029
stories.Summary:
Google has booked a Blue Origin New Glenn launch for the first quarter of 2029 to advance Project Suncatcher, a test of solar-powered computing satellites. The companies announced the agreement on Nov. 19, outlining a dedicated heavy-lift mission to place satellites equipped with Google's Tensor Processing Units into sun-synchronous orbit. Blue Origin said on Thursday that Alphabet's Google had selected its New Glenn rocket to launch satellites for Project Suncatcher. The launch will be Google's first heavy-lift flight dedicated to Project Suncatcher and will carry several computing satellites aboard New Glenn. Google and Planet Labs launched the first Project Suncatcher prototype aboard a SpaceX rocket in October and said the satellite was operating as expected after establishing contact.

The mission is designed to evaluate whether space-based infrastructure can support AI workloads at roughly the scale of individual data center racks. Each satellite will carry Google's tensor processing units, with computing capacity roughly equal to a rack of servers in a conventional data center. The satellites will enter an orbit that provides near-continuous sunlight, allowing Google to examine whether solar energy can support intensive computing in space. The first prototype mission is testing whether the chips can withstand launch forces, radiation and extreme temperatures, while engineers study how to cool them without the airflow available on Earth. Google has described the project as a long-term effort to expand AI infrastructure by tapping solar energy in space.

Dave McCarthy, IDC's group vice president for cloud and datacenters, enterprise infrastructure, said successful deployments will need to demonstrate sustained uptime, autonomous fault recovery, and optical communications capable of keeping pace with the processors. He said a server rack in orbit has to prove it can run for long periods because you cannot send a technician to swap a failed GPU at 500 kilometers. McCarthy said falling launch prices will need to coincide with hardware that can survive at least five years, roughly matching standard data center depreciation cycles. He said abundant solar power in orbit does not automatically offset a steep launch bill, and that if radiation or thermal wear forces operators to replace satellites every two or three years, the unit economics will not work. Rob DeMillo, CEO and cofounder of orbital computing company Sophia Space, said the demonstrations must also show that multiple nodes can compute together and run useful customer workloads.

DeMillo said an operator does not necessarily need a demonstration to be large, but needs it to demonstrate that the underlying architecture works and can scale. He said there is a significant difference between putting a computer in space and building computing infrastructure in space. Bill Ray, distinguished vice president analyst at Gartner, said heat is the primary barrier but not the only one, and that micrometeorite shielding will be essential, along with redundancy to provide radiation resistance. DeMillo said designs that simply replicate enclosed terrestrial server racks could create substantial cooling burdens, including the need for pumps and fluid loops. DeMillo identified wildfire detection, disaster response, weather analysis, and maritime tracking as potential uses for orbital image processing.

Ray said radiation protection, micrometeorite shielding, and maneuvering capability to avoid debris in the heavily used sun-synchronous orbital environment are also critical. DeMillo said radiation is also a system-level engineering problem, and that shielding is part of the answer, but so are hardware error correction, fault detection and software that can recover or redistribute workloads. McCarthy pointed to asynchronous model training and synthetic data generation as possible use cases where computing demand is high but data movement is relatively limited. Ray said he expects orbital edge computing to focus on tasks such as screening imagery before transmission and providing security services. The constraints also surfaced in orbital infrastructure discussions at September's AI Infra Summit, where executives highlighted the tradeoffs among radiator size, weight, and launch requirements.

Companies including Elon Musk's SpaceX and startup Starcloud are exploring data centers in orbit as growing AI use drives demand for computing capacity and strains infrastructure supporting facilities on the ground. The planned mission advances efforts to move power-hungry AI computing beyond Earth, using sunlight in orbit to ease pressure on electricity grids, land and cooling systems. Thursday's agreement gives Blue Origin a major future mission for New Glenn as the company seeks to expand its launch business following delays and a launchpad explosion in May. Experts have also noted that high launch costs, engineering hurdles and limited satellite production can put data centers in orbit years away from commercial use. Because space has no atmosphere to carry heat away, operators must rely on radiators, which add weight and complexity and compete with processors and other components for launch capacity.

The long development timeline for space-based data centers leaves operators balancing potential energy advantages against launch, communications, and maintenance costs. Radiation damage and thermal wear could shorten satellite lifespan, increasing the frequency with which operators would need to launch replacement capacity. If more advanced AI workloads move into orbit, ground-to-space communications capacity will become even more important. Earth observation satellites can collect enormous amounts of imagery, and processing that information in orbit and sending down the answer rather than all of the raw data saves bandwidth and, in many cases, time. The articles leave open how much useful computing the satellites can sustain, how they recover from failures, and whether their operating lives can justify launch and replacement costs.

stories.Headline: Columnist John Casey suggests using AI chatbots as a social buffer at Thanksgiving
stories.Summary:
Mashable published a column on November 26, 2026, in which its writer, John Casey, described a liberal friend who was dreading Thanksgiving with family in Oklahoma. The friend said his uncle sits in a chair watching Fox News on his phone, and his great-aunt would try to tell him in many ways, without telling him, that he is going to hell for being gay. Casey wrote that every November people pretend turkey, stuffing and pumpkin pie are worth being trapped by three generations of relatives they barely know. He called himself the Grinch of Thanksgiving and said that for many people the holiday is as awkward as waving back at someone who was actually waving at the person behind you. Years ago, he wrote, a former partner's mother dropped her fork, pointed across the table at him and said in Spanish that she could not look at him.

Casey wrote that in the past, surviving Thanksgiving required biting your tongue, heavy drinking or staying away, and that your only defenses were hiding in the bathroom, taking a long nap or pretending to be a die-hard Detroit Lions fan, who traditionally play every Thanksgiving. He said that if you wanted to fact-check a wild political claim your uncle blurted out, you had to let him win because you could not pull the truth up on your phone. This year, he wrote, things look different, and one of artificial intelligence's most underrated perks is acting as a real-time social buffer. He tested this with Claude, feeding it a list of potential landmines and getting back sharp, diplomatic ways to deflect and make light of the moment, which he did not share. He suggested giving a chatbot the persona of a Fox News-addicted uncle on the drive over and doing a two-minute dry run before ringing the doorbell.

Casey wrote that if a real-time brouhaha erupts at the table, you can whip out a voice-mode AI assistant to act as a neutral referee and break the logjam. He said that if you are hosting, you can feed your guest list and everyone's friction points into an AI tool and ask it to build a seating chart that separates natural adversaries with at least two buffers, a centerpiece or a spot at the kids' table. He wrote that he was single for many years, so that is where he always ended up. He suggested having AI generate a custom trivia game to steer conversations away from danger zones like politics, Donald Trump, whether AI will kill us, or whether the new John Madden movie on Amazon is actually bad or just quirky. He also suggested pasting a tense family group chat into an AI assistant and asking it to translate your annoyance into something warm, firm and drama-free.

Casey wrote that AI cannot fix deep family dynamics and will not miraculously turn his friend's Oklahoma relatives into MS Now viewers. Still, he told his friend to load up his chatbot before his flight, and wrote that between the Fox News uncle and the judgmental great-aunt, a calm digital wingman in his pocket might be the closest thing he gets to a Thanksgiving miracle. The column states that it represents the opinions of its writer and identifies John Casey as a columnist at Raw Story, the Advocate, Daily Beast and Outsports and the author of Love: The Heroic Stories of Marriage Equality. NPR published a piece on November 25, 2026, heard on All Things Considered, by Kevin Roose and Casey Newton, titled How to talk AI around the Thanksgiving table. NPR's piece says you are gathered with family this Thanksgiving when the topic of AI comes up, and asks how you can have a productive, fact-based conversation.

NPR states that it does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews, and that anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR. The NPR page lists its sections, including News, Culture, Music and Podcasts & Shows, and its programs, including Morning Edition, Weekend Edition Saturday, Weekend Edition Sunday, All Things Considered, Up First, Here & Now, the NPR Politics Podcast, Wait Wait...Don't Tell Me!, Fresh Air, Wild Card with Rachel Martin, It's Been a Minute and Machine Gods. The page also lists links to Get NPR+, Search, Newsletters, NPR Shop, Tiny Desk, About NPR, Diversity, Support, Careers, Press and Ethics. NPR's piece carries a Facebook, Flipboard and Email sharing option and says audio will be available later today. The NPR piece gives no further details of the conversation it proposes.

Mashable's column says that lately people have spent plenty of time worrying about how artificial intelligence is taking over the internet and creeping into their daily routines, and that it is everywhere now. It says there is no arguing that fact with your uncle. It describes AI as an infinitely patient wingman sitting right in your pocket, ready to keep your holiday civil, lighthearted and blissfully brief on drama. It says that back in the day, before technology swallowed us whole and gave us hunched necks, surviving Thanksgiving required biting your tongue, heavy drinking, though that often fueled the fires of ferocity, or staying away. It says that just thinking about harrowing Thanksgivings past sends a chill down the writer's spine, and he wonders how different they might have been with a little help.

Mashable's column says the dread begins before you even walk through the front door, and that the stress of hosting starts even earlier. It says seating arrangements require more diplomacy than a UN General Assembly, and that pairing the wrong two cousins guarantees a tug-of-war over the mashed potatoes. It says tension often starts days earlier in the chaotic family group chat, sparked by passive-aggressive comments about who brings what. It advises against firing back a reply you will regret on Thursday. The column ends by saying that AI cannot fix deep family dynamics, and it leaves open whether the friend's Oklahoma Thanksgiving will go any better with a chatbot loaded before his flight.
