stories.Headline: INEC chairman Amupitan says the commission sets up an AI division to fight deepfakes before the 2027 elections
stories.Summary:
The Independent National Electoral Commission established an Artificial Intelligence division inside its Information and Communication Technology Department to tackle misinformation and digitally manipulated content before the 2027 general elections. Its chairman, Joash Ojo Amupitan, disclosed this on Wednesday at the Nigeria Election Risks and Readiness Summit 2026 in Abuja. The summit was organised by the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development. Amupitan was represented by his Chief Press Secretary, Adedayo Oketola. The commission said generative AI, synthetic voice cloning, deepfakes and coordinated online campaigns had made information management a critical part of election security.

Amupitan said INEC was strengthening capacity to detect deepfakes, synthetic voices and fabricated videos, and was collaborating with media organisations, fact-checkers and civil society groups. He said INEC would give verified journalists and fact-checkers timely access to official information, and called for institutionalised partnership with independent fact-checking organisations including Dubawa, media organisations, civil society groups and the National Orientation Agency. He cited an incident during the Federal Capital Territory election in which a viral video falsely claimed National Youth Service Corps members were being killed in parts of Abuja on election day, and said INEC worked with the NYSC to verify and debunk it. He said INEC had procured about 57,000 new Bimodal Voter Accreditation System devices, replaced batteries in serviceable units and set up climate-controlled storage facilities across states. He said the voter threshold per BVAS device was cut from 1,250 to 850, with more devices for larger polling units, to keep accreditation within an estimated one to two minutes.

Amupitan said the commission would recruit about 1.41 million ad hoc personnel, with approximately 700,000 for the presidential and National Assembly elections and another 700,000 for the governorship and State House of Assembly elections. He said the registration period for ad hoc staff was extended from two weeks to two and a half weeks, and urged journalists and stakeholders to complete accreditation within the stipulated period. He explained the deadlines were guided by the Electoral Act and could not be arbitrarily extended. He said INEC was working with security agencies and political parties to identify potential election flashpoints and improve security deployment, using its Election Risk Management tool to find areas vulnerable to violence and guide targeted deployments during the 2026 Osun governorship election. He condemned political violence and attacks on journalists, election officials and party supporters, warning such incidents could undermine democratic participation and the credibility of elections.

Amupitan said INEC was engaging the police, political parties and other security stakeholders through the Inter-Agency Consultative Committee on Election Security to address threats before, during and after the elections. The commission called for responsible political communication and urged parties and their supporters to avoid inflammatory statements and actions capable of escalating tensions. The summit featured a panel session titled “Preventing Electoral Violence and Strengthening Election Security Ahead of 2027”, with Gloria Korang, programme manager at the West Africa Network for Peacebuilding; Bukola Idowu, executive director of Kimpact Development Initiative; Raphael Mgbaegbu, head of social research at NOI Polls; and Safiya Bichi, senior manager at YIAGA Africa, moderated by Tolulope Adeleru-Balogun of News Central Television. European Union Ambassador to Nigeria and ECOWAS Gautier Mignot said credible elections required more than voting and the announcement of results, depending also on a fair pre-election environment, access to reliable information and transparent resolution of electoral disputes. Mignot said the credibility of Nigeria’s elections had implications for democratic stability across West Africa.

Norway’s Ambassador to Nigeria, Svein Baera, called for the protection of journalists, fact-checkers, editors, election officials and observers, saying those working to safeguard electoral integrity must perform their duties without intimidation, and commended CJID and its partners for supporting media development and efforts to strengthen accountability and democratic processes in Nigeria. The summit was convened by CJID as part of its 2026 Media and Development Conference, under the theme “Securing the Vote and Protecting the Frontliners.” Amupitan said elections could be influenced by false information even before voting commenced, and that fabricated audio recordings, doctored videos and false election results could trigger panic, discourage voter participation and spark communal violence. He said the commission was adopting a zero-tolerance approach to communication gaps but acknowledged that tackling false narratives in a highly connected society required collaboration. He warned that false content could undermine public confidence in the electoral process, discourage voter participation and trigger panic or communal violence, particularly when circulated through coordinated online campaigns.

The presidential and National Assembly elections are scheduled for 16 January 2027, while the governorship and State House of Assembly elections will hold on 6 February 2027. The articles leave open the AI division’s staffing, funding and launch date, and do not say which of the 57,000 BVAS devices are new purchases rather than replacements. They do not name the states receiving climate-controlled storage facilities or give the number of devices allocated to larger polling units. They do not specify how the 1.41 million ad hoc personnel will be distributed beyond the two roughly 700,000 groupings, or state the accreditation deadline date. They do not say when the Election Risk Management tool will be applied to the Osun election or what specific flashpoints have been identified.

stories.Headline: QAI orders a 54-qubit IQM Radiance quantum computer for its Seoul data center
stories.Summary:
IQM Quantum Computers Plc has received a new order from QAI Co., Ltd., a South Korean quantum-AI data center and cloud infrastructure company, for an IQM Radiance R3 54-qubit quantum computer. The order was announced on November 25, 2026, and covers a complete on-premises quantum computing solution for QAI's data center in Seoul. The total order value is between EUR 8 million and EUR 10 million, and it will be recognized as revenue in 2027. The IQM Radiance R3 system is expected to be delivered and installed on-premises at QAI's data center by the end of 2027.

The order includes the IQM Radiance R3 system itself along with associated services for the South Korean company's data center operations. IQM Quantum Computers describes itself as a global leader in superconducting quantum computers, delivering full-stack quantum systems and cloud platform access to enterprises, research institutions, universities, high-performance computing centers, and national laboratories worldwide. The company's on-premises deployment model gives customers direct ownership and control of their quantum infrastructure, which appears to be the arrangement QAI has chosen for its Seoul facility. IQM was founded in 2018 and is headquartered in Finland, with major operations in Munich, and it employs over 450 people across Europe, Asia, and North America.

The broader infrastructure investment landscape is expanding rapidly as artificial intelligence drives demand for data centers and related power systems. Preqin data shows infrastructure fundraising rebounded sharply in the third quarter of 2026, with $62 billion raised across 21 funds, bringing the year's total to $101 billion across 65 funds. Rene Lubianski, managing partner for infrastructure at Brookfield Asset Management, said infrastructure is a cornerstone of the private markets giant's business during the group's third-quarter earnings call on November 6. The firm has raised roughly $50 billion in capital commitments across its infrastructure strategies over the past year, and the latest vintage of its flagship infrastructure strategy had received $26 billion in commitments, with $13 billion coming after the end of the quarter.

Lubianski said the firm is well on track to exceed its $30 billion target in early 2027, and at that size the fund would surpass the $28 billion raised for its predecessor to become the largest closed-end infrastructure fund ever raised. He added that if current momentum continues, it could also become the largest closed-end private fund ever raised in any sector. Investor appetite is strengthening even as infrastructure owners hold assets longer, with portfolio companies owned by the 50 largest infrastructure general partners having an average holding period of 7.6 years in 2025, up from 6.1 years in 2021, according to Boston Consulting Group. A Goldman Sachs survey of some 225 institutional investors found that 43 percent of respondents have a more favorable outlook on infrastructure investment compared with a year ago, while 49 percent with a target allocation to infrastructure said they were under-allocated.

stories.Headline: UK cyber center reports rise in AI-driven attacks exploiting weak security foundations
stories.Summary:
The National Cybersecurity Center, which is the cybersecurity unit for the United Kingdom government, has observed a marked rise in cyberattacks driven by artificial intelligence. These incidents have occurred in recent months, with several specific cases involving autonomous hacking tools reported since September. Hackers are increasingly using these agentic tools to identify and exploit simple weaknesses to breach various networks and systems. These attacks have caused significant intrusions and resulted in operational downtime for the affected organizations.

The current threat landscape requires a renewed focus on basic cybersecurity defenses and the implementation of established best practices. These AI tools often target internet-facing systems to rapidly test easy-to-guess passwords or abuse API endpoints used by developers. The rise in these attacks coincides with the release of open-source autonomous penetration testing tools, specifically naming Artex and Cairn. These tools allow malicious actors to find vulnerabilities in minutes that may have gone unnoticed for years.

The National Cybersecurity Center stated in a blog post that the exploited issues are not novel memory corruption flaws or unpatched vulnerabilities. Instead, the unit explained that these are unmitigated weaknesses resulting from years of accumulated technical debt within organizations. The NCSC noted that while AI makes it easier to find and exploit flaws, it does not make established security controls obsolete. They emphasized that building strong foundational cybersecurity has never mattered more than it does now.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation has also issued a warning regarding the unprecedented speeds at which these AI-powered attacks are carried out. This suggests a broader trend where autonomous tools enable faster exploitation of known weaknesses across different regions. The UK government maintains that many of these intrusions are preventable if organizations address their underlying security foundations. No further future actions were specified beyond the urgent need for stronger foundational defenses.

stories.Headline: AmCham and Korea AI policy chief discuss US-Korea AI cooperation in Seoul
stories.Summary:
The American Chamber of Commerce in Korea held a roundtable meeting on Wednesday to discuss strengthening artificial intelligence cooperation between the United States and Korea. Ha Jung-woo, the vice chair of the Presidential Council on National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, met with the chamber and member companies in Seoul. The participants focused on ways to advance the ambition of Korea to become one of the world's top three AI powers. This closed-door event took place at the chamber's office located in Yeouido, which is in the western part of the city of Seoul. The meeting brought together government policymakers and executives from several global technology companies to share industry perspectives and discuss national AI strategy.

The discussions required expanding infrastructure like data centers and making advances in semiconductors, AI models, and software to strengthen the national AI ecosystem. Ha Jung-woo outlined three government megaprojects focusing on semiconductors, AI data centers, and physical AI to accelerate transformation across industries and public services. The meeting included representatives from Apple, Amazon Web Services, Corning, Palo Alto Networks, PTC, Qualcomm, and the safety testing provider UL Solutions. Participants explored how to leverage complementary strengths in digital infrastructure and advanced manufacturing while cooperating on cybersecurity, AI safety, and international standards. These efforts aim to foster a sustainable and inclusive global AI ecosystem through international cooperation in energy, infrastructure, and cybersecurity.

Ha Jung-woo stated that the three major megaprojects are central to efforts to accelerate AI transformation in everyday life and public services. He said that Korea would continue expanding international cooperation in energy and AI safety to help foster a sustainable global AI ecosystem. James Kim, the Chairman and CEO of AMCHAM, said that the chamber strongly supports the ambition of Korea to be a leader. Kim noted that the complementary strengths of both nations in semiconductors and AI technology present tremendous opportunities for bilateral cooperation and growth. He described artificial intelligence as one of the most promising areas for the next phase of the bilateral economic partnership between countries.

Representatives from global firms like Apple and Qualcomm discussed how US companies could help expand infrastructure and speed up AI adoption in manufacturing. The participants explored the role of public-private partnerships in enhancing the competitiveness of Korea and accelerating transformation across various key industrial sectors. The meeting affected executives from across the AI value chain who sought to share their business perspectives with the Korean government policymakers. These industry leaders discussed how government and industry could work together to expand computing infrastructure and advance the development of AI software. The discussions highlighted the importance of building a trusted AI ecosystem through the establishment of international standards and improved cybersecurity measures.

The AMCHAM AI Leadership Council was launched in July to bring together executives from across the AI value chain to share perspectives. This council serves as a bridge to promote closer public-private cooperation on policies related to artificial intelligence and overall industry innovation. The background of the meeting involves Korea's strategic push to integrate AI into manufacturing and other key industries to increase global competitiveness. The government's national AI strategy prioritizes the development of physical AI and the expansion of data centers to support its technological goals. These initiatives are part of a broader effort to ensure that AI transformation reaches public services and the daily lives of citizens.

The AMCHAM AI Leadership Council will continue working with the Korean government to promote a predictable and business-friendly policy environment for AI. James Kim pledged that the chamber would continue talks with the government to encourage further AI investment and innovation in Korea. The participants will look for ways to build on the complementary strengths of the United States and Korea in advanced manufacturing. The articles leave open the specific details of how the three megaprojects will be funded or the exact timeline for implementation. It remains unspecified how the mentioned global companies will specifically contribute to the expansion of the Korean AI infrastructure and manufacturing.

stories.Headline: Saudi Arabia directs every citizen and visitor to get an AI agent for public services
stories.Summary:
Saudi Arabia is preparing to move its digital government to an agentic model in which artificial intelligence agents deliver public services, Middle East Online reported on Wednesday 25 November 2026. Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman directed that every citizen, resident and visitor be given a smart agent to streamline access to public services. Minister of Communications and Information Technology Abdullah Alswaha revealed the directive on Wednesday. He spoke in a session titled Logistical and Technological Capabilities Connecting the World at the 2027 Budget Forum. The shift moves the Kingdom from a digital government to what the article calls an agentic government.

The Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority has launched the initial pilot phase of the smart assistant with 500 users ahead of a wider rollout. Alswaha said the Tawakkalna Shamel AI agent will officially launch in February 2027. The Kingdom aims to fully transition to using AI agents to serve citizens by 2028. The minister said government platforms have been consolidated from 800 down to 400, offering more than 1,800 services. A study published by the Digital Government Authority in January 2025, titled AI Agents and Large Action Models in Digital Government, explains that these systems combine language comprehension, planning, command execution and direct interaction with applications.

Alswaha said the agent is engineered to comprehend requests, identify the required service, interact with relevant government systems and follow through until the transaction is completed, within approved permissions and regulatory controls. He said the agent will coordinate steps on the user's behalf via an interactive interface powered by natural language and voice commands. He said the initiative aims to restructure government operations, boost institutional productivity, lower transaction costs and redirect human capital toward roles requiring judgement, expertise and high-level decision-making. He said decisions involving legal rights, financial obligations or administrative exceptions will remain subject to defined tiers of human approval and oversight. The article says the project's outcomes will hinge on public authorities building a reliable, transparent ecosystem that balances speed of execution with human oversight.

The article says the initiative opens doors for technology and AI firms to develop localised solutions while driving investment in cloud infrastructure, data management and cybersecurity. It says the shift broadens the beneficiary base to citizens, residents and visitors alike. It says the project raises questions over who bears responsibility when an agent makes a mistake, how a citizen can appeal a decision rendered by an automated system, and what safeguards guarantee personal data is never used beyond the purpose for which it was collected. It says the Digital Government Authority's own study warned of risks surrounding security, privacy and diminished transparency, calling for stronger encryption, rigorous access controls, continuous auditing and clear regulatory frameworks. It says the 2025, 2030 Digital Government Strategy projects that digital transformation initiatives will deliver a cumulative contribution of roughly 11.4 billion riyals to GDP and create more than 26,000 jobs by 2030, though these remain strategic targets and estimates rather than realised returns.

The article says the move builds upon a digital public infrastructure that has expanded significantly in recent years. It says the trajectory reflects an effort to move away from fragmented service channels toward a unified user experience that minimises the time and effort required to complete administrative procedures. It says that previously users had to identify the relevant authority, log into its specific platform, fill out forms and track their applications. It says a practical example is a citizen instructing their AI agent to renew a passport, with the agent verifying identity and permissions, retrieving data from government databases, checking eligibility criteria, fees and documentation, preparing the application, prompting for approval on steps requiring explicit consent, then submitting it, tracking progress and notifying the user of the outcome. It says executing this workflow requires integrating the agent with Application Programming Interfaces, government databases, digital identity verification systems and electronic payment gateways, all underpinned by a comprehensive audit trail for every transaction.

The article says the architecture could eventually evolve into a network of specialised agents, one for passport services, another for healthcare and a third for education, communicating with one another to complete cross-departmental procedures. It says the initiative places Saudi Arabia in the global race to pioneer smart government models, reinforcing its ambition to become a regional hub for AI research and application. It says the transformation's success will not be measured solely by how widely AI agents are adopted but also by the state's ability to establish robust frameworks for accountability, transparency and the protection of rights. It says the project's ultimate success will depend on the performance of the initial pilot and the Kingdom's capacity to scale it safely and efficiently. It says the initiative is an attempt to redesign how the state operates, turning AI into an executive intermediary between the individual and public institutions.

stories.Headline: Pinterest lets parents limit AI-generated content teens see
stories.Summary:
Pinterest announced that it is expanding its parental controls during the week of November 24, 2026, to help manage teen experiences. The company is adding new tools that allow parents to limit the amount of AI-generated content their children see on the app. These updates were reported by Jay Peters for The Verge and Sarah Perez for TechCrunch on November 24, 2026, in the United States. The platform is introducing these changes to give parents more direct control over the recommendations that appear in their teen's feeds. This move aims to let users dictate the type of experience they want to have while using the social media application.

The new system requires parents to use an updated Parental Controls page to adjust the amount of AI-generated content for teens. Parents can now tweak settings to decide if videos can autoplay and manage the volume of push, browser, in-app, and email notifications. The redesigned page also allows parents to configure settings related to personalized ads to better manage the overall user experience for children. These tools are part of a broader set of updates that include standard options for adjusting notifications and other general account settings. The company is implementing these specific controls to address how AI-generated content fills user feeds and recommendations on the platform.

Pinterest is responsible for these changes and claims that providing these tools is a good first step for the platform's users. The company has previously fought its own battle against AI content that appears in feeds even when certain restrictive settings are enabled. Pinterest introduced settings to restrict AI-modified content in 2025, but the company acknowledges that some of this material still appears. By putting these tools in the hands of parents, the company seeks to allow families to manage the exposure to AI. The platform is positioning itself as a leader in providing these specific parental controls for AI-generated content in user recommendations.

Some parents say that the prevalence of AI-generated content is harming the well-being of children in favor of corporate profits. The children's advocacy group Fairplay expressed similar concerns in a letter sent in April to Google CEO Sundar Pichai and YouTube. This letter was signed by over 200 experts and organizations calling for the removal of AI content from the YouTube Kids app. They also requested that AI-generated videos be barred from being recommended to any users who are under the age of 18. These groups believe that social media platforms must do more to protect minors from the influence of artificial intelligence content.

The articles state that Pinterest is one of the first major social platforms to allow parents to control AI-generated content recommendations. Other platforms have focused on limiting access to specific AI features, such as the AI chatbot provided by the company Snap. Meta announced a global pause on teens' access to AI characters after the company retooled the product based on parent feedback. WhatsApp currently allows parents to adjust how teens use Meta AI to create content or receive answers to their various questions. Most social media platforms generally provide very few controls for parents regarding AI-generated content that fills the feeds of their children.

The next step for the platform is to integrate these new parental controls into the redesigned Parental Controls page for all users. Parents will now be able to access the updated settings to limit AI content and manage video autoplay for their teens. The articles leave open whether these new tools will successfully stop AI-generated content from appearing in the recommendations for teens. It remains unclear if other major social media platforms will follow the example of Pinterest by adding similar AI-specific parental controls. The reports do not state if Pinterest plans to introduce further restrictions on AI-generated content beyond these new parental settings.

stories.Headline: Amazon and Meta negotiate restoring Meta's Muse AI agent to Amazon shopping
stories.Summary:
Amazon and Meta are negotiating to restore Meta's personal AI agent Muse to Amazon's e-commerce platform, Fortune reported on Wednesday, November 25, 2026. Amazon blocked Muse in September, a move that cut the agent off from Amazon's shopping site. Meta makes Muse, which the article describes as the most widely used personal AI agent. Amazon runs the e-commerce platform Muse was blocked from. The renewed talks between the two companies follow that September blockade.

Restoring access would let Muse work again on Amazon, whose advertising business is worth nearly $70 billion. Amazon blocked Muse to safeguard that advertising business, because AI agents could let shoppers bypass sponsored product listings. Muse already works with Amazon rivals Walmart and Best Buy. Walmart announced on Tuesday that its Black Friday deals can be shopped directly through Muse. Walmart says the agent can find items, build a basket and complete a purchase with a key search and price point in mind, such as a Black Friday TV deal under $500.

Amazon is responsible for the September block, and Meta is responsible for Muse. The articles do not give direct statements from either company about the talks. PwC's Ali Furman said AI is more like a knowledgeable friend at the mall who can give advice, not yet the checkout counter everyone anticipates. Furman said a majority of consumers use AI agents for advice to find gift ideas or compare prices, but not to make the purchase, going to a retailer's website instead.

A recent Salesforce survey of shoppers in the US, UK, Canada and Australia found that 31% have tried a personal AI agent. Only 19% of those users have used one at checkout, roughly 6% of those polled. Salesforce expects AI to influence more than one in five holiday orders, including by helping shoppers research and discover products. Shoppers are the people affected, along with Amazon, Meta, Walmart and Best Buy. This holiday shopping season will be a major testing ground for agentic commerce.

The articles say Amazon blocked Muse in September to safeguard its advertising business. They say AI agents could allow shoppers to bypass sponsored product listings. They report that Muse is already working with Walmart and Best Buy. They describe Muse as the most widely used personal AI agent. They say renewed discussions between Amazon and Meta come after Walmart's Tuesday announcement about Black Friday deals through Muse.

What happens next depends on whether Amazon and Meta reach an agreement to end the blockade. The articles leave open whether the talks will succeed and when Muse might return to Amazon. They leave open the terms Amazon might seek over ads and search, which Fortune called key issues. They leave open how many shoppers will trust AI to complete purchases on their behalf. They leave open how the holiday season will test agentic commerce.

stories.Headline: US researchers develop a language model that rewrites its own weights to boost accuracy
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and other US universities developed a language model that rewrote its own weights. This process allowed the model to improve its results without undergoing traditional training. The team reported these findings in a paper published around November 26, 2026. The model acted as both the editor and the subject during this self-rewriting process. It diagnosed its own failures and edited internal weights to boost its performance.

The work focused on Qwen3.5-27B, which is an open model with 27 billion parameters. The model was placed in a Python environment to inspect and alter its own weights. It reviewed graded answers to practice questions and compared its edited form with its unedited version. Accuracy on unseen maths problems rose from 57.2% to 63.8% on a set of 490 problems. This represents an improvement of 6.6 percentage points through the use of only forward passes.

Jiajun Fan, a PhD student and first author, said the model finds what is going wrong. He stated that the model rewrites responsible weights and keeps changes only if they hold up. Fan noted that because the gain is written into the weights, every answer costs the same. He claimed that there is no training pipeline to build and no cluster to rent. Fan argued that the wall between training and inference is a limit of tools, not intelligence.

The researchers found that the model reduced incomplete answers rather than correcting factual mistakes. In tests, the model often fell into repetitive loops until it hit its token limit. After edits, the share of answers cut off at the limit fell from 33.6% to 26.1%. Over eight sessions, the model submitted three edits and withdrew five to reach its final accuracy. The process used no teacher model, reward model, or second model to achieve these gains.

The team conducted a separate experiment where they damaged eight rows in one weight matrix with noise. The model examined 112 of its own matrices and identified the damaged one without original weights. This repair lifted performance on text maths problems from 0.0% to 33.0% for the model. On six unseen image benchmarks, performance rose from 7.3% to 70.2%, which was 83% of the undamaged level. This suggests that changes discovered in one setting may carry over to other tasks.

The researchers said this behavior appeared only at larger model sizes within the model family. A 2B model made no edit, while 4B and 9B versions damaged their own performance. Each session behind the largest gains took a few hours on one GPU. The team argued this approach could reduce the infrastructure needed to modify a model. The articles leave open how this method might scale to even larger models or different architectures.

stories.Headline: Insight UK adviser Rob O'Connor says AI lets attackers exploit retail flaws before Black Friday defenders can patch them
stories.Summary:
Insight UK warned on 25 November 2026 that retailers face faster cyberattacks during the Black Friday shopping period, with artificial intelligence shrinking the time available to fix vulnerabilities. Rob O'Connor, Senior Cybersecurity Advisor in the Office of the CISO at Insight UK, said attackers are not relying on entirely new methods but are using AI to move more quickly from discovery to exploitation. He said organisations had an average of 21.5 days in 2025 to address a vulnerability before it was exploited, while in 2026 that window has reportedly fallen to minus 23 hours, meaning attackers exploit flaws almost a day before defenders know of them. He said defenders have not seen the same gains in speed, because security teams still need to assess vulnerabilities, prioritise the most serious risks and deploy fixes without disrupting critical systems.

O'Connor said many businesses limit software updates and infrastructure changes before major sales events to avoid outages or disruption to checkout systems, websites and fulfilment operations, and that this can create another weakness if a serious flaw emerges during a freeze. He said the risk is no longer confined to a retailer's own systems, because many businesses depend on the same payment providers, cloud infrastructure, eCommerce software and logistics networks, so a breach at one external provider could hit several retailers at once. He said a single attack on a major technology provider could bring multiple retailers to a standstill, disrupting online orders, payments and deliveries at the busiest time of year. He said cybercriminals see retailers and their suppliers as one interconnected network of potential targets and will exploit whichever weakness gives them the greatest impact.

O'Connor said temporary change freezes, while common in retail, may now need to be handled differently, because the balance of risk has shifted as attackers move faster. He said the priority should not simply be identifying what needs patching but understanding which vulnerabilities are exposed, actively exploitable and capable of affecting the business, and that for the most critical vulnerabilities resolution needs to happen in hours rather than weeks. He said retailers also need to ensure their emergency patching processes work during peak trading rather than relying on normal change windows. He said the short-term risk of a patch causing disruption needs to be weighed against the potentially much greater cost of an attacker exploiting an unpatched vulnerability.

The breakdown came as Microsoft Corp reassessed some neocloud projects and Meta Platforms, Inc. explored ways to sell excess AI computing capacity. Nebius stock suffered a sharp technical breakdown, raising questions about whether enthusiasm for the AI cloud boom is beginning to fade. The articles were published on November 25, 2026, by Benzinga staff writer Surbhi Jain and by TradingView. NBIS traded well below its 50-day average of $174.05 and its 200-day average of $179.72.

The stock also slipped below its eight-day and 20-day averages of $95.57 and $122.49, respectively. The relative strength index stood at 32.21, approaching the conventional oversold threshold of 30. The moving average convergence divergence remained negative, with its MACD line at a negative 24.60 below the signal line at a negative 22.59. A Nov. 5 report said Microsoft had tightened oversight of some data-center projects involving neocloud providers, including Nebius, amid concerns about project risks and a focus on expanding its own infrastructure. In July, Meta was reportedly developing a cloud business to sell excess AI computing capacity, potentially putting the social media giant in competition with specialist AI infrastructure providers. Meta remains a major Nebius customer, and the plans were still in development and could change. The articles say these developments add to investor questions about the economics of the AI infrastructure boom. The articles attribute the death cross and the figures to Nebius and to Benzinga Pro data.

The articles state that the death cross does not guarantee further losses. They say that with shares trading far below both major moving averages, a sustained recovery will likely require more than another big AI contract. The articles describe Nebius's AI infrastructure ambitions as getting bigger while investors become less forgiving about the time and money needed to deliver them.

stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics announced its regular executive promotions for 2027 on November 24. The company reduced the total number of promotions to 131 from 161 a year earlier. This change represents a reduction of 30 people or nearly 20 percent. The reshuffle focused on rewarding talent in strategic growth areas like semiconductors and robotics. The DX division saw promotions fall sharply from 92 to 61. The DS division promoted 70 people, increasing its share of total promotions to 53.4 percent. The 131 promoted individuals include 39 executive vice presidents, 78 vice presidents, two fellows, and 12 masters. Executive vice president promotions fell from 51 to 39, and vice president promotions declined from 93 to 78. These changes occurred within the company's semiconductor and finished product divisions.

Samsung made its performance-focused approach clear through these specific personnel changes. The company promoted key talent who contributed to HBM4 development and foundry orders. It also rewarded those who worked on the commercialization of physical AI, including humanoids. The company aimed to elevate technical talent driving the AI semiconductor business. This merit-based strategy was intended to lift both organizational tension and execution.

Engineers specializing in humanoid design, walking, and control technology were tapped as vice presidents. A record 11 women were elevated during this specific reshuffle process. Samsung Electro-Mechanics also carried out its largest executive reshuffle in five years by promoting 15 people.

The company promoted Ha Kyung-soo and Park Tae-hoon to executive vice president for their HBM4 work. Kim Myeong-o and Park Jin-pyo were also promoted to executive vice president for DRAM development. Jang Se-jeong was promoted for overseeing AI server solid-state drives and on-device AI storage. stories.Headline: India calls for inclusive AI governance and warns against using tech for strategic one-upmanship
stories.Summary:
India warned against using technology for strategic one-upmanship during a United Nations Security Council high-level open debate on November 24, 2026. Ambassador Harish Parvathaneni, the Permanent Representative of India, delivered the statement during this specific event convened by the nation of Latvia. The debate focused on the theme of conflict resolution in an era of rapid technological change and international security. India called for inclusive governance of artificial intelligence to ensure that technological transformation does not deepen existing global inequalities. The Indian envoy asserted that responsibility for using lethal autonomous weapons systems must always rest with human beings.

The proposal requires that technology remains human-centric and serves as an instrument of peace while respecting sovereignty and international law. India specifically called out the use of licensing regimes and export control to instrumentalise technology for the purpose of strategic one-upmanship. The envoy stated that countries of the Global South should not be treated as mere consumers without agency in AI development. He highlighted that AI systems can inadvertently perpetuate biases related to socio-economic background, language, and gender during their deployment. India supports inclusive international cooperation on technology governance through the United Nations, with regard to national priorities and developmental needs.

Ambassador Harish Parvathaneni said that technology may inform human judgement but it cannot and should not ever replace that human judgement. He stated that the risks associated with AI are real and the international community must address them without any hesitation. The envoy claimed that the potential misuse of emerging technologies by non-State actors and terrorists is a matter of grave concern. He noted that deliberately manipulated, inaccurate, or incomplete data through AI can undermine the process of critical decision-making. Parvathaneni emphasised that technology should strengthen international cooperation, serve all of humanity, and advance the cause of lasting peace.

Secretary General Antonio Guterres voiced concern that today's wars have become proving grounds for targeting enabled by artificial intelligence. He asserted that killer robots must have no place in the future and called for negotiations for a legally binding instrument. Guterres stated that algorithms are increasingly shaping life-and-death decisions, from target selection to the gathering of military intelligence. He warned that integrating AI with nuclear command, control, and communication systems is a recipe for a global catastrophe. The UN chief said that technology companies must reckon with legal risks if their services contribute to violations of international law.

The articles state that rapid technological advances are fundamentally transforming the international security landscape and the nature of modern conflict. Artificial intelligence and autonomous systems present unprecedented opportunities but also introduce new risks across the entire cycle of a conflict. India has made robust advancements in emerging technologies, cybersecurity, and digital infrastructure to protect critical information infrastructure and civilian services. India is committed to addressing lethal autonomous weapons within the framework of the Convention on Prohibitions or Restrictions of Certain Conventional Weapons. This specific framework seeks to balance humanitarian considerations with military necessity regarding the use of these advanced weapons systems.

India called on the international community to address threats posed by the misuse of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence. The envoy stated that technology should be leveraged for the protection of peacekeepers, humanitarian personnel, and all innocent civilians. The articles leave open how the international community will specifically regulate the development and deployment of these emerging AI technologies. It remains unclear how the proposed legally binding instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems will be negotiated among different nations. The text does not specify the exact timeline for implementing the inclusive international cooperation on technology governance through the UN.

stories.Headline: Apple adds Mac controls in macOS 27.3 beta 2 to limit AI agent file access
stories.Summary:
Apple introduced new Mac security controls in macOS 27.3 beta 2 on Nov. 16, 2026, according to Fox Wilmington and Fox News reports dated November 24, 2026. The changes give Mac owners greater control over what apps, including AI agents, can access on their computers. Apple separated its existing Device Control and Data Access permission system into two settings, System & App Protection Override and Accessibility. The update adds clearer warnings when apps request powerful permissions and more detailed information about what an app could access. Apple says permissions already granted will remain in effect after the update, and the new approval experience mainly applies when apps request permissions going forward.

Starting with macOS 27.3, some apps requesting Full Disk Access will let users choose specific protected folders instead of granting access to everything. Other apps may continue using the existing approval process depending on their purpose, and Apple is introducing a more consistent process for granting permissions. Users will select the requesting app from a list rather than navigating different approval methods. When configuring System & App Protection Override, users can choose which apps an AI tool may control and select Ask First or At Any Time for each approved app. Apple is adding a transparency indicator that appears when an app controls another app through this permission system.

Apple warns that an app with Full Disk Access can read or modify sensitive files and may delete or export information without asking again. The company says the System & App Protection Override permission can allow an app to control a Mac and monitor activity, including keystrokes, when unrestricted access is granted. Apple says the changes focus on making permissions more visible and giving people greater control over what they approve. Apple says the changes will not prevent users from installing AI agents or using apps that genuinely need broader permissions. Apple is also allowing developers of certain backup and accessibility applications to request special permissions that preserve their existing functionality.

In September, a journalist claimed that Meta's Muse AI app had read his private messages without his permission, and Meta disputed that account, saying the Messages integration requires explicit permission. A security vulnerability in OpenAI's ChatGPT Mac app could have allowed attackers to access sensitive information, and OpenAI patched the flaw before it was publicly reported. The articles say these incidents highlight security concerns surrounding increasingly capable AI software and that even legitimate applications can create privacy risks with broad access. Mac owners are affected, along with developers of backup and accessibility applications, and users can review permissions in System Settings under Privacy & Security. The articles list Full Disk Access, Files & Folders, Accessibility and Automation as sections to check, and say users can revoke access or remove an app and add it again to choose specific folders.

The articles say AI assistants have become increasingly useful and that an AI agent can go further by interacting with apps and taking actions on a user's behalf. Examples given include asking an AI agent to organize a Downloads folder or find a receipt buried in email, tasks that may require permission to access information stored on the Mac. The articles say some legitimate applications, including backup software and security tools, require extensive access to function properly, and removing their permissions could prevent certain features from working. The articles leave open the date of the broader software release and do not say how many apps or users the changes affect.

stories.Headline: InfoQ authors propose evals, grounding and release gates for AI-drafted suspicious activity reports
stories.Summary:
On 24 November 2026 InfoQ published an article on engineering around non-determinism with evals, grounding and release gates for AI-drafted suspicious reports. The article was written by participants of the online InfoQ Certified Architect Program, and it represents the capstone of their work. It reflects the cohort's collective learnings on the intersection of AI and modern software architecture. The article explains how non-deterministic AI components can be incorporated into a dependable agentic system that reduces the cost of doing business. That system also increases drafting and review speed and maintains the quality of the final report.

A Suspicious Activity Report is a formal document submitted by regulated entities and financial institutions to law enforcement or financial intelligence units such as the UK's National Crime Agency. It flags known or suspected instances of money laundering, fraud or terrorist financing. The Inverted Pyramid Plot Model for SAR narratives opens with the lead, a short summary of the most noteworthy details and the main story event. It answers the five W questions of who, what, when, where and why, then gives a body of crucial details supported by evidence, facts and patterns. The narrative closes with a tail of concluding remarks, and the article gives an example of 10% of active customers detected, investigated and reported at $50 in human labour cost per case.

The article says a drafting agent should refuse to draft when the evidence is missing, and stopping with an explicit "insufficient context" signal is safer than a fluent narrative built around gaps. It says an LLM judge is itself non-deterministic, so its version should be frozen and paired with a deterministic fact-checker for names, dates and amounts. It says building agentic systems on probabilistic LLMs requires engineering around them with evals, context engineering, observability, regression runs and human-in-the-loop controls that contain the effects of randomness rather than removing it. It says grounding the system in authoritative case evidence and a knowledge-augmented graph data system helps ensure every material claim is supported by traceable data. It says versioned models, prompts, policies, retrieval configurations and reviewer actions make the system observable, reversible and suitable for regulated production environments.

The article says regulators penalize institutions for systematic data deficiencies, missing narratives or failing to report suspicious transactions adequately, and public enforcement actions can undermine the confidence of investors, business partners and customers. It says such cases are typically investigated and reported by in-house employees in a very secure environment, and that if suspicious activity volumes increase the cost of investigation and reporting increases as well. It says the quality of reports is directly proportional to the quality of investigation and editorial style of the human workforce, and that there is a lack of consistency. It says the manual system cannot keep pace with an increase in demand, and that there is a cost to the business and the customer for every investigation and reporting. The article says the proposed solution is a multi-agent system with access to selected LLMs via a gateway, supported by a tailored knowledge graph built from operational data.

The article describes a Data Query Planner Agent that fetches the quality data required and stops the agentic automation with feedback to the user if the data is not present. It describes a Data Reranker Agent that re-ranks the returned data for relevance to the context, and a Drafter Agent that produces a narrative from factual data against a defined SAR schema and cites supporting source identifiers. It describes a Judge Agent that runs deterministic checks and an independent judge to assess factuality, completeness, consistency and style, and a Coordinator Agent that publishes the report for human review once quality is of decent standard. The article says the investigation of the network is already done, so there is no need for community detection and the GraphRAG approach is not considered, and that data is carefully labelled and collected for security and privacy.

The article says the architectures described are representative examples used to compare traditional and AI-based designs, and that they do not describe real systems currently in use and have no correlation with any particular financial institution. It says the traditional system has a human agent view investigation notes prepared by another human agent and then draft the report, which another peer reviews before submission to a financial intelligence unit. It says detection happens through manual oversight or machine learning models, investigation goes for thorough investigation and peer review, and reporting must reach the national financial intelligence unit within a tight deadline. It says the design was changed to support background automation, with the case sent to a queue for processing by the Agentic System as soon as the investigation is complete. It says the AI Agent has drafted the first version before the human agent picks the case, and that low-quality drafts create repeated draft-and-review cycles and additional human editing that increase the cost per report.

TechGig published its own report on the same day, 24 November 2026 at 06:55 PM IST, saying LLM deployment in regulated systems requires engineering non-determinism with evals and grounding. It says evals are crucial for continuously testing model output quality, assessing instruction following, generation capability and narrative-specific correctness, and that they check factual accuracy, completeness and adherence to narrative structures like the Inverted Pyramid Plot. It says regression evals with a golden data set are essential for testing the system before any model upgrade or prompt or configuration change. It says observability monitors the decision-making trajectory from initial intent to final outcome, checking LLM model reasoning, RAG performance and system failures, and that human-in-the-loop control remains vital for accountability through risk-tiered routing and evaluation of human edits. The articles leave open what happens next beyond the proposed design and the stated need for evals, regression runs and human review.

stories.Headline: Korean ETF managers add Anthropic cautiously after SpaceX losses
stories.Summary:
Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in its Nasdaq debut on Nov. 19, 2026, and its shares fell from a first-day close of $97.17 to as low as $83.05 the next day. Korean ETF managers are taking a more cautious approach to Anthropic after its shares swung during their first days of trading. The move follows steep losses in funds that held SpaceX after its volatile Nasdaq debut. The AI company behind the Claude chatbot set a record for the largest IPO in history, surpassing SpaceX, according to the article. Its shares closed at $97.17 on the first day, 17.1 percent above the $83 offering price, before closing at $88.91 the following day.

Hana Asset Management plans to spread purchases for its new AI-focused fund over three days, beginning on the second trading day after Anthropic’s listing. Samsung Asset Management’s actively managed AI Agent fund held Anthropic at a 4.29 percent weighting on its first trading day. Mirae Asset Global Investments plans to include Anthropic in a new global LLM ETF scheduled to list on Nov. 24, the third day after Anthropic began trading. Nineteen South Korean ETFs had added Anthropic shares by the second trading day after its Nasdaq debut, with combined holdings valued at 88 billion won, or $65.5 million. The Kodex US AI Agent Active ETF, managed by Samsung Asset Management, had the largest exposure at 19.4 percent, and all other funds had allocations below 5 percent.

Samsung Asset Management gave SpaceX a weighting of around 25 percent in its passive KODEX ETF, buying shares on the day of the IPO. Mirae Asset Global Investments’ TIGER U.S. space tech ETF added SpaceX based on the stock’s closing price on the second trading day after its listing. Hana Asset Management previously added SpaceX to its passive aerospace-themed ETF as part of a scheduled index rebalancing. An official at a local asset manager said strong demand for AI- and space-related investments at the time made planned allocations an effective marketing tool when SpaceX went public. The same official said investor sentiment has shifted since then, particularly toward AI-related investments, making Anthropic a harder sell to investors.

Five major space-themed ETFs holding SpaceX fell by double digits, and Samsung Asset Management’s KODEX, Mirae Asset Global Investments’ TIGER and Shinhan Asset Management’s SOL each lost more than half their value. The value of SpaceX shares held by 15 domestic ETFs stood at 597 billion won, nearly seven times that of Anthropic, on the second trading day after its June listing. The Time US Nasdaq 100 Active ETF, the largest fund among the 19 run by Timefolio Asset Management, has allocated just 0.6 percent to Anthropic, making it the fund’s 44th-largest holding out of 45 stocks. Financial regulators cautioned against the promotion of Anthropic-related investments over concerns about potentially misleading or exaggerated marketing claims. Some firms faced questions during the rocket maker’s listing over whether they had overstated their exposure to the stock in their ETFs.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell more than 5 percent Friday, entering correction territory. The sell-off spilled over into Korea, with the Kospi falling below 4,600 intraday Monday, more than 50 percent below its June 19 intraday record high of 9,385.59. Markets recently rebounded after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. The lukewarm response contrasts with SpaceX’s listing, when Korean asset managers rushed to add the company to their ETFs despite concerns over high valuations. The subsequent sharp correction in SpaceX shares following their inclusion in ETFs has also contributed to the subdued appetite for Anthropic, with related ETF products yet to recover their previous highs.

More asset managers are expected to add Anthropic to their ETF portfolios in the coming days as market conditions stabilize and the stock’s initial volatility subsides. Mirae Asset Global Investment has listed Tiger Global LLM Active ETF on the Korea Exchange on Tuesday, announcing a target allocation of 25 percent to Anthropic. Passive ETFs, which can include newly listed stocks only after they have traded for at least two sessions, are also expected to begin adding Anthropic shares. The articles do not state when the remaining managers will complete their purchases. The articles do not state whether the regulators’ caution will extend to the new funds.

stories.Headline: IrisKey.ai introduces a 26-gate governance architecture for autonomous AI
stories.Summary:
IrisKey.ai introduced a 26-gate governance architecture for autonomous AI systems, the Coventry-based company said on 25 November 2026. The company said the design is intended to enforce authority before AI agents carry out consequential actions. The proposed system is patent-pending, according to IrisKey.ai. The company said the architecture is designed to separate what an AI system can do from what it is allowed to do. IrisKey.ai said the framework would verify authority, control delegated permissions and support the withdrawal of access when authorisation changes.

The 26-gate concept is intended to create a structured series of checks before execution, IrisKey.ai said. The company said these are designed to address whether authority can be verified before an action takes place, whether delegated permissions remain within defined limits, and whether revoked access can be prevented from being used. IrisKey.ai said the architecture is intended to work across different AI models, software environments and operational settings. The company has not disclosed the detailed design because the work sits within its intellectual property programme. IrisKey.ai said the architecture is not meant to replace cybersecurity systems or regulatory governance, but to sit between AI decision-making and execution.

Adam McCrum, Founder at IrisKey.ai, said the rise of more autonomous systems had exposed a gap between policy and technical control. McCrum said artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly capable, but that capability and authority are two very different things. He said the company is building systems that can reason, make decisions, communicate with other agents and execute actions across digital environments. He said a fundamental question remains about what technically prevents an AI system from performing an action it was never authorised to carry out. McCrum said a governance policy cannot physically stop an unauthorised API call, and a compliance dashboard cannot guarantee that a revoked permission has stopped being used.

McCrum said the issue becomes more acute when AI agents interact with other systems or receive delegated permissions across multiple operational environments. He said the question in those cases is not only what the system has the technical means to do, but whether the action remains valid under the authority originally granted. He said technical enforcement is needed as AI moves into real-world operations, designed into the architecture itself. IrisKey.ai pointed to financial services, healthcare, industrial systems, transport, defence and public-sector operations as areas where enforcement of AI permissions could be significant. The company said automated systems in such sectors may handle transactions, sensitive records, operational workflows or interactions with physical infrastructure.

IrisKey.ai said capability alone is not enough when actions carry financial, safety or security consequences. The company said the central issue is how to ensure autonomous systems act only within explicitly authorised limits. IrisKey.ai said it is pursuing a commercial model centred on intellectual property licensing and independent technical evaluation, rather than building its own foundation model. The company said it is seeking discussions with organisations that want to test whether the proposed framework could be applied to existing AI agent platforms, cybersecurity tools, enterprise automation systems and financial technology. IrisKey.ai said any external assessment would need to examine implementation feasibility, integration requirements, enforcement behaviour and underlying security assumptions.

IrisKey.ai said it has not announced independent validation of the full 26-gate architecture. The company said performance and security outcomes would require testing. McCrum said the wider AI market should give as much weight to control mechanisms as it does to advances in reasoning and automation. He said the principle behind the company's work is that authority must come before autonomy, and that permissions must remain verifiable, constrained and enforceable as systems become more capable. McCrum said the future of AI will depend not solely on how intelligent systems become, but also on whether meaningful technical boundaries can be established around their actions.

stories.Headline: Taiwan passes bill to give all citizens cash payments from AI industry tax revenues
stories.Summary:
The Taiwanese government decided to provide cash payments to share economic achievements from the artificial intelligence industry boom with its citizens. Taiwan's Legislative Yuan passed a bill on November 20 to grant these payments to all citizens regardless of age or income. The main opposition Kuomintang led the effort to pass this legislation despite formal opposition from the ruling Democratic Progressive Party. This bold decision aims to return tax revenues generated by the AI industry boom back to the general public. The Legislative Yuan passed the measure with 50 votes in favor and 46 votes against the proposed cash distribution.

The Special Act for Sharing Economic Fruits with the Entire Nation and Stabilizing Livelihoods requires payments of 20,000 New Taiwan Dollars. This amount is equivalent to about 810,000 won and will be distributed to every resident without any income based exclusion criteria. The received money will be exempt from income tax and excluded from seizure, collateral, and any form of compulsory enforcement. The Executive Yuan must submit a special budget bill to the Legislative Yuan within one month of the special act taking effect. Payments must then be completed within three months after the special budget takes effect to fulfill the requirements of the bill.

The main opposition Kuomintang led the bill and claimed that local election results will determine whether the bonus is paid. The ruling Democratic Progressive Party maintains that further increases are difficult without considering fiscal conditions for the country's general budget. This ruling party stated that its proposed 2027 budget already includes a payment of 10,000 New Taiwan Dollars per person. The Executive Yuan raised concerns over the fiscal burden and stated the plan could be unconstitutional due to the cost. They claimed that distributing 20,000 New Taiwan Dollars to all citizens would require about 471.4 billion New Taiwan Dollars in resources.

Online opinion appears to favor the cash payments according to a poll conducted by the China Times News Network. In that poll, 92 percent of more than 8,000 participants responded that they strongly support the proposed AI bonus payments. The ruling and opposition parties have clashed ahead of local elections over how much excess tax revenue should be refunded. Citizens of all ages and income levels are affected by this decision as the bill targets every resident of Taiwan. The clash between the two parties centers on the amount of money that should be returned to the public.

Taiwan houses major companies across global AI supply chains, including TSMC, which is claimed to be the world's largest foundry company. The AI semiconductor industry boom has driven up economic growth rates and increased tax revenue, leading to calls for sharing achievements. Taiwan has previously distributed consumer vouchers and cash several times to stimulate the economy and boost overall national consumption. These past payments include 3,600 New Taiwan Dollars in the late 2000s and 3,000 and 5,000 New Taiwan Dollars during the pandemic. In 2023, the government paid 6,000 New Taiwan Dollars per person, and last year it distributed 10,000 New Taiwan Dollars per person.

The government must now determine if the Executive Yuan will submit the required special budget bill to the Legislative Yuan. It remains uncertain whether and when the cash will actually be distributed to the citizens of Taiwan despite the bill. The two political parties continue to disagree, so it is expected to take time to finalize the payment details. The articles leave open whether the ruling party will accept the fiscal burden of 471.4 billion New Taiwan Dollars. Final decisions on the exact amount and the timing of the distribution are not yet confirmed by the government.

stories.Headline: Onclusive finds AI citations vary by category as Webflow reports median brands appear in 16% of AI answers
stories.Summary:
On November 25, 2026, The Drum published a member article by Aya Elbaoudi of Onclusive, a field marketing assistant, arguing that brands’ AI visibility problems are local, sectoral and specific. Onclusive analyzed 1,972 unique earned-source domains cited by five AI systems, ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity and Grok. The analysis covered 12 industries, 24 categories and six countries: France, Italy, Mexico, Spain, the UK and the US. On November 24, 2026, IT Brief Australia published a report by news editor Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin on Webflow research finding most companies have limited visibility in AI answer engines. Webflow’s study found the median company appeared in 16% of responses across a sample of 2,000 websites.

Onclusive said the closer you get to the question your audience actually asks, the less the global list matters. Its analysis split the 12 industries into 24 product and service categories, and it said sources AI systems cite can change from one category to the next within the same industry. It said the top of its Industry Citation Guide is led by Il Sole 24 Ore, El Economista (Mexico) and Les Echos, ahead of Forbes and CNBC. It said Reddit appears in retail’s top sources nearly three times as often as in automotive’s, with about 29 mentions against 11. It said Toyota holds a 24.7% share of voice in hybrid SUVs and appears in 92.5% of AI answers there, while in electric cars its visibility drops to 1% and Tesla is chosen in 95% of answers.

Onclusive said B2B sectors such as banking, enterprise software, insurance and pharma lean on journalism, institutional sources and regulators. It said B2C sectors such as consumer tech, retail, fashion and travel draw more on reviews, creators and community discussion. It said regulated industries such as healthcare and telecoms are shaped heavily by government and policy sources. It said a source that dominates in the US might barely register in France, Italy or Spain. It said the same source can be essential context in one category and background noise in another.

Webflow said the median company was cited with a link only 6% of the time, and appeared 15% of the time whenever any company was mentioned. It said the systems got facts wrong roughly one-third of the time when a company was mentioned, producing an accuracy score of 63 out of 100, with message pull-through at 24 out of 100 and median sentiment at 57 out of 100. It said B2B SaaS and software companies were mentioned 20% of the time against 14% for B2B industrial and manufacturing groups, with citation rates of 13% and 6% respectively. It said companies in the Forbes AI 50 were mentioned 31% of the time against 16% across all 2,000 websites, and cited 8% of the time against 6%. It said Progressive had the strongest visibility in the Ad Age Top 50 US Ad Spenders group, with a mention rate of 44%.

Onclusive said its analysis identified 70 media sources linked to 220 articles where Toyota is either absent or described negatively, including Edmunds, KBB and Auto Express. It said its AI Visibility Playbook sets out six steps, from mapping cited sources to measuring change in AI answers over time, and includes a 90-day plan for PR, comms, content and digital teams. Webflow said its assessment covered 2,000 websites and used 123 scoring gates, drawing on roughly 325,000 lines of code, more than 29,000 automated tests, more than 5,200 lines of prompts and 100 source modules across more than 500 large language model sessions. Webflow said it queried four answer engines with buyer-style questions and scored responses against a common rubric, measuring quality metrics across the 1,579 domains mentioned at least once. Webflow said Forbes AI 50 companies’ content had been updated within the previous six months at three times the rate seen across the wider sample, and those businesses were recognised as thought leaders 60% more often.

Webflow ranked Krea.ai highest overall among the Forbes AI 50, followed by Abridge, BaseTen and Cohere, and ranked AllState highest in the Ad Age group, followed by Capital One, Pfizer and Progressive. It said none of the Cannes Grand Prix winners reviewed reached the top tier of its scoring, with Columbia, Heineken, Suncorp Insurance and Adidas ranking highest in that group. It said Google, represented by deepmind.google, ranked as the most mature in the MANGOS group of Meta, Anthropic, Nvidia, Google, OpenAI and SpaceX, with Nvidia following on a mention rate of 86%. Onclusive said the next phase of generative engine optimization is about finding the handful of sources that repeatedly shape the answers you want to influence in your industry, market and category. Webflow said that for many brands the issue is not only whether they appear in an answer, but whether the answer links back to them and describes them accurately.

Sen. Marsha Blackburn has only a few weeks left to get her signature kids’ online safety bill across the finish line before she trades her seat on Capitol Hill for the Tennessee governor’s mansion. She said she would be honored to lead that charge. OpenAI has named Gary Bornstein, a top partner and co-head of the litigation department at Cravath, Swaine & Moore, as its lead defense lawyer for a Texas trial in a lawsuit brought by Elon Musk's X Corp and SpaceX Super Intelligence. OpenAI said Bornstein will serve as lead trial counsel in federal court in Fort Worth, where the case is set to be heard by a jury in March. The lawsuit by Musk's companies was filed last year and alleged that Apple conspired with OpenAI to monopolize the market for generative AI chatbots. Apple settled with Musk's companies in September, and neither company has disclosed the terms. Musk's companies have designated John Hughes of Bartlit Beck as their lead trial attorney.

The trial before US District Judge Mark Pittman would mark the second trial between Musk and OpenAI in less than a year. In May, a jury in federal court in Oakland, California, ruled against the billionaire tech entrepreneur in his separate lawsuit accusing OpenAI of straying from its original mission to benefit humanity. OpenAI was founded by Sam Altman, Musk and several others in 2015, Musk left its board in 2018, and OpenAI set up a for-profit business the next year. In the Texas case, Musk's companies are represented by lawyers from Axinn Veltrop and Stone Hilton, in addition to Bartlit Beck. Hughes, a partner at Bartlit Beck, in 2018 was lead trial counsel to a group that sued Harvard University over its admissions practices, a case that led to a US Supreme Court ruling ending race-conscious college admissions practices.

Bornstein and another lawyer for OpenAI, Cravath's Lauren Moskowitz, are separately representing Fortnite maker Epic Games in a court fight against Apple over its app store business practices, and Bornstein served as lead counsel to Epic. In addition to Cravath, OpenAI is represented by Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, whose team includes Stephen DiPrima and Kevin Schwartz. X and SpaceX Super Intelligence did not immediately respond to requests for comment, and OpenAI and Bornstein also did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The case is X Corp and SpaceXAI v OpenAI in the US District Court for the Northern District of Texas, No. 4:25-cv-00914-P.

stories.Headline: Princeton public affairs school adds seven undergraduate courses on AI risk and other policy topics
stories.Summary:
The Princeton School of Public and International Affairs is offering seven new undergraduate courses for the spring semester, as registration opens next week, according to the school. The offerings reflect the school's stated effort to adapt to evolving trends in public policy, from the state level to the international stage. The courses cover topics including artificial intelligence risk, the effectiveness of youth programs, state constitutions, emerging policy problems, African societies, religion and politics, and Iran's role in the Middle East. Two further new courses led by other departments are cross-listed with the school, one on war and climate change and one on families in algorithmic and authoritarian times.

One course will examine artificial intelligence as a technology and industry, weighing existential and loss-of-control scenarios alongside risks such as cyberattacks, bioterrorism, bias, labor disruptions and concentrations of power. Students will study competing frameworks including effective altruism, cybersecurity and perspectives focused on socioeconomic harms. Another course, on youth programs for people ages 0 to 30, will teach students to judge the credibility of evidence and to avoid being fooled by data. A seminar will explore the revolutionary origins and impact of America's state constitutions, noting that in 1776 no nation was governed by a written constitution. The Problems of Tomorrow, taught by Eduardo Bhatia, asks students to identify emerging challenges likely to grow in importance over the next 10 years.

A course on contemporary African societies will cover fertility transitions, health and illness with a focus on epidemics, and migration and urbanization, and how these shape and are shaped by war, ethnic politics, religion, education, aid and climate change. A course on religion and politics will examine religion as a factor in struggles over social, political and economic power. A course on Iran traces its strategic evolution from ancient Persia through the Pahlavi monarchy and the 1979 Islamic Revolution, then the 47 years of tension with the West including the hostage crisis and cycles of sanctions. The cross-listed course on war and climate change examines the environmental footprint of modern war and the link between fossil fuel economies and war since the 19th century, while the other cross-listed seminar asks when families nurture democratic citizens and when they feed authoritarianism.

The school's undergraduate program office is the contact for questions about the courses. The article names no individual instructors except Bhatia and gives no further details on enrollment, class sizes or scheduling beyond the spring semester. It does not say what happens after registration or how the courses will be evaluated. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Bloomington mayor Kerry Thomson declines to sign artificial superintelligence ban, letting it lapse into veto
stories.Summary:
Mayor Kerry Thomson announced on November 19, 2026, that she will not sign Ordinance 2026-29, which the Bloomington Common Council passed on November 4, 2026, to prohibit the distribution and deployment of artificial superintelligence within city limits. The ordinance was sponsored by Councilmember Dave Rollo, and the mayor said she had discussed it with him at length and appreciated his openness to revisions. Under Indiana law, the mayor must approve or veto an ordinance within 10 days of receiving it from the legislative body. If the mayor takes neither action, state law considers the ordinance vetoed. The ordinance would prohibit the distribution and deployment of artificial superintelligence within city limits, and the mayor said it leaves significant questions about how the City would identify violations, what authority it has to regulate them and what enforcement would require.

She said the potential need to monitor private digital activity is especially troubling given recent work to strengthen protections against government surveillance. She also said passing a law carries responsibilities beyond stating a principle, and that the City must be confident it can implement and enforce the laws it adopts. She said legislation meant to protect must not unintentionally create new risks. The mayor said Bloomington is working hard to grow its innovation economy and that artificial intelligence plays an important role in that work, already contributing to advances in research, medicine, education and many other fields. She said the City is committed to creating more high-skill jobs, growing local wages and keeping talented people in Bloomington, and supports entrepreneurs and researchers in technological innovation guided by clear community values and ethical responsibility.

She said she appreciates Council's efforts to address the risks of increasingly autonomous AI systems and the national conversation the legislation has helped advance, and that those risks deserve serious consideration. She also said the City needs to be careful about creating unnecessary barriers that discourage those very people from investing in the community. The mayor said she has a responsibility as mayor to lead the team that implements and enforces ordinances, and she looks forward to continuing work with Council to support Bloomington's research and innovation economy while establishing clear, enforceable safeguards. She said she will not sign the ordinance as written. Because she took neither approval nor veto action, Indiana law considers the ordinance vetoed.
