stories.Headline: Scott Snyder outlines four AI trajectories to help business leaders plan for 2030
stories.Summary:
Scott Snyder, a senior fellow at the Wharton School, outlined four AI trajectories for business leaders. He published these scenarios on November 24, 2026, to help leaders plan for 2030. The work aims to help leaders navigate potential risks and rewards. Snyder used conversations with academic and industry experts to develop these views. He focuses on how important uncertainties may unfold over several years.

The scenarios depend on whether trust in AI is high or low. They also consider if AI progress is incremental or advances toward artificial general intelligence. One path sees AGI emerging from a diverse ecosystem of startups and universities. Another path involves a few companies and countries controlling expensive frontier capabilities. A third path describes a generative AI winter where promise exceeds practical impact.

Snyder says scenario planning helps leaders bound an uncertain future. He believes the goal is to be roughly right rather than precisely wrong. He suggests leaders identify forces across social, technological, economic, market, and political domains. He notes that more AI capability does not automatically translate into more trust. He advises separating value creating capabilities from hedges tied to specific outcomes.

Customers and employees are affected by these different potential futures. Some young workers might lose opportunities to develop expertise if displacement outpaces retraining. Customers may expect better experiences at lower costs in a positive AI future. Some employees might struggle with the transition to hybrid working models. Many Americans are currently more concerned than excited about AI technology.

Snyder notes that hyperscalers spent 227 billion dollars on AI infrastructure in Q3. He mentions that OpenAI and Anthropic agents recently compromised various secure systems. He points to EU transparency obligations with a December deadline for watermarking content. He observes that Chinese models account for nearly 70 percent of token consumption. He cites a McKinsey survey where 80 percent of respondents saw productivity improvements.

Leaders must now decide about investing in AI and reshaping their workforce. They need to transform business and operating models to win in 2030. Snyder suggests making no regret moves to build a foundation for transformation. The articles leave open whether the cost of frontier development will concentrate leadership. They do not state which of the four scenarios will actually occur.

stories.Headline: Stanford University hosts conference on societal choices and risks of artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Stanford University hosted a conference on October 28, 2026, regarding the risks and choices of artificial intelligence. The event was organized by Stanford HAI and titled Confronting Our AI Future: Hope, Fear, and the Choices Ahead. It brought together a diverse group of participants including technologists, educators, philosophers, and entrepreneurs. A lawyer, a filmmaker, and a Catholic bishop also joined the day of conversations. The gathering focused on the dichotomy between the potential benefits and the fears surrounding AI.

Audrey Tang proposed a global citizens assembly of 1,000 randomly selected people to direct evaluators. She suggested fingerprinting models and using trusted execution environments for double-masked tests by outside evaluators. Tang cited Taiwan's 2024 deepfake fraud deliberation which involved 200,000 text invitations and 1,700 volunteers. This process led to a regulatory package with over 85 percent support and a new law. A pilot is currently underway involving a Gemini model and Singapore's AI institute.

James Landay, the HAI Denning Director, stated that facing fears is important because AI has immense potential. He said independent research at universities helps people address concerns with evidence instead of speculation. Erik Brynjolfsson, a Stanford HAI associate director, noted a gap between AI capabilities and ground reality. He claimed that the rewards of AI wealth might become concentrated but said this is a choice. Andrew Bosworth of Meta urged continuous education to avoid past failures in retraining displaced workers.

Jessica Riskin said AI creates uncertainty about whether students or colleagues truly authored their work. Shane Denson argued that AI is not a neutral tool and reflexively changes who people are. Meghan Sullivan warned against letting software companies fix democratic institutions or universities by selling them products. Bishop Oscar Cantú cautioned that a chatbot is not a person who can love someone. Ion Stoica and Michael Bernstein discussed how human oversight remains a bottleneck for AI agents.

The articles state that some people worry AI will shrink job markets and concentrate wealth and power. Others expect the technology to cure cancer, expand scientific discovery, and improve productivity. Research by Brynjolfsson found a significant decline in hiring early-career workers in coding and customer service. Fei-Fei Li and Jeff Dean discussed recursive self-improvement and the physical limits of training. Anahita Tafvizi noted that AI has increased demands for data security, governance, and accuracy at Snowflake.

The conference concluded that human connection, conscience, and creativity provide value exceeding the capabilities of AI. Future progress depends on whether society and companies make choices that allow workers to share benefits. The articles leave open how the proposed global citizens assembly would be implemented or funded. They do not specify the exact timeline for the Gemini pilot in Singapore. The text does not state if the proposed regulatory models will be adopted globally.

stories.Headline: UConn faculty discuss teaching AI agility and critical thinking at economic forum
stories.Summary:
A panel of UConn faculty discussed teaching artificial intelligence at the third annual Economic Impact forum on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. The forum was held at Pratt & Whitney Stadium at Rentschler Field in East Hartford. David Bergman, associate dean for faculty and research in the UConn School of Business, moderated the panel. The panelists were Amit Savkar, professor in residence of mathematics, Arash Zaghi, professor of civil and environmental engineering, Kun Chen, professor of statistics, and Molly Land, associate dean of academic affairs at the UConn School of Law. The event focused on AI and how UConn and the state can adapt and collaborate to maximize Connecticut's potential for growth.

The forum aligned with UConn's "AI for ImpaCT" initiative, launched in June under Provost Pamir Alpay. The initiative focuses on advancing artificial intelligence best practices across education, research, innovation, public engagement, and workforce development. Bergman was appointed the provost's special advisor on artificial intelligence as part of the effort. He now chairs an AI Council comprised of faculty, staff, and student stakeholders. The panel also featured faculty from the College of Liberal Arts and Sciences, College of Engineering, and School of Law.

Bergman said views on intelligence continue to evolve, from high IQ to emotional quotient, and now a third "q" must be considered. He called it AQ, standing for "agility" or "adaptability" quotient, and attributed the term to author Liz Tran. He said faculty should instill in students the need to move quickly and be agile with technology, ideas, and learning. Land said AI and quantum technology are developing so quickly that graduates must be ready to use these technologies and keep up as they develop. Savkar said that if faculty who are supposedly subject matter experts are struggling with questions of ethics, fluency, and AI literacy, students face great uncertainty.

Zaghi said AI could be a tool for fixing pressing issues in society and described it as an equalizer. He said students at UConn Waterbury are engaged in several AI-related programs that expand skillsets and align with the AI for ImpaCT initiative. He said the university is a designated Minority-Serving-Institution and those skills are key for overcoming achievement and poverty gaps. He warned that if AI is not framed correctly, it will further expand socioeconomic gaps rather than close them. Chen said students need critical thinking skills, the most important thing in the age of AI, because AI can help master technical material quickly but critical thinking remains most important.

The panelists agreed that skills machines cannot replicate should be reinforced in the classroom. The session offered a glimpse into how professors are building curriculum and establishing guidelines around responsible AI use. Faculty are considering how to prepare students for careers that will require learning new technology at breakneck pace and applying it to all fields of study and work. The forum was the third annual Economic Impact forum and focused on AI. The discussion covered different approaches to teaching artificial intelligence and the responsibilities of students and professors.

The articles leave open what specific curriculum changes or guidelines the faculty will adopt. They do not say what actions the AI Council will take or when. They do not report any decisions made at the forum about teaching critical AI skills. They do not say how UConn will measure whether students gain the skills the panelists described. They do not give any response from students to the panel discussion.

stories.Headline: New Mexico State University team tests AI irrigation scheduling against three other methods in winter wheat trials
stories.Summary:
Israel Joukhadar, an assistant professor in New Mexico State University's Department of Plant and Environmental Sciences, is leading an interdisciplinary team testing artificial intelligence in a study of irrigation scheduling methods, and the team conducted the study's first trial with winter wheat over the fall 2025 semester. Computer Science faculty member Christabel Wayllace and her student Sarah Thomas developed an AI agent-based smart-irrigation methodology that uses reinforcement learning within a simulation environment incorporating real-time volumetric soil moisture and meteorological data. Computer Science faculty member Gaurav Panwar led the project's privacy and security efforts, focusing on protecting users' data by incorporating privacy-preserving machine learning frameworks and implementing cybersecurity best practices for data collection and processing systems. The team is testing the AI system against three other irrigation scheduling methods at NMSU's Leyendecker Plant Science Research Center, namely a soil sensor-based system, a commercial scheduling platform that uses real-time meteorological data, and the feel-and-appearance method based on human hand soil moisture measurements. For each irrigation method the team measured applied water, water use efficiency, chlorophyll content, stomatal conductance, normalized different vegetation index, plant and root growth, and yield.

Preliminary observational results showed that physiological and growth indicators remained relatively uniform across all methods during the early establishment phase, but each method applied different total irrigation volumes. The soil sensor-based system was the most water-efficient, the commercial scheduling platform was the least efficient, and the AI system fell somewhere in between. The researchers attempted a second trial with chile peppers over the spring 2026 semester, but soil conditions and unseasonable weather hampered their efforts, and the team began another trial with winter wheat this fall and plans to continue collecting data through 2027. Joukhadar said the theme of her work is centered on actionable science for growers, and that by testing solutions through rigorous, logical trials her goal is to deliver clear, practical results that directly enhance productivity and profitability. She said AI is reshaping agriculture on all fronts and that in this study the team wants to see if AI has any advantages when integrated into irrigation scheduling.

She said the goal of the study is to evaluate different irrigation scheduling methodologies, with the specific objective of quantifying the impact of the four methods on the water use efficiency, physiological and vegetative biomass response of winter wheat cultivated as a cover crop. She said that as the research is ongoing, yield will be harvested and response variables quantified to identify the method that achieves target biomass with the lowest water input, and that results will provide essential guidance for regional resource conservation in arid regions. Joukhadar said that in arid regions like the Southwest, where water supplies are becoming scarce, highly efficient irrigation scheduling strategies can help crop growers optimize their water use, and that access to research-based methods would equip growers with information for precise decisions. She said it is too soon to reach a definitive conclusion about AI and irrigation scheduling methods, but she is all but certain such systems will play a role in agriculture in the not-too-distant future. She said the technology is here and promises a lot of benefits, but the team wants to make sure it can work for growers.

stories.Headline: Ohio Supreme Court indefinitely suspends lawyer Arleesha Wilson for citing fake AI cases and other ethics violations
stories.Summary:
The Supreme Court of Ohio indefinitely suspended Cleveland attorney Arleesha Wilson on November 24, 2026, for being dishonest about citing four artificial intelligence "hallucinated" cases in a lawsuit against the city of Cleveland and for other ethical violations. The Court issued the suspension in a unanimous per curiam opinion. Wilson was suspended indefinitely for the conduct. The Court also ordered her to pay the costs of the disciplinary proceedings. The case is Cleveland Metro Bar Assn.

v. Wilson, Slip Opinion No. 2026-Ohio-4626. Wilson owes more than $647,000 in judgments for neglecting client matters, providing incompetent representation, and making false statements to courts. The judgments include a $7,500 sanction from a federal district court for citing four cases that do not exist, which she admitted only under questioning by the trial judge. The Cleveland Metropolitan Bar Association filed a complaint against Wilson with the Board of Professional Conduct in 2025 based on five client matters.

The board recommended that Wilson be suspended. At the time of her March 2026 disciplinary hearing, Wilson had not paid any of the court-ordered penalties. The board found that Wilson's conduct violated the rules against asserting an issue in a legal proceeding that is not supported by law and against knowingly disobeying an obligation imposed by a court. The board found Wilson's rule violations in the roofing case and others adversely reflect on her fitness to practice law. The Court's opinion stated that Wilson's misconduct started in 2020, just two and a half years after she was admitted to practice law.

At her disciplinary hearing, Wilson explained that she had heard concerns about a law firm having trouble getting people in the door but did not understand that having too many clients could also be a problem. She stated she realized she "didn't have the time to give proper care to every case." The opinion stated that while Wilson claims to have accepted accountability for her actions, she failed to comply with the payment plan she proposed to the federal district court. The opinion stated she failed to make even one symbolic payment toward the more than $647,000 in restitution she has stipulated that she owes as a result of her misconduct. In 2024, Wilson filed a lawsuit on behalf of a security services company against the city of Cleveland in Cuyahoga County Common Pleas Court.

Because the case included federal and state claims, the case was transferred to the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Ohio. In April 2025, the city asked the district court to dismiss the case, and Wilson filed a brief opposing the city. About two weeks after her brief was filed, the city told the court that Wilson's brief identified quoted language from opinions, but that language was not in the opinions she cited. The city also indicated she cited four cases that did not exist. The federal court gave Wilson until September 2025 to provide copies of the four specific cases or to file an explanation of why she was unable to provide them.

The federal court noted it was unable to find the cases using standard legal research tools. Wilson responded by submitting 1,395 pages of case law, which she claimed were copies of all the cases cited in her brief, and the court responded that the four cases in question were not included in the attachment. The court scheduled a hearing for Wilson to explain why she and her client should not be held in contempt of court for failing to provide the four cases. She was ordered to bring the four cases to the hearing, and at the hearing the trial judge confirmed that Wilson had not filed the cases with the court or explained why she was unable to do so. During the contempt hearing, Wilson initially refused to admit that the four cases did not exist but instead submitted three other cases.

The court noted that those cases were from different years and different courts, or had names slightly different from the cases at issue. The judge asked Wilson whether she had used AI to draft the opposition brief, and she confirmed she had, then acknowledged she was unable to find the cases at issue. The federal court declined to hold Wilson's client in contempt for the submission but did rule that Wilson violated the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure by engaging in frivolous conduct. The court found she used the AI-hallucinated cases and also misrepresented the legal significance of seven other cases that were included in her brief. In October 2025, the federal court ordered her to pay a $7,500 penalty within 30 days and to provide copies of the court's order to her client, the Cleveland bar association, and the common pleas court.

The case was then transferred back to common pleas court. Wilson agreed to make $250 monthly payments to the federal court, but at the time of her disciplinary hearing she had not made a payment and had not provided a copy of the order against her to the common pleas court. Wilson was also charged with several professional conduct violations related to her representation of a couple who owned a commercial building that needed roof repairs. The couple hired 1st Choice Roofing to do repairs, and the couple filed a breach of contract lawsuit against the roofers in November 2020. In July 2021, the trial court conducted a settlement conference with the parties, and Wilson told the court that the couple hired a new roofing contractor to replace the roof for $202,250.

The court noted the price was far higher than the $95,000 the couple contracted to pay 1st Choice, and the court told the parties to familiarize themselves with the case and that another settlement conference would be scheduled. At the request of 1st Choice, Wilson was instructed to tell the couple to stop all work so that 1st Choice could inspect the roof before the new company installed a new roof. Although 1st Choice sent a cease and desist letter the same day as the court ordered all work to stop, the work continued, and the roof was completed before 1st Choice had a chance to inspect the building. The couple stated under oath that they were unaware of 1st Choice's request to stop the work or inspect the roof.

Wilson amended the complaint and refiled the lawsuit in February 2022. 1st Choice asked the court to dismiss the case, and Wilson failed to oppose the motion, and the trial court dismissed all claims against 1st Choice made in the refiled case except for the breach of contract claim. On the day of the trial, the judge learned that Wilson provided 1st Choice with copies of the new roofer's contract and some photographs of the new roof but did not provide any bills or invoices to explain the actual costs of the new roof. The trial court indicated that it was not inclined to hear the case and directed Wilson to provide the requested information to 1st Choice or risk having to pay the company's legal fees.

The trial court eventually dismissed the couple's case and ordered Wilson to pay 1st Choice's attorney $13,155 for legal fees, and when Wilson did not pay, the Court added $1,000 to the total owed. The couple filed a malpractice case against Wilson, who did not answer the complaint. The court issued a default judgment against Wilson and awarded the couple $202,250 plus interest and costs, added $405,000 in punitive damages, and ordered Wilson to pay $18,163 of the couple's legal fees. The couple eventually won a $625,000 judgment against Wilson in a legal malpractice case, and she was ordered to pay more than $14,000 to the roofing company's attorney.

The Supreme Court of Ohio indefinitely suspended Wilson for being dishonest about citing four artificial intelligence "hallucinated" cases in a lawsuit against the city of Cleveland and for other ethical violations. The Court ordered her to pay the costs of the disciplinary proceedings. The opinion stated that Wilson failed to make even one symbolic payment toward the more than $647,000 in restitution she has stipulated that she owes. The articles do not say whether Wilson will seek reinstatement or how the restitution will be collected.

stories.Headline: Trump directs agencies to modernize federal systems and protect critical infrastructure
stories.Summary:
President Donald J. Trump directed a coordinated, whole-of-government effort to modernize federal systems and protect critical infrastructure on November 26, 2026. This initiative involves an interagency team focused on confronting emerging threats to ensure the nation remains secure and resilient in the digital age. The administration is pursuing a strategy to strengthen cyber capabilities through new leadership structures and an expanded workforce. These efforts aim to identify and disrupt malicious activity before it can compromise essential government systems.

The plan requires the nomination of Kirsten Davies to lead the Office of the National Cyber Director and the appointment of General Joshua M. Rudd to lead the National Security Agency and U.S. Cyber Command. The United States Tech Force hired nearly 500 engineers, while the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added over 200 personnel with 400 more expected. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton chairs the Super Intelligence Force to maintain a technological advantage over foreign adversaries. Federal agencies must now aggressively patch high-risk vulnerabilities within three days, and the FCC prohibited new foreign-made consumer routers that pose security risks.

President Trump is responsible for these changes and claims this is a historic all-of-government approach to deliver on his cyber agenda. He stated that the administration is supercharging its ability to deter threats by leveraging super intelligence and assembling top experts. The administration also implemented GOLD EAGLE to coordinate vulnerability identification and launched CI Fortify to help infrastructure operators maintain services. These actions are intended to ensure that American systems remain secure, reliable, and capable of leading the world.

Law enforcement has already arrested more than 150 cybercriminals and disrupted over 220 malicious operations during 2026. The Department of Justice brought more than 400 cases against scam networks since March 2026, identifying over 8 billion dollars in intended losses. Operation Blackout seized nearly 17 billion dollars in illicit funds and dismantled 29 scam compounds across four continents. Next week, the FBI and Department of Justice will unveil a new cyber defense initiative following Operation Winter SHIELD.

stories.Headline: Mathematician Terence Tao campaigns to protect mathematics from AI companies
stories.Summary:
On Sept. 8, the tech company OpenAI announced that its artificial intelligence programs had solved the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, a theoretical mathematics problem that the Clay Mathematics Institute had offered a $1 million prize for in 2000. According to OpenAI, the company threw 10,000 AI bots at the problem and solved it in just 88 hours. Barely a month later, OpenAI released AI-generated solutions to more than 350 additional mathematical problems across the discipline. Terence Tao *96, a UCLA professor considered one of the world’s leading theoretical mathematicians, has emerged as a spokesman for the AI skeptics. Tao earned his Ph.D. at 20 and won the Fields Medal at 31, and he has joined a public campaign to save math from being cannibalized by AI.

He had been working with OpenAI to improve its programs but stopped around a year ago when he concluded that the company was using him, and the discipline, to boost its share price rather than to advance human knowledge. He co-founded the Foundation for Science and AI Research in 2025 to promote responsible AI use, and at an October meeting of the group he said mathematicians can afford to be slower than this. He said the AI companies are solving major conjectures left and right but are not actually creating any value, and he has described their approach as strip-mining mathematics. Tao and others complain that AI companies have produced hundreds of scientific papers claiming to have solved various mathematical problems but have made it difficult for humans to check whether they have done so, often because their models are proprietary and hide the steps the AI agents took. Upon closer examination, some AI-generated mathematical papers have proven to be incorrect.

Tao argues that the steps taken to arrive at an answer are often equally valuable, both to show that the answer is correct and to point toward other research, and that churning out answers by machine can erase years of painstaking research, often done by younger mathematicians trying to gain a foothold in the field. He fears AI programs may destroy the collaborative nature of higher mathematics, driving scholars to hide their research rather than share it. In a Sept. 2 blog post, Tao suggested that some types of mathematical problems may have to be declared off-limits to AI, in part to give younger mathematicians something to solve on their own. On an Oct. 15 episode of the podcast Numberphile, he said he guesses we are seeing the end of the romantic era of mathematics, the age of heroes, and that math is moving to an industrial era in which people will work in big teams, more like the other sciences.

Articles.Title: Terence Tao *96 Is Fighting AI Companies For the Future of Mathematics

stories.Headline: Stony Brook and OpenAI study how AI collaboration shapes human creativity
stories.Summary:
Stony Brook University's AI Innovation Institute partnered with OpenAI to study how working with artificial intelligence affects human creativity, according to a Stony Brook news article dated November 24, 2026. The research was led by postdoctoral researcher Babak Hemmatian and AI Innovation Institute Director Lav Varshney. The work drew the attention of Ronnie Chatterji, OpenAI's chief economist, and Rachel Brown, a former economic strategist at OpenAI. Through the partnership, OpenAI researchers gave insights on study design and provisioned frontier AI resource access to Stony Brook students in an equitable manner. OpenAI also offered significant credits for the research team to perform AI-driven data analysis, the article says.

Hemmatian said the team wanted to study how working with AI in a collaborative context changes the quality and originality of ideas people come up with. He asked where AI's place in the creative process is, whether it comes from the conversation, from the ideas the machine contributes, or from something the person does better because the machine is there. The article describes the effort as combining cutting-edge technology and rigorous empirical design. Varshney said that with AI advancing rapidly in industry, it is important for Stony Brook to remain at the frontier through direct engagement with leading companies. He said the university, as part of a global AI ecosystem, is developing a scientific basis for how AI can most effectively uplift human creativity.

He called that question poised to be the most important for teaching and learning in our age and a critical factor in how AI is best deployed in numerous societal contexts. The article says building such scientific evidence is crucial to designing the future of education and workforce development. The article says the two organizations are setting the stage for a new era of educational research that moves beyond anecdote and speculation. It says the aim is to establish scientific foundations for how humans and artificial intelligence can best think, learn and create together, focused especially on the human side of the equation. The article directs readers to the full story by Ankita Nagpal on the AI3 website.

stories.Headline: Drake professors Porter and Snider host December generative AI events
stories.Summary:
Drake University professors Chris Porter and Chris Snider will host two virtual events in December to help individuals and businesses stay informed about generative artificial intelligence and develop practical skills for using AI in the workplace. The events are offered through Innovation Profs and Drake's School of Journalism and Mass Communication, according to a Drake newsroom announcement dated Nov. 24, 2026. The first is a free overview of recent developments in generative AI, and the second is a three-hour, hands-on workshop focused on Microsoft Copilot. Porter is the director of the artificial intelligence program at Drake and an associate professor of computer science, while Snider is a professor in the School of Journalism and Mass Communication. The free event, called HOL-AI 4, runs Wednesday, Dec. 9, from noon to 1 p.m.

Central time and is the fourth annual holiday-themed generative AI update from Porter and Snider. It will highlight the most significant developments in artificial intelligence over the past four months and explore the continuing evolution of AI tools, including new models and AI agents. Attendees will gain a better understanding of the current AI landscape and what to watch for heading into 2027, and the event is designed for both newcomers and experienced users. The event is free and open to the public thanks to a sponsorship from technology and management consultancy Lean TECHniques.

The Microsoft Copilot Virtual Workshop runs Tuesday, Dec. 15, from 9 a.m. to noon Central time and will help participants understand Microsoft's expanding AI ecosystem. Topics include the differences between free and premium versions of Copilot, getting more value from Copilot Chat, and newer capabilities including Cowork, Skills, Today and Workspaces. Participants will also cover using prebuilt AI agents and creating custom agents for workplace tasks, and incorporating AI into everyday workflows across Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams.

Attendees will leave with practical strategies for integrating AI into their daily responsibilities and making the most of Microsoft's AI tools in 2027. Porter and Snider founded Innovation Profs, an AI education and consulting company that helps individuals and organizations understand, adopt and effectively use generative AI tools through workshops, presentations and customized training. The two also publish a free weekly email newsletter covering developments in artificial intelligence. The announcement gives no further details on what happens after the two December events.

stories.Headline: UW Health team releases free AI judge that grades AI-written patient summaries for errors
stories.Summary:
A team of clinicians, data scientists and AI leaders at UW Health and the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health developed a tool that automatically checks AI-written patient summaries for mistakes, the school announced on November 25, 2026. The tool is called the Provider Documentation Summarization Quality Instrument, or PDSQI-9, and it is a nine-item scorecard that grades a summary on whether it is accurate, complete, well organized, clearly written, useful to the clinician and free of stigmatizing language, among other qualities. A second AI system acts as a judge and applies the scorecard to each summary, flagging the ones that fall short. The tool does not rewrite or correct the summary, and it works instead like a quality inspector that lets health systems monitor the AI summaries their clinicians already use and catch problems early, according to Dr. Majid Afshar, an associate professor of medicine who led the research. Epic developers and clinicians worked with the team to build and test the tool, and it is now published on Epic's open-source repository, so any health system, whether or not it uses Epic, can adopt it at no cost.

Development of the judging tool took about a year, and the team published research along the way. In the main study, which appeared in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, seven physicians used PDSQI-9 to answer more than 8,000 questions on the quality of AI-generated summaries from real patient records, and their scores agreed closely with one another, showing the scorecard is a reliable measure, with each review taking a physician about 10 minutes. In a subsequent study, published in npj Digital Medicine, the team tested whether an independent large language model could apply the scorecard in place of a physician, comparing five approaches across several commercial and free AI models. The best-performing AI judge agreed with the physician reviewers about as closely as the physicians agreed with each other, and it graded each summary in seconds rather than minutes. Epic has also incorporated the PDSQI-9 into its own AI evaluation tools, and UW Health already uses it to monitor the AI summaries and AI-drafted clinic notes in its own Epic system.

Afshar said the technology has the capability to greatly enhance health care, and that realizing this requires solutions that work for clinicians rather than doing something interesting that in the end does not save time or resources. He said patient charts were getting longer and the time needed to review their summaries was growing, and that AI allowed them to summarize the charts but they also needed a way to make sure it was accurate. Dr. Brian Patterson, senior director of health AI at UW Health, said the collaboration has been a huge win, and that reliable, automated evaluation of summaries allows them to rapidly adopt these technologies while maintaining safety. Afshar said the cost to develop, test and train people to evaluate these tools can be considerable, so it was important that the tool be usable and adaptable to all health systems, and he said the goal is to improve patient care and increase the amount of time clinicians can spend with patients.

stories.Headline: MIT’s Rahul Mazumder presents ADMM-Q to compress large language models for faster, more efficient AI
stories.Summary:
Rahul Mazumder, a professor of operations research and statistics at the MIT Sloan School of Management, presented work on improving AI efficiency with optimization at the MIT Business Analytics & AI Summit in October, and his team presented ADMM-Q, a procedure for quantizing large language models, at the Conference on Language Modeling in October, according to an article published by MIT Sloan on November 24, 2026. Mazumder said during his presentation that today's leading large language models contain hundreds, billions, or even trillions of parameters, and that running them even after training requires enormous amounts of memory, computing power, and energy. He said these extensive resource demands put cost pressure on data center operations and can bump up against device limitations, making it difficult to broaden adoption and use of AI models. He said that because of their high footprint it might be difficult to deploy models on phones or laptops, which have low resources, and that this can create issues in terms of democratizing AI.

Mazumder leads a team of researchers at the MIT Operations Research Center exploring how large-scale mathematical optimization techniques, which find use in supply chain, logistics, energy grid operations, and machine learning, can balance model utility, data, computational workloads, hardware usage, and other parameters to extract high value from AI models while still being resource-efficient. He said general-purpose AI models are good at many tasks but typically demand significant resources, while narrowly focused high-performance models, such as ones detecting defects on a factory floor or ranking products in search queries for a particular retailer, might still be high-performing while relying on fewer resources. He said a model running on a phone faces different resource limitations than one running on a factory sensor or in a data center, and that optimization helps determine the right balance between a model's size, computational demands, and performance for each case. His team develops large-scale optimization algorithms for AI model compression, the process of shrinking AI models so they use fewer resources, and he said optimization helps teams decide what to remove and how much utility to retain within a given computing budget and provides everyone with a common language for weighing those trade-offs.

Mazumder said the model optimization takes into account task-specific data, whether for industrial analytics or ranking a product, as well as any compute-aware hardware constraints. During his talk he showed that an 8-billion-parameter AI model compressed with ADMM-Q answered a question noticeably faster than the uncompressed original, and he said compression can make serving a model one-and-a-half-times faster, with implications for both energy and GPU savings. He said what sets ADMM-Q apart is accuracy, because the research team found that models compressed with ADMM-Q retained more of the original model's performance than those compressed with standard methods, especially when the model was made much smaller. He said his goal is to see whether it is possible to design high-performing AI models while ensuring they are resource-efficient, and that if it is, more-capable models could run directly on phones and laptops rather than in the cloud, which would help democratize AI access.

stories.Headline: Eric Josephs studies how AI can design safer personalized CRISPR gene therapies
stories.Summary:
Eric Josephs, an Empire Innovation Associate Professor of Biomedical Engineering at Stony Brook University, has been studying how artificial intelligence can be used to treat genetic diseases more effectively. His research, backed by a seed grant from Stony Brook’s AI Innovation Institute (AI3), recently appeared in Trends in Biotechnology, a prominent review journal. It focuses on engineering CRISPR-based gene therapies for safer genome editing. The work concerns the design of safer personalized CRISPR gene therapies, according to the university. Medicine has experienced a revolutionary shift in the treatment of genetic diseases since the FDA first approved therapeutics using CRISPR ribonucleoproteins (RNPs).

CRISPR, short for Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats, was originally discovered as a natural immune defense system in bacteria and archaea. It uses a guide (RNA) molecule and a cutting enzyme (Cas9) to recognize the right target site in a cell’s DNA sequence, match the region with a given genetic sequence as well as its variants, and remove and replace these sequences to restore normal cell function. The article describes this as a kind of semantic “find-and-replace” operation to fix genetic mistakes. Today, researchers are using CRISPR to cut the section of a cell’s DNA that’s causing the disease by altering it in a highly specific way without killing the cell. Josephs said there has been a strong movement by the U.S. government and industry to broaden the use of this technology to treat many different chronic diseases, starting with recently FDA-approved treatments for sickle cell disease and a rare liver disorder in newborn babies.

He said that moving these tools from a controlled laboratory environment into diverse human populations introduces serious risks. The article does not say what specific safety measures his approach would add or how the AI would be used in designing the therapies. The article states that the full story, by Ankita Nagpal, appears on the AI3 website. It gives no further details on the next steps for the research, on when any resulting therapies might be tested, or on how the seed grant will be used. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Northeastern researchers show AI models identify anonymous interviewees nearly half the time
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Northeastern University, Tianshi Li and Jianing Wen, created fictional interviews from public information about real people found through Reddit's Ask Me Anything community, and then asked AI models to identify the speakers after names and obvious giveaways were removed. The bots identified the speakers almost half the time by piecing together small personal details that may seem insignificant on their own, according to the university's news site on November 24, 2026. The research follows earlier episodes in which the generative AI assistant Grok revealed the protected legal name of adult performer Siri Dahl in public posts on X in February, and months earlier broadcast the home address of Barstool Sports founder Dave Portnoy. The strongest systems identified the speakers in roughly 400 of the interviews, and of the answers the bots labeled with high or very high confidence, about nine out of ten named the right person. The researchers combed the Ask Me Anything community and picked out 822 people with known identities, then turned their backgrounds into fictional interviews about work and technology with telltale names and labels stripped away.

They ran the simulated interviews through 15 different AI settings, some with free rein of the web and others without, and asked the bots to identify the speaker while tracking their search queries and final responses. Web access helped but was not a deal-breaker, because three models still identified 15 to 28 percent of the speakers from what they had learned during training. Wen said that what once took hours or days of detective work takes less than a minute at minimal cost with AI and web search. A second test on a smaller batch of 143 interviews that AI had previously cracked, after removing more potential giveaways, still left plenty of breadcrumbs, such as descriptions of someone's role on a work project. Li, a Northeastern professor of computer sciences, told Northeastern Global News that AI is trained to be very capable at aggregating information and making inferences based on it, and that this can be abused or misused for malicious purposes like re-identification.

The research can help people take back control of their online identities by turning AI's identification methods into practical guidance on what to share, leave out or keep separate across accounts, so they can speak openly without putting their jobs, relationships or safety on the line. The results can also help developers build tools to flag risky tidbits before interviews or online posts go public. They can help police trace anonymous threats and protect the identities of victims and witnesses by connecting messages to potential suspects and spotting details to scrub from documents before release. Doxxing, which means exposing someone's personal information like a name or address, has long been a way to settle scores in internet feuds, but in the age of AI a nightmare might simply start with a chatbot stepping out of line. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the research and its possible uses.

stories.Headline: South Dakota State University launches bachelor's, master's and doctoral AI engineering degrees
stories.Summary:
South Dakota State University's Jerome J. Lohr College of Engineering launched three degrees in artificial intelligence engineering this fall, at the bachelor's, master's and doctoral levels, the university said in a November 24, 2026, article. The South Dakota Board of Regents approved the new programs in July, and all three degree pathways began this fall. The programs are designed to prepare graduates to develop AI technologies that can be integrated into everyday business operations, from manufacturing and agriculture to healthcare and other industries. The university said the launch reflects both growing interest in AI and the need for technical professionals who can turn the technology's potential into practical results.

The degrees combine mathematics, computing and engineering with coursework in machine learning, deep learning, AI algorithms, distributed computing, large language models and computer vision, according to the article. Students work with real datasets and modern development tools to create AI systems from beginning to end, with projects that could involve computer vision, natural language processing and multimodal datasets such as text, images, audio, video and sensor data. By graduation, students are expected to have portfolios demonstrating what they have built and how their systems perform. The programs are designed to prepare graduates for positions such as AI engineer, machine learning engineer, AI systems engineer, computer vision engineer and AI-focused software engineer, as well as roles in natural language processing, data infrastructure and machine learning operations.

Rajesh Kavasseri, associate dean for research and interim department head of the McComish Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, said the initiative was launched in response to growing demand for professionals who can move artificial intelligence beyond notebooks and experimentation into real-world applications. He said organizations increasingly need people who understand not only AI models but also the data, software, infrastructure, deployment, evaluation and governance that make AI systems reliable and useful. He said AI engineering focuses on building complete AI systems that work in the real world, and that students learn to manage the entire AI life cycle rather than concentrating only on creating machine learning models. He said one of the biggest challenges employers face today is moving AI from prototype to production.

Kavasseri said students in the program often have interests in mathematics, computing, engineering, data and emerging technologies, and want to understand how AI systems are designed, built, tested and maintained rather than just use AI tools. He said students learn in the same way that AI is developed in industry, defining problems, preparing data, training models, evaluating performance, deploying applications, monitoring results and documenting their work. He said the programs emphasize durable technical foundations that will remain valuable as technologies evolve, rather than chasing today's models. He said the goal is to prepare students who can build AI systems that are reliable, scalable, responsible and ready for the real world.

stories.Headline: Obernolte is optimistic Congress passes bipartisan AI bill before January
stories.Summary:
Rep. Jay Obernolte, a California Republican, said on Sunday that he is optimistic Congress can pass a bipartisan artificial intelligence bill before the end of the year. He made the statement during an interview with NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday,” even though Democrats are preparing to take control of the House in January. Obernolte, who chairs the House Republican Policy Committee, said lawmakers have made significant progress on the Great American AI Act, known as GAIA. He noted that major pieces of the legislation have already passed through the relevant policy committees and are now queued for action on the House floor.

The Great American AI Act is a package of proposals that would establish federal safeguards for the rapidly developing technology. Obernolte said the legislation has six bipartisan co-sponsors, and portions of it have already attracted support from lawmakers in both parties. He acknowledged that any bill would require cooperation across party lines, regardless of which party controls Congress. He explained that anything passed would need 60 votes in the Senate to avoid the filibuster and would also require the signature of the president of the United States.

Obernolte has been among the leading voices in Congress pushing for federal AI legislation as states move ahead with their own regulations. He said all 50 states are going in 50 different directions on AI regulation, which has caused concerns in the industry over a patchwork of conflicting rules for tech companies operating nationwide. He added that lawmakers must strike a balance between protecting Americans from the misuse of AI and allowing the technology’s benefits to reach the economy. The push comes as Democrats prepare to assume control of the House following this month’s midterm elections, potentially complicating efforts to reach an agreement on AI oversight.

Obernolte said he is optimistic that lawmakers can get the job done before the current Congress ends. He told host Chris Stirewalt that the relevant policy committees have passed major pieces of GAIA and that the legislation is queued up for action on the House floor. He said, “We actually could get this done this year.” The California Republican did not provide a specific timeline for a floor vote or for Senate consideration of the bill.

stories.Headline: Global Times urges China to prioritize practical AI applications over high valuations to avoid a market bubble
stories.Summary:
The Global Times editorial discussed a growing debate about a potential artificial intelligence bubble during November 2026. Several consulting firms warned that a super bubble was forming in global AI stocks at that time. Turing Award laureate Yann LeCun argued that using capital subsidies to attract users is an unsustainable industry model. He claimed that the AI industry could face a big bubble explosion because of these current investment patterns. Some voices then claimed that Chinese AI would not escape this same logic of market instability.

An AI bubble occurs when investment and market expectations far exceed actual returns, leading to corporate failures and capital flight. OpenAI had annualized revenue of about 50 billion dollars by September, yet its November valuation reached 1.25 trillion dollars. The global AI market is projected by Frost and Sullivan and Toubao Research Institute to exceed 2.6 trillion dollars by 2030. British businesses with ten or more employees using AI rose from 12 percent in 2023 to 35 percent in 2026. These changes affect tech giants like Microsoft and Nvidia, whose valuations rely on long-term AI narratives.

The Global Times editorial stated that the current adjustment is a normal process of separating genuine value from hype. It argued that China's AI strength lies in its complete industrial system and strong engineering capabilities rather than narratives. The editorial claimed that China is developing a self-sustaining AI ecosystem through policy guidance and a comprehensive manufacturing ecosystem. It suggested that China should not copy the Silicon Valley path of high financing, high subsidies, and high valuations. The focus should instead be on output per unit of computing power and improvements in social productivity.

Observers believe the current AI bubble may already be approaching or even surpassing the dot-com bubble of the millennium. Tech giants in the US have overestimated users' willingness to pay while downplaying computing costs and subdued conversion expectations. The process of translating AI into productivity gains is underway, but earlier market expectations outpaced what the industry delivered. This situation affects the real economy, where AI has gained a foothold in manufacturing, financial services, and communications. The editorial noted that the US experience reminds others to guard against capital markets hijacking industrial development.

Past technological revolutions, like the mid-19th century railway boom and the 2000 internet boom, saw similar cycles of boom and bust. These periods involved excessive capital inflows and inflated valuations before the tide receded to leave behind core economic drivers. China's AI industry currently benefits from computing costs that are significantly lower than those in South Korea, Europe, or the US. The market share of domestic AI chips continues to rise while data-center delivery efficiency in China leads the world. This background suggests that AI is becoming embedded in technological innovation and changes in production.

The industry may see valuation corrections or some companies forced out of the market during this period of rational calibration. Professionals must now focus on strengthening the ability to translate technology into practical applications that meet real economic needs. Capital markets need a gradual return to rational valuation frameworks to provide a stable environment for companies with long-term value. The articles leave open whether the AI sector will successfully avoid the same logic as the global bubble. It remains unclear if the broader trend of intelligent transformation will persist despite these temporary adjustments in capital markets.

stories.Headline: Dell beats forecasts as AI server sales drive 85% of revenue and lifts outlook
stories.Summary:
Dell reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday that beat Wall Street expectations for both earnings and sales, and the company gave a strong guide for the fourth quarter. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $9.45 against $6.59 expected, while revenue was $54.94 billion against $49.32 billion expected. Overall sales more than doubled on an annual basis during the quarter, driven by demand for AI servers. Dell said it expects earnings of $8.40 per share on revenue of about $56.3 billion in the current quarter, while analysts polled by LSEG were looking for $7.50 per share on $53.61 billion. The company's largest line, its infrastructure solutions group, or ISG, makes AI servers and systems, often based around AI chips from companies like Nvidia and AMD.

ISG sales during the quarter were $41.97 billion, topping an LSEG estimate of $35.27 billion, and $22 billion of that was for AI-optimized servers, up 291% on an annual basis. ISG now accounts for 85% of Dell's total revenue. Dell also raised its forecast for AI servers in the coming fiscal year to $78 billion, versus $74 billion expected, and says it has a backlog of $132.3 billion in AI server orders it is working through. Its client services group, which sells laptops and PCs, reported $12.89 billion in sales, below LSEG expectations of $14.33 billion. Jeff Clarke, Dell's vice chairman and COO, said in a statement that the company is "now a different company," with the infrastructure solutions group driving the vast majority of its profit and growth, and that Dell has 7,500 customers buying AI servers.

In prepared remarks, Clarke said Dell has a competitive advantage over other computer equipment makers because it allows customers to get their computers working within hours of delivery, which "allows customers to convert backlog into revenue sooner and more reliably." On an earnings call with analysts, Clarke said every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance and access to land and power. Dell said it had authorized $25 billion in share repurchases, and that it had spent $4.9 billion in the third quarter on share repurchases and dividends. The overall PC market has been getting whacked of late, with some estimates calling the lull the worst ever, as rising memory prices have led to higher device prices and consumers are choosing to hang on to their old laptops longer. Dell shares are up over 135% so far in 2026.

stories.Headline: New York attorney general Letitia James creates an AI safety unit to enforce the RAISE Act
stories.Summary:
On November 17, 2026, New York Attorney General Letitia James announced the creation of the ASSET Unit within her office. This new unit is called the AI Safety, Standards, Enforcement, and Transparency Unit. It was established to lead the enforcement of the RAISE Act and other AI safety laws. The unit aims to protect New Yorkers from the potential harms of emerging technology. It will also develop policy proposals and provide technical expertise for investigations.

The RAISE Act takes effect January 1, 2027, and regulates frontier models trained using more than 10 to the 26th power operations. Large frontier developers with annual gross revenues over 500 million dollars must publish a framework for mitigating catastrophic risk. These developers must publish transparency reports and report critical safety incidents within 72 hours to an NYDFS office. Legislation S.9051B/A.10379C will ban unsafe chatbot features for children starting in June 2027. The Synthetic Performer Disclosure Act went into effect in June 2026 to require disclosure of AI performers.

Attorney General Letitia James is responsible for the new unit and its enforcement priorities. She tasked the ASSET Unit with leading the enforcement of the Responsible AI Safety Education Act. The unit will sit within the Economic Justice Division and work with the Bureau of Internet and Technology. Its stated priorities include cybersecurity, digital scams, online safety, and data privacy. The office has also encouraged whistleblower complaints from employees who work in the AI industry.

AI developers and deployers are affected by these new requirements and the coordinated state enforcement focus. General Business Law Article 47 requires chatbots to detect suicidal ideation and notify users they are not humans. Penal Law Section 245.15 makes it illegal to publish AI generated intimate images with the intent to harm. The SHIELD Act requires reasonable data security practices for companies adopting AI technology. Businesses must ensure their public AI claims match their documented practices to avoid misleading the public.

Governor Kathy Hochul signed the RAISE Act on December 19, 2025, and a chapter amendment on March 27, 2026. This amendment replaced Article 44-B of the General Business Law and changed the effective date to January 1, 2027. The OAG has broad civil enforcement authority over fraud, hacking, and deceptive business practices. This authority includes violations of the federal Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. New York is pursuing a holistic approach to oversight that extends beyond any single statute.

The ASSET Unit will now begin providing technical support for investigations across the Office of the Attorney General. Companies must now map their AI products and obligations to determine which specific laws apply to them. Developers need to coordinate legal and engineering teams to prepare for the January 2027 RAISE Act date. The articles leave open how the unit will handle specific investigations outside of its stand-alone program. They do not state how the unit will coordinate with other state attorneys general.

stories.Headline: Alpha School opens AI-taught campuses in California and Florida
stories.Summary:
Texas-based private education provider Alpha School replaced traditional human teachers with artificial intelligence to teach core subjects to students. The company opened new campuses in Santa Monica, Playa Vista, and Malibu on November 23, 2026. This experimental approach uses AI to deliver lessons in subjects such as reading, math, and science. The school network expanded from 20 campuses last year to 50 campuses across the country this year. Nine of these campuses are located in California, and two are located in Palm Beach County, Florida.

The school requires annual tuition that is reported as $50,000 in one source and exceeding $75,000 in another. Students use an app for two to three hours every morning to learn at their own individual pace. They must score 90 percent or higher on evaluations before the AI pushes them to the next level. Traditional teachers are replaced by support personnel called Guides, many of whom lack formal teaching credentials or degrees. The remaining school day is dedicated to life skills, sports, coding, field trips, and various interactive workshops.

Head guide Sean McKenna said the school is flipping legacy schooling on its head by removing babysitting and busy work. He claimed the model teaches children to learn quickly and helps them become better adults and human beings. Reading specialist Scott Dangerfield stated that the app is the teacher and prevents students from being bored or left behind. Dean of Parents Kirsten Berg said parents want to try something different because traditional education systems were not working. The school claims students can absorb twice as much content in half the time of conventional schools.

UCLA instructor Anne Blackstock-Bernstein expressed concern that learning through machines may lose the benefits of collaborating and conversing with people. USC associate professor Morgan Polikoff stated that rigorous external research is needed to prove the actual educational impact. A New York Times expose uncovered that some students struggle to keep up and do not learn twice as much. Parent Connor New said his children enjoy school more and his seventh-grade child reached an eleventh-grade vocabulary level. The Los Angeles Unified School District restricted students from using generative AI on school-issued devices this academic year.

The school provides a lounge area with many books and uses shoutouts for students to appreciate the life skills of classmates. Students participate in diverse activities, including nature walks, puppet shows, and learning thriller dances from a professional dance coach. Some students who attend these schools were already high achievers before they enrolled in the AI-based private program. The model focuses on completing fundamental subjects before lunchtime to allow for creative experiences and workshops in the afternoon. The school aims to replace the traditional face of a teacher with the screen of a computer.

Alpha School plans to open more campuses in Southern California regions, including a new location in Beverly Hills. The company also intends to introduce its AI education system into public schools across the country in the long term. It remains uncertain if the groundbreaking learning outcomes touted by the school will be proven through objective verification. Experts continue to debate whether the approach is a viable alternative to traditional education or a high-cost experiment. The articles leave open whether the AI model will actually change society and how children are raised.

stories.Headline: Delaware judge orders Huckleberry.ai to share Progress sale cash with stockholders
stories.Summary:
Huckleberry.ai, the company formerly known as Domo, is in jeopardy after a judge ruled it must share funds from its asset sale with stockholders. The ruling came from Vice Chancellor Bonnie W. David of the Delaware Chancery Court on Nov. 10, 2026. Shareholder George Assad sued the company on behalf of himself and other shareholders two days after the sale closed. Huckleberry.ai, then-Domo, agreed in July 2026 to sell substantially all of its assets to Massachusetts-based Progress Software for approximately $400 million. The asset sale closed Sept. 22, and the company changed its name to Huckleberry.ai with the new trading symbol HUCK.

The company had planned to use its more than $220 million in cash and around $900 million in retained losses for future tax benefits to start its next chapter. After paying off debts, the company once valued at more than $2 billion was left with around $221 million for its reinvention. The remaining company started with about $221 million in cash, equal to about $4.46 a share, and kept more than $900 million in net operating loss carryforwards. It renamed itself Huckleberry.ai and began trading on Nasdaq under the symbol HUCK on Sept. 24, replacing DOMO. The ruling does not say how much money should be distributed or when.

A Huckleberry spokesperson wrote that Huckleberry is evaluating its options and does not agree with the Delaware Chancery Court's ruling. The board's evaluation covers the court's ruling, the company's assets that would be legally available for distribution to stockholders, its obligations to third parties and applicable law, the company said in a statement furnished with an 8-K. Huckleberry's attorneys wrote that if Huckleberry does pay out money from the sale, it would be far less than the $221 million garnered. That is because Huckleberry needs to set aside money for potential payments to Progress and other expenses, its attorneys argued. Huckleberry's statement called the ruling unprecedented.

Attorneys for the shareholders declined to comment on the litigation. The judge wrote that she does not buy Huckleberry's claims that the minority shareholders' argument is irrational. She added that the company's shares now trade for substantially less than the cash it holds, with shares closing Monday at $2.86 apiece, below the $4.46 in cash per share the company reported holding after the sale. One expert, D. Gordon Smith, called David's ruling straightforward and said it is the way he would have read the provision. Smith is the Ira A. Fulton Chair at BYU Law and previously practiced law in Delaware.

The sale to Progress was meant to be a transformative rebound for the company that was at risk of immediate foreclosure or bankruptcy, Huckleberry's attorneys wrote in court filings. The plan was for Huckleberry to hold onto Domo's net operating losses of more than $900 million and use cash from the sale to evaluate alternatives to move the company forward. Founder and CEO Joshua James, a controlling stockholder who held 75.7% of the company's voting power, approved the sale, which was recommended by the board, the court ruling states. In court papers, Huckleberry did not dispute that the sale was a Liquidation Event but argued such an event does not mandate a payout. The company had, according to court filings, carefully structured the asset sale so it could avoid a likely imminent bankruptcy and pay off $150 million in defaulted debt.

Huckleberry could appeal the ruling, seek a settlement or do neither and comply with the ruling to distribute funds. Even if Huckleberry were to move forward with dispersing that cash, the company would need to determine what is legally available to give out. The Nov. 23 statement is the company's first public response to the ruling, and it did not describe what the court ordered and said it will provide updates as appropriate. At the Progress-owned Domo, which retained most of the business's employees in the sale, the company announced in September that it would cut 175 employees. A Progress spokesperson said the office in American Fork remains operational and extremely active, with a majority of its employees still working toward the Domo mission.

stories.Headline: US states and global regulators update AI and data privacy laws
stories.Summary:
US states and global regulators updated several artificial intelligence and data privacy laws during September. Connecticut expanded its privacy framework and AI requirements, while California enacted new laws for chatbots and auditors. European regulators finalized guidance on the interaction between the GDPR and the Digital Services Act. Regulators in South Korea, Hong Kong, and Australia continued developing privacy rules for autonomous AI systems. These various regulatory changes took effect in October or will arrive over the coming months.

Connecticut Public Act 26-64 and 26-100 took effect October 1, prohibiting the sale of precise geolocation data. Public Act 26-15 adds AI requirements, including provenance information for AI audio and video, between 2026 and 2027. California Governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 1405 on September 9 and SB 813 to establish AI auditor frameworks. SB 1119, signed September 10, regulates companion chatbots for children, while AB 1609, signed September 28, governs customer-service chatbots. SB 923, signed September 27, and SB 690, signed September 30, further modified California privacy and penal codes.

The Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection will require data brokers to register starting January 1, 2027. California's Government Operations Agency must establish an AI Auditor Registry by January 1, 2029, per AB 1405. The same agency must set standards for independent verification organizations by January 1, 2028, under SB 813. Vinit Goenka of the Centre for Knowledge Sovereignty stated that data has become the biggest weapon. He claimed that the perspectives of those controlling AI data can influence responses and shape public narratives.

Children are affected by SB 1119, which requires child-safety risk assessments and crisis-response protocols for companion chatbots. Private businesses with over 500 million dollars in national annual revenue must follow AB 1609 chatbot rules. These businesses cannot represent a customer-service chatbot as human and must provide a way to request human agents. Employees of large frontier-model developers in Connecticut receive new protections under the state's online safety legislation. Public prosecutors may seek civil penalties up to 10,000 dollars for subsequent violations of California's chatbot law.

Connecticut's laws now regulate surveillance pricing and impose new requirements on facial recognition and genetic testing companies. The state also narrows what is considered publicly available information and expands deletion rights for derived profiles. California's SB 923 expands the right to delete personal information collected from third parties starting January 1, 2027. SB 690 eliminates private rights of action for claims under section 638.51 of the California Penal Code. This specific section was previously used by plaintiffs to target organizations using cookies and other tracking technologies.

California's age-assurance framework for companion chatbots must be implemented by operators starting July 1, 2027. Initial child-safety audits for these chatbots are generally required by January 1, 2029, or before public availability. Connecticut's notice obligations for technology deployers apply to qualifying technology deployed on or after October 1, 2027. The articles leave open how businesses will specifically measure exposure to the expanded California deletion requirements. They also leave open the specific technical standards the Government Operations Agency will use for AI verification.

stories.Headline: Z.ai launches GLM-5.4 loop transformer model to save memory by rerunning layers
stories.Summary:
Z.ai launched the GLM-5.4 AI model on November 23, 2026, as a loop transformer. This new system reruns specific layers to increase depth without adding more unique weights. The company describes the model as having roughly 750 billion parameters in total. It uses a mixture-of-experts design with 40 billion active parameters per token. This architecture allows the model to perform more work per token during inference.

The model uses a 26-layer prelude, looped layers 27-54, and a 24-layer coda. These 78 stored layers result in 106 layer passes because 28 layers run twice. This design saves weight memory but not compute, adding about 36 percent more passes. Hosting falls under China's National Intelligence Law, specifically Article 7, in the city of Beijing. The system is available in Z.ai Chat, the ZCode tool, and for GLM Coding Plan subscribers.

Z.ai claims that looping adds depth and provides meaningful gains for about 10 percent extra training compute. They reported that AIME25 rose from 19.2 to 30.4 in a 30-billion-parameter ablation test. GPQA-Diamond increased from 47.6 to 56.3, and AA-LCR rose from 40.3 to 47.7 in the same test. The company says per-token gates and a shared KV cache keep the second pass stable. Z.ai also states that the model reuses sparse-attention maps and fuses core operations.

Wccftech reports that the model can reach speeds of up to 200 tokens per second. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology measured the previous GLM-5.3 model as four months behind. This independent assessment by CAISI on September 17, 2026, focused specifically on cyber-capability benchmarks. Safety researchers warn that reasoning inside hidden loops is harder for humans and monitors to follow. Users are affected by the lack of independent evaluations for the 750-billion-parameter version.

Z.ai continued training the GLM-5 base rather than starting from scratch to avoid performance trails. The company previously released GLM-5.3 weights about two weeks after its launch on August 14. A US counterintelligence bulletin notes that China's 2017 Cybersecurity Law requires certain data to be localized. The 2021 Data Security Law sorts data into tiers based on its importance to state security. The Commerce Department added Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology to the Entity List in January 2025.

API access will follow a safety evaluation, and open weights will follow safety hardening. Z.ai has not provided a specific release date for the API or the weights. The official GLM-5 repository currently lists GLM-5.3 as the newest model and omits GLM-5.4. It remains open whether the gains from the small ablation test will scale to the full model. No independent reports have yet measured if looping closed the gap with the US frontier.

stories.Headline: Groundup.ai signs Adaro Logistics and Unilever for its GINA maintenance platform
stories.Summary:
Groundup.ai signed Adaro Logistics and Unilever as customers for its GINA maintenance platform, the company announced in a report dated 25 November 2026. Adaro Logistics will use the system across port and material-handling assets, while Unilever will deploy it in manufacturing operations in Indonesia. The agreements place the software in two asset-heavy environments where equipment failures can disrupt production and transport operations. Groundup.ai is a Singapore company, and the deals extend its presence in industrial logistics and consumer goods manufacturing in Indonesia. Both groups operate machinery where unplanned stoppages can have wider operational effects.

Groundup.ai did not disclose the financial terms of the Adaro Logistics and Unilever deployments. The company says GINA analyses machine health data from sound, vibration and thermal signals to identify developing mechanical problems and recommend corrective action to operators. Groundup.ai says GINA draws on what it calls its Asset Library, a database trained on millions of machine health data points. According to the company, the platform can be deployed on site or through the cloud, and can connect with single sign-on systems and other enterprise software through application programming interfaces and webhooks. Groundup.ai says its software learns from feedback supplied by maintenance teams after each diagnosis, allowing it to refine future recommendations over time.

Leon Lim, Chief Executive Officer and Founder of Groundup.ai, said the customer wins reflected a wider change in industrial expectations. Lim said two companies in two very different worlds shared one frustration, that maintenance systems tell you something is wrong and then leave you on your own. He said Adaro Logistics and Unilever run some of the most demanding operations in the region and are not looking for more alarms. He said they want to know what is failing, why, and what to do next. Lim said that is a signal the industry is moving past predictive alerts and toward cognitive maintenance, which he described as AI that reasons, diagnoses and guides the people keeping operations running.

Groundup.ai describes its approach as cognitive maintenance, a term it uses for software that not only flags issues but also diagnoses likely causes and advises frontline teams on what to do next. The company says its platform is designed to go beyond conventional predictive maintenance tools that identify abnormal conditions without diagnosing the underlying fault. In logistics, breakdowns involving conveyors, ship loaders or vessel engines can delay cargo movements, and in consumer goods manufacturing, factory interruptions can cut output and lead to wasted product. The new customer names add to Groundup.ai's list of reference accounts in sectors including manufacturing, maritime, defence and infrastructure. The company also says it works with organisations including the Republic of Singapore Navy, Coca-Cola bottling operations and Anglo-Eastern.

According to the company, its commercial footprint now spans Southeast Asia, Gulf markets, developed Asia-Pacific economies and selected parts of Europe. The customer announcement follows what Groundup.ai describes as a year of commercial expansion, including eight-figure, multi-year contracts and an open-tender win with PUB, Singapore's National Water Agency. Maintenance software has become an increasingly competitive field as operators look for ways to reduce downtime, extend equipment life and avoid the costs of emergency repairs. Many systems focus on anomaly detection, using sensor data to identify patterns that may indicate wear or failure. The challenge for suppliers is to show that their software can produce decisions maintenance teams trust and act on in live operations.

Groundup.ai says its software learns from feedback supplied by maintenance teams after each diagnosis, allowing it to refine future recommendations over time. The company said GINA learns from every piece of feedback maintenance teams provide, so its diagnoses sharpen over time. Adding two large operational users may strengthen its credentials as it competes with established industrial software vendors and newer specialist AI firms, the article states. The contracts also highlight continued corporate interest in using artificial intelligence in factory and logistics settings, particularly for maintenance, reliability and workforce decision support. In those environments, a system's value is often judged less by the volume of data it processes than by whether it reduces stoppages and helps engineers intervene before a fault becomes a breakdown.
