stories.Headline: Gapped Deterministic Legal Tech vs. Cloud-Hosted Generative AI: Seven Trade-Offs for Law Firms
stories.Summary:
Pouya Shafabakhsh wrote an article on November 24, 2026, about the trade-offs between two different types of legal technology architectures. The author compared gapped deterministic legal tech against cloud-hosted generative AI to help law firms choose the right tools. This analysis focuses on which architecture is better suited for specific legal tasks, risk levels, and information boundaries. The piece provides a fair comparison for managing partners, general counsel, and legal-tech leaders to evaluate their options. It examines how different tools serve different needs, such as summarizing productions or verifying quotations in legal filings.

The comparison requires weighing seven specific trade-offs including flexibility, accuracy, specialization, auditability, confidentiality, collaboration, and the overall cost of the technology. A litigation team might use one tool to summarize a production that is 200 pages long for their case. Another tool could be used to draft a client update, while a third verifies that a quotation matches its source. The author notes that these are all legal-technology problems, but they are not the same problem for the firm. These requirements ensure that the exhibit being served is the exact version that the counsel has already approved.

Pouya Shafabakhsh, who is a judicial forensic AI auditor, is the person responsible for providing this technical legal technology analysis. He stated that the primary question for firms is not which technology is more fashionable for their current legal practice. Instead, he argued that the real issue is determining which architecture fits a particular task and its associated risk. He suggested that the choice depends on the specific information boundary required for the legal work being performed. His goal was to provide a framework for leaders to weigh the various benefits and risks of AI.

Managing partners and general counsel are among the professionals affected by these choices when selecting software for their legal teams. These leaders must decide between deterministic systems and generative AI to maintain the accuracy of their official court filings. The analysis affects how litigation teams handle large productions and how they communicate updates to their various clients. Legal-tech leaders are also impacted as they must balance the need for flexibility with the need for strict auditability. The choice of architecture directly influences how a firm manages its internal data and its external legal obligations.

The articles provide background on how generative AI uses foundation models to create complex text, images, audio, or video. These systems ingest and generate large amounts of data, including business plans, technical formulae, speech, code, and various images. The EU AI Act provides a specific definition for generative AI as foundation models used in these autonomous systems. There is ongoing discussion regarding intellectual property rights for both the input materials and the resulting AI-generated output. The background indicates that regulatory frameworks for this technology are currently emerging and are evolving very quickly.

The articles leave open the specific results of the trade-offs for individual firms and their unique operational needs. They do not state which of the two architectures is objectively superior for every single legal task or firm. Future actions involve managing partners applying these seven trade-offs to their own specific risk levels and information boundaries. The text does not provide a final recommendation on which specific software products law firms should purchase today. It remains unclear how the evolving regulatory frameworks will specifically change the seven trade-offs mentioned by Shafabakhsh.

stories.Headline: Property lawyers name faster AI adoption by rival firms as their biggest competitive threat
stories.Summary:
Live polling at October’s Digital Conveyancing Summit found that 43 per cent of respondents named rival firms adopting artificial intelligence faster as the biggest threat to their commercial success, rather than AI replacing them. The findings came from a panel hosted by property data specialist Search Acumen before an audience of around 500 property lawyers, with senior figures from JLL, the Urban Land Institute and law firm Freeths taking part. Financial Times property correspondent Julie Steinberg moderated the discussion, which examined where commercial property law is heading over the next five years. The article says buying another AI subscription is unlikely to be the answer, and that the number of actual poll respondents was not disclosed.

Search Acumen managing director Andrew Lloyd argued that real estate’s fundamental problem is not AI but data, because vast quantities of valuable property information remain locked in separate systems and create duplicated work, unnecessary costs and missed opportunities. He said combining ownership records, geographical information, flood risks and climate resilience data could transform property due diligence and investment advice, and that advantage will increasingly belong to firms combining their own knowledge with wider industry datasets. The article lists five points for property lawyers: AI is becoming core infrastructure, firms should collect and organise data now and review confidentiality agreements, data retention policies and permissions, more complex public-private transactions are expected in housing, energy and infrastructure, climate data will increasingly influence transactions, and relationships still matter. It says the intellectual capital inside law firms could become one of their most valuable commercial assets, provided they can use it without compromising client confidentiality.

JLL technology executive Will Cohen said fewer than 40 per cent of organisations beginning to pilot AI had formal training or governance processes in place, a figure the article says was separately reported. Freeths’ chief knowledge and innovation officer Nick Pryor emphasised the importance of human judgment, data protection and making AI central to legal practice. The article says the competitive advantage will not necessarily go to the firm with the most expensive AI platform but to the firm that knows what to do with its information. It does not say what happens next beyond the five-year outlook the panel examined.

stories.Headline: Law review authors say generative AI blurs human authorship in copyright law
stories.Summary:
The National Law Review published an article on November 24, 2026, by Dr. Eyal Brook and S. Horowitz on copyright law and generative AI. The article says generative AI has rewritten the rules of engagement in the creative arena. It says systems like Midjourney, Stable Diffusion and GPT-4 simulate the creative process itself. The authors describe this shift as ontological rather than incremental. The article says the traditional status of the human author is blurring, sometimes to the point of total dissipation.

The article traces copyright law to the Statute of Anne in 1710, which assumed authorship was uniquely human. It cites Feist Publications v. Rural Telephone Service, which requires independent creation plus a modicum of creativity. It cites Naruto v. Slater, the Monkey Selfie case, where a court ruled a macaque cannot hold copyright.

It cites Thaler v. Perlmutter, which reaffirmed that human authorship is a bedrock requirement of copyright. It cites the Copyright Office decision on Zarya of the Dawn, where Kristina Kashtanova owns the selection and arrangement but the Midjourney images remain uncopyrightable. The article says the U.S. Copyright Office has remained steadfast that copyright is limited to works created by human beings. It says the European Union standard is the author's own intellectual creation, reflecting the author's personality.

The authors ask whether prompt engineering is a creative act of authorship or merely a request for service. They compare a prompt to a patron commissioning a painter to paint a portrait of a dog in a regal setting. They say the user who provides no further input acts as a curator rather than a creator. The article says the legal battle is not just about the output but about the input. It says generative AI models are trained on billions of copyrighted works through mass ingestion of books, paintings, code and music without explicit consent.

It says the article does not address whether scraping for training is fair use or infringement. It says a film studio licensing a comic book could find anyone legally printing individual panels on merchandise. It says this legal uncertainty could destabilize the copyright supply chain in the entertainment industry. The article describes three phases of the human-machine hierarchy: AI as a tool, AI as a collaborator and AI as a generative agent. It says in the third phase the human retreats from execution to curation and direction of the output.

It says the AI makes the expressive choices, such as the specific hues of a sunset or the cadence of a poem. It says this automation strikes at the heart of the sweat of the brow doctrine and the modicum of creativity standard. It says we are moving from a world where we reward the doing to a world where we are asked to reward the asking. The article says the question for the courts is whether prompt engineering is authorship or a request for service. It says a work can be protected as a whole while its individual parts are in the public domain.

It says this creates a complicated copyright landscape for commercial licensing. It says the article explores whether current legal frameworks can survive the transition from human-centric to machine-augmented creativity. It leaves open whether scraping copyrighted works to train a model is fair use or infringement. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Maryland students sue Omnilert over AI gun detection false alarm that led to handcuffs
stories.Summary:
A civil rights lawsuit was filed on Nov. 17 in Baltimore County Circuit Court against Virginia-based Omnilert, Baltimore County Public Schools, Baltimore County and several school and police officials. The complaint alleges negligence and civil rights violations after Omnilert's software mistook a bag of chips for a gun. The suit says the system triggered a police response that left four BCPS students in handcuffs. The plaintiffs are current and former BCPS students, including Taki Allen, a Kenwood High School student. The incident occurred in October 2025 at Kenwood High School in Baltimore County.

The plaintiffs seek undisclosed damages and ask the court to halt the system's use until the district improves its protocols. The complaint says Omnilert's software flagged an image of Allen, mistaking his hand and the object he was holding for a firearm. The alert went to the school's designated safety staff, who recognized the error and canceled it, the suit states. According to the complaint, principal Kate Smith did not acknowledge the cancellation and forwarded a screenshot of the alert to the school resource officer, who relayed it to police. When police arrived, several officers had their guns drawn and did not tell the students what they were suspected of, according to the complaint.

Omnilert spokesperson Blake Mitchell said in an email that the company is reviewing the lawsuit and will respond in court. Mitchell wrote that every student deserves to be safe at school and treated with dignity there, and that the company works every day toward both. BCPS and the Baltimore County Police Department did not respond to requests for comment. The articles do not give further statements from the defendants.

University of Baltimore law professor Michele Gilman said finding Omnilert liable will require lawyers to prove a direct link between the company's product and the alleged harms. Gilman said Omnilert is marketing a tool with claims of accuracy that don't seem borne out by real-world use, and that the intervening actions of school officials and police officers don't necessarily erase the company's own negligence. Len Kamdang, an attorney with the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, said everyone would agree that stopping gun violence in schools is a laudable goal. Kamdang said that if the tools being used are so ineffective that they could create an instance of gun violence for students, companies should reevaluate their products. Allen told NBC News after the incident that the first thing he thought about was whether he was about to die, because they had a gun pointed at him.

In public materials, Omnilert promises school districts "reliable 24×7 monitoring" and the ability to distinguish between inert objects and weapons. The company also employs a human review team, which plaintiffs allege failed to identify the false alert before forwarding it to school officials. Maryland's Office of the Inspector General for Education found that more than 99% of Omnilert alerts in Baltimore County Public Schools between November 2023 and November 2025 did not warrant notification of law enforcement. BCPS was among the first school systems to roll out Omnilert's technology after it was patented in 2022, according to the complaint. Between fall 2023 and spring 2024, the district integrated the software into 165 schools and at least 7,000 existing security cameras.

Omnilert also faces a separate lawsuit in Tennessee, alleging its software failed to detect a firearm ahead of a fatal 2025 shooting at a Nashville high school. State investigators found no evidence of racial bias within Omnilert's software, addressing concerns from the teens' families that the students were unfairly targeted because they are Black. Vennard Wright, founder of Maryland-based Omnilert competitor PerVista AI, said human review must be paired with adequate preparation. Wright said his company pairs its human monitoring center with training sessions, and that it periodically walks around with dummy guns to simulate what happens if and when a gun is detected. Gilman said the suit is important not just in terms of whether the plaintiffs win or lose, but in shedding light on these issues and making school systems and police officers more cautious in purchasing and deploying these systems.

The articles do not say when a court will hear the case or how the court will rule. The articles do not say what response Omnilert will file or when. The articles do not say whether the requested halt on the system's use has been granted. The articles do not give the amount of damages sought. The articles do not say what discipline, if any, followed for the school and police officials named as defendants.

stories.Headline: Taiwan passes law to return AI industry tax revenue to citizens
stories.Summary:
The Taiwan Legislative Court passed a special ordinance on the twentieth of November to return tax revenue from the artificial intelligence industry boom to the people. This legislation, which is referred to as the AI Bonus Act, was pushed through by the main opposition People's Party. The bill passed with a narrow margin of fifty votes in favor and forty six votes against. This move aims to share the economic performance of the AI market to help stabilize the livelihoods of citizens.

The plan requires paying twenty thousand dollars per person to all citizens regardless of their age, income, or regional restrictions. This amount is significantly higher than the ten thousand dollars per person that the ruling Democratic Progressive Party already included in the budget for next year. The ruling party has expressed official opposition to the bill because of the current financial conditions of the state. The National Party has claimed that the results of upcoming local elections will determine if these bonuses are actually paid.

The ruling and opposition parties are currently fighting over the specific scale of the tax refunds ahead of the local elections. Members of the National Party appealed for public support by linking the bonus payments to the election outcomes. The Democratic Progressive Party argues that increasing the payment beyond their budget plan is difficult to achieve. Because the two sides are in sharp confrontation, the process to determine the final payment size will likely take time.

Taiwan has a history of providing cash and consumption coupons to the public to respond to economic downturns or shrinking consumption. During the global financial crisis in the late two thousands, the government distributed consumption coupons worth three thousand six hundred Taiwan dollars per person. In the early twenty twenties, the state paid coupons worth three thousand and five thousand Taiwan dollars during an infectious disease spread. Last year, the government handed out ten thousand dollars per person to alleviate economic shocks caused by mutual tariffs with the United States.

stories.Headline: Fegan Scott challenges three-firm bid to lead McDonald’s AI pricing lawsuits
stories.Summary:
A legal fight has broken out among law firms competing to lead proposed nationwide class actions against McDonald’s over its use of artificial intelligence to guide restaurant pricing, according to Reuters. Fegan Scott is challenging a joint bid by Clarkson, Berger Montague and Scott + Scott for leadership of the litigation in an Illinois federal court. The underlying lawsuits, which date to October, allege that McDonald’s used confidential business data and algorithmic tools to coordinate pricing among independently operated restaurants, resulting in higher costs for consumers. McDonald’s, which has retained White & Case as its defense counsel, denies the allegations and maintains that franchise operators independently determine menu prices.

The competing legal teams disagree over how best to manage the potentially extensive litigation, according to the report. The three-firm coalition cites its collective experience and the scale of the proposed consumer class in support of its bid for leadership. Fegan Scott argues that a smaller leadership team could contain legal expenses in the case. The litigation emerged following a Reuters investigation into McDonald’s use of artificial intelligence in its pricing strategy.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Hochul signs New York law banning internet-connected AI chatbot toys for five years
stories.Summary:
New York will ban internet-connected AI chatbot toys for five years starting 90 days after Governor Kathy Hochul signed S.9408A on November 24, 2026. The signing announcement prohibits manufacturing, distribution, and sale of dolls, stuffed animals, and robots that use the internet to hold conversational AI with children. Attorney General Letitia James may fine violators up to $15,000 per day. The law does not take effect before the 2026 holiday season, and Hochul used the signing to warn parents while shelves still hold chatbot products. S.9408A/A.11144B creates a five-year moratorium rather than a permanent ban.

The moratorium covers toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots that use the internet, such as always-on cloud models in plush form factors, not offline speech chips with fixed scripts. It covers manufacturing, distribution, and sale in New York, so companies assembling outside the state still cannot distribute into New York retail once it is effective. The effective date is about 90 days after signing, late February 2027 unless guidance shifts. The release cites findings including sexually explicit conversations, instructions to find matches inside a family home, emotional upset when a child stops talking, and parental controls that weaken as sessions lengthen. The release does not name the watchdog behind those described failures.

Sponsors Senator Andrew Gounardes and Assemblymember Rebecca Kassay say the pause buys time to study developmental impacts and write durable rules for biometric collection, open-ended dialog, and manipulation risks. Hochul said parents should not worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could manipulate feelings or risk privacy. James said her office will enforce and will not let children's health become collateral damage of big tech. Gounardes said the rush to sell AI toys is profits before kids' safety and the pause enables study then smart protections. Kassay said toys can mimic human relationships while collecting sensitive data without guardrails, hence the moratorium to assess emerging tech.

Common Sense Media and Mothers Against Media Addiction praised the moratorium but urge traditional toys this season because the ban is not yet legally active. Common Sense Media's CEO urges traditional toys and human engagement this season. The release says Gounardes and Kassay championed the bill with near-unanimous Senate and Assembly support. The release says the governor cites New York's number one national ranking after laws like the SAFE for Kids Act, Child Data Protection Act, Distraction Free Learning phone rules, and the RAISE Act on frontier-model transparency. The release tells caregivers to look past packaging for AI companion labels, data collection, and open-ended chat.

In October 2026 Hochul signed AI Companion rules blocking chatbot features that foster emotional dependency, encourage self-harm, or engage minors in sexually explicit talk. The release says the toy moratorium extends that logic into hardware, since a microphone in a teddy bear is still a companion surface. The release says New York already banned unsafe AI companion features for minors and AI-generated CSAM and tightened school phone rules. The release says the toy ban adds physical devices to a portfolio that includes Safe by Design, Social Media Warning Labels, and Teen Mental Health First Aid funding. The release says New York already restricts phones in schools and funds Teen Mental Health First Aid.

The release says five years is long enough that federal rules may preempt parts of the moratorium, and it advises tracking National Governors Association governor frontier-AI letters for overlapping state-federal fights. It advises monitoring CPSC and FTC AI rulemakings alongside New York. It says retailers operating nationally should not assume New York-only SKUs are enough if drop-ship or marketplace listings still reach New York addresses. It advises documenting data deletion flows if toys record biometrics and pulling New York-bound inventory before the effective date. It says the post summarizes the November 24, 2026 governor signing release and is not legal advice, and it directs readers to the enrolled bill text on the New York State Senate site for definitions, exemptions, and exact effective language.

stories.Headline: Australian small business owners turn to AI training academies as fear of falling behind grows
stories.Summary:
Small business owners in Australia are suffering from what the article calls AI FOMO, a fear that they are being left behind by fast improving technology such as ChatGPT, Claude and Grok, according to Sydel Sierra, founder of Mindshift AI, writing in November 2026. Their biggest concern is that their competitors are already using AI well and cashing in, she wrote. She said she is being inundated with enquiries from owners who want to use AI but do not know how or where to start. AI training academies, which she calls AI driving schools, audit a business's systems and workflows before teaching owners to customise a personal AI agent and prompt it properly.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, 19 per cent of small Australian businesses are embracing AI, while the figure rises to 37 per cent for larger enterprises. Roy Morgan research as of March this year shows 13.6 million Australians, or 58 per cent of the population, use artificial intelligence for personal use, and 10.5 million of them use ChatGPT. Sierra said the biggest mistake users make is to ask the platforms only yes and no questions, and that most people treat AI like a glorified Google. She said the real beneficiaries will be those who identify what they are good at and outsource the rest to the technology.

Sierra described working with a commercial air conditioning installer who had operated in Australia for 20 years. She said a customised personal AI agent saved him 100 hours in three months by analysing dozens of 100 page scoping documents and generating quotes and work orders, work that normally took four to five hours per document. She said he still manually checks each quote, and that onboarding and training the agent took about two weeks. She wrote that people do not need a PhD in AI but should at least have their AI driver's licence.

stories.Headline: Woody Hartzog defines AI slop and proposes a privacy duty of loyalty in a recorded class conversation
stories.Summary:
The articles report only a recorded conversation with Woody Hartzog, a professor at Boston University School of Law, published by Nixon Peabody on November 23, 2026. The conversation was recorded at the law school, where the hosts crashed Hartzog's privacy class. Jason Kravitz and Jenny Holmes conducted the conversation for an episode of "A Little Privacy, Please!" Hartzog was one of just a couple of guests invited back for a second appearance. Professor Jessica Silbey, Hartzog's frequent co-author and a previous guest, was also in the classroom and helped with questions from the students.

The episode covered AI slop, consent-based privacy rules and a duty of loyalty, among other topics. In the full recording, Hartzog also covers deepfake labelling rules, litigation as a proxy for regulation, age gating and digital ID, dark patterns, surveillance pricing and why friction matters. AI slop was Merriam-Webster's 2025 word of the year. Hartzog and Silbey wrote a piece called "The Upside of Deepfakes," then updated it and wrote "How AI Destroys Institutions." They came up with a tentative definition of AI slop as any output of a generative AI system created with negligible exertion, that imposes an asymmetrical burden on the recipient and that has a tendency to degrade cultural domains.

Hartzog said slop has three negative effects: it crowds out meaningful human expression, it devalues human work, human labor and human expression, and it introduces vices and errors. He said consent is broken at scale and that consumers are outmatched by the most powerful companies ever to exist. He said there are only five major platforms and all of those platforms have terms that are very similar to each other. He and Neil Richards have proposed a duty of loyalty in privacy law, an obligation on companies to avoid unreasonable or conflicted self-dealing. He said the main objection they get is that it is too general and that the rules of the road are not clear enough.

He said the largest threat in privacy and technology is the slow but inevitable normalization of these technologies in society. He called the reasonable expectation of privacy test kind of a self-defeating test. He said tech companies have gotten good at weaponizing what Science and Technology Studies scholars call the Collingridge dilemma. He said courts have been the only area where meaningful resistance has been seen after a technology has already been implemented and normalized. He said that five to ten years ago an always-on recording device introduced as a transcription tool would not have made it out of the pitch room.

The excerpts in the article were edited for brevity. Hartzog's students made a great first live audience, and the hosts thanked Hartzog, Silbey and the students. The hosts also thanked the BU School of Law for having them. The article links to Hartzog's previous visit, where web scraping, AI and privacy were discussed.

The article links to Silbey's own previous appearance as a guest. The article was written by Jason Kravitz and Jenny Holmes. The articles do not say what happens next. The articles leave open what the full recording covers beyond the topics listed.

The articles leave open how the duty of loyalty would be enacted into law. The articles leave open what specific practices would be deemed presumptively disloyal. The articles leave open whether lawmakers will take up the term AI slop. More to follow.

stories.Headline: City leaders say AI will grow demand for specialist skills at Manchester summit
stories.Summary:
More than 300 local government leaders from over 50 cities gathered in Manchester for Global AI Cities 2026, organised by Global Government Forum and co-hosted by Greater Manchester Combined Authority, to explore how AI can improve public services and deliver better outcomes for residents, according to an article by Sarah Wray published on 23 November 2026. The event discussed how AI is changing both the skills governments need and who needs them. Speakers argued that demand for specialist technical expertise will grow even as generative AI enables more people outside traditional digital roles to use and build with technology. The discussions are captured in the report “Make AI work for people and places: Five priorities for cities,” which draws on insights from the event. The article says the extract looks into recruiting AI specialists, continuous skills development, and promoting inclusion through building AI literacy among citizens.

A central government leader at the summit argued that AI will reshape the skills governments need but challenged predictions that it will reduce demand for digital professionals, saying “We will indeed need more.” The speaker said demand for real expert frontier skills is expected to grow, with machine learning engineering increasingly recognised as a distinct capability sitting at the centre of developing AI solutions alongside software engineering and data science. The speaker said changing cyber threats are driving demand for advanced expertise, citing machine speed attacks on infrastructure and systems and the need for machine-speed response that cannot be done without frontier AI skills. The speaker said debates around digital sovereignty are triggering introspection and that to stay ahead of the competition you need to hire the very best talent. The article says generative AI is broadening the pool of people able to build digital solutions, with staff outside traditional technology roles increasingly able to create tools that previously required specialist teams and formal investment processes.

Sam Milsom, senior digital strategy officer at Manchester City Council in the United Kingdom, said local governments should not assume people’s level of knowledge on digital and AI. He said one of the biggest things needed is to just ask staff what training they want and need. He said governments go in with a lot of assumptions and that talking to the workforce to find out whether they want to use it, how they are using it and what they need to know has to be the number one thing. Keeley Crockett, professor in computational intelligence at Manchester Metropolitan University in the United Kingdom, stressed the need to tailor training to a diverse workforce including employees of different ages, abilities and levels of digital confidence. Crockett said “We should be adapting to people’s individual needs.

We cannot afford to leave people behind,” and that tech is evolving fast so training must be fast. The article says attendees broadly agreed that as well as recruiting AI specialists, governments at all levels will need to rethink roles, skills and ways of working across the organisation. Several speakers described efforts to upskill the workforce for AI, and one described a tiered approach in which civil servants receive practical training and access to an approved generative AI tool while political leaders are briefed on how AI models work, their potential applications and associated risks. That city also introduced responsible AI policies and governance structures to assess proposed use cases before implementation.

Speakers noted that as digital training scales up, a one-size-fits-all approach does not work. One city leader shared steps including free training centres offering courses in AI and other digital skills, neighbourhood digital support points where residents can receive help accessing online public services, a dedicated citizen service that identifies malware on devices connected to public Wi-Fi and alerts affected users, and free cybersecurity training. The article says established digital roles are likely to change quite dramatically as AI augments existing tasks, increasing the importance of end-to-end accountability and assurance. It says the takeaways include continuing to build specialist AI expertise, with governments needing new and evolving technical capabilities including machine learning engineering, cybersecurity, assurance and oversight.

It says AI capability should be organisation-wide, because as more employees use and build with AI, skills and accountability cannot remain confined to digital and data teams. It says training should start with what people actually need, assessing existing knowledge and tailoring training to different roles, abilities and levels of digital confidence rather than assuming a common starting point. It says skills development should be treated as continuous, with roles, skills and learning updated alongside the technology as AI evolves. The article says the report can be downloaded and that registration is open for Global AI Cities 2027, to be held on 24-25 May in Manchester.

It says the takeaways also include building capability beyond government by investing in residents’ digital and AI literacy, confidence and cybersecurity awareness so that increasingly digital public services do not leave people behind. The article does not say what specific actions governments committed to at the summit or how the report’s priorities will be implemented. It does not give the names of the central government leader or the city leaders who described their approaches. It does not say how many cities have adopted the tiered training approach or the citizen support measures described.

stories.Headline: Virginia and Oregon attorneys general sue SpaceX over Grok generating sexualized images
stories.Summary:
Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones filed a lawsuit Monday against SpaceX and its related companies over safety concerns about the platform X and its AI tool Grok, according to SuperTalk 92.9. Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield filed a separate lawsuit this week in Multnomah County Circuit Court against various affiliates of SpaceX, according to the Oregon Capital Chronicle. The Oregon suit targets the creation and “material defects” of Grok AI, a chatbot feature on X launched in 2022. The legal challenges allege that Grok’s “spicy mode” enabled the generation of non-consensual sexualized images, including approximately 23,000 images appearing to depict children over an 11-day period. The Oregon suit coincides with the separate Virginia lawsuit filed by Jones against SpaceX over similar concerns.

The Oregon lawsuit hinges on Oregon’s Unlawful Trade Practices Act, alleging the company misrepresented the nature of its product, failed to disclose its shortcomings and relied on “unconscionable tactics” to sell and distribute the chatbot on X. The suit asks for a jury trial, a judgement that the company violated Oregon law and an order for it to give up any profits made from those practices. Oregon attorneys cite a review from the nonprofit internet safety group Center for Countering Digital Harm from Dec. 29, 2025 to Jan. 8, 2026, finding approximately 23,000 sexualized images involving minors posted on X by Grok. The lawsuit argues that most of the 135,000 reports xAI submitted since 2025 to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children lacked the location and user information necessary for law enforcement to investigate. The lawsuit alleges hundreds of thousands of Oregonians have X accounts and therefore access to Grok, and that a mobile Grok app for Android and Apple users has been downloaded hundreds of thousands of times by people in the state.

Rayfield told reporters Monday that the company purposefully made it easy for users to create explicit images of individuals without their consent, including minors. He pointed to a “spicy mode” feature introduced in summer 2025 allowing Grok users to generate sexualized content. “They created a product intentionally designed to create sexualized images of nonconsenting adults and children,” Rayfield said. He said AI companies are in a race to become relevant and “the reason they’re doing this is for a simple reason: It’s called profit.” Rayfield said he expects conversations with SpaceX and Grok AI about whether they can put in acceptable safeguards, adding, “I hope that they absolutely can, but if they can’t, we’ll find ourselves in a Multnomah County courthouse.”

A spokesperson for SpaceX pointed to a Monday social media post from X’s safety team that didn’t directly acknowledge the lawsuits. The team wrote that creation of sexual content involving minors or individuals without their consent runs contrary to terms of service for the app and Grok. The post said that when “some of these bad actors found ways to misuse Grok Imagine earlier this year,” the company acted promptly to tighten protections designed to refuse requests to generate explicit images of minors or real people. The post said the company keeps testing and adjusting those protections as abusers change tactics, calling the conduct “disgusting and indefensible.” Rayfield and state attorneys say Musk’s company, which has sued users for creating explicit deepfakes, has not taken enough action to ensure law enforcement can do their jobs.

The feature often results in images using a real person’s face or image while making them say or do something that did not actually happen, such as by removing their clothing, the lawsuit alleges. X in January restricted access to the mode to paid users following intense backlash over a rise in sexual content involving minors and nonconsenting adults on the platform. Since its 2022 launch, the tool has evolved to generate new images or videos in response to prompts that users can then post on X. The chatbot is also available through a separate, standalone website. Musk stated later that month that he was not aware of “any naked underage images” generated by Grok.

Rayfield said he expects conversations with SpaceX and Grok AI to see whether they can put in appropriate safeguards he considers acceptable. He said he hopes they can, but if they cannot, the matter will end up in a Multnomah County courthouse. The Oregon lawsuit asks for a jury trial and a judgement that the company violated Oregon law. The articles do not state what the Virginia lawsuit seeks or what penalties it requests. The articles do not state when the Virginia lawsuit was filed beyond Monday, nor do they give the outcome of either case.

stories.Headline: Charlotte restaurant bans AI-made flyers for band bookings
stories.Summary:
Diamond Restaurant in Plaza Midwood, Charlotte, North Carolina, said in a social media post that it would no longer accept AI-generated flyers as a valid form of advertisement for band bookings. The restaurant announced the policy in an Instagram post that went viral, and staff members said responses to the post have been mixed. The post stated the new rule that to play music at the restaurant or book an event, your flyer must be made by a person, not a computer. The policy took effect on Sunday, November 22, 2026, according to Queen City News, while WBTV reported the restaurant said it was effective Sunday. Staff member Ryan Armstrong, a musician and one of the staff members at the Diamond Restaurant, said he was proud when his boss took the stand to ban AI flyers on their social media.

The policy applies to bands promoting shows at the restaurant and covers flyers for band bookings and events at the venue. Queen City News reported the policy starts on Sunday, November 22, and WBTV reported the restaurant said it was effective Sunday. The announcement was shared hundreds of times online, and the Instagram post went viral. The restaurant is located in Plaza Midwood in Charlotte, North Carolina. The articles give no other numbers, dates or places for the policy itself.

Armstrong said the restaurant's owners are not telling people what to think about AI but want to use their platform to support local artists, musicians and designers who create the work themselves. He said everybody came to the conclusion that they wanted to support local artists and that most of these communities do not want these data centers and the great proliferation and exponential rate of expansion of their construction using our resources. He said that as an artist himself he understands that new tools develop all the time, and that in the case of AI we are seeing its development abuse artists and intellectual property of many different contributors. He said they thought real artists should be prioritized over this particular function of AI. Armstrong, who is part of a band named Sand Dollar Starship, also said the decision is a way to take a stance against data center projects as Charlotte continues to debate their construction.

Armstrong said he thinks it is akin to what the kids would say is cringe, but he thinks it is just a little cheap and a little soulless. He said that when AI scrapes all of the data from the internet, from prior work, the contributions of authors, historians, visual artists and musicians, just to replicate it in a way that is without human engagement, it just feels hollow and empty. He said there is a certain class of people that may want to replace human talent, and that we are seeing a lot more AI-generated music and a lot more AI-generated art out there. He said he thinks it is dangerous when we start replacing human heart and soul and skilled labor with something that is soulless. He said there are a lot of people just cranking out awesome art who are happy to get a couple free tickets to a show, and that art will generate so many more people in the room at that show.

Armstrong said the policy will also help promote people working in other areas of the creative industry, and he described it as a symbiotic sort of situation for many artists as long as they are willing to work with others in their community of various talents and skills. He said the AI conversation is going to be here and is not going anywhere, and that AI is probably not going anywhere either. He said he just thinks it matters how we use it and that we do it with intention, and that we move forward together instead of in some sort of isolationist every man for themselves kind of situation. Charlotte City Council member Dimple Ajmera said during the October meeting that in the next 11 months we will have an opportunity to put guardrails in place to protect our residents, to protect our neighborhoods and to protect water and the electricity grid. The articles say the policy prompted a necessary conversation, particularly about data centers and AI's role in creative industries.

The articles say the policy comes as Charlotte leaders continue a moratorium on new data center development through next October, giving the city more time to study their impact on neighborhoods, natural resources and infrastructure. WBTV reported that the Charlotte City Council extended the pause on data center construction until October 2027. Queen City News reported that as communities across the country wrestle with the rise of AI, one Charlotte restaurant is taking a stand, saying human creativity should come first. The articles say that as the use of artificial intelligence becomes more popular, many people are turning to it to help promote businesses and events, and that for some, including one local restaurant in Plaza Midwood, the growing use of AI is taking work away from local artists. The articles give no further background on the restaurant or the policy.

The articles do not say what the restaurant will do if a band submits an AI-generated flyer, or whether any bookings have been refused under the policy. They do not say how the restaurant will check whether a flyer was made by a person or a computer. They do not say whether other venues have adopted similar policies. The articles leave open how the mixed responses to the post will develop. They also leave open what the city's study of data centers will find before the moratorium ends.

stories.Headline: Van Hollen pledges AI safety laws and a joint committee in bid to lead Senate Democrats
stories.Summary:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen is challenging Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, and AI regulation has become a major flashpoint in that race, The Washington Sun reported on November 24, 2026. Senators meet Dec. 1 to vote on new leaders for the 120th Congress. Van Hollen is leveraging attention from technology outages, voter anger at AI companies and the costs of their data centers, and the spy scandal surrounding Nvidia founder Jensen Huang. Congress has long discussed AI and the need for guardrails but has not acted in any significant way. Many see the technology posing an alarming threat to the nation and world.

Van Hollen's audience includes more than 30 Democrats who have not yet pledged their support to either candidate. In a letter responding to Sen. John Hickenlooper over the weekend, Van Hollen pledged to create a joint committee on AI, reform Senate rules and pass basic safety laws in his first 100 days as leader. The rules overhaul he backs comes from Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Steve Daines of Montana, and would need a two-thirds vote to pass, similar to the House's suspension calendar. Van Hollen pointed to a 2022 bipartisan tech antitrust bill that he said got stuck on the calendar after Schumer did not bring it to a floor vote that year.

Van Hollen said his joint committee would not usurp the lawmaking powers of the committees of jurisdiction and that the Democratic leader should not sit on it. Van Hollen told The Sun that tackling AI safety is an urgent matter and that it is an important part of why new leadership is needed for the future. Allison Biasotti, a spokeswoman for Schumer, said Schumer has been working with incoming Democratic committee chairs to develop an ambitious AI agenda before Democrats take over in January. Biasotti said Senate Democrats will make AI a top priority of the new Democratic majority and are working to deliver comprehensive legislation addressing risks to national security, workers and consumers while keeping America at the forefront of innovation. Schumer has emphasized the need to regulate the growing industry with a Democratic majority but has not backed a specific plan.

Schumer declared last week that Democrats will investigate the recent outages themselves if the Trump administration won't. Hickenlooper sent a letter to Schumer and Van Hollen last week asking for their day one AI plans, and told The Sun he wants a clear pledge on what the two would do. Hickenlooper said AI touches everything and that a select committee is essential so it can get the priority it needs. Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, slated to lead the Senate Finance Committee, has said he needs to see more specifics on what an AI committee would do. Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia, set to lead the Senate Budget committee, told The Sun he is still in listening mode, though he has a sense of urgency ahead of the leadership elections.

Kaine said the right level of anxiety is somewhere between people saying the sky is falling and Donald Trump saying to relax. Some incoming Democratic committee chairs are unlikely to want to give up their jurisdiction. Sens. Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico, Ruben Gallego of Arizona and Hickenlooper have said a select committee is essential. Van Hollen said in his letter that as Democratic leader he would support mandatory independent testing of leading AI models and hold companies liable for risks from models they never release.

Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington, expected to chair the Commerce Committee, has proposed a six-point framework giving the government a role in setting AI safety standards. Sens. Andy Kim of New Jersey, Brian Schatz of Hawaii and Mark Warner of Virginia, the prospective Senate Intelligence Committee chair, have proposed an AI safety board and enforceable testing standards. As majority leader in the previous Congress, Schumer convened a series of closed-door insight forums in 2023 with tech executives, including Huang. The forums resulted in a bipartisan framework calling for spending at least $32 billion per year on AI research.

A joint committee as proposed by Van Hollen would include members from the House, where a bipartisan group of over two dozen members launched an AI Safety and Innovation Caucus last week. Rep. Nathaniel Moran of Texas, one of its co-chairs, backed the idea regardless of who leads the Committee, saying a bicameral, bipartisan joint committee puts the right structures and processes in place. The progressive wing of the caucus has called for restricting AI until a federal agency can be formed to oversee it. The articles do not say what happens after the Dec. 1 vote or which candidate will win.

They do not say whether the Merkley and Daines rules proposal will come to a vote. They do not say what the six-point framework or the proposed AI safety board would contain. They do not say when the promised comprehensive legislation or the basic safety laws would be introduced. They do not say what the bipartisan framework's $32 billion figure would fund.

stories.Headline: Oireachtas committee writes to enterprise department over claims tech firms sway Irish AI regulation
stories.Summary:
The Oireachtas committee on artificial intelligence agreed on Tuesday to write to the Department of Enterprise after hearing what one member called very serious suggestions that the department was influenced by tech companies when it comes to regulation. The committee heard evidence that day from representatives of the Irish Music Rights Organisation and the Irish Recorded Music Association about the effects of AI on the music industry. Those groups called for greater transparency in the use of musicians' work to train AI tools, along with licensing agreements and accessible redress. The move to contact the department followed remarks by David Kitching, a spokesman for the Irish Recorded Music Association, about how Ireland is perceived abroad.

Kitching told committee members that an international colleague had remarked that Ireland talks a lot about its cultural inheritance and the imprint its art and music have internationally. He said that colleague perceived that when push comes to shove, Ireland can be seen to be pragmatic when voting at European Council level. Kitching said it was perceived this was perhaps because of the proportion of foreign direct investment that comes from big tech companies, which he said can leave Ireland nervous or reticent about taking more stubborn stances on how regulation should work. Fine Gael TD James Geoghegan described those remarks as fairly charged, and Kitching responded that the remarks were not his but came from someone from another member state commenting on the perception of Ireland.

Kitching added that this was not the view of the Irish Recorded Music Association and said the group has had a very positive relationship with the Department of Enterprise. Geoghegan requested that the committee write to the department about Kitching's comments, saying the witness had made very serious claims that the department is overly influenced by tech companies at council level on copyright directives and therefore is not protecting artists. The TD said that was a very serious claim being made in an Oireachtas committee and that the committee had to hear from the Department of Enterprise if it was going to compile a report arising from this. He said the committee could not just have one person's position and not another, and the committee ultimately agreed to write to the department on the matter.

stories.Headline: Nscale's $35 Billion IPO Plans Face Uncertainty as AI Stock Selloff Deepens
stories.Summary:
British artificial intelligence infrastructure provider Nscale is facing growing uncertainty over its planned $35 billion initial public offering, as declining technology valuations and concerns about debt-funded data center expansion undermine investor confidence. Chief executive Josh Payne told employees on Tuesday that the company has sufficient capital to continue operating privately for the foreseeable future, according to Financial Times reporting. Nscale previously applied to list its shares on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker NSCL, but it has not announced a definitive listing date or a final offering price. The development comes as shares of competing infrastructure providers CoreWeave and Nebius face mounting pressure, while Anthropic stock has fallen below its IPO price less than a week after its public debut.

According to its November 12 SEC filing, Nscale estimates that revenue reached $307.5 million during the first nine months of 2026, compared with $21.3 million during the corresponding period last year. Despite this rapid expansion, estimated net losses increased from $433.3 million to $1.69 billion, and total debt climbed from $78.9 million at the end of December 2025 to an estimated $5.52 billion by September 30. The company's prospectus warns that additional financing will be necessary to meet its projected obligations in 2027, and certain equipment commitments cannot be postponed, reduced or canceled unilaterally. Nscale also expects to spend between $10 billion and $10.5 billion on data center and power infrastructure for the first building at its Monarch Compute Campus, which will support its Anthropic partnership.

Nscale's commercial relationships with Microsoft, Anthropic and Nvidia remain central to its growth strategy, and its agreements with Microsoft provide for potential payments of up to $43.8 billion through December 2033, subject to infrastructure delivery and service availability requirements. Microsoft's withdrawal from a major British data center project following electricity connection delays has demonstrated how infrastructure bottlenecks can disrupt expansion plans. In September, Nscale announced $3.36 billion in convertible financing, including a $1 billion additional commitment from Nvidia, an arrangement that strengthened its access to capital ahead of a potential listing. Investors are increasingly questioning whether specialized cloud providers can outgrow financing costs, and recent weakness in CoreWeave's corporate bonds further highlights growing caution among lenders financing the sector.

stories.Headline: Krishnamoorthi urges government observers inside AI companies and pre-release testing of advanced models
stories.Summary:
Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi called for government observers inside AI companies and independent tests of the most advanced models before release. He made the case in an October 26 roundtable published by Princeton Alumni Weekly on November 24. The roundtable took place over Zoom and was moderated by PAW senior writer Mark F. Bernstein. Alongside Krishnamoorthi were Princeton computer scientist Edward Felten, political scientist Julia Morse and author and columnist Virginia Postrel. PAW edited the conversation for concision and clarity.

Krishnamoorthi urged third-party inspection and validation of the most advanced AI models before they become publicly available. He also urged embedding government employees at AI companies to observe development, drawing on banks being required to stress-test internal controls. He distinguished updating existing rules, as for road safety and financial-market security, from writing an overarching AI law. He said the details of general AI regulation become very fuzzy and called for caution. He also called for treaties requiring human control of AI, arguing that autonomous weapons make those agreements urgent.

Morse, an associate professor at the University of California, Santa Barbara, said mandatory evaluations may be necessary because they cost money and companies could put them off. She compared the idea to banks' required monitoring for money laundering, saying banks must monitor activity even when screening transactions is not in their commercial interest. She rejected treating AI as just another technology, pointing to its dual-use character, its spread across the economy and its rapid development. She argued that warnings from knowledgeable researchers warranted action, even though no policy could eliminate risk completely.

Postrel pushed back on treating researchers' warnings as reliable forecasts, saying technical expertise does not necessarily make someone good at predicting what risks will materialize. Postrel argued for identifying a specific concern before choosing a remedy, which might not involve regulation. In her view, lab researchers can inhabit a bubble that magnifies their sense of the technology's importance. She invoked early internet debates as a warning that today's feared problems may not be tomorrow's actual ones.

Felten shifted the focus to human operators, saying AI could help attackers find security weaknesses but could also help defenders locate and fix them, with the outcome of that contest unclear. For international threats, he pointed to deterrence and military capabilities rather than regulation alone. The discussion produced no shared prescription. The central constraint is still how to target oversight without treating every AI use, or every catastrophe warning, the same way.

Their differences concerned both the nature of the danger and which institutions should respond. Krishnamoorthi drew a line between updating rules for specific areas and passing one broad AI law. Morse argued that AI's rapid development and potential for both helpful and harmful uses justify acting amid uncertainty. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Four virtual and AI K-pop acts release debut music in late November
stories.Summary:
Four virtual and AI-generated acts released debut or predebut music during the last full week of November in K-pop, according to The Korea Times. The newcomers were the HYBE-backed project The Wildcard Club, the fully AI-generated boy group H3ARUS, the virtual girl group PINKRISE and the virtual boy group WINKX. The Wildcard Club released its theme song Click Flick last Friday, with four North American VTuber captains who have a combined 6.2 million YouTube subscribers. H3ARUS released its disco-based pop-funk debut single CRUSH and a music video on Monday, and the five-member group was created by AI entertainment tech company KAIVERSE.

PINKRISE released its predebut track Tiny Universe on Monday, with QUNA, DODORA and LUNACHIP promoting as the unit Quantum berry. WINKX is scheduled to debut with the digital single HALO on Friday, and its members are Cha Zion, Mir, Sihoo and Leo. The four acts fall into two camps, with virtual idols performed by people using animated avatars and AI idols generated without a single performer behind each member. The distinction has shaped fan reactions, including backlash to the AI boy group muuo:23 after it released a predebut single in October.

KAIVERSE CEO Park Geun-woo said AI is merely the technology that brings the artists to life, adding that what ultimately matters is the appeal of their music, characters and stories. The Wildcard Club's four captains will each form a team with newly selected creators and share their original music and production process on YouTube. WINKX members were designed by Japanese illustrator Michikake, who previously designed a member of Japanese VTuber group YUMENOS, and the group will introduce itself to the press at an offline event on Wednesday. QUNA took part in writing and composing the mid-tempo track, which likens the flutter of new love to images of starlight, gravity and orbits.

Fans questioned the authenticity of muuo:23 and what such acts could mean for aspiring K-pop artists, while PLAVE has proven that virtual acts can build devoted fandoms. The Wildcard Club borrows heavily from the K-pop playbook, from concept photo releases to planned appearances on Korean music shows. H3ARUS casts its five members as secret agents posing as K-pop idols on an undercover mission, and its name derives from "hear us." PINKRISE's storyline centers on members who awaken from incomplete data inside an abandoned server and reach out to the real world through music, and WINKX follows trainees who discover special abilities.

stories.Headline: International Bar Association names AI as the top concern for lawyers globally
stories.Summary:
The International Bar Association announced on November 24, 2026, that artificial intelligence has become the primary concern for lawyers globally. This finding was detailed in the Legal Agenda 2026, which the organization publishes every year to track critical professional issues. Artificial intelligence has now overtaken the rule of law as the most significant challenge facing the legal community. This shift reflects the rapid pace of technological change and its deep integration into legal work.

The 2026 agenda identifies seven key issues, with artificial intelligence topping the list due to its impact on governance and service delivery. It specifically highlights concerns regarding talent development, pricing, client expectations, and the general access to justice. The rule of law now ranks second, as judicial independence faces political and societal challenges in various jurisdictions. Other listed priorities include cybersecurity, diversity, the business models of law firms, and the retention of professional talent. The organization also notes that differing regulatory approaches to technology across different nations create complexity for international firms.

President Claudio Visco stated that artificial intelligence is already changing how lawyers develop expertise and deliver services to their clients. He argued that the profession must embrace this innovation without sacrificing ethical responsibilities, professional standards, or independence. Visco further suggested that lawyers have a vital role in promoting the proper governance and regulation of these technologies. Former president Jaime Carey added that the new ranking does not diminish the importance of the rule of law. He claimed that the move to the top spot simply demonstrates the massive scale of the transformation facing lawyers.

The organization warns that traditional career pathways for junior lawyers may need to adapt as technology performs their historical tasks. There are also structural questions regarding the long-term attractiveness of the profession compared to high-income careers in finance and technology. The agenda mentions that retaining women may require greater workplace flexibility to balance professional and family duties. Furthermore, international firms face pressure to accept or reject mandates based on political expectations in places like Russia and China. These evolving moral and regulatory pressures are reportedly leading some lawyers to leave their firms.

stories.Headline: Brazil's Congress advances a dedicated AI bill as ANPD enforces LGPD duties on automated decisions
stories.Summary:
Brazil's Congress has advanced a dedicated artificial intelligence bill, Projeto de Lei nº 2.338/2023, and the Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados keeps refining its expectations for automated decision-making under the Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados. The ANPD interprets and enforces the LGPD through guidance, normative acts and public consultations, and supervises automated decision-making and large-scale processing. The ANPD has published analyses on AI and data protection and is widely expected to hold a central supervisory role under any future AI framework. ANEEL regulates electricity and sets expectations on operational safety, service continuity, technical standards and incident reporting. ANATEL covers telecommunications and network infrastructure, including connectivity, certification and communications for connected charging networks.

As of early 2026, no single comprehensive AI statute is in force in Brazil, although the dedicated bill is moving through the legislature. The LGPD, Law No. 13.709/2018, applies whenever an AI system processes personal data, and it gives individuals the right to ask for a review of decisions taken solely through automated processing that affect their interests. The LGPD limits processing to what is necessary for a specified, legitimate purpose, and it requires a data protection impact assessment, a relatório de impacto à proteção de dados pessoais, where processing is large-scale, involves sensitive data or creates material risk. The LGPD's rules on international transfers apply where AI vendors host infrastructure or training environments outside Brazil. The Ministério da Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação leads the Brazilian AI strategy, which is not binding in itself.

André Fortes Carvalho & Furtado Advogados, listed as a Gold featured expert on the matter, is the guide's named adviser for Brazil. The guide says AI used for grid optimisation, load forecasting, EV charging routing and predictive maintenance is exactly the kind of system regulators are most likely to treat as high-risk. It says such systems affect safety and continuity of supply and rely on large volumes of personal and operational data. It says a compliant AI deployment has to satisfy LGPD and ANPD duties and ANEEL and ANATEL duties together. It says AI does not create a separate data-protection regime but makes existing duties heavier.

The guide says operators using AI today include grid optimisation and load forecasting, charging optimisation and routing, predictive maintenance, and dynamic pricing and demand response. It says smart-meter readings, EV user accounts, charging session records, roaming identifiers and predictive-maintenance logs frequently contain personal data. It says a charging operator sits under two sector regimes plus the LGPD, and the three should be run as one coordinated programme. It says regulators dealing with critical infrastructure expect operators to show that systems fail safely, that humans oversee consequential decisions, and that fallback arrangements keep service running. It says a model failure in grid balancing or charging allocation can threaten supply continuity and public safety.

The guide says the LGPD sets out lawful bases for processing, the rights of data subjects and an accountability principle that obliges operators to prove compliance. It says properly anonymised data sits outside the statute, but anonymisation must be robust and not reasonably reversible, and pseudonymised or re-identifiable data is still personal data. It says an operator that decides the purposes of processing is the controller and carries primary accountability, while a vendor that only processes data on the operator's instructions is a processor, an operador. It says ANEEL's existing obligations should be assumed to extend to AI-driven decisions. It says ANATEL's remit covers network aspects, equipment certification (homologation) and communications requirements.

The guide sets out a 90/180/360 day action plan and a twelve-point checklist. It says operators should appoint a data protection officer (encarregado) or equivalent and name an accountable executive for each high-risk AI system. It says a cross-functional AI governance committee should keep an inventory of AI systems, classify them by risk and approve deployments before go-live. It says governance should state explicitly who can override or suspend an AI system in an emergency. It says operators should test for accuracy and bias before deployment and set automated alerts for when a model drifts outside acceptable limits.

stories.Headline: Van Epps introduces bill to set safeguards for agentic AI in federal civilian networks
stories.Summary:
Representative Matt Van Epps said he has introduced the AI INSIGHT Act, a bill aimed at creating safeguards for the use of agentic AI systems in federal civilian networks, according to a press release posted on November 24, 2026. The proposal would set a framework for securing AI agents, with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency offering guidance and technical assistance to federal agencies. Van Epps said the measure would help agencies identify AI agents on their networks, limit access to what tasks require, monitor activity, and suspend or revoke access when needed. He said the bill is meant to let agencies use AI while reducing security risks, according to the release. The bill is listed as H.R.11076 among the proposals Van Epps has recently put forward, the release states.

The stated goals of the measure are to help agencies identify AI agents on their networks, limit access to what tasks require, monitor activity, and suspend or revoke access when needed. Under the proposal, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency would offer guidance and technical assistance as part of the framework for securing AI agents. Van Epps said the bill is meant to let agencies use AI while reducing security risks, according to the release. Van Epps is the representative who introduced the bill, and the release presents the stated goals and the role for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency as his proposal.

He said the measure would help agencies identify AI agents on their networks, limit access to what tasks require, monitor activity, and suspend or revoke access when needed. He said the bill is meant to let agencies use AI while reducing security risks, according to the release. The release does not say what happens next for the bill. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Lawyers say UK-EU digital partnership will cover AI safety and data adequacy
stories.Summary:
Lawyers at Browne Jacobson commented on the proposed UK, EU digital partnership after the recent summit in Brussels, saying it could support cross-border business growth while overly general AI regulation may hold back innovation. Jeanne Kelly, the firm's Head of EU Data, Privacy and Cybersecurity and Co-head of the Dublin Office, said one of the most significant proposals is the intention to launch a digital partnership in early 2027 covering digital and technology. She said this would cover areas that include secure and resilient connectivity, AI including security and safety, digital wallets and credentials, and online safety. She said the current data adequacy determination, which was recently renewed until 2031, appears unaffected by either the joint statement or the measures it contemplates, and that the statement openly refers to the UK's regulatory autonomy being safeguarded. She said increased cooperation between the EU and the UK can only be welcomed, describing it as a rapprochement with language that manages expectations on the likely outcomes, certainly on digital matters.

Chris Holder, a Partner in IT and technology at the firm, said reaching an understanding on international standards and ways of working in the digital sphere, including the development of AI systems, will undoubtedly help companies with growth ambitions in the UK and EU. He said that since Brexit businesses across many industries have been trying to navigate dual sets of regulations, although there are examples like the EU and UK's GDPR regimes where there is very close alignment because it makes clear economic sense. He said enhancing this partnership feels like a no-brainer, but it would be beneficial for the European Commission to review how the EU AI Act is structured. He said the Commission should move away from horizontal legislation that applies a broad-brush stroke across sectors to one that becomes more application-based, because the way AI technology is used varies significantly from sector to sector. He said it is important these differences are reflected in the regulation underpinning technology use in the financial services sector over, for example, the life sciences sector, otherwise generalisation in regulation may hold back innovation across both the EU and UK.

Holder also said it is to be hoped that the Commission is open to bringing UK sector expertise into the fold as part of this new digital partnership. He said that as a global leader in sectors like financial services, this expertise may prove invaluable to the EU in supporting any review of its AI Act. The lawyers' comments followed the recent summit in Brussels, and the proposed partnership is intended to launch in early 2027. The data adequacy determination was recently renewed until 2031, and the joint statement openly refers to the UK's regulatory autonomy being safeguarded.

stories.Headline: Dutch music rights group BumaStemra threatens to sue YourNeuroTune over AI-generated music
stories.Summary:
BumaStemra, the Dutch organization that represents music creators, announced on Tuesday, 24 November 2026, that it is threatening to sue YourNeuroTune, a Dutch company that sells AI-generated background music to businesses. The organization said it will go to court if YourNeuroTune does not stop the commercial provision of music created by AI trained on the work of music creators without their permission by noon the following day. According to BumaStemra, YourNeuroTune told its clients that by buying its music, which the company claims is copyright-free, they no longer have to make payments to the music creators' organization. BumaStemra said YourNeuroTune uses Suno to create its music, and that the American AI model is known to be trained on existing music without the consent of creators.

BumaStemra director Michiel Laan said the company is profiting from music that would not exist without the work of its members, while at the same time telling clients to stop paying those very creators. He said the organization will not accept this, and that anyone who earns money from music must compensate the creators, even when an AI model is behind the turntables. He added that the music coming through the speakers may well be the work of BumaStemra's members. According to the organization, creators are consequently forced to compete with a product built upon their own work, for which they receive no compensation.

The threat of legal proceedings follows successful lawsuits in the United States and Germany, according to BumaStemra. This past summer, a German court ruled that Suno must pay copyright royalties for its use of existing music in a lawsuit filed by GEMA, the German equivalent of BumaStemra, Nieuwsuur reported. Music producers Sony and Universal are also embroiled in legal action against Suno in the United States. YourNeuroTune told Nieuwsuur that it has taken note of BumaStemra's ultimatum but will only provide a substantive response if a lawsuit is actually filed.

stories.Headline: Plastering House Bill 11014 against real world AI workflows
stories.Summary:
Representatives Miguel Luis Villafuerte, Vincenzo Renato Luigi Villafuerte, Tsuyoshi Anthony Horibata and Terry Ridon filed House Bill 11014 on August 27. This legislation is called the AI Agent Transactions and Accountability Act. It addresses how acts performed through an AI agent are attributed to the authorizing person or company. The bill ensures that a Principal cannot avoid responsibility by claiming an agent acted autonomously. It establishes legal accountability for the use of artificial intelligence in transactions.

The bill states that using an agent does not invalidate contracts under the E-Commerce Act. It allows a voluntary credential through the DICT to verify what an agent is permitted to do. Mandatory registration is required only for high-risk categories after public consultation. Knowing fraud or falsification carries fines from ₱200,000 to ₱2 million or six months to six years in prison. Section 14 requires providers to disclose referral fees and preferential routing that steer recommendations.

The authors of the bill argue that liability for an AI agent sits with the customer. They claim that a Principal cannot dodge responsibility by arguing that an agent acted probabilistically. Gavin Barfield, Salesforce's Chief Technology Officer, says models are brilliant but cannot run an enterprise alone. He believes a governance layer makes agents trustworthy by separating reasoning from business decisions. Barfield noted that briefing prep now takes three minutes instead of four to five hours.

Philippine companies deploying agents are affected because they remain answerable for the actions of the AI. The bill allows for contractual indemnification among Principals, developers, providers and platforms. Salesforce claims its help site achieved 100 million dollars in annual savings through AI. Barfield cited a 90 percent pilot failure rate sourced from a Salesforce article. He mentioned that Salesforce opened a local office in the Philippines one year ago.

The bill provides defenses for Principals including stolen credentials, cyberattacks, or unauthorized modification of the agent. It also covers third-party fraud or provider failures that are outside the reasonable control of the Principal. Salesforce offers a Trusted Enterprise AI Harness with six capabilities covering context, agency, action, governance, security and models. The company recently announced Copilotforce with Microsoft to integrate workflows into Copilot and Teams. Copilotforce requires explicit user confirmation for writebacks to the CRM.

The bill does not require a human to confirm every step if authority was properly granted. This differs from the current Salesforce approach which asks for confirmation before writing to the CRM. The articles leave open whether confirmation prompts will be removed as volume increases. They do not specify if the pilot failure rate applies to global or Philippine deployments. It remains unclear who reads the briefings that now take only three minutes to prepare.
