stories.Headline: Clients blindly trusting AI legal advice increase pressure and emotional labor for lawyers
stories.Summary:
Lawyer Huang Qin passed away after collapsing during a communication with a client. This event occurred on November 13, when Hubei Maple Leaf Law Firm released her obituary. The 48-year-old lawyer died following continuous high-pressure overwork and extreme exhaustion. She was handling a case for a legal aid recipient named Duan. The collapse happened after she told the client that his lack of trust broke her heart.

Duan insisted for three to four months that Huang Qin follow AI legal advice. This pestering delayed the case and included calls and texts at 9 p.m. Other lawyers, like Lin Liming from Beijing Yingke (Dongguan) Law Firm, noticed this trend since 2025. Lin Liming handled a divorce case where a party doubted a judge's property decision. This party relied on AI, which wrongly claimed the judge's decision was incorrect.

Lin Liming stated that incomplete case descriptions lead AI to provide wrong answers. He noted that AI often fabricates false laws and cases through hallucinations. Lawyer Xie He from Guangzhou Luoya Law Firm said AI caters to users. She claimed AI-generated documents can be unprofessional, emotional, and irrelevant to the case. Xie He warned that lawyers bear the liability for faults, not the AI.

Clients who blindly trust AI are driving lawyers to experience extreme mental exhaustion. These parties use AI to question the competence and professionalism of their lawyers. This behavior affects the judicial resource allocation of court mediation and trial systems. Legal aid recipients are often affected, as they may distrust randomly assigned free lawyers. Some clients miss first instance opportunities by following AI instead of hiring lawyers.

The articles state that AI can create information illusions for those lacking professional knowledge. Many people now use social media tutorials to learn about suing with AI. Legal aid lawyers are often young professionals who join the pool for experience. Article 46 of the Legal Aid Law forbids refusing or delaying legal aid services. This law applies to the random assignments handled by the judicial bureau.

Lawyers now face higher communication costs and more emotional labor due to AI. Some lawyers choose to compromise with clients, while others take a stronger attitude. It remains unclear if technology increases the burden or brings new opportunities. The articles leave open whether this trust crisis will permanently change the agency relationship. They do not state if new regulations will limit AI use in courts.

Articles.Title: Clients who are blindly superstitious about AI are driving lawyers crazy. - 36Kr

stories.headline_source: Clients who are blindly superstitious about AI are driving lawyers crazy.

stories.Headline: Anke Krebs presents a 2026 guide on German AI patent law for pharmaceutical businesses
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a 2026 guide on AI patent law in Germany for pharmaceutical businesses, published by Global Advisory Experts on November 25, 2026. The guide is written for general counsel, R&D heads, patent managers and patent attorneys at pharmaceutical businesses. It aims to help them size up legal risk quickly and adjust their filing and enforcement approach for AI-assisted drug discovery in Germany. The guide covers the Patent Act (PatG), the European Patent Convention (EPC) and EPO and DPMA practice. It is a Germany legal pharmaceutical guide with a read time of 16 minutes, updated in 2026.

The guide states that in 2026 generative models are routinely used to suggest molecular scaffolds, plan synthesis routes and rank candidates for clinical development. It says AI does not alter the substantive tests of novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability and sufficiency of disclosure. It says neither the PatG nor the EPC contains a dedicated AI clause, and the existing rules are simply applied to new facts. It says the EPO's Legal Board of Appeal confirmed in the DABUS cases (J 8/20 and J 9/20) that an AI system cannot be designated as inventor. It says the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) entered into force in 2024 and is being phased in.

The guide draws on the experience of a German Patent Attorney holding a doctorate in chemistry (Dr. rer. nat.), with a background in pharmaceutical patent litigation and cross-border enforcement. It names Anke Krebs of dompatent as the featured expert on this matter, a Gold Member. It says the German Patent and Trade Mark Office (DPMA) examines German applications on the facts, applying the usual novelty and enablement analysis whether or not an AI tool contributed. It says German national practice is aligned with the EPO posture that a human inventor is required.

It says the EPO requires credible technical teaching on how to produce and use the claimed compound. The guide says sufficiency is the biggest patentability risk for AI-derived pharmaceutical claims, and applicants usually need experimental support: synthesis, characterisation and at least indicative activity data. It says training data can be prior art where public, and that material accessible before the priority date can form part of the prior art for novelty and inventive step. It says Germany regulates employee inventions through the Employee Inventions Act (Arbeitnehmererfindungsgesetz, ArbnErfG), under which an employee who makes a service invention must report it to the employer, who may claim it, and the employee is entitled to reasonable compensation.

It says UK and US courts have rejected AI inventor claims in DABUS litigation. It says WIPO's work on AI and IP offers a comparative view of how different jurisdictions handle inventorship and ownership. The guide says most of the significant pharmaceutical patents in force in Germany are European patents, granted by the European Patent Office under the EPC and then validated nationally. It says the substantive tests for AI-assisted inventions are essentially identical in both systems.

It says the EPO's guidance on AI and patents is the more developed public reference. It says the EU Artificial Intelligence Act sets expectations on data governance, transparency and risk management that affect how pharma companies document and govern their AI-assisted discovery pipelines. It says none of these instruments overrides the PatG or the EPC. The guide says companies should check that internal invention-disclosure processes handle AI-assisted inventions properly, that reporting duties are met, and that compensation reflects the actual human contribution.

It says the answer to blurred ownership with contractors, tool vendors and data-science consultants is contractual clarity: assignment of any inventive contributions and express allocation. It says ignoring the statutory procedure can cause ownership and remuneration disputes that come to light years later in litigation or licensing. It says a broad claim to a class of AI-generated molecules with no supporting data is vulnerable to attack. It says AI can speed up ideation, but the patent still depends on real experimental evidence.

stories.Headline: Bill Gates warns AI transition may bring two decades of turbulence and inequality
stories.Summary:
Bill Gates, the Microsoft cofounder, warned that the spread of artificial intelligence could trigger one of the most turbulent periods in human history, according to an essay published Aug. 26, 2026, on Gates Notes, his personal website. The essay was titled The turbulent age of AI is already here, and in it he wrote that even under the best circumstances the transition to this new era of artificial intelligence will be one of the most turbulent periods in human history. He said the world is still not ready to face the changes and that action will be needed to keep the technology from widening inequality. He also said artificial intelligence could become a tool to reduce inequality or, on the contrary, a source of injustice, depending on the decisions made by governments, companies, and societies.

The warning was reported by El Cronista on Nov. 25, 2026. In an interview with the Decoder podcast from The Verge, published Oct. 22, 2026, Gates warned that over the next two or three years significant negative consequences could emerge in the job market and digital security. He believes AI could make cyberattacks easier by giving more powerful tools to those looking to exploit computer vulnerabilities, and that automation could affect different jobs and speed up changes that companies and workers are not yet prepared to handle. Gates said young people can use the technology's capabilities to make an impact and take part in shaping policies to manage its consequences.

In the interview he said that if you are 20 years old today, over this 20-year period you can take advantage of the things AI still can't do, use it to make a positive impact and propose policies. Gates also raised the possibility that society could decide to keep certain activities under human control, even if robots and artificial intelligence become technically capable of doing them. During the interview he explained that he spoke with an AI system about the possibility of reserving job categories for people and keeping a share of the job market under that condition. Among the alternatives he mentioned were early retirement and shorter workweeks, and he said we'll have to make real decisions.

He also noted that some communities, such as the Amish, choose not to live on the technological frontier, a choice that could extend to other people in the future. Gates estimates the transition could last about 20 years, with winners and losers before a more abundant future is reached. During that time, the combination of artificial intelligence and robotics could make the production of goods and services easier but also create inequality, job problems, and social tensions. For that reason, he says governments must prepare, establish oversight mechanisms, and make sure the benefits of technology do not end up concentrated in a few sectors.

stories.Headline: UK regulators tell Meta to make Muse terms fairer for consumers as three bodies set out existing rules
stories.Summary:
On 24 November 2026, the day Meta's Muse agent launched in the UK, three regulators published their positions on consumer AI agents. The ICO set out its privacy expectations in a blog, the Competition and Markets Authority said UK consumer protection law applies to AI products, and the Financial Conduct Authority posted an update on what financial services rules mean for agent makers. None of the three announced a new rule. The four regulators in the Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum had said a month earlier that existing legal and regulatory frameworks apply to personal AI agents.

The CMA's agentic AI and consumers page, with guidance for businesses, was published on GOV.UK on 9 March 2026. The DRCF joint statement on personal AI agents came on 30 October 2026, declaring existing frameworks apply across four remits. On 16 November 2026 the four chief executives wrote to the Chancellor and three other ministers about the forthcoming launch of a number of personal agentic products, calling it a step-change in the way AI is being used. Muse launched on 24 November 2026, with statements from the ICO, CMA and FCA. ICO agentic AI guidance is due in spring 2027.

The CMA says the same consumer protection rules apply to these new products and technologies as to any other product or service. It says terms and conditions should not contain surprises for the consumer about where responsibility lies if something goes wrong. The CMA says it engaged with Meta over the past several weeks on reflecting consumers' statutory rights in its terms, and that Meta then made changes to make them fairer for consumers. The CMA says it will be closely reviewing how Muse is presented and functions in practice. ICO chief executive Paul Arnold said the ICO had told Meta before launch what data protection law required of it, and that Meta has committed to a voluntary monitoring and reporting scheme with the ICO.

The ICO says consumer agents raise some novel questions about how the law applies to some aspects of processing. It warns that the dynamic nature of data access permissions may pose data security risks, and that meaningful transparency may be hard if people are not told about risks peculiar to agents. The FCA says that just because a business describes itself as a technology provider does not mean it does not need to be authorised to provide financial services in the UK, and that this boundary is set by Parliament. The DRCF letter says some firms have engaged early and constructively, but engagement has not been consistently early or open across the relevant regulators. The CMA and ICO published joint tips telling people to start in the most limited mode and check permissions regularly.

The DRCF's 30 October statement says firms should think carefully about how consumers can understand when and how an agent acts on their behalf, how authority to act is given, how their personal data is used, how commercial interests that may influence its recommendations are communicated, who is accountable for the agent's decisions and how to obtain redress. The regulators say they are working together and with Government to identify potential gaps in compliance and further regulatory challenges that arise from personal AI agents. The DRCF letter says partners' own obligations continue to apply when customers use personal AI agents. The FCA says responsibility stays with a regulated firm and its senior managers when it uses agentic AI, including a third party's. The CMA says similar products are likely to be introduced in the UK in the coming months.

The ICO's agentic AI call for evidence closed the week before Muse launched. The ICO's guidance, due in spring 2027, is meant to give greater regulatory certainty. The FCA lists activities that could bring an agent inside its perimeter: payment services, financial promotions, an authorised information service, credit broking or intermediation, and financial advice. The FCA says some products may require FCA regulation at launch or evolve in a way that makes regulation apply. The CMA says it is still talking to Meta.

The CMA expects more launches in the coming months. The DRCF has a shared form for consumers to report problems with Muse or other agents. The FCA's consumer page asks people to understand what protections, if any, they might have if something goes wrong before letting a tool make transactions. The articles leave open what the ICO's spring 2027 guidance will require on permissions and transparency, and how liability is shared when a partner acts on an agent's instruction. They also leave open whether the FCA's Agentic Policy Sprint changes any expectations, and what redress applies when an agent makes a costly mistake.

stories.Headline: LexisNexis’s chief AI officer predicts lawyers will judge legal AI by holding-level evidence in 2027
stories.Summary:
LexisNexis published a release on November 25, 2026, in which its Chief AI Officer set out five predictions for how lawyers will judge legal AI in 2027, arguing that better answers will need better evidence behind them. The release says every new generation of models raises what legal AI can do, and that 2027 will raise that ceiling again, but that lawyers decide usefulness at the floor, by asking what an answer stands on and whether they could stand on it before a court or a client. It says litigators told the company this year that knowing a case is still good law is only the start, and that they also need the specific holding that fits their client's facts and supports the argument they have to make. The first prediction is that research will start from the client's facts rather than from a topic, with systems moving from what happened to the client to a holding that fits, explaining where the comparison is weaker and which adverse holdings matter. The second is that the question of whether a case is still good law will be answered holding by holding, because a single case often decides several issues that later courts may follow, limit or distinguish, and the release gives the example of a decision on a defendant's right to a timely appeal that a later court distinguished and that now carries a caution signal.

The third is that the most dangerous AI errors will be the believable ones, and the release cites Mata v. Avianca in 2023, when lawyers were sanctioned after submitting cases invented by a general-purpose chatbot, which it calls the easier problem to catch compared with a real case, cited correctly and summarized well, whose holding does not support the argument or fit the facts. The fourth prediction is that smarter models still need trusted legal intelligence underneath them, because the law keeps changing after they are trained, and the release says the leading systems in 2027 will draw on legal intelligence that is already structured and verified. The fifth is that firms will judge legal AI by how fast they can trust the answer, asking how many unsupported or inapplicable authorities slip through and how long verification takes, since a draft produced in seconds offers less value if its authorities take hours to verify.

The release says LexisNexis built the Point of Law Graph, which it describes as a legal knowledge graph that maps how individual points of law connect across court decisions and helps Lexis+ with Protégé find authority at the level of a specific legal issue, and it says the graph goes one step further than the Shepard's Signal by showing which specific holding a later court followed, limited or distinguished, and on what facts. The release says three things set the graph apart: it works at holding level rather than case level, tracing a rule from the case that states it to cases that apply it on different facts and to decisions that clarify its limits; it is grounded in verified legal knowledge, drawing on Shepard's citation analysis, headnotes and LexisNexis editorial expertise, with automation building connections at scale and legal experts reviewing the results; and it is built for verification, with Shepard's Verify using the same point-of-law knowledge to help assess whether a cited authority supports the proposition it is cited for. In internal LexisNexis testing on a set of legal research questions, the release says, adding point-of-law retrieval from the graph to case-level retrieval raised answer usefulness by about 10 percentage points, as scored by the company's legal experts. The release says the work ahead starts with the client's facts and follows the evidence through, that in 2027 lawyers should be able to see the holding an answer relies on, how later courts treated it, where the facts match or differ and what to check before use, and that the company is building toward this with customers in the LexisNexis Customer Innovation Lab.

The most recent item is an AI Pulse Check piece dated November 25, 2026, which says regulators want AI model, version and prompt disclosure in submissions, and that panelists weighed hype against value in AI-for-biology deals. Responsibility is placed on manufacturers and on the people named in the panels, with regulators cast as the party that will test companies against their own internal AI policies.

The articles paraphrase no single official statement beyond that, and they give no date for the December AI playbook other than the month. The context they offer is a series of AI Pulse Check discussions running from November 10 to November 25, 2026, alongside Manufacturing Intelligence pieces on where to slow AI and how to guard its data. stories.Headline: Politicians and advocacy groups call for stricter artificial intelligence regulations
stories.Summary:
Various politicians and advocacy groups called for greater controls over artificial intelligence on Tuesday, November 24, 2026. Former Utah Senator Mitt Romney criticized the current American strategy for rushing the technology without safeguards to compete with China. He suggested that selling necessary chips to China while ignoring regulation smelled of corruption and profit. President Trump recently stated that he agreed to joint guardrails with China, though he did not provide specific details.

These advocates argue that the government must implement stringent regulations to control how the technology evolves. Isabelle Freiling, an assistant professor of communication at the University of Utah, believes that broad public debates are necessary to give regulations legitimacy. She argues that a small group of tech leaders with conflicts of interest should not determine the future of the field. Clark Dice of the Utah Civic Compact also called for guardrails to ensure humans remain accountable for important decisions.

Dice compared the technology to a savant toddler that lacks the life experience to put information into proper context. He expressed concern that over-reliance on these tools could cause human cognitive abilities to atrophy over time. Some tech leaders have argued against such rules, claiming it is difficult to regulate something that is not fully understood. They also suggest that strict regulations might limit the potential benefits of the technology.

stories.Headline: Law students present AI bills by cabinet portfolio at Toronto Met event
stories.Summary:
Michael Bryant wrote an opinion article published by the Toronto Star on Nov. 25, 2026, about the AI Legisla-Thon hosted by the Lincoln Alexander School of Law at Toronto Metropolitan University. Students at the school presented legislation over two days at the Legisla-Thon on TMU's downtown campus. Teams of about six students presented AI bills on child protection, labour and employment, autonomous weapons, residential tenancy, clinical patient safeguards, insolvency, and critical care. The event was part of a mandatory second-year class taught by Prof. Jake Effoduh. Bryant attended the Legisla-Thon and wrote that he was struck by the students' confidence and fluency.

Bryant wrote that every cabinet minister in every provincial and federal government in Canada should be legislating in the AI field. He wrote that the federal Artificial Intelligence and Data Act, part of Bill C-27, died on the order paper when Parliament was prorogued on Jan. 6, 2025. He wrote that the 2026 AI for All national strategy is a policy road map only and does not revive AIDA. He wrote that the federal Parliament has no jurisdiction and zero expertise in fields such as health care, education, energy, environment, infrastructure, policing, courts and corrections. He wrote that the feds could take the same approach to AI governance as they do with their dated privacy legislation, permitting provinces to opt in to the prescribed rules.

Bryant wrote that Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon has been monitoring the work of Prof. Effoduh and his classes, including the Legisla-Thon. Bryant wrote that the Prime Minister's Office must know that all federal ministries require legislative amendments on AI. He wrote that Solomon's ministry is likely collaborating with those ministries, through an intergovernmental quagmire, to develop a legislative strategy, building on past failures. Bryant wrote that the Carney Government has not been able to pass such a law. Bryant wrote that Bill C-27 died on the Order Paper, facing a litany of "but what about" questions and failing to cover the infinite priorities packed into it.

Bryant wrote that the students got it right and that the young Lincoln Lawyers of TMU say AI regulation should be broken down into more familiar terrain, organized by existing Cabinet responsibilities. He wrote that the most impactful level of government under our constitutional system is provincial. He wrote that the task is unmanageable if confined to a single bill, forcing all-or-nothing votes, keeping provisions from expert committees, and blurring accountability. He wrote that there is significant political currency for politicians who convince their constituents that they are responsive to rampant public fears about AI. He wrote that it is a toss-up as to which most occupies voters' minds, cost of living or AI.

Bryant wrote that frontier models have developed so rapidly in a legal vacuum, outside Europe. He wrote that global economics and local budgets do not stand in the way of AI regulation. He wrote that the only limitations are legislative capacity, policy development, and leadership. He wrote that the opposite of the students' confidence and fluency is true of most politicians, who are far less knowledgeable and comfortable with the concepts and functions of AI. Bryant wrote that the demographics of these decision-makers are a handicap for legislative leadership.

Bryant wrote that nothing stops a federal or provincial ministry from enabling its Minister to bring forth a government bill. He wrote that the PMO and Premiers' Offices try to keep their cabinets on a short leash, but that there are exceptions, speaking from experience. He wrote that developing AI policy and governance ought to be every legislator's job. He wrote that many politicians are overwhelmed by the task of governing AI, especially the late adopters. Bryant wrote that the students' discomfort-alleviating approach leaves open who is schooling who.

stories.Headline: Intel faces shareholder lawsuit alleging misleading PC and AI disclosures
stories.Summary:
Intel has been hit with a shareholder class action lawsuit alleging misleading disclosures around its PC market slowdown and inventory buildup, according to a report published on November 25, 2026. The complaint claims Intel executives overstated benefits tied to AI infrastructure and data center activity while downplaying offsetting headwinds in its core PC business. Shareholders argue that Intel failed to fully explain how excess inventory and weaker PC demand could affect results and operational risks. The report describes Intel as a large US semiconductor producer with a reported market value of about $317.1 billion, designing and manufacturing computing hardware across PCs, data centers and related services in the United States, Ireland, Israel and other international markets. The lawsuit questions how clearly management described the trade-offs between heavy AI and foundry spending and pressure in the PC franchise as the AI narrative took hold.

The report states that Intel's 2026 capital spending is now expected to be more than $20 billion, with 2027 planned to be significantly higher. It says the legal action undercuts one pillar of the bullish case, which assumes Intel can keep scaling fabs and packaging while retaining trust in how it reports PC demand, inventory and AI driven benefits. The report adds that the core AI infrastructure angle pitting Intel against Nvidia and AMD is unchanged by itself, because the claim targets communication rather than the existence of data center demand or foundry build out. The report says that if plaintiffs succeed in showing disclosures around the Client Computing and Physical AI Group were incomplete, the perceived risk attached to that capital program and to future guidance could rise.

It notes the unresolved piece is how any potential settlement costs, disclosure changes or management distraction might interact with already-flagged risks around high capex, foundry losses and volatile shares. The article was produced with the assistance of AI automation, based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St, and states it is general in nature and not financial advice. It also says Simply Wall St has no position in any stocks mentioned. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Gene Quinn moderates a webinar on California’s AI law and patent practice
stories.Summary:
A webinar titled Verify, Don’t Delegate, about what California’s AI law means for patent practice, is scheduled for December 15, 2026, at 12 PM ET and is sponsored by Patsnap. IPWatchdog founder and CEO Gene Quinn will moderate the conversation, which features USPTO rules expert John White of Harness IP and Sivon Kalminov, head of intellectual property at Canon U.S.A., Inc. The session will examine where California’s SB 574 intersects with federal patent practice, which requirements clearly apply, and what remains unresolved. Organizers say attendees will leave with a clearer understanding of what the law requires and how to use AI in patent practice without surrendering professional judgment. Effective January 1, 2027, California will become the first state to impose statutory requirements governing attorneys’ use of generative artificial intelligence, a claim the article presents as the state’s own. SB 574 prohibits attorneys from delegating the practice of law to AI and restricts the entry of confidential and other nonpublic information into systems without appropriate access controls.

The law also requires attorneys to take reasonable steps to verify AI-generated output and correct erroneous or hallucinated material. It further requires disclosure of AI use for documents submitted to a court and personal verification of every citation in a court filing, whether generated by AI or not. The article says that without Congressional action it seems virtually certain that other states will follow California’s lead, raising the question of whether SB 574 will become a template. It notes that some provisions expressly govern court filings and do not map neatly onto patent prosecution before a federal agency, while nondelegation, confidentiality, verification, and correction are written broadly as duties of attorneys using generative AI in the practice of law. The USPTO permits practitioners to use AI subject to existing duties of competence, candor, confidentiality, supervision, and signature certification, and imposes no general requirement to disclose AI use, although AI-related information may still require disclosure when material to patentability.

The overlap raises difficult questions for California attorneys practicing before the USPTO, for parties appearing before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board, and for mixed teams of attorneys and registered patent agents who may perform the same work but are not regulated by SB 574 in the same way. Panelists will discuss which SB 574 duties apply broadly to California attorneys and which are specific to court submissions, and how the law interacts with USPTO rules and guidance, including existing disclosure and materiality obligations. They will also cover how the law affects mixed teams of California attorneys, attorneys licensed elsewhere, and registered patent agents, and what access controls and confidentiality protections should be required before sensitive invention or client information enters an AI system. The webinar will address how to build human-review, source-verification, approval, and documentation checkpoints into AI-assisted workflows. It will also cover what in-house departments and law firms should incorporate into AI policies, outside-counsel guidelines, and training before the law takes effect.

stories.Headline: The Chicks and Willie Colón join a lawsuit accusing Suno of misusing artists' identities
stories.Summary:
The Chicks, Willie Colón and Sam Moore joined the legal fight against AI music, Billboard reported on Nov. 25, 2026. The acts and their estates were among a slew of artists added Tuesday, Nov. 24, to a case filed this summer against Suno. The case accuses the AI song generator of breaking the law by allowing users to conjure up a beloved musician’s identity when they enter a name as a prompt. The case was filed by Jason Isbell as a novel action centered on artists’ likeness rights. It differs from earlier lawsuits over AI labs using copyrighted music to train models.

Lawyers for the artists wrote that Suno built and trained a model to index musicians by name. They wrote that it encoded musicians’ identities into its AI model to create its commercial product without consent. They wrote that it now exploits those identities by publicly using musicians’ names to Suno’s considerable commercial benefit. The lawsuit was also joined by 10 more artists, including David Longstreth of Dirty Projectors and Carl Craig, a pioneering DJ of Detroit techno. Franz Nicolay of The Hold Steady and Kealiʻi Reichel, a top Hawaiian music artist, also joined.

A spokeswoman for Suno told Billboard on Wednesday, Nov. 25, that the company believes the claims are without merit. She said Suno would defend itself in court. She said Suno exists to help people create new, original music, not to trade on anyone’s name. She said the company prohibits any unauthorized use of an artist’s work. An attorney for the artists did not immediately return a request for comment.

Artists as big as Madonna and SZA have spoken out against AI music. Dozens of stars like Billie Eilish, Katy Perry, Luis Fonsi and the estates of Bob Marley and Frank Sinatra joined an open letter in 2024. The letter called unlicensed music AI an assault on human creativity that must be stopped. Few have taken actual legal action, though an indie country singer named Tony Justice is litigating a class action against Suno. Isbell’s case was joined by Camper Van Beethoven frontman David Lowery and a handful of others.

The biggest case yet came from the owners of Elvis Presley’s intellectual property, who launched landmark cases against Suno and Anthropic this fall. The Chicks, who have a long history of outspoken advocacy, represent by far the biggest living musical act to yet sue over AI. Suno has argued that its current models don’t allow users to prompt its AI model with specific artist names. When users do enter artist names, the platform says it translates that request into descriptive musical characteristics. Those characteristics can then be used to direct the model to generate a song.

Isbell’s lawsuit, filed on Aug. 31, claims those safeguards can be easily duped by merely using spaces, such as Taylor Swift with “t a y l o r s w i f t” or Bad Bunny with “b a d b u n n y.” The case claims that even when a name is translated into musical styles, the model clearly still exploits an artist’s identity. It claims the platform is built to identify musicians by name and generate identity-evocative output on command. Suno has already asked a judge to dismiss those accusations, arguing they are legally faulty. In a motion earlier this month, the company’s lawyers argued there’s nothing unlawful about merely using an artist’s name to describe music.

More artists could be added to the case in the future. Since the case was filed as a proposed class action, it ultimately seeks to represent millions of other artists in making the same claims against Suno. Suno’s lawyers wrote that when people describe styles of music, they often use artists’ names as shorthand for the genre they perform in. They wrote that the case turns on the premise that the law somehow condemns that universal practice. They wrote that in reality it does not and that the First Amendment would not allow it to.

stories.Headline: Visa, Mastercard and FIS reports find consumers warming to AI payments as model performance and trust lag
stories.Summary:
Research reports from Visa, Mastercard and FIS say that consumers are warming to artificial intelligence in payments, but the reports also find room for improvement in how well the models perform and how much people trust them. The reports were covered by American Banker in a story published on November 25, 2026, which framed the findings around the challenge banks face in drawing consumers to AI payments. The story was written by John Adams, the executive editor of payments for American Banker, who interviews top executives in payments, cryptocurrency and fintech and hosts podcasts and conference panels. The key insight the story draws from the three reports is that consumers are warming to AI, while model performance and trust still need work.

The story sets out what trust means for consumers through Jim Johnson of FIS, who said that for consumers trust is whether they can get a refund if something goes wrong and whether the fix can happen quickly. Johnson also said that when something goes wrong, consumers do not want to talk to a bot. The story adds that the strategy of blocking all external agents cannot last forever, and that frameworks described as know your agent are in the works. It also says that defensive policies may shield banks from early AI fraud, but that leaving consumers exposed creates a major retention risk. The reports from Visa, Mastercard and FIS are the source of the findings on consumer attitudes, model performance and trust.

The story does not name any bank, regulator or other body as responsible for the challenge, and it records no statement from any of them beyond the remarks attributed to Johnson of FIS. The context the story gives is that banks weigh defensive policies against the retention risk of leaving consumers exposed, and that blocking all external agents is a strategy that cannot last forever. It says know your agent frameworks are in the works, without saying who is developing them or when they might arrive. The story does not say what happens next beyond those points, and it gives no date for any change.

stories.Headline: New York judges oppose Hinchey bill on AI misconduct over judicial independence fears
stories.Summary:
New York judges expressed their opposition to a proposed bill on November 25, 2026, regarding the use of artificial intelligence. Senator Michelle Hinchey of Ulster introduced this legislation to stop the inclusion of fabricated legal materials in judicial decisions. The bill aims to prevent the use of fake cases and quotations that might be generated by AI tools. These judges believe the new rules could negatively impact the independence of the judiciary. The proposed legislation seeks to clarify when the use of fabricated authority constitutes judicial misconduct in the state.

This change would address the growing use of artificial intelligence within the court systems of New York. The Association of Justices of the Supreme Court of the State of New York warns that the bill risks creating political pressure. They also argue that the proposal raises significant concerns regarding the separation of powers. Senator Michelle Hinchey stated that existing laws leave too much uncertainty about what qualifies as misconduct.

Bianka Perez, who serves as the president of the Association of Justices, represents the judges pushing back. The judicial association claims that the bill could chill the independence of those serving on the bench. They believe the legislation might allow outside forces to influence judicial decisions through misconduct charges. More to follow.

Articles.Title: NY Judges Warn AI Misconduct Bill Could Chill Judicial Independence

stories.Headline: Lenovo launches a multimodal AI urban super agent for the city of Dunhuang
stories.Summary:
Lenovo and Dunhuang jointly released the Urban Super Agent on November 20. This event occurred alongside the release of a white paper co-produced by Lenovo and IDC. The project introduces a unified multimodal interaction portal for the city of Dunhuang. It aims to move smart city implementation toward a fourth stage of development. This new system shifts the role of AI from observation to execution.

The system requires three modules called the Urban Digital Portal, Urban Task Kernel, and Urban Asset Library. It uses the Lenovo Wen Tian AI infrastructure and the Lenovo Wanquan Mixed Token Factory in Gansu. The project creates four unifications regarding entry, scheduling, memory, and capabilities for the city. It includes the Dunhuang Cultural Gene Bank to support content generation and creative product creation. The system also uses NFC chips in products to increase agent reach by over 50 percent.

Lenovo is responsible for the Tianqi Agent solution used for government and enterprise customers. The company stated that the Urban Digital Portal acts as a one-stop service steward for the city. Lenovo claims the Urban Task Kernel serves as an assistant that undertakes full-process tasks. The company also provides Baiying Agent-as-a-Service and Token-as-a-Service for its commercial customers. These tools help Dunhuang manage tourist services, urban governance, and industrial operations.

Tourists are affected by the agent through personalized itineraries and digital travel logs. The system has driven more than 13 million consumption orders through the ticket stub economy. Professor Ling Hong of Fudan University believes AI is now a basic capability for urban operation. He suggests that the significance of the project depends on whether the sample can be replicated. Other cities like Yichang, Hohhot, and Foshan have also deployed the Urban Super Agent.

The articles state that previous smart city models focused on data aggregation and visual dashboards. These older systems left government departments isolated and required manual coordination for cross-domain issues. IDC predicts that 70% of Chinese cities will deploy AI agents across all systems by 2027. The State Information Center expects the low-altitude economy market to exceed 1 trillion yuan in 2026. This growth creates high scheduling pressure for ground digital infrastructure.

Lenovo has deployed this agent in 11 cities since the global debut in 2025. Future steps include promoting the interconnection of AI standards between different cities. The articles leave open whether this architecture can be reused in manufacturing or megacity governance. It remains unclear if the system can move from customized experiments to reusable public infrastructure. Most current cases remain in the deployed stage rather than the verified effectiveness stage.

stories.Headline: Hong Kong Monetary Authority promotes agentic AI to manage on-chain financial crime risks
stories.Summary:
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority promoted the use of agentic AI to manage on-chain financial crime risks during November 2026. Raymond Chan, the Executive Director for Enforcement and AML, delivered a speech on this topic on November 17. He highlighted how this technology can combat illicit activity and fraud occurring with accelerating speed. The supervisor emphasized that banks must maintain accountability over these agentic systems. This initiative supports a broader strategy to make Hong Kong a world leader in digital asset innovation.

The HKMA published a discussion paper on agentic AI governance in the banking sector on November 2. This paper describes significant opportunities to enhance risk management, anti-fraud capabilities, operational efficiency, and customer experience. It requires banks to establish risk-based governance arrangements across the AI lifecycle to ensure alignment with intended outcomes. The framework suggests steps like ensuring human oversight, performing adequate validation, and monitoring for AI model risks. These efforts occur alongside the licensing of HSBC and Standard Chartered to issue stablecoins under the supervisory framework.

Raymond Chan stated that digital assets present unique risks due to their speed, global reach, pseudonymity, and limited reversibility. He argued that integrating blockchain analytics, customer due diligence, and scam intelligence into an AI agent would make AML controls more effective. Chan noted that a permanent public trail on the blockchain provides valuable evidence not possible with cash. He explained that agentic AI could analyze both on-chain transfers and off-chain transactions to flag anomalies like rapid fund layering. The HKMA aims to use the ART Framework to improve service delivery and financial crime risk mitigation.

The HKMA warned that adopting AI poses heightened risks including unintended actions, ambiguous accountability, data compromise, and operational disruption. Banks are the primary entities affected because they are the point where illicit on-chain and off-chain flows converge. International bodies like the G20 and Financial Services Board have also issued guidelines on AI governance. Supervisors in the US, UK, and Singapore have similarly drawn attention to the need for responsible AI governance. Elliptic also highlighted the role of agentic AI in responding to evolving threats while stressing the need for robust standards.

The HKMA has been engaged in supervisory activities involving the adoption of digital assets and AI by the banking sector. This includes undertaking substantial work to enable innovation in tokenization through its tokenization sandbox arrangements. The agency seeks to promote financial sector growth and competitiveness through a comprehensive regulatory framework. These activities are part of a wider effort to manage the systemic impact of digital asset risks. The supervisor believes that advanced technology is necessary to build a more complete picture of criminal funds flows.

The HKMA will continue to explore the development of agentic AI to provide banks with more powerful monitoring capabilities. Banks are expected to implement the proportionate governance arrangements described in the November 2 discussion paper. The agency will monitor how these tools mitigate risks associated with tokenization and stablecoins. The articles leave open how specifically the HKMA will measure the success of these AI agents in practice. They also leave open the specific timeline for the full deployment of these agentic systems across the banking sector.

Articles.Title: Crypto regulatory affairs: Hong Kong supervisor highlights agentic AI for on-chain risk management - Elliptic

stories.Headline: 10th Circuit requires human verification of AI-assisted court filings
stories.Summary:
The 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Denver instituted a new rule on Friday, November 25, 2026, to address artificial intelligence hallucinations. This mandate requires that all court filings utilizing artificial intelligence undergo a mandatory human review process. Attorneys and pro se parties must now certify that a human has verified every quotation and cited authority within their documents. This action follows several years of discovered fake citations caused by large language models producing false information.

Starting at the beginning of next year, the court can penalize violations by striking noncompliant documents or waiving the affected issues. Judges also have the authority to dismiss or affirm an appeal based on these failures. Furthermore, the court may impose monetary sanctions or require the offending party to pay some of the opponent's attorney fees. These strict requirements aim to ensure the accuracy of legal citations in an era of generative technology.

The court implemented these changes because large language models have frequently produced hallucinations that led to fake citations in legal filings. According to Law360, this trend has persisted for four years since generative AI first debuted on a mass scale. Data consultant Damien Charlotin noted that cases involving hallucinated citations worldwide have decreased this year due to better models and increased awareness. The 10th Circuit now requires human verification to prevent these errors from compromising the judicial process.

Articles.Title: 10th Circuit addresses AI hallucinations with new human fact-check rule

stories.headline_source: 10th Circuit addresses AI hallucinations with new human fact-check rule

stories.Headline: Pre-school AI rostering tool halves principal’s scheduling time
stories.Summary:
A new artificial intelligence-enabled rostering tool for pre-schools was demonstrated on Nov 23 at M.Y World @ Rivervale Shores, a pre-school in Sengkang, during a visit by Senior Minister of State for Social and Family Development Goh Pei Ming. The tool generates staff rosters and suggests replacements for absent educators while ensuring that teacher-child ratios are met, and it also sets aside two hours of non-teaching time each week for teachers to plan lessons and engage parents. Joey Lim, the centre principal, who oversees almost 60 staff and spends at least six hours a week on scheduling, estimates that the tool can halve the time she spends on rostering arrangements. She said it would let her focus more on professional development activities and on engagement sessions with other stakeholders.

The tool is one of 14 projects supported by the $2 million Early Childhood Innovation Sandbox, which the Early Childhood Development Agency said received over 60 proposals in its inaugural grant call in May, with the 14 chosen on factors such as relevance, scalability and potential impact. M.Y World Preschool aims to implement the tool at its Rivervale Shores and Ang Mo Kio centres from January 2027, a move that could benefit almost 100 employees. Its chief education officer, John Fong, said the sandbox funding gave the school resources to make innovative changes, and that without it such tailor-made solutions would be costly and progress might be slower. The other supported projects include an oral health surveillance tool proposed by PAP Community Foundation Sparkletots Preschool, which analyses photos of children's teeth to assess urgent dental care needs, and a facial recognition system proposed by Star Learners that verifies parents' and guardians' identities at drop-off and pick-up and sends real-time alerts to educators.

Poh Soon Tat, head of IT and group ventures at Star Learners, said the operator wants to see whether these changes can shorten wait times for families and give educators more time to focus on the children in their care. ECDA chief executive Ku Geok Boon said the strong interest in the sandbox showed the sector's commitment to addressing everyday challenges through innovation. The agency said the solutions aim to address operational challenges and reduce educators' administrative workload so they can focus more on supporting children's learning and development and partnering families. The next grant call will be in the second quarter of 2027, with more details to be announced on the ECDA website at a later date.

Articles.Title: AI tool to halve rostering time among govt-funded innovations for pre-schools

stories.Headline: Brookfield agrees $1.7 billion deal to buy PGP Glass from Blackstone and plans AI-led efficiency push
stories.Summary:
Brookfield, a global investment firm, agreed to acquire the speciality glass packaging manufacturer PGP Glass from Blackstone in a deal valued at $1.7 billion, according to Reuters, and the agreement was announced on Monday, November 23, 2026. Brookfield will acquire PGP through its flagship private equity strategy, and the investment will involve Brookfield Capital Partners and affiliate Brookfield Business Corporation. The transaction requires regulatory and government approvals, with completion expected during the first quarter of 2027. The deal marks a major investment in India's premium glass packaging industry, and it will transfer PGP Glass between two major global investment firms.

PGP Glass manufactures premium packaging for cosmetics, perfumes, pharmaceuticals and speciality food and beverages, and the company serves leading international brands across more than 70 countries. It operates three manufacturing facilities across India and Sri Lanka, and its services include product design, mould-making, speciality glass manufacturing and decoration. The company also maintains an extensive global logistics and warehousing network, and its integrated operations enable customers to access multiple packaging services through a single manufacturer. Brookfield sees considerable growth opportunities as global demand for premium glass packaging increases, and it plans to strengthen existing customer relationships while entering new international markets. Targeted investments in manufacturing capacity will support the company's expansion plans.

Artificial intelligence will play an important role in Brookfield's strategy for PGP Glass, and the investment firm intends to improve production efficiency through AI-driven operational changes covering sales planning, manufacturing operations and quality control. Aditya Joshi, Brookfield's private equity head for Asia Pacific and the Middle East, said that as demand for high-quality packaging continues to increase worldwide, Brookfield brings the scale and operating expertise to accelerate PGP's growth through an AI-led transformation program. Blackstone's Amit Dalmia praised PGP's operating performance and sustainability achievements under its ownership, saying the management team under Vijay Shah delivered outstanding operating performance, outpaced its peers and demonstrated leadership in sustainability. Shah welcomed Brookfield as the company's next investment partner, highlighting its international presence and experience managing businesses across economic cycles, and he acknowledged Blackstone's contribution towards PGP's manufacturing expansion and operational improvements.

The acquisition comes amid changing conditions in the global glass packaging industry, where European and North American manufacturers face rising costs and reductions in production capacity. These pressures could create opportunities for efficient manufacturers such as PGP Glass, and premium glass packaging also benefits from established demand and limited substitution risks. Brookfield manages assets exceeding $1 trillion across infrastructure, energy, private equity, real estate and credit, while Blackstone manages nearly $1.4 trillion across its global investment businesses. Brookfield will focus on international expansion, manufacturing improvements and technology-driven growth following the transaction.

stories.Headline: Review authors assess physical nonlinear activation functions for optical neural networks
stories.Summary:
A review paper on physically implemented nonlinear activation functions in optical neural networks was published in Nature Reviews Electrical Engineering on 25 November 2026, with a DOI listed as doi.org. The authors named on the paper are Martin Jakobi, Alexander W. Koch and Shiqiang Yang, with an ORCID identifier given as 0000-0003-0896-267X. The review covers nonlinear physical activation function devices and their optical signal modulation mechanisms in free-space and on-chip optical neural networks. It states that optical neural networks including free-space and on-chip architectures are promising for energy-efficient computing in the era of large neural network models with billions of parameters. It states that nonlinear processing units for activation functions are an essential building block in optical neurons with complete functions.

The review states that optical-electro-optical nonlinear activation functions based on Mach, Zehnder interferometers and micro-ring resonators achieve above 90% classification accuracy, picojoule-per-operation power consumption and subnanosecond latency in single-chip end-to-end optical neural networks. It states that all-optical nonlinear activation functions without electrical and optical signal conversion are promising for femtojoule and attojoule per-operation energy efficiency and 100-GHz bandwidth. It states that the future of practical optical neural networks requires nonlinear activation function devices with power consumption at the level of femtojoule per operation. It states that these devices should use the mathematical forms of rectified linear unit and its variants and modulation mechanisms based on cascaded optical-electro-optical and all-optical approaches. It states that scalable photonic systems are also required.

The review states that optical neural networks require reconfigurable and cascaded physical nonlinear activation functions to construct optical neurons with complete functions for nonlinear feature transformation. It states that optical nonlinear activation functions including optical-electrical, optical-electro-optical, electrical-optical and all-optical types mimicking their digital twins have been implemented in both free-space and on-chip optical neural networks. It states that electrical-optical conversion in the optical propagation process and optical-electrical conversion in the detection process are the mainstream configurations of nonlinear activation functions in free-space diffractive neural networks. It states that in backpropagated and feedforward network architectures, updating the parameters before and after nonlinear activation functions during in situ training processes is critical for mitigating the simulation, reality gap induced by hardware. It states that training must include both cascaded linear and nonlinear processing units to ensure parameters are optimized in situ for inference tasks including classification, localization and generation.

The review states that software-defined, programmable and small-footprint nonlinear activation functions are possible solutions towards scalable and reconfigurable optical neural networks with millions of parameters. It states that complementary metal oxide semiconductor compatibility is another possible solution. It states that efficient in situ training capabilities are also a possible solution. It states that these solutions are aimed at mainstream complex classification, detection and generation tasks in machine-vision and language processing applications. It states that all-optical nonlinear activation functions are especially promising through new configurations including structural nonlinearity and field programming.

The review includes six figures, covering a timeline of nonlinear activation function devices of hybrid types including electrical-optical, optical-electrical, optical-electro-optical and all-optical types. It includes figures on electrical-optical and optical-electrical nonlinear activation functions in free-space optical neural networks and on optical-electro-optical nonlinear activation functions in optical neural networks. It includes a figure on all-optical nonlinear activation functions in optical neural networks. It includes a figure on nonlinear activation functions in backpropagation and backpropagation-free training of optical neural networks. It includes a figure on the outlook for optical neural networks implementing physical nonlinear activation devices.

The review states that scaling optical neural networks for inference tasks including classification, localization and generation requires training that includes both cascaded linear and nonlinear processing units. It states that the parameters of optical neural networks must be optimized in situ. It leaves open which device configurations will reach the stated targets of femtojoule per-operation power consumption and 100-GHz bandwidth in practical systems. It leaves open how the simulation, reality gap induced by hardware will be mitigated in backpropagated and feedforward architectures. It leaves open which of the possible solutions, including software-defined and programmable nonlinear activation functions and complementary metal oxide semiconductor compatibility, will enable scalable and reconfigurable optical neural networks with millions of parameters.

Articles.Title: Physically implemented nonlinear activation functions in optical neural networks

stories.headline_source: Physically implemented nonlinear activation functions in optical neural networks

stories.Headline: New York governor Kathy Hochul signs a five-year ban on AI-enabled toys
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a bill on Tuesday that bans the sale, distribution and manufacture of AI-enabled toys in the state for five years, announcing the measure from a toy store in Harlem. The ban is set to begin in mid-February and applies to anyone statewide, with violations carrying a fine of $15,000 per day. Hochul said the products are harmful to children and described the move as a warning that some toys out there could hurt kids. She said that when tech companies and unregulated AI pose a threat to children and babies, she is going to have something to say about it. The toys covered by the ban are often stuffed animals integrated with chatbots that children can talk or text with, and the articles describe tests in which some of them went rogue when led into certain conversations.

NBC News testers watched one toy describe gang-rape and historical execution methods in graphic detail, while another tested by Common Sense Media was found encouraging kids to jump from roofs and windows. That same testing found the toys urging users as young as 5 to believe the chatbot was as real as their human friends. The ban bars businesses from selling, distributing or manufacturing the techie toys to anyone statewide, and the $15,000 per-day fine applies to violations. Hochul was joined by State Senator Andrew Gounardes, a Brooklyn Democrat who authored the ban bill and evoked the menacing Talky Tina doll from the 1962 "Twilight Zone" episode. Gounardes said that what the show's writer and host Rod Serling warned of in 1963 is actually here, pointing to the headlines appearing day after day.

He asked who knows what these chatbots are saying, what data they are collecting on children and what they are doing with it. He said kids deserve a real childhood, real toys and real connections, and the ability to play with their friends in the streets and at home. Hochul declined to expand on how AI toys would be handled after the ban but suggested she would speak on wider AI regulatory plans at her January state of the state address. The articles describe the ban as the latest cautionary measure she has taken against AI in New York, noting that she banned data center construction for one year in July, a move that frustrated tech proponents but satisfied AI-skeptical citizens. The articles do not say what happens to AI toys already owned by families or what steps would follow once the five-year period ends.

Articles.Title: NY bans AI toys for 5 years as lawmakers evoke creepy ‘Twilight Zone’ Talky Tina doll

stories.headline_source: NY bans AI toys for 5 years as lawmakers evoke creepy ‘Twilight Zone’ Talky Tina doll

stories.Headline: Researchers release DailySafe benchmark for tracking evolving safety risks in multimodal AI
stories.Summary:
Xuankun Rong, Xinhao Deng, Wenzheng Jiang, Ziheng Peng, Siyuan Liang, Wenke Huang, Pablo Arbelaez and Mang Ye posted a paper on arXiv on 25 November 2026 introducing DailySafe, a benchmark for what they call Dynamic Safety Awareness in multimodal large language models. The benchmark consists of 195 naturalistic multi-turn, multi-image interactions spread across 10 everyday domains and 42 task categories. The authors say it is grounded in authentic user dialogue topics and documented safety knowledge, so that safety-critical evidence is progressively revealed across conversational turns and visual observations. They describe the work as bringing multimodal safety evaluation closer to real-world everyday AI assistance, and they state that DailySafe is publicly available.

The paper argues that existing safety benchmarks mainly focus on isolated harmful requests or adversarial scenarios, and so overlook the safety risks that may arise as ordinary tasks unfold. In practice, the authors write, users pursue legitimate goals through multi-turn, multimodal interactions in which seemingly benign requests may become safety-critical when considered alongside earlier actions and visual observations. They define Dynamic Safety Awareness as the ability to track evolving task conditions, recognize implicit contextual risks, and provide safe and helpful assistance. DailySafe uses case-specific safety annotations to assess whether models can recognize and appropriately address evolving risks while still supporting users' legitimate goals.

The authors are responsible for the benchmark and frame it as a way to evaluate whether multimodal large language models can provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities, a question they say remains insufficiently explored. They present the benchmark as capturing realistic scenarios in which safety-critical evidence emerges gradually rather than in a single request. The paper states that DailySafe is publicly available, and it gives a link for access. The abstract does not report results for any model, and it does not say what happens next beyond the release of the benchmark.

Articles.Title: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions

stories.headline_source: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions

stories.Headline: KEPCO reports breach of 1.5 million customer and supplier records via external attacker
stories.Summary:
South Korean state-owned electric company Korea Electric Power Corporation disclosed a data breach affecting approximately 1.5 million customers and suppliers, according to a report published on November 25, 2026. The company said the incident involved KEPCO ON, its integrated customer service portal, and its supplier relationship management platform. KEPCO attributed the breach to an external attacker and noted the growing sophistication of AI-driven cyberattacks. The company did not confirm that AI was used in this specific incident.

Hackers stole personal information from KEPCO ON for 650,487 individuals, including names, addresses, phone numbers, unique ID numbers, customer numbers, and card and bank details. From the supplier relationship management systems, information for 869,761 individuals was exfiltrated, including names, email addresses, company addresses, and employee IDs for KEPCO staff and partners' employees. KEPCO suspended the affected services immediately after discovery, blocked external access, and conducted a thorough system review. The company has since notified affected individuals and reported the incident to relevant authorities.

South Korea's Personal Information Protection Commission has launched an investigation into the incident, and it noted that KEPCO received an email from the hacker and verified sample data. KEPCO has notified affected individuals and reported the incident to the relevant authorities, while the commission's investigation continues. The articles do not say what further action the company or the regulator will take. More to follow.

Articles.Title: KEPCO data breach impacts 1.5 million customers and suppliers

stories.Headline: Gilbane starts building New York's 74.5 million dollar Empire AI data center at the University at Buffalo
stories.Summary:
Gilbane broke ground on the Empire AI data center on November 19, 2026. Governor Kathy Hochul announced the start of this project in New York. The facility will be located at the University at Buffalo in Amherst. This new center will focus on research and education for the state. It is exempt from a statewide data center moratorium ordered by the governor.

The construction budget for the facility is 74.5 million dollars. It will initially use up to five megawatts of power in total. The site will house the Empire AI Gamma supercomputer for university researchers. The center will connect to the Baker Chilled Water Plant for cooling. It will use clean hydropower to run the high performance computing infrastructure.

Roger Treichler is a senior project executive at the construction firm Gilbane. He said Gilbane is proud to deliver a facility that expands computing resources. Treichler stated the project shows how technology and environmental stewardship work together. He noted the plan supports capturing and reusing heat across the North Campus. He said the facility helps researchers tackle challenges in healthcare and climate science.

The University at Buffalo will use heat from the facility to warm buildings. A system of pipes and geothermal wells will recover energy from the center. This technology will redistribute heat to the campus to reduce overall energy consumption. The project specifically serves researchers who need powerful computing resources for their work. The facility adds to two earlier systems that already serve the research community.

Governor Hochul paused certain state environmental permits for new data centers in July. This order was meant to study effects on water use and energy demand. The order exempts facilities used for research and names the Empire AI consortium. A second supercomputer in downtown Buffalo cost 40 million dollars to build. That system has 11 times the AI training capacity of a 2024 system.

Gilbane targets substantial completion of the data center for late 2027. The state expects the construction to reach full completion by early 2028. Treichler said finishing touches will continue on the site after substantial completion occurs. Remaining work includes testing building systems and commissioning the facility before operations begin. The articles do not state when the supercomputer will be fully operational.

stories.Headline: ChatGPT 5.5 Thinking and Gemini 3.5 Flash identify exact judo kata techniques in only 20.0 and 13.3 percent of clips
stories.Summary:
Two commercial multimodal artificial intelligence systems, ChatGPT 5.5 Thinking and Gemini 3.5 Flash, were tested on judo kata video clips by sports scientists and engineers at Universidad Europea de Madrid. The evaluation ran between June 16 and June 20, 2026, with each of 30 clips submitted three times to each platform, for 180 total submissions. The study was published on November 25, 2026, in an article on bioengineer.org. The models were asked to name the exact technique, the parent kata, the functional category, a justification and a confidence rating from 0 to 5. The systems identified the exact technique in only 20.0 percent and 13.3 percent of clips under a majority-of-three rule.

The stimulus set held 30 short competition clips from public YouTube broadcasts of official judo kata tournaments. The clips covered five katas, Nage-no-kata, Katame-no-kata, Ju-no-kata, Kime-no-kata and Kodokan Goshin Jutsu, with six clips from each. Each clip showed one complete technical execution of five to fifty-five seconds, from the establishment of grips to the final position, filmed from an unobstructed lateral view showing both tori and uke. Sessions began from clean application states with cross-session memory disabled, and video files were scrubbed of metadata and labeled with neutral numeric strings. A post-collection keyword audit found scoreboard text in two Kodokan Goshin Jutsu clips, which ChatGPT noted in its justification text, and sensitivity analyses excluding those submissions and clips confirmed no change to the conclusions.

The authors said the two desktop configurations differed in reasoning mode and compute allocation, so comparisons reflect the two specific products as configured rather than their underlying model families. They said the exploratory sample of 30 clips produced wide confidence intervals that preclude claims of equivalence between the platforms. They said video processing ran through proprietary desktop interfaces without direct control over frame rates, compression or internal tool settings. They said consumer video ingestion pipelines may sample frames at opaque frequencies, preserving macroscopic postural indicators such as stance and relative positioning while temporal downsampling strips fine dynamic transitions, unbalancing phases and micro-timing of grip entries. They said modern multimodal assistants can offer coarse semantic orientation within structured movement environments but are unsuitable as autonomous evaluators without rigorous human oversight.

ChatGPT correctly identified the parent kata in 19 of 30 clips, or 63.3 percent, and Gemini in 20 of 30, or 66.7 percent. Functional category accuracy was 15 of 30 (50.0 percent) for ChatGPT and 11 of 30 (36.7 percent) for Gemini. On first submissions only, ChatGPT identified 6 of 30 techniques (20.0 percent) and Gemini 3 of 30 (10.0 percent), and first-attempt category recognition favored ChatGPT by 30.0 percentage points, 16 of 30 against 7 of 30. The paired technique difference was 6.7 percentage points with confidence intervals from minus 8.6 to plus 22.4 percentage points, and paired statistical differences were undetectable under the primary endpoint. ChatGPT gave identical technique labels across all three repetitions for only 5 of 30 clips, and Gemini for just 2 of 30, with mean pairwise agreement of 34 percent and 16 percent.

ChatGPT never abstained across 90 technique submissions, and Gemini abstained once across its 90 evaluations. Of ChatGPT's 68 incorrect exact-technique submissions, 54 carried confidence ratings of 4 or 5, or 79.4 percent, while 73 of Gemini's 75 technique errors were high confidence, or 97.3 percent, and 67 errors (89.3 percent) carried the maximum score of 5. Confidence and correctness correlated at 0.127 for ChatGPT and 0.131 for Gemini, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values of 0.574 and 0.553. Across all 180 submissions the platforms cited Nage-no-kata 66 times against a balanced expectation of 36, and recognized Kodokan Goshin Jutsu only 11 times. Two independent judo experts blinded to the generating systems evaluated the outputs, with unresolved discrepancies settled by consensus.

Coding reliability reached a Cohen's kappa of 1.00 for technique identification, 0.88 for parent kata and 0.86 for technique category. The authors noted that traditional markerless pipelines extract geometric landmarks and kinematic coordinates but require calibrated camera installations, dedicated software configurations and substantial biomechanical interpretation by domain experts. They noted that generalist vision-language models accept natural video alongside text prompts and return natural-language categorical judgments without user-side calibration or kinematic coordinate extraction. They noted that judo kata consists of strictly codified, sequentially organized techniques cataloged by the Kodokan Institute and judged under explicit International Judo Federation standards. They noted that the capacity of generalist models to interpret complex technical gestures and signal uncertainty when visual evidence is insufficient had remained largely unvalidated in formal movement science.

The article leaves open whether the findings extend beyond the two products as configured, given the wide confidence intervals and the authors' statement that equivalence between platforms cannot be claimed. It leaves open how proprietary frame sampling, compression and internal tool settings affected the results, which the authors said they could not control. It leaves open whether the scoreboard text in the two Kodokan Goshin Jutsu clips affected any outcome, though sensitivity analyses found no change. It leaves open how the systems would perform on larger samples, since the exploratory set of 30 clips was small. It leaves open whether other multimodal systems or configurations would show the same pattern of high-confidence errors and rare abstention.

Articles.Title: Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Models Fail Exact Judo Kata Recognition Despite High Confidence
