stories.Headline: Wells Fargo holds customers liable for mistakes made by their AI agents
stories.Summary:
Wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers, specifically about AI agents, starting on Tuesday, according to WIRED. The bank’s new terms state that “Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK,” the article reported. In late October, JPMorgan Chase changed its terms to ban third-party agents that log in with your credentials, WIRED reported. That same day, Bank of America warned its customers not to share login info with agents, according to WIRED. Citibank and PNC have also changed their terms to include warnings about agents, WIRED reported.

The survey in Bankers Journal for the American Bankers Association found 27% are likely to let an AI agent autonomously manage their bank accounts in the next 12 months. It also found 20% say an AI agent has already asked them for login credentials or a card number. The survey also found large majorities are concerned about AI moving money, want businesses held to the same standards as banks, and say they should not be required to give a bank’s AI agent their passwords. In the past few weeks, several major institutions, including Chase, Schwab, Citigroup and Wells Fargo, blocked outside AI agents such as “Muse” from logging in to accounts using customers’ credentials, according to News 3 Las Vegas. Many of those banks now say any actions taken by a customer’s AI agent, including mistakes, will be the customer’s responsibility, the article reported.

Wells Fargo’s warning to early adopters could not be clearer, WIRED reported, with the bank’s new terms stating use of any AI Agent is at the user’s own risk. Kacy Kim, an associate professor of marketing at Bryant University who studies consumer behavior and emerging tech, said “Consumers authorize goals, not every click,” according to WIRED. Kim expects some consumers to feel like it’s unfair to be held accountable for their agent’s mistakes, but she doesn’t expect these policy moves by financial institutions to scare off the early-adopter crowd already using the tools as part of everyday life, WIRED reported. Sucharita Kodali, a Forrester analyst who focuses on ecommerce and consumer behavior, said “All of our data shows that most people don’t even know what agents are, much less use them,” according to WIRED. Kodali sees banks as fundamentally risk-averse, so taking proactive measures now makes sense, even if most agentic issues remain edge cases, WIRED reported.

Luca Cian, a professor at the University of Virginia who studies consumer psychology and AI, said “People are very comfortable with AI buying toilet paper,” according to WIRED. Cian sees consumers as increasingly comfortable turning to AI tools for shopping advice but often only automating boring buys, like household supplies, WIRED reported. Cian said “Banks are doing two things at once,” adding “They’re locking the door to outside agents and building their own,” according to WIRED. Users have interacted with Wells Fargo’s tool that answers questions using generative AI over a billion times, WIRED reported. American Express announced that some agentic mistakes, like ordering too many of a certain item, may be eligible for reimbursement in the future through the card provider if you can’t get your money back from the original retailer, according to WIRED.

Natalie, who uses AI at work, said “The only thing I use it for is to generate graphics for my work, and that is just a shortcut,” according to News 3 Las Vegas. When asked whether she uses AI in her own personal banking, Natalie said “Uh, no. I just go on the app usually,” adding “But I like better going in person to the teller line and speaking with a person. Call me old school.” Asked whether she trusts AI for banking, Natalie said “No, especially with the recent news reports,” News 3 Las Vegas reported.

UNLV cybersecurity professor Dr. Yoohwan Kim said AI agents should be treated like new employees who need limited access at first, according to News 3 Las Vegas. Kim said “So agents like human beings, like new employees; on day one they don’t know anything, so you give them just a little permission,” the article reported. Kim said an AI agent can gradually learn routines and what it is allowed to access and, if a user chooses, handle low-risk tasks such as writing an email, according to News 3 Las Vegas. But he said banking and sending money are high-risk because transactions may not be reversible, the article reported.

Kim said “So you gradually release the access or the permission to agents,” according to News 3 Las Vegas. Kim also warned that AI agents can be manipulated because they follow instructions and may not recognize suspicious activity, the article reported. “You can put instructions inside the PDF file or image file. We don’t see it, but agents can see it, so they can be redirected to wrong websites or wrong actions,” he said, according to News 3 Las Vegas.

Articles.Title: Consumers weigh risks as banks warn AI agent mistakes could be customers’ liability

stories.Headline: Oak Park parent urges districts to adopt clear AI policies protecting student privacy
stories.Summary:
Stacey Belmont, a member of Screen Sense Oak Park and an Oak Park parent, wrote in a letter published by Wednesday Journal on November 24, 2026, that her child was asked to use AI to alter photos for an assignment so students could better envision themselves in an earlier time period. She said alarm bells went off in her head because of the potential privacy issues involved in feeding children's images to AI. In the same week, she wrote, her oldest child was given an assignment requiring her to record her speech with AI, and when she asked for an alternative she was told there was none and to accept the consequences to her grade if she chose not to do it. Belmont said these experiences led her to research whether Oak Park school districts have official AI policies, and she found the results were mixed.

Belmont wrote that District 200 has what it calls a policy but that it is actually more of a guideline, which does not address students' rights and options to forgo AI when it violates their personal values and merely discusses using it to enhance education without substance or clear boundaries. She wrote that District 97 similarly has district guidance but no firm policy. Without official policies, she wrote, teachers are put in the position of determining AI's appropriateness for use in schools and then making judgment calls about what is considered private or sensitive, and they are likely not aware of the many ways AI uses the data it is fed. She called this an unfair position for teachers and a disservice to children and the wider community.

Belmont wrote that the districts need clear policies on AI use, something Screen Sense Oak Park is advocating for, and she listed what such a policy should do. It should protect student privacy and prohibit disclosure of children's sensitive data, allow older students to opt out altogether and receive alternative non-AI-dependent assignments, and require parental consent for younger students who are not cognitively mature enough to consent to the potential consequences. She added that it should line up with the values of the community and consider its impact on the planet, and support the development of critical thinking, creativity and problem-solving. She wrote that it is time for D97 and D200 to act because AI is not going away any time soon.

Articles.Title: Schools need clearer AI policies

stories.Headline: Congressional Research Service releases a guide organizing federal AI policy research into twelve topics for lawmakers
stories.Summary:
The Congressional Research Service released a new report on November 24, 2026, providing Congress with a comprehensive topical guide to federal artificial intelligence policy research. This new resource organizes selected work from the research agency into twelve distinct topic areas to help lawmakers navigate complex legal and policy issues. The guide includes a variety of written and audiovisual products that examine legislation, executive branch actions, and various AI-related policy challenges. These categories specifically cover critical sectors such as national security, defense, health care, infrastructure, finance, patents, and the integrity of elections. The guide tracks several key executive actions, including an explainer on Executive Order 14409 which was published in the Federal Register on June 5.

This specific order directs federal agencies to prioritize cybersecurity and create a voluntary framework for government access to certain advanced AI models. The report also details court outcomes regarding the federal government and Anthropic, noting a California district-court injunction on August 27 and a D.C. Circuit ruling on September 25. Additionally, the guide references the TAKE IT DOWN Act, known as Public Law 119-12, which became law on May 19, 2025, to prohibit the nonconsensual publication of intimate images. The Congressional Research Service is responsible for this guide and notes that advances in machine learning, generative AI, and facial recognition offer potential benefits across many sectors.

However, the agency also expressed significant concerns regarding the spread of misinformation, potential shifts in the job market, and various security risks. The report further includes information on cyber and artificial intelligence provisions found within the National Defense Authorization Act for the 2026 fiscal year. These entries aim to provide a centralized location for members of Congress to review how the government is managing the rapid evolution of AI technology. More to follow.

stories.Headline: LexisNexis adds citation and quote checks to Protégé as states tighten legal AI rules
stories.Summary:
New York’s October 26, 2026, guidance on the risks of using artificial intelligence in preparing court papers specifically names LexisNexis as an authoritative source attorneys can use to independently verify AI-generated citations and quotations. The guidance reinforces attorney accountability under existing duties and does not generally require special disclosure of AI use under its statewide approach. California’s SB 574, signed September 30, 2026, and effective January 1, 2027, adds statutory requirements addressing verification, professional responsibility, confidentiality, and disclosure. Pennsylvania’s court advisory committee has published a proposed AI notice and compliance certification for public comment, and New York’s pending S9794 and A9097 would impose additional certification or disclosure obligations. Those proposals are not current requirements, but they show that expectations continue to develop.

The article organizes these expectations into four practical categories: verify authorities, retain professional responsibility and judgment, protect sensitive information, and document or disclose AI use as applicable. Lexis+ with Protégé brings together verification capabilities, attorney-directed skills and drafting tools, and security safeguards that the article says help attorneys address these expectations in their everyday work. Shepard’s Verify checks citations against LexisNexis legal content and Shepard’s citation information, provides Shepard’s Signals where available, and flags unmatched citations for further review. Shepard’s Verify will soon check quotations and paraphrased statements against cited sources, flagging inaccurate quotes, misleading context, and unsupported or overstated characterizations of case law. The article notes that matching a citation to a real authority does not establish that it supports a particular proposition or quotation.

Protégé’s Skills provide reusable instructions for specific tasks, and custom skills can reflect a firm’s preferred workflows, document standards, and review processes. For complex drafting and analysis, attorneys can review, edit, and approve a proposed plan before execution, then follow progress and assess the results. Protégé operates within the LexisNexis environment, supported by privacy, security, and governance controls, and customer data is not used to train or fine-tune LexisNexis AI models. New York’s guide recommends recording the tools used, the tasks performed, and the verification steps taken, while California’s new law requires disclosure of generative AI use for court-submitted documents. Shepard’s Verify offers downloadable PDF reports that attorneys can retain as part of their verification records.

Tony Muljadi, Vice President of Large Law at LexisNexis, said that as expectations for legal AI evolve, attorneys need technology they can trust and practical ways to verify its work. He said LexisNexis has for decades helped attorneys research the law and validate the authorities they rely on, and that Lexis+ with Protégé builds on that foundation. He described the company’s commitment as helping customers put AI to work with the sources, safeguards, and oversight that responsible legal practice demands. The article states that the attorney remains responsible for applying the rules governing each matter and must still determine what disclosure is necessary and submit it in the form their court requires.

stories.Headline: RoboStrategy courts Korean pension funds and insurers for physical AI robotics investments
stories.Summary:
RoboStrategy, a fund from the United States, held its first institutional investor relations event in Korea. The fund targets professional investors, insurers, and pension funds to raise new capital. This event took place on the 22nd of November in the Cheongdam-dong area of Seoul. The fund focuses on investing in physical AI companies and unlisted robotics firms. It seeks to attract institutional investors from the Korean market to grow its assets.

The fund listed on the Nasdaq in May of this year with a market capitalization of 810 billion won. It has invested in Figure AI, a humanoid manufacturer valued at about 50 trillion won. The fund is currently in early talks with insurers, pension funds, and professional investors. These discussions aim to secure capital for further investments in the robotics sector. The event in Cheongdam-dong served as the primary venue for these institutional briefings.

Co-Chief Executive Andrew Kang outlined the fund's plans during the event on the 22nd. He stated that the fund is in early talks with various institutional investors in Korea. Kang forecast that the robotics industry will see a major leap within three to six months. He presented these views to the gathered professional investors and pension fund representatives. The fund's leadership believes the timing is right for significant growth in physical AI.

The fund is courting pension funds, insurers, and professional investors who manage large capital pools. These institutional investors are the primary parties affected by the fund's capital raising efforts. The fund targets those interested in unlisted robotics companies and advanced humanoid technology. Professional investors in Seoul are the specific group being courted for this venture. The fund aims to integrate Korean institutional capital into its global investment strategy.

RoboStrategy invests specifically in unlisted robotics companies and firms specializing in physical AI. The fund has already backed Figure AI, which produces humanoid robots for various uses. It entered the public market via the Nasdaq exchange in May of this year. The fund operates with a market capitalization of approximately 810 billion won. It focuses on the intersection of artificial intelligence and physical robotic hardware.

The fund will continue its early talks with Korean insurers and pension funds to raise capital. It expects a major leap in the robotics sector within the next three to six months. The articles do not state the specific amount of capital the fund wants to raise. They do not mention if any Korean institutions have already committed funds to the venture. It remains open whether these early talks will lead to formal investment agreements.

stories.Headline: AI giants integrate models into enterprise workflows to drive profitability
stories.Summary:
AI giants are shifting their focus toward enterprise workflows to ensure profitability. This transition occurred as the secondary market stopped equating technological breakthroughs with future earnings. Anthropic officially went public with an offering price of 83 USD. Its stock price fell after an initial first-day increase of 17 percent. This shift happened as companies moved from providing conversation assistants to business executors.

Anthropic defines Claude as a virtual collaborator that handles complex multi-step tasks. Claude Code helps engineers with planning, writing, testing, and debugging project development. Claude Cowork targets non-technical personnel for research, drafting, and data analysis. By September 2026, Cowork adoption surpassed that of Claude Code. Enterprise adoption grew from 20 customers in December 2023 to 11,900 by the third quarter of 2026.

Robin Li Yanhong stated that intelligent organizations are the new factories of the AI era. He launched the Kuku agent to connect enterprise cloud disks and chat records. Anthropic claims its Recursive Self-Improvement technology creates a computing multiplier for better performance. This technology helped Opus 5.5 reduce single-task costs by about 40 percent. Baidu also uses this technology to optimize its ERNIE-5.5-Flash model reasoning speed.

Tencent connected its Hunyuan model to WeCom and Tencent Docs for automated business flows. Its WorkBuddy enterprise version reached a 60 percent penetration rate among China's top 100 enterprises. WorkBuddy has more than 10 million daily active users. Baidu's Famou 3.0 now covers 25 of 41 industrial categories in China. ByteDance uses Feishu to connect data and approval nodes into a closed loop.

AI initially entered the market as free conversation assistants to capture user traffic. Companies like DeepSeek and Doubao provided free versions to attract users. This model failed because advertisements damage the objectivity and professionalism of productivity tools. Enterprise customers offer higher unit prices and more stickiness than individual users. Giants now seek to build commercial moats through deep integration into business flows.

Companies will continue integrating AI into internal code bases and development specifications. This creates path dependence because migration and labor costs for replacement are incalculable. Anthropic plans a capital and research loop where revenue growth funds further model development. The articles leave open how enterprises will overcome natural inertia and resistance to change. They also leave open the specific costs of introducing AI from zero to one.

stories.Headline: Trapit Bansal leaves Meta to start new AI research from scratch
stories.Summary:
Trapit Bansal, an IIT Kanpur alumnus, announced in a post on X that he has left Meta after 16 months at the company. At Meta he was a founding researcher at TBD Lab within its Superintelligence Labs, where he contributed to the development of Muse AI models. Before joining Meta in July 2025, he spent over three years at OpenAI, where he focused on AI reasoning research and was a co-creator of the o1 reasoning model. His departure suggests a return to exploring new research ideas, and he said he is starting from scratch again to find out what comes next.

His time at Meta was part of a significant AI hiring initiative by Mark Zuckerberg in 2025 to build advanced AI models. His compensation package from Meta was reportedly $100 million, which is about ₹800 crore, though these details were not publicly confirmed. His career began in India, where he earned degrees in Mathematics and Statistics from IIT Kanpur, followed by research roles at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru. He later pursued a PhD in Computer Science at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, with internships at companies including Facebook, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI.

Bansal has not yet disclosed specific plans for his next venture, so what he will work on next remains unknown. The articles give no further details on the timing of his departure beyond the announcement or on any response from Meta. They also say nothing about who might replace him at TBD Lab or how the Muse AI models will be affected. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Developer open-sources 11,011 AI-generated bird stickers built from scraped photos
stories.Summary:
A birdwatching app called Bird Trace: Birdwatching Logbook appeared on the App Store in recent days, and its installation package is as large as 1GB, while a typical popular science field guide app usually takes up around 100MB. The developer crammed massive bird stickers directly into the local package to save server resources, and the interface copy and update notes show a pervasive Claude-generated style. The app's built-in materials come from an open source project called the Global Bird Sticker Library, and a supporting bird website called Bird Album supports retrieval in 15 languages. The developer says he cannot write code at all, burned more than 1 billion Tokens through Vibe Coding, and used up the weekly quota of multiple $200 top-tier memberships. In less than a week, with one computer and 8 windows running AI scripts, he turned 11,064 existing bird species worldwide into white-bordered stickers and announced the project was officially open source.

The checklist was later adjusted to 11,011 species and 91 subspecies following an update. The author bulk-scraped real photos from iNaturalist and Wikimedia Commons, stitched them into 3×3 nine-square grids, and fed them to a generative image model for redrawing. Among the reference photos of these 11,064 bird species, only 1,986 are actually licensed under open licenses such as CC0 and CC BY. The rest are marked non-commercial use, no derivative works or all rights reserved, and 2017 of them have no recorded license agreement at all. The author first used the PolyForm Shield 1.0 license that restricts use of competing products, later changed it to CC BY 4.0, and wrote that anyone who does not want a photo used should send an email to raise an Issue and it will be removed within 7 days.

The author recommends that everyone use these stickers to make courseware for nature education and bird cards for children, and provides CDN interfaces bound to the IDs of eBird and GBIF. He added a disclaimer in the documentation saying these are illustrations, not field guide plates, and that error correction from bird lovers is the most needed contribution. He admitted that the reference photo scraped for the Peregrine Falcon was taken from a low angle under a tree, with the feet blocked by belly feathers and branches, and the AI filled in a pair of thin claws. He classified ornithologists who expressed deep indignation and other independent developers who kept criticizing the project as remnants of the old era, workers who rejected the textile loom. He is quite proud that self-media outlets and ordinary users are piecing together popular science texts, images and short videos from the stickers.

The r/birds section of the overseas birdwatching community Reddit said feeding other people's hard work into a plagiarism machine can never be whitewashed by an opt-out mechanism implemented after the fact. Ornithologists have expressed deep indignation, and other independent developers have kept criticizing the project. Self-media outlets and ordinary users who do not have professional identification capabilities are using the stickers, which have serious errors in basic biological features such as feather color and beak shape, to piece together expert-level popular science content that spreads freely on social platforms. In the first version of the open source repository there are as many as 3,388 defective works that do not meet the AI passing line of 80 points set by the project itself, and 109 of them are even below 70 points. The image library has never undergone systematic review by even one ornithology expert.

During testing, the author himself found that the generative image model frequently creates ridiculous, bizarre monsters, with irises that are originally red or teal drawn as lifeless solid black eyeballs, toes fused into a lump of flesh, and hummingbirds forcibly given a pair of long sparrow-like legs. For rare bird species that cannot find good reference photos, the author patched together several incomplete photos, sent the result to another AI reviewer for scoring, and kept the relatively best one from the bad lot. The Sulphur-crested Cockatoo, the author's favorite bird species and the original inspiration for the project, came out with its folded wing feather area completely wrong. The article cites Lu Xun's Mr. Fujino, in which Mr. Fujino tells Lu Xun that anatomical diagrams are not fine art and the real object cannot be changed. The article says the idea that aesthetic effect is more important than facts still has a huge market in the AI circle.

In November the author re-ran all the more than 10,000 images with another set of AI standards and announced that all of them passed the line. The author's principle is to neither fall back on using real photos nor leave the entry blank, but to pick the relatively best one from the bad lot. The article says the author adheres to the agile development thinking of launching and getting it working first, then relying on the community to raise Issues for iterative error correction. The article states that translating this logic of pollute first, govern later to the field of natural science is undoubtedly a disaster. The article leaves open whether professional review was conducted before the product was launched and pushed to the public for popular science purposes.

stories.Headline: Ghana education minister Haruna Iddrisu proposes coding and AI subjects for basic schools pending Cabinet approval
stories.Summary:
Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu announced on Monday at the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission in Accra that basic schools will introduce new subjects. Students from kindergarten to Primary Six will study coding, robotics, artificial intelligence, and electronics once the Cabinet approves a revised curriculum. These subjects are not currently in force because the Cabinet has not yet signed off on the changes. Mr. Iddrisu has mentioned these potential curriculum updates during various gatherings since December 2025.

The proposed changes require a revised basic school curriculum that also includes financial literacy for students. Researchers are currently presenting evidence on digital learning to help create a draft AI-in-education roadmap for 2027 to 2030. While the 2027 Budget provides for 10,000 recruitment places for various education staff, no specific costs for the new subjects have been released. There is currently no official start date for the classrooms, no list of required equipment, and no timetable for teacher training.

Minister Haruna Iddrisu stated that the government intends to use artificial intelligence to improve learning outcomes and develop competitive human capital. He clarified that the policy aims to empower teachers with technology rather than replacing them with artificial intelligence. The Minister warned that the country must prevent the use of these tools from creating lazy learners who take shortcuts. He believes that such shortcuts could prevent the production of quality graduates for the needs of the country.

stories.Headline: Tidal bans fully AI-generated tracks and will remove over 29 million songs starting December 9
stories.Summary:
The music streaming service Tidal announced on Tuesday that it will ban and remove millions of songs created entirely by artificial intelligence. This decision follows a massive surge in submissions where over 43 percent of tracks uploaded in the last 90 days were AI generated. The company intends to stop the flood of low quality content that is currently inundating its digital platform. This aggressive move aims to protect the visibility of human musicians against a tide of automated audio.

The removal process will begin on December 9 and is expected to delete more than 29 million songs by the end of the year. Under these new rules, the platform will reject between 80,000 and 85,000 tracks every single day. Tidal is also banning distribution services from delivering tracks that are 100 percent AI generated based on their metadata. While fully automated songs are banned, the service will still accept music that was created with AI assistance.

Robert Anderson, who leads Tidal Music, stated on X that previous efforts to demonetize AI tracks in June were not enough of a deterrent. He explained that the sheer scale of these uploads means authentic artists are getting buried under a mountain of synthetic content. The company noted that 27 million tracks, or 6.3 percent of its library, are fully AI generated. They further observed that 96 percent of those specific automated tracks have received no streams at all.

Tidal claims to be one of the first major platforms after Bandcamp to ban AI music in such an outright manner. Other services like Deezer are introducing filters, while Spotify and YouTube Music have chosen to label the content instead of removing it. The company believes that drastic action is necessary to maintain the authenticity of the music discovery experience for its subscribers. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Sanders and Schneier propose a three-point plan for Democrats to unite on AI regulation
stories.Summary:
Democrats must unite on AI regulation, according to a three-point plan by Nathan E Sanders and Bruce Schneier published in the Guardian on 25 November 2026. The authors said this month's elections showed the American public's urgent demand for change. They said the elections also revealed that Democrats had not presented a compelling plan around AI. They said AI companies and their boosters tossed around hundreds of millions of dollars in the 2026 elections. They said the Trump administration lined up unequivocally alongside industry oligarchs.

The authors said an October survey shows 84% of voters say AI threatens American workers. They said 57% say the Trump administration has not taken AI risks seriously enough or at all. They said 80% of Democrats and 61% of Republicans want stricter AI regulation. They said voters say by nearly a seven-to-one ratio that companies developing or deploying AI should be liable for the harms of their products. They said Congress has not established that accountability.

The authors proposed curbing the power of big tech, building AI that works for everyone, and putting people in charge of where the technology is used. They said they would match and extend Massachusetts' policy preventing companies from foisting pollution and price spikes on datacenter host communities. They said they would require datacenter developers to match their power consumption with new clean energy and install energy storage systems. They said they would levy an excise tax on the energy used by large AI datacenters. They said they would direct the funds to a counterbalancing reduction in payroll taxes and to support unemployment insurance.

The authors said Democratic senators-elect Sherrod Brown in Ohio, James Talarico in Texas, Troy Jackson in Maine and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan all ran and won against giveaways to tech billionaires. They said Vermont senator Bernie Sanders has advocated that the government acquire shares of AI companies. They said California representative Ro Khanna has called to give workers a say in AI use in their workplaces. They said New York governor Kathy Hochul has signed safeguards for consumers using AI companions into law. They said South Korea offers free universal AI access to its 52 million residents.

The authors said they studied examples from around the world in their book Rewiring Democracy. They said a datacenter developer in the UK secured more than £200m of public guarantees for a project before backtracking on promises to use renewable energy. They said Switzerland and Spain are building public AI already. They said a bipartisan coalition including New Mexico senator Martin Heinrich and New Jersey senator Cory Booker have proposed a permanent federal AI research program. They said Warren has proposed the Accountable Capitalism Act, which would give workers at least a 40% share of the largest corporations' board seats.

The authors said the congressional caucus must walk into the Capitol in January prepared to take immediate legislative action. They said that includes rejecting AI billionaires' campaign funds and barring Congress members from stock trading. They said Congress should insist that states receiving federal energy and economic grants require their cities to execute transparent, binding and enforceable agreements with datacenter developers. They said Congress should invest in a permanent federal AI research program. They said they would bar companies from consolidating control of the full AI stack across chips, compute infrastructure, and model development.

Articles.Title: Democrats must unite on AI regulation. Here’s our three-point plan | Nathan E Sanders and Bruce Schneier - The Guardian

stories.Headline: Maryland students sue Omnilert and school officials over AI chip bag gun alert
stories.Summary:
Four current and former students from a Maryland high school filed a federal lawsuit. They were detained at gunpoint after an AI system mistook chips for a gun. This incident occurred approximately one year before the lawsuit was filed in November 2026. Armed police officers accosted the students and held them in handcuffs. The students reported that they feared for their lives during the encounter.

The lawsuit names Omnilert, the company that created the AI gun detection system. Other defendants include the Baltimore County Police, the board of education, and individual officers. Kenwood High School principal Catherine Kate Smith is also named as a defendant. The plaintiffs allege unlawful detention and search due to human and technological errors. The incident involved a bag of Doritos that the AI identified as a firearm.

Omnilert expressed regret over the incident but shifted blame to those acting on alerts. The company stated its system is designed to identify threats for human review. It claimed the process functioned as intended to prioritize safety through rapid verification. Principal Kate Smith sent a text message with laughing emojis after the event. She wrote that the patrol car found it was just a bag of chips.

The students involved were the ones affected by the armed police response. Some officers on the scene expressed that the AI cameras were stupid and unreliable. One officer told the students that AI is not the best during the encounter. Two school administrators had canceled the alert within two minutes of receiving it. They determined the footage showed nothing more than a student holding a bag of chips.

Omnilert uses AI to detect guns by analyzing images from school camera systems. The company's profile rose after its tech failed to detect a real school shooting. In that separate event, a student killed one person and injured another before suicide. The current lawsuit follows a pattern of false positives in AI gun detection technology. The principal manually sent a screenshot to SRO John Douglas after the alert ended.

The legal process will now determine if the defendants are held personally accountable. A judge must decide which of the named defendants remain in the lawsuit. The articles do not state when the court will hear the case. It remains open whether the school will change its use of AI technology. The text does not say if the students received a settlement.

Articles.Title: Students Detained At Gunpoint After AI Says Their Bag Of Chips Is A Gun File Federal Lawsuit - Techdirt.

stories.headline_source: Students Detained At Gunpoint After AI Says Their Bag Of Chips Is A Gun File Federal Lawsuit

stories.Headline: Indiana Supreme Court distributes AI toolkit for judges and launches mental health pilot
stories.Summary:
The Indiana Supreme Court published its 2025-2026 annual report on Nov. 19, highlighting changes and improvements the court made across the judicial branch during the fiscal year. The report says the court continues to seek improvements to state courts' use of artificial intelligence and distributed a model toolkit for judges across the state to use in their own implementation of AI. The AI model toolkit was phase two of the court's AI Governance Committee's work to establish internal guardrails on AI use in state courts. During phase one, the committee developed and distributed a foundational policy for Supreme Court staff to use in responsible AI decision making. In total, the committee developed four tools to help judges draft their own AI policies, including a starter pack summarizing key rules judges should understand before using AI.

The tools also include a checklist for organizing and planning a policy, guidelines on how to regulate AI within the framework of the Code of Judicial Conduct and the Rules of Professional Conduct, and a buyers' guide for judges who may want to purchase off-the-shelf AI software for their courtrooms. In October 2025, the court's Office of Behavioral Health launched an assisted outpatient treatment pilot program, convening a statewide cohort of 10 county teams who received training and technical assistance to support local outpatient treatment programs. The programs are court-ordered civil commitments for individuals with severe mental illness caught in a cycle of hospitalization and arrest, according to the annual report. In April 2026, the court's Behavioral Health Committee published its inaugural report of 16 priorities to help judges and court staff navigate defendants' behavioral health challenges, focusing on education, connection to treatment, competency and data and funding. Indiana's behavioral health office was created as a result of Indiana Supreme Court Chief Justice Loretta Rush's work in state and federal task forces focused on the issue.

In May, Rush told The Indiana Lawyer she wanted to build a team that could identify and promote resources to help judicial officers address behavioral health challenges while ensuring justice is served. Rush said judges do not get a pass for behavior if someone commits a crime because of substance abuse or something else, describing the dual roles a judge has. Last fiscal year, the Supreme Court reviewed 790 cases, heard 39 oral arguments and handed down 47 majority opinions, according to the annual report. The court received 790 cases and disposed 809 cases, leaving 131 cases pending as of June 30. The court distributed more than $22 million in grant funds across the state, including more than $72,000 to court improvement programs and more than $40,000 to educational scholarships.

stories.Headline: Manitoba education minister Tracy Schmidt expands school cellphone ban to include smart watches and AI glasses
stories.Summary:
Manitoba Education Minister Tracy Schmidt sent a directive to school leaders last week telling them to add smart glasses, smart watches and other wearable technologies to the cellphone ban that has been in place in the province's schools since September 2024, the Manitoba government says. The November 17 letter went to all school division superintendents as well as principals of independent schools that receive public funding, and it said students increasingly have access to personal devices that offer messaging, social media, internet browsing, photography, recording, artificial intelligence tools or other cellphone-like functions. The directive was issued one week after the Hanover School Division in southeast Manitoba became the first division in the province to ban smart glasses in its schools, according to the government, with a letter to parents citing privacy because the glasses can record audio and video without others readily knowing. Schmidt said in a statement that guidelines must evolve with technology so students learn in healthy, safe environments that support their education and well-being, and the original ban was meant to reduce distractions in classrooms and minimize the harmful impacts associated with social media and online platforms.

Kara Brisson-Boivin, director of research at the Ottawa-based digital media literacy group MediaSmarts, said Manitoba is on the right track but she would like to see rules set at the federal level rather than a patchwork of 13 provinces and territories regulating the same technological challenge in different shades of grey. She said policing the technology should not fall on school staff who are already overrun with day-to-day challenges, and she is not convinced a blanket long-term ban is right because students with visual and hearing impairments could be aided by such devices, though she said not enough is known yet about the potential benefits. Meta, one of several makers of AI glasses, says on its website that its product has an LED light that blinks to alert others when the wearer takes a picture or records video, and the glasses automatically disable the camera if they detect the capture light was covered or tampered with. Brisson-Boivin said that light is difficult to recognize, especially for children and youth, and online criticism says the LEDs are small and easy to miss in direct sunlight, in bright indoor lighting, from the side or in crowded spaces.

Logan Hassett, 14, told CBC he could not understand why watches are included because there is not as much to do on them and it is easy to see if someone is staring at their watch, while Kaitlynn Seavers, who bought a smart watch for her 10-year-old son, said a ban goes too far and parents should teach their kids when to use one. Tracy Cosser, assistant director of the Manitoba Child Care Association, called the crackdown a really good idea, saying parents want to stay connected to their children but devices that can take video and images infringe on privacy. Brisson-Boivin said it makes good sense to slow the integration of new technology in a controlled way and study the benefits as well as the harms, and she said Manitoba is taking important steps but a broader conversation is needed across the country about the role and place of wearable technology. She said AI, like any other technology, is a tool that can be used to hone skills but should not be used to replace them.

Articles.Title: Smart watches, AI glasses now outlawed in Manitoba schools - CBC

stories.Headline: A Chicago teacher says Title I schools lag on AI access and training
stories.Summary:
Sofia Gonzalez, an English teacher for English learners at a Title I high school near Chicago, wrote in EdSurge on November 25, 2026, that AI development has accelerated faster than anyone could have imagined since ChatGPT was released to the public four years earlier. She described watching AI become part of the fabric of K-12 education while educators on the ground struggle to incorporate it into policy, student learning and instructional practices. At her school, part of a high school district near Chicago, teachers and administrators completing a recent survey indicated little to no use of AI in their day-to-day work. Her newly created AI team is making progress as it navigates how to create consistency in use, practical guardrails and official guidelines, though she said they still have a long way to go. She learned through colleagues across her district of four different campuses that she is not alone in trying to keep up with the AI race.

A recent study from the University of Chicago’s Becker Friedman Institute for Economics found that lower AI integration is associated with a higher share of disadvantaged students. The study concluded that schools serving more disadvantaged students, along with charter and private schools, lag well behind traditional public schools on AI integration. Gonzalez wrote that many Title I schools, which receive federal funding for serving a high proportion of low-income students, are still trying just to gain access to AI tools and platforms such as Claude and ChatGPT. She said staff lack the training to begin to use AI to close academic and opportunity gaps. In Chicago Public Schools, she wrote, Title I schools have a particularly hard time accessing AI tools and resources because of how large the CPS system is.

Gonzalez wrote that she started applying to fellowships centered on AI and experimenting with AI tools in developing her curriculum, lesson plans and ideas for student projects and activities. She tells her students that AI can’t write their essays or short answers, that they have to use it responsibly and with integrity, and that she will put their writing through an AI tracker the entire school year. She wrote that she hears the contradiction of promoting effective AI use for learning while threatening consequences for dishonest use, which makes the messaging feel confusing and counterproductive for students and teachers. She said her district has taken steps to establish guidelines through its staff handbook and policy development, creating a starting point for using AI with integrity. Her district’s AI committee has also recently developed a seven-step action plan for AI integration.

The seven priorities Gonzalez listed are: establish a representative committee, conduct a needs assessment or environmental scan, develop foundational principles and ethical framework, categorize AI use cases and draft specific guidelines, get stakeholder feedback and iteration, plan for implementation, training and communication, and establish a review and adaptation mechanism. She wrote that her school is also forming a team and designating lead teachers willing to engage in AI implementation. She said all Title I schools can prioritize professional development for interested educators and staff so more teachers feel equipped to integrate AI with their students. She wrote that providing premium access to AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Canva and Class Companion for every student may require reallocating funding within a school’s fiscal budget. She cited EdTrust’s 2024 report, “Navigating the Promise and Peril of AI for Students of Color,” which asserted that students of color must have access to the same AI technologies as their peers without exceptions, alongside universally accessible safeguards.

Gonzalez wrote that Title I schools already face an array of disparities, including limited resources from lack of sufficient funding while serving Black, Latino and immigrant students who rarely see themselves reflected in the teachers and staff who serve them. She wrote that those students often lack resources such as quality technology, high-speed internet and functioning Chromebooks for optimal learning. She said that schools forcing quick adoption of AI without access to AI tools or effective guidelines and guardrails could compound existing challenges and harm student achievement. She wrote that her students are still hesitant to use AI tools because the lines are still blurry between using AI as a thought partner and using it as the sole generator of their work. She said access to the AI tools they have is still limited and the tools aren’t available to all their students.

Gonzalez wrote that Title I schools need continued support and resources to avoid being outrun by the fast pace of AI innovation in teaching and learning. She wrote that the way forward is to keep having conversations that are raw, real and authentically honest. She warned that if schools don’t, AI will surely outpace them and continue to widen the equity gap for the most marginalized students and the teachers who serve them. She wrote that all students deserve equal and fair access to AI to enhance their learning and prepare them for the technology-driven society that awaits them. She wrote that the only thing teachers and students in schools should outrun are the odds.

stories.Headline: Large firms increase use of open-weight AI models to reduce costs
stories.Summary:
Nearly six in ten senior executives at large companies plan to increase their use of cheaper open-weight AI models over the next year, according to a Capgemini study released on Thursday, November 12, 2026. The shift comes as AI bills have overshot budgets for many firms. The survey of 500 executives at enterprises with annual revenue above $1 billion across 10 countries found that open-weight models handled 72 per cent of traffic on the OpenRouter multi-AI provider in September. Those models, however, accounted for only 27 per cent of AI spending. Capgemini also said open-weight tokens were on average 87 per cent cheaper than closed ones.

Fifty-nine per cent of the executives said their AI spending over the past year had run significantly above their expectations or budgets, by 24 per cent on average. Another 53 per cent said they were worried about AI costs, up from 45 per cent the previous year. Half of the respondents said they would keep closed models where the complexity of a task justified the extra cost. The findings point to a mixed approach rather than a full move away from proprietary systems.

Companies appear to be weighing price against performance task by task. Capgemini, the IT consulting firm that helps companies embed AI into their existing platforms, conducted the study. The report reflects its own survey findings and its view of where enterprise spending is heading. The trend echoes a decision by SAP, whose finance chief said last month that the company was replacing some of its costliest AI models with cheaper ones where performance held up.

Anthropic, which launched its IPO roadshow this week, also warned in its prospectus that customers may shift to cheaper options, including open-weight models. Open-weight models, such as those from DeepSeek or Mistral, can be downloaded and run anywhere, while closed options such as Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini are accessible only from the cloud. The survey indicates that enterprises are likely to keep expanding their use of cheaper models while retaining premium closed systems for demanding work. The articles do not say how the spending pattern will change beyond the next year.

stories.Headline: OpenAI cuts unauthorised reasoning extraction success rate to 0.2 per cent in GPT-6.2 Astra
stories.Summary:
OpenAI said on 21 November 2026 that it had strengthened safeguards in its latest AI models to prevent unauthorised attempts to extract their internal reasoning and replicate advanced capabilities, and that the success rate of such attacks had fallen sharply after the security upgrades. In an update on its efforts to combat adversarial distillation, the company said the average success rate of attacks trying to extract protected reasoning from an earlier request fell to 0.2 per cent in its latest model, GPT-6.2 Astra, compared with 54 per cent in GPT-6 Astra under its original safeguards. The success rate for attacks targeting reasoning generated in the current request also declined to 0.9 per cent from 22.9 per cent, according to internal adaptive evaluations involving automated red-teaming. Distillation is a machine-learning technique through which one AI model learns from data generated by another, and OpenAI said unauthorised distillation can let another model reproduce advanced capabilities without inheriting the safety protections of the original system.

OpenAI warned that this could create risks in sensitive areas such as cybersecurity and biological research, where capabilities developed for defensive or legitimate purposes could be repurposed for harmful activities. The company said it had placed particular emphasis on protecting its models' chain-of-thought, the intermediate reasoning steps generated while working towards an answer, which can contain details not included in the final response and can provide valuable training material for competing models. An internal study found that AI models trained on exact reasoning traces generally performed better in cybersecurity benchmarks after supervised fine-tuning than those trained on reasoning summaries, and the advantage persisted at higher inference budgets following additional reinforcement learning. To address the threat, OpenAI said it is combining model-level safeguards, input and output classifiers, API restrictions and investigations into coordinated extraction campaigns.

OpenAI said it had detected multiple unauthorised distillation campaigns on its platform this year, with weekly enforcement actions ranging from thousands to tens of thousands of accounts, and that the pace of such activity increased significantly over the summer. The company also said it shares indicators of compromise with other AI model providers to help identify and disrupt similar activities across platforms. Highlighting the broader national security implications, OpenAI said foreign actors could reproduce advanced capabilities developed by US AI companies and deploy them without comparable safeguards. It called for stronger coordination among AI developers, deployment partners and governments, arguing that protecting frontier models from unauthorised capability extraction would be essential as advanced AI systems become more widely available.

Articles.Title: OpenAI improves AI models' safety, reducing unauthorized extraction attempts by over 50% - ET CIO

stories.Headline: Florida court lets hotel subpoena opponent’s AI chats in defamation case
stories.Summary:
A federal court in Florida ruled on October 21, 2026, that a litigant can subpoena his opponent’s AI chatbot conversations because they might reveal his intent, according to Fisher Phillips attorney David Walton. The Fontainebleau Florida Hotel sued Shmuel Botach in federal court in Miami in 2025, alleging he published defamatory statements about the hotel and continued an online campaign against it, its personnel and its lawyers. According to the hotel, some of that conduct involved AI-generated content, and the hotel is seeking punitive damages against Botach. The hotel served a document request and prepared subpoenas to four AI service providers seeking Botach’s AI chat communications. Magistrate Judge Marty Fulgueira Elfenbein rejected a blanket claim that the chats should be shielded as litigation-preparation materials but left room for specific chats to be protected if properly identified and logged.

The hotel sought Botach’s AI chat communications concerning the hotel, the litigation, the hotel’s lawyers, any hotel employee, owner or representative, any court order in the case, and the two judges presiding over the case. The court allowed the requests about the hotel, its lawyers, and its employees, owners and representatives, along with any deleted chats on those subjects. It cut the requests about the litigation, court orders and the judges as too broad. Florida’s statutory cap on punitive damages does not apply if the hotel can prove Botach had a specific intent to harm it, which makes his state of mind central to the issue of damages. The court authorized subpoenas seeking deleted chats directly from the AI providers.

Botach objected across the board, arguing the chats were protected work product, among other things, relying on a landmark Michigan court decision covered earlier this year. The court said Botach’s AI chats could show more than the final public statements ever would, and that if he used AI tools to generate, revise or refine statements about the hotel, his prompts could reveal why he created them, the instructions he supplied and the effects he sought to achieve. The court was careful to say it was not deciding that the chats would prove malice, only that they were related closely enough to the damages issues to be discoverable. The court agreed that work-product protection is not limited to lawyers and that a party’s own materials can qualify if prepared because of litigation. The court determined that chats used to create, revise or spread public statements about the hotel ordinarily would not qualify, even though the defendant is a litigant.

The court said the party claiming protection has to prove it for each document, and that the fact a chat was created after the lawsuit was filed is not enough. If specific chats truly were litigation preparation, Botach can withhold them, but he has to list them on a privilege log. In the court’s words, using AI does not automatically establish either discoverability or protection. The decision lands in the middle of several earlier rulings, applying ordinary discovery rules chat by chat rather than treating AI chats as automatically protected or automatically fair game. The earlier decisions include Shealy v.

Seaside Investments in Massachusetts state court, Morgan v. V2X in Colorado federal court, United States v. Heppner in New York federal court and Warner v. Gilbarco in Michigan federal court. Walton wrote that the ruling should prompt employers to rethink what they allow managers to type into AI tools.

He said the holding could apply to any claim where someone’s state of mind matters, which he said covers a lot of workplace litigation, including punitive damages rulings, retaliation claims, and wage and hour or leave cases where willfulness is a key element. He gave the example of a supervisor asking an AI chatbot to help find performance problems for an employee the supervisor wants to discipline. He said employers should train managers and HR staff to assume that anything they type into an AI tool about an employee could become evidence in a case one day. He said whether a provider still has a deleted conversation depends on the tool, the account type and its retention settings, and that employers should not count on the delete button as a failsafe. Walton said protecting genuine litigation-preparation chats is much easier when AI use tied to a dispute happens at a lawyer’s direction, in a company-approved tool, and separate from everyday business use.

The articles do not say whether Botach has produced a privilege log or withheld any specific chats. The articles do not say whether the AI providers have responded to the subpoenas or produced any communications. The articles do not say whether the hotel has yet shown the specific intent to harm that would lift Florida’s cap on punitive damages. The articles do not give a trial date or any further scheduled proceedings in the case. The articles do not say whether Botach has appealed the October 21 ruling.

stories.Headline: Western Cape High Court sets aside Phala Phala panel report, halting Ramaphosa impeachment
stories.Summary:
South Africa's Western Cape High Court on Wednesday, Nov. 25, set aside in its entirety the independent panel report that found President Cyril Ramaphosa may have a case to answer over cash stolen from his Phala Phala farm. The court declared invalid all proceedings arising from that report, which halts the parliamentary impeachment process built on it. Judge President Nolwazi Mabindla-Boqwana, reading a summary, said the Section 89 panel fundamentally misconstrued its functions and went beyond its lawful remit, making several errors in law. Full reasons have not been released, and no date was given for them.

About $580,000 in foreign currency was stolen from sofa cushions at the Limpopo farm in February 2020, and the theft became public in June 2022. Ramaphosa denies wrongdoing and says the money came from the sale of 20 buffalo. In late November 2022, the Section 89 panel found he had a case to answer, and the National Assembly, where the ANC then held a majority, voted the report down on Dec. 13, 2022. In May 2026, the Constitutional Court ruled that vote unconstitutional on a challenge by the EFF and referred the report to an impeachment committee, after which Ramaphosa filed a new review arguing the panel relied on hearsay and ignored his submissions, and the full bench heard it in early September.

The EFF, MK party and UAT opposed the review. ATM MP Vuyolwethu Zungula said there was one law for the president and another for the citizens, and that his party would consult lawyers and other parties on an appeal. An appeal court could restore the report. National Assembly Speaker Thoko Didiza said she would study the judgment and its implications, and it was unclear whether the impeachment committee would go ahead with a meeting on Thursday to choose an evidence leader.

stories.Headline: Self-represented litigants cause most courtroom AI misuse according to a legal study
stories.Summary:
A legal study published in the Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance revealed that unrepresented litigants misuse generative artificial intelligence. This analysis was released by November 25, 2026, and focused on common law and hybrid court systems. Researchers found that self-represented litigants were responsible for 69 percent of incidents involving defective automated submissions. Qualified legal practitioners accounted for 27 percent of recorded episodes, while others included witnesses, third parties, and judicial officers. The study used an international repository from the Centre for the Future of the Legal Profession tracking 1027 proceedings.

The dataset included ten jurisdictions, namely Australia, Hong Kong, New Zealand, Singapore, Canada, India, Ireland, South Africa, the United Kingdom, and the United States. The study specifically examined regulatory mechanisms in four Australasian jurisdictions, which are Australia, Hong Kong, New Zealand, and Singapore. It applied a theoretical framework of responsive regulation formulated by Ian Ayres and John Braithwaite to conceptualize courts as regulators. This model uses an enforcement pyramid that escalates from informational guidance and education to financial penalties and criminal prosecution. The authors constructed two distinct regulatory pyramids to separate licensed legal practitioners from self-represented lay individuals.

The authors stated that generative models produce forensic injuries, including fabricated judicial precedents and inaccurate summaries of doctrine. They argued that adversarial common law systems depend on the integrity of materials submitted by participating parties. The researchers claimed that responsive regulation is compromised by the one-shot nature of self-represented litigation compared to regular advocates. They noted that unrepresented individuals often lack the technical and legal literacy required to identify probabilistic hallucinations. The authors concluded that courts must refine case management and support systems because artificial intelligence cannot be forced back.

Opposing counsel and judicial staff are affected because hallucinatory precedents impose heavy investigative friction on their work. In the United States, fabricated authorities have occasionally migrated into substantive judicial rulings, which the study says endangers the rule of law. Some judges vigorously strike out flawed documents, while others merely disregard defective citations and resolve the underlying substantive dispute. Unrepresented litigants are affected because they often litigate without representation due to financial distress or ineligibility for legal aid. This variability in judicial responses introduces regulatory unpredictability and incentivizes resource-constrained litigants to gamble on unverified artificial intelligence.

The background involves the proliferation of low-cost generative models that introduce fabricated citations and distorted statutory summaries into court pleadings. In New South Wales, practice notes mandate active disclosure of machine use, while other regions encourage responsible technological integration. Practitioners are bound by the Legal Profession Uniform Law and the Australian Solicitors Conduct Rules to owe duties to the court. In Re Mr Dayal, an Australian federal magistrate referred an attorney to regulators for using automated tools to compile fictitious authorities. The Federal Court of Australia in Wamba Wemba directed indemnity costs against a law firm for a junior solicitor's errors.

Courts have used financial deterrents, such as 2980 Australian dollars in Valu and 8371.30 Australian dollars in JNE24. A Singapore court assessed 800 Singapore dollars against counsel, and the Singapore High Court set aside an action in Forbes Monaco APAC v Seiji. In Gribble v Essential Energy, a statement of claim containing fictitious citations was struck out with leave to replead. The articles leave open how courts will balance severe sanctions like criminal contempt with public commitments to open access to justice. Future efforts may include targeted pre-filing certification protocols and regulatory pluralism to preserve institutional fairness and public confidence.

stories.Headline: Manufacturers find AI value in planning and inventory work, not just the shop floor
stories.Summary:
A column published by ET CIO on 24 November 2026, written by Dr Sanjay Kukreja, Chief Technology Officer at eClerx, argues that manufacturers often look for artificial intelligence on the shop floor, in vision cameras, predictive maintenance and robotics, while many of the everyday decisions that decide whether targets are met happen elsewhere. He points to planning meetings, catalogue spreadsheets and conversations with distributors as the places where AI is quietly proving its value. The piece cites Deloitte's 2026 survey of more than 140 manufacturers, which found that 84% already see measurable value from AI, yet only around one in five use cases has been scaled consistently across sites. It also cites Deloitte's 2026 enterprise survey, which reports that 40% of Indian respondents describe their AI use as significant or full, against a global average of about 28%. The column suggests three starting points, beginning with inventory decisions such as how much to stock, where to hold it and when to reorder, where AI-driven analytics can connect sales history, inventory positions and supplier lead times and flag items needing human attention.

It says AI can extract product specifications from source documents, validate them against agreed standards and flag inconsistencies before listings are published, while human teams approve the final output. A third area is market intelligence, where AI can bring together fragmented public information on competitor pricing, availability and demand shifts, though the column says pricing, channel strategy and market positioning remain human judgements. It adds that the strongest candidates for AI share four traits: frequent work, existing data, a measurable outcome and a clearly identified individual who owns the result. Kukreja advises manufacturers to start with one workflow, establish a baseline, keep a human in the loop and review the results after 90 days, and he says measurement should be built in before the first model is developed. He writes that Deloitte's respondents reported an average improvement potential of around 20% across core operational measures, which he would treat as a benchmark to test against rather than a promise to make to the board.

He also stresses governance, asking who reviews the output, what checks are required before anything goes live and how decisions are documented. He applies a simple test, that the expected impact must justify the effort involved, including data preparation, team readiness and the governance required to deploy AI responsibly, and if it does not, the use case can wait. The column says every workflow that delivers results leaves behind cleaner data, clearer ownership and a team that has seen AI work in practice, which makes the next implementation easier and faster. It notes that adoption is no longer the only challenge and that the bigger question is where AI can deliver meaningful, scalable impact. The views are attributed solely to the author, and ET CIO states that it does not necessarily subscribe to them.

stories.Headline: Moldova's economy ministry submits draft AI law for public consultation ahead of 2028 rollout
stories.Summary:
Moldova is set to adopt a law regulating artificial intelligence, with the draft bill prepared by the Ministry of Economic Development and Digitalisation and submitted for public consultation, Logos Press reported on 25 November 2026. The bill defines which actions will be prohibited, sets out conditions for the use of AI systems, and establishes obligations for companies and public bodies. It also sets out citizens’ rights, in particular the right to be informed when interacting with an artificial intelligence system. The law is expected to come into force on 1 January 2028. Implementation will take place in phases until 2031.

Prohibited practices include using AI to create intimate images or videos of a person without consent, known as nudification. The law bans systems that manipulate people through subliminal or misleading techniques, and systems that exploit the vulnerability of children, older people or those in difficult life circumstances. It prohibits systems assigning people a social rating based on behaviour to restrict rights or access to services, and programmes predicting the likelihood of a crime solely from profiling or personal characteristics. AI analysis of the emotions of employees at work, and of pupils and students, is banned except in strictly defined health or safety cases.

Real-time remote biometric identification in public places faces strict rules, and law enforcement agencies will not be able to use such systems arbitrarily. Use is restricted to serious situations such as searching for victims of abduction or human trafficking, tracing missing persons, preventing terrorist acts or identifying suspects in serious crimes. As a rule this will require court authorisation, and in emergencies authorities must obtain it within 24 hours. Citizens have the right to know when they interact with an AI system such as a chatbot. AI-created or altered images, audio and video appearing genuine must be labelled, as must AI-generated texts on matters of public interest unless a human has editorially reviewed them.

Public authorities will be prohibited from making adverse decisions affecting citizens’ rights based solely on AI results, so a social assistance request cannot be rejected on an automated decision alone and a human must make the final decision. Those affected have the right to clear explanations and the opportunity to lodge a complaint. AI systems in healthcare, transport, education, recruitment, credit decisions, the justice system and law enforcement will be classified as high-risk and subject to stricter security and oversight requirements. The National Agency for Communications Regulation (ARCOM) will coordinate implementation as the single point of contact, liaising with authorities responsible for personal data protection, financial market supervision and human rights protection. Fines of up to 2 million lei or 1 per cent of annual turnover apply to prohibited practices.

Breaches of requirements on high-risk systems and transparency may bring fines of up to 1.5 million lei or 0.75 per cent of annual turnover. Providing false information to the authorities may lead to fines of up to 1 million lei or 0.5 per cent of turnover. Small and medium-sized enterprises and start-ups are offered free consultations and access to a testing environment. A three-year grace period has been established for them, so unintentional breaches that have not caused serious harm will receive warnings rather than fines. Transparency requirements and rules for public bodies become mandatory in 2029, and technical requirements for high-risk AI systems will be introduced between 2030 and 2031.

The draft bill was prepared by the Ministry of Economic Development and Digitalisation and submitted for public consultation. The document defines prohibited actions, conditions for use of AI systems and the obligations of companies and public bodies. It also sets out citizens’ rights, including the right to be informed when interacting with an artificial intelligence system. The law is expected to come into force on 1 January 2028. Implementation will take place in phases until 2031.

Transparency requirements and rules for public bodies will become mandatory in 2029. Technical requirements for high-risk AI systems will be introduced between 2030 and 2031. The articles do not state when the public consultation ends or when the bill will be adopted. They do not say what penalties apply after the grace period for small and medium-sized enterprises and start-ups. They do not name the other authorities beyond the areas of personal data protection, financial market supervision and human rights protection.

stories.Headline: Nexent Capital launches $1 billion fund for quantum-ready AI infrastructure and advanced energy
stories.Summary:
Nexent Capital IFSC Private Limited announced on 25 November 2026 the launch of Nexent Capital ADGM Fund I, a closed-end fund targeting US$1 billion in capital commitments with a hard cap of US$1.6 billion. The fund is dedicated to quantum-ready AI infrastructure and advanced energy investment, and it will deploy capital across five complementary strategies. Those strategies are infrastructure private equity in AI and data-center assets, private credit and structured capital, special-situations M&A, growth equity and PIPEs, and liquid public equity exposure within the AI and data-center value chain. The fund is structured as an ADGM-domiciled Qualified Investor Fund as the master fund, with a GIFT City-based IFSCA-regulated Alternative Investment Fund acting as its feeder. Nexent Capital ADGM Limited is being established as the fund's licensed ADGM Fund Manager.

The fund has an anchor commitment of US$20 million from the Tyagi family office and line of sight to an identified pipeline of quantum-ready AI infrastructure and advanced energy projects across North America and India. That pipeline includes data-center and power assets sponsored by affiliates of the Nexent Capital and Tryfacta platform, and the fund's minimum investment is US$500,000. Nexent Capital IFSC is working with a large Abu Dhabi-based fund administrator that globally manages over $3.4 trillion in assets, and it is progressing formal engagement of legal counsel and an auditor as part of its path to FSRA authorisation and first close. The fund is targeting a first close within approximately six months of FSRA authorisation, with a final close targeted six months thereafter, and it is preparing for FSRA authorisation. Adesh Tyagi, Managing Partner of Nexent Capital IFSC Private Limited, said AI is being built on a foundation of physical infrastructure, namely power, land and compute, that most capital is not positioned to finance at the scale or speed the moment demands.

He said the fund, with its GIFT City feeder, is designed to meet that gap directly and to give institutional and family-office investors a disciplined way to back the infrastructure and energy assets underpinning the next decade of AI growth. Abhimanyu Tyagi, Director of Nexent Capital IFSC Private Limited, said the pipeline is not theoretical but is built on relationships and projects the platform has been developing for years, from data-center conversions to gigawatt-scale energy campuses. He said that gives investors in the fund a head start that most new vehicles in the space simply do not have. The launch comes as global investors increasingly look to deploy capital into the physical infrastructure underpinning AI growth, including power generation, data centers and advanced energy systems. It also comes as GIFT City and the Abu Dhabi Global Market continue to develop as complementary gateways for structuring cross-border alternative investment vehicles.
