stories.Headline: Congressional Research Service urges Congress to evaluate defense against agentic AI cyberattacks
stories.Summary:
A new report from the Congressional Research Service warns that agentic artificial intelligence could automate complex cyberattacks that usually require entire teams of hackers. The document highlights a mid-September 2025 operation that Anthropic attributed to a Chinese state-sponsored group known as GTG-1002. This specific group allegedly automated between 80 percent and 90 percent of a campaign that targeted approximately 30 different organizations. Some researchers have since questioned whether this particular attack was actually as autonomous or successful as the initial reports claimed.

The report suggests that Congress should evaluate if the Department of Defense is appropriately postured to detect and respond to these autonomous threats. It notes that the Cybersecurity and Information Systems Information Analysis Center has found no official government policies specifically addressing agentic AI yet. Under Section 1535 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, which became Public Law 119-60 on December 18, 2025, the Secretary of Defense must establish an AI Futures Steering Committee by April 1. Additionally, the report questions if voluntary partnerships with the Department of Commerce Center for AI Standards and Innovation should be made mandatory.

The Congressional Research Service describes agentic AI as systems that can pursue specific goals while requiring very limited human supervision. The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency claims that its AI Cyber Challenge showed AI agents can fix open-source vulnerabilities faster than human teams. This capability could potentially support a strategy of AI-on-AI defense to counter the speed and scale of autonomous attacks. The AI Futures Steering Committee is expected to deliver its official findings to congressional defense committees by January 31, 2027.

Congress may use these upcoming findings to determine the necessary authorizations, appropriations, and general oversight for Department of Defense agentic AI programs. Lawmakers are also considering the reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015, which was part of Public Law 114-113. This specific information-sharing law is currently set to expire on December 11 under an amendment found in Section 2011 of Public Law 119-103. These legislative steps aim to address the evolving capabilities of militaries exploring autonomous decision-making and operations.

Articles.Title: Agentic AI Cyberattacks Raise Questions for Congress on Defense

stories.headline_source: Agentic AI Cyberattacks Raise Questions for Congress on Defense

stories.Headline: Germany plans to coordinate EU AI Act market surveillance through its Federal Network Agency
stories.Summary:
The article says that in 2026 the EU AI Act in Germany is an operational matter, not a policy debate for later, and that Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 is being phased in across the Union. It says duties for prohibited practices, high-risk systems and general-purpose AI models are arriving on staggered timelines. It says that in 2026 national enforcement structures, market surveillance and data protection scrutiny begin to take shape in Germany. It says the guide was written by Global Advisory Experts and published on November 25, 2026. It says the guide covers conformity assessment, technical documentation and an investigation playbook designed for German conditions.

The article says the Act is the first broad, cross-sector law on artificial intelligence anywhere in the world, a claim it attributes to no one else. It says the Act takes a risk-based approach, so the greater a system's potential to harm health, safety or fundamental rights, the heavier the duties. It says that because the Act is a regulation it applies directly in every Member State, so German businesses do not need to wait for a national transposition statute. It says the core obligations come straight from the EU text and are supplemented by national enforcement and designation measures. It says prohibited practices and AI literacy duties applied in the first phase, general-purpose AI transparency and documentation duties follow, and high-risk requirements apply later.

The article says each Member State must designate competent authorities for market surveillance and for notifying bodies. It says Germany's federal structure and its group of technically capable regulators suggest enforcement will involve several bodies working together rather than one super-regulator. It says national planning has identified the Federal Network Agency (Bundesnetzagentur) as the intended central coordination point for market surveillance, and that the final designation should be verified against official German government sources. It says the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy publishes German policy and implementation material and is a key reference for national strategy. It says the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) issues guidance on measures relevant to the security of AI systems, and its standards are likely to influence how conformity is assessed in practice.

The article says the Regulation creates EU-level governance, including the European Artificial Intelligence Office within the Commission and the European Artificial Intelligence Board, to promote consistent application, while day-to-day enforcement stays with national authorities. It says a compliance position accepted in one Member State is not automatically shielded from scrutiny elsewhere, and guidance or decisions from other national authorities can shape the German approach. It says industry observers expect German market surveillance bodies to draw on established product-safety enforcement techniques, since much of the high-risk regime rests on the EU's existing product legislation. It says the Federal Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information (BfDI) and the state data protection authorities provide the enforcement strength on the data side.

It says coordination between AI Act surveillance and GDPR enforcement is expected to define the German landscape, and a single system can face scrutiny under two regimes at once. The article says likely triggers for regulatory action include market surveillance inspections started by the authority, whether routine or intelligence-led. It says complaints from users, competitors, consumer bodies or affected individuals are a trigger. It says data protection referrals, where an AI system's handling of personal data raises GDPR issues that overlap with AI Act duties, are a trigger.

It says incident reports from post-market monitoring, including serious incidents that providers must report, are a trigger. It says the Act sorts systems into prohibited, high-risk, limited-risk and minimal-risk tiers, and that misclassification is itself an enforcement risk. The article says high-risk systems include many used in critical infrastructure, employment, essential services and safety components of regulated products. It says technical documentation for high-risk systems must cover the system description and intended purpose, design and development choices, data governance and the datasets used for training, validation and testing.

It says the documentation must cover risk management records, human oversight measures, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity metrics, and a post-market monitoring plan with records showing it operates. It says providers of high-risk systems must run a post-market monitoring system and report serious incidents to the relevant authority. It says many high-risk systems can rely on an internal conformity assessment by the provider, while others, particularly systems covered by existing product-safety legislation that involves notified bodies, need a third-party conformity assessment body. More to follow.

Articles.Title: EU AI Act in Germany: A 2026 Guide to Compliance, Enforcement and Investigations - Global Advisory Experts

stories.Headline: Intuit study finds AI adoption makes employers more attractive to junior accountants
stories.Summary:
Research commissioned by Intuit, and published on 25 November 2026, found that employers showing off their AI capabilities while recruiting are more likely to attract entry-level accounting candidates. The study, commissioned by Intuit QuickBooks, surveyed 1,003 people in the UK aged 18 to 24 between 1 June and 11 June 2026. It reported that 89% of candidates want embedded AI tools, structured training and modern career pathways from the start of their employment. Respondents also considered conversational AI tools built into financial software very useful for data analysis, reporting, research, brainstorming, summarising insights and automating workflows. The findings put candidate confidence at a high level, with 91% believing AI technology will lift their career prospects and feeling prepared for roles where it plays a central part.

A total of 68% believe their skills will lead to faster career progression, while 35% expect to move into higher-value advisory positions earlier in their careers. Preparation varied across the group, with 47% naming self-directed learning as their main preparation for AI, 32% citing university education and 20% pointing to work experience. On training, 46% of candidates expect regular workplace training and 36% anticipate ongoing training throughout their careers. The research also flagged a possible disconnect between candidate confidence and readiness for risk, since automating traditional junior tasks could leave graduates without the practical experience needed to underpin sound professional judgement. Intuit sorted future accountants into four personas, the largest being highly engaged users who favour strong governance at 34%, followed by cautious adopters who seek oversight at 26%.

Confident users who tend to underestimate potential risks made up 23%, and the remaining 16% were uncertain about the technology and its implications. Overall, 88% of respondents said a firm's AI adoption makes it more attractive. The study was commissioned by Intuit QuickBooks, which published the findings on 25 November 2026. It covered 1,003 UK respondents aged 18 to 24, surveyed between 1 June and 11 June 2026. The articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Hassan plans hearings and legislation to require AI safeguards against terrorist planning
stories.Summary:
U.S. Sen. Maggie Hassan is set to become New Hampshire's senior senator in January and to chair the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, which oversees the Department of Homeland Security and guides policy on cybersecurity and artificial intelligence regulation. She recently directed the Government Accountability Office, the congressional watchdog, to study whether common artificial intelligence models such as ChatGPT can be used to plan terrorist attacks on the United States. The report found that the tools can easily plan out violent attacks, which prompted Hassan to call for more investigation and regulation. Hassan discussed artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and her plans for the next legislative session with Morning Edition host Rick Ganley.

Hassan said she wants to hold hearings with experts to learn about the vulnerabilities of artificial intelligence systems and to investigate the cause of major technology outages around the country. She wants to implement legislation that regulates artificial intelligence, including prohibiting tech companies from releasing new models without proving they have safeguards to stop them from being used to plan violence or terrorist attacks on the United States. The GAO study found that users can easily bypass safeguards on artificial intelligence models within about 12 hours and come out with detailed instructions to conduct a terrorist attack. Hassan said the results were not surprising but were deeply concerning, and the models provide instructions on how to build a weapon and offer advice on what events to target, when to attack and how to avoid law enforcement.

Hassan said she wants to ensure that artificial intelligence companies report attempts to dangerously manipulate the technology to law enforcement and to explore defenses against potential attacks, such as a defensive model or other tools. She said she wants to work with other committees in Congress that oversee artificial intelligence safety and to introduce a comprehensive package of legislation quickly, and to work with private companies to balance regulation and market competition. She said the Senate should thoroughly investigate the cause of outages at major technology companies and government systems in recent weeks. She said the administration should take artificial intelligence more seriously as a threat to national security.

Articles.Title: Hassan says AI regulation, investigating tech outages will be top priorities in January

stories.headline_source: Hassan says AI regulation, investigating tech outages will be top priorities in January

stories.Headline: Anthropic launches Enterprise Frontier Safeguards to detect harmful AI activity with zero data retention
stories.Summary:
Anthropic launched a public beta of Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, a capability that lets organizations detect potentially harmful AI activity across multiple interactions while keeping zero data retention, the company said on November 25, 2026. The system uses automated safety systems to analyze conversations stored in customer-controlled cloud environments and to flag suspicious behavior for security teams to investigate. Anthropic said the tool addresses a gap in legacy zero data retention safeguards, which screen individual requests for signs of misuse even though sophisticated attacks can span several interactions that each look harmless alone. The company pointed to its September threat intelligence report, which documented an operation targeting roughly 50 organizations in which an AI agent delegated attack tasks to other agents and kept stolen credentials between sessions.

When the system detects a potential threat, it creates a Safety Case that security teams can retrieve from their cloud storage or access through an API, and cases can be integrated into security information and event management systems. Anthropic said the cases contain neither prompts nor responses, and the monitoring can help identify both deliberate misuse and AI agents acting beyond their users' intentions, such as exploiting software vulnerabilities to gain unauthorized access to internal databases or external systems. Organizations store AI inputs and outputs in their own cloud environments, and according to Anthropic neither the company nor its cloud partners retain copies once the information has been transferred to customer-controlled storage. Customers configure access policies and audit logging and encrypt safety data with their own keys, while provider-side access to conversation content is restricted to automated safety monitoring systems, and Anthropic said neither its personnel nor cloud provider personnel can review it and the information is not used to train models or classifiers.

Omar Santos, a Distinguished Engineer at Cisco, said customers can keep sensitive data in their own environments protected with their own encryption keys while still preserving the specialized safety mechanisms frontier capabilities require, and he called that balance critical to broader adoption of advanced AI in security-sensitive organizations like Cisco. EFS is available through the Claude Platform, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock and Claude on Google Cloud, and for Amazon Bedrock and Google-managed deployments the respective cloud provider operates the safeguards with the entire data flow remaining within its environment. Support for Microsoft Foundry is coming soon, and depending on the deployment customers can use Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage and are responsible for the associated storage and usage costs. Anthropic said eligible organizations will receive instructions on how to get started.

Articles.Title: Anthropic wants to catch rogue AI activity without retaining your data

stories.Headline: AI helps pinpoint submerged invasive weeds impacting our aquatic environments
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Earth Sciences New Zealand have developed a portable artificial intelligence detection system that spots target weeds in underwater video and records exactly where they are. They collaborated with partners including the Department of Conservation, Land Information New Zealand, Boffa Miskell and Ngāti Tarāwhai on the tool. The system has already been tested in Queenstown’s Lake Whakatipu, the Kawarau River, Lake Wānaka on the South Island and Lake Ōkataina on the North Island. It was successful in detecting lagarosiphon, one of New Zealand’s worst freshwater weeds, according to the organisation.

The system combines underwater cameras, machine learning and a portable detector module to identify invasive weeds in live-streamed video, and the software is trained to recognise the target species by analysing video frames as the camera moves through the water column. Each detection records the GPS location, the time and the number of instances in the frame, and these records can be displayed in mapping applications such as ArcGIS so managers can direct efforts to specific locations. The technology has initially focused on two of New Zealand’s most problematic invasive freshwater plant species, lagarosiphon and hornwort. Divers could then focus on management interventions rather than looking for what the article calls the needle in the haystack.

The project was led by Earth Sciences NZ researcher Dr Daniel Clements, who said detecting submerged weeds in an early stage of invasion has been a challenge for managers tasked with protecting aquatic resources. He said traditional surveillance often relies on divers searching extensive areas of the underwater environment, which can be time-consuming, costly and limited in the area that can be covered. He said finding invasive weeds early can make a real difference to achieving cost-effective management, and that combining underwater video with AI lets infestations be identified and mapped so managers focus efforts where they are needed most. Clements said collaborators see the potential of the technology and have provided technical input and early-stage development funding, and the project has worked with Ngāti Tarāwhai Iwi Trust, which supported trial deployments at Lake Ōkataina.

DOC Freshwater Technical Advisor Phoenix Hale said the department was eager to target these species because of their economic, social and environmental impact. Hale said both weeds form dense underwater growths that can reach the surface and smother native plants that fish and invertebrates rely on, and that they spread when fragments are carried on boats, trailers and fishing gear, making them difficult to eradicate, though finding them early gives the best chance to act. Clements said his goal is to partner with organisations interested in using the technology to refine it and make sure it is fit for purpose and deployable at large scale in the field. He said more needs to be done to take the innovation from its current prototype to large-scale field use, that the team wants to partner with prospective users to get the system into action, and that he welcomes enquiries from interested parties.

Articles.Title: AI helps pinpoint submerged invasive weeds impacting our aquatic environments

stories.Headline: South Korea study group meets Wednesday to discuss revising AI Basic Act and extending enforcement pause
stories.Summary:
South Korea's AI Basic Act study group and the National AI Strategy Committee are scheduled to hold a joint on-site meeting on Wednesday, Nov. 25, at the Seoul office of GIST in Jung-gu, Digital Daily reported Tuesday. The session is meant to gather views on revising the law and on adding further grace periods before enforcement begins. No decision has been announced, and the report gives no start time. The Ministry of Science and ICT set a pause of at least one year when the Act took effect on Jan. 22, 2026. The pause cannot end before Jan. 22, 2027, about two months from now.

The Act's enforcement ladder runs from a fact-finding investigation to a corrective order and only then to a fine. MSIT has described the pause as covering fact-finding investigations, corrective orders and fines. The fine cap is 30 million won, about $22,500, a figure Cooley says applies to failing to notify users that AI is in use, failing to designate a local representative and ignoring a corrective order. Draft rules allow machine-readable watermarks users cannot see, paired with at least one visible or audible notice that content was AI-generated. Digital Daily counted 19 amendment bills filed within about six months of the Act taking effect.

Lee Sang-yong, a professor at Konkuk University Law School and chair of the study group, is scheduled to give a progress report, according to Digital Daily. Sangchul Park, a professor at Seoul National University Law School, is scheduled to present key discussion points. In July 2025, Digital Daily reported Park's view that subordinate rules alone would not be enough and that a Japan-style overhaul deserved study. Lee presented on revising the Act at the Kim & Chang AI Law and Policy Forum seminar on Sept. 4, 2026. Law Times' account of that seminar did not report a stated position on a grace period.

At the September 2025 MSIT briefing, industry was reported to be asking for three years at least. In April 2025, Democratic Party lawmaker Hwang Jung-ah introduced a bill to postpone enforcement of key provisions by three years. A Startup Alliance survey found that 98 percent of 101 startups did not feel ready for compliance, according to the Stimson Center. The National Human Rights Commission raised concerns about postponement in a September 2025 letter, and a joint civil-society comment followed days later. In an Oct. 1, 2025 submission, the Institute for Digital Rights and allied groups argued that a fine grace period would effectively suspend regulation of minimal duties such as prior notice and designating a domestic agent.

Korea's Act was modeled on the EU's AI Act, and the EU has already moved its calendar. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on AI, was published in the Official Journal on July 24 and entered into force July 27. Stand-alone high-risk systems, such as those used in education and employment, now face obligations from Dec. 2, 2027, and high-risk AI embedded in regulated products moves to Aug. 2, 2028, a deferral of about 16 months for the first group. Brussels moved its deadlines by statute, while Korea's pause is an administrative policy. A compliance guide describes the pause as ministry policy rather than statute, a third-party reading rather than a statutory finding.

Neither MSIT nor the committee has announced an extension, and published policy trackers list no extension notice or fixed end date. Nothing public says whether an extension would cover all provisions, only some, or specific sectors, and Digital Daily reports the topic of amendments but no specific proposals. The meeting's outcome and any readout are unknown. For operators, the practical reading is that Jan. 22, 2027 is the earliest possible start of enforcement, not a fixed one. The labeling and notice duties apply now regardless of when investigators begin to use them.

Articles.Title: South Korea AI Basic Act Fine Pause May Outlast January 2027 as Study Group Meets Wednesday - Tech Times

stories.Headline: Polar and Crusoe plan 40MW Norway AI facility for late 2027
stories.Summary:
Polar Data Centers announced on October 21, 2026 that it is expanding its partnership with Crusoe with a new facility, DRA02, at its Tørdal campus in Norway. The announcement said DRA01, Polar's facility in Tørdal, is now live and providing 12MW of IT capacity. DRA01 is powered by 100% hydroelectric energy and supports Crusoe Cloud, Crusoe's AI cloud platform and AI services. Polar and Crusoe first announced their partnership around DRA01 in June 2025. The press release was issued from London, United Kingdom, through EINPresswire.com.

DRA02 is expected to go live in late 2027 and plans to deliver an additional 40MW of critical, liquid-cooled IT capacity. The new facility is also powered by hydroelectric power. Crusoe plans to deploy NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 at DRA02 to support the next phase of its AI cloud expansion in Norway. DRA01 combines modular infrastructure, advanced cooling technology, and resilient electrical systems designed around the requirements of the latest GPU deployments. DRA01 was recognised as "Most Successfully Delivered Data Centre" at the Data Centre World Awards 2026.

Andy Hayes, CEO of Polar, said the company's ambition has always been to help customers develop the future of AI, and called the Crusoe relationship a great example of that in action. He said Polar has successfully delivered DRA01, Crusoe is live and operating in Norway, and the companies are now moving forward together with the next phase. Hayes said the expansion into DRA02 demonstrates the strength of the collaboration and the confidence that comes from successful delivery. He said it is about much more than bringing capacity online, and about creating the infrastructure, operational performance, and customer relationships that enable customers to continue scaling. Cully Cavness, Crusoe's Co-founder, President and Chief Strategy Officer, said the expansion with Polar in Norway lets Crusoe serve some of the world's most innovative companies with reliable access to Crusoe Cloud's AI cloud services.

Cavness said what makes Tørdal stand out is that it runs on 100% renewable hydroelectric power, which he said aligns with Crusoe's value of bending the arc of energy towards sustainability. He said Polar has been a solid partner to help Crusoe scale its presence in Europe. The move from initial deployment into stable operations represents an important milestone for the partnership, according to the announcement. The companies said the milestone demonstrates their ability to deliver and operate infrastructure for the world's most demanding AI workloads.

The expansion significantly increases the scale available to support Crusoe Cloud's continued growth in Europe and beyond, the announcement said. The announcement described Polar as a European developer and operator of AI-ready data center infrastructure. It described Crusoe as the AI factory company. Polar said it is building a growing European platform of AI-ready infrastructure, combining renewable power, resilient design, high-density cooling capability, and a customer-led approach to development and operations.

Crusoe said it provides a reliable, scalable, cost-effective, energy-first solution for AI infrastructure, harnessing large-scale energy sources, building AI-optimized data centers, and delivering a powerful AI cloud platform. The announcement said the expansion reflects Polar's approach to developing long-term customer partnerships by delivering initial capacity successfully, operating it reliably, and creating a platform that can scale as customers' requirements grow. The announcement said the move into DRA02 takes the relationship to its next stage and supports Polar's wider vision to accelerate AI infrastructure. It said Polar aims to create the infrastructure platform customers need to develop the future of AI.

The articles did not state the cost of DRA02 or the terms of the agreement between Polar and Crusoe. The articles did not state how much capacity Crusoe plans to use at DRA02 beyond the 40MW planned for the facility. The articles did not state when construction of DRA02 began or whether it has started. The articles did not state how many NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems Crusoe plans to deploy at DRA02.

stories.Headline: SpaceX leases spare AI computing to Anthropic and Google for billions monthly
stories.Summary:
SpaceX earns more than half its revenue from leasing computing infrastructure, according to a report by The New York Times. Anthropic reportedly pays SpaceX approximately $3.1 billion every month for computing capacity. Google's arrangement with SpaceX reaches $800 million, the report said. The division was renamed SpaceXSI and reportedly earns billions of dollars monthly by supplying processing capacity. Anthropic has become its largest customer under an agreement reportedly valued at approximately $3.1 billion monthly.

Both agreements could remain active until 2029, although either customer can withdraw by providing 90 days' notice under their contractual arrangements. In August 2026, Musk reportedly renamed an engineering team's group conversation to express frustration about SpaceX's competitive position in artificial intelligence development. The revised name read "Sell compute because we can't compete," according to internal communications reviewed by The New York Times. Musk reportedly began demanding weekly explanations from selected engineers about their activities and consumption of specialized computing resources. Musk indicated that Anthropic's relationship with SpaceX could expand rather than contract despite their competitive interests.

Musk warned employees against misusing expensive GPUs, which provide the computational capacity required to train and operate sophisticated AI models. "Anyone wasting GPUs on bullshit while we are failing to compete will be asked to leave immediately, as this constitutes a betrayal of your team," said Elon Musk. Musk reportedly has privately acknowledged that commercial leasing currently offers better financial returns than allocating those resources toward internal AI development. Musk said Anthropic told him its highest probability outcome is that it would like an incremental 10 gigawatts of compute from SpaceX. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei described the existing arrangement favourably, citing the quality of SpaceX's computing resources and their working relationship.

The arrangement creates an unusual commercial relationship because companies competing against Musk's AI ambitions also depend heavily upon his infrastructure. His AI business, xAI, entered the market after ChatGPT's 2022 release and subsequently invested billions in computing facilities to challenge established competitors. One notable achievement involved constructing the Colossus facility in Memphis, Tennessee, in 2024. Musk subsequently announced that his company had installed more than one million specialized processors to support demanding AI tools. Internal documents reportedly indicated that xAI used less than half of Colossus's available capacity in the previous year.

This underutilization helps explain why leasing spare capacity became financially attractive while internal development continued struggling against established rivals. The company redirected resources away from certain projects, including Grok Imagine, after about 60 employees working on image and video generation were laid off. The report claims Musk is questioning whether developing artificial intelligence capabilities at his SpaceX firm can compete financially with renting computing infrastructure to rival companies. The dilemma comes as Anthropic and Google pay substantial monthly fees to access processing resources that SpaceX originally developed for its own artificial intelligence ambitions. The internal tensions emerge alongside the rapid growth of SpaceX's infrastructure leasing operation.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: SpaceX earns billions renting AI compute to Anthropic and Google

stories.headline_source: SpaceX earns billions renting AI compute to Anthropic and Google

stories.Headline: US senator Frank Warner drafts a bill to regulate AI agents acting for users online
stories.Summary:
On 29 June 2026, US Senator Frank Warner published a discussion draft of a bill on the safety of AI agents, titled the Artificial Intelligence Access, Gatekeeper Exchange, and Nondiscriminatory Transfer Act of 2026. The draft is open to feedback and comments until the bill is officially presented to Congress. The article describes the bill as a continuation of an earlier Warner bill from 2019, known as the Augmenting Compatibility and Competition Enabling Service Switching Act. The bill is not intended to stifle innovation but would establish a federal framework to protect consumers' freedom of choice, promote fair competition and ensure that AI agents act in the best interests of the users they represent. The framework would grant individuals the right to choose and designate artificial intelligence agents, defined in the bill as Custodial User Agents, to act on their behalf online.

Large online platforms with at least 50 million customers or subscribers in the United States in any of the preceding 12 months would have to maintain an interoperable interface enabling these agents to act for users in a fair, non-discriminatory and functionally equivalent manner. The Federal Trade Commission would be instructed to issue regulations and monitor compliance, including by creating a new register to track designations, assess agents and catalogue trusted providers. NIST would be directed to identify technical protocols and standards to support interoperability between platforms, including protocols for verifiable delegation such as revocable and scoped delegation credentials, verification of agent registration, real-time revocation and verifiable logs of actions taken on behalf of users. Under Section 3(b), once an individual has designated an agent, it may manage the individual's online interactions, e-commerce decisions, user-generated content and account settings on large online platforms. Section 3(c) requires the FTC to ensure, within 180 days of the Act coming into force, that the process by which an agent gains access to a large online platform is secure and properly authenticated and allows the individual to revoke the authorization and notify the platform of the revocation.

Providers must be accredited by registering with the FTC and must reasonably safeguard the privacy and security of users' data, maintain real-time records of actions taken on the user's behalf and make them available to the user, and establish reasonable measures to ensure agents comply with the regulations. Providers may not manage a user's interactions to benefit the agent at the user's expense, cause reasonably foreseeable harm or act inconsistently with the user's instructions, and they may not collect, use or share users' data except as reasonably necessary to provide the services, including for advertising, behavioural profiling, sale or any other secondary commercial purpose, or delegate powers to another entity without the user's express, specific and revocable authorization. Breaches may result in deregistration with the FTC or other enforcement actions, and large online platforms must facilitate and maintain an interface accessible to agents on fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory terms, with functionally equivalent access for competing third-party agents, failing which the FTC may intervene. The article says the spread of agent-based artificial intelligence brings various risks, which the United States aims to make practical and secure through earlier implementation than in Europe.

stories.Headline: NTT DATA warns that tightening Asian data rules may force banks to run separate AI instances by country
stories.Summary:
Paul Sommerin, the managing director for financial services industry business consulting in Asia Pacific and India at NTT DATA, spoke at the NTT R&D Forum 2026 in Tokyo. He explained that tightening data rules in Asia could force banks to run separate AI instances in each country. This shift is driven by governments increasing their control over data generated within their own borders, a concept known as data sovereignty. Sommerin noted that India has already begun cracking down on data leaving the country, and Indonesia is considering similar measures.

These changes may require banks that currently use a single AI platform across Southeast Asia to build separate systems for each nation. Regulators are primarily concerned with the location of personal, financial, and health data, as well as the impact of AI on jobs and worker skills. Other priorities include national security and the ability of AI to identify threats, such as the use of crypto or payments to fund domestic activities. Regulators now expect banks to trace the origin of customer funds rather than simply flagging unusual amounts.

Sommerin stated that the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority, and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority are very insistent on AI oversight and governance. He said that NTT DATA now proactively approaches regulators on behalf of clients before AI projects go live, especially when the work falls outside current rules. He suggested using regulatory sandboxes in Singapore, Hong Kong, and Australia to test new services under supervision. He believes firms must show governments the economic value that AI brings to both the organization and the country.

The transition to production is currently slowed by legacy core banking systems from the early 2000s that spread customer data across many different platforms. Sommerin mentioned that the investment needed to modernize these systems is a significant challenge for finance chiefs already paying off old debts. He cited a project with Aichi Bank in Japan that saved about 14,000 hours by using AI in corporate lending. NTT DATA also signed a memorandum of understanding in June 2026 with AXS to explore linking bill payment networks between Singapore and Malaysia.

stories.Headline: Automakers integrate agentic AI into production and development by 2026
stories.Summary:
Automotive manufacturers and suppliers integrated agentic artificial intelligence into their core production and development infrastructure by the year 2026. These companies moved from using bounded pilot projects to deploying autonomous systems that make decisions previously reserved for humans. AI now inspects welds, schedules production, monitors equipment for failure, and writes vehicle code. These systems also talk to drivers from the dashboard and assess every resistance spot weld in real time. AI agents now inspect finished vehicles and enhance both drivability and safety.

GM uses AI and simulation to shorten vehicle development to roughly two years and reduce physical testing. BMW integrates intelligent systems at nearly every production stage and plans to extend agentic AI into vehicle development. Horse Powertrain launched the kAIros initiative to pair an AI Factory with digital twins for autonomous decision-making. This kAIros initiative targets a 50 percent reduction in time-to-market for the company. The Commerce Department's Connected Vehicle Rule prohibits covered software linked to Russia or China starting with model year 2027.

Foley and Lardner stated that automotive companies must now navigate product liability, negligence, and warranty risks. They said that companies should establish clear accountability and maintain an inventory of every AI system in use. The firm recommended that manufacturers maintain human oversight and test systems in digital twin environments before production deployment. They suggested that companies strengthen vendor contractual protections and continuously monitor AI performance for drift. They also advised preserving records to allow AI-driven decisions to be reconstructed for legal reasons.

The EU AI Act and various US state laws affect companies by classifying AI systems by their risk level. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has proposed rules addressing design requirements for automated driving systems and certain ADAS-equipped vehicles. Tier 1 suppliers are affected because flawed signals from AI demand-forecasting agents can cause minimum-volume disputes and OEM penalties. Third-party AI vendors create risks because they often update models and change data sources without providing notice. These legal and operational exposures impact any manufacturer or supplier deploying autonomous AI agents.

The articles state that AI has matured from experimental tools into autonomous, production-scale systems across the automotive industry. This shift includes software-defined vehicles, digital twins, predictive maintenance, and warranty and quality analytics. Development pipelines for advanced driver-assistance systems and automated driving systems also utilize these matured AI capabilities. Earlier AI systems only made recommendations for humans, but the newest agentic systems act on their own. This transition from advisory tools to autonomous agents creates new legal and operational risks for the industry.

Companies must now build governance programs to adapt to a patchwork of overlapping and shifting global obligations. They need to define when human approval is required before an agent acts and maintain manual fallback plans. The Commerce Department's Connected Vehicle Rule also prohibits covered hardware linked to Russia or China starting with model year 2030. The articles leave open how specific liability will be allocated between vendors and deployers when autonomous agents fail. It remains unclear how companies will successfully reconstruct every AI-driven decision to demonstrate reasonable care in court.

stories.Headline: Researchers find limited evidence for the strongest claims about AI harming cognition, information and relationships
stories.Summary:
A group of researchers published a review in Nature Human Behaviour on November 25, 2026. They examined empirical evidence regarding eight ways that artificial intelligence impacts people. The authors include Rebecca Anselmetti, Shahar Avin, Vanessa Cheung, and Madga Dubois. Other contributors are Tom Eccles, Anna Gausen, Kobi Hackenburg, and Keno Juechems. The team also includes Hannah Rose Kirk, Lennart Luettgau, Brendan McGrath, and Ishan Mishra.

The study notes that one billion people worldwide now use artificial intelligence systems. It reviews evidence from model evaluations, user studies, and analysis of consumer chatlogs. The researchers also utilized agent-based simulations to study the impact on human users. They looked at claims about cognitive abilities, information ecosystems, and human relationships. The review also examined mental health, persuasion, manipulation, emotional dependence, and social engineering.

The authors are responsible for reviewing the emerging research on these impacts. They stated that there is limited evidence for the strongest narratives of concern. These narratives argue that AI may be undermining cognitive abilities and polluting information. They also suggest AI could corrode relationships and damage mental health. The researchers noted that many uncertainties still remain to be resolved.

Popular narratives of concern suggest that users are vulnerable to social engineering. These claims suggest that AI could make people susceptible to manipulation and persuasion. The affected group consists of the one billion people using these systems globally. These users may face risks related to emotional dependence on the technology. The research aims to see if empirical evidence supports these specific claims.

The articles provide background on the current state of artificial intelligence research. They mention that research into the impact of AI on people is nascent. The study draws on various methods to evaluate how these systems function. It contrasts popular concerns with the actual data found in recent studies. This background sets the stage for evaluating the validity of common fears.

Future work must resolve the many uncertainties that currently remain in the field. The researchers indicate that more study is needed to understand these impacts. The articles leave open whether the strongest narratives of concern will be proven. They do not provide a final conclusion on all eight ways AI impacts people. Further empirical evidence is required to reach more definitive results.

stories.Headline: AI hip fracture models predict costs but no study evaluates their economic value
stories.Summary:
A scoping review of 236 studies published between 2018 and 2025 found that artificial intelligence and machine learning models for hip fracture care consistently forecast the clinical drivers of episode costs but have almost entirely failed to evaluate actual monetary expenses or economic value. The review was reported in BMC Health Services Research by Shu, Li, Wang and Peng in 2026, and it was described in a Scienmag report by Blake Davidson dated November 26, 2026. Across eight years of peer-reviewed literature, the researchers identified an extensive body of work optimizing predictive algorithms for surgical complications, prolonged hospital stays and post-acute discharge destinations. Despite the substantial financial burden of managing hip fractures in older adults, formal health-economic evaluations measuring cost-effectiveness or budget impact remain entirely absent from the analyzed artificial intelligence literature.

The research team conducted a comprehensive scoping review adhering strictly to the PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines, designing a structured Boolean search that combined thirteen anatomical hip terms with forty-six machine learning and artificial intelligence descriptors. The primary query was run in the OpenAlex database on July 23, 2026, and was paired with a parallel PubMed search reconciled at the record level, while an expanded variant-term search and a known-item recall benchmark were added at peer-review revision. Eligible sources were restricted to English-language journal articles or reviews published from 2018 through 2025 that implemented an explicitly named computational intelligence method within hip fracture clinical pathways. The search initially retrieved 432 candidate records from OpenAlex, yielding 230 eligible publications, and three further studies came through PubMed reconciliation, two through the supplementary query and one through the known-item recall benchmark, for a total analytic sample of 236 papers. Two reviewers screened and extracted the data independently and applied an investigator-defined six-level classification ladder whose uppermost rung corresponded to the CHEERS 2022 reporting guidelines, with three analytical lexicons used to check that charting thresholds did not obscure health-economic concepts.

Diagnostic imaging, automated fracture detection and procedural guidance systems formed the largest single focus with 92 publications, or 39.0 percent of the reviewed literature, while clinical outcome forecasting and healthcare resource prediction formed the second dominant concentration with 87 articles, or 36.9 percent. Only 16 studies, representing 6.8 percent of the analyzed records, incorporated any explicit references to financial costs or hospital payment mechanisms. Exactly one study, representing 0.4 percent of the sample, constructed an explicit quantitative model simulating monetary expenditure alongside a specific healthcare payment scenario, and not a single paper in the reviewed abstract cohort presented a formal health-economic evaluation. Screening with the broadest thematic lexicon surfaced only six additional context-only mentions, none of which delivered an economic appraisal, and an audit of all 135 openly accessible full-text manuscripts, comprising 57.2 percent of the dataset, found zero cost-effectiveness analyses, cost-utility calculations, budget-impact models or formal health technology assessments.

The authors concluded that while predictive algorithms reliably detect the primary drivers of episode-based expenses, health economics remains an urgent, unaddressed necessity before these digital tools achieve clinical deployment. The absence of economic scrutiny did not stem from a shortage of economic methodology within hip fracture scholarship, because the identical search strategy identified 11 formal economic evaluations published during the same period that investigated hip fracture clinical pathways without machine learning techniques. In addition, 17 artificial intelligence publications explicitly cited the TRIPOD predictive model reporting standard, which confirmed that authors adhered to specialized algorithmic reporting frameworks even as none cited the CHEERS health-economic guidelines. The review therefore points to a gap between algorithmic risk stratification and real-world costs, reimbursement mechanisms or rigorous health technology assessments, and it frames formal economic evaluation as the missing step before clinical deployment.

stories.Headline: Fujitsu launches a vulnerability assessment service with OpenAI to verify exploitable flaws
stories.Summary:
Fujitsu Limited announced on November 25, 2026 that it has expanded its collaboration with OpenAI and joined the Daybreak Defense Network, OpenAI's cyber defense partner program. The announcement came from Kawasaki, Japan, according to JCN Newswire. As its first offering through the program, Fujitsu launched a vulnerability assessment service on November 25, 2026. The service combines OpenAI Daybreak's cyber defense capabilities with Fujitsu's proprietary vulnerability assessment system. It provides end-to-end support, from vulnerability discovery and exploitability verification to remediation guidance and post-remediation retesting.

The service combines dynamic testing of running systems with static source code analysis within the scope authorized by the customer. Reports include the summary and cause of discovered vulnerabilities, the specific location in the source code, Proof of Concept Code to reproduce the vulnerability, and proposed remediation methods. After customers implement fixes, Fujitsu retests to check whether those fixes are effective under the conditions of the assessment. If remediation is found to be insufficient, Fujitsu reports the findings and supports the review of additional countermeasures. Fujitsu will offer the service to customers in Japan and overseas.

Shuda Shinichiro, Global CEO and Senior Managing Partner of Uvance Wayfinders at Fujitsu, said AI continues to advance and cyberattacks are becoming increasingly sophisticated, with attackers analyzing systems at the code level. He said simply using AI to detect large numbers of potential vulnerabilities is not enough, and what matters is verifying whether vulnerabilities can actually be exploited. He said Fujitsu is pleased to expand its collaboration with OpenAI into cybersecurity and introduce the new service. He said bringing together advanced AI technologies and the expertise of Fujitsu's cybersecurity specialists will help customers strengthen their cyber defenses. He said Fujitsu will contribute to a safer and more secure digital society.

Dino Mizushima, Head of GTM Partnerships at OpenAI Japan, said the Daybreak Defense Network aims to bring frontier AI into companies' day-to-day cyber defense work. He said Fujitsu's experience building and operating enterprise systems is an important part of this effort. He said Fujitsu's security specialists play a key role by reviewing the results of AI-assisted assessments. He said validating vulnerabilities from an attacker's perspective helps customers determine which risks to address first based on exploitability and potential impact. He said that together with Fujitsu, OpenAI will help more companies in Japan turn those findings into concrete steps.

In May 2026, Fujitsu began collaboration with OpenAI, combining OpenAI's advanced AI technology with Fujitsu's knowledge of system construction and operation. Fujitsu said the cybersecurity landscape is undergoing significant change amid advancing generative AI and AI agent technologies and their expanding corporate use. Fujitsu said companies face challenges in securing highly skilled human resources to quickly discover and address vulnerabilities and in managing growing volumes of diagnosis and response operations. In 2026, Uvance Wayfinders' Security Consulting, led by Takeshi Sato, conducted red team tests for approximately 30 organizations and successfully penetrated all of them. In internal verification before the launch, Fujitsu discovered new vulnerabilities that were difficult to detect with conventional methods, even for expert teams, and confirmed they could be practically exploited in a real environment.

Going forward, Fujitsu will utilize OpenAI Daybreak's cyber defense capabilities across various areas of cybersecurity beyond vulnerability assessment to further expand its cybersecurity services. Fujitsu will leverage its own AI technologies, including the enterprise-grade generative AI "Takane" and the AI platform "Fujitsu Kozuchi," alongside its system construction and operation expertise. Fujitsu said it will support customers in a wide range of challenges, including advancement of the Software Development Life Cycle and system renewals such as modernization and migration. The articles do not say how many customers have adopted the service or what it costs. The articles do not give a date for further service expansions.

stories.Headline: OpenAI publishes a preprint claiming to prove the matrix multiplication exponent is exactly 9/4
stories.Summary:
OpenAI published a preprint on November 25, 2026, that it says proves the matrix multiplication exponent, written ω, is exactly 9/4, according to a post by Deedy on X. The post says the preprint runs 111 pages and addresses a problem that is 57 years old. Deedy writes that the problem ranks 31st on ProofAtlas’s list of the top 500 open problems in mathematics and is arguably second only to P versus NP in algorithms. The question at issue is how many steps it takes to multiply two n by n matrices, where the schoolbook method takes n cubed and the true cost is n to the power ω. The post traces the history of bounds on ω, starting with Strassen in 1969, who beat 3 for the first time with 2.807. Schönhage reached 2.522 in 1981, and Coppersmith and Winograd reached 2.376 in 1990, according to the post.

It says 36 years passed from 1990 to August 2026 to shave off 0.005, bringing the figure to 2.3712. The post states that in November 2026 OpenAI proved the upper and lower bound is 2.25, and it links to a GitHub page and to ProofAtlas rankings. The post presents the result as OpenAI’s claim, and it does not name the authors of the preprint or describe the proof itself. Deedy, the account that posted the summary, says it is wild to see things taught in university change before our eyes. A reply from the account Somi says exactly 9/4 is a clean answer after decades of shaving off decimals.

The articles give no statement from OpenAI beyond the linked preprint and no independent verification of the claimed proof. The articles do not say how the result would be checked, who would review the 111-page preprint, or when any verification might come. They give no reaction from mathematicians or from anyone outside the accounts quoted above. They also do not say what the claimed exact value of 9/4 would change in practice beyond the stated cost of matrix multiplication. More to follow.

stories.Headline: UAE minister Al Kaabi presents people-centred AI approach at Bridgetown AI safety summit
stories.Summary:
Noura bint Mohammed Al Kaabi, Minister of State, participated in the Bridgetown Special Summit on AI Safety, held in Barbados on 25th November, 2026, according to WAM. The summit brought together government leaders, senior officials, experts and representatives of international organisations to strengthen international cooperation in the field of artificial intelligence. It was co-chaired by Mia Amor Mottley, Prime Minister of Barbados, and Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations. The summit was held alongside the second meeting of the United Nations Independent International Scientific Panel on AI. Discussions focused on the opportunities presented by artificial intelligence and the importance of ensuring its safe and secure adoption.

During a roundtable titled 'AI for Humanity', Al Kaabi underscored the importance of ensuring that artificial intelligence reflects the languages, cultures and heritage of the communities it serves. She highlighted the UAE's people-centred approach to artificial intelligence, noting that the country became the first in the world to appoint a Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence in 2017. Al Kaabi underlined the UAE's investments in AI education and talent development, including integrating artificial intelligence into public school curricula from kindergarten to Grade 12. She also cited the establishment of the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence as part of those investments in education and talent. Her Excellency further showcased the UAE's Falcon family of AI models, including Falcon Arabic and the recently launched Falcon-Emirati, developed specifically for the Emirati dialect.

Al Kaabi emphasized the role of artificial intelligence in safeguarding cultural heritage during the summit proceedings in Barbados. She highlighted the efforts of the International Alliance for the Protection of Heritage (ALIPH), co-founded by the UAE and France. She pointed to its HeritageWatch.AI initiative, which leverages artificial intelligence and satellite imagery to identify threats to heritage sites. The UAE's participation reflected its approach to international cooperation on AI, which places people at its centre. That approach is built on exchanging best practices and ensuring the safe and secure adoption of AI, according to the articles.

The articles state that the summit brought together government leaders, senior officials, experts and representatives of international organisations. Mia Amor Mottley, Prime Minister of Barbados, co-chaired the summit together with Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations. The second meeting of the United Nations Independent International Scientific Panel on AI was held alongside the summit. Discussions at the summit focused on the opportunities presented by artificial intelligence. They also focused on the importance of ensuring its safe and secure adoption.

The articles give the dateline as Barbados, 25th November, 2026, with WAM reporting the participation of Noura bint Mohammed Al Kaabi, Minister of State. The summit was co-chaired by Mia Amor Mottley, Prime Minister of Barbados, and Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations. It was held alongside the second meeting of the United Nations Independent International Scientific Panel on AI. The roundtable at which Al Kaabi spoke was titled 'AI for Humanity'. The articles describe the UAE's participation as reflecting an approach to international cooperation on AI that places people at its centre.

stories.Headline: Avanade's Ben Beath says firms must redesign work to gain 200% to 300% from AI
stories.Summary:
Ben Beath discussed how to create value from artificial intelligence during a video interview with ISMG. This conversation took place on November 24, 2026, at the Microsoft Ignite 2026 event. Beath serves as the chief AI officer for the company known as Avanade. He explained that organizations must redesign business processes to maximize the return on their AI investments. He argued against simply layering new technology onto existing work patterns to achieve better results.

The AI Reality Report from Avanade found that only 18% of global organizations fundamentally reshaped their AI usage. However, 75% of these organizations claim they are doing better with AI than they actually are. Layering AI onto existing processes yields about 30% productivity gains according to the data provided by Beath. Building AI into the business can yield 200% to 300% through new revenue opportunities for the company. This approach requires alignment and a specific perspective on both governance and security for the enterprise.

Ben Beath is responsible for scaling AI adoption and integrating agentic systems into various enterprise operations. He stated that rethinking how a business operates is hard work for any organization to undertake. Beath believes that velocity is the right way to think about AI adoption rather than focusing on speed. He noted that human oversight must evolve as AI agents gain authority to make decisions of consequence. He also explained how Avanade uses Agent 365 to help employees build more intelligent AI agents.

The reports indicate that many global organizations are affected by what Beath calls the AI reality gap. These companies claim higher success rates with AI than their actual process redesigns would suggest. C-suite leaders are the primary group Beath works with to scale these complex AI adoption strategies. The data shows a significant difference in value between simple layering and full business reinvention for firms. Most organizations are currently failing to fundamentally reshape how their teams use these new artificial intelligence tools.

Beath has more than 20 years of experience in digital transformation and innovation for various businesses. His professional expertise includes enterprise AI strategy as well as generative AI and machine learning technologies. He previously co-founded the digital agency Loud & Clear along with PlayHQ Sports and FanHub Media. He was also a co-founder of the company called Sidekicker before his current role at Avanade. These experiences inform his view that business reinvention is necessary for achieving high returns on AI.

The next step for organizations is to move beyond simple productivity gains toward new revenue opportunities. Companies must decide if they will continue layering AI or commit to the hard work of redesigning. The articles leave open how exactly human oversight should evolve as agents gain more decision making authority. It remains unclear how many organizations will close the AI reality gap in the coming years. The text does not specify the exact timeline for achieving these 300% gains in revenue.

stories.Headline: Germany, Italy, Poland and Sweden join France in setting up international AI defense center
stories.Summary:
Germany, Italy, Poland, and Sweden joined France to set up an international artificial intelligence center for defense, the French Defense Ministry announced. These four European countries officially announced their intention to join the new organization during a first establishment conference held in Rennes. The conference took place on November 19 and 20, and the announcement was made public by the ministry on a Monday. This international effort seeks to create a center that focuses on the use of artificial intelligence for various defense purposes. The participating nations intend to work together to build a new center dedicated to the field of artificial intelligence in defense.

The new organization is called the International Center for Artificial Intelligence in Defence, which is also referred to by the acronym ICAID. The center requires the cooperation of France, Germany, Italy, Poland, and Sweden to establish its initial operational framework and goals. It aims to build an international community of interest to share best practices and anticipate technological advances in the field of AI. The center will draw on operational feedback to ensure that AI solutions closely meet practical needs and support military operations. The initiative remains open to other like-minded nations that wish to join the effort to accelerate AI readiness for operations.

The French Defense Ministry is responsible for the announcement and the overall coordination of this new international artificial intelligence defense initiative. The ministry stated that France and its partners aim to accelerate AI readiness in support of military operations through the ICAID. They said the center will establish an international network for sharing best practices and anticipating future technological developments in AI. The ministry explained that the center will use operational feedback to ensure that AI solutions address practical defense needs effectively. Officials reaffirmed that the initiative is open to other nations that share similar goals regarding the use of artificial intelligence.

The articles do not provide specific quotes from other individuals, but they mention that other like-minded nations are welcome to join. The nations affected by this initiative include France, Germany, Italy, Poland, and Sweden, who are the current founding members. These countries will be affected by the acceleration of AI readiness and the adoption of new technologies for their military operations. The international community of interest will be affected by the sharing of best practices and the anticipation of technological advances. Military operations in these participating nations will be affected by the practical AI solutions developed by the new center.

The background provided is that France initiated the creation of the International Center for Artificial Intelligence in Defence to support military operations. The center was established to create a network where nations can share best practices and anticipate future advances in AI. It was designed to ensure that artificial intelligence solutions are based on operational feedback to meet practical defense needs. The first establishment conference was held in Rennes to formally bring the participating European nations together for this specific purpose. This initiative is part of a broader effort to accelerate the adoption of artificial intelligence within the defense sectors of Europe.

The next step will be for the participating nations to work together on drafting the founding texts for the center. The goal of the member nations is to reach full operational capability for the center in the course of 2027. The articles leave open which other like-minded nations might decide to join the initiative in the future. It is not stated which specific founding texts will be drafted or how the operational capability will be measured. The articles do not specify the exact funding or the leadership structure that will govern the center once it is operational.

stories.Headline: US Department of Commerce plans to blacklist Singaporean AI firm Megaspeed over chip export violations
stories.Summary:
The United States government intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence company from doing business in America following a recent Nvidia scandal. The US Department of Commerce announced this plan on Monday to blacklist the firm known as Megaspeed Ltd from American trade. This action follows accusations that a former executive of the company worked as a spy for China during a romantic relationship. The relationship was with Jensen Huang, who is the head of Nvidia, and it led to increased scrutiny by US officials. This situation created heightened concerns that the company was funneling advanced AI computer chips from Nvidia into the country of China.

The Commerce Department plans to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are banned from buying or selling US goods. This Singaporean company is mainly a developer of data centres and has significant business dealings in China with the retailer Alibaba. The US intelligence apparatus believes that Alice Huang, a former executive, was working as an asset for the government in Beijing. This specific relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang became public through media reports that emerged during the previous month. The US has blocked China from buying this specific type of advanced AI technology since the year 2022.

The US Department of Commerce stated that it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years before the affair incident occurred. Officials said they suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping Chinese companies obtain advanced chips from Nvidia. President Donald Trump said he convinced the company and made a deal to reinstate Jensen Huang on Monday after his resignation. The board of Nvidia then reinstated the CEO after the intervention by the president of the United States regarding the matter. The White House, the Commerce Department, and Megaspeed were all asked for comment by the BBC regarding the planned ban.

China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use this scandal as a pretext. The Chinese government stated that the US should not use the situation to impose a technological blockade on AI technology. The US intelligence apparatus claims that the activities of Alice Huang created national security concerns within the United States of America. The company Megaspeed was not well known within the US until the media reports about the affair surfaced last month. Another alleged affair involving Jensen Huang also surfaced days after the first one, which led to the CEO's initial resignation.

The US government suspects that Megaspeed was helping to get Nvidia chips into the hands of various companies located within China. This activity would violate US export controls that have been in place to restrict Chinese access to AI technology since 2022. Megaspeed is based in Singapore, but its largest customer is the major Chinese online retailer known as Alibaba. The company primarily focuses on the development of data centres as its main business activity before the recent blacklist announcement. The US intelligence community viewed the romantic link between the two individuals as a risk to national security interests.

The US government has not yet specified when the ban against Megaspeed Ltd will officially go into effect for the company. The Commerce Department continues to monitor the situation after its two year investigation into the suspected violation of export controls. The articles leave open whether the US will impose further restrictions on other companies tied to the recent Nvidia scandal. It remains unclear if the Chinese government will take further diplomatic actions in response to the planned American technological blockade. The BBC is waiting for responses from the White House and Megaspeed regarding the announcement made on Monday.

stories.Headline: Nvidia reports 103 percent revenue growth as AI chip demand outstrips supply
stories.Summary:
Nvidia released its third quarter fiscal 2027 results on November 17, showing that the artificial intelligence build-out continues at an impressive pace. The company reported that its revenue increased by 103 percent year over year to reach a total of 115.8 billion dollars. Data center revenue drove this growth by increasing 110 percent to 107.6 billion dollars during the same period of time. Nvidia also increased its revenue growth estimate for fiscal 2028 from 70 percent to a new target of 75 percent. The company stated that demand for its chips is currently outstripping supply due to a huge backlog from cloud providers.

stories.Headline: Galveston police adopt Veritone Investigate AI to speed active and cold case work
stories.Summary:
The Galveston Police Department announced in a November 19 news release that it will begin using an artificial intelligence platform called Veritone Investigate to help move active and long-running cold case investigations along more efficiently, according to Houston Public Media. The Galveston City Council approved the use of the AI-powered tools in a 5-0 vote at a council meeting on November 12. The service package with Veritone runs for one year and costs approximately $75,000, according to city documents. The California-based company Veritone works with about 450 agencies across the U.S. for public safety, most of which are in California, and CEO and President Ryan Steelberg said the partnership with Galveston is one of the company's first entry points into Texas.

Steelberg said police departments are struggling to manage increasing volumes of digital evidence, which makes it harder to find information that moves cases forward. He said the investigative tool would help agencies process audio, video, images and documents and make the material searchable, and would also use AI-driven tools to get information relevant to an investigation. He said the AI is not trying to solve the case for the department but is trying to organize the data. Galveston Police Chief Doug Balli said that entering just one case into Veritone would save the average investigator hundreds of man-hours in reviewing information and generating leads, and that investigators need technology that helps them move from evidence to insight quickly, especially when they are working both active and cold cases. Balli did not respond to Houston Public Media's request for comment about the new technology.

Steelberg said the information used with Veritone Investigate will be safeguarded like any other investigation and that the process for public records requests will not change. He said nothing will change in terms of the controls, audit logging and jurisdiction, and that the purpose is for data to go into a secure environment where the AI models that are invoked are containerized and secure. The department's decision comes alongside heavy scrutiny from residents around Harris and Galveston counties who have expressed privacy concerns about Flock Safety cameras, which use AI technology to automatically read license plates, especially in light of Houston-area cases of alleged misuse by law enforcement. It also comes around the same time that Harris County officials decided to pull a no-bid contract for a controversial AI facial recognition technology, Clearview AI, from a commissioners court meeting agenda.

stories.Headline: China and ASEAN designate 2027 as the Year of AI cooperation
stories.Summary:
China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations declared 2027 as the Year of AI cooperation on Monday, November 16, 2026. This announcement occurred as the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 Upgrade Protocol prepares to enter into force on December 1, 2026. The upgraded deal moves beyond traditional trade liberalization to cover emerging areas like the digital economy and green development. It aims to shift the regional relationship from simple market opening toward deeper institutional cooperation and coordinated standards. This new framework will address global challenges by creating a more stable and predictable regional market and industrial chain.

The protocol, signed in October 2025, includes a standalone chapter on supply-chain cooperation for the first time in a bilateral agreement. It covers hard connectivity in logistics and digital infrastructure, plus soft connectivity for electronic payments, invoices, and bills of lading. The agreement empowers a regional market of nearly 2.1 billion people through high-level commitments and improved customs procedures. China and ASEAN will establish sub-committees on standards, small and medium-sized enterprises, green development, and the digital economy. These measures will reduce business costs by encouraging the mutual recognition of conformity assessment results to avoid duplicate testing.

An official from the Ministry of Commerce of China said the upgrade reflects a commitment to multilateralism and free trade. The official stated that the deal will create a safe and open environment for digital trade and investment. MOFCOM will support local governments and industries by organizing targeted outreach and training for enterprises to understand new rules. The ministry noted that these arrangements will provide fresh impetus to Asia-Pacific economic integration amid global trade uncertainty. They believe that improving system compatibility through digital cooperation will enhance the competitiveness of regional products more than tariffs.

Poh-Yian Koh of FedEx China said AI adoption must translate technology deployment into better decisions and measurable customer value. Robin Li of Baidu warned that AI risks becoming a bubble if it does not translate into practical business value. Yang Ting of Agilent Technologies noted that AI helps life sciences customers make faster decisions and improve data quality. Fang Ling of Alstom stated that AI can improve rail reliability but requires rigorous validation in real operating environments. Winnie Ma of VF Corp said realizing AI potential requires responsible governance and a combination of technology and creativity.

China has remained the largest trading partner for ASEAN for 17 consecutive years, while ASEAN has led for China for six. In 2025, the value of bilateral trade between the two sides exceeded 1 trillion dollars, up 18 times since 2002. Business leaders recently met at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation CEO Summit 2026 in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, to discuss AI productivity. Executives highlighted China's AI Plus initiative and its large manufacturing base as key opportunities for multinational companies to validate applications. They noted that China's digital infrastructure and market scale provide a strong environment for the adoption of new technologies.

The two sides will now review relevant provisions under the protocol's future work plan and hold further AI consultations. APEC economies are called upon to share practical experience and expand digital skills to make AI applications more accessible. The Ministry of Commerce will continue working with ASEAN to advance practical cooperation and implement the new trade rules. The articles do not state when the specific sub-committees will be formed or the exact date for AI consultations. It remains open how businesses will specifically measure the tangible productivity gains mentioned by the various regional business leaders.
