stories.Headline: Investors hold $1.4 trillion in margin debt as AI data center spending outpaces revenue growth
stories.Summary:
Margin debt, money investors borrow from brokerage firms to buy stocks, reached a record $1.5 trillion in June, according to data compiled by the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, and stood at $1.4 trillion at the end of October, about 3.6% below that June peak. Adam Spatacco wrote the article for The Motley Fool, published on November 24, 2026. The article says investors are borrowing unprecedented sums to participate in the stock market's ongoing rally, which it says introduces another layer of risk into an already frothy market. It says enthusiasm surrounding AI infrastructure and software helped propel the S&P 500, Nasdaq Composite and Dow Jones Industrial Average to record highs over the past four years. The article says the rapid accumulation of debt over the last year or so suggests investors are developing more of an appetite for risk.

The article gives borrowing levels during other periods of unusually high speculation: $300 billion in March 2000 during the dot-com bubble, $416 billion in July 2007 prior to the great financial crisis, $936 billion in October 2021 during the pandemic-era rally, and $1.5 trillion in June 2026 during the AI-fueled bull market. It says today's borrowing levels dwarf the historical figures in absolute dollars but that the stock market has become considerably larger. It says brokerage firms require investors to maintain a minimum level of liquidity in their margin accounts, and that if declining stock prices cause an account to fall below that threshold, investors could face a margin call requiring them to deposit additional collateral or reduce their positions. It says brokerages also have the authority to liquidate positions without obtaining an investor's permission. It says forced selling across several accounts at the same time puts additional downward pressure on stock prices, triggering more margin calls and creating a destructive cycle.

The article says elevated margin debt doesn't necessarily mean a stock market crash is imminent and that borrowing often increases alongside rising stock prices. It says margin debt is better viewed as a potential amplifier of market volatility rather than a reliable predictor of when a crash or drawdown will occur. It says declining balances can reflect forced liquidations rather than voluntary reductions in risk. It says investors who buy stocks using their own capital have more financial flexibility to endure prolonged downturns than those whose brokerage firms can force them to sell at unfavorable prices. It says nobody knows whether today's borrowing levels will culminate in another stock market bubble bursting event.

The article says the S&P 500 declined by 49% following the dot-com bubble and nearly 57% during the financial crisis. It says the index fell 34% during the COVID-19 crash and 25% during the 2022 bear market. It says that despite these setbacks the S&P 500 eventually recovered and reached new record highs. It says history suggests staying diversified and remaining invested through volatility is a more prudent approach to building long-term wealth than attempting to predict the next market crash. It says the practice of borrowing from a brokerage firm to buy stocks is more commonly known as leverage and allows investors to increase purchasing power without committing an equivalent amount of their own capital up front.

The article illustrates leverage with an example: an investor with $10,000 who borrows another $10,000 has $20,000 invested, and a 25% increase generates a $5,000 gain, a 50% return on the original capital. It says a 25% portfolio decline would lose $5,000, or half of the original investment, and a 50% decline effectively wipes out the original capital. It says borrowing can be lucrative when stocks are rising but that leverage works in both directions. It says one of the most dangerous aspects of using leverage is that investors do not necessarily control when their positions are sold. It says much of Wall Street's attention is focused on whether AI stocks are overvalued.

The article says margin debt is at historically high levels and describes it as one of Wall Street's biggest threats. It says the article explores what smart investors can do about it. It leaves open whether today's borrowing levels will culminate in another stock market bubble bursting event. It does not say when any crash or drawdown might occur. It does not give a date for any forced liquidation tied to the October figure.

Dell Technologies reported fiscal third-quarter results on November 24, 2026, and its most telling disclosure came on the earnings call, according to articles by Omor Ibne Ehsan. Vice chairman and COO Jeff Clarke said Dell has taken about $180 billion of AI orders over the past four quarters. He added that a majority of new orders are based on Vera Rubin NVL72, the next rack-scale AI system from Nvidia. Both stocks fell in the regular session, with Dell falling 11.83%, or $39.63, before the report and closing at $295.28. At 7:59 p.m.

ET Dell traded at $297.91, up 0.89%, while Nvidia fell 5.86% to $155.38 and traded at $151.95 at 7:59 p.m. ET, down 2.21%. The majority of orders phrase applies only to new bookings, and Dell gave no Vera Rubin share of backlog, revenue, or shipments. Dell's press release never names the platform, and Dell disclosed no Vera Rubin margin figure. Dell booked $60.2 billion in AI orders, slightly below the prior quarter's then-record $60.9 billion, yet the AI backlog rose from $95 billion to a record $132.3 billion.

That increase was about $37.3 billion, or about 39%, and orders are getting in faster than Dell can ship. AI-optimized server revenue reached a record $22.0 billion, up 291%, and CFO David Kennedy guided to roughly $23.5 billion for the fourth quarter. Dell Technologies raised its fiscal 2027 AI server outlook to $78.0 billion from $74.0 billion, and Infrastructure Solutions Group revenue rose 198% to $42.0 billion. The PC unit brought in $12.9 billion, up 3%, a mix that shows Dell is now mainly an AI infrastructure company. Dell Technologies raised its fiscal 2027 non-GAAP EPS outlook to $29.68 from $25.50, yet the stock trades at a P/E of about 17x.

The stock sits about 50% below its 52-week high of $595.51, and the risks are thin hardware margins and a schedule set by Nvidia's ramp. Dell prices deals to delivery dates, and Nvidia benefits most directly from this mix, with a 60.4% operating margin against Dell's 7.44%. Clarke said Dell has priced Vera Rubin with the expected delivery date with all of its customers, and because memory and other component costs are rising, pricing each deal to its ship date moves timing risk off Dell's margins. Clarke said, "We've had no customers reschedule business," and more than 7,500 customers now use Dell AI Factories. Clarke said: "Demand continues to exceed supply."

Dell is one of the largest builders of Nvidia-based servers, so its mix gives an early, customer-level read on how quickly buyers are moving to the next platform. Nvidia said Rubin generated nearly $20 billion in its first quarter of production shipments, and Dell also played up PowerEdge servers built on Advanced Micro Devices processors, which limits its reliance on one chip vendor. That concentration also creates dependence, because when most new orders target a platform still ramping, Dell's revenue timing rests on Nvidia's supply. Nvidia, at a $3.75 trillion market cap and amid a leadership transition and board investigation, carries separate questions beyond Vera Rubin demand. The November 25 session opens at 9:30 a.m.

ET after 8:30 a.m. ET PCE and GDP data, and markets close November 26 for Thanksgiving. After-hours trading is thin, so those prices can shift at the open. Dell's valuation looks modest against its outlook, and the bullish case on demand holds if AI server revenue lands near $23.5 billion and the backlog remains above $132.3 billion. At the fourth-quarter report, any customer delays would weaken the bullish case on demand.

stories.Headline: HPE shares fall as rising AI server costs shrink margins despite strong revenue forecast
stories.Summary:
Shares of Hewlett Packard Enterprise fell about 16 per cent on Tuesday, November 24, as investors focused on the company's shrinking margins amid soaring costs, even though strong AI demand boosted its full-year revenue outlook. The stock had more than doubled this year through Monday's close, but it was set to lose about $10 billion in market value if the losses held. On Monday, HPE had soared more than 17 per cent as an Nvidia-fueled rally lifted AI stocks. The drop came as the company's upbeat forecast was overshadowed by concerns about profitability in its AI business.

HPE forecast an adjusted operating margin for the fiscal year ending October 2027 of between 14 per cent and 15 per cent, down from 15.1 per cent in fiscal 2026. At its Cloud and AI unit, which includes servers and storage and is a key growth driver, HPE expects an annual fiscal margin of about 14 per cent, down from 15.2 per cent in the previous fiscal year. Robust demand for AI servers helped drive a 50 per cent jump in HPE's fourth-quarter revenue to $14.55 billion, topping estimates. The company now expects fiscal 2027 revenue growth between 27 per cent and 35 per cent, up from its earlier forecast of 13 per cent to 17 per cent.

HPE finance chief Marie Myers said on an earnings call that costs were rising faster than pricing and that margins would take a hit in the second half of the year as the company ships more AI servers. Art Hogan, chief market strategist at B Riley Wealth, said that when input costs go up and not enough is passed along, margins have to take a hit, and that this clearly showed. He added that this raises concerns that pricing tailwinds are beginning to fade, and that supply shortages expected through 2028 will take a bite out of margins. Bob O'Donnell, chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research, said the market seems acutely sensitive to any potential changes in profit margins at tech companies these days, and that HPE's solid numbers and robust forecast certainly did not seem to justify the market's reaction that day.

stories.Headline: AI builder Will Thomas sees his model beat him in Fantasy Premier League
stories.Summary:
Will Thomas has played Fantasy Premier League for over 15 years, and last season the AI he built finished above him for the first time. He told Reuters it was a bit of a surreal moment and that he thought he was being beaten by his own creation. Thomas is an Englishman and the CEO and founder of Scoreline.ai, which delivers subscriber-based content including data, insight and analytics for fantasy sports players. Among its products is Fantasy Football Hub, which has around 60,000 paying subscribers and focuses on FPL, the official fantasy competition of the English Premier League. FPL offers match tickets and replica kits as prizes and had over 13 million registered teams in the 2025-26 season.

Scoreline.ai's purpose-built model finished in the top 0.5 per cent of those teams, ranking 67,829th in the world. A Reuters analysis of nine FPL teams, seven of which were run on the directions of AI chatbots, showed the chatbot teams scored an average of 499 points in the first eight gameweeks of the 2026-27 FPL season. The chatbot teams were operated by Scout Digital, a sports marketing firm that gives each separate chatbot the same instructions every week and, in most cases, has a staff member log in to carry out its decisions. Their performances were in line with the average human benchmark of 502, but about 75 points below the average of the top 1,000 human players. Scout Digital said newer versions of each AI model are used as they are released.

Thomas said there are still human managers beating the model, but it is getting harder to do, and he has a PhD in team leadership at the University of Sussex. Scout Digital managing director Mike Lewis said that so far they are two seasons in and the improvement they have seen is huge. Lewis said that in 2025-26 Scout Statto comfortably won, and that this season is looking neck and neck. Daniel Groos, head of AI at Groos Analytics, who built the open-source forecasting model OpenFPL, said the hardest question remains whether a player will even be in action on any particular gameweek and not dropped, rested or injured. Jonas Sand Labakk, the 2023-24 FPL champion, told Reuters that where you need human input is the expected minutes for players, because rotation, injuries and managerial choices are where he thinks the models miss the most.

Groos added that overall machines have an advantage because humans tend to be influenced by a spectacular performance, media narratives or a favourite player. The chatbot teams make about as few transfers as the best human managers, and the gap in transfer volume is small. The chatbot teams' captain picks trail those of the top 1,000 human players, and they also leave more points on the bench than the typical manager. The top 1,000 do not play against the grain, owning more popular players than the average manager, not fewer, which undercuts the idea that beating the field takes contrarian bets. Thomas also argues that the machines are weakest at the start of a season, when new managers and players give the models little data, and that fans of specific teams may have a slight insight advantage.

However, the early numbers do not clearly show that. The chatbot teams Reuters analysed were level with the official average in gameweek 1 of this season, pulled ahead in gameweek 2, and had dipped just below it by gameweek 8. According to industry research, Thomas is one of around 245 million people who play fantasy sports, where players take the role of manager or coach and build a virtual team made up of athletes whose real-life performances earn them points. As a control, Scout Digital also has a team titled Scout Statto, which is managed by the firm's co-founder Simon Gold and run without the use of AI tools. Beginning this season, FPL features its own conversational AI assistant titled FPL Companion.

While some predict a future where fantasy sports become a battleground purely for competing versions of AI, Groos does not expect the human element to disappear completely. Groos said the winning formula may turn out to be neither human intuition nor AI-based insights, but a combination of both. Labakk echoed that, adding that he thinks the best possible way is an engaged manager with the models rather than an AI with the models. Marcus Adebayo, 34, a software project manager from South London, uses Gemini by letting it do the structural heavy lifting but picks the team himself. Adebayo said treating it as a co-pilot works brilliantly, provided you are honest enough to admit that when the plane hits turbulence, it is usually because you grabbed the controls.

stories.Headline: Ohio mother criticizes elementary school for sending AI generated letter with typos
stories.Summary:
An Ohio mother of two children criticized her son's elementary school for sending a notice generated by artificial intelligence. This parent, who goes by Lyssa, posted a viral video on TikTok about the incident in November 2026. She kept her son home because he had a fever and obtained a medical note for the absence. The school sent an attendance overview sheet that accused the child of chronic absence despite the doctor's note. This notice included a reprimand stating that every hour counts, which the mother found to be condescending.

The letter used the word mieses instead of misses and wrote absenteessn instead of absences in one specific sentence. Another error in the text printed the word hours as bours, while a slogan promised that togettier they make a difference. Under Ohio House Bill 410, the Ohio Department of Education flags students as chronically absent if they miss ten percent of hours. This limit includes both excused and unexcused absences, which makes providing doctor's notes feel like a waste of co-pays. Lyssa pointed to creepy design choices and spelling errors as evidence that the school ignored its own tech guidelines.

Lyssa said the school district only wants money and does not care about children or the parents they send letters to. She questioned why the school used AI as a shortcut and failed to proofread the document before sending it out. The mother claimed that a simple letter written by a human principal would have been a sufficient way to communicate. She insisted that someone must take the education of children seriously because the school staff appeared to be very lazy. Lyssa also warned that external textbook publishers across the country are relying on AI for assignments and for lesson plans.

A school staff member on the Reddit forum r/antiai expressed frustration over low effort AI graphics used at various student events. This user claimed that genuine human art pieces were replaced by tapestries of AI slop that looked like no effort. Another Reddit user said they were confused and sad about the state of education compared to the early twenty ten period. This person noted that teachers used to lecture against excessive internet use, but now it seems everyone embraces the rot. These individuals and the mother are affected by the growing use of generative AI for official communications and event materials.

The articles state that the mother's TikTok video calling out the school has currently reached a total of 45,000 views. The background provided shows that New York City Public Schools enacted an AI and screen time policy for 2026 to 2027. The mother's frustration stems from a strict attendance policy that counts medical absences toward the chronic absence limit for students. She believes that unchecked AI content is being used to educate students in ways that are not being properly monitored. The reports indicate that parents are not buying the use of AI slop to scold them about school attendance.

The New York Post reached out to the parent for further comment, but they did not immediately receive a response. The articles leave open whether the school district will respond to the claims about its use of artificial intelligence tools. It remains unclear if the school will change its attendance policy regarding the use of medical notes for sick children. The text does not say if the teacher who sent the letter will face any disciplinary action for the errors. There is no information on whether other parents at the school have complained about receiving similar AI generated attendance notices.

stories.Headline: FUJIFILM Business Innovation Singapore launches Apeos C7072 Series A3 color MFPs with AI and cloud features
stories.Summary:
FUJIFILM Business Innovation Singapore announced on November 24, 2026, the launch of the Apeos C7072 Series, a new generation of A3 color multifunction printers. The company said the series uses cloud capabilities and AI technologies to help organizations make better use of their know-how. It said the series also reduces environmental impact through energy savings, resource circulation and more efficient maintenance services. The company said the Apeos C7072 Series is the first MFP from FUJIFILM Business Innovation to incorporate its AI technologies. It said the series uses technologies developed under its AI technology brand, REiLI Business.

The company said the series captures information including paper documents, electronic files and faxes, and organizes and structures it in the cloud. It said all models feature a newly developed duplex automatic document feeder and support high-speed scanning of up to 300 pages per minute for two-sided originals. It said the Apeos Cloud Extension cloud service automatically stores scanned documents and fax data in the cloud. It said recycled plastic accounts for 50% of the device's total plastic content by weight, with a four-tray configuration. It said recycled materials account for 5% by weight of all steel sheets used in the device, with a four-tray configuration.

The company said the series will continue to expand its functions and services through the cloud after installation. It said the series evolves into an information-utilization platform. It said AI-enabled power savings and more efficient maintenance, together with an environmentally conscious design, help reduce environmental impact throughout the product lifecycle. It said the design framework sets and evaluates environmental quality targets from the design stage, taking the entire product lifecycle into account. It said the series encourages customers to adopt AI by organizing and structuring dispersed information.

The company said the series is among the highest speeds in the industry for two-sided scanning, based on its internal research of A3 color MFPs. It said the industry-first AI-controlled energy-saving feature analyzes device usage patterns and automatically optimizes the time before the device enters low-power or sleep mode. It said Smart WelcomEyes reduces the activation time from approximately three seconds on the previous Apeos C7071 Series to approximately one second. It said the devices support paper weights from 52 to 300 g/m2 and long paper up to 320 x 1,200 mm. It said the new Finisher A4 can bind up to 10 sheets without metal staples.

The company said much organizational information remains stored in a variety of formats, including paper documents, electronic files or emails, and is not readily available for use in AI applications or business systems. It said organizations need to organize and structure accumulated information so it can be applied to both AI and business operations. It said it believes preparing information accumulated within organizations for use by AI and in business operations will become a new role for MFPs in the AI era. It said the optional functions of Apeos Cloud Extension enable customers to centrally manage digitized documents in the cloud. It said a separate agreement is required for those optional functions.

The company said APIs and MCP are expected to expand opportunities for integration with AI agents and a variety of SaaS applications. It said it aims to expand integration with external business services to support the entire process from information utilization to task execution. It said the Apeos Cloud Extension requires registration. It said the generative AI-powered OCR is based on its internal research, using the measurement method specified by the International ENERGY STAR Program. It said the low power consumption claim is based on its internal research, using the measurement method specified by the International ENERGY STAR Program.

stories.Headline: West Virginia students learn welding as AI concerns grow
stories.Summary:
As artificial intelligence continues to change the workforce, some West Virginia high school students are turning to skilled trades for a sense of job security, the articles state. At the Monongalia County Technical Education Center in Morgantown, students are learning hands-on skills that could prepare them for careers less dependent on emerging technology. High school junior Graham Young is focused on developing skills that could lead to a career in welding, while some other students are concerned about how artificial intelligence could affect their career opportunities. The story was produced by journalism students at WVU’s Reed School of Media, and a photo of Young working on a project in Morgantown on Friday, Oct. 30 is credited to James Bickom of the WVU Reed School of Media. The articles were published on Nov. 25, 2026, by timeswv.com and register-herald.com.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, the median annual salary for welders in the United States is nearly $54,000, and the industry is projected to have more than 40,000 job openings each year over the next decade. More than 90,000 high school students in West Virginia completed a technical education course during the 2024-25 school year. At M-TEC, students are learning different welding techniques and gaining practical experience that could help them enter the workforce after graduation. The training gives students an opportunity to explore different areas of welding before deciding which career path they want to pursue. Young hopes to eventually work in structural or pipeline welding, two fields that could take him to different parts of the country.

Young said he has a passion for steam locomotives and that welding is one of the only trades directly applicable to the steam locomotive preservation world. He said he would be lying if he said the money was not an allure, calling the money a very big allure to the job. Young said he would like to go into either structural or pipeline welding, naming a city like New York, Pittsburgh or Chicago for structural work, or pipelines out west. Welding instructor Don Robinette said he has noticed more students expressing interest in skilled trades, particularly as concerns surrounding artificial intelligence continue to grow. Robinette said a lot of high school students want to get into it due to some of the AI that has been going on, that they are afraid of what is going to happen, and that welders and plumbers are going to be needed.

At Morgantown High School, counselor Alex Eddy works with students as they explore their options after graduation, and Eddy says artificial intelligence has become part of those conversations as students begin thinking about job security. Eddy said a lot of those kids are kind of thinking just what AI may look like, what it may affect, jobs in the future, and that they are thinking about that and considering it. One student said the class is doing stick welding and hopefully will get into other kinds of welding later in the year, that they are doing different jobs, and that it gets them ready to go into the different trades. Although artificial intelligence could change how certain jobs are performed, Robinette believes there will continue to be a demand for workers in hands-on fields like welding and plumbing. While artificial intelligence continues to raise questions about the future of employment, students like Young are already preparing for the workforce by developing skills they hope will remain in demand.

As artificial intelligence and automation become more common across industries, educators are beginning to see students consider how technology could influence their future careers. For educators like Eddy and Robinette, helping students understand their career options is becoming increasingly important as technology changes the job market. For Young, the future may still be uncertain, but his career goals are becoming clearer with every project he completes. The articles state that the story was produced by journalism students at WVU’s Reed School of Media, with more available on their website. The articles give no further background on the event.

The articles do not state what happens next beyond the students’ continuing training and Young’s stated hopes for structural or pipeline welding. They leave open which specific career path Young will pursue and where he will eventually work. They do not say how many students are enrolled at M-TEC or how the welding program will change. They do not state whether the students’ interest in trades will continue to grow. They give no further details on the event beyond what the students and educators said.

Noah Holdings Limited hosted the 19th Global Black Diamond Summit in Singapore starting November 23, 2026. The event drew hundreds of clients from various countries and regions to explore wealth security. Representatives from global asset management firms, business, government, and academia also attended the gathering. The summit focused on asset allocation and long-term investment judgments during the AI era. This specific event in Singapore was titled The Anchorage and ended on November 25, 2026.

The summit requires high-net-worth families to understand risk and avoid relying on any single future view. It focuses on the Singapore headquarters of Noah Holdings and its global Chinese family clients. The event theme was Safe Passage, Wider Horizons, and it addressed balancing growth with protection. Participants discussed how AI brings both opportunities and divergent views while markets fluctuated throughout the year. The gathering maintains a private character built over the past 18 years of annual events.

Chairwoman Norah Wang said families must understand if their net AI exposure is positive or negative. She stated that underlying cash flows may carry hidden concentration risk for families wealthy on paper. CEO Zander Yin said disciplined asset allocation helps maintain perspective when markets diverge and fluctuate. Yin noted that Noah uses AI to turn two decades of industry knowledge into institutional intelligence. He claimed that continued research and prudent judgment are needed to identify long-term opportunities.

Professor David Lee suggested evaluating asset allocation by a family's ability to meet financial commitments. He said families should assess liquidity needs using dates and currencies of debts and education expenses. Former MP Seng Han Thong noted that the second generation values investment autonomy and professional management. Former Ambassador Chan Heng Chee said the new world order would be an asymmetric multipolar order. These speakers addressed entrepreneurs to help them assess emerging opportunities in Asia and globally.

The articles state that Noah Holdings was founded in 2005 and is headquartered in Singapore. The firm has allocated more than 153 billion US dollars in cumulative assets for clients. It operates across nine countries and regions using three platforms for investment and legacy planning. stories.Headline: Lianlian DigiTech launches an AI business card to enable automated agentic payments for global enterprises
stories.Summary:
Lianlian DigiTech announced the launch of the LianLian XCard on November 25, 2026, in Hangzhou, China, to help enterprises operating globally. This new AI-powered business card aims to close the loop between AI task execution and agentic payments for various international businesses. The company designed the card to combine multi-currency payments, business expense management, and exclusive AI benefits for its corporate users. Eligible users have been able to apply for the card since November 18 through the AI Workforce platform, LianLian XWorker. This product allows authorized AI agents to initiate payments within predefined authorization limits to procure AI tools and manage global spending.

The card supports payments in more than 140 currencies and covers over 120 payment scenarios, including SaaS subscriptions and business travel. Users can link the card to the LianLian Agent Wallet and define purchase intent, permissions, and budgets within the platform. Payments executed through LianLian XPay use single-use payment tokens and dynamic security credentials so agents do not access actual card numbers. Activation provides 20 million complimentary AI model usage credits through the LianLian RouterBrain platform for marketing, content creation, and customer service. The system offers shared corporate spending limits, individual card limits, and a use now, pay later option for AI services.

Lianlian DigiTech is responsible for the launch and claims the card helps businesses streamline spending and advance AI-enabled global operations. The company stated that the card enables a seamless transition from task execution to transaction completion for advertising and procurement. They described their AI Workforce platform, LianLian XWorker, as a global business partner that coordinates AI agents around specific business objectives. The firm believes that payments are evolving into essential infrastructure that connects business decisions, agentic execution, and global commercial resources. They intend to continue expanding global business payment capabilities to enable more trusted agentic transactions and seamless international operations.

The product affects enterprises operating internationally that need to manage digital service procurement and everyday operational expenses as they expand globally. These businesses can now allocate budgets across teams and projects while using card-level statement reporting to streamline their financial reconciliation. The collaboration with Visa allows the use of Visa Intelligent Commerce Connect to power the business spending and expense management. This partnership helped an AI agent complete the first live B2B transaction in Asia Pacific using a tokenized payment credential. Other affected users include those who can earn additional AI credits through eligible spending to turn expenses into AI resources.

Lianlian DigiTech and Visa have been working together to explore new technological capabilities to advance trusted agentic payments and risk management. An AI agent previously demonstrated the ability to identify procurement needs, evaluate suppliers, place orders, and complete payments within limits. The LianLian XWorker platform is registered in the Visa Agentic Directory to facilitate these advanced types of automated commercial workflows. The company developed the LianLian RouterBrain as an AI computing infrastructure platform to provide the necessary credits for various AI models. These background developments aim to extend AI capabilities beyond standalone assistance and into the realm of real-world business execution.

Lianlian DigiTech will continue to enhance services and benefits based on the actual usage and transaction records of the card users. The company plans to provide additional benefits to eligible users as they continue to navigate the AI era and markets. The articles leave open how the specific additional benefits will be structured or which users will qualify for them later. stories.Headline: Colorado hearing officer dismisses Kipp complaint over Independence Institute AI video
stories.Summary:
A hearing officer in the Colorado secretary of state's office dismissed a complaint last week regarding an AI-generated political video. State Senator Cathy Kipp filed the complaint, alleging that the video violated state laws against unlabeled deepfake political content. The hearing officer, Macon Cowles, issued his decision on November 19 to dismiss the case against the video. The video was produced by the right-leaning Independence Institute to criticize a specific ballot measure before the election. This legal dispute centered on whether the AI-generated content required a specific disclosure under current Colorado state law.

The 2024 law requires a disclosure when generative artificial intelligence depicts a political candidate close to an election date. The video criticized Proposition NN before the November 3 election, a measure sponsored by Kipp and referred by the Legislature. Proposition NN passed with over 57 percent of the vote to let the state retain more revenue for education. The AI-generated video showed Kipp as a grocery store cashier who refused to give a customer their change. While the video had a closing line stating it was AI-generated, it lacked the text required by law.

Hearing officer Macon Cowles stated that the law applies to content that falsely appears to be authentic and truthful. He determined the video was parody and satire, which he wrote are protected by the First Amendment of the Constitution. Cowles wrote that no reasonable viewer would believe Kipp agreed to play a cashier who keeps a customer's money. He noted that Kipp is a public figure and this AI criticism is akin to a political newspaper cartoon. The Independence Institute conceded the video was not true but asserted that no viewer would consider it true.

Independence Institute CEO Jon Caldara said they were grateful the officer saw the video as a joke with a point. Caldara stated that nobody believed Kipp moonlights at a checkout counter and that voters deserved to hear their argument. Senator Cathy Kipp expressed disappointment that the complaint was dismissed in a text message sent to the Colorado Newsline. Kipp stated it was important for the Legislature to find out how the law they passed would be interpreted. She argued that laws must keep up as AI-generated imagery and deepfakes become increasingly prevalent and harmful.

The law at the center of this case was passed by Colorado lawmakers in 2024 to regulate campaign materials. The Independence Institute used the video to illustrate what they believed Proposition NN would do with taxpayer money. The video portrayed Kipp stealing grocery change to give to children for their education, which the institute admitted was false. Critics had already raised free speech concerns about the disclosure requirements of the law after it took effect in 2024. The hearing officer concluded that reasonable viewers would not believe the events in the video actually happened.

The decision made by Macon Cowles is subject to review by the deputy secretary of state before it becomes final. The articles do not state when the deputy secretary of state will complete this review or what the result will be. There is no information regarding whether Senator Kipp intends to appeal the decision or take further legal action. The text does not mention if the Independence Institute plans to release similar AI-generated videos for future elections. It remains open whether the Legislature will amend the 2024 law based on this specific legal interpretation.

stories.Headline: GoVeda launches an AI agent that searches patents and research to answer IP questions
stories.Summary:
GoVeda launched its AI IP Intelligence Agent for innovators and IP professionals on Nov 25, 2026, and the company said it is now available at www.goveda.com. Users ask any question about a technology, a patent or an idea in their own words, and the Agent researches more than 220 million patents from 108 countries and regions, more than 350 million research papers and the live web. It then returns a clear answer or a finished report, according to the announcement. The issuer said it is solely responsible for the content of the announcement. For innovators, the company said the Agent is affordable and takes an idea from start to a filed patent without IP expertise, and startups, R&D teams and university labs use it to explore a technology, size up competitors, map the landscape, check whether an idea is new and find who could license or buy it.

When an idea is worth protecting, GoVeda's end-to-end filing service takes it to a filed patent, backed by registered patent practitioners at a fraction of typical professional fees. For IP professionals, in-house IP teams, search firms and law firms use the Agent for prior art, novelty, FTO and invalidity searches, landscapes and patent valuation. Most tasks take 15 to 55 minutes, and every patent cited links to its record for review, so teams get a report they can check, edit and deliver at a fraction of the usual cost. Every task uses two kinds of models together: GoVeda's own IP models search, read and count patents so every answer rests on real patents, searching by meaning and across languages, and GoVeda said it refined them working with patent examiners on search and examination tools, while a frontier AI model from OpenAI or Anthropic plans the steps and writes the result. In examiner-grade patent analysis tests, the Agent identified 81.8% of the references examiners cited, compared with 40% to 68% for frontier AI models tested on their own, the company said, at a small fraction of the cost of traditional IP work.

Dr. Tai Cheng, CEO and Co-Founder of GoVeda, said general AI models can talk about patents but miss too much of what matters, and that the company built its own IP models and paired them with frontier AI models so any innovator can get answers they can act on and IP professionals can deliver more and better work at a cost both can afford. GoVeda said it does not use customer data to train AI models, its security controls are audited under SOC 2 Type II, and organizations can deploy GoVeda inside their own infrastructure. GoVeda describes itself as a venture-backed, AI-native company based in Singapore that builds the AI infrastructure for innovation, providing startups, R&D teams and university labs with an end-to-end solution from idea to filed patent and helping in-house IP teams, search firms and law firms deliver faster, more accurate work at lower cost. The articles give no further details on what happens next.

stories.Headline: Maverick Medical AI showcases CodeAgent within Microsoft Dragon Copilot at RSNA 2026
stories.Summary:
Maverick Medical AI, Inc. announced on November 24, 2026 that it will showcase CodeAgent™, its real-time AI documentation assistant, within Microsoft Dragon Copilot at RSNA 2026. The announcement was issued from Wilmington, Delaware, under a GlobeNewswire release dated Nov. 24, 2026. The release was published on finance.yahoo.com on November 24, 2026 at 06:00:00Z and carried by The Manila Times on November 25, 2026. The showcase is set for RSNA 2026, where Maverick will demonstrate real-time documentation guidance connecting radiology reporting with autonomous, billing-ready coding. Microsoft Dragon Copilot works alongside PowerScribe One, a Microsoft radiology reporting solution used by hundreds of healthcare organizations in the United States.

The offering brings Maverick's Clinical-to-Revenue Intelligence into radiologists' reporting workflows to address documentation issues in real time, reduce physician rework and accelerate reimbursement. Powered by Maverick's proprietary Clinical-to-Revenue Foundation Model, CodeAgent identifies documentation gaps, coding opportunities, compliance and payer-specific risks as radiologists complete their reports. The integration surfaces Maverick's intelligence across documentation and reimbursement requirements alongside the PowerScribe One report. Available through Microsoft Marketplace, CodeAgent works alongside mCoder™, Maverick's autonomous coding solution, to support a single intelligence layer spanning physician documentation through autonomous, billing-ready coding. Maverick will also demonstrate CodeAgent's enterprise dashboard, which gives clinical and operational leaders visibility into alert rates, alert-to-action rates and associated financial impact.

Yossi Shahak, CEO and Founder of Maverick Medical AI, said working with eight of the ten leading radiology firms is a testament to the accuracy and consistency the company delivers. He said that precision comes from understanding radiology, from the clinical detail in each report to the coding and payer requirements it must satisfy. He said the collaboration with Microsoft brings that expertise into the reporting workflow, giving radiologists guidance in real time. He said this helps organizations reduce rework and accelerate reimbursement. Maverick said it chose to integrate with Microsoft's radiology reporting tools to deliver this guidance within the workflow radiologists already use.

Vikram Chhabra, Vice President, Diagnostics Solutions, Microsoft, said the future of radiology AI will be built through an ecosystem of innovation, with partners like Maverick Medical AI central to how Microsoft extends AI capabilities across diagnostic imaging. He said that through Microsoft Marketplace, health systems can adopt CodeAgent in one trusted place, with IT in control. He said they can put it to work in the reporting workflow radiologists already use, bringing Maverick's impact directly to them. The articles say the offering is aimed at radiologists and the healthcare organizations using PowerScribe One. The articles say the dashboard's insights help organizations track corrective action and identify opportunities to improve documentation workflows.

The articles describe Maverick Medical AI as bringing Revenue Certainty to the hospital revenue cycle with Clinical-to-Revenue Intelligence. They say Maverick, powered by its proprietary Clinical-to-Revenue Foundation Model, orchestrates autonomous workflows across physician documentation, coding, compliance, medical necessity and denial prevention. stories.Headline: Nasdaq falls about 4% as AI stock selloff and Trump tariffs unsettle Wall Street
stories.Summary:
On Wednesday, U.S. stocks ended mixed as technology shares sold off and bargain hunters helped the S&P 500 and Nasdaq recover from steeper losses ahead of Thanksgiving, according to Reuters. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 346.96 points, or 0.69 percent, to 50,365.85, while the S&P 500 lost 6.03 points, or 0.08 percent, to 7,195.06 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 121.93 points, or 0.52 percent, to 23,611.61. The Nasdaq had fallen more than 4 percent earlier in the session, and the Nasdaq 100 briefly dropped 20 percent from its record closing high, nearing bear-market territory. Nvidia shares fell 4.7 percent and an index of semiconductors declined 1.3 percent, while technology stocks were down more than 1 percent. Volume was low, and the market was scheduled to close on Thursday for Thanksgiving and to close early on Friday.

The selloff came as investors weighed a rout in AI-related stocks and new U.S. tariff proposals on 14 trading partners, which Washington described as a move to combat structural excess industrial capacity and which revived global trade tensions. Fears of increased regulatory scrutiny of the AI sector following the Democratic sweep in the U.S. midterm elections added to worries about AI stocks, and the article said Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of AI leader Nvidia earlier this month but the company's board reinstated him on Monday. U.S. economic data showed third-quarter growth was faster than initially estimated while inflation rose further in October, which the article said reinforced expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027. The extra tariffs could cloud the outlook for investors already grappling with the prospect of rates staying higher for longer, as inflation has accelerated and oil prices have risen steadily due to the US-Iran war.

Oliver Pursche, senior vice president and adviser for Wealthspire Advisors in Westport, Connecticut, said there are all these potential headwinds but also a certain amount of conditioning of buying on the dip, which he said is part of what was being seen. He said broad selloffs tend to throw the baby out with the bathwater and that investors were taking advantage of some of those discrepancies. While technology was down more than 1 percent, materials and real estate led S&P 500 sector gainers. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 2.08-to-1 ratio on the NYSE, which had 43 new highs and 594 new lows, while on the Nasdaq 2,730 stocks rose and 2,016 fell, a 1.35-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 19 new 52-week highs and 11 new lows, and the Nasdaq Composite recorded 34 new highs and 465 new lows.

stories.Headline: Agricultural engineers create a contactless AI system to estimate yak body weight
stories.Summary:
Agricultural engineers developed a contactless passive stereo vision system to estimate the live body weight of farmed yaks. This new technology was created to work on resource-constrained edge computing hardware in high-altitude conditions. The research team completed the project by November 25, 2026, to improve livestock monitoring. This system removes the need for physical restraint on dedicated scale platforms during the weighing process. It uses dual-view cameras and lightweight artificial intelligence to achieve high accuracy.

The system uses a side-view camera at 120 centimeters high and 110 centimeters from the fence. An overhead dorsal-view camera is installed at 240 centimeters high above the yak back. Testing occurred at an indoor facility in Ya’an, Sichuan, China, during three seasonal campaigns. Sampling dates included July 7, 2025, September 5, 2025, and January 13, 2026, over 190 days. The study used 29 male Maiwa yaks aged three to four years weighing 170.0 to 366.5 kilograms.

The researchers stated that traditional weighing protocols induce acute stress in livestock and present safety hazards. They claimed that mechanical scales are limited by high construction costs and rough alpine terrain. The team noted that yaks rarely remain stationary, which often distorts mechanical scale readings. They explained that dense seasonal fur coats obscure body silhouettes and hinder conventional two-dimensional imaging. The authors said their passive stereoscopic arrangement reduces hardware complexity while maintaining robust matching.

The system affects farmed yaks and animal handlers by eliminating the need for physical handling bottlenecks. It replaces active illumination sensors that suffer from restricted operating ranges and high solar illumination. It also avoids laser scanners which the researchers described as having prohibitive cost and power demands. The technology helps monitor growth, feed efficiency, reproduction, and health for this essential livestock species. It provides a viable way to acquire weight on farms without using active scale platforms.

The researchers used a 120-centimeter-wide experimental chute equipped with two independent binocular camera modules. They developed a MobileLKA architecture to replace heavy attention mechanisms with Large Kernel Attention modules. This pipeline detects the animal torso and localizes key anatomical measurement points using neural networks. The system converts two-dimensional landmark coordinates into three-dimensional dimensions through stereoscopic depth extraction. Gaussian process regression was used to map these morphometric dimensions to the live body weight.

The framework achieved a coefficient of determination of 0.965 and a root mean square error of 8.33 kilograms. It also reached a mean absolute percentage error of 2.60 percent during the animal-disjoint cross-validation. The researchers found that combining side and dorsal features was critical for the best accuracy. Winter measurements showed an absolute error of 1.40 centimeters compared to 1.35 centimeters in summer. The articles leave open how the system performs with different livestock species or larger herds.

stories.Headline: Knox County Schools plans to convert a Tennessee trade school into a data science academy next fall
stories.Summary:
Knox County Schools announced last week that it plans to convert Byington-Solway Technology Center, a career and technical education school serving high school students in Karns, into a data science academy by next fall. The district said the new Byington program will initially enroll 50 students next fall to study data analysis and modeling, programming languages, and research methods. The announcement drew pushback from community members and former students concerned about losing access to skilled trades education. Byington serves 350 students each semester, and its current offerings include electrical and structural trades, cosmetology, audiovisual production, early childhood education, and veterinary sciences. The district plans to increase enrollment at the data science academy to 200 students over the next four years.

The district said current Byington juniors and seniors will have a way to complete their trade programs, though details are sparse on where that will take place. Officials are in talks with the local Tennessee College of Applied Technology to strengthen an existing dual enrollment program, the district said. Students can access CTE programs through dual enrollment with nearby trade schools, and district officials say nearby high schools may absorb some of Byington's shuttered programs next year. The district maintains Byington's conversion is not a cost-cutting measure, though Knox County Schools faces a $4 million budget crisis this year. The district can make the change without school board approval.

Keith Wilson, the district's assistant superintendent for academics, said last week the district must constantly assess what the future demands and the future workforce needs are and continue to look at its programs. Wilson acknowledged in a local radio interview that any time the district has changes to programming, that is a tough place to be. He said the district certainly recognizes the value a lot of students have seen with the programs offered at Byington and that the staff there is wonderful. He said change is a difficult piece to work through. A district spokesperson said last week the goal is to develop analytical and problem-solving skills that can be applied across a wide range of in-demand careers and postsecondary opportunities.

Colten Roberto, a Byington welding graduate who now works as a welder at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory with a salary well above the Tennessee household average, said it is sad but seems crazy. Roberto said there is a shortage of tradesmen and women in every field, not just welding. He said AI cannot take his job because there is too much of a human aspect in welding, and he cannot see AI crawling under a house to fix a stopped up drain or working on heavy machinery. Kendra Lynn Dill, a 2020 Byington graduate who completed its early childhood program, said she thinks it is important that the trades stick around because not every kid has the option to go to college out of high school, or at all. Dill said the district has not told families what will happen to the preschool when Byington transitions, and she said AI is not going to teach her kid or feed her kid.

Roberto discovered a different way to learn when he stepped into a welding class at Byington his freshman year of high school. He spent half of every school day at Byington and got by in his traditional academic classes at nearby Karns High School, but writing papers or spending time on the computer never felt right, while the hands-on construction, mechanics, and welding courses did. Dill worked in the school's on-site preschool to earn credits toward state early childhood provider certification, and her now-husband studied plumbing, carpentry, and electrical work at Byington. The couple's young daughter now attends the same preschool where Dill gained hands-on experience. Tennessee faces a critical shortage of early childhood educators, and more than half of Tennessee childcare providers reported recent staffing shortages.

Dill and others plan to lobby the board in December to oppose the proposal. Data science programs that taught tech skills like coding were considered forward-looking just a few years ago, encouraged by some in the tech industry as a reliable pathway to lucrative careers. Now, some districts are rethinking their curriculums as software engineering and entry-level tech job opportunities have dried up amid the AI boom. Meanwhile, proposals to open AI-focused schools have faltered in the face of strong community pushback. The articles do not say what the school board will do when it is lobbied in December.

stories.Headline: Steinbach developer Scott Jodoin launches AI website to track local government records and voting choices
stories.Summary:
Steinbach software developer Scott Jodoin created a website that uses AI to comb through online local government sources, CBC reported on Nov. 25, 2026. Jodoin said he found combing through years of municipal records and video too daunting ahead of October's municipal election in the southeastern Manitoba city. He said he remembered he is a software developer with access to artificial agents that can do exactly that. He started adding AI-generated reports on local election issues in Steinbach and on the voting records of individual councillors and candidates. The site uses data collected as far back as 2015, when city council meetings were first broadcast on YouTube.

Jodoin encourages people to use chatbots and other AI programs with his site to find what people have said about any topic. He said the site shows "literally, 'This person said this on this exact date,'" calling these facts that can be collected to understand the full story. He suggested advocates of a particular issue could use it to see what does or does not work with specific councillors or council as a whole. He said he hopes people can understand the history behind an issue and make a genuinely useful contribution without wasting time. He includes instructions on his website on how to enter AI prompts for the topics people want to look up.

Jodoin said his AI tool can help increase government transparency and that AI is the future of democracy. He said AI, like any tool, needs to be used properly. He said he has no plans to create another AI-driven website for next year's provincial election or for other governments. He said he wants to meet with Steinbach Mayor Earl Funk and city administration to have them consider incorporating his AI program into the city's website. He said he has no intention of replacing traditional journalism, saying AI will never solve asking the right questions and that journalists understand broader context and are more critical than ever.

Steinbach voter Matthew Heinrichs learned about the website through social media and said it helped him change his vote. Heinrichs said he had an idea of who he did not intend to vote for after watching a live Steinbach council candidate forum. He said he had not seen that candidate's written pieces or other content elsewhere, and that the AI captured things said in the debate he had not caught. He said the site frames councillors' voting choices on a purely analytical surface level and is missing all the wisdom of the choices made. He said AI can break down the language barrier for candidates whose first language is not English and can bridge gaps for those who cannot articulate things in depth.

Federal Chief Electoral Officer Stéphane Perrault told a parliamentary committee this month that people are already using AI to inform their election decisions, but said the accuracy of that information is a growing concern. In September, Elections Canada hosted a global conference with the United Nations to discuss responsible AI and elections. Nathalie Smuha, an assistant professor of law at the University of Toronto whose research focuses on digital technology and democracy, said it is inevitable that AI will become more widely used by voters and that education is the best way to prepare people. She said people need to learn how to ask the right kind of questions on politically sensitive matters like voting and to pinpoint answers to the evidence and follow it themselves. She said automation bias, the tendency to rely on automated systems, is becoming a problem, saying people are inherently lazy and these tools help us be more lazy, and that the political sphere is even more sensitive because so much is at stake.

Smuha said it is important to consider safeguards like specifically engineered AI programs rather than generic chatbots for research on government or elections. She said such a tool would ideally be built not just by a public authority but also by independent researchers coming together to make sure what it says is verifiable. She said she believes AI can be used safely by independent developers like Jodoin but is concerned about future ownership of the technology as it becomes a regular part of the democratic process. She said it is great that these tools enable us for the first time to peruse huge amounts of public information about what public officials do, which can help citizens hold government to account if the information is accurate and they verify it. Jodoin said he wants to meet with Funk and city administration about incorporating his program into the city's website, and the articles do not say whether that meeting has happened or what the city has said.

stories.Headline: House panel examines AI risks to financial stability at Dec 2 hearing
stories.Summary:
The House Financial Services Committee will hold a hearing on Dec. 2 to examine the opportunities and challenges facing the financial services industry as artificial intelligence raises concerns about financial stability. The hearing is titled "The Future of Financial Services: Opportunities, Challenges, and the Path Forward" and will feature witnesses representing the payments, banking, asset management and consumer advocacy sectors. Rep. French Hill (R-AR) chairs the committee, and Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA) is the ranking member. The five scheduled witnesses are Erik Syvertsen of AngelList Asset Management, Jim Johnson of FIS, Blake Breathitt of Adyen, Erica Khalili of Lead Bank and Tom Feltner of Americans for Financial Reform.

The Federal Reserve's Financial Stability Report, released Nov. 13, identified AI as the most frequently cited potential threat to financial stability, with 87% of the 23 market contacts surveyed naming it as a risk, up from 50% in the spring survey. Hunton Andrews Kurth reported on Nov. 3 that JPMorgan Chase, Charles Schwab, Citigroup and Wells Fargo each moved between Oct. 13 and Oct. 20 to block or contractually restrict customer-directed AI agents from accessing financial accounts. The FDIC and the Conference of State Bank Supervisors announced on Nov. 24 their support for the Third-Party Assessments and Standards Council, a voluntary, industry-led effort to develop common third-party risk management standards. The Fed's report also found that debt issuance related to advanced computing infrastructure exceeded $680 billion by October, more than five times the $130 billion issued in 2023.

The public comment period on federal regulators' proposed third-party risk management guidance closes Dec. 16, two weeks after the hearing, and the proposed guidance is non-binding and seeks to help financial institutions manage risks associated with third-party service providers. Rep. Bill Foster (D-IL), a committee member, unveiled a discussion draft of the Real-Time Regulatory Study Act on Nov. 5, which would direct the Federal Reserve Board, in coordination with other financial regulators, to develop, test and publicly release open-source software to assess the feasibility of real-time financial oversight. The legislation remains a discussion draft and would not require financial institutions to adopt the software developed through the study. The Federal Reserve and other federal financial regulators extended the comment period on the proposed third-party risk management guidance to Dec. 16.

stories.Headline: EDDA and ONYX preview edge AI surgical navigation on a medical computer at RSNA 2026
stories.Summary:
EDDA Technology and ONYX Healthcare USA said on November 25, 2026 that they have begun a joint technology collaboration to run EDDA's IQQA-eFusion surgical AI application on the ONYX ACCEL-JS3000, a medical AI computer built on the NVIDIA IGX Thor platform, according to the press release issued by EDDA Technology. The companies said they will show an early preview of the work at ONYX Healthcare USA booth 1906 during the RSNA 2026 technical exhibits at McCormick Place in Chicago, which run from November 29 to December 2. The release said the demonstration is meant to address a growing challenge for surgical and imaging equipment makers, because real-time AI guidance in the operating room, such as overlaying 3D anatomy on live laparoscopic video, needs more computing than most systems carry today. According to the release, sending that data to a data center or the cloud adds latency, network dependency and data-governance overhead, and the ACCEL-JS3000 is designed to put server-class AI performance inside the imaging system itself, from the radiology suite to the operating room. The release said EDDA's IQQA-eFusion is designed to overlay patient-specific anatomic structures, including vascular anatomy and lesions, onto laparoscopic video to support real-time deep 3D visualization and navigation, with GPU-accelerated 3D visualization and anatomical analysis processed locally without a round-trip to the cloud, and with 4K laparoscopic video captured through the system's integrated SDI input and processed on the device.

It said the ACCEL-JS3000 combines the NVIDIA IGX Thor T7000 platform, built on the NVIDIA Blackwell architecture with a 14-core Arm Neoverse-V3AE CPU, with an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU. The release listed capabilities including AI performance of up to 5581 TOPS with RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU expansion, NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking with 2 × 200GbE for high-bandwidth imaging data streams, a functional safety architecture for mission-critical AI applications, 4K SDI capture and front-panel display support, and a 900 W medical power supply with a thermal design tuned for performance at low acoustic noise. The release said ONYX engineers will be available at the booth to discuss integration into OEM systems. Brian Wang, Director of Product Management at ONYX Healthcare USA, said according to the release that real-time surgical navigation cannot wait on a round-trip to the cloud and that the AI has to keep pace with the live video in the operating room, and he said the ACCEL-JS3000 brings NVIDIA IGX Thor performance into a medical-grade platform built for long product lifecycles so that innovators like EDDA can focus on clinical applications instead of compute infrastructure. Dr. Xiaolan Zeng, Chief Strategy Officer at EDDA Technology, said according to the release that surgical AI has the potential to transform how surgeons visualize and navigate complex anatomy during procedures, and that IQQA-eFusion is designed to support real-time fusion and visualization of patient-specific 3D anatomical models with intraoperative surgical views.

Zeng said running IQQA-eFusion on the ACCEL-JS3000 and NVIDIA AI infrastructure provides the edge AI computing performance needed to support these computationally demanding capabilities directly in the operating room, and that the companies look forward to offering RSNA attendees an early glimpse into the emerging possibilities of AI-powered, image-guided laparoscopic and robotic surgery. The release said the integrated ACCEL-JS3000 and EDDA IQQA-eFusion solution is works-in-progress and has not been cleared or approved by the U.S. FDA. It described ONYX Healthcare as a designer and manufacturer of medical-grade computing solutions, including medical panel PCs, medical displays, embedded systems and AI computing platforms, with a focus on reliability, long-term product availability and medical device integration. It described EDDA Technology as an innovative leader in surgical AI and intelligent robotic solutions for precision surgery, and said the company has built a proprietary technology platform to facilitate pre-surgical planning and simulation, intra-operative navigation and post-operative evaluation. The release gave no date for when the collaboration might produce a cleared product or move beyond the preview.

stories.Headline: Joseph reports that the ARTEX AI hacking framework drives breaches worldwide
stories.Summary:
The podcast episode covers ARTEX, an AI hacking framework that Joseph reported is behind a number of breaches around the world, and 404 Media spoke to the people distributing it. The episode was published on November 25, 2026, and it also includes Sam's report on a Google plan for a 24/7 AI-powered TV channel that puts the viewer as the main character. In a subscribers-only section, Matthew reports on a data center being built that the articles describe as definitely not a data center. The episode is available on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube, with bonus content for paid subscribers. The articles give no further numbers, dates or names about ARTEX itself, beyond the framework's name and the claim in a linked headline that the code is already copied everywhere.

The episode points listeners to four related stories: the AI hacking tool causing havoc around the world, Google's 24/7 AI TV channel, a University of Michigan mailer promising its data center isn't really a data center, and a study finding Black neighborhoods are twice as likely to house a data center. Paid subscribers get an email from the podcast host Transistor with a link to the subscribers-only version, and the same email should contain a link to an extended video version. That link also appears in the show notes of the podcast player, and subscribers can add the subscribers feed to their app of choice. Joseph is described as an award-winning investigative journalist focused on generating impact, whose work has triggered hundreds of millions of dollars worth of fines and shut down tech companies. The articles do not say who distributes ARTEX beyond that 404 Media spoke to those people, and they give no statement from Google or from anyone behind the framework.

The episode's own description says only that Joseph's story concerns the framework and the breaches, and that Sam and Matthew handle the other two segments. No one quoted in the articles responds to the breaches or to the TV channel plan. The context the articles provide is limited to the episode's rundown and its links to the related stories, with no further detail on how ARTEX spreads or what happens next with it. The same page lists other 404 Media items, including a Muse agent suing Meta, the Justice Department using Pangram, and a Treasury CIO vibe coding a game during a hack, but none of these are part of the episode's described segments. What happens next, according to the articles, is only that listeners can hear the full episode and subscribers can access the bonus content and extended video.

stories.Headline: EA adds late commentator John Motson to EA Sports FC 27 using AI and archival recordings with family permission
stories.Summary:
Electronic Arts used generative AI and archival recordings to add John Motson to EA Sports FC 27. The company announced this move to the BBC on 25 November 2026. They obtained permission from the late commentator's widow and his son for the project. This digital recreation allows the deceased voice to appear in the football video game. The feature becomes available to players on 26 November.

The game includes a synthesized voice created from old recording sessions and generative AI. This is the first time the series, formerly called Fifa, has featured a deceased commentator. The voice allows Motson to comment on modern players like Chloe Kelly and Bradley Barcola. EA paid the family for the rights to use the likeness and the voice. The company did not disclose the financial terms of this specific deal.

Mat Prior, senior game design director, said the studio wanted to pay tribute to Motson. He stated the team would not move forward without the full support of the family. Prior claimed AI was the only way to make the project happen for the game. He also said there are no future plans to replace any human commentators with AI. The company claims the technology is not there to replace people in any way.

Fred Motson said it means an awful lot to have his father's voice in the game. Guy Mowbray called the use of AI for this project a nice and non-scary application. Peter Caulfield of Save Our Voices Now expressed disquiet that Motson could not consent personally. Caulfield argued that family members should not automatically have the right to allow AI voice cloning. Commentator Derek Rae said he was excited but unsure if he would ever follow suit.

John Motson died in February 2023 at the age of 77. He was the main commentator for BBC Sport for several decades during his career. Motson covered 29 FA Cup finals, 10 European Championships, and 10 World Cups for the BBC. He was the first commentator for the game series, appearing from Fifa 96 until Fifa 2005. He also made a brief cameo in the Fifa 19 title.

The game will now feature a voice that combines old lines with new AI synthesis. Derek Rae continues to spend many days recording dialogue in studios for the series. He noted that AI can easily handle routine surnames like Brown, Smith, and Jones. The articles do not state if other deceased figures will be added to the game. They leave open whether other current commentators will agree to similar posthumous voice deals.

stories.Headline: Anthropic migrates its Messages API from Python to Rust and uses the Python service to verify it
stories.Summary:
Anthropic migrated its Messages API, the primary way customers access Claude, from Python to Rust, the company said in a post published on November 25, 2026. The Messages API was built in 2023 and written in Python, which was widely used internally for much of Anthropic's research code. From early 2024 to fall 2026, API traffic grew roughly 1,800 times, the post said. Claude wrote a first version of the API's core request path in about a week. Anthropic said it used the production Python service to verify the migration.

The migration covered both the input and output paths of the API, according to the post. Anthropic said the Rust API uses about 70% less CPU per request and cuts median time to first token by about 20%. The company said it shipped the Rust API without ever taking the service offline or freezing feature development. By May 2026, Claude was writing more than 80% of the code Anthropic merged, the post said. An earlier incremental rewrite in Rust, which parsed model output and was called from Python, reduced CPU usage by about 8% to 10%.

Anthropic said it turned the production Messages API itself into a verifier to test the new Rust version on production traffic. The company said this helped it find where the two versions differed and automatically dispatch agents to fix those differences. Anthropic said it ran the model once and replayed the model output to Rust because Claude is nondeterministic. The company said it worked without reading user requests or Claude's replies to them, recording instead the shape of each difference. Anthropic said it had to ensure a request only counted once toward a customer's limits and bill.

The post said the Rust API passed about 98% of its tests in April, yet only about a quarter of inputs matched on production traffic. Anthropic said it had about 700 integration tests, and that an audit of ported tests found more than 100 weakened assertions. The company said just 20 binary options make over a million combinations, which it said translates to 12 days of tests at a second each for one model. Anthropic said Python escapes certain characters such as an emoji in JSON tool calls by replacing them with text codes, while Rust wrote those characters as is.

The post said a single common bug can cause many mismatches in live traffic. The post said the Messages API passed requests to the model and sent back what the model wrote, and one engineer at the time called it "basically a request forwarder." Anthropic said the API developed shared dependencies with Python libraries owned by its research and inference teams, which made it hard to move. The company said that by late 2025 every request had to be validated, converted into a prompt, tokenized, and screened by safety classifiers.

Anthropic said Python added overhead each time it created an object, freed memory, or handed work to the next task. The post said that in 2024, after one engineer suggested migrating to Go or Rust, another temporarily settled the question by saying the API would not be rewritten in either. Anthropic said the incremental rewrite created new sources of overhead, with each token crossing between Python and Rust three times. The company said it questioned whether the usual reasons to avoid a full migration still held as the effort required dropped.

Anthropic said it compared every stage before and after the model call, and the results had to match exactly. The post said the company used checkpointing, in which both API versions handle a request using the same steps that produce results it could compare step by step. The post did not say when the Rust migration began or how long the full migration took. More to follow.
