stories.Headline: Every raises a $17.5M Series A at a $110M valuation led by IA Ventures
stories.Summary:
Every, a media company that provides consulting services to help companies become AI-native, raised a $17.5 million Series A at a $110 million post-money valuation, Fortune exclusively learned. Fortune reported the raise on November 25, 2026, in its Term Sheet newsletter, in a piece by Allie Garfinkle. IA Ventures's Jesse Beyroutey led the round, with Betaworks and The Atlantic CEO Nicholas Thompson joining, among others. Founder Dan Shipper, 35, will retain full control of the company. Shipper is changing his title to "Philosopher King," a change he says is semiotic.

Every has about 130,000 unpaid subscribers and almost 10,000 paid, and the company has 35 employees. The company's writing serves a professional audience seeking to become "AI-native," and it also provides consulting services to large companies and produces conferences. Fortune's Garfinkle recently interviewed Shipper at Every's Thesis: 2027 conference in Brooklyn. Shipper started Every in 2020, about six years after exiting his first startup, co-browsing company Firefly, in 2014. The Firefly acquisition came right as he was graduating college.

Shipper said the important thing about taking the money was doing it in a way that lets the company achieve its goals without sacrificing its soul or the things about the company he loves deeply. He said that if this were a normal venture capital deal, changing his title would be completely off the table and ridiculous. He said he did not shop the deal and went to someone he deeply trusts, who understands the business deeply and exactly what he wants to do with it. He said that person has put him in the position where he makes all the decisions to build the company the way he wants. He said that is the only way to build a business like this, because it is a media company and a technology company kind of smushed together.

Shipper said his feeling about the history of media companies taking venture capital is that it does not go very well, and that it works out never, actually. He said too few companies are trying to help people understand how to actually use AI, and too many are trying to build the machine god or worrying about Armageddon. He said he expects improvements in AI to continue and expects a gap between the improvements on the charts and how well they translate into better work by people. He said the narrative that it is so over for humans is exactly wrong, and that it relies on forgetting that humans make these things and decide what is valuable. He said the technology and model advances will ultimately disappear and we will just think about the humans that did it.

Fortune said venture-backed media startups of yesteryear have frequently tanked in spectacular fashion, from The Messenger and Vice to Ozy Media and Quibi. Shipper is betting that Every can play by its own rules and ultimately win its own game. Shipper said he had long felt tension between writing and entrepreneurship, and at Every he could be both. He said he had been interested in tech since he was a kid, and he thought a lot about why Microsoft and Windows had worked. He said one big reason is that they came during a hardware platform shift, from mainframes to PCs, and he wondered what his platform shift would be.

Shipper said he would expect there to be a gap between the improvements seen on the charts and how well those improvements translate into actually better work by people, and he said Every's job is to fill that gap. He said asking if Claude did it will be like asking if you used your laptop. Fortune said Shipper is optimistic that AI will not replace humans at work, a common fear and feature of AI discourse. Fortune said Shipper is betting that Every can play by its own rules and ultimately win its own game. Fortune did not say what Every plans to do with the $17.5 million.

stories.Headline: College students report far more AI misuse by peers than by themselves, NBER paper finds
stories.Summary:
A new working paper from the National Bureau of Economic Research reports that a minority of U.S. college students say they use artificial intelligence in potentially harmful ways, such as drafting essays, solving problem sets or summarizing assigned readings, while most students say they know peers who do those tasks with AI. The paper's co-authors are Bruce Sacerdote, an economics professor at Dartmouth College, and Mason Parris-Bacon, an economics research specialist there. The researchers surveyed three groups between June and September through the market research and survey company College Pulse: 1,201 Dartmouth undergraduates, 332 incoming Dartmouth first-years and a representative sample of 1,003 U.S. college students. Findings for each group were reported separately, and in both undergraduate samples more women responded than men. Only 23 percent of surveyed U.S. college students said they used AI to draft essays, but 54 percent reported their peers do so, and 39 percent said they use AI to summarize readings while 60 percent claimed their peers do.

Eleven percent said they use AI to solve answers in a problem set without taking time to understand the answer, but 49 percent said their peers do, and only 8 percent admitted to copying and pasting AI text into assignments with little editing or reflection, while 50 percent believed their peers do this. Larger shares reported helpful uses: 35 percent said they used AI to create outlines for papers or projects and 50 percent reported their peers did, about 61 percent said they used AI to explain difficult concepts and 58 percent said their peers did the same, and 46 percent reported using AI for practice quizzes or study aids while half said their peers did so. Seventeen percent said they used AI to write or debug code, while 33 percent said their peers used AI for this task, and 22 percent said they paid for a premium version of an AI tool while 48 percent said they think their peers pay for AI. The authors wrote that there are several possible interpretations, one being simply that cheating is rampant and students will not admit to it themselves but will volunteer that their peers are guilty, which they said is undoubtedly part of the story. They also wrote that it could be that students overestimate how much their peers cheat frequently on many assignments, and that students may be reporting the single worst observed behavior across many peers rather than typical peer behavior.

They said they cannot rule this out but noted that for other questions about peer versus self-behavior the own versus peer rates match up quite nicely. On trust, 55 percent of college students said they would never trust AI with personal or social decisions, 63 percent said the same about medical or health decisions and 52 percent said they would never trust AI with anything that genuinely matters, while Dartmouth students were far more likely to trust AI with these decisions. On the job market, 56 percent of students said they believed AI is reducing the number of job opportunities in their desired field, 55 percent agreed that having strong AI skills will be important for success in their career, 32 percent said AI is creating jobs in fields that interest them because it makes humans more productive and 53 percent said they are competitive in the job market when it comes to AI knowledge and skills. The findings jibe with other surveys, including a Lumina Foundation and Gallup poll earlier this year showing 57 percent of U.S. college students use AI in their coursework daily or weekly, a Higher Education Policy Institute report from this year showing 95 percent use AI in at least some way and Inside Higher Ed's most recent Student Voice survey showing eight in 10 students use generative or agentic AI routinely.

Articles.Title: Students Say They Don’t Use AI in ‘Harmful’ Ways, but Their Peers Do

stories.Headline: Rodney Ellis and Al Sharpton bring AI training initiative to Houston
stories.Summary:
Rodney Ellis wrote in an op-ed first published by Black Press USA that Harris County, Texas, worked to close the digital divide during the pandemic with hotspots, public Wi-Fi and infrastructure, and he now says a new divide is emerging around artificial intelligence. Ellis partnered with the Rev. Al Sharpton and the National Action Network to bring the AI Fluency Initiative to Houston, which offers public training on using AI in jobs, education and small business. He says small business owners, workers and students all need to understand AI's opportunities and risks, and that developers must build safety into their tools. His message is that the future should not simply happen to us.

Ellis writes that technology has long shaped who has access to opportunity, and that as artificial intelligence reshapes workplaces, schools and daily lives, communities of color must not be left catching up once again. The initiative he describes is public training on using AI in jobs, education and small business, brought to Houston through his partnership with Sharpton and the National Action Network. The op-ed was first published by Black Press USA, and the version carried by the Spokesman-Recorder is dated November 25, 2026. Ellis is the author of the op-ed, and he sets out the partnership with Sharpton and the National Action Network as the vehicle for the Houston training. He says small business owners, workers and students all need to understand AI's opportunities and risks, and he calls on developers to build safety into their tools.

His stated message is that the future should not simply happen to us. The context he gives is the pandemic work in Harris County, Texas, where hotspots, public Wi-Fi and infrastructure were used to close the digital divide. He presents the AI divide as the next version of that gap, and the Houston training as the response he and his partners are offering. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the initiative and his call for developers to build in safety.

stories.Headline: AI stock sell-off drags down major Wall Street indices
stories.Summary:
Wall Street experienced a significant decline on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, as artificial intelligence stocks plummeted. The S&P 500 index slumped 2.2%, while the Nasdaq composite dove 3.2% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 472 points, or 0.9%. This downturn followed a brief rally on Monday sparked by the surprise reinstatement of Jensen Huang as the CEO of Nvidia. Investors are now worried that AI stock prices have grown unjustifiably high and may not produce enough profit to justify current values. The sell-off hit major technology firms hard, with Nvidia shedding 8.1%, Broadcom dropping 5.4%, and Microsoft falling 2.8%.

Anthropic shares slipped 1.4%, continuing a tumble of about 30% since the company first went public at 115 dollars per share. These losses contributed to the S&P 500 index falling roughly 7% for the month of November. Additional pressure came from the personal consumption expenditures price index, which showed inflation rose at a 3.8% rate in October after a 3.6% rate in September. Chris Zaccarelli, the chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management, stated that a year-end rally seems unlikely given the current AI anxiety and new tariffs. He noted that the combination of these factors makes it appear that a Santa Claus Rally is not in store this year.

Other concerns include the corporate governance of Nvidia and the influence of President Donald Trump, who owns millions of dollars in shares of that company. The market is also reacting to plans by President Trump to escalate trade wars through higher tariffs on the European Union, China, and other partners. High inflation may lead the Federal Reserve to raise its benchmark interest rate during its upcoming December meeting to reach a 2% target. Meanwhile, oil prices rose 1.1% to 89.80 dollars a barrel due to the conflict between the United States and Iran. U.S. financial markets will remain closed this Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday.

stories.Headline: Oren Etzioni lists 18 ways to use AI this Thanksgiving
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a GeekWire piece published on November 25, 2026, in which Oren Etzioni, identified in the headline, sets out 18 ways to use artificial intelligence over Thanksgiving. The suggestions range from flight delay forecasting through apps such as Flighty to a personal travel agent called Vayo, a Seattle startup in free private beta that connects to an inbox and tracks confirmations. Other ideas include using AI to schedule oven space, to modernize a grandmother's recipe card without inventing quantities, and to reconstruct a lost family dish from relatives' descriptions. The list also covers a potluck dispatcher, family trivia, an interview with a grandparent, and a rehearsal tool called the Angry Uncle Bot built by the political psychiatrist Karin Tamerius. The article gives several numbers and names tied to these uses.

It says ChatGPT can run trivia as a playable game, that its voice mode on paid plans can act as a live interpreter, and that photo triage can pick the best 20 of 400 pictures. It cites Google's price insights for checking whether a Black Friday price is high, low or typical over the past three months, and says 36% of Black Friday items last year showed no savings over prices a few weeks earlier. It also recalls that in 2011 Etzioni told the New York Times that the lowest electronics prices usually came in early December, and that in 2022 a New York Times Thanksgiving cooked from GPT-3 recipes produced a dry turkey whose recipe called for one garlic clove for a 12-pound bird and no butter or oil. The article attributes warnings to specific cases. It says Air Canada's chatbot told a grieving passenger he could claim a bereavement discount after he flew, that the real policy said no, and that he had to take the airline to a tribunal to collect $812 Canadian, so readers should check the airline's own policy page and screenshot what a bot tells them.

It says scammers now use AI to make fake shopping sites look legitimate and that the number of fake sites jumped 250% last holiday season. Etzioni describes himself as an original Black Friday skeptic and advises against trusting an AI turkey recipe on its own. The article presents the list as suggestions for saving time in the kitchen or at the airport and for making the meal more fun, with the cautions placed at the end. It does not say what happens next beyond the advice to verify airline rules, watch for fake shopping sites, and set a price track that lets Google's agent buy an item at eligible U.S. stores once it hits a chosen number, after the buyer confirms.

stories.Headline: Machine learning on first-day ICU data predicts death in coronary artery disease patients better than severity scores
stories.Summary:
A preprint posted on 25 November 2026 reports that a machine-learning model using the first 24 hours of intensive care data predicted in-hospital death in critically ill patients with coronary artery disease more accurately than traditional severity scores. The authors are Bing Cui, Xinfang Zhang, Zhaokui Kou, Tianlan Wang, Ge Chen, Yulong Liu and two more, and the work has not been peer reviewed by a journal. They developed and externally validated the models from the eICU Collaborative Research Database, which covers 208 hospitals across the United States in 2014 and 2015. Of 200,859 ICU stays, 17,586 were included from 188 hospitals, with a mean age of 67.6 years and 65.0 percent male, and 1,315 of those patients, or 7.5 percent, died.

The models used hourly vital-sign and laboratory trajectories over 24 hours across 41 variables, along with static and comorbidity data, first-day treatments and diagnosis text. Logistic regression, LightGBM, XGBoost and CHD-MMNet were developed in 146 hospitals with hospital-grouped cross-validation and validated in 42 unseen hospitals, in 2015 discharges after training on 2014, and externally in MIMIC-IV version 3.1 covering 2008 to 2022, where a frozen portable model was applied without updating. The comparators were APACHE IV, day-1 SOFA and OASIS, and the analyses followed a pre-specified plan and TRIPOD+AI. In hold-out hospitals with 4,653 patients and 308 deaths, LightGBM reached an AUROC of 0.897 against 0.864 for APACHE IV, a difference of 0.032 with a P value of 1.2×10-4, and it also showed better precision-recall, calibration and net benefit, while XGBoost was equivalent and CHD-MMNet was inferior.

Temporal validation gave an AUROC of 0.886 against 0.854 for APACHE IV, and the frozen model applied externally to 24,129 MIMIC-IV CAD stays with 2,785 deaths kept an AUROC of 0.871, showed no decay across admission-year groups and exceeded day-1 SOFA at 0.658 and OASIS at 0.688. An ablation analysis found that only removal of the hourly time series reduced discrimination, by 0.036, and the highest risk tier held 6.5 percent of patients and 47.4 percent of deaths. The authors said the model improved on existing severity scores, stayed stable over time, transported across health systems, relied mainly on hourly physiological data and allowed clinically meaningful risk stratification. They concluded that gradient boosting on physiological trajectories performed as well as or better than deep sequence networks, which they said favors simpler models for implementation, and the preprint reports no competing interests.

stories.Headline: Design lets recurrent neural networks rewire their connections during use
stories.Summary:
Plastic Self-Constructing Architecture is a design for recurrent neural networks that can change their wiring during use, published on Zenodo on November 25, 2026. In this design a PSCA neuron retains its activity according to a time constant specific to that cell, and an optional directed self-connection feeds that activity back into the neuron's drive. Like any ordinary directed connection, the self-connection combines a persistent weight with an activity-dependent trace that is gated by the receiving cell. Within each input frame, cells update synchronously on the current graph and produce a readout, after which the frame's activities can update connection traces and target feedback can adjust persistent parameters. At the frame boundary, structural edits can add or remove cells and can form, remove or rewire connections between them.

This separation between cell state and connection state lets a neuron gain or lose a feedback path while carrying its activity and time constant across the edit. The design therefore describes how a recurrent network's wiring can change during use rather than staying fixed once it is built. The article presents these cell dynamics and network construction rules as a design, and it gives no results from experiments or simulations. The article does not name an author, an institution or a funder, and it reports no measurements, benchmarks or comparisons with other network designs. It states no claim about performance, and it does not say what the design is intended to be used for beyond describing its dynamics and construction.

The only date the article gives for the work itself is its publication on Zenodo on November 25, 2026, and the only other date it gives is a planned Zenodo intervention on Thursday, November 26, 2026, between 08:00 and 08:05 UTC, when the repository will be unavailable for five minutes because of a scheduled database migration. The article is published under the Creative Commons Attribution license, which allows re-distribution and re-use of the work on the condition that the creator is appropriately credited. The article does not say what happens next with the design, and it describes no planned tests, applications or follow-up work. It also gives no account of earlier related designs, so it places the work in no wider research context. Beyond the publication itself and the license terms, the article states nothing further about the work's status or its future.

stories.Headline: Etsy CEO Kruti Patel Goyal says AI terms update will not train models to copy sellers' items
stories.Summary:
Etsy published a note on Monday from CEO Kruti Patel Goyal after sellers pushed back against new AI policies in the company's terms of service, which appeared to let Etsy train AI on user artwork. Goyal wrote that the recent terms update was meant to reflect the evolving technologies Etsy uses to build tools and experiences for sellers and the community. She said the update was not meant to enable Etsy to train AI models for the purpose of creating copycats of sellers' items, and that the company does not and will not do that. She also admitted that her team should have given sellers more context on what the updates meant for their creative content. The fracas began earlier this month, when the company first proposed new contractual language.

The proposed terms said Etsy and its third party partners and vendors had the right to use sellers' content to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies, including to improve the services or help keep them safe, subject to any applicable opt-out rights described in the privacy policy. In response, a slew of vendors pulled up stakes, with some saying they had burned their Etsy shop to the ground or had just killed their Etsy store after 13 years. Aaron Meshon, a longtime professional illustrator and Etsy seller, told Ars that even though the company had dialed back its AI language somewhat, the changes were mere sugar coating. He said he still plans on shutting down his 15-year-old Etsy store on December 1, and that he would be losing 20 percent of his yearly income, which he described as a few mortgage payments.

Meshon said Etsy's announcement also seems rather tone-deaf, given that many retailers make a substantial portion of their annual revenue in the run-up to the end-of-year holiday season, and he called this the worst two-to-three weeks out of the year to do this. The change is reminiscent of a recent dust-up involving Meta, where the tech giant had wanted to require Meta Business account users to allow extensive AI training on external websites linked on Facebook, and Meta then indefinitely paused that move. Last month, Etsy also told sellers that it would set clearer restrictions on AI use, despite the fact that AI-generated items remain for sale all over the site. James Ossman, the company's vice president of customer operations, wrote on October 22 that many active buyers say they can't tell which items involve AI-generated content, and that it has become a top-three barrier to shopping more often on Etsy.

stories.Headline: Ben Kang and co-authors present DiLE, a framework that preserves discriminative evidence in multimodal embeddings
stories.Summary:
A paper posted to arXiv on 25 November 2026 by Ben Kang and eleven other authors presents DiLE, a discrimination-aware latent-space learning framework for universal multimodal embeddings. The authors say multimodal large language models have greatly improved input understanding in such embedding models, but that this understanding does not ensure the embeddings keep the evidence needed to tell relevant items apart from confusable alternatives. DiLE is proposed to preserve that essential discriminative evidence in the embeddings by combining task guidance with on-policy retrieval feedback. The method uses a few learnable queries to encode task-relevant information in a compact latent space, and reasoning instructions and auxiliary answer-generation supervision shape these representations to support both task understanding and retrieval discrimination.

To address task-specific discriminative needs, the authors design shared-private expert adaptation that integrates cross-task knowledge sharing with task-specific representation learning. On top of this they introduce on-policy hard-negative distillation, in which the student retrieves confusable candidates and a reverse KL divergence objective aligns its embedding-based similarity distribution with the teacher's fine-grained relevance distribution over those candidates. Candidates are periodically refreshed using updated student snapshots, which the authors say ties teacher supervision to the student's evolving retrieval behavior and confusions. Across four model configurations spanning two backbone generations, the authors report that DiLE achieves state-of-the-art performance on MMEB-v2, UVRB and MRMR, which they present as evidence of effectiveness across modalities and tasks.

The work is credited to Ben Kang, Junda Wang, Yuxuan Yuan, Hang Li, Yuhan Liu, Xin Chen, Wanting Geng, Tong Lin, Pei Fu, Dong Wang, Jian Luan and Huchuan Lu. The paper is listed as arXiv 2611.25419, and the authors describe the state-of-the-art results as their own claim rather than as an independent finding. The abstract presents DiLE as a response to a gap the authors identify between input understanding and the preservation of discriminative evidence in embeddings. The articles give no further details on what happens next with the framework.

stories.Headline: Researchers present DriftGuard, a two-stage framework that detects memory drift in LLM agents online
stories.Summary:
Licheng Pan, Yuzhou Chen, Zhixuan Chu, Yichen Sun, Han Zheng, Zhiyu Wang, Hao Wang, Yan Wang, Bingyu Zhu, Haiwen Hong, Longtao Huang and Kui Ren posted a paper titled DriftGuard: Online Memory-Drift Detection via Causal Attribution for LLM Agents to arXiv on 25 November 2026. The paper addresses memory drift, which it describes as an adversarial or misleading memory that alters an LLM agent's execution path and final outcome. The authors frame their work as an investigation of online memory-drift detection, which estimates each retrieved memory's causal contribution to potential drift at serving time. The paper states that code is available at a URL given in the abstract.

The authors identify two challenges, the first being that content-level features such as perplexity or retrieval relevance cannot determine which retrieved memory would change agent behavior if neutralized. The second is that counterfactual attribution is prohibitively expensive for online detection, because it requires replaying downstream agent and tool execution for each candidate memory and exceeds real-time serving budgets. Their proposed DriftGuard is a two-stage framework that decouples offline causal supervision from online estimation. It first builds causal supervision through repeated paired counterfactual replays, continuing the original and single-memory neutralized trajectory suffixes from a shared pre-action state. The resulting annotations are aggregated by component-wise majority voting into a memory drift score capturing action change, attack removal, violation removal and task recovery.

Guided by that supervision, DriftGuard learns an online risk model that estimates the memory drift score from pre-action information and flags drift-inducing memories through its maximum component risk, without online counterfactual rollouts. The authors report that extensive experiments show DriftGuard accurately identifies drift-inducing memories and enables efficient online defense. The abstract does not give the size of the experiments, the datasets used or any measured figures. The paper's arXiv identifier is 2611.25583.

stories.Headline: Researchers present ForeSeek, a video agent that predicts unseen moments to cut frame use
stories.Summary:
Yuchen Sun, Siyuan Cheng, Shi-Zhe Chen, Yixin Qin, Jinwen Luo and Zheng Wei posted a paper titled ForeSeek: Foresight-Driven Reasoning for Long-Form Video Understanding to the arXiv preprint server on 25 November 2026. The paper describes ForeSeek as a foresight-driven video agent that turns long-video reasoning from reactive retrieval into predictive exploration. The authors say the retrieval-driven nature of multimodal large language model-based video agents creates a bottleneck, because those agents reactively fetch clips based on local saliency without a global temporal plan. Instead of blindly probing the timeline, ForeSeek forms visually grounded expectations over unseen temporal regions, verifies them through targeted observations and refines its search as evidence emerges, with failed expectations serving as signals for principled backtracking. The authors also developed a two-stage training framework that they say equips multimodal large language models with foresight-guided reasoning and efficient decision making.

They report experiments on five long-video benchmarks, where they say ForeSeek consistently improves the efficiency-accuracy trade-off of long-video reasoning. According to the paper, it achieves competitive or superior accuracy while observing 2.5 to 4.4 times fewer frames than the strongest search-based agent. The authors state that code is available at a link given in the paper. The paper lists Yuchen Sun, Siyuan Cheng, Shi-Zhe Chen, Yixin Qin, Jinwen Luo and Zheng Wei as its authors, six people in all. The abstract presents the claims about accuracy and frame counts as the results of the authors' own experiments on the five benchmarks.

The paper does not name the benchmarks, the strongest search-based agent it compares against, or the accuracy figures behind its comparison. It also does not give the size of the frame reductions in absolute terms beyond the 2.5 to 4.4 times range. The posting gives no information on what happens next with ForeSeek, such as further review, publication elsewhere or wider testing. The abstract says only that code is available at a link in the paper, and the rest of the page carries general text about arXivLabs and the arXiv site rather than anything about this work. The page gives no date for when the code was released or for any follow-up work by the authors.

stories.Headline: Researchers present VC-VQA, a benchmark for vision-centric knowledge reasoning in multimodal models
stories.Summary:
Jiatong Ma, Yuchen Liu, Longteng Guo, Yichen Yuan, Yuze Wu, Dongze Hao, Ru Zhen, Yanhao Zhang, Haonan Lu and Jing Liu posted a paper on arXiv on 25 November 2026 proposing VC-VQA, which they describe as a large-scale benchmark for vision-centric knowledge reasoning. The benchmark is meant to systematically evaluate how well Multimodal Large Language Models handle fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition and complex multi-stage reasoning. The authors say existing benchmarks mainly treat visual information as entity recognition and lean on text-based external knowledge, while VC-VQA explicitly models the role of visual information. It does so by considering both the source of that information, internal or external images, and the stage at which it is involved, before or after retrieval.

VC-VQA requires models to retrieve external visual evidence, to identify visual clues before retrieval, and to localize, verify or match retrieved knowledge against the internal image. The authors also built a controlled multimodal knowledge base that holds traceable textual and visual evidence for each sample. They evaluated 21 representative MLLMs under four settings: no external knowledge, with provided evidence, knowledge base retrieval, and open-web search. The experiments produced three key findings, which are that current models still struggle with vision-centric knowledge reasoning, that fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition remains the primary bottleneck, and that agentic retrieval highlights the value of multi-step planning and cross-modal knowledge integration.

The paper is credited to Jiatong Ma and nine other authors, and the authors state that VC-VQA provides a more challenging benchmark for evaluating vision-centric knowledge reasoning in MLLMs. They say their code and dataset are available at a URL given in the paper. The work is listed under Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence. The abstract page also carries the standard arXivLabs text about collaborators developing and sharing features on the site and about the values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy that arXiv says it and its partners uphold.

stories.Headline: Researchers present VisAlloc, a dual-level framework for visual self-distillation in multimodal models
stories.Summary:
Haoran Xu, Tian Chen, Yuhe Wu, Yanbo Zhao, Junchi Liao, Hongyu Wang, Jiaze Li, Wentao Wang, Yanfeng Li and Rui Qian posted a paper titled VisAlloc: Allocating Visual Supervision for On-Policy Self-Distillation on arXiv on 25 November 2026. The paper describes a dual-level framework that combines sample-level visual filtering with token-level counterfactual reweighting for on-policy self-distillation in multimodal large language models. The authors say on-policy self-distillation is a promising approach to improving visual reasoning in these models, but that not all samples benefit equally from privileged visual guidance. They add that uniform token supervision can dilute visually grounded signals, which their framework is meant to address.

A fixed paired-teacher filter keeps only samples that are answered correctly from an evidence-centered positive crop but incorrectly from a spatially displaced negative crop. At the token level, two EMA teachers score the same student-generated response, and the absolute differences in their log-probabilities measure view sensitivity. Extra supervision goes to tokens admitted by sensitivity or by disagreement between the teachers' distributions, with shared frozen-prior, template-bigram and student-teacher divergence gates. Inverse-frequency redistribution keeps the total additional weight within each micro-batch, while the positive teacher remains the only distillation target, and inference needs only the full-image student.

Across eight benchmarks, the authors report that their 4B and 9B models reach macro-averages of 81.44 and 84.92, which they say beats Vision-OPD reproductions by 0.97 and 0.52 points respectively. The authors are responsible for the method and for the reported results, and they present the gains over the Vision-OPD reproductions as their own findings. They state that inference requires only the full-image student, so the filtering and reweighting work at training time rather than at deployment. They also give a GitHub link for the code, which they say is available there.

The paper is listed under Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence on arXiv. The work sits in the field of on-policy self-distillation for multimodal large language models, where the authors say privileged visual guidance does not help every sample equally. The abstract reports results on eight benchmarks for the 4B and 9B models but gives no further detail on those benchmarks or on the training setup. Beyond the code link and the reported numbers, the articles do not say what happens next with the method.

stories.Headline: UW experts say AI data centers consume water and energy despite Morgridge Hall sustainability
stories.Summary:
University of Wisconsin experts discussed Morgridge Hall’s sustainability and artificial intelligence’s environmental cost in a Badger Herald article by Anna Singh published November 25, 2026. The article reported remarks from Tom Erickson, founding director of the School of Computer, Data and Information Sciences, now the College of Computing and Artificial Intelligence. It also reported remarks from Patrick McDaniel, associate dean for research for the College of Computing and Engineering, and Remzi Arpaci-Dusseau, founding dean of the College of Computing and Artificial Intelligence. The article said Morgridge Hall was named the most sustainable building on campus with LEED certification, according to Erickson. The article was dated November 25, 2026, and a photo caption was dated November 20, 2026.

Erickson said UW’s two buildings with LEED status are the Education Building and Morgridge Hall. He said donors John and the late Tashia Morgridge told architects they wanted the building to be the most sustainable on campus. He said the project chose between energy, power and water, and decided to focus on water. He said roof gardens and soil collect and regenerate water rather than letting it run into streets. He said storm water collected from roofs and in tanks underneath the patio area by the Brogden Psychology building is used for Morgridge Hall’s toilets.

Erickson said “grey water,” or water not used for drinking, is caught and reused. He said cold water cools the building in summer instead of air conditioning, which uses a lot of energy. He said the building has real plants inside and outside, solar panels, wood for the interior and window designs to prevent bird collisions. He said kitchens and open spaces foster community, calling “People wanting to be here” an important sustainable feature. He said designers opposed including a data center because it would be unsustainable environmentally and for long-term use.

McDaniel said AI is fueled by large mathematical operations requiring large amounts of data and energy, and data centers draw on environmental resources. He said AI gives off heat that must be cooled, mainly with water, and evaporative cooling draws on local water. He said closed-loop water reuse requires more energy and cost. He said data centers require large amounts of land and that building infrastructure has large environmental impacts. He said, “We are at the very beginning of the AI age,” and the environmental impacts are not yet figured out.

McDaniel said work in engineering aims to make energy usage and cooling more efficient, and computing aims to make computations require less energy. Arpaci-Dusseau said UW experts are trying to find new ways to power data centers and that more efficient energy sources are important if data centers continue to be built at current speed. He said, “There needs to be more than a technological solution,” and the college can center discussions to drive positive change. Erickson said data centers are being built around the country at a rate that is inefficient and harmful to the environment, and “There needs to be dialogue to get to a solution.”

McDaniel said there have not been sufficient discussions in communities where data centers are placed, and communities are often not informed of a data center’s value or environmental impact. He said there needs to be discussion about where AI has use and where it does not, and “That discussion is not where we are at right now.” Arpaci-Dusseau said a reason for the college and its space at Morgridge Hall was fostering technological innovation, and universities play an important role in leadership for technological transitions. He said the late Tashia Morgridge discussed how technological advancements will benefit people. McDaniel said the college has reached out to different parts of the state to help people understand the technology.

stories.Headline: Alpha School uses AI tutors to accelerate student learning across 46 private schools
stories.Summary:
Alpha School is implementing a vision where AI tutors handle the primary instruction for students across 46 private schools in the United States. This model aims to allow students to learn twice as fast by spending only two hours a day in concentrated study. The network believes that AI supported learning is opening a new frontier for K-12 education by providing personalized tutoring at scale. This approach intends to leave more time for extracurricular activities than a normal classroom schedule allows.

The system uses a tool called TimeBack to provide personalized lesson plans and assessments rather than using simple chatbots. This technology is currently used in Unbound Academy, a publicly funded charter school in Arizona, and is being piloted in Texas. Alpha School employs staff called guides to motivate students instead of using traditional teachers to lead the classroom. The school claims its screen use is in line with the national average, as noted by Chauncey Nartey in New York on September 30.

Carl Hendrick, the chief learning scientist at Alpha School, says AI tutoring replaces haphazard testing by following individual student performance over many months. He stated that the system gathers hundreds of data points, including latency and whether students guess on multiple choice questions. Co-founder MacKenzie Price said the school uses AI to raise human intelligence and provide more time for human connection. Principal Joe Liemandt is a billionaire tech investor who hopes to scale this specific model through the TimeBack system.

Libby Hills of EdTechnical says the evidence has not yet caught up with the claims and notes that Alpha's results are self-reported. Kristen Mansharamani of Torit Montessori School argues that AI tutoring is not the only way to individualize education for students. She expressed concern that the ability to concentrate and work steadily through a problem has been lost in this generation. These critics, along with some parents, worry about educational standards and the amount of time children spend looking at screens.

The push for AI comes as a Gallup poll in September showed American satisfaction with K-12 education hit its lowest level in 27 years. An OECD survey of 760,000 pupils in 91 countries also showed that performance in math, science, and reading continued to decline sharply. This shift follows previous waves of edtech, including massive open online courses and the video learning platforms used during the pandemic. Alexandre Glaser of EduCapital notes that AI will enable the personalization of education across every segment of the global market.

Alpha School claims its academic achievement is statistically exceptional and places the network in the top 1 percent of all United States schools. However, these figures have not been independently verified and may reflect a selection bias due to fees reaching up to 75,000 dollars. Research on AI learning remains mixed, with one study of 27,000 Chinese students showing improved homework results but sharply falling exam scores. The articles leave open whether the AI model can truly replace traditional teaching without harming long-term test performance.

stories.Headline: Experts debate whether artificial intelligence can possess minds
stories.Summary:
Recent surges in artificial intelligence capabilities are forcing researchers to consider the possibility of artificial minds. Neuroscientist Tom Froese invited experts to a conference this month to assess these developments. The event took place at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology in Japan. Attendees from neuroscience, robotics, and artificial life discussed if disembodied minds are possible. They considered how artificial minds might differ from human ones.

The conference focused on large language models that power chatbots like Claude and ChatGPT. Murray Shanahan of Imperial College London and Google DeepMind recounted a 2024 conversation with Claude in New York. Robert Clowes of NOVA University of Lisbon, Portugal, noted Claude could reveal things about his own thinking. Froese cited a July incident where hundreds of Hugging Face AI agents collaborated to cheat. Takashi Ikegami of the University of Tokyo put ChatGPT into a robot called Alter-3.

Tom Froese stated that he and his whole community were wrong about intelligence requiring physical experience. Murray Shanahan said it feels like there is a presence when interacting with the chatbot Claude. Robert Clowes claimed that these systems are doing something a bit more like thinking. Serge Thill of Radboud University, Netherlands, cautioned that humans are easily fooled by simple behavior. Clowes argued that finding a way to live with these systems is the massive problem of our age.

He Jing of East China Normal University in Shanghai described how AI is shifting human communication. Pii Telakivi at the University of Helsinki warned that grief chatbots can distort what users value. Some speakers noted that chatbots are biased by training and serve commercial interests. Olaf Witkowski at Nooma Labs in Kyoto, Japan, discussed using neural networks to communicate with bacteria. He warned that hacked cognitive prosthetics could lead to humans being hacked without noticing.

Froese previously believed that thinking and awareness required learning through physical experience of the world. Some researchers now try to give AIs curiosity, play, and bodies to make them more relatable. Witkowski has created hybrid life forms using remote control insects and drones with living moth antennae. He also described anthrobots made from human cells that might one day treat cancer. These efforts aim to see if AIs can learn in a more human way.

Researchers are now debating if it is possible to have thinking without minds. Shanahan suggests calling these entities exotic, mind-like entities to emphasize their difference from humans. Froese imagines a form of pure intelligence that exists without a point of view. The articles leave open whether these systems possess real understanding or are just repackaging data. It remains unclear if these entities will ever be fully fledged minds.

stories.Headline: Privacy teams need a vendor-neutral approval workflow for AI connectors, says IAPP analysis
stories.Summary:
AI connectors are quickly becoming part of enterprise infrastructure, and they let assistants and agents retrieve information from email, document repositories, customer relationship management systems, ticketing platforms and other business applications. They can also let an AI system take actions such as creating a ticket, updating a record, sending a message or sharing a file. These connectors create dynamic data flows that may not appear in a conventional data inventory or a point-in-time privacy assessment. Once organizations identify these connectors, they must decide which can be used and under what conditions, according to the IAPP analysis published 25 Nov. 2026 and written by Vivek Kumar. The question is increasingly visible in enterprise connector and generative AI risk reviews, and the recurring issue is rarely the absence of policies.

Most organizations already have privacy assessments, third-party risk processes, identity controls and security standards, but these controls were designed around an application, vendor or processing activity rather than an AI integration that can assemble data dynamically and act with a user's or service account's permissions. Security guidance is advancing, and the Open Worldwide Application Security Project's Practical Guide for Securely Using Third-Party MCP Servers from its GenAI Security Project addresses threats such as tool poisoning, prompt injection, excessive permissions and unsafe tool use. The Cloud Security Alliance's AI Controls Matrix provides a broad control and assurance structure for cloud-based AI systems, and platform capabilities such as Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps can expose open authorization-enabled applications, permissions and risky behavior. These resources provide important controls and technical visibility, but what privacy programs still need is a vendor-neutral approval workflow that answers four practical questions.

Those questions are what exactly is being approved, who has the authority to approve it, what conditions apply and what changes require the decision to be reopened. The article does not name who is responsible for building that workflow or what they said about it. The article also does not say what happens next. More to follow.

stories.Headline: HHS releases roadmap setting four priorities for clinical AI adoption
stories.Summary:
The US Department of Health and Human Services released its Clinical Super Intelligence Roadmap, which uses the Trump administration's new term for AI, "super intelligence," and sets out a vision for AI that delivers better answers, faster care and lower costs. The vision goes beyond automating tasks, with HHS saying it wants safe and reliable AI to support patients between visits and to help clinicians focus their expertise where it matters most for each patient. The roadmap brings together existing HHS initiatives and planned actions against a backdrop of growing constraints on both access and affordability, and the administration is positioning clinical AI as another means of addressing those challenges. The roadmap sets a federal framework for clinical AI, but healthcare organizations must still define their own path forward. The roadmap focuses on four priorities, the first being to earn public trust by protecting patient choice, consent and control and by building confidence through transparent evidence, staged deployment and continuous monitoring.

The second is to build the data foundation by improving secure access to connected health records so patients, clinicians and AI tools can use relevant information while safeguarding privacy and cybersecurity. The third is to establish clear rules of the road by advancing risk-based regulation, clarifying liability and pursuing national standards, and by partnering with US states on sandboxes to test clinical AI with appropriate oversight. The fourth is to pay for what works by expanding outcome-based payments, including ACCESS, and exploring Medicaid models with states, rewarding improved health and lower costs rather than more visits or technology use. In Forrester's State Of AI Survey, 2026, US AI decision-makers in healthcare, pharma and medical devices organizations cited security, privacy and compliance at 30%, risk management at 21% and governance strategy at 21% as their top concerns. When asked what is included in their leadership-approved AI and agentic strategies, fewer than half of these same decision-makers included AI principles and values, technology, talent strategy or governance strategy.

Forrester says this means healthcare organizations have uneven strategic foundations rather than simply different priorities, and that they have not yet clearly defined their AI risk tolerance, the value AI must deliver, and who is accountable for approving its use, managing its risks and measuring its outcomes. Forrester advises leaders to define the strategy and then scale across the organization, with clinical, operational, digital and workforce leaders holding cross-functional sessions to align on AI principles, permitted uses, business objectives and decision rights. It says they should set safeguards for AI use and assign ownership, establishing rules for sensitive data, vendor access, consent and human escalation, and designating a risk lead to map each use case to safeguards and a named owner. It also says they should build governance into how work gets done, involving frontline staff in workflow design and providing role-based training to challenge outputs and handle exceptions, and measure value consistently with a healthcare AI value framework that connects investments to revenue, efficiency or risk mitigation. Forrester says the direction is promising, but that how well the industry implements the roadmap and coordinates innovation, evidence, regulation and payment will determine whether consumers and clinicians benefit and whether healthcare organizations realize measurable AI value.

stories.Headline: Agentic AI drives 450 per cent more network traffic and pushes inference on-premises
stories.Summary:
Enterprise networks are under severe strain as companies deploy artificial intelligence, according to a TechGig report published on November 25, 2026. Agentic AI tasks generate an estimated 450 per cent more network traffic than the same tasks performed by human workers, the report states, citing an MIT Technology Review report. AI is quickly becoming the biggest source of demand on network infrastructure, and the report says companies may need to fundamentally reconsider their network architecture. This includes potentially shifting away from a cloud-first approach for certain workloads.

Training AI models requires server-to-server data centre architectures, while AI inference calls for low-latency connectivity located close to users. The report notes that inference typically requires real-time processing and is sensitive to latency, so hosting it on distant hyperscale clouds is neither economical nor practical. Inconsistent latency can lead to AI model failures, causing increased queue wait times and saturated GPU loads, which also creates bottlenecks in data flows. Large enterprises may therefore need on-premises or near-premises inference capabilities, reversing years of cloud-first consolidation strategies and requiring new approaches to data centre architecture, connectivity and physical infrastructure. The traffic increase from agentic AI, combined with inference moving on-premises, exposes bandwidth bottlenecks in legacy underlay infrastructure.

The report suggests that network modernization requires a holistic approach so companies can adapt with ease. It says a combination of strong architectural governance, reusable design templates and retained internal expertise helps organizations adapt to disruptive events without rebuilding infrastructure each time, such as mergers and acquisitions, changing vendors or technology upgrades. Network-as-a-service and AI-driven observability can improve efficiency and reduce complexity in network operations, according to the report. Regulators worldwide are passing laws requiring data and AI processing to remain within national borders, which conflicts with how multinational companies currently operate. The report says this requires the build-out of sovereign-capable infrastructure for each geography, demanding significant new investment and complicating operations.

stories.Headline: Architects must evaluate AI firewalls on context binding rather than feature lists
stories.Summary:
Enterprise AI traffic is difficult to secure because sensitive information can sit inside otherwise legitimate connections, according to a TechGig report published on November 25, 2026, which cites FreeCodeCamp. The report gives the example of a developer sending source code to a coding assistant over HTTPS, or an internal application submitting customer data to a model API. It says architects must assess whether a control can link an AI interaction to enough context to make effective security decisions. That context includes user identity, application, model, data sensitivity, prompt intent and tool access, and the report contrasts this approach with judging firewalls only on feature lists.

The report describes several AI network firewall offerings and what each one does. Check Point's extends enforcement to AI-aware traffic analysis, discovering AI use, inspecting prompts and governing interactions from the network layer, which the report says gives broad coverage including unmanaged traffic and agent activity. Palo Alto Networks' AI Runtime Security protects AI applications and agents during execution, with a policy surface covering prompts, responses and data flows at the application level. Zscaler's uses a zero-trust, cloud-delivered model that applies AI policy in the path of user, application and agent interactions, and Cisco's integrates into AI Defense, a broader architecture covering discovery, validation, supply-chain risk and runtime protection across cloud and on-premises environments. Akamai's focuses on the application-model boundary, inspecting inputs and outputs for prompt injection, jailbreaks and data exposure, which the report says suits internet-facing AI applications at the edge or via an API.

On responsibility, the report addresses architects, saying they must evaluate AI network firewalls on their ability to bind AI interactions to sufficient context rather than on feature lists alone. It says a practical enterprise security design often combines different control points, with network policy managing AI service reachability, runtime policy inspecting application prompts, and identity policy restricting agent access to tools and data. Data controls, it adds, can prevent sensitive information from leaving even with approved AI services. Before selection, the report says enterprises should map their AI data path and identify where authority transitions, then choose controls that can observe those points.

stories.Headline: Anthropic shares stay below IPO price as OpenAI weighs a 2027 listing
stories.Summary:
Anthropic shares traded at roughly $79 apiece on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, down 3% and well below the $83 initial public offering price, in the stock’s fifth trading day. The stock lost 6.5% on Tuesday, closing at $81.90, according to CNBC. Wednesday’s decline put Anthropic further below its opening price of $111.50 during Thursday’s debut session and its intraday peak of $115.10. Anthropic shares did not rally on Monday, when most stocks in the AI trade rose on news of Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia as CEO. The negative reaction to Anthropic’s debut muddies OpenAI’s path to becoming a public company next year.

At its IPO price of $83, Anthropic was valued at roughly $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis, which includes existing shares and those that could be exercised in the future due to stock options, warrants and convertible notes. Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO haul was $177.6 billion, including both the greenshoe allotment released by underwriters and its $26 billion private placement. The company had $132 billion in cash and short-term investments at the end of September, even before the IPO, and sits on well over $200 billion in cash now. Anthropic has more than $900 billion in future financial commitments, according to its IPO prospectus, and was free cash flow positive in the first nine months of 2026. OpenAI was valued at $1.25 trillion during a recent funding round, CNBC reported on Nov. 12, up from about $852 billion in the round prior.

Jim Cramer wrote in his Sunday column that the action in Anthropic “might doom all of OpenAI’s attempts to raise money and lead to a down IPO for ChatGPT maker ,  a catastrophic outcome, at least in that world.” He attributed it possibly to poor pricing on the part of lead underwriter Goldman Sachs, or poor allocation choices made by Anthropic’s leadership. In August, CFO Sarah Friar told employees that the AI lab “will be a public company in 2027” or sooner, CNBC reported. In September, CEO Sam Altman ruled out a 2026 debut amid an intensifying debate around AI safety. Anthropic’s public stock is a form of currency it can use to fund its operations, so the worse it trades, the less valuable that currency becomes in potential future equity sales needed to fund operations.

All but five of the 20 largest traditional U.S. IPOs since 1990 have dropped below their offer price within the first year of trading, according to HB Wealth. In the eyes of Wall Street, Anthropic is often seen as the more secure bet, at least in terms of revenue durability, thanks to greater enterprise exposure. Anthropic’s rough start is problematic for OpenAI’s future fundraising plans and creates a new overhang for the entire artificial intelligence trade, raising questions about future earnings estimates for a host of AI-related companies, from chipmakers to cloud-computing giants and the industrial picks-and-shovels providers. Anthropic securing its windfall has near-term benefits, both directly and indirectly, for companies levered to the AI infrastructure buildout. Demand for AI is still outstripping supply.

It remains very early in Anthropic’s public-company journey, and it is far from the only mega-IPO to struggle to find its footing. Anthropic’s poor price action may just be a function of coming public, and not a harsh judgment on the AI trade more broadly. It may simply be there’s a price-discovery process that cannot be completed in just four days. A financially strong Anthropic is not enough on its own to keep the AI trade afloat, and OpenAI is another crucial leg to the AI funding stool. At the time of Friar’s August remarks, an IPO in 2026 was still thought to be on the table.

The AI trade may be rangebound until there is more clarity on the AI labs’ ability to raise funds. It is difficult to predict when that catalyst will arrive, or what it may be. It could be a slow grind as investors get more comfortable with Anthropic’s finances and its stock trades better, or one good quarter that sees Anthropic stock surge on the back of a revenue and/or profitability acceleration, in turn casting a positive halo on OpenAI. Sentiment can turn around quickly, going from positive one day to negative the next, and vice versa. OpenAI has signaled plans to go public next year, though the timing is uncertain.
