stories.Headline: Hitachi develops framework to check AI infrastructure decisions before execution
stories.Summary:
Hitachi said on 25 November 2026 that it is developing an orchestration framework called the Integrated World Infrastructure Model, which combines AI models, physics-based simulations, digital twins and domain expertise to support reliable decision-making across critical infrastructure. The company said the framework is meant to evaluate AI-generated recommendations against operational and safety requirements before they are executed, rather than relying on a single model of the physical world. Hitachi described a four-step process in which AI models propose actions, specialized models and digital twins simulate their effects on interconnected assets, and the proposed actions are then checked against engineering constraints, operating rules and safety requirements. Under the final step, actions that meet the required conditions may be authorized within predefined boundaries, while novel, uncertain or irreversible decisions are escalated for human review. Hitachi said the framework is designed to coordinate specialized models across infrastructure systems so that decisions can be evaluated in a broader operational context.

As an example, the company said growing electricity demand in North America from data centers, electric vehicle infrastructure and other sources is increasing the complexity of generator interconnection studies. Hitachi said it announced a strategic partnership with Southwest Power Pool, a regional transmission organization, in 2025, and that through the partnership it is developing an integrated AI-based solution with the objective of reducing generator interconnection analysis times by 80% while supporting more informed planning decisions. Looking ahead, Hitachi said it aims to use the framework to coordinate generator interconnection, power flow, equipment layout and profitability assessment models. Ahmed Farahat, Lab Manager and Director of Applied AI R&D at Hitachi America's Industrial AI Laboratory, wrote that the challenge for Physical AI is not simply developing more intelligent models or collecting more data but ensuring that AI-generated decisions are reliable and appropriate for the physical environments in which they are applied. He wrote that in mission-critical infrastructure an incorrect decision can disrupt operations, damage equipment or put people at risk, and that intelligence alone is not enough.

He said routine actions that have been extensively simulated, verified and shown to be reversible may be performed autonomously within clearly defined boundaries, while novel situations, uncertain outcomes or actions with irreversible consequences should remain subject to human judgment. He also said established industrial protection mechanisms, including relays and interlocks, must continue to provide protection when AI-generated decisions are incorrect, and that human operators remain essential. Farahat wrote that one of the greatest challenges will be verifying systems that continue to learn, because traditional engineering certification generally assumes that a system's behavior remains substantially consistent after testing, and AI systems that adapt over time challenge that assumption and require new approaches to continuous verification, governance and oversight. He said Hitachi is developing technologies that help engineers create simulations, extract domain knowledge and integrate specialized reasoning models, and that the Integrated World Infrastructure Model provides a framework for orchestrating these capabilities and evaluating AI-generated recommendations before they affect real-world operations. He wrote that the future of Physical AI will depend not simply on who develops the most intelligent model but on whether those models can be integrated into systems that consistently operate within established safety and operational boundaries.

Articles.Title: Beyond Intelligence: Building Reliable Physical AI for Critical Infrastructure

stories.headline_source: Beyond Intelligence: Building Reliable Physical AI for Critical Infrastructure

stories.Headline: WEX COO says payments winners will rely on proprietary data and change management as AI spreads
stories.Summary:
The payments industry’s artificial intelligence race is running into a differentiation problem, because if every provider can deploy sophisticated automation, the value of any one company’s technology becomes harder to explain. Carlos Carreido, chief operating officer for Americas payments and mobility at WEX, discussed that question with PYMNTS for the “What’s Next in Payments” series’ November edition, titled “From Good to Great in 2027.” He said that when a company holds proprietary data no one else can have, the task is to understand how to use it for the advantage of its customers and to offer them value. He added that great companies will be able to stay true and keep doing what they do best. The discussion took place as financial services firms enter 2027, and it framed the answer as lying less in the AI capabilities a firm acquires than in the operational advantages it already possesses.

New research from WEX found that 44% of enterprises plan to adopt agentic AI within two years, according to the article. AI may improve fraud detection, automate payment workflows and help businesses identify inefficiencies, but the effectiveness of those capabilities can depend on how well a provider understands the underlying transactions, spending patterns and customer requirements. Capabilities that once required significant internal development may become more accessible to competitors, reducing the advantage of deploying a particular tool and putting greater emphasis on proprietary information, specialized expertise and customer relationships. The article also says a more efficient payment method does not automatically produce a more efficient business, because companies must persuade employees, finance departments and suppliers to abandon familiar processes before they can capture the benefits. That makes organizational adoption a critical variable in the return on technology investment.

Carreido said payments companies need professionals who combine deep industry knowledge with the willingness to adopt unfamiliar technologies, and he said it is not easy to find people like that. He contrasted his experience in the United Kingdom, where business check usage is relatively limited, with the continued reliance on checks among U.S. companies. He said the change needed in an organization that moves away from something it has always done, such as paying a supplier by check instead of a more effective mechanism, is a huge change-management effort, and he noted that the persistence of checks illustrates a broader problem for financial technology providers. He said he cannot think of a company in the future that would be successful without embracing what AI has to offer, but he also said companies can get lost in the hype, get distracted and just do AI for the sake of AI.

The article says the competitive question for 2027 is shifting from who can adopt AI to who can make it economically consequential. It says AI alone won’t determine who wins in payments, and that as automation becomes widely accessible, competitive advantage could shift toward proprietary data, specialized expertise and the ability to turn emerging technologies into measurable customer value. It describes payments modernization as having a change management problem, since U.S. businesses still rely heavily on paper checks despite more efficient alternatives, and it says Carreido argues that overcoming entrenched processes and employee resistance can matter as much as adopting new technology. The article says the next payments advantage may come from execution rather than innovation, and that the winners in 2027 may be those that turn AI investments into tangible business outcomes.

Articles.Title: When Every Payments Company Has AI, What Separates the Winners?

stories.headline_source: When Every Payments Company Has AI, What Separates the Winners?

stories.Headline: Chinese AI experts and investors debate model futures amid chip shortages and US restrictions
stories.Summary:
Researchers and investors in China discussed the future of their artificial intelligence models in late 2026. These professionals shared their views through the Chinese technology media outlet called Intelligent Emergence. The discussions focused on the challenges of compute shortages and the transition to domestic chips. They also examined issues regarding training data, model scaling, and the commercialization of these technologies. These conversations occurred against a backdrop of tightening United States restrictions on advanced computing resources.

The current situation requires developers to navigate new United States export control rules on advanced chips. These rules cover data centers that remotely provide large-scale computing resources to Chinese companies. In November, NVIDIA announced that Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on November 12. The board then unanimously decided to reinstate Huang as president and CEO on November 23. Huang now faces a closed-door congressional hearing scheduled for December 1.

Zhipu Chief Scientist Tang Jie stated that the gap between Chinese and American models might not have narrowed. Lin Junyang of Alibaba previously claimed there was only a 20 percent chance of China leading in three to five years. Yao Shunyu expressed a more optimistic view, stating the probability of leading was actually quite high. An investor advised startups to prioritize securing GPUs over building teams or raising capital. A data professional noted that GPU shortages force teams to do fine-tuning instead of reinforcement learning.

Independent foundation model companies are affected by acute shortages because they lack their own cloud infrastructure. Startups face rising rental prices for high-end GPUs as exports are restricted by the United States. Some researchers at major technology companies report that they never have enough GPUs for experiments. One researcher noted that securing one or two servers for an experiment can take half a day. Others mentioned that the number of available Blackwell-series GPUs has recently decreased.

The industry saw a series of high-performing Chinese large language models released in rapid succession during the summer. Nathan Lambert claimed the performance gap between Chinese and American models narrowed to three to five months. In September, OpenAI and Anthropic strengthened anti-distillation measures to prevent the extraction of reasoning content. The price of an eight-GPU NVIDIA B300 server in China exceeded RMB 20 million. This price was five times higher than the price at the beginning of the year.

Major technology companies and leading developers will gradually release next-generation foundation models by early next year. Some researchers believe that smaller models are sufficient for most everyday use cases to control costs. Others are exploring machine-written kernels to optimize GPU computations and reduce inference costs. It remains uncertain if Jensen Huang's return will bring high-end chips back within reach of Chinese companies. The articles leave open whether developers can secure enough resources for the next round of training.

Articles.Title: Inside China's AI Industry: How Researchers and Investors See the Future of Chinese AI Models

stories.headline_source: Inside China's AI Industry: How Researchers and Investors See the Future of Chinese AI Models

stories.Headline: Nvidia shares jump 31% as Huang returns as CEO and AI debt concerns mount
stories.Summary:
Nvidia shares jumped more than 31% on Monday after Jensen Huang was reinstated as the company's CEO, and the move lifted technology stocks and the wider market after a sharp sell-off the previous week, according to CNBC. The rebound came even though Anthropic's stock market debut on Nov. 19, which the article describes as the largest ever, failed to lift the broader sector. Nvidia then closed about 5.9% lower on Tuesday. The article frames the swing as a sign that investors are asking harder questions about what the AI build-out will cost and when it will pay off. Man Group analysis cited by the article says Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Alphabet are on track to spend more on capital projects than their businesses generate in cash in both 2026 and 2027.

PIMCO, citing Goldman Sachs data, expects the biggest AI companies to raise about $250 billion through bond sales this year, while borrowing across the wider AI industry, including chipmakers, utilities and data center developers, could reach $300 billion to $570 billion. Man analysis found that heavy spenders and debt issuers such as Oracle, Alphabet and certain chipmakers fell by 25% to 45% between their June peak and Friday's close, while Apple, which the article says has sat out the AI spending race, was up almost 20%. The article also says Anthropic is already bringing in cash and is close to breaking even on free cash flow. Dan Taylor, deputy chief investment officer and CIO equities, systematic at Man Group, said investors are getting choosier about where the capital goes and when it might pay off, and he expects the market to fragment beyond the old trade of buying chipmakers and selling software. He said the era of spending first and asking questions later seems to be over, and that mega-cap tech spenders have room to rebound but will likely need to show more spending discipline and rebuild free cash flow.

Matthew Rees, head of global bond strategies at L&G Asset Management, said bond markets have been more bearish on Big Tech hyperscalers than equity markets, partly because of the sheer volume of issuance, and he said BBB names like Oracle and SpaceX are trading more like single B. Cole Smead, CEO and portfolio manager at Smead Capital Management, said there are vast capital needs in the AI story but just not enough money to go around, and he questioned whether buyers of data center debt are being paid enough for the risk. Taylor said the past week showed that a mega-IPO like Anthropic no longer lifts the whole market, and he said Nvidia and the semiconductor complex need the big spenders to keep spending heavily on AI capacity even as those same companies need to rebuild free cash flow. He said it is hard to see how both sides get what they need at the same time. The article gives no further scheduled events or decisions beyond those expectations.

Articles.Title: AI debt worries grow as Nvidia rebound masks Big Tech spending squeeze

stories.headline_source: AI debt worries grow as Nvidia rebound masks Big Tech spending squeeze

stories.Headline: ActivTrak CTO Matthew Finlayson builds a Jira routing agent that reaches 95% accuracy
stories.Summary:
Matthew Finlayson, CTO at ActivTrak, spent the past year building four iterations of an AI agent designed to route customer issues to the right engineering team, as he wrote in a November 25, 2026 article. The first iteration used Claude Code with an MCP connector to Jira, and he would hand it an issue and a prompt, and it would tell him who should look at it. For the second, he turned that workflow into an agent in n8n, a low-code framework. The third ran on Claude Managed Agents, Anthropic's hosted agent platform, but he wanted it to have access to tools and data that the environment couldn't reach. For the fourth, he rebuilt the agent on Google's agent platform, where ActivTrak runs its production infrastructure, which gave it access to the codebase and issue tracker.

At ActivTrak, the customer support team handles 90% of customer issues themselves, while 10% involve product problems that require escalation to engineering. Routing those escalations was a bottleneck, and roughly 100 times a week someone had to apply substantial domain knowledge to identify the right engineering manager. The first version of the routing agent assigned only about 60% of issues correctly, and it also made people up, hallucinating names and combining first and last names from different people. Engineering managers flagged incorrect assignments in Jira and explained which team or person should have received each ticket, and through that review process the agent reached about 95% routing accuracy. The agent now saves each of ActivTrak's seven engineering managers about 2 hours a week, and its actual operational cost is pennies a month, a figure that excludes the time Finlayson spent building and refining it.

Finlayson said the biggest surprise was discovering how much the routing process relied on knowledge the managers couldn't fully articulate. He said he couldn't have asked any of the managers to write the complete set of routing rules upfront, but they could review a routing decision and say they would have sent it to a particular person for a particular reason. He said building the agent meant turning the group's fragmented judgment into explicit rules. He said the agent explains its assignments in Jira, stating that it is a bot and assigned the ticket there for stated reasons, and that anyone can put a thumbs down on it. He said he stopped short of building automatic learning from each correction because each additional refinement saved less time.

Finlayson wrote that separate testing by his department showed how differently models can interpret the same restrictions, under rules that included a prohibition on giving employment recommendations. He wrote that Gemini would go out of its way not to answer questions it felt crossed a specified line, Opus would get excessively creative trying to find ways to answer without violating the premise, and Sonnet followed the restriction more literally. He wrote that a new model release or even a new model family, such as a move from Claude Opus to GPT-6 or Gemini 4, can change response patterns even when the surrounding tools and instructions stay the same. He wrote that when the agent broke for a week, several managers came to him, noticing the manual work had come back. He wrote that when one team's responsibilities changed, ActivTrak had to adjust the routing rules.

Finlayson wrote that he kept asking across each iteration whether the agent justified the work of building it, including how often it routed an issue correctly, what it cost to run, and how much manual routing it removed. He wrote that a reporting issue could have different causes, with an incorrect report sometimes indicating a front-end problem and sometimes a data problem, and that data ingestion belonged to one team unless the data came from an HRIS system, which another team handled. He wrote that he also built tools to ask whether an issue is a regression, whether a recent change caused it, where in the code the problem lives, and which developer touches that area, making four tools with routing. He wrote that he started with a concrete metric, how much time engineering managers were spending in the Jira project before and after the agent went live. He wrote that managers redirect the remaining roughly 5% of incorrect assignments, just as they did before the agent existed.

Finlayson wrote that before building another agent he needs to ask whether the workflow is fairly static or whether the team or process will change substantially, which changes the ROI calculation significantly. He wrote that he suspects by next year he will have multiple agents running to take over tasks for his team, and that some he may purchase rather than build. He wrote that whether he builds or buys, he will want to understand how an agent handles exceptions, adapts to workflow changes and justifies the effort required to maintain it. He wrote that low operating costs mean little if the system needs constant intervention to stay useful. He wrote that he encourages other technology leaders to build an agent themselves, and that documenting the workflow, investigating incorrect results and deciding whether another improvement is worth the effort gave him a clearer understanding of automation's true cost and value and of the work his team does every day.

Articles.Title: I built an AI agent. It broke my assumptions about my own team

stories.headline_source: I built an AI agent. It broke my assumptions about my own team

stories.Headline: Financial Times reports tech stocks slide as AI trade confidence fades
stories.Summary:
Tech stocks slid as confidence in the AI trade faded, according to the Financial Times on 25 November 2026. The article names no companies, gives no index levels and reports no percentage moves for the session. It offers no figure for how far prices fell or which stocks led the decline. The report carries no named author and no source for the shift in sentiment. The article as published is behind a subscription wall, so the body of the story is not available.

What remains visible is the headline and the date and time of publication, 06:00 GMT on 25 November 2026. The page shows only subscription offers and site navigation around the headline. No details of the trading session, the size of the fall or the companies involved appear in the accessible text. The available material does not say what the slide requires or changes for investors or markets. The Financial Times is responsible for the report, and the accessible text contains no statement from any person about the slide.

No investor, executive or official is named or paraphrased in what is visible. The article gives no explanation for why confidence in the AI trade faded. It also gives no context on earlier AI-driven gains or on the wider market. Nothing in the accessible text says what happens next. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Meta staff warn AI moderation makes mistakes at scale
stories.Summary:
Meta employees expressed concern about the company replacing human moderators with artificial intelligence. These insiders claim the technology leads to mistakes with potential for sweeping political consequences. The company has experimented with AI driven moderation since 2017 to filter violent extremist content. This push toward AI has occurred alongside mass layoffs across the company. These cuts severely affected staff responsible for reviewing content on Meta platforms.

In March, Meta announced it was transforming its approach by rolling out more advanced AI systems. This change affects content moderation across Facebook and Instagram to improve enforcement. Some content moderation teams were cut by half or two thirds of their staff. Meta previously paid outsourced moderators in Kenya as little as 1.50 dollars per hour. These workers viewed graphic content and described struggling with severe mental health issues.

One employee said that gutting human reviewers leads to mistakes because AI struggles with nuance. They stated that automated algorithms work at a greater speed than humans. This speed means mistakes can happen at a greater scale than before. Another employee claimed AI offers plausible deniability for the company to hide behind. They suggested AI allows Meta to obscure controversial decisions regarding political content.

Martha Dimitratou of Repro Uncensored said these takedowns could shape the political future of nations. Affected accounts include the US No Kings account and those posting queer content. Repro Uncensored tracked takedowns in the US, Turkey, the EU, and Brazil. Accounts backing Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva were also restricted or suspended. Users now find it more difficult to get help with nuanced cases.

Repro Uncensored documented 210 account takedowns in 2025 and 657 in early 2026. Meta adjusted its algorithm in late 2023 to limit posts from people in Palestine. The company has used a system since 2022 to prioritize specific Arabic dialects. Meta says its latest AI tests make 13 percent fewer mistakes than humans. These systems reportedly find 10 percent more actual violations of community standards.

Meta says any claims of enforcement based on political advocacy are baseless. The company states that everyone on its platforms is subject to the same rules. Users are given the opportunity to appeal decisions if they think Meta is wrong. The articles leave open whether political considerations influence how the algorithms are designed. It remains unclear how the opaque systems of levers and factors actually function.

Articles.Title: ‘It’s been really a mess’: Meta insiders concerned over push to AI content moderation

stories.headline_source: ‘It’s been really a mess’: Meta insiders concerned over push to AI content moderation

stories.Headline: House oversight subcommittee examines responses to AI-enabled cyberattacks at Dec 2 hearing
stories.Summary:
A House Oversight subcommittee will hold a hearing on Dec. 2 to examine how organizations can prevent, detect and disclose cyberattacks enabled by artificial intelligence, following reports of a breach involving unclassified U.S. intelligence systems. The hearing, titled "Defend, Detect, Disclose: Responding to AI-Enabled Cyber Incidents," will take place before the Subcommittee on Economic Growth, Energy Policy, and Regulatory Affairs of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee. Rep. Eric Burlison (R-MO) chairs the subcommittee, and Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-FL) is its ranking member, while the full committee is led by Chair Rep. James Comer (R-KY) and ranking member Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA). The hearing follows reports that unclassified open-source intelligence systems used by the Central Intelligence Agency, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency were breached, as Reuters reported on Nov. 24.

The hearing is a joint session with the Subcommittee on Cybersecurity, Information Technology, and Government Innovation, which is chaired by Rep. Nancy Mace (R-SC). According to the committee's announcement, lawmakers will examine existing liability protections, potential legislative changes and the Federal Trade Commission's investigations into major AI companies. Scheduled witnesses include Neil Chilson, head of AI policy at the Abundance Institute, Sam Rubin, senior vice president of consulting and threat intelligence at Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42, and Morgan C. Plummer, vice president of policy design and delivery at Americans for Responsible Innovation. Nextgov/FCW reported that ARTEX, an AI-based hacking framework, is believed to have been used in the intelligence system breach, and the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center issued an advisory on Nov. 13 warning that malicious actors had exploited ARTEX, an autonomous penetration-testing framework powered by large language models.

Industrial Cyber reported that attackers have used the technology since at least August to target industries including energy, manufacturing and telecommunications. The Trump administration is also weighing changes to cybersecurity incident reporting policies, and on Nov. 12 the White House Super Intelligence Force urged federal agencies to provide at least 12 months of regulatory liability relief to companies that voluntarily report cybersecurity vulnerabilities and AI-related incidents in good faith, CDO Magazine reported. The task force also called for clearer reporting requirements that reduce duplication across federal agencies, and its recommendations are not yet binding. Abroad, the European Commission confirmed that it had been targeted by an AI-enabled cyberattack, and European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said on Nov. 19 that it was an AI-generated cybercampaign, according to Brussels Signal.

Cybersecurity companies have also lobbied Washington on AI-enabled cyber defense, with Palo Alto Networks Inc. reporting $120,000 in third-quarter lobbying through Miller Strategies LLC and Wiz Inc. reporting $120,000 in the fourth quarter of 2025. The Dec. 2 hearing will examine whether existing federal laws adequately address AI-enabled cybersecurity threats and whether additional legislation is necessary. For cybersecurity companies and critical infrastructure operators, the White House task force's proposed liability protections could affect voluntary incident reporting and regulatory compliance. Palo Alto Networks will have an opportunity to address lawmakers directly through Rubin's scheduled testimony as Congress considers whether to strengthen cybersecurity requirements and revise existing legal protections.

Articles.Title: House Panel to Examine Responses to AI-Enabled Cyberattacks

stories.headline_source: House Panel to Examine Responses to AI-Enabled Cyberattacks

stories.Headline: Most firms do not track accuracy of their AI agents, survey finds
stories.Summary:
Parloa, an agentic customer experience company for enterprise customer service, and the research and advisory firm Metric Sherpa polled 531 customer experience professionals and 238 executives at vice president level or above in the United States, according to a report published by Sifted on 25 November 2026. The survey set out to find what metrics are being tracked in what the companies call the hybrid AI-CX era, how those metrics compare with what executives want to see, and whether the resulting insights are used across different functions. What the two firms found, the report says, is little visibility into how AI agents perform, data sets held in silos, and few links between AI and real business outcomes. The report states that no finding is more pressing than the lack of accuracy tracking, with only 27.9% of executives saying accuracy data reaches them at all.

The survey reports that 78.5% of customer experience operators do not track hallucination or accuracy for the AI agents they have bought. Confidence in customer experience does not match visibility either, because 94.7% of operators said they trust their metrics reflect the real customer experience while 89.5% said there is at least one part of that experience they know they cannot see. The report notes that the survey covers American results but that the urgency carries globally, since the EU AI Act puts pressure on companies deploying high-risk AI systems to enforce accuracy and prove it. It adds that confidence in customer experience rose alongside AI maturity, but concern about undetected AI errors did not fall with it, and that operators and executives alike keep deploying AI without being confident in its safety or having measures to guarantee it.

The report says leaders should be able to answer several questions before widening an AI agent's remit, including which interactions the AI handles, how factual accuracy is measured, how quickly errors are detected, assigned and corrected, who can pause expansion when the evidence does not exist, and whether accuracy data reaches the executives responsible for customer outcomes. It describes customer experience observability products that are being built to answer such questions, noting that less than a third of respondents were familiar with the term at the start of the survey while over half said they would find such tools valuable. Such products, the report says, can assess every interaction, whether handled by AI or a human, against the same quality standard. For European companies, the report says, not knowing will not be an answer that gets by much longer, and it advises companies building or buying AI to start with a lens on AI accuracy.

Articles.Title: How much do you know about your AI agents?

stories.headline_source: How much do you know about your AI agents?

stories.Headline: MIT researchers find generative AI could increase market risk by reducing portfolio diversification
stories.Summary:
Andrew Lo, a professor at MIT and founder of the Alpha Simplex Group, recently led a team of researchers to analyze the potential drawbacks of generative AI in investment analysis. The team conducted simulations to determine what might happen as more investors rely on these tools to make their financial decisions. They specifically examined how the widespread use of large language models could impact market stability and portfolio diversification. The study was designed to predict future market behavior since AI-driven investments have not yet taken a major share of overall market action. The researchers tested seven different large language models by presenting them with 64 distinct scenarios involving various fundamental and price inputs for a stock.

These scenarios varied based on factors such as valuation, price momentum, the volatility of the stock, and the consensus views of analysts. The team measured the correlation between the fundamental gap, which is the difference between the current share price and the fair value, across these different inputs. They discovered that as the capability of a model increases, as measured by the ELO capability score from the LMSYS Chatbot Arena benchmark, the models tend to give the same answer regardless of the input factors. This suggests that more capable models remove noise but may become stubbornly resistant to changing their views even when market circumstances shift. Andrew Lo and his colleagues concluded that if many investors use the same dominant model, they will likely buy and sell the same stocks.

This behavior would ruin the diversification effect for individual portfolios and make the overall markets significantly riskier. Even if investors use different models like ChatGPT, Claude, or DeepSeek, the results remain similar because these tools rely on the same input data. The researchers found that portfolio volatility remains well above the theoretical minimum because of this model resistance to input changes. Consequently, investors using AI may stubbornly stick to a specific decision even when the underlying financial environment changes. More to follow.

Articles.Title: The downside of AI for investment analysis

stories.headline_source: The downside of AI for investment analysis

stories.Headline: AI shifts IT teams from running technology to governing how organizations work
stories.Summary:
The first in a two-part series on how AI is transforming the IT function explores the impact the technology is having on how the department operates, its remit, and how tech roles are changing. Ironically, the very tech industry that invented AI has become one of the sectors most disrupted by it, with high rates of task automation and workforce change already evident. To date, the technology has been deployed in two key areas: the first is automating repetitive, manual operational tasks to boost productivity and efficiency. The second is boosting tactical decision-making, with initiatives around strategic decision-making still mostly at the pilot stage, points out Soumendra Mohanty. He is Chief Strategy and Chief Innovation Officer at data science solutions provider, Tredence.

But the upshot of this increased automation, combined with executive anticipation of the promise that AI offers, is that leaders are increasingly expecting IT teams to become "partners for business change" rather than take a more traditional operations-centric approach. In other words, says Mohanty, the focus is on what initiatives and new projects you can take on to support business stakeholders looking into revenue generation opportunities or enabling new business streams. That's where the shift is happening more and more, which implies that the current composition of IT teams will have to change quite a lot. The pyramid structures they run under will also have to become thin, leaner, and much more efficient. So, there's a crunch happening at that end as well.

Ankur Anand, Chief Information Officer of technology recruitment consultancy Harvey Nash, agrees. He believes the IT function's remit in many organizations is shifting from one of running technology to running how the organization works. AI doesn't sit inside a system you can draw a box around, he says, and it sits in workflow, decisions and process alongside legacy and modern platforms. So, IT is inheriting questions that used to belong to operations, HR, and legal. We spent a good part of this year assessing AI tools across our own recruitment stack, and the decisive questions were almost never technical.

They were about candidate data, whether a screening tool introduces bias, and what we'd tell candidates we were doing. Those are legal, HR, and ethics questions. They landed on my desk because the technology landed on my desk. Moreover, in Anand's view, governance is becoming the "new center of gravity". This involves more concentration on data quality, model risk, and guardrails defining what AI should and should not be used for.

At a more individual level, meanwhile, roles are becoming less siloed, Mohanty believes. As more traditional IT tasks are automated, tech workers are having to move from what they've been doing manually into "how do I now build value-add services on top of what these AI models are providing us?". This could be the right kind of problem-solving or ticket resolutions being undertaken in a highly autonomous manner. In other words, many IT teams are having to get on top of working with AI models in a way they have not necessarily done so before, often in collaboration with other teams. At the same time, as departmental leaders now require information and support more swiftly than ever, it is becoming clear that AI, data science, and analytics teams need to change.

They can't operate in their silos anymore. They can't say, "I'm the data guy - don't talk to me about algorithms". The data scientists can't say, "Don't talk to me about your ticket or problem-solving". Everything has to come together more and more, so cross-functional knowledge in the IT team is going to become the most critical. This, Mohanty believes, will lead to a shift in the team's size, shape, and skillsets.

There's a compression happening, he says, and many of these things that were siloed by nature have to come together. Hence there'll be better efficiency and collaboration, and of course, cross-functional upskilling has to happen. You don't need 20 people to do one report, for example. You probably need two or three, some functional, some technical, coming together and producing a report with the help of AI agents. But in his opinion, it will be less about AI taking people's jobs and more about tech employees' willingness to upskill and work with the technology.

Mohanty explains that there'll be a certain consolidation impact. Largely what we're seeing is that much of the spare capacity and additional roles that'll emerge will be on the enterprise value creation side. Which is a good thing as people have been in the industry doing a certain type of work for years and so have built that industry and process knowledge and understanding of where things can go wrong. They've got that very critical business knowledge that no AI can provide. So, leveraging that capacity for enterprise value creation, that's what enterprises are looking for.

The organizations furthest ahead on AI are hiring more people, not fewer. Firms running large-scale implementations are 24% more likely to be growing technology headcount than their peers - 51% against 41% - and mostly in AI and data. Leaders do expect hiring to fall for some existing roles over the next two years, but the team is changing shape, not shrinking. For instance, he indicates that software engineers, enterprise architecture, and first-line helpdesk positions are now in less demand. This, he says, is because AI is undertaking more coding activities.

Increasingly decentralized software delivery means there is less need for heavyweight architecture roles, while looking after internal support has become one of the most common AI use cases. Anand, who has first-hand experience of the shift, explains how this situation is playing out in one area of his organization. We're part of the way through replacing our own IT service management platform, and the interesting part isn't the technology. It's that the first-line role changes character. Password resets, access requests, and joiner-mover-leaver tasks are the easiest things in the department to automate, so the value of the person on the desk moves to curating the knowledge the automation draws on.

That's a different job, and not everyone on a service desk wants it. But new roles are starting to emerge too. These include AI and data engineering, AI product ownership, AI security and governance. They also consist of various orchestration roles, where people design and supervise AI work rather perform it themselves. Anand again illustrates the point using changes made in his own team.

We recently had to map and enrich around a million candidate records against standard industry job titles and skill sets. Done the traditional way, that's months of analyst work. We did it with a small team directing AI and then checking what came back. Nobody's job on that project was to classify records. The job was to design the approach, spot where the model was confidently wrong, and decide what good looked like.

That's an orchestration role in practice, and it draws on quite a different skill from the one it replaced. Outsourcing and direct headcount are both rising, often within the same organizations as leaders bring in-house what is core to them and flex the rest. Structures are flattening in parallel, with fewer larger delivery teams and more multi-skilled product teams, with AI carrying more of the load underneath. Kyle McNabb is Principal of Advisory Research and IT Advisory at AI and digital transformation consultancy, The Hackett Group. He agrees that despite all the change, the end of the IT function is certainly not nigh.

Instead, he predicts that moving forward key elements, such as ticketing, infrastructure architecture, and application maintenance and helpdesk, will "be distributed into lines of business". Application delivery design will be absorbed into lines of business, but security's not going away and will be beefed up more at the core. Architecture that's usable doesn't go away. IT leadership or infrastructure doesn't go away.

But the scope of traditional IT gets narrower, while the business takes on more ownership of solutions that help them change how they work. At the same time, however, McNabb believes that the importance of IT will be "elevated" as it takes on more of a facilitation role relating to AI oversight and governance. This includes how it manages performance using ThinOps while also ensuring the operational environment runs effectively. He explains that while the marketing department, for example, will have developers and data architects who know how they're using Snowflake better than IT does, they'll go to IT and say they need more capacity from an infrastructure standpoint.

They'll also plug into a core, standard IT operating environment rather than create their own. The IT department will have a smaller core, surrounded by a considerably wider network of partners, platforms, and agents. Less time will be spent building and more spent curating and assuring because the scarce skill becomes judgement: knowing what good looks like and being able to verify work you didn't write yourself. The second of this two-part series tomorrow will look at how AI is impacting tech leadership roles and what IT execs need to bear in mind when planning for the future.

stories.Headline: House panels hold joint hearing on AI-enabled cyberattacks on Dec 2
stories.Summary:
A House subcommittee hearing on artificial intelligence-enabled cyberattacks that was originally scheduled for Dec. 2 was canceled as a standalone session but will proceed on the same date as a joint hearing of two House Oversight and Government Reform subcommittees, according to a Nov. 25 announcement. The hearing, titled “Defend, Detect, Disclose: Responding to AI-Enabled Cyber Incidents,” was originally scheduled before the Subcommittee on Cybersecurity, Information Technology, and Government Innovation, chaired by Rep. Nancy Mace (R-SC), with Rep. Shontel Brown (D-OH) serving as ranking member. According to the committee's Nov. 25 announcement, the hearing will proceed jointly with the Subcommittee on Economic Growth, Energy Policy, and Regulatory Affairs, chaired by Rep. Eric Burlison (R-MO). The full committee is led by Chair Rep. James Comer (R-KY) and ranking member Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA).

The Dec. 2 joint hearing is expected to examine existing legal protections and whether additional legislation is necessary to address emerging cybersecurity threats. The White House AI Task Force met Nov. 12 to discuss AI-powered cyberattacks and voluntary incident reporting, and the discussions included potential legal protections for critical infrastructure operators that disclose cybersecurity vulnerabilities and attacks. The task force urged agencies to grant at least 12 months of regulatory liability relief to companies that voluntarily disclose AI-related incidents, according to AI Weekly. On Nov. 13, the Federal Bureau of Investigation warned about ARTEX, an open-source, large language model-based penetration testing framework, saying some cyberattacks using it achieved privileged access in under three hours. CNN reported Nov. 24 that hackers breached an unclassified system shared by the Central Intelligence Agency, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, and an initial investigation pointed to the suspected use of ARTEX, according to people familiar with the matter.

In Congress, a Nov. 23 press release announced that Reps. George Whitesides (D-CA) and Josh Gottheimer (D-NJ) introduced legislation to defend critical infrastructure against AI-driven cyberattacks. The White House's discussions about voluntary incident reporting and liability protections come as lawmakers consider legislation to strengthen critical infrastructure defenses against AI-enabled cyberattacks. The articles do not say who will testify at the Dec. 2 joint hearing or what the expected outcome is.

stories.Headline: AI Magazine ranks Salesforce, Microsoft, LangChain and AWS among ten agentic AI platforms
stories.Summary:
AI Magazine published on November 25, 2026 a ranked list of ten agentic AI platforms that it says are delivering measurable value to enterprises, naming Salesforce, Microsoft, LangChain and AWS among the offerings included. The publication said it aimed to capture the full stack of the agentic AI landscape by looking at a broad array of players in the field. The list also includes Kore.ai, CrewAI, UiPath, IBM, ServiceNow and Google Cloud alongside those four companies. The article cites McKinsey in noting that nearly two-thirds of enterprises worldwide have experimented with agents, while fewer than 10% have scaled them to deliver tangible value. The article describes each platform and the figures its maker gives for it.

Kore.ai says its Artemis platform is AI-programmable for the agentic enterprise and that its agents thrive in complex, high-volume, regulated workflows, and the firm has deepened partnerships with Microsoft and AWS, serving as a launch partner for Microsoft Agent 365 and earning the AWS Advanced AI Competency designation. CrewAI combines an open-source, multi-agent harness with its Agent Management Platform, which is built on the MIT-licensed CrewAI framework and lets organisations design Crews of autonomous agents and Flows that mix deterministic steps with agents. LangChain says its technology is used by 35% of the Fortune 500, has crossed a billion open-source downloads and ingests at least a billion events daily on LangSmith. UiPath says customers achieve 45% faster process cycles on average, claims more than US$10m in documented average savings per enterprise customer, and says eight of 10 top global healthcare firms and seven of 10 top global banks run on it. IBM describes watsonx Orchestrate as an open, hybrid and trusted platform with an AI Gateway for discovering third-party agents, models and MCP servers across platforms such as Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft and Google.

ServiceNow says its AI Platform has a single data model connecting to more than 450 systems, and NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang has previously said ServiceNow is destined to be the best platform and the operating system of enterprise AI agents. AWS delivers its offering primarily through Amazon Bedrock, a fully-managed service giving access to models such as Claude, Llama 2 and Amazon Titan, with Bedrock Agents using the reasoning of foundation models, APIs and data to handle user requests. Google Cloud delivers through Vertex AI Agent Builder and its Gemini models, with sandboxed code execution, persistent memory banks and compliance controls. Salesforce says more than 18,000 companies already run on Agentforce, including Fujitsu, Indeed and OpenTable, and that Gartner named it a Leader in the 2026 Magic Quadrant for Conversational AI Platforms. Microsoft's offering spans Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio, Azure AI Foundry and the open-source Microsoft Agent Framework, with access to models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta as well as its own Phi family.

The article attributes the descriptions and figures to the companies themselves and to the executives it names, including Kore.ai, CrewAI CEO João Moura, UiPath CEO Daniel Dines, AWS CEO Matt Garman and Salesforce CEO Marc Beinhoff. Claims such as UiPath's savings figure, LangChain's Fortune 500 share and Salesforce's customer count are presented as what each firm highlights or notes rather than as independently verified facts. The ranking itself is the publication's own selection, and the article does not describe a method beyond saying it aimed to capture the full stack. The context the article gives is that agentic AI is fundamentally reshaping enterprises, with many rushing to build out pilots as soon as possible, while McKinsey's finding suggests most have not yet scaled them to deliver tangible value. The article does not say what happens next beyond the publication of the list.

stories.Headline: Unit 42 says AI agents execute attacks at machine speed and urges edge AI defenses
stories.Summary:
Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 reported on 25 November 2026 that AI-driven attacks have moved from theoretical risks to real-world threats, with criminals using AI to accelerate attacks at scale. The unit said it observed attackers using AI agents to carry out context-aware commands with real-time decision-making during intrusions. In one campaign it observed, a highly persistent threat actor using AI generated 117 unique scripts across multiple languages and executed more than 8,000 unique commands in just 12 days. By contrast, normal attackers usually run dozens of commands with a few scripts over similar time periods, according to the unit.

The unit described a sharp behavioral difference between human operators and AI agents in one attack it observed, where humans acted first and an agentic AI attacker followed. In the human phase, the time between commands averaged roughly 24 seconds, and the hackers made typographical errors, repeated manual checks and showed environment confusion. In the agentic phase, the unit observed flawless, zero-syntax-error commands with a median gap of just 1.4 seconds. Because of that machine-speed execution, the unit said Mean Time To Respond metrics must improve considerably and that attack isolation and near real-time response are now critical mandates.

The unit said defenders must employ AI-powered tools right where attacks happen and must understand the behaviors that separate AI-based attacks from normal operations. It argued that running AI on the edge, specifically on endpoints and Next-Generation Firewalls, is a major strategic necessity, since edge AI can process telemetry instantly and make split-second decisions to terminate malicious web shell sessions or block privilege escalation locally. In its own product deployment, the unit said edge AI operated in milliseconds rather than the minutes taken by agentic LLMs, and it can work without cloud access or continuous connectivity. The unit also said agentic AI attackers share a foundational weakness, because they enter an environment without information and must perform extensive reconnaissance, port sweeping and environment enumeration.

The unit said collecting telemetry across network, endpoint, identity and cloud sources, normalizing it into a single schema and stitching related events into context-rich stories lets AI analytics engines establish baselines of normal organizational behavior. It said threat actors lack that context, so their automated attempts to map the terrain inevitably trigger detectors against established baselines and expose their presence. The unit said detection alone was never enough and that organizations must combine real-time detection with automated response for instant isolation and remediation. It said every attack it observed triggered alerts and that deep forensic investigations let it reconstruct the attack lifecycles, adding that existing tools such as XDR solutions, network monitoring and active prevention rules remain essential.

stories.Headline: DeepMind launches Humanity's First Exam to test AI model consistency on everyday tasks
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind launched Humanity's First Exam to test if AI models are consistent. This new exam checks if models get easy questions right every single time. The test was released on November 25, 2026, according to the report. It focuses on reliability rather than the ability to solve impossible problems. The exam uses 544 everyday questions covering text and images.

The test includes 20 foundational capabilities grouped into sets of four related questions. Tasks include counting objects, naming colors, tracking positions, basic arithmetic, and following strict formatting. It also tests the ability to spot false premises built on untrue things. A live leaderboard is hosted on the site Kaggle for data scientists. A Kaggle contest runs through December 15 for submitting questions models miss.

DeepMind says frontier models made significant progress on the exam over six months. They state the scoring is harsh because one slip fails a whole set. A model must get all four versions of a question right to pass. DeepMind's technical report traced 73 percent of wrong answers to visual perception. This means photo questions are currently the soft spot for these models.

Casual users are affected because they trust quick answers and rarely double-check them. A model that miscounts items on a shelf will fail a user. One sample prompt asks for the color of letters in a neon sign. The correct answer for that specific task is green, yellow, white, blue, blue. This represents the kind of simple work a child can do.

The exam name winks at a brutal benchmark called Humanity's Last Exam. This new test goes in the opposite direction by focusing on easy tasks. Top models reach roughly 95 to 98 percent on a single try. However, strict scoring puts the best score at barely an A-minus grade. These skills are used in requests like totaling a receipt from photos.

OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra placed first with a score of 90.7 percent on the test. GPT-6.2 Sol followed in second place with a score of 87.5 percent. Gemini 4 Neon ranked third with a score of 85.6 percent. The articles do not say how DeepMind will update the exam. They leave open how models will improve their visual perception scores.

Articles.Title: 😺 DeepMind's Humanity's First Exam Tests AI Consistency

stories.Headline: SalesHood launches an MCP integration that lets sellers pull approved content into AI assistants
stories.Summary:
SalesHood this month launched an MCP integration that brings its enablement platform into AI tools including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Glean and Perplexity, CX Today reported on 25 November 2026. Bloomreach has acquired the answer engine optimization platform AthenaHQ, the article said. Richardson Sales Performance surveyed 1,105 senior sales and revenue leaders at large organizations in North America and Europe. Gartner's latest Magic Quadrant for Revenue Enablement Platforms predicts that by 2030, 80% of interactions with revenue enablement platforms will happen through AI agents and embedded workflows rather than the platforms' own interfaces. The article said sellers are asking ChatGPT, Claude and Copilot for help with customer conversations, and buyers are asking AI tools which brands and products to consider.

The SalesHood integration lets sellers ask their preferred assistant for approved talking points, a customer story or a demo video, and then add the content to a Digital Sales Room, subject to their approval. Bloomreach plans to connect AthenaHQ's work to its customer engagement platform, from the first point of discovery through to personalization and loyalty. Richardson found that 62% of leaders at organizations that met or exceeded their quotas reported a positive financial return from AI, compared with 39% of leaders at organizations below 90% of their quotas. Richardson notes that quota attainment was self-reported, so the findings show correlation, not cause. Seventy percent of respondents said humans outperform AI in the activities that matter most in complex deals, while 88% expect skills AI cannot replicate to set their best sellers apart in 2027.

The article quoted SalesHood saying that sellers have already picked their AI and asking them to switch is a losing fight. Bloomreach said that from a customer's first moment of discovery through to lasting loyalty, it is giving businesses AI purpose-built to both win customers and keep them. Andrea Grodnitzky, Chief Marketing Officer at Richardson Sales Performance, said the difference came down to how leaders responded. Gartner's report says revenue enablement platforms are becoming an embedded intelligence layer across CRM, collaboration tools and AI assistants. The article said the enablement platform still holds the content, permissions and controls.

The article said brands can influence their product information, pricing, content and availability, but they do not fully control how an AI assistant chooses what to recommend. It said the next challenge is measuring whether appearing in an answer engine moves a customer from discovery to purchase. It said the risk for leaders is not simply that sellers use unapproved AI, but that they use it without access to the current messaging, content and buyer context that would make the answer useful. It said organizations that report stronger AI outcomes also report greater confidence in their forecasts and better returns from seller development. It said the goal is not to add another assistant, agent or content tool to the stack, but to make the work around it more consistent.

The article said the usual route through the revenue tech stack is starting to change, with sales teams traditionally going to an enablement platform for training, approved messaging and buyer content. It said marketing teams have worked to bring customers to brand websites, search pages and campaigns, and now AI assistants are inserting themselves at both ends of that journey. It said the work is moving beyond the dashboards and interfaces that revenue teams know well. It said this week's news from SalesHood, Bloomreach and Richardson Sales Performance shows what that could mean in practice. It said the technology may be changing, but the issues for business leaders are familiar: trusted information, visibility, governance and people.

The article said AI is not replacing the revenue tech stack overnight, but is changing where people experience it. It said a seller may ask an AI assistant for approved messaging rather than search an enablement platform, and a buyer may discover a product through an AI-generated answer rather than a search engine. It said the data, content, permissions and processes behind those interactions still need to be managed. It said the practical work for business leaders remains the same: keep product and customer information accurate, define who can access it, test AI in real workflows, and measure whether it improves outcomes that matter. It said the front door may be changing, but the need for trusted context and disciplined execution is not.

stories.Headline: European IT spending rises 9.9% in 2027 on AI-optimized server demand
stories.Summary:
European IT spending is set to rise by 9.9% in 2027, according to a forecast reported by IT Pro on 25 November 2026, with growth driven by demand for servers built to handle artificial intelligence workloads. The report frames the increase as a surge tied to that AI-optimized server boom across the region. The figure covers European IT spending as a whole for the 2027 calendar year. The articles give no further dates, names or numbers beyond the 9.9% figure and the year 2027.

The forecast implies that European organizations will spend nearly a tenth more on IT in 2027 than in the year before, with AI-optimized servers named as the main force behind the increase. The articles do not break the total down by country, vendor or category, and they do not say what the baseline year's spending was. No company, agency or individual is named as the source of the 9.9% figure. The articles also give no detail on what the servers are, who buys them or what they cost.

The articles name no one as responsible for the forecast and carry no statements from any person or organization about it. No spokesperson, analyst or executive is quoted, and no explanation is offered for why AI-optimized servers are driving the growth. Because no one is named, there are no remarks to paraphrase on the record. The only attributed element is the 9.9% figure itself, reported by IT Pro.

The articles give almost no context beyond the headline figure and the year it applies to. They do not say what happens next, whether the forecast could change, or how it compares with earlier estimates for European IT spending. No follow-up announcement, report or event is mentioned. stories.Headline: Infobip predicts AI agents will handle bookings, refunds and purchases for customers in 2027
stories.Summary:
Infobip, a global AI-first cloud communications platform based in Vodnjan, Croatia, released five predictions on November 25, 2026 about how customer engagement will change in 2027, according to a press release distributed by Business Wire. The company said AI agents will handle multi-step tasks such as changing bookings, processing refunds, completing purchases and resolving service requests. It said voice AI has already moved from pilots into live service and sales. Infobip said clear permissions, business rules and execution controls will be essential, with human handover when needed. The predictions say consumers will increasingly use personal agents to compare products, make purchases, change bookings and seek support, and some journeys may start through a personal AI assistant rather than a brand's website or app.

Businesses must make services and transactions accessible to authorized agents acting on customers' behalf, the release said. Customers will expect their identity, history and intent to carry across agents, voice, RCS, WhatsApp, apps and human support, with real-time data, customer memory and orchestration helping preserve context. Businesses must also verify that agents acting for customers are authorized and ensure that calls, messages and AI agents claiming to represent brands are genuine, the release said. Silvio Kutić, co-founder and CEO at Infobip, said 2027 will see AI move from conversation to action, with agents taking on more tasks for customers and businesses. He said action has to be useful and reliable, with the right context and authority and human support when needed.

He said businesses will focus less on what AI can do and more on the outcomes it delivers. The release said authentication, consent, disclosure, transparency and human oversight will underpin trust as fraud and impersonation remain concerns and AI-generated interactions and content become more common. The release said businesses will prioritize measurable outcomes such as faster resolution, lower costs, increased revenue, retention and reduced risk, and should scale use cases that justify investment and change or stop those that do not. It said that as AI-assisted development makes tailored software easier to build, some organizations may build the applications that differentiate them while relying on specialist providers for communications, identity and orchestration. The release did not say what happens next beyond these predictions.

stories.Headline: SolarWinds CTO says AI shifts IT work from investigation to verifying agents
stories.Summary:
Krishna Sai, senior vice president and chief technology officer of SolarWinds, said in an interview published by TechInformed on 25 November 2026 that AI moves IT work rather than removing it. Sai said AI shifts work from investigating problems to verifying and governing the agents that do the investigating. He said AI multiplies whatever a company already has, good or bad. He said organizations with brittle systems and poor-quality data will get more of the same. He said those with solid foundations will see the benefit.

Sai joined SolarWinds in June 2021, when he says its tools worked as separate point products. He said bringing them onto a single platform with the data in one place laid the groundwork for layering AI across the suite. He said he cofounded and served as CTO of two startups. He said he held engineering leadership roles at Polycom, Groupon and Atlassian. He said AI raises the level of abstraction and moves everything to a higher level than where people typically operate.

Sai said IT professionals' days are defined by toil, assembling data, chasing alerts and repeating the same fixes. He said AI can offload some of that toil and have immediate benefits. He said people's time shifts away from assembling data, chasing alerts and repetitive work toward making higher-level decisions. He said everyone is comfortable asking questions of AI but organizations need to put things in place for AI to act in their environment. He said one requirement is autonomy, with different levels so teams can start small with a narrowly scoped problem in a narrowly scoped environment.

Sai used the example of self-driving in a Tesla, which he said has different autonomy modes including chill mode, standard mode, hurry mode and Mad Max mode. He said organizations don't jump into Mad Max mode on day one and can begin with small tasks such as disk space management and build trust gradually. He said a second challenge is determinism, because AI is a probabilistic system and a language model asked the same thing three times may give three different answers. He said pairing AI with established IT and ops systems is important, along with good context, permission levels, evaluation systems, containment, observability of the agent itself, verification processes and escalation paths. He said a retailer whose checkout systems slow down is a good example, where an AI agent can automate much of the investigative work and, with the right controls, parts of the response.

Sai said the so-called AI productivity paradox comes down to how and at what layer productivity is measured. He said AI can make individual tasks dramatically faster but IT operates as a workflow around how tasks come together to achieve a business outcome. He said one of his engineers used AI to work through huge volumes of log data much faster but then had to spend time verifying the insights it generated. He said productivity should be measured at the level of verified outcomes such as reducing alert noise, reducing total effort or reducing incident frequency. He said organizations often get AI tool sprawl instead of traditional IT tool sprawl and should look at their enterprise AI stack.

Sai said SolarWinds has a unified AI gateway that all of its AI tools leverage, giving teams flexibility in model choice plus auditing, cost controls and safeguards against sensitive data leakage. He said scaling AI across an organization requires thought and used the analogy of driving a Ferrari, which performs incredibly on an empty road in Montana but gives a completely different experience through New York City, Jakarta or Bangalore. He said he has an agent that converts topics from his backlog into podcasts he listens to while driving. He said he grew up in the south of India and drinks South Indian filter coffee, a strong and hot brew with a layer of froth in a special two-piece metal container with a whole ritual. The interview was edited for length and clarity.

stories.Headline: Synthesis earns AWS AI Competency in generative and agentic consulting
stories.Summary:
Synthesis Software Technologies has achieved the Amazon Web Services AI Competency in the Generative AI Consulting Services and Agentic AI Consulting Services categories, according to an announcement dated 25 November 2026. To earn the competency, the company demonstrated its established AI delivery practices and provided evidence of customer implementations running in production. The assessment covered how Synthesis designs, implements and supports AI solutions, as well as the value its work has delivered to customers. The two categories cover distinct capabilities, with generative AI helping employees retrieve knowledge and produce content while agentic AI lets software agents interact with enterprise tools and carry out multi-step tasks within defined boundaries. Synthesis says the recognition gives it faster access to AWS generative AI tools and services, and it describes joint programs that combine its industry experience with AWS's scalable generative AI solutions.

The company says these will provide rapid time to market across back-office and front-office functions, including operations, technology and marketing. For organisations adopting agentic AI, Synthesis says boundaries must be built into the system, with appropriate monitoring and opportunities for human intervention. Paul Spagnoletti, Executive Head of Revenue at Synthesis, said a working proof of concept is only the beginning and that the real test is whether a business can depend on the AI system every day. He said banking and payments systems have to work with existing technology and meet strict security and oversight requirements, which takes far more than getting a model to produce the right answer. Michael Shapiro, Managing Director at Synthesis, said the recognition is valuable for what the team can do with it next, and that the relationship with AWS gives access to programmes and support that can help customers get significant AI projects under way.

He said Synthesis will help customers identify where the technology can deliver real returns and then put in motion secure and robust engineering. Synthesis says an AI project also needs a credible operating model before it goes live, and that customers should weigh implementation and ongoing support costs against the improvements they expect and decide how to measure those benefits. Responsibility for handling exceptions needs to be clear, especially when software agents take actions across business systems, and employees may need training as familiar processes change. Without that preparation, the company says, a system that performs well in testing can be difficult to manage at scale. Synthesis says it draws on its experience in cloud architecture, software engineering and managed operations to plan for those demands before deployment and to provide support afterwards.

stories.Headline: Nvidia and Anthropic shares fall 8% as Nasdaq 100 drops over 4% on rate hike fears

On Wednesday, November 25, 2026, stocks extended their declines as the chip sector sold off and the Nasdaq 100 sank more than 4%, according to a Yahoo Finance report by Ines Ferré. The AI trade extended its declines, with semiconductor stocks leading the Tech sector lower. The report attributed the pressure on growth stocks to expectations of a December rate hike by the Federal Reserve, following the tariff announcement and the inflation data.

stories.Headline: Virginia Tech-led team publishes statistical test for AI medical imaging
stories.Summary:
A Virginia Tech-led team published a new statistical test for AI medical imaging on Nov. 23, 2026, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team includes researchers from the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, Texas Tech University and Princeton University. Virginia Tech News reported the work the same day in an article by Kelly Izlar. The tool combines computational topology and statistics to compare complex image data. The researchers tested it on synthetic mammograms compared with real patient data.

The method's job is to decide whether AI-generated medical images are faithful enough to stand in for real patient data in clinical trials. The team tracked how breast cancer responds to different radiation doses. The National Science Foundation funded the research through a joint partnership with the National Institutes of Health and the Food and Drug Administration. The announcement gives no sample sizes, error rates or number of synthetic images used. The paper's exact title as it appears in PNAS and any product name for the method are not established in the sources.

Yulia R. Gel, a professor of statistics at Virginia Tech, said the goal is that clinical trials with synthetic data reach the same conclusions as with real people. Statistics graduate student Jaidev Goel, one of the paper's leading authors, told Virginia Tech News that statistics has always supplied the stress tests for new tools. Goel also said people should not buy into AI hype blindly. Virginia Tech says the tool bridges computational topology and statistics to measure and compare complex image data. The announcement does not spell out which topological features the team extracted or how the statistical test is built.

Virginia Tech explains that deploying a more powerful, more precise MRI in a hospital requires FDA approval. The university adds that the FDA is exploring AI-generated synthetic data alternatives that could compress trial timelines to months. The team is in talks with FDA on pre- and post-market use, confirmed as talks only. A systematic literature review and meta-analysis in npj Digital Medicine examines how AI implementation affects efficiency in medical imaging. Approval for routine clinical use is not confirmed, and no evidence was found for it.

Generative adversarial networks, introduced in 2014, showed that neural networks could produce convincing images. Medical researchers soon tried them on scans, mostly to augment small datasets. Computational topology studies the shape of data and summarizes structure such as connected regions, loops and gaps. Statistics turns a comparison into a decision by asking whether two collections of images differ by more than chance would explain. The announcement does not give cost or an implementation date.

The research is real and published, while the commercial and regulatory consequences remain forecasts. Independent replication on other modalities will tell us far more than the first paper can. The method exists to say no when a synthetic set falls short. A pass on one generator, one organ and one dose range tells us little about another generator. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Microsoft and the FAA show routine changes outpacing human checks as AI speeds up software work
stories.Summary:
In mid-November 2026, two failures in a single week showed how much modern life depends on systems few people see, according to an analysis published by the IAPP on 25 Nov. 2026. On 12 Nov., Microsoft's cloud office services went down worldwide for about a day, and the next day the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration halted every departing flight in the country for over four hours. Neither failure has been linked to AI, and in both cases a routine change to the system caused a problem that existing safeguards did not detect or contain. The article says this weakness matters more as AI reshapes how software is built, because documented incidents over the past year have shown AI tools may generate or apply changes faster than people can check or fully understand them.

According to Microsoft's early explanation, a fault introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade laid dormant until a later network change exposed it. Microsoft has said the outage was a technical issue, unrelated to a cyberattack or to AI agents, and a full post-incident report is still to come. The FAA's ground stop followed routine maintenance, and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said L3Harris, the contractor that runs the FAA's telecommunications network, was replacing copper lines with fiber at a remote FAA site when a router being replaced started flooding other routers in the air traffic control system. Officials did not link the outage to SMART, the FAA's new AI-powered air traffic planning system, which had been expanded nationwide only three days earlier, and the outage instead revealed a design weakness because the FAA's backup communications run on the same network, so there is no independent backup.

For privacy and AI governance professionals, the article says responsible use of AI in development is not only about the tools but also about whether the human capacity to review their output keeps pace. The IAPP describes itself as a policy neutral, not-for-profit association founded in 2000 with a mission to define, promote and improve the professions of privacy, AI governance and digital responsibility globally. The article is an analysis published for IAPP members, and it does not say what further steps Microsoft, the FAA or L3Harris will take beyond the full post-incident report still to come from Microsoft.
