stories.Headline: Analyst upgrades Nebius to Buy after 70% selloff on cheap valuation
stories.Summary:
On November 24, 2026, Seeking Alpha published an analyst article by Juxtaposed Ideas that upgraded Nebius Group N.V. (NBIS) to Buy after what the author described as a 70% selloff in the stock. The author wrote that since a Hold rating in August 2026, Nebius had suffered steep declines, with the stock breaching the Q2 2026 to Q3 2026 trading floor of $150s. The piece was published at 10:40 AM ET and carried the headline claim of a meltdown the author had been waiting for. The author disclosed a beneficial long position in NBIS, CRWV, AMZN, GOOG and PLTR through stock ownership, options or other derivatives. The upgrade rests on the author's estimate that the selloff brought NBIS to an end of FY2026 EV/Sales of 4.64x and FY2028 EV/Sales of 1.25x.

The article cites $38.7B in remaining performance obligations, rising lease prices and contract prepayments covering roughly 100% of new capacity costs as support for growth, cash flow resilience and faster payback prospects. It also points to a preferred sovereign AI infrastructure partnership with PLTR as implying further US commercial growth as more enterprises demand open-source AI models. The author frames the Buy rating as preferably acted on upon a bounce, for an improved margin of safety amid falling-knife risks. The author lists project timing delays, financing and dilution risks from aggressive capex, data center moratoriums and volatility pending the bottoming of the AI trade as risks that may constrain a recovery. The article states that market rotation away from AI and Big-Tech sectors has finally occurred, which brought NBIS down to the author's estimated valuations.

The author notes the analysis is for informational purposes only and should not be considered professional investment advice. Seeking Alpha's disclosure states that past performance is no guarantee of future results and that no recommendation is being given as to suitability for any particular investor. The article does not say what happens next beyond the author's view that a bounce may offer a better entry, and it gives no further dates or figures for the company's plans. The author's position disclosure and the site's disclaimer accompany the rating change, and the piece invites readers to do their own research before investing. No company statement or independent confirmation of the figures appears in the article.

stories.Headline: Together AI makes preemptible GPU compute generally available at half the on-demand rate
stories.Summary:
Together AI made preemptible GPU compute generally available on Together GPU Clusters on November 24, 2026, covering Kubernetes and Slurm deployments in all regions, according to the company. The interruptible nodes use the same NVIDIA accelerated compute as standard nodes and cost a flat 50% of the on-demand rate, with no bidding or spot market pricing. Customers can add preemptible capacity when creating a cluster or to one already running, and the nodes draw from unused supply and can be reclaimed when that capacity is needed elsewhere. Standard nodes remain the default because they are provisioned synchronously and are never preempted, while preemptible nodes fill in asynchronously as spare capacity becomes available. Usage is metered every one to two minutes and billed sub-hourly, so customers pay roughly for the minutes a node runs rather than a full hour.

Customers set targets in multiples of eight GPUs, and the documentation distinguishes desired_preemptible_gpus from allocated_preemptible_gpus so they can see when live capacity falls short of the target. After a reclamation the cluster keeps its target and automatically provisions replacements as spare capacity returns, without another capacity request. Reclamation starts with a drain window of at most five minutes and ends with node removal regardless of whether work has finished, and there is no minimum node lifetime. On Kubernetes, reclamation cordons the node, emits a TogetherPreemptionNotified warning and sends pods a SIGTERM signal, and workloads can set terminationGracePeriodSeconds to use up to the full drain window for checkpointing, while pods without that setting get the default of 30 seconds. On Slurm, preemptible and standard nodes share partitions and the same scheduling feature, so the scheduler cannot target preemptible nodes or keep a job off them, jobs still running when a node is removed are killed, and only jobs submitted with --requeue are resubmitted.

Together AI recommends the capacity for checkpointed or retryable work such as short experiments, configuration sweeps, fine-tuning, evaluations, distillation, batch inference and temporary inference bursts, and it said it already uses preemptible clusters for internal research, development and testing and for non-critical production workloads. The company said multi-day runs without checkpoints, user-facing serving without fallback and workloads with strict service-level objectives are not suitable. A cluster can consist entirely of preemptible nodes, but Together can reclaim all of them, and while data on shared volumes persists, shared volumes and the Slurm control plane remain reachable while no nodes are running only in some regions and on a best-effort basis, so customers needing continuously reachable shared storage need at least one standard node. Nodes cannot be converted between standard and preemptible types in place.

stories.Headline: Together AI adds Tencent Hy4 multimodal model to its serverless inference platform
stories.Summary:
Together AI added the Tencent Hy4 model to its serverless inference platform on November 24, 2026. This action provides developers with access to a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model. The new offering allows users to process both images and text. It is the first model in the Hy family with these vision capabilities. The launch targets enterprises that struggle with the costs of self-hosting.

The model uses 770B total parameters and 49B active parameters per token. It features a 1M-token context window and supports tool calling and JSON output. Users access it via the tencent/Hy4 string through the Together chat completions API. Input tokens cost $0.83 per 1M, while cached input tokens cost $0.042 per 1M. Output tokens are priced at $2.50 per 1M tokens.

Together AI demonstrated the model reading a chart screenshot to return structured JSON. The company also showed the model reproducing that chart as one HTML file. Another demonstration showed the model generating a functional browser game from one text prompt. Together AI claims its neutral catalog helps enterprises avoid the risk of model lock-in. This strategy counters platforms that remain primarily optimized for the proprietary OpenAI ecosystem.

Futurum data show that self-hosting costs hold up 50% of AI pilots. Many enterprises cite AI agent reliability and hallucination as a top production challenge. Specifically, 55.4 percent of enterprises identify these reliability issues as a major barrier. IT operations and cybersecurity are top areas for planned agentic deployments over 18 months. Customer experience automation is also listed as a leading priority for these firms.

Tencent trained Hy4 to operate professional software including CAD tools and Blender. The company evaluated the model on financial research, office work, and game development. These evaluations included the use of Unity, Godot, and the Unreal Engine. The model follows the Hy4 Preview version by adding computer-use and image input. It is described as a frontier-class open-weight model for managed inference platforms.

Observers will watch if Hy4 workloads move to production in Q1 2027. It remains open whether this pricing accelerates the shift of stalled pilots. The market will see how rival platforms respond to these multimodal features. It is unclear if JSON output will demonstrably reduce production hallucination failures. The speed of enterprise procurement requiring multi-model API compatibility is also unknown.

stories.Headline: Recent graduates use AI to apply for jobs while employers use AI to screen them
stories.Summary:
The article reports that recent college graduates are using artificial intelligence to search for openings, polish resumes and apply quickly to many jobs, while employers are turning to AI-powered screening tools to sift through the larger number of applications. Mahathi Vinapamula, a recent San Jose State graduate who earned a business administration degree in May, estimates she applied to about 500 jobs during a yearlong search. She said an AI hiring agent has several times determined whether she receives a second interview with a human. Raciel Diaz, a recent San Francisco State University graduate, said the advent of AI onto the job market has been a pain in his ass. The article was published by EdSource on November 25, 2026.

A survey of more than 3,000 hiring managers by the AI-powered hiring platform Hirevue found that 43% of organizations now use artificial intelligence to screen resumes and 40% use AI to communicate with candidates. According to the latest data from Braven, a nonprofit that helps college students launch their careers, 54% of San Jose State students who graduated in 2024 and participated in Braven’s courses landed a full-time job requiring a bachelor’s degree or enrolled in graduate school six months after graduation. For the class of 2025, that rate dropped to 43%. Braven works with employers and mentors to prepare students for their job search. Vinapamula recently ended her hunt for a marketing job and will instead pursue a master’s degree at Santa Clara University.

Christie Brodbeck, Hirevue’s vice president of customer science, said final hiring decisions remain with a human, but with more AI-polished, look-alike resumes and cover letters, employers are also using application exercises to assess candidates’ skills. Sue Harbour, associate dean and executive director of UC Berkeley Career Engagement, said relationship building has always been important but will give students a leg up today more so than ever. She said students should work smarter, not harder, by tapping their networks rather than simply applying to more jobs. Diana Phuong, executive director of Braven Bay Area, said graduates have struggled to secure jobs because some companies in the region are hiring fewer entry-level workers. Phuong said it is not what you know, not what your resume says, but who you know and who knows you in this world.

Brian Justie, a senior research analyst at the UCLA Labor Center, said the renewed importance of networking is ironic considering how some AI proponents argue the technology can help reduce equity gaps. He said it brings the process of getting a job back to an old model probably based only on existing connections, such as which of your dad’s friends can make the intro that gets you a foot in the door to a face-to-face interview. Jesse Rothstein, director of UC Berkeley’s Center for Studies in Higher Education, said the overall labor market has slightly softened in recent years and reduced demand for workers is more pronounced for recent college graduates. He said employers are able to offload some of the cost of the job search to the job seeker because there is less demand for workers.

Iman Noor, a San Jose State senior majoring in accounting, secured a full-time position at Deloitte before graduating next spring after getting a referral from a friend who works at the professional services firm. The article says the job market for new college graduates has slowed in recent years, and the omnipresence of artificial intelligence means job seekers often need to apply to more positions to land an interview. It says applicants are using AI to polish cover letters and mass apply to positions, and employers are turning to AI-powered screening tools in response. Rothstein said that during the Great Recession employers developed a norm of conducting more interviews than before to give them more opportunities to assess candidates.

He said employers are now using AI to sort through applications, and job seekers are questioning whether positions are real or not. Diaz said he started and stopped his education at various Bay Area community colleges before graduating from San Francisco State last spring, and along the way worked as a full stack developer, caregiver and receptionist for the city of Walnut Creek. Vinapamula hopes the additional education and opportunities to network at Santa Clara University will help her land a full-time job next spring. She said she likely will have to continue braving the gauntlet of AI hiring agents.

She said she understands why companies are using them but thinks she would have better luck speaking to an actual human. Diaz said he has almost gone through the stages of grief, was really sad, really depressed and really angry, and now throws his application everywhere no matter what company it is. He acknowledged that networking is not his strongest skill and he is trying to improve. The article leaves open whether Vinapamula or Diaz will land full-time jobs.

stories.Headline: OpenRouter removes three AI providers after data exposure incidents
stories.Summary:
OpenRouter removed three artificial intelligence providers from its platform in November 2026 after an investigation revealed they violated data policies. The security firm Dragos discovered that sensitive information, including credentials and unique tracking links, had leaked through test prompts. Dragos sent two million prompts through the platform and found that at least three providers exposed data to unauthorized parties. OpenRouter subsequently off-boarded Together AI, Phala, and Novita, while Atlas Cloud voluntarily withdrew its models for security testing.

The removal process affected requests involving models such as MiniMax and DeepSeek V4 Flash. OpenRouter revoked Zero Data Retention eligibility for 125 endpoints as a precautionary measure and notified all potentially affected customers. Investigations showed that Together AI suffered a repository credential exposure, Phala had a server compromise, and Novita experienced a routing misconfiguration. The platform is now conducting technical verification of network paths to ensure requests are not forwarded to third parties.

OpenRouter stated that no breach occurred on its own systems and that it takes data policy enforcement very seriously. The company expressed gratitude for the report from Dragos and is adapting those testing techniques for ongoing monitoring. OpenRouter is requiring validation and assurances before restoring Zero Data Retention eligibility to any removed endpoint. The affected providers are currently strengthening their data retention policies and security controls to prevent future incidents.

OpenRouter will continue to raise the security bar for any providers that wish to remain on the platform. Users who may have been affected by these leaks are advised to rotate any potentially exposed secrets. The company is encouraging all involved providers to create public incident write-ups to explain the failures. OpenRouter will maintain a live list of security announcements as providers address the findings from the researchers.

stories.Headline: Nvidia leads tech sell-off as AI cost concerns return and Huang rally fades
stories.Summary:
Technology stocks experienced a significant sell-off on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, led by sharp declines in Nvidia and other semiconductor companies. This downturn occurred as the brief market rally sparked by the return of CEO Jensen Huang faded away. Investors renewed their concerns regarding the high costs of artificial intelligence build-outs and the overall sustainability of AI profitability. Fresh inflation data further reduced the appetite for growth stocks, contributing to the broader market decline.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 1 percent, while the VanEck Semiconductor ETF, which tracks the sector, edged down 2 percent. Nvidia shares slumped 5 percent on Wednesday after previously recording one of its best days on record on Monday. Micron Technology also declined 5 percent, while Oracle fell more than 4 percent. Other chip names including Advanced Micro Devices, Marvell Technology, and Intel all dropped about 2 percent or more. Amazon, Tesla, and Alphabet each declined about 2 percent, and Microsoft lost more than 1 percent.

Venu Krishna, the head of U.S. equity strategy at Barclays, described the current market situation as panic. He stated that the growth narrative for artificial intelligence has hit a wall, which may lead the market to expect a macro shock. Bankim Chadha of Deutsche Bank characterized the return of Jensen Huang as a circuit breaker for the market. These analysts suggest that the excitement over the leadership change failed to calm fears about the high spending required for AI.

The market is now digesting a hot inflation reading that suggests higher interest rates could further dent demand for growth stocks. While most AI-linked stocks plummeted, the AI lab Anthropic climbed more than 4 percent after its shares dropped below the initial public offering price. Investors remain cautious about whether the artificial intelligence trade can maintain its momentum amid these economic pressures. The industry continues to monitor how these macroeconomic factors will influence future tech investments.

stories.Headline: Global capability centres bring core IT in house as AI reshapes outsourcing
stories.Summary:
Global Capability Centres are increasingly taking ownership of core IT capabilities and moving strategic technology in-house, according to TechGig, which published the report on August 27, 2026. The shift is driven by factors including artificial intelligence and software-defined vehicles, and it is creating demand for new, specialised AI vendors. This changes traditional outsourcing models, in which critical technology and engineering functions were fragmented across many external service providers. The report says this evolution does not mean IT vendors will disappear.

The traditional outsourcing model often left enterprises with a disjointed view of their technology estate, according to Prashobh Chandralayam, Global GCC Leader at Kyndryl, who spoke to Moneycontrol. He said an enterprise's IT budget could be spread across 10 to 15 vendors, each handling different segments of the same platform, and that this fragmentation hindered modernisation. The GCC model offers a consolidated approach that brings these capabilities under one roof. In the automotive sector, Sharad Bairathi, Founder and Managing Director of Volkswagen Group-owned Embitel Technologies, told Moneycontrol that software-defined vehicles have pushed automakers to internalise more development. He said original equipment manufacturers, including Volkswagen, sought greater control over areas such as edge analytics and cloud technology, moving away from vendor dependency for every change.

Pari Natarajan, CEO of Zinnov, said at a recent Bengaluru press conference that vendor consolidation is not imminent, according to the report. He said that on the AI side the number of vendors will become dramatically more fragmented, and that enterprises are increasingly willing to experiment with new AI-native service providers, especially in slower market conditions. The report describes an emerging hybrid model in which GCCs own architecture, intellectual property, governance and strategic technology capabilities, while external providers continue to play a role in specialised domains, particularly AI. It says the question is not whether IT vendors will disappear but how much of an enterprise's core technology they will continue to control. For Indian engineering talent and the IT services sector, the report says, the shift means increased responsibility for critical architecture and IP decisions within GCCs, alongside new opportunities for AI-focused tech startups.

stories.Headline: SAP CEO Christian Klein says India can lead in applying AI across industries
stories.Summary:
SAP CEO Christian Klein said in a recent interview that India is well-positioned to take the lead in applying artificial intelligence across industries such as manufacturing, finance and life sciences, according to TechGig. He noted that AI models are becoming commoditized and that the real opportunity lies in applying them to improve productivity and business outcomes. Klein highlighted India's talent pool, its significant investments in AI infrastructure and a pro-business government as factors that create a conducive environment for AI innovation. He also pointed to companies such as TCS, Adani and Airtel as actively building the infrastructure needed to support AI ecosystems.

Klein said during his visit to India that geopolitical tensions are affecting IT spending, but he noted a strong upward trend in IT investments as companies increasingly see AI as a solution to challenges posed by inflation and supply chain disruptions. He said that if inflation remains high, companies need to find productivity improvements somewhere in their operations, and that AI can become a very strong lever for that. He emphasized the importance of workforce transformation and warned that the risk for Indian IT and software services companies lies in failing to align their workforce with AI advancements. He expressed optimism about the Indian IT ecosystem despite potential short-term disruptions, as new categories of work emerge alongside automation.

SAP is hiring aggressively in India for roles such as full-stack AI developers and data engineers to support the development and deployment of AI solutions tailored for enterprise use cases, according to the article. The company is also investing in partnerships with top universities to engage with students early in their education and enhance their skills in AI development. Klein's insights reflect what the article describes as a strong belief in India's capacity to leverage its unique strengths to become a frontrunner in the global AI landscape. The articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: CNCF finds virtual machines host 53% of production applications as AI workloads grow
stories.Summary:
The Cloud Native Computing Foundation and Linux Foundation Research published new research finding that virtual machines host an average of 53% of production applications, InfoQ reported on November 24, 2026. The report surveyed 492 cloud-native practitioners and technology leaders in September 2026. Among organisations expanding their VM footprint, 34% identified AI and agentic workloads as a contributing factor. The research challenges the assumption that cloud-native adoption necessarily means moving away from virtual machines. The survey found that 51% of respondents run at least half of their production applications on VMs.

The VM share rises to an average of 64% in organisations with more than 10,000 employees, compared with 45% among organisations with fewer than 500 employees. Some 71% of respondents who provided both current and expected workload figures anticipate their VM share remaining within the same range over the next year. Among organisations expanding their VM footprint, 47% cited security and isolation as a contributing factor. MicroVM sandboxing adoption is expected to increase from 20% current use to 30% planned use, while confidential computing is expected to grow from 12% to 26%. Some 61% of respondents described their VM and container administration teams as collaborative or fully integrated.

The report identifies hardware-level VM isolation, containers running inside VMs, and MicroVM sandboxing as approaches organisations are using to contain AI workloads. The survey was sponsored by CNCF and Broadcom. The report states that its results should be read as reported industry perspectives rather than a complete census of cloud-native deployments. The research states that VMs continue to offer isolation and support for workloads that depend on dedicated operating systems or established virtualisation environments. The report states that Kubernetes and containers remain important but are not necessarily the right execution model for every workload.

Among respondents using VMs, 8% reported using KubeVirt, the CNCF project that allows virtual machines to be managed through Kubernetes resources and APIs. The report states that technologies such as KubeVirt and Kata Containers show how virtualisation can integrate with container orchestration. The report states that MicroVMs provide lightweight environments to isolate short-lived or potentially untrusted workloads. The report states that AI agents increasingly generate and execute code, interact with tools, and access external systems. The report states that virtual machines offer a stronger isolation boundary than conventional containers, which share the host operating system kernel.

The report states that the findings suggest organisations are increasingly combining virtual machines and containers to accommodate different application and security requirements. The report states that containers provide portability and efficient application packaging. The report states that the findings reinforce a shift in how cloud-native infrastructure is evolving. The report states that for platform engineering teams, the research highlights the need to accommodate different execution environments without fragmenting operational practices. The report states that AI makes isolation, resource utilisation and workload security increasingly important infrastructure considerations.

The report states that the figures on MicroVM sandboxing and confidential computing represent reported intentions rather than confirmed deployments. The report states that KubeVirt brings VM lifecycle management into existing Kubernetes operational practices without requiring applications to abandon their virtualised environments. The report states that its findings provide a useful indication of where infrastructure priorities are moving. The report states that managing different workload types is increasingly becoming a shared platform engineering responsibility. The report states that the findings point towards continued coexistence rather than a wholesale migration to one deployment model.

stories.Headline: Seven in ten engineers admit they do not fully understand AI-generated code they approve
stories.Summary:
CodeRabbit sponsored the LeadDev AI Code Review Report 2026, which was published in November 2026 and reported by SD Times. The survey found that seven in ten engineers say they do not fully understand the AI-generated code they approve. LeadDev Research conducted the survey of 377 engineers and engineering leaders in the U.S. and Europe. The survey ran between Sept. 29 and Oct. 17, 2026, and 325 respondents completed the full survey. The report was released from San Francisco.

Only 26% of respondents are very confident they understand an AI-generated change as thoroughly as a human-written one. Fifty-eight percent understand the intent but not every detail, and 11% say they are mostly checking that it runs and passes tests. Forty-five percent of organizations now name code review as the single biggest bottleneck in software delivery. That is more than unclear requirements at 19%, QA and testing at 17% and CI pipelines at 7% combined. Half say pull requests per developer have risen at least 25% since adopting AI coding tools, and 67% say PRs have grown in size.

Harjot Gill, CEO and co-founder of CodeRabbit, said writing code is no longer the hard part and that understanding, validating and trusting it is. He said reviewers are being asked to approve code faster than anyone can understand it, and nearly half of teams ask the coding agent to grade its own homework. He said you cannot review agent-scale code at human scale and that teams have to fight AI with AI, but not the AI that wrote the code. He said what is needed is independent validation grounded in a team's own codebase context and standards, with humans making the final call. Michael Hill, Managing Editor of LeadDev, said AI made code creation abundant and pushed the burden downstream to review.

Eighty-two percent of respondents say developers still manually review most or all AI-generated code before it is merged. Seventy-four percent always or usually have a human verify what an AI review tool flags, while 47% of teams rely on the same AI coding agents that wrote the code to review it. Only 18% say reviewers regularly have enough context to judge a change's architectural impact and blast radius, and 68% say reviewers do not consistently know which changes need deeper scrutiny. Only 14% of organizations have clearly defined, consistently applied standards for reviewing AI-generated code, while 42% apply guidelines inconsistently and 42% leave it to each team. When an AI agent writes the code, another AI agent reviews it and an automated system merges it, 48% say the person who requested the change is accountable for how it behaves in production and 14% say the person who approved it.

More teams say review cycles have slowed since adopting AI, at 38%, than say they have sped up, at 25%. More organizations track AI token usage at 30% than escaped defects at 22%, and 24% track no code review metrics at all. The report recommends that engineering leaders plan for review capacity the way they plan for build time and on-call load. It also recommends triaging every change before review, giving reviewers the context behind each change, deciding what approval means and tracking escaped defects and reviewer workload as well as throughput and token spend. Hill said that of the 377 engineers and engineering leaders surveyed, 45% name review capacity as their biggest delivery bottleneck and only 18% say reviewers consistently have the context to judge what an AI-generated change could break.

Hill said that where review is holding up, organizations are using specialized agents to give human reviewers the context behind each pull request and focusing the attention of senior engineers only on critical changes that need their input. Earlier in November 2026, CodeRabbit announced it had grown annual recurring revenue from $10 million to $100 million in just over a year. CodeRabbit says it has surfaced more than 100 million issues that developers have used to fix bugs, security flaws and standards violations before code reached production. CodeRabbit says those issues came across 20,000 customers, 400,000 monthly active users, 300,000 open-source projects and more than 8.5 million connected repositories. The full report is available at https://leaddev.com/the-ai-code-review-report-2026.

The articles do not say what CodeRabbit or LeadDev will do next with the report's recommendations. The articles do not say whether any organization has adopted the recommended review capacity planning, triage or tracking practices. The articles do not give a response from any organization named in the survey findings. The articles do not say how the survey sample was selected beyond the 377 respondents in the U.S. and Europe. The articles do not say what happens to the 42% of organizations that apply guidelines inconsistently or the 42% that leave review standards to each team.

stories.Headline: Ez-ai founder runs company back office with AI agents but keeps payment and email approval
stories.Summary:
Skene Bennellick, the founder of Ez-ai.nz, wrote in an article published by IT Brief Australia on 25 November 2026 that he runs his own company with no account managers, no bookkeeper and no admin staff, because most of the back office is handled by AI agents he built for himself. He said he has spent about 13 years in AI and automation inside large organisations, working as a business analyst, a solution designer, a developer and a product owner. According to his account, the agents write his call plans, take meeting notes and actions, write and send a daily newsletter, produce explainer videos, manage search visibility and ad spend, shortlist government tenders, build invoices, chase payments, record expenses, prepare wages and tax payments for his approval, set aside GST, keep his pipeline and cash forecast current, and audit client systems daily and propose fixes for his review. He wrote that the agents prepare the work and he approves it, and that the email agent drafts replies but cannot send them, because he reads each one, changes what needs changing and presses send himself. He said anything new that touches invoices, payments or client email starts in a test mode where the only person it can email is him, until he has watched it work on real data.

He described a payment system that once treated "accepted by the bank" as "paid", although a payment can be accepted and then declined, and said it now waits for the bank's final answer and emails him straight away when a payment is declined. He said the gap between what a system thinks happened and what really happened is where most agent failures live, and that logging, alerts and a human check matter more than which AI model is chosen. He wrote that he uses four questions before handing anything over: what the problem is, what it costs today, where the freed time will go, and whether the number moved at 30 and 90 days. He said a single, well-defined process often costs a few thousand dollars, while a system that runs a whole workflow is more like $15,000 to $25,000, plus running costs for AI usage, hosting and care, which he said are usually smaller than people fear but never zero.

He said six hours a week at $45 an hour is about $14,000 a year, but that unless those hours go somewhere on purpose, such as more quotes out, faster replies or more time with customers, the work expands to fill the time and nothing on the bottom line moves. He said that if a provider, including him, gives vague answers on where a person approves the work, what happens when the system is unsure and how he will find out if something has quietly stopped, the risk is the client's. He wrote that the public conversation about AI is mostly about whether it will replace people, but that running his own company on it has changed the question for him to which decisions you are willing to hand over and which you are not. He said that question cannot be answered from a slide deck, but by putting agents on real work, watching closely and moving the line one step at a time.

stories.Headline: WatchGuard director says shadow AI reveals gaps in SaaS visibility
stories.Summary:
Mick McCarter, director of product for Zero Trust Access at WatchGuard Technologies, said in an article published by IT Brief Australia on 24 November 2026 that shadow AI exposes a wider weakness in how organisations manage and monitor their software environments, and that the real issue is SaaS visibility. He said employees use AI tools without the knowledge or approval of their organisations, often before the risks have been assessed, and that cloud applications let staff adopt new tools in minutes without involving IT. He pointed to WatchGuard's 2026 Cybersecurity Hygiene Report, in which 64% of employees admitted to using unauthorised AI tools for work while fewer than 40% of respondents maintained an accurate software inventory. He said these findings suggest many organisations do not have a complete understanding of their SaaS environments.

McCarter said an accurate software inventory is only a starting point, because an approved application can still introduce vulnerabilities through its integrations, permissions and the resources it can access, and he used OAuth connections as an example of legitimate applications receiving access that creates an exposure the organisation does not know about. He said security teams need to understand how applications connect to one another, what data and resources they can access, and how users and identities interact with them. He said SaaS environments are not static, since applications gain new integrations and permissions and an application judged secure at approval may present a different risk months later, and that traditional software asset management and periodic reviews cannot necessarily keep pace. He said effective SaaS security requires continuous visibility across applications, identities, configurations and integrations, so that unmanaged applications, excessive permissions, insecure configurations and unusual activity are found as they emerge rather than after a security incident.

McCarter said the attention given to shadow AI is an opportunity to address the broader issue, but that trying to control every AI application individually is unlikely to be sustainable, because new tools will keep emerging and AI capabilities will become part of existing SaaS applications. He said organisations should move away from treating each new application or technology as a separate security problem and instead keep an ongoing understanding of their SaaS ecosystem, including which applications employees use, how they connect, what permissions they have, what they can access and how identities interact with them. He said this does not mean abandoning application controls or acceptable-use policies, which remain important parts of security governance but need the visibility and context that make them effective. He said shadow AI is a warning sign that organisations may have lost sight of what is happening across their wider software environments, and that addressing the visibility gap will better equip them to manage unauthorised AI adoption and the broader risks of a connected and constantly changing SaaS ecosystem.

stories.Headline: 3forge CEO Robert Cooke argues enterprises need shared data and application foundations for AI
stories.Summary:
Robert Cooke, the chief executive of 3forge, wrote an article published by IT Brief Australia on 25 November 2026 arguing that large enterprises need a shared data and application foundation for AI. He said large enterprises often run sprawling technology estates where a surge in AI-generated applications and automated workflows has not been matched by a unified approach to data access, system interaction and governance. The 2026 MuleSoft Connectivity Benchmark Report, which he cited, found that surveyed organizations manage an average of 957 applications, yet only 27 per cent are connected. Cooke said this divided environment produces fragmented handoffs, where developers copy data between platforms and repeat business logic, which can create conflicting versions of the same rule. He gave the example of three applications independently deciding whether a market is open, where a calendar update made in only one could produce conflicting answers within the same workflow.

Cooke said the same report found IT teams spend an average of 36 per cent of their time designing, building and testing custom integrations between systems and data. He said AI agents and automated workflows intensify the problem because they are not only new data consumers but may also invoke operations and take part in business processes. He cited KPMG's Q2 2026 survey of U.S. C-suite and business leaders at enterprises with at least $1 billion in revenue, in which 58 per cent cited data readiness and access as the biggest challenge to deploying AI agents. Cooke said chief data officers must decide which recurring capabilities should stay application-specific and which should become shared infrastructure, and he argued the answer increasingly requires two reusable foundations, one for data and one for applications, with operational control spanning both.

He described four friction points: extending governance along the entire path rather than at static permission points, bridging real-time and historical data, moving AI-enabled applications from prototype into production, and connecting data, logic and execution without brittle handoffs. Cooke said separate data fabric, AI application and governance initiatives may each succeed while fragmentation persists where they meet. He pointed to e-commerce, gaming and financial services as industries showing how reusable capabilities let developers focus on differentiated work, and said these patterns point to a data fabric for governed enterprise data access and an application engine supplying reusable capabilities for business-specific software. He said the two should operate as a continuum rather than two distinct layers, with source systems remaining authoritative and external applications consuming the fabric through governed interfaces.

Cooke said the objective is coordination, not architectural uniformity, and that governance must extend across the operating environment, covering what data an agent can access, what operations it can invoke and how its activity is supervised, including auditing the data an agent accesses and tracing which information informed a decision. Cooke recommended starting with a bounded workflow, preserving the wider estate and expanding when later use cases can reuse what has been established. He said each implementation should leave behind reusable connections, models, transformations, controls and runtime capabilities so the next project starts from a stronger foundation. He said this lets governance requirements be addressed at the architectural level, so compliance with institutional policies becomes part of how applications operate rather than something each project implements separately.

stories.Headline: Companies curb tokenmaxxing as AI costs and security risks rise
stories.Summary:
The rise of "Tokenmaxxing," which is the excessive use of AI tokens by engineers, has prompted companies to take a closer look at how AI resources are being used, according to an article by Pejman Tabassomi, Field CTO at Datadog, published by IT Brief Australia on 25 November 2026. AI models can generate thousands of tokens in the space of a few minutes, especially for intensive tasks and workloads, but the cost of running AI models is escalating faster than expected. Many organisations have used token consumption as an indicator of productivity, which has incentivised Tokenmaxxing to the extent that engineering teams at Meta created a "token leaderboard" to rank token usage. Datadog's 2026 State of AI Engineering report found that token usage per request more than doubled year over year for median customers and quadrupled for 90th-percentile power users among Datadog-monitored services. For organisations, the challenge is to find the right balance between AI cloud spend, return on investment and security, though tightening controls on AI usage too far risks slowing innovation.

Tokenmaxxing can be managed through context optimisation, which means reducing token costs throughout an agent request by restricting the context processed by the LLM to what is necessary while maintaining response quality. By optimising outputs, it is possible to filter out irrelevant search results and deduplicate repetitive content, and this process also allows teams to break down sessions with an AI model to identify what contributes to the end-to-end cost of a request. As AI usage grows, so too do the security risks, and Tokenmaxxing has contributed by generating higher volumes of sensitive data inputs and outputs, increasing exposure to threat actors using new techniques that teams are still learning to address. One example is prompt injection, where an attacker manipulates the information or instructions provided to a model, and Datadog's researchers found that prompts can also be injected through instructions delivered via retrieved documents, tool results or files in a trusted workspace. Other risks include supply chain compromises, where attackers target popular third-party tools, libraries, registries and even Model Context Protocol servers, and data leakage, where sensitive data can leak into LLM datasets unless it is actively scanned or blocked.

The first step in managing these security risks is to create an inventory of the AI models, agents and tools that engineering teams are using, since AI agents are made up of models, instructions, data and tools. Unified monitoring and observability lets teams trace how a prompt leads to an action and place controls along that path, and guardrails can help block unsafe prompts or tool calls before they reach downstream systems. As AI use continues to grow, organisations must control Tokenmaxxing while maintaining the productivity and innovation benefits that AI offers, and reducing unnecessary token consumption needs to be paired with visibility into the models, agents, tools and data involved. Unified monitoring, observability and appropriate guardrails can help organisations put controls in place, identify potential security risks and support AI use without disrupting established workflows.

stories.Headline: AWS lets AI agents buy marketplace products with spending limits and audit trails
stories.Summary:
AWS introduced new buying tools in AWS Marketplace for human users and AI agents on 24 November 2026, according to IT Brief Australia. The update adds agent purchasing, a new data category and broader procurement features, along with approval workflows for people who do not hold AWS accounts. AI agents can now discover and buy select products through the x402 agentic payment protocol using AgentCore payments, which is part of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Those transactions are billed in USD through an existing AWS account, keeping agent purchases within the billing and budget controls finance teams already use. Customers can set spending limits before an agent transacts, audit every agent-initiated transaction in AWS CloudTrail and monitor transaction health through dashboards in AgentCore Observability within CloudWatch.

Sellers that want to support agent purchases must register with AWS Marketplace and integrate with the AWS Marketplace x402 SDK, going through the same registration and review process as other marketplace sellers. AWS is also adding data as a service as a new product category, so customers and their agents can discover, evaluate, subscribe to and pay for commercial datasets through the marketplace website tools, APIs and an MCP server, without separate vendor onboarding. The agent mode conversational interface now supports customers who start with a business problem rather than a named product, and it can explain pricing models, suggest configurations based on budget, flag purchase order thresholds and summarise licence terms, though human confirmation is still required before any purchase is completed. A trust agent feature works with Drata and Vanta to gather compliance documentation from participating vendors and show trust centre information inside the marketplace workflow, and for supported Amazon Machine Image products a deployment agent can create a deployment plan that buyers review before confirming deployment through AWS CloudFormation. Customers can now create approval policies based on spend thresholds or product type, send agreements to approvers who can respond through a browser using a one-time passcode, and route transactions into procurement systems including Coupa and SAP Ariba, while some US customers can buy select software without setting up an AWS account first.

Nandhan Puppala, General Manager of Uber AI Solutions, said the next frontier in AI would be defined by the quality and readiness of real-world data, and that bringing the company's multimodal datasets to AWS Marketplace would help enterprises unblock data pipelines and accelerate their path to production. Nikki Santoro, Chief Executive Officer of IMDb, said demand for trusted entertainment data was accelerating and that the marketplace would simplify how customers discover, procure and integrate IMDb data. AWS linked the new data category to the growing use of AI agents that consume data directly, giving examples including investment analysis using firmographic and funding data, agricultural robotics trained on synthetic field data and venue management systems checking live weather information. AWS framed the trust agent feature as a response to slow procurement cycles when compliance teams are involved late in the process.

stories.Headline: IHL Group ranks GK Software first in food, drug, convenience and mass retail POS study
stories.Summary:
GK Software has been ranked the leading provider in the food, drug, convenience and mass retail segment in IHL Group's latest point-of-sale market study, according to a report published on 23 November 2026. The study assessed 19 international POS and mobile POS providers against 147 criteria, including functionality, architecture, unified commerce, internationalisation, resilience, artificial intelligence and market strength. GK also ranked second overall across the broader field covering food, softlines, general merchandise and hospitality, and it placed first among 11 vendors assessed in fuel and convenience. Within the food, drug, convenience and mass retail category, analysts gave GK the highest functionality rating among the 10 providers serving that market, citing self-checkout, store resilience, omnichannel processes and regulatory support as areas of strength. In apparel, fashion and emerging formats, GK ranked third out of 19 vendors, with the report citing platform architecture, internationalisation and sector-specific functions such as markdown, price optimisation, virtual try-on support and RFID-assisted checkout.

The study ranked GK second among all providers in AI, machine learning and agentic systems, pointing to products including GK AIR, GK Vision and the GK Agentic Framework, and said the company's AI tools are already used in business processes or pilot programmes, ranging from price optimisation and personalised offers to loss prevention at self-checkout. GK also ranked first among the 19 vendors for its responses on bounded AI autonomy and AI audit evidence. Analysts rated GK CLOUD4RETAIL among the strongest platforms in the field, citing its microservices-based design, integration options and headless implementation model, and the study ranked GK first among the 19 vendors on headless, decoupled implementation. The report said the company has more than 572,000 installed POS, mobile POS and self-checkout devices across 68 countries, and IHL ranked it second highest on its growth, direction and resilience axis. Michael Scheibner, Chief Executive Officer of GK Software, said retailers are looking for platforms that effectively combine resilience, openness, unified commerce and AI in ways that create measurable business value, and that being recognised among the leading providers in areas such as AI, platform architecture and retail operations confirms the company's strategy of delivering a flexible platform that helps retailers across industries adapt, innovate and grow.

Orit Bar-Ad, Chief Innovation Evangelist at GK Software, said the company offers AI that is already in productive use today, with proven returns from fully automated personalisation, recommendation and price optimisation for millions of items to computer vision-powered loss prevention at self-checkout, and that it places the utmost importance on transparency, auditability and compliance with regulatory requirements such as the EU AI Act. She said the company's agentic architecture is open, model-agnostic and can be flexibly operated in the cloud, in a hybrid environment or entirely on-premises. The findings reflect a market in which suppliers are becoming harder to distinguish on core selling functions alone, with vendors increasingly separated by performance at the edges of the transaction, including resilience, order management, implementation, international reach and AI in production. IHL said the next phase of competition in retail transaction systems will depend less on basic selling functions and more on the ability to remain operational during system failures, support changing regulatory requirements and introduce AI use cases in a controlled way. The report said GK's standing in food retail, platform architecture and AI positions it strongly for that shift.

stories.Headline: Denodo executive says AI sovereignty demands domestic compute and data control
stories.Summary:
The article, published on 24 November 2026 by IT Brief Australia, was written by Ravi Shankar, the Senior Vice President and Chief Marketing Officer at Denodo, and it describes AI sovereignty as a new form of geopolitical and economic competition that goes beyond data residency alone. Shankar says AI sovereignty covers control over the infrastructure, governance frameworks, compute power and data ecosystems that underpin AI innovation, and he warns that nations failing to act decisively risk becoming structurally dependent on a handful of dominant players, most notably the United States. He reports that the United States operates more than 5,000 data centres with 3,000 more planned, which he says is more than the rest of the world combined, creating what he calls a profound asymmetry in access to the computational backbone required to power AI. Because AI is compute-intensive, he writes, countries without sufficient domestic infrastructure face a choice between constraining their ambitions or outsourcing their AI workloads to foreign providers, which brings latency, cost pressures, regulatory friction and systemic exposure. Shankar says the Australian government has been courting US cloud providers to invest locally, with Microsoft committing A$5 billion towards expanding AI and cloud infrastructure in Australia and AWS planning to invest A$13 billion by 2027.

He notes that amendments to Australia's Security of Critical Infrastructure Act now classify critical data storage and processing providers as nationally significant assets, reflecting concern about foreign dependency and cyber resilience. He cites projections that AI will expand from 0.3 per cent of US GDP today to more than 15 per cent within the next decade, and he says hyperscale data centres in the US cost upwards of US$5 billion each, while Microsoft alone has committed more than US$200 billion to expand its data centre footprint. He adds that India has allocated approximately US$200 billion toward AI development, and that Australia's National AI Centre reports more than one-third of businesses are already adopting AI technologies while many still face infrastructure and compute constraints. Shankar argues that AI sovereignty is achievable but requires intentional investment and a rethinking of national strategy, including domestic data centre infrastructure that leverages regional advantages such as lower energy costs and labour efficiencies. He points to early signs of this shift, saying Australia is positioning itself as a data centre hub for Asia and that industry analysts estimate its data centre market will exceed US$12 billion within five years, with Sydney emerging as one of the Asia-Pacific region's fastest-growing digital infrastructure hubs.

He says infrastructure alone will not unlock the full value of AI, because critical data remains siloed across organisations and systems, and he proposes a logical approach to data integration that enables secure, governed access to distributed data with zero-copy. He cites McKinsey as noting that chief data officers looking to scale AI will need to treat data as a core enterprise asset, and he says that principle applies equally at a national level. Shankar concludes that AI sovereignty is not about isolation but about control, resilience and growth, and that it is increasingly about determining where innovation happens, who captures economic value and which nations retain strategic control in the AI era. He says countries that invest in domestic infrastructure, secure data assets and enable seamless access to information can reduce external dependency while fostering innovation from within. He adds that the countries that act now will protect their digital futures and define the next era of global economic leadership.

stories.Headline: iVisa updates AI customer service checks after chatbot blocks user request for human agent
stories.Summary:
In October, Rocky Scopelliti attempted to cancel a China arrival card order and receive a refund from the customer support team at iVisa. He interacted with an AI assistant named iVy, which twice claimed to be a real person before eventually admitting it was an AI. Despite an explicit request to speak with a human, the chatbot acknowledged the request but only invited the user to ask another question. No handover to a human agent occurred during the exchange, even though the company employed 86 support agents at the time.

iVisa apologized for the incident and confirmed in writing that the AI assistant had generated all of the responses. The company stated that the false claims of being a human were hallucinations and that early incorrect responses prevented the handover from triggering. To address these failures, iVisa said it is introducing stronger checks on closed conversations and clearer disclosure regarding its AI. The company also provided a full refund for the order in question.

The event highlights a design risk for businesses that place AI at the front door of customer service. Rocky Scopelliti argued that customers need a direct route to human judgment that the AI model cannot block. He suggested that businesses should implement a visible control or direct reply route to ensure requests reach a person. This approach would allow a business to triage cases by urgency and ensure that a named service owner takes ownership of the issue.

stories.Headline: Businesses should test an AI receptionist by making it transfer a call before buying one
stories.Summary:
Matthew Walker, founder of Valory AI, wrote on 24 November 2026 that businesses should test an AI receptionist by making it transfer a call before they buy one. He described a caller ringing an accounting practice on a Tuesday morning to sort out payroll and asking to speak to Sam, and said the AI receptionist takes their name, says it will check if Sam is free and puts them on hold. Walker said Sam is in a meeting in his example, and asked what the caller hears next, saying he would ask that question early in any demo. He said the answer matters if the caller is a potential new client, and that at the very least they should know who has their enquiry and what happens next. Walker said Valory built screened live transfers and had to decide what counted as a successful handoff, because a phone can ring, go to voicemail or be picked up by someone about to walk into a meeting.

He said that on a route set up for screening the caller agrees to a short introduction and the receptionist tries an approved number, and the staff member hears who is calling and a brief reason before accepting or declining with their keypad. He said the introduction is kept short because it could end up on voicemail, so it is no place for someone's tax details. He recommended testing with two phones, letting the introduction play and the staff member accept, then speaking both ways to confirm the two people actually reached each other, and then repeating the call with the second phone left on the desk to see what the caller hears when nobody answers. Walker said businesses should check that a callback note lands with the person who will make the call and shows why the caller rang and which number they asked to use. He said there is a decision for the business on whether a first-time enquiry goes straight to Sam or to someone in intake, and who takes it when Sam is away, and he suggested starting with one team, a clear set of calls and a named person who owns the messages.

He said every supplier should be given the same example, where the caller spends a minute with the AI receptionist, a minute on hold and five minutes talking to a staff member, and asked when the AI charge stops, who charges for the time on hold and whether there is a separate phone charge for the conversation. He said Valory's November pricing study could read pricing records for five of the seven providers selected, which gave headline prices for ten plan or payment options, but across those five providers the wait and the transfer could not both be priced, and he said a written quote is where to go for actual numbers. Walker said businesses should ask for both examples priced, then for a normal month and a busy one, using the same call volumes and mix with each supplier and getting totals in Australian dollars including GST where applicable. He said the transfer cost might barely register if most calls are quick questions about opening hours, but it is worth knowing what longer calls will do to the bill if much of the work starts with a caller asking for someone. He said the two calls should be run before switching over with whoever will be on duty that week, and that those staff will spot things a sales demo can miss, such as a shared inbox everyone assumes someone else is watching.

Articles.Title: Before you buy an AI receptionist, make it transfer a call - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Sepanta CEO Omid Pakseresht says AI growth beats cost-cutting
stories.Summary:
Omid Pakseresht, chief executive of SEPANTA, wrote in an article published by IT Brief Australia on 24 November 2026 that the next large AI opportunity is growth rather than cost-cutting. He said the dominant question around AI for the past two years had been how much work can be automated. He called that the wrong question and said the bigger opportunity is what happens after businesses become more efficient. He asked what new products can be built, which markets can be entered and which revenue streams become possible. He said that is where he believes the real AI opportunity lies.

Bain & Company estimates that AI could put $4.7 trillion of global business profit at stake between 2025 and 2035, he wrote. Only $1.1 trillion of that comes from productivity gains, while innovation accounts for $2.2 trillion and shifts in market share $1.3 trillion. He said roughly three-quarters of the opportunity sits beyond efficiency. Gartner forecasts worldwide AI spending of $2.67 trillion in 2026, up 49.5% from the previous year, he wrote. Spending on AI agents and assistants alone is expected to more than double again in 2027, reaching $65.5 billion.

Pakseresht said he worries that many businesses are still organising that infrastructure around the wrong objective. He said he hears a familiar language from corporate teams: automate repetitive tasks, reduce manual work, increase productivity and lower costs. He said there is nothing wrong with any of that, but efficiency is the floor and growth is the point. He said the most interesting conversations are not about replacing people but about giving people back time, connection and bandwidth. He said that is a different purchase from a cost programme and harder to buy because the return cannot be pointed to on a headcount line.

He said most large organisations do not lack access to technology but have too much of it, with a dozen AI tools each doing something useful. He said none of them necessarily understands how the business actually runs, and that value leaks out in the gaps between systems. His co-founder and SEPANTA's CPTO, Dr Nima Pakseresht, described the problem simply: organisations have tools but not yet a system that connects those tools to the reality of the business. Pakseresht said SEPANTA is working with global brands, including a global leader in consumer goods, and has developed patent-pending technology across data trust, control and scalability. McKinsey's latest State of AI survey found that around 80% of organisations are pursuing efficiency gains from AI, he wrote.

He wrote that the small group McKinsey identifies as high performers stands apart by also using AI to pursue growth and innovation. The Office for National Statistics reports that improving business operations is the most common use of AI, cited by more than 60% of larger businesses, he wrote. He said developing new offerings and exploring new markets remain minority uses, which tells him we are still relatively early. He said SEPANTA has grown without institutional venture capital as a deliberate choice and has raised from the crowd three times. He said a funding round is one verdict from one room delivered once, whereas revenue is a verdict customers re-run every month and can withdraw.

He said the first phase of AI's evolution was about proving machines could do things humans previously did. He said the next phase is about what businesses can become when those capabilities are connected to the organisation as a whole. He said if AI reduces time spent on repetitive work, the prize is what people can do with the time they get back. He said the next decade of AI will be defined by what businesses choose to do with the capacity that automation creates. He said that is the opportunity he sees for businesses willing to look beyond cost-cutting, because efficiency is the floor and growth is the point.

Articles.Title: AI's next $4.7 trillion opportunity is growth, not cost-cutting - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: BCG finds 81% of Singapore workers use AI but only 18% have strong strategic clarity
stories.Summary:
Boston Consulting Group published a report on November 24, 2026, regarding the use of artificial intelligence in Asia-Pacific workplaces. The study surveyed 6,349 employees across nine countries, including Singapore, to examine how technology changes work. It found that while 81 percent of Singapore workers use these tools regularly, only 18 percent have strong strategic clarity. This indicates a significant gap between the widespread adoption of technology and the direction provided by management.

Strong strategic clarity requires employees to know that AI is a priority and understand their specific role in the strategy. It also involves receiving clear guidance on how to utilize the time saved through these digital tools. In Singapore, only 12 percent of workers engage in deep use, which means using AI for at least half of their daily tasks. These employees save an average of 7.2 hours per week, which is lower than the regional average of 9.4 hours.

Jeff Walters, a Managing Director and Senior Partner at BCG, stated that putting tools in the hands of employees was the easy part. He explained that measurable impact now depends on how companies rebuild their work processes around the technology. Romain de Laubier, the Asia-Pacific Regional Chair at BCG X, said that strategic clarity must be the top priority for companies. He also advised that organizations should measure the value created and establish guardrails for responsible use.

stories.Headline: Personal AI is making your people better and your firm worse
stories.Summary:
Christian Chadwick, co-founder and chief executive of Chaidojo, wrote in an article published by IT Brief Australia on 24 November 2026 that personal AI is making individual people better while quietly making professional firms worse, and he based the piece on a conversation he had a few weeks earlier with the director of an engineering consultancy. That director told him his firm needed nothing new for AI because his team already put their reports and data through Claude and got good answers back, and when Chadwick asked who had set it up and who else could run it the same way, the answer to both questions was the same person. Chadwick wrote that the firm is not behind on AI and by most measures is ahead, which he described as the problem, and he said he hears a version of it in many conversations with the leaders of professional firms. Chadwick argued that most AI rollouts assume that if each person gets faster the firm gets faster too, but that this breaks for professional work, where a firm sells reports, packs and figures that several people draft, check and sign to the same standard whoever worked on them. He wrote that when everyone builds their own prompts, skills and custom assistants, everyone does the job slightly differently, so adoption goes up and consistency goes down, and no adoption dashboard shows it.

He said the bigger loss from shadow AI runs the other way from the usual worry about client data leaking out, because people are writing down what good work looks like into accounts the firm does not own, cannot review and could not recover if the person left, which makes a firm's strongest AI users its biggest key-person risk. He added that fluent drafts from personal set-ups arrive with no record of sources, assumptions or doubts, so the time saved in drafting reappears at sign-off. Chadwick wrote that the missing layer is the software around the model, sometimes called the harness, which holds the structure and controls and makes AI multiplayer by turning a personal chat into a firm's way of working. He described a monthly monitoring report whose workflow is written once and kept in the firm's own cloud or on its own servers, setting out the steps, the template, the checks and a few past reports the partner was happy to sign, and versioned like a procedure so changes are reviewed before they go live. In his example code reconciles the readings against last month and the permitted limits, a model drafts the commentary in the firm's style, anything that does not reconcile or was read two ways is flagged rather than smoothed over, and the draft lands in a shared review queue where the reviewer sees the flags first and every figure next to the file it came from.

He said IT would see one list of workflows, who can run them and which clients' files each one can reach. Chadwick said the answer is not to ban personal AI or buy more of it but to stop treating the workflows people build as personal tools, and to collect shadow AI rather than stamp it out because what people have built is the best map a firm has of where AI genuinely helps. He advised firms to stop measuring adoption and instead measure how far apart two people's versions of the same job are, how long it takes to get from data to a signed-off report and how often drafts come back, and to accept slower drafts if they are faster to check. He also advised moving one piece of work off personal accounts, starting with the recurring report clients judge the firm on, and rewarding people for sharing rather than for being the expert. He wrote that the engineering director's team is getting real value from what one person built, and that the firm will only keep that value if it stops belonging to one person.

Articles.Title: Personal AI is making your people better and your firm worse - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Author-it releases MCP to connect approved AI assistants to cloud documentation
stories.Summary:
Author-it released Author-it MCP for its cloud documentation platform on 25 November 2026, letting customers connect approved AI assistants to content held in Author-it libraries, and the company said the feature forms part of the 2026.R4 release for Author-it Cloud customers. The Wellington-founded software company said the tool lets AI assistants work inside documentation systems while remaining subject to the same controls already applied to human users, and it supports Claude at launch, with support for ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot planned later. Author-it MCP uses the Model Context Protocol, which the company described as an open standard for linking AI assistants to business systems, and in practice this allows customers to use an AI assistant already approved by their security team rather than adopt a separate tool from the documentation vendor. Users can ask the assistant to search and read content, check material against a style guide, draft new or revised topics, and handle translation work, and the assistant operates in the live library rather than a separate copy, but any content change requires user approval before it is applied. The assistant cannot publish or delete content, it operates only within the permissions of the signed-in user, and administrators can restrict access to specific areas of a library, while before an import is accepted the system checks the full file and rejects the entire import if any check fails.

Every change made through the assistant is recorded in the object history and the previous version is retained, and in launch webinars the product team demonstrated the system carrying out seven tasks in a live library, including reviewing topics against a style guide, building index keywords, filling glossary gaps, writing alt text for images, converting repeated passages into reusable topics, translating a translation job while preserving elements and IDs, and drafting troubleshooting topics from support tickets. One part of the demonstration focused on restrictions rather than output, with the assistant rewriting six topics against a style guide and then stopping when it reached a release state the user was not allowed to edit. Vikram Arumilli, Chief Executive Officer of Author-it, said companies are investing heavily in AI and many of their projects stall on the same problem, which is that the AI has no trusted, current knowledge to work from, and he said customers have spent years building exactly that in Author-it, so Author-it MCP lets their AI work directly with that approved, structured content inside the controls they already rely on. Adrian Winks, Chief Customer Officer, said every content team he talks to has had the same memo from above to use AI, then security adds that it must be only this one, so the company was never going to bolt its own chatbot onto Author-it and ask customers to trust yet another AI, and he said it is the customer's AI, not Author-it's, and the company is not in the business of selling AI models. Winks said each person's AI assistant works with their permissions and nothing more, and that customers decide what it can change using the release states and workflow they already run, so there is nothing new to learn and they can fence it into one corner of the library if they want.

The release also reflects a broader shift in how documentation teams assess routine maintenance work, with Author-it arguing that jobs such as alt text creation, glossary upkeep, index management and duplicate-content clean-up are becoming more important as AI systems increasingly read and respond from published documentation. Each object in Author-it collects metadata from the moment it is created, including who created it, when it was created and how it relates to other content, and the company says this structure gives AI assistants more context than systems that rely on large undifferentiated stores of information. Winks said the minute knowledge lands in Author-it it picks up a dozen or so pieces of metadata without anyone lifting a finger, and he said many AI knowledge projects pour everything into one big blob and then spend months trying to stitch the context and meaning back in, whereas Author-it would much rather it is built in from the start, deliberately and under the customer's control. Prompts that prove useful can be saved as reusable skills, allowing teams to repeat common jobs such as content reviews or glossary maintenance with a short prompt rather than recreating the instructions each time, and organisations that need to distinguish AI-made edits for compliance reasons can use a dedicated release state for AI-edited work or a separate user account for the assistant.

Articles.Title: Author-it launches MCP to connect approved AI assistants - IT Brief Australia
