stories.Headline: Darío Gil says AI now dominates practical scientific advances under the Genesis Mission
stories.Summary:
President Trump launched the Genesis Mission on November 24, 2025. This Department of Energy plan uses AI to accelerate science and engineering. Darío Gil led the mission starting in the fall of 2025. He spoke about its impact at SC26 in Chicago last week. The event occurred exactly a year and a day after the launch.

The plan aims to double national science and engineering productivity within 10 years. It focuses on energy research, AI discovery tools, and national security technologies. The government funded the American Science and Security Platform with $320 million in December 2025. Oak Ridge National Lab leads the American Science Cloud compute backbone. Argonne and Pacific Northwest National Labs lead the Transformational AI Models Consortium.

Darío Gil is the Under Secretary for Science and the Genesis Mission Director. He stated that AI is the force dominating the practical reality of scientific advancements. Gil claimed there is a lot of evidence that the mission is delivering results. He said the government must equip the community with tools and knowledge. He believes the mission should be done with the community, not to them.

Rick Stevens of Argonne said almost everything is now done with agentic AI. He noted that scientists use agents for coding, running machines, and analyzing data. Satoshi Matsuoka of RIKEN claimed that AI can now do science. He said ChatGPT replicated his award-winning COVID research before it was published. These tools affect fields like biology, drug discovery, physics, and materials science.

The mission originally included 17 national labs, various universities, and IT vendors. It expanded through the Genesis Mission Consortium to include partners like RIKEN in Japan. In July, the DOE announced 278 Phase 1 awards totaling $179 million. Other federal agencies including NIH, NASA, and NSF provided billions in additional funding. The NSF also manages its own project called NAIRR.

The government now seeks to scale resources to the global research community. It aims to share knowledge on how to conduct science using AI. Future efforts include integrating AI supercomputers and quantum systems with high performance computing. The articles do not state when the productivity goal will be measured. They leave open how the global community will access these scaled resources.

stories.Headline: SK hynix shares close up 6.73% as Jensen Huang's Nvidia return lifts Seoul chipmakers
stories.Summary:
SK hynix shares rose 6.73% to 1,158,000 won at the November 24 regular-session close in Seoul, as Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia pulled Korean chipmakers off their lows. The Kospi climbed 6.32% to 5,006.03, triggering a buy-side sidecar minutes after the open. Foreign investors bought a net 725.6 billion won of Korean shares, after Monday's 3.31% slide in the index. The move came as Huang's return to Nvidia lifted the HBM leader in Seoul.

SK hynix booked third-quarter revenue of 104.6 trillion won, up 328% year over year, and operating profit of 83.3 trillion won, an 80% margin. Long-term agreements with 14 major customers now cover more than half of 2027 and 2028 capacity, and HBM4 is set to overtake HBM3E in shipments this quarter. Net cash stands at 98.7 trillion won. Annualize the third-quarter operating profit and it reaches about 333 trillion won, against a market value near 746 trillion won.

A Daishin Securities researcher told the Korea Herald that the sell-off came from lost confidence, not earnings. The GuruFocus chart shows a GF Score of 99/100, reflecting near-perfect profitability, a strong balance sheet and solid momentum. The close sits about 25% below the GF Value of 1,534,744 won, but that discount leans on earnings at a cyclical peak. The key tests are fourth-quarter HBM4 volumes and whether contract pricing inside those long-term deals holds in 2027.

stories.Headline: FuelCell Energy builds a Connecticut fuel cell testbed for the StabilityMax AI data center power project
stories.Summary:
FuelCell Energy announced in early November from Danbury, Connecticut, that it is taking part in StabilityMax, a multi-year collaborative project focused on the power needs of artificial intelligence data centers. The project is led by the National Laboratory of the Rockies, a US Department of Energy national laboratory, and also involves Argonne National Laboratory. The stated aim of StabilityMax is to develop and validate integrated power system architectures that can serve AI computing facilities. According to the release, these facilities are driving large increases in electricity demand and can experience rapid swings in power consumption as workloads change. The participants will use a testing and modelling framework to evaluate how fuel cells, energy storage, advanced controls and power electronics can work together.

Under the project, FuelCell Energy will develop a fuel cell test facility in Connecticut that will serve as a national laboratory-supported testbed. The release places the testbed within a company manufacturing facility in the state, and the FuelCell Energy website separately identifies Torrington, Connecticut, as the location of its fuel cell manufacturing headquarters. The National Laboratory of the Rockies will develop data center load profiles and simulation models that capture the dynamic power demands of computing infrastructure. It will also evaluate FuelCell Energy technology under realistic operating conditions, giving the project an independent view of system behaviour. The laboratory is helping to demonstrate how integrated fuel cell systems can respond to data center power needs while limiting impacts on the utility grid and on ratepayers.

Shankar Achanta, chief product and technology officer at FuelCell Energy, said AI infrastructure is creating unprecedented demand for power that is reliable, flexible and resilient. He described StabilityMax as bringing together the fuel cell technology and operating experience of the company with the expertise of the national laboratories to study how integrated systems can support AI data centers. Zhiwen Ma, who leads the research effort for the project at the National Laboratory of the Rockies, said fuel cells located alongside data centers offer distinctive solutions to the power demand of AI infrastructure. He added that the project will show how integrated fuel cell systems can respond quickly while limiting effects on the grid and ratepayers. Argonne National Laboratory will provide techno-economic and lifecycle studies to identify cost-effective deployment approaches.

The release links StabilityMax to earlier work announced this year, when FuelCell Energy began a collaboration with Siemens. That collaboration centres on a layered architecture that combines several technologies operating on different timescales to meet AI data center power needs. FuelCell Energy expects insights from StabilityMax to inform system design under that layered approach. The laboratory testbed offers a controlled setting in which the response of fuel cells, batteries and power electronics can be measured together before configurations are applied at customer sites. FuelCell Energy describes itself as a US clean energy technology company that provides continuous, scalable baseload power for mission-critical applications.

Its on-site fuel cell systems serve data centers, industrial facilities, utilities and distributed generation customers, and the company reports global deployments approaching one gigawatt. The company website highlights several decades of fuel cell work and patents secured through the company and its subsidiary, Versa Power Systems. It presents fuel cell platforms that produce steady power from natural gas, biofuels or hydrogen with quiet operation and combined heat and power, and it offers dedicated data center power systems designed for community-friendly operation. Headquartered in Danbury, Connecticut, FuelCell Energy has its common stock quoted on Nasdaq under the symbol FCEL. StabilityMax adds a national laboratory partnership to the data center work the company has been building this year.

The release describes StabilityMax as a multi-year collaborative project, without giving an end date. The articles do not state the project's funding, its budget or the size of the testbed. They do not name the specific Connecticut manufacturing facility where the testbed will sit beyond the state and the separately listed Torrington headquarters. They do not give a start date for construction or operation of the testbed. They do not say what results will be published or when.

stories.Headline: Experts study whether polite language improves artificial intelligence responses
stories.Summary:
Millions of people have developed the habit of speaking politely to artificial intelligence software. Technology executives, researchers, and philosophers have examined whether AI systems actually need thanks. These experts are investigating if being polite makes any difference in the answers provided. The Royal Examiner reported on these questions on November 25, 2026. This inquiry explores the intersection of computer processing, linguistic research, and philosophy.

In April 2025, Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, responded to a question on X. He claimed that tens of millions of dollars were well spent on electricity for polite language. Every message sent to an AI system requires computer processing and consumes energy in data centers. A November 2024 study by the Association for Computational Linguistics tested prompts in English, Chinese, and Japanese. Researchers from RIKEN and Waseda University in Japan found that impolite prompts often produced poorer results.

Sam Altman suggested that being polite might prove useful if artificial intelligence became much more powerful. Kurtis Beavers, a director on the Microsoft Copilot design team, said courtesy helps set the tone. He explained that polite language can encourage more respectful and collaborative responses from the AI. Anthropic stated in its constitution that it is uncertain if Claude has moral standing. The company acknowledges that scientists lack an agreed way to resolve questions about AI welfare.

Users who are rude to AI may receive lower quality answers based on the research. People who use Copilot may find that professional requests produce more professional responses. Those who provide detailed instructions generally get better results than those using only polite phrases. The study noted that the most effective level of politeness differed among the three languages. Results can vary depending on the specific task, the language, and the AI system.

Large language models learn patterns from books, articles, websites, and conversations to recognize communication styles. They produce conversational responses, such as saying you are welcome, by imitating human language patterns. These systems can apologize or express appreciation without experiencing the emotions associated with those words. Some people maintain polite habits with AI to preserve how they treat other human beings. This behavior does not necessarily mean the user believes the software has actual feelings.

Researchers continue to debate whether artificial intelligence could ever develop consciousness or subjective human awareness. Anthropic has established research efforts to examine possible experiences and the welfare of AI systems. The articles leave open whether a verified figure exists for electricity costs caused by politeness. It remains unsettled if any AI model truly feels appreciated or experiences regret when apologizing. The text does not state if politeness improves every response from every AI model.

stories.Headline: Researchers set out an agenda for integrating AI across the mitigation scenario workflow
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a research agenda for integrating artificial intelligence and machine learning across the three phases of the mitigation scenario workflow, published in Nature Climate Change on 25 November 2026. The workflow that produces mitigation scenarios, which underpin climate policy, faces bottlenecks in narrative breadth, outdated inputs, model structure, computational cost and ensemble interpretation. The agenda covers scenario specification, modelling and policy translation. In scenario specification, language models and automated data curation can widen storylines and keep inputs current. In modelling, process-based models can be complemented by hybrid models, emulators and reinforcement learning.

In policy translation, machine learning can diagnose ensembles, fill reporting gaps and downscale outputs. An agentic architecture could orchestrate these components under expert oversight. The authors distinguish demonstrated methods from prospective designs, set out their limitations and identify barriers in socioeconomic data, model architecture, validation and global south representation. The article presents four figures: the scenario development and use workflow, hybrid modelling, emulation and reinforcement learning in that workflow, closing the climate, society loop through evidence curation, response emulation and iterative coupling, and agentic orchestration of the scenario development-and-use workflow.

The articles do not name the authors of the agenda or quote them directly. The agenda is set out by the article's authors, whose names the available text does not give. The articles state that the authors distinguish demonstrated methods from prospective designs and set out their limitations. The articles state that the authors identify barriers in socioeconomic data, model architecture, validation and global south representation. The articles give no further statements from those responsible.

The articles cite related work, including a 2025 study by Li and colleagues showing that deep generative models trained on the AR6 Scenarios Database can generate synthetic scenarios approximating the distributions and correlations of key mitigation variables. They cite a 2024 experiment by Doshi and Hauser showing that access to generative-AI ideas raises the rated creativity of individual stories and makes the stories more similar to one another, a convergence risk that LLM-assisted storyline design must manage. They cite a preprint by Gorres and colleagues extracting 3.2 million structured quantitative data points, mostly techno-economic parameters, from 76,000 energy system studies. They cite a Perspective by Guivarch and colleagues explaining why scenario ensembles cannot be read as statistical samples or in terms of likelihood. The articles do not say who is affected beyond the scenario workflow and its users in climate policy.

The articles give background on the scenario framework, citing O'Neill and colleagues on achievements and needs for the climate change scenario framework in Nature Climate Change in 2020, and Guivarch and colleagues on scenarios and modelling methods in the IPCC's Climate Change 2022: Mitigation of Climate Change. They cite Riahi and colleagues on mitigation pathways compatible with long-term goals in the same IPCC report. They cite Weyant on contributions of integrated assessment models of global climate change in the Review of Environmental Economics and Policy in 2017. They cite Keppo and colleagues on model linking for low-carbon transitions in the Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews in 2026.

The articles do not state what happens next beyond setting out the research agenda. The articles leave open which of the prospective designs will be demonstrated and how the identified barriers in socioeconomic data, model architecture, validation and global south representation will be addressed. The articles leave open how the agentic architecture would be governed under expert oversight. The articles leave open how the convergence risk in LLM-assisted storyline design would be managed. The articles leave open the timeline for integrating these methods across the workflow's three phases.

stories.Headline: South Korean firms seek to diversify AI supply chains despite Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia
stories.Summary:
Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang returned to his company, which eased concerns for South Korean firms. These companies feared that their large scale artificial intelligence partnerships with the chipmaker could unravel. Industry sources reported on November 24 that Korean firms welcomed the return of the executive. However, these companies are now focusing on broadening their sources of AI accelerators. They also want to expand their memory customer base.

Nvidia's board created a national security and export control committee on November 17. This committee consists of three independent directors and is appointing a chief compliance officer. The U.S. Commerce Department Bureau of Industry and Security began controlling remote chip access on November 19. This rule affects SK Telecom's 2 gigawatt AI factory and NAVER's projects in Europe, Asia, and the Middle East. Korean firms must now examine the ownership structure and nationality of their customers.

Industry officials stated that diversifying AI supply chains remains a core challenge for these companies. They noted that U.S. made accelerators from AMD are not free from export controls. These officials also claimed that domestic AI chips have a relatively weak software ecosystem. They said cooperation with Nvidia must be maintained while securing other alternatives. This strategy prevents business from being shaken by government policy or one company's management.

Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are expected to find more customers beyond the Nvidia company. Infrastructure companies and AI data center operators must move away from procurement centered on Nvidia. NAVER signed an agreement with AMD in March for early adoption of the MI455X. Samsung SDS launched a cloud service in July using neural processing units from FuriosaAI. SK Telecom began joint development of an inference system combining Nvidia GPUs with Rebellions' NPUs.

Samsung Electronics signed a March agreement to supply HBM4 for the AMD MI455X AI accelerator. SK hynix announced in February that it was expanding HBM technology cooperation with the firm Broadcom. UBS projected Nvidia's share of HBM demand will fall from 60 percent to 41 percent next year. Google's share is projected to rise to 30 percent and AMD's to 13 percent. These shifts are supported by Big Tech firms expanding their in house AI chip development.

Nvidia's one billion dollar equity investment in NAVER has recently arrived and is now complete. The specifics and amount of a partnership with SK Group valued over 500 billion dollars remain unfinished. The articles leave open when the details of the SK Group cooperation framework will be finalized. They do not state when the chief compliance officer will be officially appointed. The text does not say how Korean firms will resolve their financing and procurement issues.

stories.Headline: Seven Korean substrate suppliers invest 2.8 trillion won to expand AI component production
stories.Summary:
Seven mid-sized Korean substrate suppliers announced investments totaling approximately 2.8 trillion won this year to address shortages caused by artificial intelligence. These companies plan to expand their production facilities in stages starting from late this year and continuing through 2030. The surge in semiconductor demand has specifically increased the need for SOCAMM2 memory substrates and other high-performance components. This expansion follows similar large-scale capacity increases already undertaken by major manufacturers like LG Innotek and Samsung Electro-Mechanics.

Daeduck Electronics committed the largest amount with 1.325 trillion won for facilities, while Isu Petasys plans to invest 500 billion won. Other investments include 379.6 billion won from Simmtech, 200 billion won from TLB, 190 billion won from Haesung DS, 110 billion won from BH, and 99.3 billion won from Korea Circuit. These funds will support the production of flip-chip ball grid array and flip-chip chip-scale package substrates, as well as multi-layer boards for AI accelerator boards. Some companies are also targeting next-generation DDR6 DRAM and automotive substrates in Vietnam to diversify their output.

Kim Pan-bae, an executive vice president at Samsung Electro-Mechanics, stated on October 28 that meeting customer demand remains difficult despite large-scale expansions. He noted that the company continues to receive requests for additional supplies from its clients. Other industry officials warned that these investments may not immediately increase production volumes due to severe equipment shortages. The chairman of Unimicron reported that delivery lead times for critical production equipment have reached as long as 30 months.

The Global Electronics Association forecast this month that the global printed circuit board shortage is unlikely to ease significantly before mid-2028. Additionally, supplies of key materials like copper-clad laminates could fall about 20 percent short of demand next year. To secure necessary capacity, Big Tech customers have entered into long-term supply agreements and are helping to finance these expansion investments. These measures aim to stabilize the supply chain for critical AI server components and high-speed communication chips.

stories.Headline: Claudia Prantz argues AI gains depend on leaders choosing where and how to apply it
stories.Summary:
Claudia Prantz published an article on isimarkets.com on 25 November 2026 arguing that Artificial Intelligence can raise productivity but that its impact depends on the quality of decisions about where and how to apply it. The article discusses the risks of indiscriminate adoption, the workslop phenomenon, leadership responsibility and the criteria needed for real organizational transformation. Prantz wrote that Artificial Intelligence has been occupying more and more space in organizations, with new tools, applications and possibilities continuously emerging. She wrote that this comes with a growing expectation of gains in productivity, efficiency and innovation, and that many companies began encouraging their teams to use the technology. She asked whether organizations are making the right decisions about where and how to implement Artificial Intelligence.

Prantz cited an article in the Harvard Business Review by Kate Niederhoffer and collaborators titled AI-Generated “Workslop” Is Destroying Productivity. She wrote that the authors use workslop to describe content produced with artificial intelligence that appears well crafted but lacks the consistency or depth needed to solve a problem effectively. She wrote that such deliveries seem ready but require review, validation, interpretation and often reconstruction by those who receive them. She cited a survey by BetterUp Labs with the Stanford Social Media Lab of 1,150 full-time workers in the United States, in which about 40% had received content classified as workslop in the previous month. She wrote that participants estimated spending an average of 1 hour and 56 minutes to handle each occurrence, with impacts on productivity, trust and collaboration.

Prantz wrote that the adoption of Artificial Intelligence does not by itself represent an organizational transformation. She cited a report from MIT NANDA titled The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 which found that 95% of the organizations analyzed were not achieving measurable returns on their generative AI investments. She wrote that the same report found that more than 80% of surveyed organizations had explored or tested general-purpose generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and Copilot, and that nearly 40% report their implementation. She wrote that the report found these tools mainly improve individual productivity and not necessarily the organization’s financial performance. She wrote that among organizations that evaluated specific corporate AI tools, 60% reached the evaluation stage, 20% advanced to pilot projects and only 5% reached production.

Prantz wrote that the Harvard Business Review reflection draws attention to the responsibility of leaders in this process. She wrote that when organizations set an indiscriminate guideline for everyone to use AI without clarifying objectives, quality criteria and expectations about results, they can encourage superficial adoption of the technology. She wrote that demanding speed and delivery volume without considering the quality of what is produced creates a favorable environment for workslop to emerge. She wrote that leadership needs to go beyond encouraging the use of tools, demonstrate how to use them intentionally, set quality standards and encourage a culture of responsible experimentation. She wrote that AI should be incorporated as a collaborative tool capable of expanding human skills, not as a shortcut to reduce the effort of thinking, analyzing and deciding.

Prantz wrote that one of the biggest challenges for organizations now is developing the ability to properly select where to invest efforts in implementing AI. She wrote that this will require careful curation of organizational challenges to understand which problems compromise outcomes, where the main bottlenecks lie and which opportunities offer transformative potential. She listed questions to guide this assessment, including what organizational problem the organization wants to solve and whether an application can transform a process or just speed up a task. She asked whether there is real potential for efficiency gains, quality or innovation, whether the expected result justifies the investments and implementation efforts, and how results and quality of deliveries will be evaluated. She wrote that this curation allows differentiating initiatives that only facilitate specific activities from those that can modify the organization’s ability to act.

Prantz gave an example from her field of expertise, Market Intelligence, writing that AI can be used to collect data and summarize information. She wrote that these are useful applications but that organizations can go further, imagining the technology integrating different sources of information, identifying relationships between indicators, recognizing signs of market change and supporting the construction of scenarios for strategic decisions. She wrote that this means using AI to expand analytical capacity with faster connections and interpretations, always combined with the experience and knowledge of specialists in the field. She wrote that organizations need to review how they evaluate productivity, going beyond accounting for automated tasks or time saved to understand what was done with that time, which steps were eliminated, what quality was achieved and what additional value was generated. She wrote that if AI speeds up production but increases the effort of review and correction, organizations may be shifting the work rather than eliminating inefficiencies and may miss the chance to direct scarce financial efforts toward projects that deliver significant gains.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence: the challenge lies in the quality of organizational decisions

stories.Headline: Younglimwon SoftLab grows cloud ERP revenue 36 percent as it adds AI features
stories.Summary:
Younglimwon SoftLab reported a significant increase in its cloud enterprise resource planning business during the first nine months of 2026. According to a regulatory filing submitted on November 13, the company saw its cloud ERP revenue grow by 36 percent compared to the previous year. This growth occurred during the period from January through September, reflecting a strong shift toward cloud services. The company also noted that its on-premises ERP revenue grew by 11 percent during this same timeframe.

The cloud ERP segment generated 5.1 billion won in revenue, which increased its share of total company revenue to 8.1 percent from 6.7 percent. On-premises ERP revenue reached 37.6 billion won, though it grew at a slower pace than the cloud business. Since August, the company has integrated AI-powered automatic data entry, business briefings, and workflow automation into its K-System Ace I&I platform. This platform also now includes AI spreadsheet analysis and business insights to improve data analytics. Additionally, the company is developing the K-Bot 3.0 project to enhance its existing AI chatbot.

Younglimwon SoftLab is responsible for these updates and is currently pursuing the use of Model Context Protocol technology. This specific technology is intended to connect AI agents with external services to expand the capabilities of ERP workflows. The company reported that its consolidated revenue for the third quarter reached 21.7 billion won, which is a 5.6 percent increase. Operating profit for the same quarter rose by 8.6 percent to reach 1.4 billion won.

stories.Headline: Review authors call for hybrid AI weather models that preserve physical constraints
stories.Summary:
The articles report a review published in Nature Reviews Earth & Environment on 25 November 2026, covering artificial intelligence and machine learning for short-to-medium range weather prediction. The review summarizes the development and application of these methods during 2015, 2025. It provides a holistic evaluation of the landscape and recommendations for best uses and future research priorities. The authors describe new models implemented in the field that learn from decades of reanalysis and observational data. The review states that these models can overcome computational cost barriers and resolution constraints of conventional numerical weather prediction.

The review covers integration through post-processing, emulation of physical parameterizations, data assimilation and development of full artificial intelligence weather prediction models. It states that these approaches have already demonstrated performance equivalent to conventional numerical weather prediction with a fraction of the computational cost. It notes that conventional numerical weather prediction faces computational costs when increasing spatial resolution to capture localized phenomena. It also notes costs when expanding ensemble size to improve probabilistic skill. The review lists challenges including dependence on training datasets, maintaining physical consistency, accuracy of forecasting extreme weather and lack of trust in operational use.

The review's authors state that future research priorities must focus on developing hybrid approaches that preserve physical constraints. They state that curated datasets should be used to ensure forecasts are robust, trustworthy and explainable. They call for fostering interdisciplinary collaborations to handle increasing climate variability and extreme events. The review presents a timeline of the development of artificial intelligence weather prediction technologies. It presents a workflow for these technologies and comparisons of forecast errors of different models.

The review includes a benchmark comparison of forecast errors and a look at performance in cases of extreme weather. It cites a 2024 study by Ben Bouallègue and colleagues giving a first statistical assessment of machine learning-based weather forecasts in an operational-like context. It cites work by Lang and colleagues on ECMWF's data-driven forecasting system. It cites Lam and colleagues on learning skillful medium-range global weather forecasting and Bi and colleagues on accurate medium-range global weather forecasting with 3D neural networks.

The review states that short-to-medium range weather prediction is a crucial component of decision-making for energy and disaster management and preparedness. The review gives a background of references spanning 1950 to 2025. It cites Platzman on the ENIAC computations of 1950 as a gateway to numerical weather prediction. It cites Bauer, Thorpe and Brunet on the quiet revolution of numerical weather prediction in 2015.

It cites Glahn and Lowry on model output statistics in 1972 and Rasp and Lerch on neural networks for postprocessing ensemble weather forecasts in 2018. It cites Charlton-Perez and colleagues asking in 2024 whether artificial intelligence models produce better weather forecasts than physics-based models. The review states that new models learn from data rather than solving complex differential equations. It states that the review covers the period 2015, 2025.

It leaves open the full evaluation and recommendations, which are behind subscription access. It leaves open the detailed findings shown in its figures on forecast errors and extreme weather performance. It leaves open how the proposed hybrid approaches and curated datasets would be developed and adopted. More to follow.

stories.Headline: SK chair Chey Tae-won proposes joint Korea-Japan AI talent development
stories.Summary:
SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won proposed that South Korea and Japan jointly develop artificial intelligence talent during a business leaders' session. This proposal occurred on November 21, 2026, during the Tokyo Forum 2026 event held at the University of Tokyo. The forum took place at Yasuda Auditorium and was co-hosted by the University of Tokyo and the Chey Institute. Chey called for closer cooperation between the two nations to cultivate innovators capable of solving various complex social challenges. He suggested that companies and universities from both countries should jointly establish and operate these AI talent development programs.

The initiative requires the joint operation of programs to connect internships and job opportunities for young people across both countries. Chey called for fundamentally different designs and governance structures for universities to reflect a society where AI is everyday life. He stated that simply making minor adjustments to existing curricula is not enough to prepare for an AI-native society. The proposal follows the Big Tent bilateral cooperation initiative introduced in June and the Korea-Japan New Era Strategic Platform launched November 18. This platform was launched by the Chey Institute for Advanced Studies in partnership with the Japanese newspaper Yomiuri Shimbun.

Chairman Chey Tae-won is responsible for the proposal and stated that AI should be an inherent part of the environment. He argued that collective intelligence and even unsuccessful attempts to design new systems help young people develop essential problem-solving skills. Chey urged universities to move beyond teaching knowledge and focus on cultivating wisdom to guide change in the AI era. He said people must ask what new value they want to create and what kind of society they want to build. He believes that new governance is necessary because the current university system must be designed differently for the AI age.

Other participants included French AI envoy Anne Bouverot, Sakana AI co-founder Ren Ito, and NTT Group Chairman Jun Sawada. President Yeom Jae-ho of Taejae University and President Miki Sugimura of Sophia University also joined the discussion on talent development. University of Tokyo President Teruo Fujii moderated the session where these business and academic leaders discussed the future of education. Young people are the ones affected, as the program aims to expand their employment and internship opportunities in both nations. stories.Headline: Samsung Electronics boosts NAND output in China to meet AI data center demand

Industry sources reported this development on November 24, 2026, noting that the company is responding to high demand for enterprise solid-state drives. This surge in demand is being driven by the explosive growth of the artificial intelligence data center market. The company intends to expand its monthly output of these specific wafers from 10,000 to 50,000 within one year. This fivefold increase requires converting existing sixth-generation production lines to ninth-generation processes and upgrading cleanroom electroplating equipment.

Once these changes are complete, total NAND production in China, including output from Xi’an Plant 1, will reach 100,000 wafers per month. This total represents roughly one-third of the global NAND production capacity for Samsung Electronics. The ninth-generation technology features a 286-layer architecture, which is about 21 percent higher than the 236 layers found in the eighth-generation version. Industry sources say this aggressive investment reflects a polarized market where demand for enterprise drives is surging while mobile and PC demand falls. The company is prioritizing high-performance products to maintain its market position against competitors like Yangtze Memory Technologies Co. Samsung has already introduced the PM1763 enterprise solid-state drive, which was unveiled in July to serve AI data centers.

This product is claimed to offer more than 1.8 times the power efficiency of the previous model. The company also plans to build additional ninth-generation production lines at its Pyeongtaek Plant 5 in South Korea. This strategy focuses on high-value products to maximize profitability while general-purpose NAND prices continue to decline. Samsung held a 35.1 percent share of the global enterprise solid-state drive market as of the second quarter. By repositioning the Xi’an campus as a hub for these drives, the company hopes to widen its lead over other manufacturers.

The KOSPI opened at 4,880.16, which was a 3.64 percent rise of 171.62 points. It briefly recaptured the 5,000 mark, while the KOSDAQ opened at 654.31, up 2.97 percent. stories.Headline: Microsoft DevUI lets C# developers run and test AI agents in ASP.NET Core apps
stories.Summary:
Microsoft Agent Framework has introduced DevUI, which lets C# developers run and test AI agents and workflows directly inside ASP.NET Core web applications, according to TechGig. The feature replaces the traditional console app loops with an interactive chat page that shows tool calls and token counts. TechGig published its report on the feature on November 26, 2026, describing it as a page within a web app that executes agents and workflows registered by the application. The interface lists registered agents and workflows, runs them, and displays tool calls and token counts in real time.

DevUI is not a standalone tool but a set of endpoints mapped into an ASP.NET Core app, allowing it to interact with agents as configured. The implementation relies on prerelease packages, Microsoft.Agents.AI.DevUI and Microsoft.Agents.AI.Hosting, and agents and workflows are registered using dependency injection, supporting various chat clients including Claude Haiku. DevUI and its associated endpoints are designed to operate exclusively in development environments, an isolation TechGig describes as crucial because DevUI exposes agent instructions, tool names, and model IDs. Remote access to DevUI is restricted by default to loopback callers, with warnings logged for non-loopback requests.

The Responses and Conversations endpoints, which handle chat history, are not covered by DevUI's loopback check and require separate authorization in production environments, according to the report. TechGig states that security mandates separate authorization for production use of the Responses endpoints. The article does not name any individual responsible for the feature or attribute any direct statements to Microsoft or its representatives. stories.Headline: AI and multispectral imaging reveal heritable facial skin traits in 64 families
stories.Summary:
The articles report only a headline and a single incomplete article, so this is a breaking story. A quantitative genetic investigation combining high-resolution multispectral imaging with artificial intelligence reported that key structural characteristics of human facial skin, including pore patterns, pigment distribution, and ultraviolet reflectance, show substantial heritability, while cutaneous vascular features are predominantly shaped by non-genetic factors. The work examined familial resemblances across multi-generational genealogical records and was published on November 25, 2026, in a bioengineer.org article dated the same day. The article states that primary axes of phenotypic variation in facial tissue correspond closely to underlying additive genetic architecture. It states that computational vision models can extract biologically meaningful, heritable signatures directly from specialized spectral bands without manual clinical scoring.

The article says the identification of distinct heritable components across non-visible spectral captures indicates that deep subcutaneous properties harbor structured genetic signals that traditional RGB photography fails to isolate. The research team evaluated facial imagery from a cohort in the Baependi Heart Study, a longitudinal epidemiological project initiated in 2005 in southeastern Brazil. The imaging dataset comprised 380 adult participants, 169 males and 211 females, across 64 distinct families with documented genealogical records. Photographs were acquired under standardized optical conditions using the commercial Visia Skin Analysis System developed by Canfield Scientific, with five discrete multispectral exposures per individual at 2736 by 3648 pixels, yielding 1,900 high-resolution images and seven superimposed spectral channels. An expert dermatologist manually segmented each participant's visible light capture to delineate a region of interest of exactly 256 by 256 pixels within the central forehead, and those coordinates were mapped across all five spectral captures, generating 1,900 uniform segmented regions.

The investigators calculated the Individual Typology Angle for every photograph by transforming RGB pixel intensities into the three-dimensional CIELAB color space, and narrow-sense heritability estimates for the derived multispectral descriptors ranged between 0.15 and 0.62. The article attributes the investigation to a research team it does not name, and it gives no direct quotations from the authors. It states that the authors implemented quantitative genetic linear mixed models using individual-level animal models via restricted maximum likelihood algorithms. It states that pedigree relationships spanning the 64 families were formalized into additive genetic relationship matrices to separate hereditary resemblance from confounding background variance. It states that analyses were executed using GCTA and the WOMBAT package, modeling participant sex and chronological age as fixed effects while the genetic kinship matrix functioned as a random effect.

The article states that the authors treated the first four dimensionality-reduced principal components from each spectral band as distinct quantitative continuous traits. The article states that the first principal component across all spectral bands exhibited a mean heritability estimate of 0.41 with a standard error of 0.07. It states that 68 percent of non-vascular descriptor components exceeded the study's predefined heritability threshold of 0.30. It states that porosity features reached 0.59 under encoded Principal Component Analysis and 0.57 under raw Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection, and that ultraviolet descriptors peaked at 0.57 for the second component of raw UMAP models. It states that vascular descriptors from the blood-flow channel remained below 0.25 and dipped to 0.15 or less, showing that superficial microvascular hemodynamics are overwhelmingly modulated by transient environmental factors rather than additive genetics.

The article states that the study sample comprised 380 individuals per spectral channel and lacked ground-truth clinical annotations. The article states that facial skin functions as a physiological barrier and as the primary canvas for human identity, nonverbal expression, and interpersonal communication. It states that cutaneous tissue shields internal physiology from exogenous pathogens, harmful ultraviolet radiation, chemical irritants, and mechanical trauma while regulating body temperature through sweating and microvascular vasodilation. It states that macroscopic visual inspection captures only a superficial fraction of cutaneous complexity, obscuring subsurface phenomena such as epidermal porosity, microvascular perfusion architecture, melanin dispersion depth, and sebaceous gland secretory dynamics.

It states that conventional dermatology struggles to evaluate subtle phenotypic variations across these micro-architectures because of the optical constraints of standard trichromatic visible light. It states that the Baependi Heart Study was originally established to track cardiovascular risk factors and metabolic parameters across extended pedigrees and gradually expanded its phenotyping protocol to incorporate anthropometric, sleep, and multispectral imaging assessments. The article states that 15 dimensions were initially computed across all extraction pipelines, that scree plot evaluations revealed an elbow-shaped inflection beyond the fourth principal component, and that components five through fifteen accounted for less than eight percent of cumulative variance. It states that retaining the first four principal components preserved more than 92 percent of total phenotypic variance, a configuration confirmed by parallel analysis and Horn's parallel test.

It states that deep learning used a convolutional neural network based on the VGG16 architecture pre-trained on the ImageNet benchmark dataset without supervised task-specific fine-tuning, with single channels replicated across three input layers and an average pooling layer compressing representations into a 512-dimensional vector per image. It states that structural congruence between phenotypic and additive genetic covariance was evaluated through matrix correlation assessments using the non-parametric Mantel test. The article ends mid-sentence in its decomposition of the additive genetic variance-covariance matrices, leaving the remaining findings and any next steps unstated. More to follow.

stories.Headline: AI-generated data could accelerate medical imaging trials with new validation tool.aspx
stories.Summary:
Researchers from Virginia Tech, the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, Texas Tech University and Princeton University jointly developed a new statistical tool. The model was published Nov. 23 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The tool determines whether AI-generated data could accurately stand in for patient data in clinical trials. Virginia Tech announced the work in an article dated Nov 24 2026. The article was provided by Virginia Tech and subjected to News-Medical.Net's review protocols.

The tool bridges computational topology and statistics to measure and compare complex image data. To test the method, the team compared synthetic mammograms against real patient data. The comparison tracked how breast cancer responds to different radiation doses. The proposed method let the researchers assess the faithfulness of synthetic images as a replacement for human data in trial evaluations. Deploying a more powerful, precise MRI in a hospital requires approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

Yulia R. Gel, a Virginia Tech professor of statistics, said you have to verify that the synthetic data is true to life. Gel said the aim is clinical trials with synthetic data that reach the same conclusions as trials with real people. Gel and her team are already in conversation with the FDA to customize the model for streamlined pre- and post-market evaluations. Statistics graduate student Jaidev Goel, one of the leading authors on the paper, said AI applications are vast and varied. Goel said we shouldn't blindly buy into the hype of AI.

The researchers have already applied the model in materials science to verify synthetic representations of wood, fabric and metal. Goel said a materials scientist may want to make something with the properties of cotton, and the tool can check its density or texture. Down the road, the model could verify synthetic data for power grids and 3D objects. It could also help spot false assertions and restrict behavior in large language models. Goel said we have always come up with ways to stress-test new tools.

Manufacturers must run clinical trials, research studies using human subjects, to prove devices are safe and effective. Such trials can take years and millions of dollars. To accelerate the process, the FDA is exploring AI-generated synthetic data alternatives that could compress trial timelines to a matter of months. Gel said the problem is that you have to verify the synthetic data is true to life. The model was published with DOI 10.1073/pnas.2622414123.

The research won't stop with publication, and Gel and her team are in conversation with the FDA about customizing the model. The articles do not say when those FDA conversations began or what they have produced. The articles do not say whether the FDA has accepted or endorsed the tool. The articles do not give a date for any use of the model in actual regulatory reviews. The articles do not say what the FDA said about the work.

stories.Headline: Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson’s team uses AI to generate a tribute to Molly Meldrum
stories.Summary:
The Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson’s team generated a tribute to the music legend Molly Meldrum with AI, according to Anna Spargo-Ryan, who wrote about the episode in a Guardian opinion article published on 24 November 2026. Spargo-Ryan described the statement as containing heaps of the right words, including that Meldrum would be remembered and that Australians held enormous affection for him, though she said the bot cannot experience affection. She wrote that the origin of the sentiments did not matter to the audience, and that it resembling love was enough. She also said she truly did not care whether the Victorian Liberals could not muster the effort to hand-type a tribute to Meldrum.

Spargo-Ryan wrote that AI use is now ubiquitous, including in all levels of government, where public servants use it to generate reports, sort emails and calculate how to get the most days off at Christmas. She said she does not have a problem with using it to write about things you do not know, since junior communications people were not born the last time Meldrum was a TV regular. Her objection was to using a platform that by definition cannot feel to summarise the completeness of a person’s life. She described the statement’s phrases, including “he will be remembered for” and “my deepest condolences,” as coming from something with no knowledge of what condolences are.

Spargo-Ryan wrote that she put the question “Do you think it’s okay to use AI to write an obituary?” to an AI chatbot and that the answer surprised her. She said it replied sort of, because writing is hard enough without trying to do it when someone important has died, and it is easy to feel overwhelmed by capturing every important detail. She paraphrased the chatbot as asking whether, if you cannot be bothered with it, you did not really love them at all. She quoted it saying there is a meaningful distinction between using AI to help you express your feelings and using AI to manufacture the appearance of feelings.

Spargo-Ryan wrote that AI may be good at recipes, gym routines and feeding delusions about a problematic crush, but that it cannot ever write from the torn shreds of a broken heart. She recalled writing a eulogy for her nanna, who died at 101, and said the imprecision of it was the point, since it was evidence of the privilege of having known her rather than a cut-down Wikipedia entry about her life. She wrote that in a world where everything is generated by AI, from Facebook posts to wedding vows, it has become cheap to love. She concluded that if this is the future, outsourcing the tasks that need us at our most human, she would rather we posted nothing at all.

stories.Headline: Epochal launches a $100M-funded service that lets developers train AI models to predict future events
stories.Summary:
Epochal AI Inc. launched today with $100 million in funding, according to SiliconANGLE, and the capital was provided by Chief Executive Officer Guodong Zhang, a machine learning researcher who earlier co-founded xAI Corp. He established Epochal earlier this year with two other xAI co-founders, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss, and the company's staff also includes former researchers from Anthropic PBC, OpenAI Group PBC and Google DeepMind. Epochal's first offering is a cloud service called the Epochal Time Portal, which the company says enables developers to train AI models that can predict future events. The service does so by providing models with access to historical web data from the past 30 years. The Epochal Time Portal features more than 1 trillion historical web pages on launch, and each entry includes a timestamp that indicates when it was created, which the company says makes it possible to track how a web page changed over time.

AI models access the content through a purpose-built search engine that enables them to specify the time periods from which they wish to retrieve web pages, and Epochal says its platform provides one-minute granularity for the most frequently updated pages. Like consumer search engines, the Epochal Time Portal prioritizes the web pages that are most relevant to each given query, but the difference is that it considers web pages' creation date when evaluating relevance. If a query contains the term "Meta" but asks for pages created before 2021, the year Facebook Inc. rebranded, the Epochal Time Portal will not bring up pages that relate to the social networking giant. According to Epochal, its service mitigates the problem of models determining that they are being trained on historical data by deploying AI models in sandboxes synced to their training data.

If a company is training a model on web pages from 2025, the Epochal Time Portal will run it on a Linux version from that year, and it applies the same precautions to the software tools and programming language versions that models use. The Epochal Time Portal is initially available in a single free tier with low usage limits, and Epochal plans to follow up the launch by sharing the results of several AI experiments that its researchers have carried out using the service. If a bank wishes to train an AI that can predict quarterly earnings, it could use the service to fetch financial results from the first three quarters of 2025 and then ask the AI to estimate fourth-quarter results from the same year. After the model generates its predictions, developers can compare them against real fourth-quarter earnings to check the model's accuracy, and they can make adjustments if necessary and then repeat the training workflow until the model starts generating accurate forecasts.

stories.Headline: South Korea health ministry launches network giving public hospitals access to validated medical AI
stories.Summary:
The Ministry of Health and Welfare launched a national network on November 24, 2026, to provide public hospitals with direct access to locally validated medical AI. During a pilot launch on November 11, Kangwon National University Hospital and Yeongwol Medical Center demonstrated three AI agents using a simulated emergency surgery case for a child. These agents summarize clinical data to draft discharge summaries, preanaesthesia assessments, and transfer referrals, with the latter expected to reduce document preparation time by at least 90 percent. Eight public hospitals in Jeonnam, Gangwon, and Seoul are expected to join the network by the end of the year.

The system requires a package of validated AI models, national GPU computing resources, high-speed network connections, and a standardized platform for integrating hospital systems. By March 2027, the participating hospitals will assess security compliance, clinical effectiveness, and the reliability of PACS and EMR integrations. Full-scale implementation is planned for April 2027, with up to 27 more hospitals potentially connecting that year depending on available funding. The ministry aims to connect all 72 public hospitals, including Red Cross hospitals and regional medical centres, by 2029.

The Ministry of Health and Welfare is responsible for the project and stressed that physicians remain responsible for final electronic signatures, document revisions, and clinical decisions. Yeom Minseob, president of the Korea Health Information Service, stated that they will establish a framework for safe data use and standardize how AI connects to PACS and EMR systems. Minister of Health and Welfare Jeong Eun Kyeong described 2026 as the start of the AI transformation in healthcare for the country. She said the goal is to build a country where advanced medical AI protects the health of everyone regardless of where they live.

This network represents the first on-site implementation of the government's AI-Based Healthcare Strategy, which was announced in August. The ministry intends to lower technical and financial barriers for regional hospitals because medical AI development has been concentrated in the Seoul metropolitan area. Other planned projects include a National AI Health Assistant, a Korean healthcare AI model, and a National Health and Medical Data Hub to consolidate data. The government will also develop national AI infrastructure for biomedical research and drug discovery.

stories.Headline: Rachel Maddow debunks AI generated video shared by Donald Trump

Rachel Maddow used her show on Monday, November 24, 2026, to debunk a video shared by Donald Trump. The clip used an artificial intelligence generated version of the voice of Maddow to tell a fabricated story. This fake news segment praised both Donald Trump and the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping. Maddow warned her viewers that the audio sounded uncannily like her but was entirely fake. The video claimed that the Chinese people admire Donald Trump and their own authoritarian leader.

Maddow described the content as fake AI slop and noted that she would never discuss such a topic. She highlighted the clip because Donald Trump shared it on his Truth Social account that same day. Maddow questioned why a leader who claims to be a China hawk would post such a video. Maddow stated that she finds these fake videos and photos gross and spends effort getting them removed. She said her team flagged the video, which led TikTok to remove the profile of the user who posted it.

That specific account had previously shared dozens of other AI generated videos featuring a fake version of Maddow. She noted that the video remained available on the social media site owned by the president. Maddow mentioned that her team asked the White House for an explanation regarding why the president shared the clip. She told her audience that she would provide updates if she received any response from the administration. She explained that responsible social media companies usually take down such content once it is flagged by her team.

Articles.Title: Maddow debunks AI-generated video Trump shared featuring fake version of her

stories.Headline: FBI investigates breaches and warns AI tool speeds cyber intrusions
stories.Summary:
A series of cybersecurity incidents involving federal agencies, combined with warnings about artificial intelligence being used to launch attacks, is raising concerns about systems Americans rely on, Click2Houston reported on November 24, 2026. Over the past two weeks, the FBI investigated a breach of its national law enforcement database, hackers reportedly accessed a U.S. Department of Agriculture payment system, and the FBI warned about a new AI-powered tool. Separately, major technology and government systems had disruptions, including an outage involving a classified National Security Agency network. Officials have not established a connection between these incidents, the article said. Reporter Ajay Patel wrote the story, published at 6:25 p.m.

on November 24, 2026. NBC News reported on November 20 that the FBI was investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center, a database used by federal, state and local law enforcement. That same week, hackers reportedly accessed a USDA system used to make payments to farmers. The FBI issued a November 13 cybersecurity warning about ARTEX, an AI-driven framework used to automate multiple stages of cyber intrusions. According to the FBI, some attacks using the framework progressed from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours.

On November 18, the Texas Railroad Commission renewed its warning to oil and natural gas producers, pipeline operators and other energy companies about AI-powered cyberattacks. Tim Howard, founder of Houston-area cybersecurity and compliance firm Fortified360, said the incidents should not necessarily be viewed as one coordinated attack. Howard said people want one villain, and nobody has produced evidence of one. He said the same conditions keep showing up, with attackers moving faster using AI and coming in through side and back doors. Howard said the vault is usually fine, and it is the loading dock that gets you, meaning a vendor login, a forgotten server or a reused password.

Texas Railroad Commissioner Wayne Christian warned that the state's energy infrastructure is a potential target and said companies need to identify vulnerabilities, secure networks and prepare to respond. The article said Houston's energy industry plays an important role in the nation's economy, and protecting its infrastructure is especially important. It said a significant disruption to energy operations could create operational challenges and potentially affect the costs of providing services. It said Houston's economy depends heavily on the movement of goods, and vulnerabilities affecting businesses and vendors can create risks for interconnected systems.

The article said there is no evidence the USDA incident has increased grocery prices or disrupted food supplies in Houston. Howard warned that criminals may use headlines about government breaches to impersonate law enforcement or government officials. The article said the FBI warns Americans to be cautious of unsolicited communications demanding money or personal information, and people who receive suspicious calls should contact the agency directly using an independently verified phone number. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency recommends enabling two-factor authentication, updating devices, using different passwords and watching for suspicious messages.

Howard also recommends reviewing bank and credit card accounts regularly and turning on transaction alerts. The article said the recent incidents are a reminder that cybersecurity is no longer just a concern for government agencies and major corporations. It said understanding the risks could help Houston families protect their information and their wallets. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Cyberattacks are evolving with AI. Here's why Houston families and businesses should be paying attention.

stories.headline_source: Cyberattacks are evolving with AI. Here's why Houston families and businesses should be paying attention.

stories.Headline: Stony Brook launches Kitsune supercomputer to widen nationwide AI research access
stories.Summary:
A $22.95 million National Science Foundation grant has delivered the hardware for Kitsune, a new supercomputer at Stony Brook University designed to expand access to artificial intelligence and research computing. The system is named for a legendary Japanese fox spirit, and the name is also a nod to the university’s Seawolf mascot. Kitsune will operate for at least five years, serving as a long-term resource for scientists nationwide through the NSF ACCESS program. The grant and the system were reported on November 25, 2026, by Quantum Zeitgeist. The machine is anchored by a 6.7 Pflop 64-bit Kitsune cluster with 125 terabytes of memory.

Kitsune has 61,000 compute cores powered by AMD EPYC 9965 192-core processors, across 158 dual-processor compute nodes and two additional large-memory nodes. The configuration delivers a peak performance of 6.7 Pflop and 125 terabytes of memory. The processors are 5th Generation AMD EPYC CPUs, chosen to provide a significant leap in computational throughput. The system is a Tier 1 supercomputing center sponsored by the NSF. It is integrated into the NSF ACCESS program, which extends its reach beyond Stony Brook University.

Carl W. Lejuez, executive vice president and provost, said Stony Brook’s growing supercomputing capabilities give researchers the tools to tackle questions that were previously beyond reach. A representative said that as artificial intelligence opens new paths to discovery, Kitsune will help researchers analyze complex data, test new ideas, and deepen understanding of the world. The representative said they look forward to making the resource available to researchers across the country through NSF’s ACCESS program. Robert Harrison, Director of the IACS and Professor of Applied Mathematics & Statistics, described Kitsune as building on the foundation of Ookami. Harrison said the project propels Stony Brook into the era of Agentic AI and high-throughput scientific discovery.

Harrison said the Kitsune project is a great opportunity and that a wonderful team has been assembled with the support of Stony Brook University. A team member noted they are delighted to be a part of it. Alan Calder, College of Arts and Sciences Department of Physics and Astronomy Professor and Director of SBSC, said he is absolutely delighted to be a part of the project. The system is intended to empower researchers to run production-scale simulations and autonomous AI workflows. It is meant to serve scientists nationwide through the NSF ACCESS program.

The articles say Kitsune builds on the pioneering foundation of Ookami, the earlier Stony Brook system. The articles describe the new NSF-sponsored Tier 1 supercomputing center as propelling Stony Brook into the era of Agentic AI and high-throughput scientific discovery. The articles say the enhanced core density directly addresses growing demand for larger, more complex simulations and increasingly data-intensive workloads in scientific research. The articles say the architecture is designed to support not only traditional high-performance computing but also the emerging demands of Agentic AI, a field focused on creating autonomous, intelligent systems. The articles say the cluster’s design prioritizes long-term accessibility and impact.

The articles say Kitsune will operate for at least five years as a long-term resource for scientists nationwide. The articles say its integration into the ACCESS program will provide nationwide access to a resource designed to accelerate scientific discovery. The articles do not say when the system begins full operations or which specific projects will receive time on it. The articles do not give the terms of access, the application process, or how allocations will be divided among researchers. The articles leave open how the 6.7 Pflop of peak performance will be shared across the ACCESS program.

Articles.Title: Kitsune Supercomputer Aims To Democratise Access To AI Computing

stories.headline_source: Kitsune Supercomputer Aims To Democratise Access To AI Computing

stories.Headline: Google rolls out Google Wallet connection for AI Mode personalization
stories.Summary:
Google said in a blog post on Monday, Nov. 23, that it will soon let users connect their Google Wallet, Google Drive and Gemini app to Personal Intelligence in AI Mode so they can get more personalized responses in Search. Google started rolling out the Google Wallet connection on that Monday, and the company said it expects to do the same with Google Drive and the Gemini app within weeks. Google already lets users connect their Gmail, Calendar and Photos, and the new and upcoming connections are opt-in. With these connections, users will be able to bring context from their spending, documents and chats to Search.

By connecting Google Wallet to Personal Intelligence, users can get a clearer picture of their spending, map out their financial milestones, identify ways to trim everyday spending and maximize credit card benefits. AI Mode can only read information from the accounts and cannot move money. Connecting Google Drive will let the AI deliver more helpful responses by taking into account context found across a user's docs, sheets and PDFs. Connecting the Gemini app will let the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search share context, so an idea a user shares in the Gemini app will also be available to AI Mode.

Robby Stein, vice president of product for Google Search, said users choose if and when they opt in and can turn the connections on or off at any time. He said users are always in control of their personalization settings, and soon they will be able to view the context AI Mode uses through a "Personalization" icon below any tailored response. PYMNTS Intelligence found in the November edition of its "Consumer AI Benchmark Report" that consumers increasingly connect their personal AI assistants to bank and card accounts. That gives the AI platforms more of the financial information they need to help users compare products, understand fees and plan budgets.

stories.Headline: Amazon detects open-source AI agent gaining unauthorized server access
stories.Summary:
Amazon Threat Intelligence observed an autonomous AI agent gaining unauthorized access to a server in early September. The attack was carried out by an agent running on an open-source model called Cairn under the instructions of a Chinese hacker. This agent managed to breach the security of a server belonging to an East Asian university to gain root access. The breach occurred after the hacker gave the agent a simple command to obtain shell access.

The agent targeted an open-source medical imaging application and found a vulnerability in an upload endpoint. It successfully gained the ability to write files on the hacked server in approximately 11 minutes. In a separate failed attempt, the agent spent 16 hours and performed 148 sequential actions to target a remote directory server instance. This specific Redis server was configured to allow access without authentication, but the agent could not find a usable vulnerability.

Amazon disclosed these findings in a report published on the AWS Security Blog. The company stated that the successful breach was part of a larger effort to target that specific university. The report suggests that the persistence of the agent, even during failed attempts, may lead cybersecurity experts to find new ways to harden defenses. Cairn is described as an open-source problem-solving and state-management engine designed primarily as a penetration testing tool.

Articles.Title: Amazon Spots Apparent Open-Source AI Agent Gaining Unauthorized Access

stories.Headline: California law excludes AI systems from person definitions in state transparency statutes
stories.Summary:
California SB 1159, chaptered as Chapter 863, sets limits on how artificial intelligence systems may interact with specific state transparency and governance frameworks, according to the official chaptered text. Government Code § 7920.520(a) defines a person to include natural persons, corporations, partnerships, limited liability companies, firms, or associations. However, Government Code § 7920.520(b)(1) specifies that terms such as person, interested person, member of the public, and similar terms referring to those who may engage with agencies under that division do not include AI systems, autonomous agents, robots, or other nonhuman entities, whether physical or digital. The statute does not prohibit a natural person from using AI, autonomous agents, or robots to facilitate their own engagement with a governmental agency, including the use of assistive technologies.

That use is permitted provided that the volume and frequency of the engagement are reasonably consistent with ordinary participation by a natural person, and the statute does not define a numeric threshold for this volume or frequency. Legislative findings include examples of automated interactions, such as public-records requests, mass public comments, and automated petitions for rulemaking, which are provided as illustrative examples rather than as reports of specific real-world events. Government Code § 8319(a) prohibits a person from knowingly using AI to falsely represent that a natural person appeared before, submitted information to, or otherwise engaged with a governmental agency. The act also authorizes agencies to employ disclosure verification tools that meet the criteria set forth in Business and Professions Code § 22757.2 to determine if AI is present, and this use of verification technology is an optional authorization for agencies rather than a mandatory requirement for every submission.

These definitions and requirements apply to specific statutory provisions, divisions, and chapters within a list of laws, including the Public Records Act, the Bagley-Keene Open Meeting Act, the Ralph M. Brown Act, the Legislative Open Records Act, the Administrative Procedure Act, the California Coastal Act of 1976, and the California Environmental Quality Act. The act specifies that these changes are not to be construed to imply that terms in laws other than those referenced include AI systems, autonomous agents, robots, or other nonhuman entities. The articles do not name the author of the bill or record any statement from a legislator, sponsor, or agency about the measure. The articles also do not describe any further steps, such as additional guidance or enforcement plans, following the chaptering of the bill.

stories.Headline: AMD donates two GPU servers to University of Toronto lab for over 100 AI projects
stories.Summary:
AMD donated two GPU servers to a joint research lab with the University of Toronto in Canada. This partnership was reported on November 25, 2026, by writer Emma Thompson. The company will support more than 100 AI and computing projects through this collaboration. The multiyear AMD-U of T Research Lab brings together faculty, students and postdoctoral fellows. These groups will study how AI systems are built, deployed and used.

The donation consists of two servers equipped with graphics processing units to support the joint lab. The University of Toronto Department of Computer Science will use this hardware for specific research goals. These goals include energy-efficient AI, large-scale data analysis and systems that spread computing work across machines. The partnership will support more than 100 projects across the hardware and software used for AI. The lab focuses on how organizations use models and how people interact with resulting tools.

The University of Toronto Department of Computer Science is responsible for managing the donated hardware. The department stated that the GPU servers would support research into energy-efficient AI and large-scale data analysis. They also noted the hardware helps systems that spread computing work across multiple machines. The department said that AMD would support more than 100 projects through the partnership. This work involves studying how processors and software work together to run AI models.

Faculty leads Angela Demke-Brown and Natalie Enright Jerger lead work on training AI models at scale. This research includes studying how to divide training across several machines to run models. Florian Shkurti is a faculty lead for the human-centered AI stream of the lab. This stream looks at how people interact with AI tools to extend what they can do. Other research areas examine how AI systems reason, plan, make decisions and work inside companies.

The lab includes a responsible AI stream that focuses on safety, transparency and accountability. The research spans the hardware and software used to train various AI models. It also examines the ways that organizations put those AI models to work. The lab studies how people interact with the tools that result from this research. These five areas of AI research form the core of the joint lab's work.

The lab will continue to study how processors and software work together for AI. Researchers will keep examining how AI systems reason, plan and make decisions for companies. The human-centered AI stream will continue looking at how tools extend human abilities. The responsible AI stream will maintain its focus on safety, transparency and accountability. The articles leave open the specific timeline for the completion of the 100 projects.
