stories.Headline: Google AI falsely tells diners that Esin Restaurant is closing and owner Curtis deCarion corrects it
stories.Summary:
A few weeks before Nov 24, 2026, a guest at Curtis deCarion’s Esin Restaurant and Bar in Danville, California, asked if the restaurant of nearly 20 years was closing for good. The guest showed deCarion her phone, where she had googled when the farm-to-table restaurant was closing that day, meaning what time. The artificial intelligence search mode responded that Esin Restaurant & Bar was planning to permanently close its doors in March 2027. The summary said the chef-owners, Esin and Curtis deCarion, announced the closure after anchoring the Danville community since 2008 and operating in the Tri-Valley since 1998. It said the restaurant would wrap up operations at its Rose Garden center location and shared hours leading up to the false closure.

The AI summary suggested ordering the American eatery’s signature pot roast or lemon meringue tart for one last meal. DeCarion, who with his wife also owns Danville’s Revel Kitchen and Bar and Lafayette’s Social Bird Kitchen and Bar, was beside himself. Another person came into Revel and asked the bartender if Esin was closing, and deCarion’s barber in Oakland said he heard the same thing. When deCarion searched, even on different computers and phones, he got the same message. He asked AI how AI got this information, and it referred him to a Yelp posting, but when he searched Yelp he did not find the source of the error.

When he emailed the support line for his Google business page, he got an AI-generated response showing him how to update his restaurant’s hours. DeCarion and his son, a manager-in-training who holds a computer science degree from UC Santa Cruz, took matters into their own hands. DeCarion said he put up a Facebook post, sent out an email and retrained the AI. He said it took about two weeks, but it finally seemed to have fixed the issue. The Nov. 5 Facebook post told customers that it was a false rumor, and the email, sent days later, also clarified that the automated AI search summary was incorrect.

The letter made the rounds on social media and stated that the restaurant wanted to set the record straight right away and was not closing. It said the kitchen was busy preparing seasonal favorites and the entire team was there doing what they love most, welcoming people to the table. SFGATE reached out to Google for comment but did not hear back before the time of publication. According to Google’s AI overview, the culprit for the erroneous summary was likely a classic AI hallucination. It was potentially caused by blending a real commercial real estate listing next to Esin’s location in the Rose Garden Shopping Center with context bleeding from other nearby Danville closures and facts from Esin’s actual profile page.

Google’s AI overview added that because the original query asked a leading question, when is Esin Restaurant closing, search-augmented models sometimes try too hard to find a date in the search results. It said they grab an unrelated future date such as a lease term or local event and wrap Esin’s real history around it. The deCarions had trained at Johnson and Wales University’s culinary school in Charlotte, North Carolina. Before opening the Mediterranean-inspired Esin Restaurant in Danville in 2008, they ran Café Esin in San Ramon. In 2014, the couple debuted Revel Kitchen and Bar, also in Danville, and followed it up with Social Bird in Lafayette in 2019.

According to deCarion, the three restaurants are not just open and employing 230 people, they are all thriving. He said they keep having record-breaking years and that it is a big challenge to manage and keep your finger on the pulse all the time, but they work every day like it is their first day. The articles do not say whether Google responded after publication or whether the AI summary changed further. They do not say what became of the Yelp posting the AI referred to or whether the source of the error was ever found. They do not say whether the guest who first asked about the closure or the barber in Oakland took any further action.

Articles.Title: For weeks, Google AI falsely said Danville's Esin Restaurant was closing

NIQ Global Intelligence expanded its ConnectAI Charter Program in recent weeks to include Arthēa and Pernod Ricard USA, according to an article published on 24 November 2026. NIQ also formed an alliance with QuestionPro that brings together consumer intelligence data and AI driven customer experience measurement. The article says the expanded program and the new alliance capture only part of NIQ's broader AI build out.

Adding Arthēa and Pernod Ricard USA takes ConnectAI to ten client engagements that cut across food, beverages, pet care, wellness, personal care and beauty. The article says that breadth matters because it gives NIQ more varied shopper behavior data and more test beds for AI driven use cases such as demand forecasting and trend detection. The expansion ties into the idea that brands increasingly use NIQ's permissioned data and context layer instead of building their own commerce intelligence stack. It also connects to the idea that more automated client workflows, including AI agents, can raise engagement within existing accounts and support usage based revenue streams.

stories.Headline: AI agent automates water network upgrade planning and matches human engineer
stories.Summary:
A research team has demonstrated that an artificial intelligence agent combining generative large language models with steady-state hydraulic simulation tools can automate water distribution system planning and engineering assessments. The work was described as a rapid communication in Cambridge Prisms: Water. The framework couples natural language reasoning and predefined computational function calling with the open-source Water Network Tool for Resilience in Python. In an empirical suburban case study, the integrated workflow processed external land development requests, executed automated hydraulic simulations, flagged network pressure violations, and identified precise pipeline augmentation requirements. The results aligned with an independent evaluation by a human hydraulic engineer.

The framework establishes four interacting components: the user, the language model, a curated function collection, and internal utility databases. Operating via the OpenAI application programming interface, the setup deployed the gpt-4o-mini-2024-2107-18 model as its central reasoning and function-calling engine. The team validated the agent's planning accuracy using a real-world municipal network model from a suburban area in South Australia. The test network comprised 28,985 nodes, 33,200 pipes, and multiple supply sources. In the primary case study, the agent received an initial user request to evaluate a land development demand of 20 liters per second situated near node ID 15064.

The agent applied strict utility service criteria: a minimum service pressure of at least 20 meters of head, a maximum pipe velocity of 2.5 meters per second, and pressure drops from new demand of no more than 10 percent of the base scenario's minimum pressure. It automatically executed two comparative simulations: a base scenario modeling current conditions and a future scenario incorporating the additional 20 liters per second demand. The assessment identified 12 nodes where pressure reductions exceeded the allowable 10 percent margin during peak demand hours. The agent recommended upsizing approximately 196 meters of ductile iron pipe from a nominal diameter of DN100 with an internal diameter of 113 millimeters to DN150 with an internal diameter of 160 millimeters. This automated solution matched the exact technical conclusion reached independently by a professional hydraulic engineer.

The authors concluded that while generative AI agents cannot replace human engineering expertise, they offer a scalable strategy to alleviate manual workloads, accelerate developer turnaround times, and improve operational consistency. They said engineering integrity is maintained because the system depends on curated, domain-specific function libraries rather than statistical pattern matching from historical records. The researchers emphasized that further research is required to evaluate framework performance across wider scales, assess operational limitations, and analyze multi-scenario planning under conditions of future uncertainty. The human planner initiates inquiries in natural language, supplies contextual specifications, and verifies final analytical recommendations before implementation. Planning engineers retain responsibility for validating all generated findings and instructing the agent to carry out supplementary modeling rounds if adjustments are warranted.

The articles state that urban water distribution systems are foundational civil infrastructure engineered to supply communities with clean potable water at adequate service pressures. They say existing networks in most developed nations, established since the nineteenth century, now face mounting strain from urban expansion and the need to support housing affordability. The articles state that delivering new homes depends directly on timely upgrades to essential utilities such as water and electricity networks. They say water distribution planning typically spans long-term master planning, short-term capital planning, and land development assessments answering proposals from private developers or rezoning authorities. The articles state that planning engineers must manually configure operating scenarios, execute individual hydraulic runs, and interpret simulation outputs across various uncertain demand forecasts.

A secondary case study verified the agent's ability to interface with empirical field monitoring data, retrieving logger records for a specific physical pressure logger identifier and defined temporal window and generating statistical and visual comparisons between field measurements and simulated model pressures. Additional exploratory tests confirmed the model consistently handled prompts to add demands at alternative nodes, trigger ad-hoc simulations, and generate time-specific hydraulic profiles. The articles state that the language model does not invent hydraulic code or access sensitive data directly, instead identifying and triggering validated, user-defined Python functions that execute calculations locally on secured utility infrastructure. The articles state that the function library contains discrete modular routines developed with domain expertise to mirror utility design standards and criteria. The articles leave open how the framework performs across wider scales and under multi-scenario planning with future uncertainty.

Articles.Title: Generative AI Agent Integrates Hydraulic Models to Automate Water Network Upgrades

stories.Headline: Researcher finds conversational AI raises student disorganisation and impairs deep processing in trial
stories.Summary:
A randomised controlled experiment by educational researcher Viola Braun, published in Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans, found that general-purpose conversational AI increased student disorganisation and impaired deep processing compared with static worksheets. The trial recruited 317 post-dropout participants aged 18 to 61 and randomly assigned them to a worksheet control group or an AI condition. The study was published on 24 November 2026 and reported by bioengineer.org. Participants in the AI arm interacted with a deployment of Gemini 2.5 Pro served through Google Vertex AI and Cloud Run Functions. The experiment gave participants 15 minutes of study time before a test.

The trial allocated 170 individuals to the static worksheet control group and 147 to the experimental AI condition. Participants had a mean age of 24.47 years with a standard deviation of 7.37 years, and comprised 215 women, 99 men and 3 non-binary individuals. Of these, 276 held a higher education entrance qualification or above, 20 held an intermediate secondary certificate and 21 held a lower secondary qualification. Prior familiarity was balanced, with 146 reporting baseline familiarity and 171 reporting no prior knowledge. The instructional content comprised 45 curated worksheets spanning German, mathematics and English from the upper secondary curriculum of Baden-Württemberg.

Braun reported a strong positive total effect of the AI intervention on disorganisation, with an unstandardised posterior median of 0.84 and a 95 percent credible interval between 0.47 and 1.21. The direct effect had a median of 0.77 and a credible interval from 0.41 to 1.15. Braun found the unmediated total effect on deep processing was diluted, with a posterior median of negative 0.22. The serial indirect pathway through cognitive offloading and critical thinking had a posterior median of negative 0.0480 and a credible interval between negative 0.1350 and positive 0.0065. Braun formulated the cognitive dormancy model, defining dormancy as an environmentally induced suspension of metacognitive and cognitive processing during educational tasks.

The study found that interaction with the AI reduced rather than increased self-reported cognitive offloading, with a median shift of negative 0.27. The experimental group showed an inverse total effect on surface processing, with a posterior median of negative 0.27 and a credible interval of negative 0.56 to 0.01. The Bayesian structural model explained 85 percent of the variance in deep processing, 41 percent in surface processing and 27 percent in disorganisation. It also explained 29 percent of the variance in critical thinking and 9 percent in cognitive offloading.

The model's Bayesian root mean squared error of approximation was 0.048, with a 90 percent credible interval from 0.047 to 0.048. The theoretical framework departed from electroencephalography research showing that relying on AI to solve novel tasks reduced neural functional connectivity and yielded persistent learning deficits. The study focused on the dichotomy between deep processing, surface processing and self-regulatory organisation. Traditional worksheets provide rigid task boundaries and sequential scaffolding that compel students to self-organise and evaluate arguments.

General-purpose conversational engines are engineered around immediate solution delivery rather than pedagogical scaffolding. The baseline content was generated via Gemini 2.5 Pro and screened through an iterative multi-agent consensus review involving six large language models alongside expert evaluation. The conversational model incorporated retrieval-augmented generation grounded in the assigned worksheet content via a JSON content directory in cloud storage. It operated at a temperature of 0.7 under a standardised instructional system prompt.

Participants completed baseline trait inventories based on the Achievement Goal Questionnaire-Revised before learning their assignment. Achievement goals were integrated as statistical covariates to prevent confounding of the observed technological effects. The primary outcomes were analysed using a multivariate Bayesian structural equation model in R, with psychometric reliability established via McDonald's omega. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Conversational AI Increases Student Disorganisation and Impairs Deep Processing in Trial

stories.headline_source: Conversational AI Increases Student Disorganisation and Impairs Deep Processing in Trial

stories.Headline: Review finds AI medical devices improve diagnosis and personalize care across specialties
stories.Summary:
A review published in the journal Biomedical Materials & Devices reports that artificial intelligence is being built into medical devices to improve diagnostic accuracy, customize treatment plans and raise patient outcomes across many clinical specialties, according to an account of the work published by bioengineer.org on November 25, 2026. The authors describe how adding intelligent algorithms to medical equipment creates opportunities to improve clinical performance while they weigh both the technological progress and the regulatory obstacles involved. The survey covers the growing role of these devices in dentistry, medical imaging, ophthalmology, mental health, autism spectrum disorder diagnosis, oncology and general medicine, and it reports consistent gains in diagnostic precision, tailored treatment planning and therapeutic results. The paper also says the algorithms help organize, classify, investigate and display complex healthcare data so that professionals can evaluate clinical information more effectively.

In oncology the review documents that artificial intelligence has been applied to identifying acute leukemia, breast cancer and pancreatic cancer, and that the systems can also estimate broader clinical parameters such as patient survival rates and the effectiveness of care plans. In dentistry the authors report that algorithmic tools are already widely used and spreading quickly for clinical diagnosis, patient charting, treatment planning, robotics and practitioner education, while also supporting general medical delivery. The review states that artificial intelligence-based medical devices must be formally approved or cleared by the United States Food and Drug Administration to verify their safety and clinical efficacy before widespread deployment, and it presents the regulatory guidance pathways established for such devices. The authors add that while regulatory compliance presents considerable challenges, the medical device industry has shown notable resilience and creativity in addressing hurdles to development and clearance.

The review is credited to Tettey-Engmann, Parupelli, Bauer, Bhattarai and Desai and was published in Biomedical Materials & Devices, volume 4, issue 2, pages 1767 to 1787, with the digital object identifier 10.1007/s44174-025-00379-1. The authors say that despite rapid clinical adoption, large-scale implementation faces substantial technical, ethical and practical obstacles that must be systematically resolved, and that the sector must remain flexible while keeping patient safety and verified clinical results at the center of innovation. They conclude that artificial intelligence will increasingly converge with complementary advanced disciplines to accelerate customized, patient-centered care, and they identify opportunities at the intersection of artificial intelligence, medical devices and internet-enabled systems, emphasizing integrations with the Internet of Things, biotechnology, nanotechnology and personalized therapeutics. The review says that combining artificial intelligence with targeted medicines tailored to individual patient needs promises to advance personalized healthcare delivery and offers insight into the future direction of collaborative, patient-centered medicine.

Articles.Title: AI Medical Devices Advance Diagnostic Accuracy and Personalized Patient Care in Review

stories.headline_source: AI Medical Devices Advance Diagnostic Accuracy and Personalized Patient Care in Review

stories.Headline: Cisco and OpenAI launch Shirudo open source AI cyber defense system
stories.Summary:
Cisco Systems and OpenAI announced Shirudo, a self-defending AI cybersecurity system for enterprises, in a release dated November 24, 2026. The system uses eBPF based agents that observe low level infrastructure activity and trigger real time automated threat responses. It watches Linux kernels and deploys cryptographically signed shields while regular patches catch up. The platform is released as open source software, and enterprise security teams and developers are invited to contribute and extend its capabilities.

The release gives Cisco a way to plug AI directly into low level defense, which the article says aligns closely with its existing security and networking stack. For enterprises already running Cisco gear, it turns the company's AI story into something operational rather than abstract, and it pushes AI Defense style capabilities deeper into infrastructure. The article says it sits alongside projects like Hypershield, Splunk integration and the US$9.3b in hyperscale AI orders that analysts already factor into growth and margin assumptions. The article describes Cisco as a US communications technology giant with a market value of about $381.6b that builds networking, security and data infrastructure many large enterprises already rely on, which it says gives the project a direct path into existing customer environments.

The article does not name individual executives or give direct statements from Cisco or OpenAI about the launch. It says the key tell will be whether Cisco starts to cite Shirudo usage and community contributions in earnings calls or product updates. Examples it gives are the number of enterprises running shields in production or tests contributed for new vulnerabilities. Concrete metrics around shields deployed, Linux hosts covered, or joint Cisco and OpenAI reference customers would show the project is turning into real world security adoption rather than just a high profile launch, according to the article.

The launch sits alongside broader shifts in Cisco's AI security positioning that recent research has highlighted, the article says. It says the current narrative hinges on Cisco extending AI focused networking and full stack security across hyperscalers, enterprises and governments while holding margins against hardware cost pressure. Shirudo fits that thesis by reinforcing the idea that security is integrated into the network rather than a bolt on product, the article says. It adds that the article was produced with the assistance of AI automation based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St, and that it is general in nature and not financial advice.

stories.Headline: Ray Dalio warns that great AI technology does not equal a good investment
stories.Summary:
Ray Dalio, the founder of Bridgewater Associates, warned in an interview on the "Sourcery" podcast that the market's habit of equating disruptive new technology with a high-quality asset is the core cause of every historical bubble. He cited the 1920s wave of technologies such as electricity, automobiles, airplanes, movies and radio, and said early investors may still lose money in the bubble first. He said the most dangerous aspect of this round of AI mania is the extreme concentration of the narrative. He said that once leveraged investors are forced to liquidate because of rising interest rates, maturing debt or tax pressure, selling pressure will feed on itself. He said that is where the bubble will burst.

Dalio argued that the real key mechanism is that people mistake a great new technology for a great investment. He said this mistake can still happen even when the technology truly does change the world. He said that even companies with good cash flow can go through a bubble. He said the key is not whether the technology is good, but whether the assets are concentrated in the hands of people who cannot withstand volatility and lack the capacity to hold. He said investors who borrow money to buy stocks must sell assets for cash once they face repayment pressure or a heavier interest burden, and falling prices trigger more selling.

Dalio said that when a company raises $50 million at a $1 billion valuation, a value of $1 billion immediately appears on the books, and holders may be called billionaires as a result. He said that until the assets are sold and converted into cash, that wealth can neither buy bread nor pay taxes. He said bubbles are often triggered when a large number of asset holders are forced to liquidate at the same time because of maturing liabilities, tax pressure or other reasons. He said selling pressure then spreads quickly, market sentiment turns from confidence to fear, and a negative cycle begins. He said that no matter how a company describes its social mission, where the money comes from is always the core question that cannot be avoided.

Dalio disclosed that he is building a system that writes his lifetime of investment judgment standards into rules and turns them into back-testable code. He said the system could keep operating across different market environments and even continue to work after he himself is no longer involved. He recalled that when he founded Bridgewater, his method was to write down investment judgment standards and hand them to computers to execute. He said relying on a single person to weigh various factors in his head and then make decisions in the traditional way is in fact already outdated. He said the future direction is for excellent human intelligence and excellent artificial intelligence to work together.

Dalio cautioned that AI will widen the cognitive divide. He said some people use it to understand causal mechanisms more deeply, while others outsource their thinking and simply wait for the system to give them answers. He said the most important thing is always to ask why, to understand cause and effect, rather than accept everything wholesale. He placed the current turmoil within the five major cyclical forces he distilled from his study of 500 years of history: debt and money, domestic political order, geopolitics, natural events, and technological change. He said these five forces interweave and usually form a grand cycle roughly the length of a human lifetime, and that the postwar world order established in 1945 is now in a phase of profound readjustment.

Dalio said the United States effectively has four political camps: the far left, the moderate left, the moderate right and the far right. He said no single extreme camp can completely suppress the other, and that only if the moderates form a force across party lines can structural problems such as the debt ceiling and fiscal consolidation be addressed. He said what has changed is the people handling the problems, not the problems themselves. He said debt, wealth disparity and the tearing of values remain, and whether pragmatic cross-party cooperation can be formed will largely determine where markets and the economy go next. He said that if the AI trade is to move from a bubble narrative back to a healthy cycle, it must first clear three hurdles: interest rates must not force debtors to dump assets at fire-sale prices, valuations must be supported by cash flow, and holders must be able to withstand price volatility.

Articles.Title: Dalio Warns on AI Mania: Great Technology Doesn't Equal a Good Investment, and a Bubble Is Only a "Forced Liquidation" Away

stories.Headline: Cary teen Krish Senthil presents AI kidney cancer model at informatics symposium
stories.Summary:
Krish Senthil, a 15-year-old sophomore at Green Level High School in Cary, presented research at the American Medical Informatics Association's 2026 Annual Symposium in Dallas on Nov. 9, exploring how artificial intelligence could help doctors determine whether a patient's kidney cancer has already spread. He was selected through the association's High School Scholars Program after submitting his research to a committee. The work, which he has pursued over the past four to five months, focuses specifically on patients diagnosed with kidney cancer before the age of 50. His interest in medicine began in middle school, and he said he chose kidney cancer because his father is a kidney researcher and both of his parents were involved in the medical field.

Using information from a national cancer database maintained by the National Cancer Institute, Senthil developed computer models that look for patterns in patient data. He trained the models on patients diagnosed between 2004 and 2018, then tested them using data from patients diagnosed between 2019 and 2023. His research found that tumor characteristics, including size, were among the most important factors in predicting whether the cancer had spread. According to Senthil, when comparing a patient whose kidney cancer had spread with one whose cancer had not, his model ranked the patient with metastatic cancer as higher risk approximately nine out of 10 times.

Senthil said the goal is to assist doctors, not replace them, and he hopes research like his could eventually help doctors determine whether a patient needs additional testing, such as a CT scan, based on information they already have at the time of diagnosis. The research uses existing patient data, and his model has not been clinically validated for use in patient care, so additional research would be needed before it could help doctors make medical decisions. He said attending the conference was also a chance to learn from experienced professionals, noting that many of them had research of their own. Back home in Cary, he said he makes sure his schoolwork remains a priority while finding time for his research, and he hopes to attend medical school, continue improving his model and potentially expand his research to other cancers.

Articles.Title: Cary teen uses AI to study kidney cancer, presents research at national conference

stories.Headline: History professor says GPT-6.2 Astra identifies the creator of an anonymous 1808 Yale sketchbook in 22 minutes
stories.Summary:
A history professor says GPT-6.2 Astra solved a historical mystery in 22 minutes by identifying the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale, according to Mark Humphries of Generative History. Humphries wrote that he tested OpenAI’s new model, GPT-6.2 Astra, before it was released. He said he gave the model access to images of the sketchbook and a throwaway prompt asking it to identify the artist. He said that 22 minutes and 1 second later, the model answered that Louis-Guy-Charles-Guillaume de Rohan-Chabot, vicomte de Chabot (1780, 1875), probably made the travel drawings. Humphries said he had never heard of Chabot and had not suspected him.

The sketchbook is held at Yale’s Beinecke Library, which bought it from an antiquarian bookseller in 2020 after it had been in private hands for decades. Humphries said the book has a mottled leather cover and 84 pages, 34 of which feature pencil and ink drawings or watercolours. He said most are labelled and only three are dated, and the handwriting is limited to short captions. He said the unknown artist began the book in March 1808, and it opens with the Newfoundland shoreline as seen from a passing ship. He said it includes Sir John Johnson’s house southeast of Montreal, the fortifications at Chambly, Chaudière Falls at modern-day Ottawa dated 8th June, the entrance of the Rivière Creuse dated 11 June, Fort St. Joseph on Lake Huron, Fort William on Lake Superior, islands in Lake Erie, and the mountains at Lake Champlain dated 16 August.

Humphries said the model suggested testing the hypothesis by ordering copies of a microfilmed diary of Chabot’s trip that it had found in an archival inventory held in the Special Collections of Cleveland State University. He said he ordered the journal and found there are two parts, one covering Chabot’s travels in Lower Canada and the other his journey to the Upper Country. He said the first is held in a private family archive in France and the second was microfilmed by the Library of Congress as part of its Lafayette papers. He said the model traced its finding to a single footnote in a 2014 PhD thesis on aristocratic refugee families fleeing the French Revolution, written by historian Juliette Reboul. He said that after some back and forth with both archives, all three documents arrived in his inbox, and the first thing he saw was handwriting with the same distinctive letter forms as the sketchbook.

Humphries said a quick bit of research revealed Chabot had been a minor French aristocrat and Irish landowner whose family was displaced by the French Revolution. He said Chabot became a British Army officer in exile and spent most of 1808 in Canada as Deputy Adjutant General. He said Chabot’s daughter eventually married the Marquis de Lafayette’s grandson and his papers were preserved in the family archive, lost until a descendant discovered them in 1984. He said the only scholarly reference he could find to Chabot’s 1808 trip to Canada was in fur trader George Nelson’s journals, published by Harry Duckworth as Friends, Foes, and Furs in 2019. He said Nelson mentioned hearing that a “Count de Chabot” had visited Fort William, and Duckworth provided a paragraph of context.

Humphries said he came across a reference to the anonymous sketchbook in 2022 while going through the Beinecke Library catalog for work on the authorship of Alexander Henry’s Travels and Adventures in Canada and the Indian Territories. He said the sketchbook depicts an 1808 journey from Montreal to Fort William and back, and is important because it uniquely depicts Great Lakes locations destroyed only a few years later. He said he spent many hours over the years trying to identify the artist with no luck. He said the chief problem is that the route was common, with hundreds of canoes and bateaux making the same journey every year, so the artist could be any one of several thousand people. He said only a tiny fraction of written sources survive, and those are handwritten, often un-indexed and mostly un-transcribed, scattered across dozens of archives.

Humphries said he included lines about Kendall and Berczy in his prompt, and that his “assistance” only led the model on a brief wild goose chase. He said he attached his article on Kendall and Henry for context and set the model to work on Ultra effort level in goal mode, which encourages it to work longer, but that he did not need goal mode. He said he initially felt the response was too improbable to be correct and suspected the journal would prove to be something else or would disprove the result. He said he ordered the journal anyway, and that how the model learned about it remains a bit unclear. He said neither Duckworth nor any of the other experts he has shared the finding with have given Chabot much thought, if they have even heard of him.

Articles.Title: A history professor says GPT-6.2 Astra solved a historical mystery in 22 minutes by identifying the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale (Mark Humphries/Generative History)

stories.Headline: BNY and Microsoft complete a pilot where AI agents negotiate a Treasury bill trade within set limits
stories.Summary:
BNY and Microsoft completed a pilot in which artificial intelligence agents negotiated a U.S. Treasury bill trade within predefined limits, BNY announced in a Nov. 17 press release that called it an industry first. Human traders at both companies reviewed and approved the terms, and the agents could not execute the trade on their own. The release gives no size, price or date for the trade, and it does not say whether other BNY clients can use the system. BNY, which oversees $63.4 trillion in assets under custody or administration, described one pilot between two parties.

The negotiation ran on BNY's Agentic Negotiation Protocol, which the bank lists as patent pending and designed as a framework and control layer for authorized agents from different organizations. Microsoft Treasury gave its agent specific trading instructions, and the agent reached the protocol through a secure gateway. Before any price was discussed, BNY's controls validated five things: the counterparty, the security, the size, the settlement terms and the available pricing. The two agents then exchanged offers and counteroffers, and neither could go past its authorized limits. Each agent submitted the proposed terms independently to a central ledger, which checked that the terms matched, and the companies executed and booked the trade through their existing trading systems.

The protocol keeps a record of who took part, the messages exchanged, the control checks and the human decisions, which BNY said lets the negotiation be reviewed and reconstructed. The release does not name the artificial intelligence models behind the agents, explain how participants are verified or say how many offers were exchanged. The Financial Industry Regulatory Authority named three risks from AI agents in its 2026 report: agents that act without human validation, agents that act beyond a user's authority and reasoning that is hard to trace or explain. Laide Majiyagbe, BNY's global head of markets, told Bloomberg that the company is not suggesting high-touch goes away.

BNY plans to keep testing the protocol and to expand beyond two-party negotiations, with future uses possibly including other contractual negotiations and repurchase agreements, which are short-term loans backed by securities. In a PYMNTS Intelligence report based on an October 2025 survey of 60 CFOs at U.S. firms with at least $1 billion in revenue, 52% said they would be open to autonomous AI that suggests changes to liquidity or payment timing. A September 2025 report drawing on a July 2025 survey of 60 similar CFOs found 32% were highly interested in AI agents for treasury management, compared with 7 in 10 for financial planning and analysis. No CFO was willing to give agents substantial or full access, 47% would grant no access and 45% would grant limited access.

stories.Headline: John Sherman says AI lets criminals and hostile governments find security flaws faster
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is allowing cybercriminals and hostile governments to find and exploit security weaknesses faster, according to an expert cited in a report published on November 25, 2026. The report was published by KOLN and carried a timestamp of 2:45 PM CST that day, with an update noted an hour later. The expert cited in the report is John Sherman of Texas A&M University, who is identified in the article's caption material. The report presents the acceleration of attacks as a concern raised by that expert rather than as a finding of a named study. The article gives no further detail on which weaknesses, which attackers or which incidents prompted the warning.

The report does not describe any specific requirement, rule or change that would follow from the warning it carries. It gives no numbers beyond the publication and update times, and it names no agencies, companies or countries as being responsible for the attacks it describes. The only date the article gives for the warning is November 25, 2026, and the only person it names is John Sherman of Texas A&M University. The article does not say what, if anything, is being asked of governments, software makers or the public in response. It also does not say whether any particular attack has been linked to the use of artificial intelligence.

Responsibility for the warning rests with the expert the article cites, John Sherman of Texas A&M University, who is presented as saying that artificial intelligence lets cybercriminals and hostile governments work faster. The article paraphrases his position rather than quoting him at length, and it does not attribute any further statements to him beyond that point. It does not say what he recommends, what he predicts will happen next or how he believes the problem should be addressed. No government official, security agency or company is named as having responded to his warning. The article does not indicate whether Sherman was speaking about a specific incident or about the threat in general.

The context the article supplies is limited to the claim that both criminals and hostile governments are using artificial intelligence to locate and exploit security weaknesses more quickly than before. It offers no figures on the number of attacks, no examples of attacks said to involve artificial intelligence and no timeline beyond the November 25, 2026 publication date. The article does not say what happens next, whether any investigation is under way or whether any response is planned. It also does not say how the warning was delivered or to whom. More to follow.

stories.Headline: India should prepare to reuse AI infrastructure after a market crash, Arindam Goswami argues
stories.Summary:
The artificial intelligence infrastructure boom has shifted from using cash to relying on debt, according to a report by Arindam Goswami. This transition occurred as large technology firms struggled to prove that the technology was boosting their earnings. American non-financial companies issued 940 billion dollars of investment-grade bonds in the first ten months of 2026, which was a third more than the previous year. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5 percent on 5 November, while Nvidia reported revenue growth of 103 percent twelve days later. These events indicate that companies now have less time to prove the worth of their massive investments.

Fitch Ratings warned on 17 November that borrowing by the largest technology firms will make bond markets more volatile next year. The agency says markets expect the five largest hyperscalers to spend over 1 trillion dollars in 2027, up from 772 billion dollars this year. Until 2024, firms like Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta paid for data centres using profits from software, cloud, and advertising. Now, these profits cover a shrinking share of the investment, forcing companies to borrow to finance the rest. An October stability report from the IMF counted 14 deals since 2023 where large firms put 300 billion dollars of equity and 650 billion dollars of debt into weaker AI companies.

Arindam Goswami, a research analyst at The Takshashila Institution, suggests that India should prepare to use the infrastructure left behind after a potential crash. He argues that India has little capital at stake and would barely feel a sharp correction in the market. He recommends that the IndiaAI Mission tilt its compute budget toward inference in hubs with existing power and fibre infrastructure. He also suggests that public funds adapt open-weight models to Indian languages, health data, court records, and farm advisories. Finally, he believes the government should set common standards for interfaces and liability, similar to what was done for UPI payments.

The current cycle faces political pushback, such as voters rejecting data-centre-friendly measures in the 3 November midterms. In the eastern US PJM grid region, data centres added 9.3 billion dollars to power capacity costs in a single year. OpenAI pledged on 5 November to pay the full cost of power at its own campuses following these political shifts. McKinsey's State of AI 2026 survey found that while almost nine in 10 firms use AI, only 37 percent see an effect on earnings. This suggests that the real constraint is the slow pace at which organisations redesign their workflows and legacy systems.

Articles.Title: The AI boom now runs on debt. India should plan for what it leaves behind

stories.Headline: Encode AI strategy chief Nathan Calvin plans to tell worried relatives they are right to be concerned about AI
stories.Summary:
Nathan Calvin, the 30-year-old chief strategy officer at the A.I. regulation advocacy group Encode AI, does not plan to bring up the risks of artificial intelligence at Thanksgiving dinner, because he expects his relatives to raise the topic for him. He will spend the holiday with his wife’s family in New York, where someone will probably ask him whether we are all going to die, and he will not say yes. His relatives cover a wide range, since his father is a neuroscientist who likes brainstorming with chatbots, his wife’s aunt is a therapist who is wary of A.I.’s effects on young people, and his mother-in-law uses A.I. to research travel, real estate, decorating and her retirement strategy. When his father wanted to understand what it meant for an A.I. to escape its sandbox, the two of them watched a presentation about it together.

Mr. Calvin plans to tell worried relatives that they are right to be concerned about A.I., but he does not want anyone spending the holiday in dread. He said that being miserable and not enjoying Thanksgiving because you are worried about A.I. doom is not really a good idea. Thanksgiving is the season for gratitude, pie and arguing about politics with your uncle, and this year A.I. may be the topic most likely to blow up dinner, whether the technology is stealing jobs or writing the kids’ essays. For a small group of A.I. researchers, the question is more urgent, namely how to tell your family, somewhere between the stuffing and the pie, that this might be one of your last Thanksgivings together.

The article, reported by Emmy Martin from San Francisco and published on Nov. 25, 2026, does not say what specific guidance the researchers offer for the dinner table conversation. It also does not say how the relatives in Mr. Calvin’s family responded to his planned approach, or what other families plan to do. The full article content was not available in the preview, so the remaining advice and any further details of the story could not be confirmed. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Bloomberg columnist warns US officials against aggressive AI chip restrictions on China
stories.Summary:
United States government officials recently closed a long-standing loophole that previously allowed Chinese artificial intelligence labs to access advanced American chips remotely. This policy change occurred around November 2026 and aimed to restrict the ability of China to develop its artificial intelligence capabilities. The move caused the Hang Seng Tech Index to drop 13 percent over two weeks, led by the e-commerce company Alibaba Group. Alibaba had been renting compute from Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based operator involved in an alleged espionage scandal with Nvidia.

These restrictions require American chipmakers to sever ties with Chinese entities and may change how companies report their global revenue. Nvidia changed its accounting policy in October 2025 to report revenue based on customer headquarters rather than billing locations. This change is significant because Singapore previously accounted for about 22 percent of total sales for Nvidia. Advanced Micro Devices also faces pressure as China represented 22 percent of its revenue in 2025. These companies must now navigate strict export controls while facing allegations that blacklisted Chinese firms still receive firmware updates.

National security hawks in Washington are responsible for these curbs and believe that squeezing China is necessary for security. However, Bloomberg columnist Shuli Ren suggests that officials should exercise caution because the global artificial intelligence value chain is deeply integrated. Ren argues that it is almost impossible to diversify risks away and that the United States will pay a hefty price. The author notes that any hit to chipmakers would reverberate far beyond Silicon Valley and hurt broader corporate profits.

The context of this situation involves a broader market concern that earnings for American chipmakers may have already peaked. Goldman Sachs warned that the S&P 500 could retreat to about 5,600 if earnings estimates revert to their 30-year trend. Investors are worried that companies like Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices cannot meet aggressive growth expectations. Future declines in artificial intelligence investments could also diminish orders for industrial companies like Caterpillar and GE Vernova. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Tiruchi colleges train faculty to teach AI and machine learning
stories.Summary:
Higher education institutions in Tiruchi have begun integrating emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and machine learning into their syllabi and into capacity building programmes for teachers and students in recent years, The Hindu reported on November 24, 2026. A growing number of institutes are opting for faculty development programmes that focus on how to integrate AI and ML in the pedagogy as well. The Tiruchi-based tech company Bodhi Multiverse UK has conducted six AI-related faculty development programmes for city colleges this year, according to its founder and director Anantha Ganesh. Capacity building programmes for educational institutions in Tiruchi typically cost upwards of ₹850 per person depending on the course and duration.

Many institutions offer degree programmes in emerging technologies, but there is a shortage of faculty qualified to teach them, the article said. Kevin Giftson, founder and CEO of Aske AI, a company that conducts tech learning modules for colleges, developers and healthcare professionals, said the syllabus has not been updated to cater to the new subjects, which has created problems for both students and teachers. He said it would be better for students to start industrial internships in the first year of their course so that they can get exposure to the technologies in real time. At National College, teachers are encouraged to complete at least two modules in emerging technologies every year through Massive Open Online Courses offered on government portals.

Ganesh said that though there is a buzz over the entry of AI into the classroom at present, it is not actually a new phenomenon, as it has existed in multiple forms before and is still developing newer versions. He said the best results are mainly down to prompting the machine, and that if one learns how to give an AI prompt one can create a product successfully and personalise it as well. He said the rapid increase in the number of AI tools and software can be frustrating for users and creators, but the company expects this to stabilise in the coming years. D. Prasanna Balaji, principal of National College, said that though AI and ML help to present lessons in an appealing manner, they cannot replace the teacher in making students actually understand what is being taught, and that the human factor is still important for the student's educational progress.

Articles.Title: Tiruchi colleges train faculty and students to adapt to AI, ML in classroom

stories.headline_source: Tiruchi colleges train faculty and students to adapt to AI, ML in classroom

stories.Headline: Apurva.ai opens call for development organisations to submit persistent challenges
stories.Summary:
Apurva.ai, a unit of the C4EC Foundation co-founded by Nilekani Philanthropies and supported by Rohini and Nandan Nilekani, launched an Open Call to Reimagine on November 24, 2026, according to The Hindu. The call invites development organisations to identify persistent challenges and explore new approaches to addressing them. The initiative seeks to engage NGOs, social enterprises, funders and other organisations working on complex social challenges where conventional approaches have struggled to deliver desired outcomes. A spokesperson for Apurva.ai said some problems do not need another solution but a different way of thinking.

Through the open call, participating organisations can submit one persistent challenge relating to programme implementation, impact measurement, knowledge management or organisational workflows. The exercise will examine existing processes, institutional knowledge and community experiences to identify alternative approaches, including opportunities where emerging technologies such as AI could contribute. The organisation cited the example of impact assessments that can take seven to ten months to complete, saying that by the time findings become available, community needs and priorities may have changed, limiting their usefulness in programme decisions. Apurva.ai currently works with over 50 organisations globally, using AI-powered products to connect community knowledge, research and institutional learning.

The articles do not say who is responsible for running the open call beyond Apurva.ai itself, and they give no closing date, selection process or further timeline for it. The only statement attributed to the organisation is the spokesperson's remark that some problems need a different way of thinking, along with the example of slow impact assessments. The articles do not say what happens after organisations submit their challenges or when results might be announced. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Nilekani-backed Apurva.ai to tackle development challenges

stories.Headline: US prosecutors say ex-OpenAI engineer Alfozan likely recorded meetings to capture trade secrets
stories.Summary:
US prosecutors claim that former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan likely captured trade secrets by secretly recording meetings in an office conference room. The Justice Department reports that staff discovered a sophisticated recording device hidden behind a television in an executive conference room in October. Alfozan had worked for the artificial intelligence company since July 2025 and was fired on the day of his arrest. He has pleaded not guilty to the eavesdropping charge and is currently detained while the criminal case proceeds.

The government alleges that Alfozan used a hidden bug to intercept dozens of conversations throughout September 2026. Investigators found hundreds of audio files and AI transcripts on his personal computer that were meticulously categorized by date and content. Some of these recordings were allegedly uploaded to the cloud platform Dropbox for storage. Prosecutors also discovered a photograph on his mobile phone of a confidential term sheet for a strategic partnership between OpenAI and another company.

The US government argues that Alfozan should remain in custody because he has considerable resources and connections in Saudi Arabia. Prosecutors stated that he was in frequent communication with people affiliated with the Saudi government while he was recording and transcribing meetings. Alfozan has denied that he was stealing trade secrets for Saudi Arabia and is seeking bail set at one million US dollars. His lawyer argued in a November 20 filing that the defendant has no covert ties to the Saudi government.

US District Judge Vince Chhabria previously expressed concern about whether Alfozan should stay in custody without more serious criminal charges. In a filing dated November 23, prosecutors urged the judge to deny the latest request for the defendant to be released on bail. They claim that his relatively weak ties to the United States make him a flight risk before the trial. A hearing regarding the bond request was scheduled for November 24 in San Francisco.

Articles.Title: Detained ex-OpenAI engineer likely captured secrets on hidden bug, US says

stories.headline_source: Detained ex-OpenAI engineer likely captured secrets on hidden bug, US says

stories.Headline: Russia uses AI to tailor disinformation for Africa and Latin America, expert says
stories.Summary:
Marcus Kolga, a Canadian disinformation expert and senior fellow at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute, said Russia is actively using artificial intelligence and other advanced technologies to expand the geographical reach of its disinformation campaigns, in an interview with Ukrinform. He said Russia is increasingly using artificial intelligence and other technologies to tailor its propaganda to different audiences. He said it is paying particular attention to countries in the Global South, especially Africa and Latin America, where AI helps overcome language barriers and expand its information footprint. He noted that Russia had been conducting disinformation campaigns for a long time, but that these operations intensified further in 2022.

Kolga said Russia has also exploited technology to expand these operations into the Global South, including regions such as Africa and Latin America, where AI is used to translate content and target specific countries and audiences. He said AI has really helped Russia expand and support many of these information operations. He added that what has really changed is how Russia has used technology and artificial intelligence to localize many of these narratives and tailor them to specific audiences. Ukrinform reported last week that Ukraine's Defense Intelligence, known as HUR, said Russian intelligence services were using artificial intelligence to spread election-related manipulation and disinformation in an effort to divide societies across European Union countries.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Podcast guests examine how AI politics and data centre protests shape South-east Asia growth
stories.Summary:
The Green Pulse podcast episode published on November 24, 2026, featured host Audrey Tan discussing with ST tech editor Irene Tham and Rajesh Sreenivasan, a partner at Rajah & Tann Singapore, how artificial intelligence has moved from a software issue into domestic politics and international relations. The episode examined what the global rise of AI and the data centres built to power it will mean for South-east Asia and its own plans to build more such facilities. It also looked at how the developing region will balance that growth against the environmental impact of data centres, which the episode said is driving protests globally. The discussion covered how AI evolved from a technology topic into a geopolitical one, and whether South-east Asia could see more protests against data centres. The episode asked whether the Nvidia controversy and United States efforts to clamp down on chip exports would act as a natural brake on the global expansion of data centres.

It also explored why Singapore chose to make environmental sustainability a key consideration for data centres alongside cyber security. The discussion covered what Singapore's digital infrastructure bill is about, and how data centres can contribute to the development of water and renewable energy infrastructure. The episode did not give further numbers, dates or names on these points. Sreenivasan is identified as a partner and the head of technology, media and telecommunications at the law firm Rajah & Tann Singapore, and Tham as ST's tech editor. The episode framed the spread of AI into politics and international relations as something that has dominated headlines globally.

It presented the protests against data centres and their environmental impact as a global phenomenon that the region will have to weigh against its growth plans. The podcast is hosted by Tan and produced and edited by Hadyu Rahim, with Ernest Luis and Zachary Lim as executive producers. The episode is part of Green Pulse, which is described as a podcast published every Tuesday to discuss how environmental issues intersect with business, politics and society. It was published on November 24, 2026, at 10:00 AM and updated at the same time. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the questions the episode raised.

stories.Headline: Jera weighs an IPO to fund expansion as AI drives power demand
stories.Summary:
Jera, the largest producer of electricity in Japan, announced on November 23, 2026, that it is considering various ways to raise funds for expansion. The company is weighing a possible initial public offering to secure the capital needed for its growth. This decision comes as the boom in artificial intelligence creates a new source of global power consumption. The company believes that this technological shift supports the case for increased investment in the power sector. The company requires significant cash to build new power stations and strengthen its liquefied natural gas terminals.

Jera previously unveiled a 5 trillion yen investment plan in May 2024 that focuses on hydrogen, ammonia, and renewable energy through 2035. It is now reassessing how it raises capital because of the growth of data centers, which it calls a new dimension. One specific project involves a 400-megawatt data center near its Chiba thermal power station with an expected investment of 15 billion dollars. This project is a collaboration with RHAELM Holdings and Dell Technologies to develop necessary AI infrastructure. Yukio Kani, the chairman and global chief executive officer of Jera, stated that the company needs a lot of cash for the whole LNG value chain.

He explained that the rapid development of AI is increasing the need to secure funds for expansion. When asked about the current status of a listing, Kani declined to provide specific details. He noted that Jera is currently talking to its shareholders about ways to maximize the value of the company. Kani believes there is huge potential because the company operates across shipping, trading, and upstream projects. More to follow.

This future projection comes as uncertainty looms over the global technology sector. The growth in the third quarter was driven largely by the electronics sector. stories.Headline: Saudi data and AI authority launches university AI initiative to train students and staff
stories.Summary:
The Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority launched a new initiative on November 25, 2026. This program is called the Year of Artificial Intelligence in Saudi Universities. It aims to spread the use of smart technologies in research and educational institutions. The authority wants to develop national skills to keep pace with rapid technological change. It seeks to turn student ideas and academic knowledge into innovative projects and solutions.

The initiative uses three tracks to build capacity through awareness, practical training, and measuring results. It includes scientific seminars, discussion sessions, training workshops, interactive booths, and specialized consultations. The program targets university students, faculty members, and administrative staff across Saudi universities. Participants can use the Athka X platform to secure training places and track their educational outputs. The initiative aligns with the targets of Saudi Vision 2030 for a data driven economy.

The Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority is responsible for this national capacity building effort. They stated that universities are key partners in preparing national talent for modern technologies. The authority wants to link theoretical knowledge with practical application in various fields of specialization. They aim to promote the responsible use of AI, specifically regarding data protection and reliability. SDAIA seeks to strengthen the role of universities as incubators for knowledge and innovation.

The initiative affects university students, faculty members, and administrative staff through tailored training programs. Faculty members learn to use AI for teaching methods, academic content, and research activities. Students are encouraged to turn their ideas into early stage solutions for economic sectors. Administrative staff use smart applications to improve the quality of work and daily transactions. These groups will learn how AI shifts the nature of professions and required job skills.

The program provides interactive booths to collect ideas and offer specialized consultations to participants. One booth introduces SDAIA publications, while another collects student proposals for the national app Tawakkalna. A session zone helps students shape projects, and another zone reviews laws on data. The initiative focuses on raising awareness of the limits of smart systems and data protection. It builds on previous SDAIA efforts to widen the base of national AI knowledge.

The authority will document results and produce reports to measure the impact of the training. They will identify projects that can be turned into sustainable applications within the universities. The program aims to create a generation of talent to bolster the Kingdom's AI standing. The articles do not state when the specific activities of the initiative will conclude. They leave open which specific universities will participate in the various training tracks.

stories.Headline: India weighs light principle-based rules for autonomous AI agents as RBI and MeitY draft sectoral governance
stories.Summary:
Manoj Chugh wrote in ETGovernment on November 25, 2026 that India's agentic AI boom needs both strong corporate governance and a light legal floor. He said agentic AI, once a buzz word, gave way to quick pilots that are now quickly making their way into production systems. He said the Government is working furiously towards building India's AI law to protect citizens. He said the law being envisaged is hoped to cover autonomous agents, not just deepfakes. He said agents can now raise payments, accept terms and act on contracts with no human pressing the final approval button.

Chugh said Indian law is unclear on who is liable when an agent gets it wrong, whether its decisions bind anyone, and what remedy a harmed person has. He proposed light, principle-based rules with named accountability, audit logs, incident reporting and a clear definition of what an agent is. He said the RBI's FREE-AI framework has recommended board-approved AI policies for banks and other regulated entities. He said MeitY's forthcoming consultation paper is reportedly being designed sector by sector, with banking and securities among the areas it covers. He said the RBI reviews its regulations comprehensively every three to five years.

Chugh said a senior technology leader argues that while agent governance is needed, regulation would be impractical and red tape would kill the benefits. He said that leader argues that if regulated industries have strong governance, with tools to onboard, manage and retire agents, that should be good enough. Dr. Pavan Duggal, a Supreme Court advocate and Global Chair of the AI Accountability Forum, said on the Corridors & Boardrooms podcast that a technology-specific law risks becoming obsolete within months. Duggal argued instead for broad principles that can stand the test of time, with detailed rules left to secondary legislation. Dr. Gulshan Rai, who led the drafting of the IT Act in 2000 and later served as India's first National Cyber Security Coordinator, said on the same podcast that any AI law must be drafted very, very carefully.

Chugh said Dr. Rai estimates that fixing processes resolves about half of security problems and configuration another 30%, with technology accounting for only about 15%. He said RBI Deputy Governor SC Murmu has told bank boards they must take responsibility for decisions made by AI and algorithms and know how many consequential decisions have been made by them. He said Dr. Duggal points out that the Contract Act recognizes agency, but not AI as an agent. He said Dr. Duggal proposes graded liability, assigned by each party's contribution to the harm, and a presumptive burden of proof. He said Chief Justice of India Surya Kant has said that banning AI tools would be neither practical nor wise and that the priority should be clear rules for their use.

Chugh said Dr. Rai observes that regulators such as the RBI and SEBI are strict, but others are not nearly as demanding. He said agents are spreading into retail, logistics, hiring, healthcare apps and small businesses, where no sector regulator asks how they are governed. He said India's 2025 AI governance guidelines relied on voluntary compliance, with mandatory measures to follow only if that fell short. He said the government now says the time for AI regulation has come. He said Dr. Duggal recalls a company that wanted DPDP compliance for the ₹15,000 price of an ISO certificate.

Chugh said Dilip Chenoy, former Secretary General of FICCI and the first MD and CEO of the National Skills Development Corporation, described a similar discipline on the Corridors & Boardrooms podcast. He said the skill standards Chenoy helped build had to be revalidated every three years. He said Dr. Rai's view is that any technology law stays relevant for perhaps five to ten years. He said Chenoy recalled that industry pressed for an e-commerce policy in 1998, which he notes did not arrive. Chugh said strong governance and light law, together, will certainly avoid both fears.

Articles.Title: Why India’s agentic AI boom needs both strong corporate governance and a light legal floor

The use of the Claude artificial intelligence model by Japanese organizations and companies has increased tenfold over the past year. The American company Anthropic drove this expansion by focusing its sales efforts on corporate clients. These strategic business moves have allowed the firm to establish a stronger presence within the Japanese market. The enterprise focus of the American firm has led to several high profile partnerships with major Japanese corporations.

stories.Headline: KAIVERSE debuts H3ARUS, a five-member AI boy group, with the single CRUSH
stories.Summary:
H3ARUS, described by its company KAIVERSE as the first five-member AI boy group, released its debut single "CRUSH" on various online music platforms on the 23rd and unveiled the official music video as it began full activities, according to a report by Son Bong-seok published on November 24, 2026. The group is built on a universe in which five secret agents disguise themselves as idols to carry out undercover missions, and its members have different personalities and voices. The name H3ARUS comes from "HEAR US" and is meant to say listen to our voices and stories, a meaning the company says reflects the members' individuality. The debut track is a disco-based pop funk song about the intense flutter and rapidly growing feelings of love at first sight, built on a lively rhythm and an elastic slap-bass sound. The song moves from the moment of being drawn to a stranger to the desire to grow closer, expressing first-love emotions in a candid and upbeat way, with distinctive member vocals blending into a dynamic chorus.

The music video follows the five members as they fall in love at first sight with one woman and each feel different excitement, expressing their feelings in different ways while gazing at the same person. The company presents the meticulously lifelike visuals, with the members' differing appearances and moods realized through AI technology, as a key viewing point of the video. KAIVERSE says the debut is meaningful as a first step introducing both the group's musical individuality and the appeal of its characters. KAIVERSE CEO Park Geun-woo said AI is merely a technology for realizing artists and that what matters in the end are the appeal of the music and the characters and the stories within them. He added that he hopes H3ARUS grows not as a mere technological outcome but as artists who make people enjoy the music, feel affection for the members and look forward to the next story.

KAIVERSE describes itself as an AI entertech company that develops artist IP based on AI technology and plans and produces content including music, music videos and dramas. The company says it has built production capabilities in AI video content, including producing the "OASIS" music video by Kim Jaejoong entirely with AI technology. KAIVERSE plans to expand the H3ARUS universe through content covering not only music and music videos but also each member, their relationships and the stories hidden behind idol activities. Building on its technological prowess and content production experience, the company plans to expand its in-house artist IP business beginning with H3ARUS. It says it will continue to present entertainment content that combines music, characters and storytelling.

stories.Headline: South Korea egg prices climb back above 7000 won as avian flu spreads
stories.Summary:
The average retail price for 30 eggs in South Korea stood at 7068 won as of the 23rd, according to the Korea Agro-Fisheries & Food Trade Corporation, which was 6.3 percent higher than the 6650 won recorded a year earlier. After the price had dropped into the 6000-won range from mid last month to early this month, it climbed back into the 7000-won range, the article reported. The report, published on the 25th, said the rise reflects reduced discount support by large supermarket chains and the government as supply increased. The article also asked whether egg prices will rise again amid the spread of highly pathogenic avian influenza.

According to the Korea Rural Economic Institute, the average farm-gate price for 10 extra-large eggs was 1661 won in mid-month, which was 133 won lower than the same period a year earlier and 173 won lower than the 1834 won of mid last month. The institute projected that the average farm-gate price in late this month would be 10 to 30 won lower than in mid-month. It attributed the decline to an increase in the number of laying hens and in egg production, expecting 58.96 million laying hens this month, up 1.6 percent from a year earlier, and average daily egg production of about 50.4 million, around 1.9 percent higher than a year ago. Whether highly pathogenic AI spreads is a key variable for future egg prices, the article said.

In this winter season, highly pathogenic AI was first detected on the 3rd, and 10 cases were confirmed by the 24th, according to the article. Last year, following the first detection on September 12, there were six cumulative cases by November 24, so within three weeks of this season's first detection the cumulative number of cases surpassed the tally at the same point last year. The article said that if AI spreads and more laying hens are culled, egg supply could shrink again and push up consumer prices. It noted that the sharp rise in egg prices this year was also largely due to last year, when 62 highly pathogenic AI cases led to the culling of 11.34 million laying hens, tightening supply.

stories.Headline: Jiro debuts fully AI K-pop group Seoria with generated faces, voices and performances
stories.Summary:
Generative AI company Jiro introduced its fully AI-generated girl group Seoria at a press briefing in Seoul on Tuesday, presenting the four-member act as its first original AI entertainment property and a showcase for its Dropshot AI platform. Seoria, whose members are named Riye, Cora, Iseol and Freya, debuted in August with the song "Burning," and every part of the group, including its faces, voices and performances, is generated using artificial intelligence rather than performed by hidden humans. Jiro co-CEO Hwang Gil-hwan said the company wanted to attempt the most difficult thing possible and to show how far its technology could be pushed, describing the creation of an attractive person as an extremely difficult task. The company said Seoria's video content had accumulated 2.54 million views as of early November, including 1.08 million for its debut music video, and that the group landed its first brand collaboration with athleisure company Andar in October.

Jiro said it spent four months taking Seoria from initial concept to debut, generating around 5,000 character images and tens of thousands of video clips while testing whether its platform could keep characters consistent and humanlike across different content. The company built the group much like a conventional K-pop act, giving the members distinct personalities and positions and a fantasy universe inspired by a legend about a secret female warrior group from the Goryeo kingdom, which spanned 918 to 1392, and it also produced album artwork, a custom typeface, dance challenges, variety-style videos and behind-the-scenes content. Jiro co-CEO Lee Jae-seok said AI idols are not bound by the same spatial, physical or time constraints as human performers, and he said the company plans to keep releasing music while expanding Seoria into animation, films, livestreaming, advertising and other content. Music critic Lim Hee-yun said AI idols face none of the human risks associated with private-life controversies or military enlistment and that content can be produced rapidly without the usual limits of time, place or language.

Lim also said K-pop fandoms form deep bonds through personal interaction with artists, and he said whether a being created entirely by AI can move beyond temporary curiosity and keep a loyal fandom over the long term still has to be proven. On Tuesday, the Korea Music Copyright Association proposed three principles for the AI era, namely responsible AI training, protection of artists' rights and fair distribution and compensation, arguing that commercial AI training should in principle require prior permission and agreed compensation. The association also called for clearer distinctions between fully AI-generated music and music made with AI assistance, while questions over how such music should be registered and compensated remain unsettled. The association is set to hold a public hearing on Monday to discuss issues including how much human creative contribution should be required for AI-assisted works to qualify for registration, as well as standards for royalty collection and distribution.

Articles.Title: After virtual idols, could fully AI-generated stars be K-pop’s next frontier?

stories.Headline: Hanwha Aerospace builds a defense AI data center in Changwon for 2028 operations
stories.Summary:
Hanwha Aerospace announced on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, that it is building a defense AI data center in Changwon, South Gyeongsang Province. The company briefed officials from the Defense Acquisition Program Administration and the National AI Strategy Committee, including Vice Chair Ha Jung-woo, at the construction site. This project is part of a larger 55 trillion won investment plan that Executive Vice Chair Kim Dong-kwan announced in July. The company intends to use its own power generation assets to expand these data center operations both in South Korea and abroad.

The first phase of this specific project has been allocated 10 trillion won, which is approximately 7.5 billion dollars. Hanwha Aerospace targets initial operations for July 2028 and plans to equip the completed center with high-density GPU servers. The facility is designed to reach an eventual capacity of 180 megawatts to support its defense AI goals. The company is also considering the possibility of including these data centers in future defense export packages.

Hanwha stated that a dedicated facility is necessary because of the military's security requirements and the need for uninterrupted operations. They are considering a model where the military retains control of its data while defense contractors operate the facility. The company claims this approach could accelerate the adoption of defense AI by four to five years over a government-led project. An official said the facility would be foundational national infrastructure that helps solidify the position of Korea among the world's top four defense powers.
