stories.Headline: India urges human accountability for AI use in armed conflicts at UN debate
stories.Summary:
India called for human judgement and accountability regarding the use of artificial intelligence during armed conflicts at a United Nations Security Council debate in New York. Ambassador Harish Parvathaneni, who serves as India's Permanent Representative to the United Nations, delivered these remarks during a session convened by Latvia. The debate focused on the challenges of conflict resolution while the world experiences rapid technological change. India raised specific alarms about the dangers of autonomous weapons and the potential for terrorists to misuse these new technologies.

The Indian representative stated that technology must serve as a means to achieve human goals rather than being an end in itself. He argued that responsibility for the use of lethal autonomous weapons systems must always rest with human beings. Parvathaneni emphasized that any emerging technologies deployed in conflict settings must respect international law and national sovereignty. He further noted that these systems must protect humanitarian personnel, peacekeepers, and civilians from harm. India remains committed to addressing these legal and ethical questions through the Convention on Prohibitions or Restrictions on the Use of Certain Conventional Weapons.

Ambassador Parvathaneni expressed concern that non-state actors and terrorists could use manipulated or inaccurate data to undermine critical decision-making. He criticized the use of licensing regimes and export controls that some nations use to gain a strategic advantage. The ambassador claimed that countries of the Global South should not be treated as mere consumers without agency in how AI is regulated. He also warned that AI systems might perpetuate biases related to socioeconomic backgrounds, language, and gender. India supports international cooperation on governance that considers the development priorities of different nations.

India pointed to the potential for AI to assist in peacekeeping through analytical tools, satellite imagery, and early warning systems. These technologies could help the United Nations respond more effectively to crises and improve overall situational awareness. The representative mentioned the New Delhi Declaration from the India AI Impact Summit in February, which more than 90 countries endorsed. This declaration called for secure systems, investment in human capabilities, and wider access to AI resources. Electronics and IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw previously argued that AI should amplify human creativity instead of replacing it.

stories.Headline: Entire partners with Sarvam AI to offer India-hosted AI coding agents
stories.Summary:
Entire, the developer platform founded by former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke, has partnered with Sarvam AI to offer Indian developers AI coding agents powered by locally hosted models, keeping code, agent runs, and inference within India, the companies said on 25 November 2026. Under the partnership, Sarvam’s models will be available in preview on Trails, Entire’s alternative to the traditional pull request. The integration allows developers to run coding agents using Sarvam’s models while hosting private code repositories in India. The partnership targets organisations that need to meet data residency requirements, particularly those in regulated industries. Trails brings code, development flow, agent sessions, and review evidence into a single workflow, according to the companies.

Coding agents can address review findings in a loop, while developers validate changes before merging them. With Sarvam’s models integrated into the platform, developers can run agent inference within India. The partnership also allows developers to create, migrate, and host private repositories on Entire’s distributed Git forge, with India set as their primary region for data residency. Dohmke said he believes India can set the standard for agent-human collaboration at a scale never seen before, producing more code than anywhere on earth. He said that as India pursues AI sovereignty, that code and the inference behind it need to stay at home, especially for organisations in highly regulated industries.

Vivek Raghavan, co-founder of Sarvam, said India should be able to manufacture intelligence in the country, and its developers should be able to use it in the tools they rely on to build software. He added that for enterprises that need their code to stay in India, this opens up agent-assisted development even for their most sensitive repositories. Entire also highlighted the performance of its Git infrastructure in India, saying tests with ForgeMark, its open-source benchmarking tool, recorded 355 pushes per second when multiple agents pushed to and cloned from a repository simultaneously. The company compared this with 29 pushes per second for Cursor Origin, 10 for GitLab, and four for GitHub, and claimed its infrastructure was up to 89x faster than the competing platforms in the tests. Entire said its early adoption in India includes enterprise and open-source organisations such as Infosys and Open Healthcare Network.

stories.Headline: AidenAI raises $32m Series A led by A91 Partners to build enterprise AI agents
stories.Summary:
AidenAI, an enterprise artificial intelligence startup founded in 2023 by Srinivas Kamadi, a former Senior Vice President at Infosys, has raised $32 million in a Series A funding round led by A91 Partners, the company announced on 25 November 2026. The company is headquartered in Princeton, New Jersey, has a significant presence in India, and operates across six countries. It develops an AI builder platform that helps enterprises build, deploy and manage AI agents using their existing systems and AI models. BDA Partners served as the exclusive banking and advisory firm for the transaction.

The funding will be used to accelerate platform development and build industry-specific agentic AI solutions, according to the company. AidenAI also plans to build a team of more than 1,000 frontier AI engineers by the end of 2027 through its AidenAI Builder Academy, which will operate from Princeton and Hyderabad. The company aims to expand its global operations beyond its existing presence in six countries. According to AidenAI, its platform acts as a layer between AI models and enterprise systems, allowing businesses to build and manage AI agents within their existing technology infrastructure, and its engineers work alongside enterprise clients to develop and implement AI solutions. The company also offers AiDAP, a platform for modernising legacy technology.

Kamadi said the investment marks a defining milestone in AidenAI's journey as it accelerates its ambition to build a global AI builder company powered by agentic AI and frontier engineering services. He said the company sees an extraordinary opportunity to bridge the widening AI capability gap, embed intelligence into the core of enterprises, and reimagine how technology solutions are built, modernised and operated. Kaushik Anand, Partner at A91 Partners, said the firm was looking forward to working with AidenAI as it builds an AI-focused enterprise technology company. Anand said that while enterprise AI adoption is still in its early stages, AidenAI has spent the last three years helping over 30 large enterprises turn the promise of AI into live, measurable business outcomes.

stories.Headline: HKS says AI reshapes building briefs as labs shift to 70 percent dry space
stories.Summary:
HKS, an architecture firm, published an article on November 24, 2026, arguing that artificial intelligence is changing the brief itself rather than merely speeding up design work such as renders and 3D models. The article says the buildings most architects worked on last year already differ greatly from those they will design over the next decade, and that this is not about designing faster but about how AI changes the way buildings will be used. It describes AI as the next inflexion point after the Industrial Revolution, which gave the factory, urbanisation, which gave the office, and sustainability, which rewrote performance targets. The author writes from the field of science, where ten years ago about 70 percent of the space designated in a floor plan was wet laboratory space, with the rest set aside for write-up and analysis work. The article says AI is reversing that model, with labs already heading towards 30 percent wet lab space and 70 percent dry, as servers and screens edge out flasks and centrifuges.

It says that as technology takes on more analytical work, spaces that bring people together to exchange ideas, challenge assumptions and make discoveries become even more important, and that the value of human collaboration remains central to scientific progress. Wet labs are becoming more specialised and potentially more hazardous, so more secure biocontainment environments are needed, along with facilities that let staff move safely in and out, and decontamination systems are becoming far more prevalent. The firm says it is working on more level three and four containment environments designed to handle research involving potentially dangerous biological materials, including airborne pathogens. The article also says data centres will be a growth sector and part of any country's vital infrastructure, and that universities will need to rethink how they use existing spaces as AI reshapes teaching, learning and research, since a new computer-based research lab or data centre cannot simply be shoehorned into an 18th-century college building without serious reinforcement of floors and frames. On healthcare, the author says the sector has adapted quickly because groundwork in hospitals had begun before AI was a consideration, citing a hospital robotics project he worked on as far back as 2009 that created a shadow hospital with its own lifts and corridors to deliver non-medical supplies out of sight of patients.

He says considerations for diagnostics and data will be similar, with space needed for servers and cabling rather than physical movement, and that the goal is more efficient healthcare environments that reduce bottlenecks, shorten waiting times and improve the patient experience, which he ties to the firm's work with the NHS in the UK. He says he does not see the wards changing much, but that humanoid robots cannot be all that far away, and that needs for automated cleaning or even changing beds may shape the ward more than shifts in medical procedures, adding that he does not much like the sound of robots doing medication rounds or observation checks but that cost savings drive their eventual acceptance. The article says such considerations did not really exist a few years ago and that the firm now has to think this way across all of its clients, predicting the future because waiting for technological or societal change means being too late to inform clients. It says the work is no longer about simply giving the client what they want but about working with them to understand what they need and how it can be futureproofed, overlaying the client's vision with an understanding of what new technology can bring and how it will shape their building. The author says having a finger on the pulse of what is possible matters far more than knowing the practicalities of AI models themselves, and that the firms that succeed in the age of AI will not be those with the latest technology or the greatest knowledge of how to use AI models but the ones that best help clients understand how AI is changing the future they are building for.

Articles.Title: AI in Architecture: How AI Is Redefining the Brief

stories.Headline: Jay Clayton says AI helps find PHP and Java flaws as agencies patch systems
stories.Summary:
Last week, users of Microsoft Outlook found the service was not working properly, and the next day the FAA issued a rare ground stop order because parts of the digital system air traffic controllers rely on failed. The following Monday, four of the country’s largest banks found their computer systems malfunctioning, and United Airlines had a computer outage that worsened the troubles of passengers still recovering from the ground stop. On Tuesday, the National Security Agency’s internal communications network went offline, and Apple web services were disrupted. Senator Josh Hawley, a Republican from Missouri, told reporters it was like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world if all of it was a coincidence, according to the New York Times. The president said it was life, and that when you are big and powerful and have all the money, things like this happen.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Fox News that ongoing efforts to patch a vulnerability in the PHP programming language took an internal National Security Agency communications system offline on Tuesday. He added that AI is making it easier to find such vulnerabilities, which can take years to fix without using AI to find them. Tech startup Calif said in a blog post this week that, using AI, it had found a critical flaw in Java4Shell, which leaves much of the internet exposed to cyber attacks if it is not corrected. Calif called Java the beating heart of the modern economy, and Oracle, the developer of Java, released a patch for the vulnerability Tuesday. South Korea’s intelligence agency reportedly sent a separate security advisory earlier Tuesday to public institutions, warning them to fix the issue and prevent hackers from exploiting the Java flaw.

Peter Avery, chief information and security officer for the Michigan cyber security firm Velocity Security, told the New York Times he was skeptical that the events of last week were connected, saying he likes facts and that until now these are all separate issues. He said drawing patterns where they do not yet exist is human nature and part of the need to make sense of things, but can lead down a dark road, and that when you start to live in that world where everyone’s a liar and no one is telling the truth, you are starting to live in fear. The article says that ever since the digital revolution began more than 50 years ago, computers have only been able to do what humans tell them to do, through instructions created by coders. It says millions of lines of bad code exist, a phenomenon known as garbage in, garbage out, and that digital firms employ many people to check code, a tedious process that often misses even glaring errors, while AI can scan 10,000 times more lines of code in a given time than a human can.

Articles.Title: Digital Outages Are Rampant All Across America. Is AI to blame?

stories.Headline: Neysa launches partner programme to deploy AI applications on its Velocis cloud platform
stories.Summary:
Neysa, a Mumbai-based AI cloud infrastructure company, launched a partner programme to help build and deploy applications on its Velocis AI cloud platform, using Neysa's infrastructure to meet customers' computing requirements, according to an announcement reported on 25 November 2026. The Neysa Partner Programme targets software companies, system integrators and resellers, consulting firms, and technology providers working across components such as networking, storage and computing. The company will provide computing capacity, technical support, deal registration, joint proposal development, and access to its sales teams to help partners develop solutions and pursue enterprise opportunities. Neysa hopes to reach more customers with its infrastructure-as-a-service offering through this structured route.

Aniket Chandavarkar, Head of Partner GTM at Neysa, said in a statement that the programme gives partners a structured way to build solutions, pursue opportunities together and grow their AI businesses. He said the aim is to make enterprise AI adoption a shared opportunity across the ecosystem. Mushtaq Khot, Director and Chief Revenue Officer at Lauren Group, a partner in the programme, said customers moving AI workloads from pilots to production need such solutions that make business sense without compromising control over data. The programme therefore pairs Neysa's capacity and support with partners who bring solutions and customer relationships.

Neysa continues to expand its own AI infrastructure footprint alongside the partner programme. Earlier in November, it announced that an 8,192-GPU cluster powered by AMD Instinct MI350X accelerators had become operational in Mumbai. It is also preparing a deployment at STT Noida 2, designed to support up to 9,000 GPUs in its first phase, with the project expected to go live in the first quarter of calendar year 2027 and to support AI training and inference workloads for Indian enterprises and global customers. In February, Neysa raised $600 million in equity funding from Blackstone and co-investors, and the company intends to secure another $600 million in debt financing, subject to documentation, taking the proposed capital raise to $1.2 billion.

stories.Headline: Anindo Saha leads a 22-country study finding AI matches radiologists on prostate cancer MRI
stories.Summary:
A study published on November 24 in the journal Radiology found that an artificial intelligence system detected prostate cancer on MRI with diagnostic performance comparable to expert radiologists across a diverse global population. The multinational SCARLET-1 study was led by Anindo Saha, PhD, of Radboud University Medical Center in Nijmegen, the Netherlands, and colleagues. The researchers analyzed 22,445 prostate MRI examinations from 21,252 men across 46 clinical sites in 22 countries, collected between January 2012 and October 2024. External validation spanned three datasets, the PRIME trial with 476 cases across 11 countries, STHLM3-MRI with 1,108 cases in Sweden, and IP1-PROSTAGRAM with 390 cases in the U.K. The primary outcome was agreement between AI assessments and standard-of-care diagnoses of Gleason grade group 2 or higher prostate cancer. The AI system's performance was comparable to radiology readings in all three external sets, with AUC values of 0.86 in PRIME, 0.89 in STHLM3-MRI, and 0.84 in IP1-PROSTAGRAM.

AI-to-standard-of-care agreement was 83% in PRIME, 87.9% in STHLM3-MRI, and 87.7% in IP1-PROSTAGRAM. Performance was consistent across age, ethnicity, cancer location, and risk subgroups, but varied substantially across 25 sites, with 28% showing an AUC below a stated threshold. The authors wrote that the study demonstrates AI achieved diagnostic performance comparable to standard-of-care radiology readings for detecting Gleason grade group 2 or higher prostate cancer across diverse populations and clinical settings. The researchers noted that prostate MRI is the international standard of care for men with suspected prostate cancer, but subspecialty urogenital radiology expertise is concentrated at a limited number of high-volume centers. They said the findings support a potential role for AI in extending prostate MRI interpretation, particularly where subspecialty expertise is limited.

The authors suggested that site-level performance variability signals the need for careful local implementation, because AI performance may be closely linked to patient and imaging characteristics. They added that shifts in case mix over time may affect results in ways that are not immediately apparent. The authors concluded that safe clinical use will require careful operating point selection, local testing, and longitudinal performance monitoring, along with prospective evaluation of clinical, equity, and cost outcomes. They stated that further large-scale trials are warranted to provide complementary evidence. In prior work, the group developed the AI system and demonstrated its noninferiority to radiologists in detecting Gleason grade group 2 disease or higher, though those studies were conducted in standardized Western settings.

Articles.Title: AI matches radiologists on prostate cancer MRI across 22 countries

stories.Headline: Solis tells Rio Grande Valley leaders that workers who know how to use AI will replace those who do not
stories.Summary:
South Texas College President Dr. Ricardo Solis told regional business, education and economic development leaders at the college's Annual Workforce Summit in McAllen that the Rio Grande Valley faces a rapidly evolving skills challenge driven by artificial intelligence and industrial expansion. He said the region is no longer facing a simple shortage of workers, and he described the area as sitting at the epicenter of global trade and nearshoring between Asia, Mexico and the United States. Solis said he is not convinced that AI will replace jobs, but he believes people who know how to use AI will have a significant advantage over those who do not. He repeated that AI is not going to replace workers, and that those who learn to manage and use AI are the ones who will replace those without AI knowledge.

The audience included Hidalgo County Judge Richard Cortez and representatives from RioPlex, according to the article. Solis reviewed economic trends he has highlighted at the summit over the past several years and how the college has adapted its curriculum to match shifting global dynamics. About four and a half years ago, the college rapidly scaled up commercial driver's license, automotive, transportation and manufacturing training to address post-pandemic supply chain bottlenecks, and North American regions later moved toward becoming more self-sustaining as supply chains reshored and consolidated. The college became the first community college in the nation to receive approval for registered nurse apprenticeships, a claim the article attributes to the college, alongside programs in manufacturing and business.

Having flagged AI as an emerging theme at the previous year's summit, Solis predicted the next major wave will be the convergence of superintelligence and employer-driven workforce development. He said the college's enrollment has surpassed 42,000 students across its six campuses when combining more than 30,000 academic and dual-credit students with its non-credit and continuing education programs. Solis said the college's primary service area covers Hidalgo and Starr counties, and that it is actively expanding its reach across the entire Rio Grande Valley to support major industrial growth at the Port of Brownsville, Eastern Cameron County and Boca Chica. To meet demand for high-paying, high-demand technical jobs, the college is ramping up capacity in welding, automotive, electronics, precision manufacturing and mechatronics, a specialized program combining electronics and advanced manufacturing that Solis noted is unique to the college in the region.

He added that the college is eyeing significant growth in its Mid-Valley and Starr County campuses to train workers centrally for port-related industries. Solis said no college can accomplish this alone and that employers need to be at the table telling the college what skills they need today and what they will need tomorrow. He also recognized Board of Trustees Chair Paul Rodriguez and Trustee Dr. Alejo Salinas, and said the future belongs to communities that can learn faster, reskill faster and adapt faster. Following his remarks, Solis introduced the summit's keynote speaker, Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board Commissioner Dr. Wynn Rosser, who traveled from Austin to discuss statewide strategies for aligning higher education with regional economic development.

stories.Headline: Wright Research's Srivastava says AI can analyse markets but cannot pick stocks for investors
stories.Summary:
Sonam Srivastava, founder and CEO of Wright Research, told Analytics India Magazine on 25 November 2026 that she would not simply talk to AI and have it suggest where to invest. She drew a line between using AI to understand the market and relying on it to select individual stocks. She said AI holds publicly available data, such as the probability of a federal rate hike. She said evaluating an individual company needs more context, including financial statements, business updates and capital allocation. She said AI models are only as good as the data and context they have.

Srivastava said users can upload financial statements and company updates to extract key metrics, or use AI tools to summarise lengthy earnings calls. She said AI is like having another quant researcher or validator on her team. She said an AI model can work with historical information but may not understand an investor's circumstances, risk appetite, investment horizon or goals. She said expert advisers might have a better forward-looking opinion. She cautioned against treating AI-generated investment suggestions as advice, especially for larger investments, which people should get checked or validated.

The Securities and Exchange Board of India, in a consultation paper published last year, clarified that regulated entities, not software vendors, were responsible for the output of AI tools. The market regulator is preparing new guidelines for the responsible use of AI in capital markets amid concerns over AI-powered trading agents. Ambarish Khenge, CEO of Angel One, said its Ask Angel chatbot can cut through information on an IPO application and tell an investor what to worry about and why they should or should not invest. He said Angel One restricts the information available to Ask Angel and continuously tests its responses to limit hallucinations. He said the chatbot draws on the platform's research and advisory material rather than issuing investment recommendations on its own.

Khenge said information asymmetry will eventually disappear and investment decisions depend on a belief about the future, which AI cannot predict. Nithin Kamath, co-founder of Zerodha, wrote in a blog post earlier this year that there is no real information edge left in markets. Khenge said regulators, brokers and every organisation that interacts with investors must help provide accurate information and counter misinformation. He said the people making consistent money in markets are high-frequency trading firms, market makers and proprietary trading desks that built infrastructural and data moats over years. Kamath wrote that AI will help investors behave better but not dramatically increase their returns.

Groww launched GR-1, a conversational financial assistant that can analyse a user's holdings, watchlists and positions, answer questions about stocks and funds, and surface market developments. FYERS introduced FIA, an AI research co-pilot that supports natural-language stock searches, portfolio analysis, options-chain analysis and IPO research. Pocketful introduced Pocketful GPT for conversational stock research. Zerodha, Upstox, Dhan, 5paisa, Kotak Neo and Sharekhan introduced integrations using the Model Context Protocol, which allow compatible AI applications such as Claude and ChatGPT to access brokerage data, analyse portfolios, examine holdings and retrieve market information. Some of those integrations are read-only, while others also support order-related functions.

Screener AI allows users to ask questions about companies using annual reports and earnings-call documents. Trendlyne's MarketMind AI analyses financial results, investor presentations and management commentary. Concall AI focuses on earnings-call summaries, while StockInsights.ai offers research based on company filings. Startups such as Genvest, MyFi and Novelty Wealth are extending AI into personal wealth management, analysing portfolios across stocks, mutual funds and other asset classes. The article was published on 25 November 2026.

stories.Headline: Chinese firms deploy adaptive robots to advance physical AI using massive manufacturing scale
stories.Summary:
Chinese firms have begun deploying and testing adaptive robots in production to enhance their physical artificial intelligence capabilities. This movement relies on a massive manufacturing base that installed 354,200 new industrial robots in 2025, which represented 59 per cent of the global total. These robots differ from conventional models because they can perceive their surroundings and adapt to changing conditions to perform complex tasks. Recent tests at an electric vehicle factory by Xiaomi showed that humanoid robot success rates rose from 90.2 to 98 per cent between March and July 2026.

Realizing this potential requires overcoming barriers to interoperability and the sharing of commercially sensitive information between enterprises. Beijing launched the Industrial Data Foundation Action in March 2026 to standardize industrial data, followed by the Model, Data Resonance Action in April 2026 to refine training datasets. In June 2026, the Special Action for Real-World Training of Humanoid Robots and Embodied AI directed 10 province-level jurisdictions and state-owned enterprises to open operating environments. Local initiatives in Shanghai and Wuxi are also establishing shared systems to standardize data from different robotic platforms and production lines.

The National Data Administration estimates that China produced approximately 27.4 per cent of global data in 2025, with over 30 per cent of industrial data coming from equipment. Engineers at Longcheer Technology stated that operational feedback from AI-enabled robots informed frequent model updates and improved robot movements. One developer of a fabric handling robot claimed a 97 per cent success rate and estimated an investment payback period of 18 months. These advancements aim to create a cycle where industrial deployment generates data that improves AI models, which then enables more capable robots.

This industrial scale could intensify pressure on Southeast Asian manufacturers by offsetting rising wages and retaining production in China. Such a shift might weaken the labor-cost advantage of the region and complicate its export-led industrialization. Other industrial economies, including Japan and South Korea, are developing their own testbeds and shared training datasets to remain competitive. These nations must improve coordination and harmonize technical standards across borders to compete with the scale of the Chinese manufacturing sector.

Articles.Title: China’s industrial scale could power its physical AI rise

stories.Headline: Deloitte says CFOs must embed AI in finance workflows to prove ROI as pilot window closes
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence in finance has moved from an experimental novelty to a board-level mandate, according to an article published by Deloitte on 24 November 2026, which says the window to prove value is closing. The article says pilots demonstrated digital potential, but chief financial officers now face the question of how to drive return on investment without eroding controllership. It says finance teams can rewire execution and elevate internal customer experience by embedding these capabilities into workflows. The article states that a stalled finance and accounting transformation often stems from ignoring data readiness, governance and security as strict prerequisites.

The article says one global beverage producer achieved 92% touchless invoice processing and reduced manual effort by more than 80% using AI in its finance operations. It says AI tools can draft variance explanations, suggest reconciliation steps and produce consistent management commentary when a reconciliation breaks or an unexpected variance occurs. For invoices with missing purchase order details, mismatches or duplicates, the article says trained tools can extract, interpret and supplement invoice content, flag issues for review and triage exceptions to the proper owner. It says AI can summarize account history, recommend next-best actions and standardize outreach when a dispute is opened or a customer inquiry comes in.

The article recommends that leaders pilot, learn quickly and scale gradually, with budget reserved for practical use cases and a plan to expand enterprisewide. It says not every problem needs AI, and that robotic process automation and other platforms may better serve rule-based scenarios, with AI more relevant when nuance is high. It says data readiness should be treated as a prerequisite rather than a phase-two task, because output quality ties directly to the underlying data and the organization's data maturity. It says investment decisions should align with a practical value roadmap assessed over short-term and long-term horizons, and that risk management and governance should be designed from day one, with Deloitte's Trustworthy AI framework named as one tool that can help design ethical safeguards.

The article says the highest-impact use cases are anchored to outcomes finance leaders already own, manage and report, such as cycle time, cost to serve, working capital and control effectiveness. It says the differentiator is workflow integration, with AI creating the most value when triggered at the moment of work rather than used as an after-the-fact summarizer. It says AI-based tools can draft and organize evidence narratives, map evidence to control requirements and flag gaps before they become findings, with typical measures including evidence collection cycle time and fewer documentation-driven findings. The article says moving from a promising pilot to an enterprise capability requires deliberate choices as CFOs seek tangible ROI and clarity on talent, platform direction, data risk and model governance.

Articles.Title: AI in Finance: From Pilots to Performance

stories.Headline: BP moves 3,000 finance staff to Wipro in AI transformation deal
stories.Summary:
BP has signed a supplier partnership with Wipro to transform its finance operations, and around 3,000 employees in India, Hungary, and Malaysia are set to move to the Indian IT services company. The new operating model is expected to take effect in 2027, subject to applicable conditions. Under the agreement, Wipro will bring its expertise in AI, automation, and transformation to BP's finance operations. The companies did not disclose the expected cost savings or specific AI applications planned for the engagement.

BP will retain overall accountability for standards, controls, data, and technology governance, while PwC will provide controls oversight. Kate Thomson, Chief Financial Officer at BP, said in a statement that the partnership with Wipro is the best path forward for BP and its people as the company builds a simpler, stronger, more valuable BP. She added that the arrangement would give employees opportunities to develop their skills while helping BP make better use of finance technology. Wipro CEO and MD Srini Pallia said the engagement underscores the company's commitment to leveraging its deep domain expertise and Wipro Intelligence to drive large-scale technology transformation.

The transfer reflects a growing trend of Indian IT services firms taking over existing enterprise teams and operations, and these transfers also bring workforce integration and margin challenges for Indian IT firms. The agreement comes as IT services providers explore AI applications in corporate finance, and HCLTech, for instance, has been examining how AI agents could automate corporate finance functions. Wipro has been positioning AI as a growth area while facing pressure on its traditional IT services business, and its AI investments and growth prospects remain an important part of its business strategy.

stories.Headline: Peter Boockvar predicts AI capital spending growth will slow sharply in 2026
stories.Summary:
Peter Boockvar of One Point BFG Wealth Partners said on CNBC's "Fast Money" that growth in AI capital spending is set to slow sharply in 2026, in a segment published on November 24, 2026. He appeared on the program to discuss whether the AI trade is on firm footing after a volatile few weeks in the space. The segment ran about five minutes and eighteen seconds, and the page carrying it was dated the same day. The headline of the segment states his view that AI capex growth will slow sharply in 2026.

The segment framed the discussion around the recent volatility in the AI trade and whether it still stands on firm footing. The page gives no figures for expected spending, no forecast amounts and no dates beyond the 2026 year in the headline and the November 24, 2026 publication date. It names no companies in connection with his call and offers no detail on which areas of AI spending he expects to slow. The only named participant is Boockvar, of One Point BFG Wealth Partners, speaking on "Fast Money."

Responsibility for the view rests with Boockvar, who gave it in the interview, and the page attributes the slowdown call to him and his firm. The page does not set out his reasoning, so what he said beyond the headline claim is not recorded there. It also does not say what he recommended or how he positioned for the slowdown he described. No one else is quoted on the call in the article text.

The context the page gives is a volatile few weeks in the AI trade, which the segment set out to examine. What happens next is not reported, and the page carries no follow-up on the forecast or on any response to it. The surrounding page consists of links to other videos, including ones on Nvidia, the Federal Reserve and the S&P, which are not part of this story. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Experts debate whether AI supercomputing is an evolution or revolution at SC26 panel
stories.Summary:
Experts debated if AI supercomputing is an evolution or revolution during a panel at the SC26 conference. Joe Greenseid of Nvidia moderated the discussion between several industry and academic specialists. The panel included representatives from AMD, VAST Data, the University of Delaware, and ETH Zurich. They discussed whether machines built for AI differ from those used by scientists for decades. The group examined how AI has increased funding and the size of these machines.

Nicholas Malaya of AMD claimed that AI and traditional high performance computing can use the same hardware. He cited the Lux system at Oak Ridge National Laboratory as a design for both workloads. Malaya also pointed to the AMD MI430 chip as an example of a dual purpose design. Torsten Hoefler of ETH Zurich argued that AI chips use lower precision like FP4 and FP8. He noted that scientific simulations often require FP64 or double precision for accurate results.

Nicholas Malaya stated that AI training shares many commonalities with traditional high performance computing. He suggested that Slinky, which combines Slurm with Kubernetes, can support both types of workloads. Torsten Hoefler argued that inference systems must handle many requests with very little delay. He claimed that professionals who do not adapt to AI could become a lost generation. Joe Greenseid moderated these views on whether the two fields can move in one direction.

Glenn Lockwood of VAST Data doubted that a 200 million dollar supercomputer could serve both purposes. He claimed that AI developers do not need traditional tools like SSH, Slurm, or file systems. Lockwood also criticized AI theater, where organizations present traditional simulations as AI work. Sunita Chandrasekaran of the University of Delaware noted that scientists cannot easily switch between precision levels. She raised concerns about moving sensitive research data between computing centers due to restrictions.

The articles state that high performance computing has used fast memory and high speed networks for years. AI has pushed technology faster but brought new demands for software and machine usage. Malaya noted that AI coding agents helped him produce more software than in the previous six years. Chandrasekaran observed that students now prefer languages like Python, Triton, and JAX over Fortran. Researchers from other fields now bring data to these environments without much programming experience.

The panel did not settle whether the change is an evolution or a revolution. Hoefler suggested that AI agents might rewrite applications to weaken the CUDA advantage held by Nvidia. He noted that any converted code would still require checking for accuracy. The discussion left open whether AI and scientific computing can continue moving in the same direction. The experts remained divided on the necessity of compromises for dual purpose hardware systems.

Articles.Title: SC26 Panel Debates AI Supercomputing: Evolution or Revolution?

stories.headline_source: SC26 Panel Debates AI Supercomputing: Evolution or Revolution?

stories.Headline: Dell posts $54.94 billion in quarterly revenue as AI server sales surge while HP misses PC market forecasts
stories.Summary:
Dell Technologies Inc. and HP Inc. delivered strong earnings and revenue beats as they posted their latest financial results today, SiliconANGLE reported on Nov. 24, 2026. Dell reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $9.45 per share on revenue of $54.94 billion, the article said. HP reported fourth-quarter adjusted earnings of 83 cents per share on revenue of $16 billion, the article said. Dell's revenue more than doubled from a year earlier, the article said. The companies have very different prospects going forward as they try to come to terms with the diverging fortunes of the artificial intelligence server and personal computer markets they serve, the article said.

Dell's result blew past Wall Street's expectations of $6.59 per share in earnings and $49.32 billion in sales, the article said. Dell's Infrastructure Solutions Group delivered sales of $41.97 billion, far in excess of the Street's target of $35.27 billion, the article said. Around $22 billion came from direct AI-optimized server sales, and that segment was up 291% annually, the article said. Dell's Client Services Group generated revenue of $12.89 billion, below the Street's forecast of $14.33 billion, the article said. HP's profit surpassed the analyst consensus estimate of 75 cents per share, and its revenue was up 9% and above the Street's target of $15.4 billion, the article said.

Dell Vice Chairman and Chief Operating Officer Jeff Clarke said the company is now a different company, with the Infrastructure Solutions Group driving the vast majority of its profit and growth. Clarke said Dell now has more than 7,500 customers buying its AI servers. Clarke told analysts the company has a significant competitive advantage over its rivals on the software side, which enables customers to get their servers up and running in data centers within hours of taking delivery. Clarke said that allows customers to convert backlog into revenue sooner and more reliably. Clarke told analysts that every order is verified for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance and access to land and power.

Dell is raising its forecast for AI servers in the coming fiscal years and now sees sales rising to $78 billion, ahead of the Street's target of $74 billion, the article said. Dell has an order backlog of $132.3 billion for AI servers, the article said. Dell's stock rose more than 3% after hours, putting the brakes on an 11% decline earlier during the regular trading session, the article said. HP's stock briefly surged more than 17% after-hours before promptly surrendering all of those gains in under an hour, and it was down just under a percentage point at the time of writing, the article said. HP's stock is still up 25% in the year to date, the article said.

Last month, Gartner Inc. reported a 22% drop in global PC shipments in the third quarter, citing the increased costs of components such as memory chips, which have led to higher prices and compelled many people to hold onto their older laptops for longer, the article said. HP has been trying to mitigate the situation by raising its prices, but it couldn't stop its profit margins from declining in the quarter, the article said. HP has been without a CEO since PayPal Holdings Inc. swooped in to poach its former leader Enrique Lores in February, the article said. Broussard has held the fort for close to nine months, and the company named Walmsley, who formerly led the pharmaceutical giant GSK Plc, as his successor, the article said. Walmsley will assume the role full time on Jan. 4, when she's slated to take over from interim CEO Bruce Broussard, the article said.

The market was eagerly anticipating HP's guidance to try and get a lid on whether or not the PC market has any prospect of recovery in the near future, but the company disappointed by refusing to provide any, the article said. All HP would say is that it forecasts free cash flow in the current quarter to be $3 billion, plus or minus $100 million, while analysts are targeting free cash flow of $3.3 billion, the article said. The article said Walmsley will have her work cut out when she assumes the role. The article said Walmsley has a tough act to follow, for Broussard has done rather well in his efforts to cope with the PC market downturn and the higher component costs. The article did not say what Dell or HP expect in the PC market beyond the figures given.

Articles.Title: Dell and HP beat expectations, but their fortunes are diverging as AI dynamics crush the PC market

stories.headline_source: Dell and HP beat expectations, but their fortunes are diverging as AI dynamics crush the PC market

stories.Headline: Gartner forecasts global AI spending rising 47.5% to $4 trillion in 2027
stories.Summary:
Global spending on artificial intelligence is expected to climb to $4 trillion in 2027, marking a 47.5 per cent increase from the previous year, according to business and technology research firm Gartner on Tuesday. The forecast says enterprises and technology providers continue ramping up investments to support growing AI workloads, research and deployment. The report projects spending on AI infrastructure to reach $2.4 trillion in 2027, up 53 per cent from 2026, accounting for 59 per cent of total worldwide AI expenditure. AI-optimised servers are expected to remain the largest segment within AI infrastructure spending, with Gartner estimating expenditure in this category will rise from $527.6 billion in 2026 to $957.2 billion in 2027.

John-David Lovelock, Distinguished VP Analyst and Chief of Research at Gartner, said the rapid expansion of AI applications and increasing computational demands are fueling this surge in investment. He said organizations are scaling up inference workloads faster than expected, while training increasingly sophisticated AI models continues to require significant computing resources. He noted that faster than anticipated expansion of user requirements into scaling up inference workloads, coupled with increasingly compute-intensive training workloads, continues to increase spending on AI infrastructure globally. The growth is being driven by continued investments from hyperscale cloud providers and newer cloud infrastructure companies, alongside rising memory-related costs in AI server hardware.

Beyond infrastructure, organizations are also increasing investments in services and software to support AI adoption, according to the report. Gartner noted that services providers are helping businesses expand AI initiatives through strategy development, data preparation, systems integration and deployment support. At the same time, software spending is rising as vendors embed AI capabilities into existing products and enterprises adopt new platforms for managing, governing and scaling AI across their operations. The market for generative AI models is also expected to witness robust growth, with Gartner forecasting spending on GenAI models to reach $51 billion in 2027, representing an 82 per cent increase from 2026 levels.

Articles.Title: Global AI spending to hit $4 trillion in 2027 as infrastructure outlay surges - ET CIO

stories.headline_source: Global AI spending to hit $4 trillion in 2027 as infrastructure outlay surges - ET CIO

stories.Headline: OpenAI reports GPT-6 models design protein shapes and sequences using reasoning and code alone
stories.Summary:
OpenAI said on November 24, 2026 that its GPT-6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs. OpenAI published the claim in a preprint titled “GPT-6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models.” An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks, OpenAI said. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take. In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT-6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets, and redesigned antibodies also retained binding.

Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing, OpenAI said. OpenAI tested 322 minibinders against 5 targets in the lab, and 35 of them, or 10.9%, tested positive for binding to their intended target. OpenAI found 5 hits for PD-L1, 3 for IL-7Rα, 1 for TrkA, 8 for VEGF-A and 18 for IL-17A. For three targets, OpenAI saw binding in 75 of 88 designs for MDM2 (85%), 26 of 42 for VEGF-A (62%), and 8 of 59 for PD-1 (14%). Of 107 proteins made from GPT-6.2’s new sequences for three unpublished minibinder shapes, 14 (13.1%) showed binding, and of 182 designs for six small antibodies (VHHs) that bind IL-4Rα, 128 (70%) showed signs of binding.

OpenAI said the models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules. When designing a small protein intended to bind to IL-7Rα, OpenAI said, the model proposed how the two proteins might interact, then wrote and executed code to explore different protein shapes and amino acid choices that could support that interaction. OpenAI said an internal model followed an instruction on how many coils or strands each minibinder should contain with near-perfect fidelity in its three-dimensional designs. OpenAI said the unpublished structures and substantial differences in sequence give strong evidence that GPT-6.2’s capabilities extend beyond memorization. OpenAI said the results also suggest it could use GPT-6.2 to intrinsically design both a minibinder’s structure and its sequence.

OpenAI said it compared computational measurements of quality against RFdiffusion, a specialized model for protein design, and found that GPT-6.2’s three-dimensional designs scored slightly lower while its latest internal models scored higher. OpenAI said the original RFdiffusion study reported higher hit rates, but rates depend heavily on how strictly researchers filter designs before lab validation and their definition of binding. OpenAI said predicting a complete protein structure remained a clear weakness. OpenAI said it used a specialized AI model called SolubleMPNN to suggest sequences for each design, and other specialized protein models helped select candidates predicted to fold as designed and bind at the intended site on the target. OpenAI said it tested the redesigned portions of the antibodies as fragments in the lab, and of 272 fragments based on five therapeutic antibodies, 179 (66%) showed binding to the original target, PD-1 or PD-L1.

OpenAI said proteins do much of the work in living cells, driving the chemical reactions that sustain life, carrying oxygen through the blood, and defending the body against infection. OpenAI said incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. OpenAI said proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids, and the order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does. OpenAI said scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do, and the challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. OpenAI said using and coordinating specialized biology models requires substantial expertise, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training.

OpenAI said it asked GPT-6.2 to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein, and when it already knew which two atoms formed a bond, it could give the model that information and ask how the rest of the molecule would fit. OpenAI said it could switch between these tasks simply by changing the prompt, without retraining the model. OpenAI said it also asked its models to design small proteins called minibinders and marked where each should attach to its target. OpenAI said it gave GPT-6.2 the three-dimensional structures of five target proteins and marked where it wanted a minibinder to attach, and the model then wrote code to create three-dimensional designs for potential minibinders without using specialized protein AI models. OpenAI said it gave GPT-6.2 three-dimensional models of how existing minibinders fit against their targets, withheld the original amino acid sequences, and asked it to propose new ones.

stories.Headline: Goldman Sachs warns that AI infrastructure spending risks could threaten memory chip companies in 2028
stories.Summary:
Goldman Sachs released a report on November 25, 2026, warning that memory chip companies face risks in 2028. The investment bank suggests that concerns over the sustainability of artificial intelligence infrastructure funding could jeopardize these firms. A potential slowdown in investments by large cloud computing companies may reduce the demand for memory products. This uncertainty follows a period of strong AI-driven demand that supports a positive outlook for 2027.

The report estimates that hyperscaler capital expenditure will reach approximately 1.1 trillion USD in 2027 and 1.2 to 1.3 trillion USD in 2028. Memory products are expected to make up around 40 percent of the 2028 budget, which is a decrease from 44 percent in 2027. Goldman Sachs analyzed three scenarios where 2028 spending remains flat, drops 10 percent, or falls 20 percent compared to 2027. These different scenarios suggest that memory spending could be lower by 55 billion USD, 99 billion USD, or 144 billion USD.

Goldman Sachs is responsible for these findings and stated that the decline in budget share reflects an expectation for memory pricing to fall in 2028. The brokerage explained that the scenario analysis was conducted to see how spending cuts would impact the revenue and profits of memory companies. They noted that current share prices might already be factoring in these potential changes to the market. The bank remains constructive about industry fundamentals for 2027 but maintains a more measured view for the following year.

The cautious outlook for 2028 is driven by the sustainability of AI spending and higher supply coming from China. Additionally, the bank pointed to a muted demand outlook for memory used in personal computers and smartphones. These combined factors create a risky environment for the industry despite the current strength of AI infrastructure investments. The report concludes that these variables lead to greater uncertainty regarding the pace of future AI investments.

Articles.Title: AI infrastructure spending risks for memory chip companies in 2028 - ET CIO

stories.Headline: Driven Tech completes ADEX and TekBay acquisitions to expand enterprise AI expertise
stories.Summary:
Driven Tech, Inc. said in a press release issued through a wire service on November 24, 2026, that it had completed its acquisitions of ADEX and TekBay after receiving all required government and regulatory approvals. According to the release, the two deals significantly expand the company's expertise in enterprise AI, data engineering, agentic AI and cloud-native development across AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud. The release said both teams will join Driven's Applied Intelligence Business Unit, which is led by Sanjeev Pant, and that the unit strengthens the company's three strategic platforms: Pervasive Security, Applied Intelligence and AI-Driven Digital Foundations. Driven said a key example of the collaboration is Lasius, its agentic AI orchestration and security platform, which the release says the ADEX engineering team developed based on Driven's strategic vision.

Vinu Thomas, President and Chief Operating Officer of Driven Tech, said in the release that the acquisitions represent a significant milestone in the company's evolution. According to the release, he said the company is bringing together exceptional AI engineering talent with its expertise in cybersecurity and infrastructure to help enterprises move beyond AI experimentation and securely operationalize AI at scale. The release said that with the acquisitions complete, Driven will focus on integrating its expanded engineering organization, accelerating innovation and bringing new AI-driven solutions to enterprise customers. Driven Tech describes itself in the release as a technology solutions and services company delivering integrated capabilities across Pervasive Security, Applied Intelligence and AI-Driven Digital Foundations.

The release was issued through WebWire, according to the press release, which directs readers to the wire service's website for more information. The release gives no financial terms for either acquisition and does not say how many employees the two teams bring to Driven. It also does not give a timeline for the integration work the company says it will now focus on. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Council of Europe trains 20 local authority teams in Paris on responsible AI governance
stories.Summary:
The Congress of Local and Regional Authorities of the Council of Europe organised the first-ever Academy on responsible AI governance at local level, held in Paris from 17 to 19 November 2026. Twenty teams from local and regional authorities, selected in an open call, took part in the academy. The teams came from 18 municipalities and two counties, spanning the continent from Diyarbakır in Türkiye to Fingal in Ireland. The academy was organised by the Centre of expertise for multilevel governance (CEMG) at the Congress, in partnership with the Council of Europe's Steering Committee for new and emerging digital technologies (CDNET). It put into practice the Congress's call to strengthen local and regional authorities' capacity to use and manage AI.

Participants were provided with practical tools for responsible AI governance, based on the Council of Europe's HUDERIA methodology for assessing the impact of AI systems. Over three days, participants applied the methodology to a fictional AI-supported public consultation, identifying and analysing risks, mapping stakeholders and developing mitigation measures. The programme was designed to strengthen authorities' capacity to assess the impact of AI in public services on everyone they serve, from a human-rights, democracy and rule-of-law perspective. The participating authorities were Amaroussion (Greece), Bălți (Republic of Moldova), Bergen (Norway), Bitola (North Macedonia), City of Arezzo (Italy), City of Vigo (Spain), Diyarbakır (Türkiye), Fingal County (Ireland), Harghita County (Romania), Kutaisi (Georgia), London Borough of Camden (United Kingdom), Lviv (Ukraine), Nõo (Estonia), Resen (North Macedonia), Rivne (Ukraine), Shkodër (Albania), Szentendre (Hungary), Turnišče (Slovenia), Valongo (Portugal), and Ventspils Education Board (Latvia). The academy was also an official part of the "Road to Geneva" programme, leading up to the 2027 Geneva AI summit.

Opening the discussions, Congress co-rapporteur on AI Annika Vaikla (Estonia, ILDG), Deputy Mayor of Viimsi, urged authorities to use AI to give public servants more time for people, while keeping people in control. She called for AI literacy among political leaders, staff and citizens. She also called for smaller municipalities to have access to shared expertise. Deputy Mayor Vaikla is co-rapporteur for the 2026 Congress report on strengthening the capacities of local and regional authorities in the use of artificial intelligence. The articles give no further remarks from her.

The articles state that local and regional authorities are on the frontline of the AI revolution in Europe's town halls. Faced with shrinking budgets, they see real potential in efficiency gains promised by AI. They also face hard questions such as planning applications for data centres and democratic accountability for decisions informed by AI. The articles say they lack capacity in understanding and governing AI technologies, particularly smaller municipalities.

The academy served as a Congress contribution to the Council of Europe's New Democratic Pact for Europe and was held in support of the implementation of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence. The articles give no further background beyond the academy's organisation and aims. They state that artificial intelligence is already in Europe's town halls. They describe the academy as the first-ever of its kind at local level.

They state that the twenty teams were selected in an open call. They state that the programme was designed to strengthen authorities' capacity to assess the impact of AI in public services. They give no further details on the Congress report or the Framework Convention. The articles state that the academy was an official part of the "Road to Geneva" programme, leading up to the 2027 Geneva AI summit.

They state that it was held in support of the implementation of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence. They state that it served as a Congress contribution to the Council of Europe's New Democratic Pact for Europe. They give no further details on what follows the academy. They leave open what the participating authorities will do next and what the 2026 Congress report will contain.

stories.Headline: Perth and Kinross Council officials say AI-generated requests overwhelm staff and raise costs
stories.Summary:
Leaders at Perth and Kinross Council in Scotland said artificial intelligence is fuelling an “incredible” rise in the volume and complexity of correspondence from the public. Officers dealing with complaints, data compliance and freedom of information requests must wade through thousands of pages of AI-generated “gibberish” to work out which communications are genuine. Lisa Simpson, head of legal and governance at Perth and Kinross, told the council’s scrutiny and performance committee on 18 November that AI lets people produce 10, 11 or 12-page requests at the flick of a button. She said 80% of this material is “nonsensical”, so “an awful lot of time and resources” is taken up processing it. Jillian Walker, the council’s data protection officer, told councillors at the meeting that subject access requests had risen by 100% in the last two years, partly due to AI.

Subject access requests let people obtain the data an organisation holds on them by law. According to Scottish newspaper The Courier, Walker said compliance with subject access requests increased in 2025 despite the pressures. A report presented to councillors showed the 1,849 freedom of information requests received in 2025-26 was the highest number in figures going back seven years, and 21% more than in 2024-25. Walker said much of the increase in communications is also related to Scotland’s Redress Scheme, which provides survivors of historical child abuse in care homes with redress payments, emotional support and official apologies. She said staff dealing with these requests must process “thousands of pages of highly distressing records” and reply to those seeking redress in a compassionate, trauma-informed and sensitive way.

Walker praised her “highly conscientious” small team but said there is “just no way we can sustain the compliance rate we have achieved previously”. Asked whether the council could use its own AI tools to sift through AI-generated correspondence, she said that though it is “very low-tech”, staff had found the best way to decipher AI-generated text and requests was to print them off and go through them with highlighter pens. Simpson acknowledged that AI could be valuable but said there was a “time and a place” for its use. She said that in some cases the tools and technology are not being used responsibly and their purpose is to tie the council up in knots and almost grind things to a halt. She said this does not help when the council is trying to help people with genuine requests, genuine issues and genuine complaints.

According to the BBC, officials told councillors that Perth and Kinross Council is working with other local authorities to find out if the problem could be addressed at a national level. In a paper published in September, researchers from the UK-based Centre for the Governance of AI and from the Hertie School in Berlin identified 84 cases across 11 countries. In those cases public bodies or “credible observers” attributed surges in requests to public use of AI, including freedom of information requests, planning consultation responses and civil court claims. The report, “Characterizing agentic flooding of government services”, defines “agentic flooding” as a surge in the volume or complexity of requests to a service caused by AI use that substantially strains the body’s capacity.

The researchers warned that governments are likely to respond with fees or by blocking AI from accessing government websites rather than by building capacity. The report presented to councillors covered freedom of information requests received in 2025-26 and compared them with figures going back seven years. Walker linked part of the rise in communications to Scotland’s Redress Scheme for survivors of historical child abuse in care homes. Simpson and Walker both addressed the scrutiny and performance committee meeting on 18 November.

The Courier reported Walker’s statement that compliance with subject access requests increased in 2025. The BBC reported that officials said the council is working with other local authorities on whether the problem could be addressed at a national level. The September paper by the Centre for the Governance of AI and the Hertie School set out the 84 cases and the definition of agentic flooding. Officials told councillors that Perth and Kinross Council is working with other local authorities to find out if the problem could be addressed at a national level.

The researchers warned that governments are likely to respond with fees or by blocking AI from accessing government websites rather than by building capacity. The articles do not say what the council’s own next steps will be, or what the other local authorities have found. The articles do not say whether the council will adopt any new AI tools to handle the correspondence. The articles do not say what response, if any, the Scottish or UK government has given to the council’s concerns.

stories.Headline: Systematix says Indian IT firms gain from AI adoption as enterprises need integration support
stories.Summary:
A Systematix report published on November 25, 2026, said India's IT services companies could keep benefiting from growing artificial intelligence adoption, because businesses still need help integrating AI solutions, managing data and deploying them at scale, even as automation puts pressure on traditional labour-based delivery models. The report said the growing use of advanced AI models would not make technology service providers irrelevant, since enterprise adoption would continue to depend on implementation partners and specialised engineering support. It added that this reduces the risk of IT services becoming irrelevant, but not the pressure on labour-based models. The report pointed to Anthropic's move into enterprise implementation services through Ode with Anthropic, an AI services company backed by Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman and other global investors, which focuses on building and supporting solutions based on Anthropic's Claude platform for mid-sized businesses and private equity-backed companies.

The report said that move showed businesses adopting AI would continue to need assistance integrating the technology into their operations and supporting its long-term use. Anthropic has also expanded its Claude Partner Network to work with global consultancies and system integrators, including Accenture, Deloitte, KPMG and Infosys, to deploy AI solutions for enterprise clients. Systematix expects large multinational AI deployments to continue relying on system integrators, even as AI model developers expand their own implementation capabilities. It identified forward-deployed engineering as an emerging area of opportunity for IT services companies, with these engineers working closely with clients to customise and implement AI solutions based on their business requirements.

Systematix said such work would increase demand for data readiness, system integration, governance and managed AI operations, creating opportunities for technology services providers to generate revenue from enterprise AI adoption. However, Anthropic's expansion into implementation services could increase competition in the mid-sized business segment, where AI companies are seeking to build closer relationships with customers. The report said demand for forward-deployed engineers could partly address concerns about the long-term role of IT services companies, but the shift towards AI-led delivery would continue to challenge traditional models that depend heavily on employee numbers and billing hours. The findings suggest Indian IT services companies may need to increasingly focus on specialised AI implementation, integration and ongoing support as enterprises move from experimenting with AI to deploying it across business operations.

stories.Headline: MaxContact warns businesses risk wasting AI spend by treating adoption as procurement rather than workforce change
stories.Summary:
MaxContact, a customer engagement software provider, warned that businesses risk undermining their AI investment by treating it as a technology purchase rather than a workforce change programme, following a roundtable it convened that brought together contact centre analysts, consultants and industry specialists. The discussion examined how AI's rapid spread is changing working practices, with a central concern being the gap between the pace of buying and deploying AI systems and the slower work of preparing employees, managers and internal processes to use them effectively. Participants said many organisations still frame AI decisions around procurement, legal review and compliance while giving less weight to customer-facing teams and learning specialists, which can lead to systems being introduced before businesses have considered how jobs will change or what support staff will need. Sue Duris, Principal Consultant and Founder of M4 Communications, said AI is still treated as a compliance, legal and tech exercise, and that the people who understand the customer need to be in the room when these decisions get made rather than brought in after.

The issue is particularly acute in contact centres, where AI tools are increasing the amount of data available to frontline managers and supervisors and, according to the roundtable, are changing the nature of existing roles rather than simply automating repetitive work. Ben Booth, Chief Executive Officer of MaxContact, said team leaders are increasingly expected to interpret larger volumes of information without being prepared for the shift, and that they are being transitioned into data analysts without realising it. Nathan Dring, Founder and Director of Nathan Dring and Associates, said the speed of adoption has created a significant challenge for employers and described it as the biggest skill gap in business that has ever been because it has been adopted so fast. He also said learning and development teams need more confidence to put their oars out on the table, with a stronger role in shaping implementation plans rather than responding after decisions have been taken elsewhere. Marianne Withers, Founder and Managing Director of Withers Jones Collective, said customer experience leaders do not always have the same influence over decisions, and that support should focus on helping them make their case and have a stronger voice in decisions that affect their people and customers.

Participants said that if AI systems are bought mainly on cost, technical specification or compliance grounds, businesses may fail to redesign roles or adjust performance expectations in line with the new reality of work, and that employees may inherit new tools and new responsibilities at the same time without a clear plan for training or transition. In that scenario, organisations may spend heavily on AI while falling short in practice because the workforce has not been prepared to absorb the change, and participants argued that workforce readiness should be considered from the outset alongside procurement and governance rather than being handed to human resources after a purchase is made. Booth said AI implementation cannot just be about selecting the right technology, and that businesses need to think just as carefully about how roles will change, what skills people will need and how they will bring their teams with them. He said the technology implementation and the change programme have to happen together, otherwise businesses risk investing in technology without creating the conditions for people to get the full value from it.

Articles.Title: Businesses warned over AI buy-in without workforce change - IT Brief Australia
