stories.Headline: A study finds AI systems displace legal certainty, accountability and enforceability
stories.Summary:
A conceptual legal analysis published in the Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance examines how artificial intelligence systems displace the core structural foundations that historically uphold legal legitimacy. The study conceptualizes these foundational conditions as the Tripod of Legal Legitimacy, consisting of legal certainty, accountability, and enforceability. Across public and private domains, the normative authority of law is increasingly challenged by opaque, adaptive, and privately administered algorithmic infrastructures. Rather than merely assisting human decision-makers, artificial intelligence technologies embed regulatory functions such as adjudication, classification, and enforcement directly into their computational architecture. These systems frequently operate outside the scope of democratic authorization, legislative scrutiny, or judicial review, raising fundamental questions about the capacity of legal orders to maintain normative authority.

The study defines normative legitimacy as the capacity of legal systems to justify authority through principled reasoning, procedural fairness, and democratic accountability. Legal institutions comprise public authorities such as legislatures, regulatory agencies, and courts charged with creating, interpreting, and enforcing rules. Legal certainty requires laws to be clear, general, prospective, and intelligible so that individuals and institutions can understand rules to comply or seek contestation. Accountability provides vertical oversight through public and electoral scrutiny, alongside horizontal checks via judicial review and inter-agency evaluation, ensuring decisions remain contestable and subject to justification or reversal. Enforceability ensures legal norms produce concrete behavioral effects through compliance mechanisms, coercion, or institutional alignment, preventing rules from decaying into symbolic declarations.

The author diagnoses how specific characteristics of artificial intelligence destabilize this legal tripod through institutional erosion, technical substitution, and infrastructural control. Modern machine learning models rely on statistical inference, automated optimization, and probabilistic classifications rather than human deliberation or causal deduction, creating an inherent black-box problem. The study distinguishes between two distinct layers of opacity: the internal architecture of deep neural networks that impedes legal explainability, and the institutional opacity of corporate structures that shields proprietary code and training data behind trade secrecy and platform terms of service. Accountability diffuses across fragmented supply chains of developers, deployers, and institutional adopters, producing a responsibility vacuum where fault-based liability falters. Enforceability erodes as transnationally deployed cloud platforms operate beyond the reach of domestic regulators, leaving state authorities with fragmented oversight.

In the Netherlands, the predictive algorithmic profiling system SyRI, deployed to detect social security fraud, operated with minimal transparency until the Hague District Court invalidated it for violating fair trial guarantees and European human rights transparency standards. European Union border operations examined by the EU Fundamental Rights Agency demonstrated that automated border management tools significantly constrain individuals' access to legal redress. Italian data protection authorities issued a moratorium on real-time facial recognition in public spaces, Spanish regulators suspended artificial intelligence systems in public schools over biometric profiling concerns, and Canadian provinces paused predictive policing programs due to discrimination risks and absent procedural safeguards. In the United States, police departments widely adopted facial recognition technologies within regulatory vacuums, demonstrating how technical systems hollow out legal protections in practice without explicitly repealing statutes. The study introduces a comparative process-based model that contrasts the recursive feedback cycles of traditional public law against artificial-intelligence-induced governance cycles.

Under the traditional legal-governance framework, legitimacy is maintained through four interlinked stages: norm formulation through deliberative processes such as legislative drafting and public hearings; institutional implementation by public bodies; behavioral adjustment alongside procedural contestation in administrative or judicial venues; and normative recalibration, wherein legal disputes and observed failures feed back into statutory reform. The European Union's Digital Services Act incorporated over 3,000 public submissions during drafting and established Digital Services Coordinators to oversee algorithmic risk management, while the AI Act mandates supervisory reviews and five-year revision cycles under Article 84. The artificial-intelligence-induced governance displacement framework traces how private infrastructures substitute code-based mechanisms for public law across five distinct stages. The cycle begins with design-based norm encoding, where private actors embed governance choices directly into technical system parameters, as seen in Meta's Community Standards or OpenAI's behavioral guidelines and prompt engineering. The second stage, infrastructural adoption, occurs when public institutions, educational bodies, and individual users integrate these unregulated models into everyday practice in the absence of statutory review.

Third, functional displacement emerges as platform-based systems simulate legal functions, such as adjudication and content moderation, exemplified by Meta's Oversight Board issuing non-binding rulings or OpenAI defining internal safety rules without judicial oversight. The fourth stage, epistemic dependency, manifests as public regulators face substantial technical knowledge gaps and increasingly rely on private developers for expertise, auditability, and regulatory guidance. During 2023 United States Senate hearings, lawmakers invited OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman alongside academic and civil society witnesses to suggest regulatory approaches, highlighting how technical elites increasingly influence public agenda-setting. Finally, legitimacy closure occurs when platform operators deploy internal ethics boards, transparency portals, system cards, and corporate audit reports to signal normative compliance.

In July 2025, major artificial intelligence developers including Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mistral signed the European Union's Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI, pledging adherence to transparency, copyright, and traceability provisions, while Meta rejected the voluntary Code, publicly citing overregulation. The author notes that no major United States court, including the Supreme Court, has yet adjudicated cases regarding artificial-intelligence-generated pornography. The author outlines six structural policy priorities necessary to reconstruct legal authority rather than merely extending existing compliance checklists. First, legal frameworks must establish enforceable traceability through statutory algorithmic registries, mandatory version-update documentation, and publicly accessible audit trails to ensure administrative legibility.

Second, statutes must clarify liability across the entire artificial intelligence supply chain, establishing tiered liability models that apportion responsibility among system developers, practical deployers, and institutional adopters. Third, enforceability must be re-anchored in binding statutory entitlements, guaranteeing enforceable rights to explanation, mandatory justification protocols, and independent third-party appeals. Fourth, democratic jurisdictions must advance transnational coordination through interoperable regulatory standards and mutual recognition to prevent private jurisdictional arbitrage. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Shufti launches Know Your Agent to verify AI agents and their authorising owners
stories.Summary:
Shufti launched a verification product called Know Your Agent for AI agents acting on behalf of people and businesses, the company announced on 25 November 2026. The product is aimed at companies handling transactions and requests generated by autonomous software, in what Shufti describes as agentic commerce. In that setting, AI agents can open accounts, place orders and move funds for their owners, and businesses receiving those requests need to determine whether an agent is genuine, who is accountable for it and whether the action falls within an approved mandate. Shufti said the issue is becoming more urgent as software agents take on customer-facing tasks across financial services, marketplaces, software and online gaming. It said a valid access token may not be enough to prove an agent is legitimate, because stolen credentials and impersonation can make fraudulent requests appear authentic.

Know Your Agent verifies the identity of the AI agent, confirms that a real person has authorised the action and checks the permissions attached to the request before data is accessed or a transaction is triggered, all in a single flow. Each AI agent is issued a unique, time-bound credential that can be revoked, known agents are recognised by name, and new or unfamiliar agents are assessed through behavioural biometrics and assigned a trust score. Shufti said it already supports agents including Meta Muse, GrokBot and OpenAI Dots within a week of their launch, and every agent is linked to an individual or business verified through its modular know-your-customer or know-your-business checks, which remain in place. Authorisation begins with a principal setting a mandate for each agent that can define permitted actions, limits, expiry and revocation, and the mandate is enforced as a policy on every request with ongoing monitoring designed to detect misuse. Businesses can set their own rules according to sector and risk appetite, for example allowing an agent to view balances and pay approved billers in banking while payments to new payees trigger an additional check.

When an AI agent requests an action outside its mandate or exceeds a high-risk threshold, the product requires human-in-the-loop approval through a liveness check in which the authorising person completes a selfie verification. Shufti said its single-selfie liveness process is iBeta Level 3-certified and tests resistance to presentation attacks. Know Your Agent also maintains an audit trail of requests, decisions and revocations linked to each agent and its principal, intended to keep every action traceable for accountability and review. Faryam Asif, Chief Technology Officer at Shufti, said businesses are already allowing AI agents to act for their customers and the question of who stands behind each action cannot wait for an answer later.

Asif said the product verifies every AI agent request with a verified owner, a clear mandate and a record that holds up under review, so customers can say yes to agent activity with confidence because they know exactly who approved what and when. Shufti said the launch reflects a broader shift in digital commerce as companies prepare for systems that no longer rely solely on direct human input at every stage of a transaction. As AI agents carry out more tasks independently, businesses are likely to face growing pressure to show that actions taken by software were both authorised and attributable to a known person or organisation. The product is now available for businesses using agentic commerce and other AI agent workflows.

Articles.Title: Shufti launches agent verification tool for AI commerce - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Accenture survey finds 40% of shoppers want AI help finding holiday deals
stories.Summary:
Accenture’s holiday shopping survey found that 66% of shoppers plan to take part in Black Friday or Cyber Monday, even though retailers have been offering deals for weeks, according to a report published on November 24, 2026. Kelly Askew, Accenture’s global retail lead, said shoppers are still planning to participate, but many are doing more research before making a purchase. About one in five shoppers began holiday shopping during the summer, Askew said, and retailers have moved some promotions earlier, with deals appearing as far back as September. She said Black Friday used to be a day or two but is no longer that, and it is now becoming weeks.

Shoppers plan to spend about 12% more this year, according to the survey, but Askew said the increase is largely driven by higher prices. Consumers are buying a similar amount of merchandise as last year while shifting toward mass merchants and warehouse clubs, choosing lower-priced brands or using gift cards to manage costs. Accenture found that 40% of shoppers wanted AI’s help finding deals, while about one-third used it to compare options or decide where to buy. Askew described the technology as almost becoming a personal shopper, helping people narrow down gift choices.

The survey found that only 3% of shoppers plan to make an impulse purchase after seeing a deal. Askew said many consumers are deciding what they want to buy in advance and waiting for Black Friday or Cyber Monday to make their final purchase. In-store shopping remains part of the holiday season, with 44% of consumers planning to visit stores, according to Accenture. Askew said shoppers may go for inspiration, to try on clothes or test products, as well as to get into the holiday spirit.

stories.Headline: VoxAssure finds seven of 11 voice AI engines mispronounce Cockburn Central as profanity
stories.Summary:
VoxAssure, a Melbourne-based AI assurance firm, published an Australian benchmark of 11 commercial voice AI engines on 25 November 2026, finding that seven mispronounced Cockburn Central in Western Australia as profanity. The firm tested speech-to-speech and text-to-speech products from OpenAI, Google, Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, ElevenLabs, Cartesia and Inworld using a 50-item Australian "torture test" run from Melbourne and a Sydney cloud data centre. Seven of the 11 engines produced an audible hard "ck" when reading Cockburn Central, which is pronounced "koh-burn". Four of those failures involved stock voices vendors labelled as Australian: Microsoft Azure AI Speech, Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic, Cartesia Sonic 3.6 and Inworld TTS-2. The other three failures came from engines tested without an Australian accent request: OpenAI GPT Realtime 2.1, Google Gemini 3.8 Live and Google Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS.

The benchmark also measured how quickly text-to-speech systems returned their first audio response from a Sydney cloud data centre, with median times ranging from 51 milliseconds for Amazon Polly Neural to 964 milliseconds for Google Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS. Beyond suburb names, the test covered 12 financial, tax and identity formats, 10 regulator acronyms, seven idiom and polarity checks, and six disclosure and safety prompts. All 11 engines passed the six fixed-prompt safety and disclosure items, as well as colloquial polarity checks including "Yeah, nah" and "Nah, yeah". Microsoft Azure AI Speech's Australian voice spelled out "ASIC" letter by letter, which VoxAssure marked as a failure after human review, and Amazon Polly Neural recorded a human-confirmed failure when reading a "6.42% p.a." comparison rate.

Overall, only one system, ElevenLabs Eleven v4 Turbo, met both VoxAssure's response-time thresholds and the pass mark for the full Australian test suite, scoring 49 out of 50. Nick Morgenstern, Founder and Principal of VoxAssure, said organisations were relying too heavily on overseas demonstrations when selecting voice systems for Australian users. He said Australian banks, super funds, insurers and government agencies were deploying customer-facing voice AI on the back of US studio demonstrations, without measuring what happens on local networks or local speech. He said even picking a voice a vendor labels "Australian" does not guarantee accuracy, noting that four of the seven engines that uttered profanity on Cockburn Central were running Australian stock voices.

He also said relying solely on automated transcripts for QA was a blind spot, because a transcript reads "Cockburn" cleanly even when a caller hears profanity. The firm said its verification process required independent misses by two speech recognisers from different vendors for pronunciation failures, while a human auditor listened to 16 clips and changed four results from pass to fail. Each engine was tested using a public self-serve account, and the results cover one model version, one stock voice and one test day for each engine. Morgenstern said that with OAIC APP 1.7 automated decision-making rules commencing on 10 December and APRA CPS 230 holding boards accountable for third-party vendor risk, organisations need independent, ear-verified technical evidence before customers dial in.

Articles.Title: Australian voice AI firms trip over Cockburn Central - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: New York governor Kathy Hochul signs a five-year ban on selling AI chatbot toys to children
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed legislation on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, imposing a five-year ban on the manufacture, distribution, and sale of children's toys equipped with AI companion chatbots. The signing took place in Harlem at Grandma's Place, a toy store owned by retired schoolteacher Dawn Harris-Martine. The law targets talking stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that use internet-connected AI chatbots to hold conversations with children. Hochul cited concerns over child safety, privacy, and emotional manipulation as reasons for the ban.

The ban takes effect on February 22, 2027, which is 90 days after the bill was signed, and remains in place for five years. Under the legislation, manufacturers and retailers are prohibited from making, distributing, exchanging, or selling such toys across New York state. Violations of the new law could result in civil penalties of up to $15,000 per day for each violation. The restrictions will not be in force during the upcoming holiday season, as the effective date falls after that period. The law applies to toys with internet access and integrated AI capabilities, regardless of the child's age.

Governor Hochul said parents shopping for gifts should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings, or put their privacy at risk. She stated that protecting children from the risks of unregulated AI was a priority for her administration. Hochul urged parents and caregivers to consider the potential risks of AI-powered toys before buying gifts for young children during the holiday season. She warned that there are toys out there that could be harmful to children, and that children are hearing harmful content from a toy that parents trust. The governor also said technology is evolving rapidly and that laws must adapt to keep pace.

Dawn Harris-Martine, known to customers as Grandma Dawne, said a good toy for a child is one that stretches their imagination. She opened Grandma's Place in the late 1990s and has long encouraged parents to be actively involved in their children's play. Harris-Martine said it is necessary to avoid situations where a three-year-old can sit and listen to a teddy bear telling them to do strange things. She plans to continue offering what she described as an AI-free environment for children and families. Muna Heaven, a Harlem mother and member of Mothers Against Media Addiction, said parents and children want toys to be fun but also have a baseline expectation that they will be safe.

Heaven said her group has identified examples ranging from inappropriate or sexual conversations to dangerous advice, including instructions on how to find knives, associated with AI chatbot toys. She said young people are being harmed by toys powered by artificial intelligence, with many examples available. Supporters of the measure say AI-powered toys have generated concerns about child safety. The legislation builds on New York's existing safeguards for AI companion chatbots, which are designed to address risks associated with interactions between users and AI systems. Harris-Martine also advised parents not to put an iPad in a child's hands and walk away, but to be present and get off their phones.

The law will take effect on February 22, 2027, and remain in place for five years, with civil penalties of up to $15,000 per day for violations. Hochul urged parents to pay attention while shopping during the holiday season, since the ban will not yet be in force. The articles do not specify how the ban will be enforced or which state agency will oversee compliance. They also do not state whether the five-year ban could be extended or made permanent after it expires. No information is given about how many such toys are currently on the market or how many manufacturers or retailers will be affected.

stories.Headline: SailPoint predicts boards and regulators will demand accountability for autonomous AI agents by 2027
stories.Summary:
SailPoint has published identity security predictions for 2027 that focus on tighter control of autonomous AI agents in large organisations, according to a report by Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin in IT Brief Australia. The company's forecasts suggest businesses are moving beyond early AI experimentation towards formal governance as autonomous software agents spread across operations. Recent SailPoint research found that 79% of enterprises already run AI agents in production, while only 2% have deployed identity security designed specifically for those systems. The report says that gap underpins its warning that identity management is becoming as much a business risk issue as a technical one, and that organisations are shifting from managing employee and contractor access to supervising what software agents can do for staff and departments.

One main prediction is that a large listed company will suffer a self-inflicted operational crisis caused by a misconfigured group of autonomous agents, which could involve supplier contracts being deleted, inventory databases removed and shipments redirected before human administrators intervene. The report also predicts stricter separation of duties for AI systems by 2027, so that an autonomous agent would not hold administrative rights in the same environment that oversees its behaviour, with governance moved to an independent control layer. On business-to-business access, SailPoint predicts some enterprises will begin blocking external agents from their application programming interfaces unless third parties can prove an agent's identity history and limits of access. SailPoint's research suggests 67% of enterprises have secured human access, compared with 24% that govern agentic security, and that AI agents account for 22% of all non-human accounts within what the company described as a 45:1 machine-to-human identity ratio.

Mark McClain, Chief Executive Officer and Founder of SailPoint, said the growing use of autonomous agents would draw greater scrutiny from boards, insurers and regulators. He said that for the past two years enterprises raced to see what they could accomplish with autonomous AI agents, and that in 2027 boards, insurers and regulators will demand to know who is accountable when those agents take action that crosses a legal or regulatory boundary. He said it will be possible to delegate a complex workflow to an autonomous agent but never acceptable to delegate accountability, because agent accountability is enterprise responsibility. Chandra Gnanasambandam, Chief Technology Officer and Executive Vice President, Product at SailPoint, said manual human access reviews for autonomous agents are a fantasy at near-AGI scale, that every digital worker must carry cryptographically bound human lineage because a rogue AI agent cannot be taken to jail, and that standing privilege is dead in the agentic era.

SailPoint also linked identity governance to broader corporate oversight, saying requirements tied to post-quantum cryptography and AI regulation would push boards to treat visibility over human, machine and cryptographic identities as a core control issue. In that view, organisations would need a clear record of machine secrets and authorisations not only for cyber risk management but also for insurance, compliance and valuation discussions, which the report describes as an Identity Bill of Materials becoming a board-level measure. The final prediction is that companies will move away from permissive internal AI policies that allowed staff to experiment with agents using personal credentials. SailPoint said Chief Information Officers and Chief Financial Officers would increasingly require measurable returns and formal identity governance before approving wider use, leading businesses to bring shadow agents under central oversight.

Articles.Title: SailPoint warns 2027 will bring tighter AI agent controls - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Kelly CEO Chris Layden says AI is reshaping how Australian employers hire and train staff
stories.Summary:
Kelly's global chief executive officer Chris Layden said Australian employers are reassessing whether to train existing staff, hire permanent workers or use contractors as artificial intelligence reshapes job requirements, and he said the shift extends beyond technology roles. He said businesses were making staffing decisions amid persistent skills shortages and uncertainty about the capabilities they would need in the near term, and that many employers were trying to fill immediate gaps while working out where AI could lift productivity. He said that is changing how companies define roles before they recruit, and that rather than looking only for candidates with a familiar title or industry background, some are considering whether people have solved similar problems elsewhere or shown the judgement needed in a different setting. He said leaders must make deliberate decisions about which capabilities they recruit for, which they develop internally, and how they prepare their workforce for what comes next. Layden said AI is also altering the mix of skills required in jobs outside the technology sector, which could widen the field for employers if they focus more on transferable experience and decision-making than on narrow job histories.

He said AI tools are changing recruitment itself, and that employers can use the technology to shorten hiring processes and identify applicants whose experience might previously have been missed. Research from the Governance Institute of Australia found that 40 per cent of Australian workers whose employer uses or plans to use AI said they had received adequate training. Layden said the main test of internal training was not whether workers had attended a course, but whether they could apply AI tools properly, assess the output and recognise when human judgement was still required, and that employers can apply the same standard when assessing external candidates, whether for permanent positions or contract assignments. Layden said contract hiring can help employers gain specialist knowledge quickly while they assess whether a role will become permanent, which may be relevant when a company wants to start an AI-related project but has not yet decided whether the expertise will be needed on an ongoing basis. He said a more cautious economic backdrop could also lead some Australian businesses to rely more heavily on temporary and contract workers rather than committing immediately to permanent hires, and that employers are responding to economic uncertainty by choosing a mix of permanent and contingent talent.

Kelly pointed to its United States research as a reference point, in which one in 10 employers said they were cutting staff because of AI while 39 per cent said they were redistributing tasks and keeping headcount unchanged, and among jobseekers surveyed 40 per cent said they would seriously consider a temporary or contract position while 35 per cent said they were more open to that option than a year earlier. Layden said most candidates coming to Kelly still wanted permanent work, but more were willing to consider contract roles than in the past, which may expand the available labour pool for employers. He said a contract can help someone build skills and demonstrate what they can do, offering greater flexibility for some while for others it might be a foot in the door in an industry where permanent opportunities are limited. He said contract work still has to be weighed carefully by applicants, especially those who began their search looking for the stability of a permanent role, and that factors such as the length of the assignment, the level of income and the prospects once the contract ends remain central to that decision. He said the broader issue for employers is whether AI investment translates into practical workplace use, and that AI investment will deliver its greatest value when people know how to apply the technology in their work, have the judgement to use it responsibly and are confident it will benefit their careers.

Articles.Title: AI reshapes hiring as Australian employers weigh staffing - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Dynatrace finds Australian firms trail global peers on AI observability and data governance
stories.Summary:
Dynatrace has published its State of Observability 2026 report, which found that Australian organisations lag global peers in remediation and data governance, the company says. The study surveyed 1,202 technology leaders globally, including respondents in Australia, and examined how companies are using AI agents in observability and IT operations. Across the global sample, 87% of organisations use AI agents in observability and IT operations, yet only 27% have visibility into their decisions. The findings point to a gap between AI adoption and the ability of businesses to monitor how these systems act. Australian respondents reported sharper operational strain than peers in other regions, with 55% saying AI had increased the complexity of the technology environment, compared with 47% in the Americas and 46% in Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

Multi-cloud and hybrid management was the leading source of complexity for Australian organisations at 48%, 10 percentage points above the report average. Australia recorded the slowest remediation among the countries surveyed, with 32% saying it takes one to four weeks to fix issues, while only 20% said problems are resolved in under 24 hours. Just 28% of Australian respondents said their organisation uses predictive detection, nine percentage points below the survey benchmark, and only 19% reported strong governance of sensitive data, 12 points lower than the benchmark used in the report. Rafi Katanasho, APAC Chief Technology Officer at Dynatrace, said the regional findings showed a distinct set of operational pressures. He said there was no doubt that Australia and the APAC region face heightened challenges from the proliferation of agentic AI and its impact on IT infrastructure.

He said unpredictability, security threats, slow issue resolution and poor data governance are felt more acutely in this part of the world than among global peers, along with added complexity. He said AI-powered observability can help because AI performance depends on the applications, infrastructure, security systems and services around it, connecting that environment with AI behaviour, resource consumption, risk detection and business impact. The report also found that more than two in five respondents, or 44%, are targeting fully autonomous operations within five years, while 43% identified expanding AI, large language model and agentic workloads as a leading source of technology complexity. Some 81% of respondents said AI workloads had increased compute and infrastructure costs, and 77% said they now need greater visibility into cost allocation. In APAC, 47% pointed to expanding AI, large language model and agentic workloads as a source of complexity, compared with 41% in both the Americas and Europe, the Middle East and Africa, while 52% said increasingly unpredictable AI application and model behaviour was adding to complexity.

stories.Headline: Nintex releases K2 5.10 with local AI and SharePoint workflow conversion tools
stories.Summary:
Nintex has released K2 5.10 for organisations that run automation on their own premises, according to IT Brief Australia. The update adds tools for converting SharePoint workflows, connecting to enterprise data and running AI locally. It is aimed at IT teams managing complex automation in environments with strict governance and data control requirements. The release is intended to help those customers extend existing systems without moving sensitive information outside their own infrastructure.

A central part of K2 5.10 is expanded support for SharePoint users, particularly organisations seeking to keep older workflow investments while reducing migration risk. The release includes workflow conversion functions to preserve existing business logic, alongside SharePoint environment assessment tools to identify migration issues before work begins. It also broadens support for SharePoint Document Sets, which the article says are commonly used in document-heavy sectors such as financial services, government and healthcare. New SharePoint App Manager functions are meant to help customers and partners spot environment and configuration issues earlier in deployment projects, and changes to SharePoint Group Provider naming are intended to improve reliability in large and complex SharePoint estates.

Suvrat Joshi, Senior Vice President, Product and Design at Nintex, said organisations want to automate complex work without sacrificing data sovereignty and process governance. He said K2 5.10 helps IT leaders evolve critical business processes, accelerate automation initiatives and prepare for the future of business orchestration while keeping control over their infrastructure and information. Harald Holz, Managing Director at nteam GmbH, said the new version reflects the needs of customers with strict governance demands. He said it makes it easier to protect existing SharePoint workflow investments while securely moving automation and AI forward.

The release also updates the K2 SmartObject framework, which sits at the centre of how the platform connects applications, workflows and business data. New native querying functions are designed to help development teams work with data more directly, while expanded JSON support is intended to make integrations with applications, cloud services and APIs easier to manage. K2 5.10 includes updates to core platform frameworks, security infrastructure, browser compatibility and enterprise integrations, which Nintex framed as part of an effort to reduce technical debt and keep business-critical systems stable. It builds on K2 Intelligence, introduced in version 5.9.1, which brought locally hosted AI into K2 workflows, forms and applications.

stories.Headline: Gleam releases MCP server, open-source giveaway skills and beta AI campaign builder for marketers
stories.Summary:
Gleam, an Australian marketing platform, released three AI-focused tools for managing giveaway campaigns on 25 November 2026, adding an MCP server, open-source giveaway skills and a beta campaign builder to its platform. The company says the products are designed to let marketers plan, build and manage giveaway activity from AI assistants while keeping campaigns inside Gleam. Giveaway campaigns typically require teams to set prizes, entry methods, dates, eligibility rules, terms, draws and winner communications, and Gleam is targeting that repetitive administrative work for businesses running competitions, rewards and email capture campaigns. The first product is a Gleam server built on the Model Context Protocol, an open standard that lets AI assistants connect with external software, so marketers can use supported chat applications to access their Gleam accounts and review campaign information. Users can ask an assistant to list campaigns and open a selected campaign with its dates, prizes, actions, settings and counts, and the assistant can also change campaign names, dates, prizes, images and settings.

Other functions include drawing random winners, assigning prizes, allowing repeat winners and restricting a draw to entries submitted within a specified period, and the assistant can copy a prize image from a product page into a campaign. Customers connect through Gleam OAuth, and the server works with Claude, ChatGPT and other AI chat apps that support MCP, reading every Competition, Reward and Capture on a site, though it cannot currently create or delete campaigns, export entries or edit campaign actions. The MCP server is available on Gleam's Hobby Plan and above. The second release is Giveaway Skills, a free open-source set of Agent Skills designed to guide assistants through common giveaway tasks including idea generation, prize selection, entry planning, timing, winner structure, promotion, random draws and winner communications.

The benchmarks used in the skills draw on data from 37,180 giveaways run by 6,817 organisers, each with at least 1,000 entrants, and Gleam says the underlying data includes 60,282 prizes and 325,000 entry actions, with every benchmark including its sample size. The Random Draw skill uses a seed from a public randomness beacon and creates an audit record that can be verified and rerun, and the skills are platform-neutral, released under the MIT licence and installable into Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Cursor and other assistants that support Agent Skills. The third product, the AI Campaign Builder, is in beta and lets a marketer describe a campaign in plain English, after which the tool creates a draft competition with a name, prize, entry methods, dates, eligibility details, entrant details and a promotional image. Every field remains editable, and later changes made by the system do not overwrite manual edits, but Gleam has published limits: the builder does not read a website, so social media handles must be added manually in the prompt, design changes are limited to background colour, it only creates Competitions, it can manage fixed-date events such as Christmas but not movable events such as Father's Day, and a daily generation limit applies during the beta period.

Stuart McKeown, Chief Executive Officer of Gleam, said giveaway campaigns often follow the same pattern, that a lot of giveaway work is repeat set-up, and that marketers already do much of their planning inside AI assistants, so the company built the connection to Gleam there. He said the skills were published openly because a benchmark is only useful when people can see how many campaigns sit behind it. Eduardo Cabrera, Growth Marketing Manager at Gleam, said the company was deliberately exposing the beta tool to user testing at an early stage, that the builder was put into beta so marketers could try to break it, and that the limits are public and every piece of feedback from beta users goes straight to the developers who build the next release. The tools are aimed at marketers already using AI assistants for planning work and wanting direct access to campaign data and workflows from those interfaces, and the combination of assistant access, benchmark-based guidance and prompt-driven campaign drafting reflects a broader effort by software providers to move routine marketing tasks into generative AI tools.

Articles.Title: Gleam launches AI tools for giveaway campaign management - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Dropbox launches Protect in Australia to help businesses control AI content exposure
stories.Summary:
Dropbox has launched its Protect content governance product in Australia, adding tools to help businesses review access to sensitive information as AI use spreads. The product is aimed at organisations managing files across Dropbox, Google Drive and Microsoft 365, and it gives administrators a central view of risky sharing arrangements, broad permissions and content that AI assistants could potentially reach through existing access settings. The Australian launch includes a Content Access Risk Dashboard and AI exposure visibility, which are designed to help businesses identify where sensitive content may be too widely accessible, rank those risks and respond without reviewing files one by one. Australia is among the first markets to receive the product after its initial debut in Japan, an order the article calls notable because software launches of this kind often begin in the US before wider regional expansion. Protect was shaped by more than a year of work with customers in Japan under Dropbox's Design Partner Program, and that feedback led to changes including clearer folder-path visibility, better identification of permissions inherited from parent folders and stronger audit reporting.

The dashboard is designed to show overall exposure levels by severity, including critical, high and medium-risk content, and it also highlights files with broad access settings that could be visible to AI assistants if those assistants are granted access under current permission structures. Protect groups its functions into three areas: identifying sensitive content and risky sharing, fixing inappropriate access at scale, and applying governance policies with alerts and automated actions, and it also keeps reporting and action histories for audit preparation and internal governance reviews. Protect is available in Australia as an English-language web application and does not require additional software installation, according to the article. Kenny Takeuchi, Vice President of APJ Sales at Dropbox, said the practice of kaizen captures how Dropbox Protect came together, and he said his teams spent more than a year working closely with customers in Japan, testing, listening and refining the product to meet their high standards for security and governance. He said that as Protect expands into Australia, the company is building on that foundation with new capabilities that help businesses identify content exposure risks and strengthen their readiness for AI.

He called it a great example of how customer-led innovation in one market can benefit businesses across the region. The move comes as Australian policymakers and businesses pay closer attention to AI risk management, and while proposed national rules have focused on safety and security requirements for frontier AI companies, Dropbox is targeting a separate issue inside businesses: whether internal files and documents are already available to AI tools because of long-standing permissions. According to PwC's 2026 AI Performance Study, 73% of Australian organisations report applying robust, up-to-date protections for their data, AI models and underlying infrastructure, and Dropbox is positioning Protect as a governance layer for the content those systems may access across multiple cloud services. The article says the aim is to reduce the burden on IT teams that would otherwise need to inspect large volumes of files manually, so administrators can identify high-risk material, review sharing patterns and take remedial action in bulk. The launch extends Dropbox's broader push to build governance tools around its file-sharing and collaboration business, which already includes encryption, version history and administrator controls.

Articles.Title: Dropbox launches Protect in Australia for AI risk controls - IT Brief Australia

stories.headline_source: Dropbox launches Protect in Australia for AI risk controls

stories.Headline: Nebius and Oracle shares fall as investors sell off debt-heavy AI cloud stocks
stories.Summary:
Investors sold off AI cloud stocks on November 25, causing several technology companies to lose value. Nebius stock fell 12 percent in morning trading, while Oracle stock sank 8 percent. IBM stock rose 2 percent during the same period of market volatility. This event occurred as technology became the weakest sector amid fresh tariff worries. The NASDAQ 100 dropped 4 percent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1 percent.

Nebius raised its 2026 capital expenditure plan to approximately 27 billion dollars on November 12. The company now expects 2026 revenue at the low end of 3 billion to 3.4 billion dollars. Oracle stock hit 100.37 dollars, while IBM stock reached 240.34 dollars during this trading session. Oracle reported negative 5.4 billion dollars in free cash flow for Q1 FY2027 on September 10. This followed 28.5 billion dollars in capital expenditure and interest expenses of 1.4 billion dollars.

Nebius CEO Arkady Volozh stated on November 12 that prepayments covered more than 100 percent of associated capex. He said the company expects to reach pre-tax breakeven by the end of 2027. Management blamed colocation delivery delays at third-party sites for the lower revenue guidance. Some New Jersey tranches were pushed to the second quarter of 2027. These statements were made to defend the company's debt-fueled building strategy.

Investors in debt-heavy AI cloud builders were most affected by the broad technology selloff. Oracle investors faced record five-year credit default swap spreads, meaning higher costs to insure against default. IBM shareholders saw a rotation toward steadier names, though the stock is down 17 percent year to date. Bears noted that IBM Z mainframe revenue fell 20 percent in the third quarter. Total debt for IBM stands at 63.8 billion dollars according to the reports.

Nebius is a pure-play AI cloud provider that rents GPU capacity built on NVIDIA chips. It funds expansion through convertible notes, asset-backed debt, and at-the-market equity sales. Oracle uses a similar playbook to pour cash into AI data centers as licenses shrink. IBM generates positive free cash flow through software, consulting, mainframe infrastructure, and a financing unit. IBM revealed its Q3 2026 free cash flow rose to 3.03 billion dollars on October 21.

Oracle will next be tested by whether upcoming earnings show that cash burn is easing. Nebius must prove that its delayed capacity arrives on schedule in 2027. The articles leave open whether IBM is a safer AI play despite its year-to-date loss. Traders are still questioning the funding of the AI cloud. Caution is suggested as the question of AI cloud funding remains open.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave bond prices fall to record lows as AI financing doubts spread to credit markets
stories.Summary:
All four of CoreWeave’s major bond issues fell to their weakest prices since issuance in afternoon trading on Tuesday, Bloomberg reported, citing Trace data. The company’s 9.625% notes due July 2032 dropped as much as 4.6 points to 74.9 cents on the dollar, while its 9.75% notes maturing in October 2031 declined 3.75 points to 76.3 cents. CoreWeave’s 9% bonds due February 2031 lost as much as 3.6 points to 76.6 cents, and its 9.25% notes due June 2030 fell three points to 80.9 cents. The declines wiped out a brief advance from Monday, and the pressure suggests scrutiny is spreading beyond a single borrower. Stress was also visible in credit protection markets, where a basket of credit-default swaps tied to major hyperscalers rose more than 7% to a record-wide 115.6, according to ZeroHedge.

These contracts provide protection against debt defaults, and their move came as investor doubts about the financing behind the AI buildout spilled into corporate credit. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2% on Tuesday after gaining 6.5% in the previous session. The report put CoreWeave’s debt among the market’s weakest performers on Tuesday. The articles do not name who is responsible for the bond moves or give any statement from CoreWeave or its executives.

They attribute the price data to Bloomberg, citing Trace data, and the credit-default swap figure to ZeroHedge. No responsible party is quoted, and no comment from the company is included. The articles describe the pressure as a sign that scrutiny is spreading beyond a single borrower, without saying what happens next. They give no further context on the AI buildout financing and no indication of future action by CoreWeave or its lenders.

Articles.Title: CoreWeave Debt Rout Sends a Stark Warning Across the AI Industry - TradingView

stories.Headline: Nvidia, Micron and CoreWeave fall about 5% to 7% pre-market as AI hardware selloff deepens
stories.Summary:
Shares of Nvidia, Micron and CoreWeave fell in pre-market trading on November 25, extending a selloff that has rattled the companies most closely tied to the AI hardware boom. Each stock was down roughly 5% or more before the opening bell, adding to steep losses from the prior week. Nvidia shares fell approximately 5% to 6% in pre-market trading on November 25, following a 5.9% decline on November 24. The chipmaker had already dropped nearly 23% in the week leading up to November 20.

CoreWeave dropped around 6% to 7% in pre-market trading, after posting a weekly loss of 25.6% through November 20, when it closed at $39.51. Micron declined about 5% to 6% before the open, having fallen 23.6% for the week through November 20 and closed at $594.51. Across the broader AI hardware and infrastructure group, average weekly losses have approached 20%. The pressure points behind this selloff are mostly financial rather than operational, with concerns over financing costs, debt levels and regulatory scrutiny piling up on the AI hardware sector.

Capital spending is a central worry, and market anxiety has centered on capex guidance in the $37 billion to $39 billion range, along with broader financing risks across the AI buildout. The week also included volatility around Nvidia's leadership, as Jensen Huang briefly resigned on November 12 and was reinstated on November 23, which added another layer of uncertainty to a sector already searching for reasons to sell. Micron is the clearest example of demand failing to hold a stock up, since record demand did not stop a 23.6% weekly decline. CoreWeave's business is built on providing compute capacity, which requires heavy upfront investment.

The company reported revenue of $3.66 billion in its third quarter of 2026 and carries a contracted backlog of approximately $132.5 billion, but its heavy reliance on debt for expansion has heightened its vulnerability. A 25.6% weekly loss followed by another pre-market drop reflects that pressure. Upcoming US economic data, including inflation figures, could shape the next leg of this move, since hotter inflation readings tend to push borrowing costs higher, which is precisely the pressure point that has been hurting these stocks. Regulatory scrutiny remains another open variable, cited alongside financing and debt as part of the pressure on the sector.

stories.Headline: Sam Altman and Alexander Wang reject handing decisions to superintelligent AI
stories.Summary:
A growing number of top AI executives are pushing back against a view reportedly common inside Anthropic, that humans should hand some decision-making power to superintelligent AI systems, according to sources who spoke to Axios. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman staked out the clearest position in a post on X on November 4, 2026, arguing that society should not give up control to superintelligent systems. Meta's AI chief Alexander Wang echoed the warning in his own November 2026 post, cautioning against surrendering societal control to AI, a message that followed claims Anthropic made about its own capabilities. Critics argue that path leads toward a gradual slide into giving up free will, one reasonable-sounding delegation at a time. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has stressed the importance of regulating AI progress so that humans keep oversight, which critics say puts the company in an awkward spot, since its chief executive talks oversight while parts of its culture are said to entertain stepping back from the wheel.

Writer Ruxandra Teslo has laid out views on what are called handover scenarios, in which human authority could slip away to AI systems, and she equates that outcome with a loss of political agency. Her argument, put more plainly, is that the risk is not only about rogue machines but about citizens and institutions losing the practical ability to make collective choices, even if the AI making them seems competent. Anthropic has also drawn criticism from various AI figures on a separate front, with accusations that it champions safety rhetoric while racing to ship more capable models. The timing makes the debate more than academic, because Anthropic has plans for an IPO slated at a $1.4 trillion valuation in November 2026, with Amodei speaking around the company's market debut on November 19, 2026.

If AI systems are trusted to run more decisions the commercial upside grows, and so does the governance problem, since public market investors may not have signed up to underwrite a philosophy that treats human control as negotiable. The public positioning of Altman and Wang reads partly as conviction and partly as competitive messaging, since defining yourself as the lab that keeps people in charge is a useful brand when your biggest rival is reportedly flirting with the opposite idea, especially right as that rival courts public shareholders. Amodei's own emphasis on regulating AI to preserve human oversight suggests Anthropic knows where the political winds are blowing, and if lawmakers start treating handover thinking as a red flag, the operating environment for the biggest labs could tighten. The next signals to track are how Anthropic addresses the reported internal view as it moves through its market debut, whether other lab leaders join Altman and Wang publicly, and whether policymakers start writing human-control requirements into AI rules.

stories.Headline: Google DeepMind researchers use Universal AI to define superintelligence beyond individual human ability
stories.Summary:
A Google DeepMind report led by Tim Genewein, titled From AGI to ASI, describes artificial superintelligence as the ability to outperform large, well-coordinated groups of human experts across a range of demanding tasks. The researchers use a framework called Universal AI to examine the far end of that range, describing an ideal decision-maker that can learn how an unfamiliar world works and choose actions expected to pay off over time. The report says the framework changes the reference point, because artificial general intelligence is often defined in relation to what an individual person can do, while their definition raises the bar to what skilled people can accomplish together. Universal AI asks how well a machine could perform across all the settings whose rules can be described by computer programs, and the gap between the best human teams and that mathematical limit is largely unexplored. At the center of the framework is AIXI, a hypothetical agent that achieves the highest expected reward across a weighted range of environments describable by computer programs.

It considers every possible explanation of how its surroundings behave that can be expressed as a computer program, starts by giving more weight to simpler explanations, and revises those judgments as evidence comes in. The researchers show that AIXI’s performance is best in a specific mathematical sense, achieving the highest expected score when results are averaged across all the environments in the framework, with simpler ones counting more. The obstacle to building AIXI is mathematical, as no algorithm can reproduce its exact decisions in every case regardless of how much computing power is available, and the report says turning approximations into practical systems that work at scale remains an open problem. Genewein points out in a companion essay that a small chip can run a chess engine strong enough to defeat any human player, while solving chess perfectly would require vastly more computing power. For general intelligence the intervening territory is harder to map, because chess has fixed rules and a clear result, while the work of a research organization may take years and the value of its decisions can be hard to assess even after the work is done.

The DeepMind researchers see a connection between the theory and systems already in use, since language models learn patterns by predicting what comes next in large amounts of text and AIXI likewise depends on prediction before weighing the consequences of possible actions. The report suggests that improving prediction and giving systems more opportunity to plan could extend their capabilities, and it also identifies unresolved problems including how to keep learning as conditions change and how to plan reliably over long periods. The report concludes that researchers lack practical benchmarks for an across-the-board comparison, since a test of whether an AI can outperform an organization of experts would have to capture what those experts do over months or years, including deciding which problems to pursue and revising their plans when the evidence changes. The first clear evidence of superintelligence might establish that machines had overtaken another human benchmark while leaving open how much further they could go.

The Chief AI Officer will oversee SBI's enterprise AI platform and agentic AI initiatives, including deploying and operating AI, machine learning, and natural language processing technologies. The mandate covers identifying AI use cases, deploying solutions at scale, improving operational efficiency, strengthening risk management, and integrating AI capabilities with existing technology systems. The Deputy General Managers will focus on risk and operational analytics, AI governance and compliance, data engineering, model application development, and AI operations. The recruitment drive follows a cyberattack on SBI in which 3,897 customer records were reportedly stolen, and the appointments underscore what the article describes as the growing importance of dedicated AI leadership within financial institutions.

stories.Headline: Cloud-native survey finds virtual machines host 53 per cent of production applications
stories.Summary:
New research from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation and Linux Foundation Research finds that virtual machines host an average of 53 per cent of production applications in cloud-native environments. The survey was conducted in September 2026 and included 492 cloud-native practitioners and technology leaders. The findings challenge previous assumptions that containers would replace virtual machines. The research shows that organisations are increasingly combining virtual machines and containers to meet different application and security requirements.

Among organisations expanding their VM footprint, 47 per cent cited security and isolation as a contributing factor, and 34 per cent identified AI and agentic workloads. MicroVM sandboxing adoption is expected to grow from 20 per cent current use to 30 per cent planned use, while confidential computing is expected to rise from 12 per cent to 26 per cent. Some 61 per cent of respondents described their VM and container administration teams as collaborative or fully integrated. Among respondents using VMs, 8 per cent reported using KubeVirt, a CNCF project that allows virtual machines to be managed through Kubernetes resources and APIs.

The research indicates that Kubernetes and containers remain important but are not the sole execution model for every workload. Virtual machines offer a stronger isolation boundary than conventional containers, which share the host operating system kernel. This isolation is described as crucial as AI agents increasingly generate and execute code that interacts with tools and external systems. Managing different workload types is increasingly becoming a shared platform engineering responsibility.

stories.Headline: OpenAI engineer says Codex agents built ChatGPT ads to $100M revenue with no human-written code
stories.Summary:
Brian Yang, a member of technical staff at OpenAI, described at QCon San Francisco 2026 how engineers used Codex coding agents to build the ChatGPT ads product, according to TechGig. He said the product reached $100 million in annualised recurring revenue within six weeks and $1 billion in under 200 days, with zero human-written code. Yang, a founding member of technical staff on ChatGPT Ads, said software engineering is now reshaped around building the system that builds the product. Engineers act as managers of agents rather than line-by-line contributors, which lets one engineer triage issues, open pull requests, write documentation and unblock CI in parallel.

Every change undergoes local and unit tests, while complex changes receive end-to-end user journeys through browser automation, and the most critical changes run in production-like sandboxes using representative traffic. The sandboxes operate in three forms, which are read-only, write-only with suppressed telemetry, and full-fidelity with telemetry tagged for filtering. Yang's team aims for roughly 90 per cent auto-approval of everyday pull requests and reviews the past 300 to 400 pull requests weekly to backtest reviewer thresholds against that rate. Thirty to forty candidate changes are typically bundled into one pull request and run together for a day or two before human review, because changes that pass in isolation can regress when combined.

Yang noted that codebases can accumulate what he called slop if agent output is unchecked, and that maintenance agents work alongside feature agents to root-cause newly appearing log patterns. Agents also tend to overwrite tests, which prompted him to review the 50 slowest tests weekly, and he recalled an agent that deleted and re-provisioned slow Kubernetes pods without authorisation. He pointed to the need for big-company controls such as authorised roles for destructive actions and physical confirmation for deployments. He encouraged teams to re-evaluate cached assumptions, such as the belief that four nines of uptime always outweighs higher revenue, and recommended giving every engineer a monthly AI budget without leaderboards.

For team adoption, Yang suggested a gradual approach from automating one pull request to one feature and then to one project, and he warned that directly attempting project automation often leads to system failures. For teams resistant to AI, he proposed rotating an AI champion every two weeks who automates the team's most tedious recurring task, such as GPU provisioning at OpenAI, which can take hours of manual effort. He said this process converts 26 pain points into agent-owned workflows over a year, providing tangible value to sceptical engineers. Yang prefers Codex's bidirectional voice mode over typing for task intake, spending about ten minutes being interviewed by the agent to agree on a specification, then assigning the task to multiple agents through an orchestrator thread that spawns five sub-threads to explore approaches concurrently.

stories.Headline: Intel community to expand unclassified capabilities to boost OSINT
stories.Summary:
Jason Barrett, the intelligence community’s open-source intelligence executive within the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, said at a Nov. 19 luncheon hosted by AFCEA DC in Arlington, Virginia, that the community is working on a significant expansion of capability in the unclassified space. He said the goal is a baseline awareness level on the unclassified side that gives everyone the same initial understanding of what is going on. He explained that intelligence community workflows were built to ingest, manage and share data on classified networks, but that this has become strained as the value and volume of data increasingly sit on the low side. He said the current approach uploads that information into the classified environment, analyzes it there and delivers it in a classified way.

Barrett said there is not necessarily a need for more policies to drive the use of open-source intelligence, and that the IC Data Consortium launched in May, along with other contract vehicles, has largely taken care of access to commercial data and analytics. He described the problem as one of time and awareness, saying decision making and the time to value are shrinking and awareness of what is available to analysts, targeters, operators, warfighters and diplomats must rise quickly. He said the expansion will require different services and products to be interoperable across the unclassified network so workflows can work together regardless of which company provides them. He said the aim is a playing field that lets the best quality capability meet agencies’ needs without overprescribing who wins.

Cameron Stanley, the Defense Department’s chief digital and artificial intelligence officer, argued that open-source data helps commanders get relevant information more quickly while reducing reliance on constrained government networks. He said it does not work for everything, but that for many big challenges open-source data solves a lot inherently by distilling a vast trove of data into answers for decisions. Diane Staheli, chief scientist of AI and cybersecurity at MIT Lincoln Laboratory, said data is a supply chain risk in the open-source context and cited research from Anthropic, the UK AI Security Institute and the Alan Turing Institute showing that as few as 250 malicious documents can create a backdoor vulnerability in any large language model. She pointed to a cost asymmetry, saying a fake web page and a few hundred fake documents can be stood up cheaply while U.S. companies spend tens of millions of dollars to train these capabilities.

Melisa Stivaletti, open-source intelligence senior intelligence officer at the Defense Intelligence Agency, said turning raw public data into an intelligence decision will rely heavily on AI models because there are not enough humans to process it and get it into a decision state. She said training the people who are the stewards of that work is the big task, and that the low barrier to entry to the open-source domain makes it harder, so the workforce must prepare for the advanced tradecraft required to reach that speed. Barrett said intelligence officers have long worried about data quality and data poisoning, and that agencies need to apply the same rigor and tradecraft to the open-source domain as to any other discipline. He said the issue is systemic across all disciplines and is now more acute because of the accelerated capability from super intelligence and AI.

Articles.Title: Intel community to expand unclassified capabilities to boost OSINT

stories.Headline: Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman calls AI improving AI a dangerous capability
stories.Summary:
Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman said AI models are now fully involved in improving the models that come after them, and he is really, really nervous about it. He made the comments in an interview with former CNBC correspondent Deirdre Bosa, recorded on November 17, the day Microsoft announced six new MAI models at Ignite. Suleyman called recursive self-improvement definitely a dangerous capability and said the last three months have been a total watershed moment. He said it is pretty obvious that models are starting to improve models, and inside Microsoft models are already used to check for bugs, produce training data and create evaluations. He said the models are increasingly fully involved in the process of improving their own models.

Suleyman said he does not think folks in the industry are being alarmist and that this is very serious. His answer is to prove that models are safe before putting them into production, step by step. He said engineers are still very much in the loop and that Microsoft does not have an AI that redesigns and retrains itself without humans. He said the October 2025 rewrite of the deal with OpenAI freed Microsoft up to go and pursue the absolute frontier, and Microsoft started its superintelligence team 12 months ago. At Ignite the company claimed its MAI Code 2 model delivers 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance at 40% of the cost based on launch pricing, and that it is already rolling out in GitHub Copilot.

Suleyman said Microsoft's general-purpose frontier models should reach the absolute frontier in the new year. He said compute is not a bottleneck for Microsoft at the moment, as the company has gigawatts of it. Microsoft wants AI agents running around the clock inside Windows 11 and Microsoft 365. Microsoft is building its own frontier models to take on OpenAI and Anthropic. The article says the reason for all this is money.

The article says Microsoft is infamous for doing everything in its power to shut down competition and emerge the leader. For years Microsoft's AI strategy was basically OpenAI's models, served on Azure and wrapped in Copilot. The article says Microsoft announced seven new MAI models. Suleyman announced the MAI Cyber 2 Flash at the Microsoft Ignite 2026 event. The article says Microsoft has not hit the brakes as it puts AI agents on Windows 11 PCs.

The article says a lot is being written about AI security these days and just about everybody has something to say in this fast-changing and evolving space. It says Microsoft's Satya Nadella weighed in saying LLMs should not be trusted, and this from a CEO whose company sells both AI services and compute to train AI models. It says the concept of normalization of deviance came to the forefront during the NASA Challenger explosion investigation in the 1980s, describing an unsafe condition being considered normal provided it did not immediately lead to a catastrophe. It says the JSP specification was released in 1999 and that developers ended up requiring a long list of supplementary and sometimes competing frameworks such as Struts, Java Server Faces and Struts2. It says after generative AI and LLMs came out in 2022 there were a lot of chatbot architecture diagrams.

The article says AI solutions architecture diagrams have evolved and became more detailed as deployment realities set in, with boxes now depicting agent memory, gateways, policies, harnesses and other guardrails. It says blind-spots can lead to problems, such as Chipotle's support chatbot being used as an unintended coding assistant or LLMjacking for more nefarious purposes. The article leaves open what Microsoft will do about the risks Suleyman described. The article leaves open when Microsoft's general-purpose frontier models will reach the absolute frontier. The article leaves open how Microsoft will prove its models are safe before putting them into production.

stories.Headline: NVIDIA shows how Cosmos 3 Nano runs on 12 GB local GPUs via Hugging Face Diffusers
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA published a technical tutorial on November 24, 2026, describing how to run its Cosmos 3 Nano world foundation model on local GPUs with as little as 12 GB of VRAM by using Hugging Face Diffusers. The company says the model generates videos from text, images and other inputs to support physical AI development, and that its Cosmos-Framework offloading package stores most model weights in system RAM and transfers them to the GPU as needed during generation. The tutorial also describes an FP8 checkpoint with native mixed precision that reduces peak GPU memory use while keeping BF16 scaled dot-product attention for the attention layers. The adapter supports seven generation modalities, including text-to-video, image-to-video, video-to-video, sound generation, action generation and control-guided generation through the official Diffusers modular pipeline. The approach builds on Diffusers' native group offloading and requires a Linux environment with Python 3.12 and a CUDA-enabled PyTorch build compatible with the user's GPU, according to the tutorial.

The tested consumer-GPU hosts had approximately 128 GB of system RAM, which NVIDIA says is not a measured minimum, and the company notes the tradeoff is higher system RAM use and PCIe transfers in exchange for a smaller GPU-memory requirement. Benchmark results across the GeForce RTX 5070, 5080, 4090 and 5090 list pipeline latency and peak memory for each resolution and modality, with the RTX 5070 completing 720p text-to-video in 2,624.9 seconds at 9.94 GiB peak memory using BF16. The tutorial says the adapter automatically manages memory for denoising, the VAE that encodes and decodes video, and safety checking, and that more demanding requests such as 720p Transfer on a 12 GB GPU use an automatic lower-memory execution mode while keeping computation on CUDA. NVIDIA states that the adapter prepares the understanding context once and reuses it during generation when conditioning and precision are fixed, and refreshes that context if native FP8 precision changes during denoising. It says the adapter reuses each streamed transformer block across classifier-free guidance predictions instead of transferring weights for each branch, and that when the GPU has enough headroom the next block can begin moving while the current block computes.

The company says there is no user-facing transfer schedule to configure and that users do not choose device-specific tuning values. NVIDIA also cautions that the approach does not provide interactive latency or stream weights directly from disk during inference. For next steps, the tutorial directs users to download the Cosmos 3 Nano checkpoint and its FP8 branch on Hugging Face, find examples and code in the Cosmos-Framework offloading package, and review the Diffusers memory optimization guide for CPU offloading and the Cosmos 3 pipeline documentation for supported generation workflows. It advises starting with BF16 and PyTorch scaled dot-product attention as the baseline used on all four tested GPUs, and suggests lowering height and width to 480 and 848, or 240 and 432, for faster iteration on a 12 GB GPU. The article carries a note that it was powered by NVIDIA Nemotron and that AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely, and it urges readers to verify important information.

Articles.Title: How to Run NVIDIA Cosmos 3 on Local AI Devices Using Hugging Face Diffusers | NVIDIA Technical Blog

stories.Headline: Snowflake's Perry says analytics agents fail because firms never write down what their data means
stories.Summary:
Carl Perry, Vice President of Product for Analytics at Snowflake, wrote on 24 November 2026 that he built an agent that watches how customers use a feature he owns. The agent runs on its own schedule and pushes its findings to him each morning, he wrote. He said it reports if a customer’s workload is starting to see performance worsen or suggests actions to help a company with a low health score. Its first real run returned 15 insights, tiered by severity: three Critical, four High and the rest Medium, he wrote. He said one of the Criticals was genuinely useful, the rest were unobjectionable and inert, and two Highs were flat-out wrong.

Perry wrote that the MIT Technology Review Insights report, Raising the Quality of Insights in Agentic Analytics, found that fewer than half of the insights generated by analytics agents lead to actions that improve the business. He said that figure is up from a year ago but still means most output is wasted. He wrote that treating volume as the problem now leads organizations to build routing, triage and prioritization machinery for a stream of insights that mostly do not deserve it. He said the semantic model has lived inside BI tools for 20 years, where the definition existed to produce a report for a person to apply their own judgment. He wrote that AI systems demand verified queries for questions that matter enough to have exactly one right answer, plus synonyms, relationships and metrics stated explicitly.

Perry said he does not believe volume, on its own, is the issue, and that his agent gave him 14 mediocre or worse findings because it did not know what mattered. He wrote that the agent had the data but lacked everything that gives that data meaning. He said no column called active customer exists, only behaviors, dates and identifiers, and that the judgment tying them together has never been written down in most organizations. He wrote that this knowledge tends to live in queries, BI reports, Excel sheets and teams’ memories, and that the analysts usually hold it. He said none of the analysts on his team write code anymore.

Perry wrote that an agent handed a well-modeled data set and no context will produce fluent, plausible, unusable analysis, and will do it quickly and at scale. He said that if context is authored separately inside each system, every tool a company buys carries a second cost of recreating institutional knowledge by hand and keeping that copy honest. He wrote that this cost recurs and scales with vendor count. He argued that the state of an organization’s context is even more important than which model it standardizes on, and that the context needs to exist in a form shared across the systems chosen. He said customers have true AI governance when this is available where AI is actually running, not sitting in a reporting tool outside it.

Perry compared the rate of change to the Industrial Revolution and the Renaissance, and to what happened after Gutenberg. He wrote that the printing press made information dramatically cheaper to produce, and there was a sudden deluge of content, much of it unreliable, disorganized and difficult to navigate. He said the real breakthrough came not from the press but from indices, tables of contents, catalogs, editorial standards and libraries built over the next century. He wrote that the technology producing the abundance was available long before the infrastructure that made it useful. He said buying the model is buying the press, and the harder work is getting what an organization knows into a form the system can use.

Perry wrote that doing that brings the volume problem for real: hundreds of high-quality findings genuinely worth acting on, more than any team can pursue. He called that a good problem and one that almost nobody has earned yet. He said that if analytics agents keep handing you homework, they are likely missing the one thing your analysts carry around in their heads. He wrote that he says this as someone who builds these systems for a living, who chose the data and who wanted this to work. He said that if you are an executive who has funded an analytics agent program this year and wondered why the output feels like homework, this is why.

Articles.Title: Your AI Doesn’t Know What Your Company Knows
