stories.Headline: AI moves to the center of spectral interpretation as models predict molecular structures from NMR and mass spectra
stories.Summary:
The article is an update review by Jerome Workman, Jr., published on November 24, 2026, in Spectroscopy, surveying machine learning research in molecular spectroscopy from 2023 through 2026. It reports that AI moved from a supporting role to the center of how spectra are interpreted in that period. Between 2023 and 2026, models began proposing full molecular structures from routine NMR spectra and learning chemistry from millions of unlabeled mass spectra. Models also began predicting UV, vis absorption from structure alone and steering workflows in autonomous laboratories. The review covers these advances, the push for explainable models, and what still limits routine adoption.

The review surveys five fronts: spectrum-to-structure prediction from one-dimensional NMR alone or with IR data using multitask transformer models, large language models and agent-based systems that reason over spectra, self-supervised learning and public benchmarks for tandem mass spectrometry, property prediction and interpretable deep learning for UV, vis absorption and fluorescence, and explainable AI and spectroscopic data driving autonomous laboratories. A 2024 Stanford University study trained a multitask model on routine 1D spectra for molecules with up to 19 heavy atoms, a range with trillions of possible structures. That model placed the correct molecule among its first 15 predictions 69.6% of the time without being given the molecular formula. It narrowed the search space by up to 11 orders of magnitude.

The same group extended the approach to molecules with up to 40 heavy atoms using a transformer-based multitask architecture. On simulated 1H and 13C spectra, top-15 accuracy reached 60.4%, falling to 46.6% with only 1H data. A model trained only on simulated spectra scored 0% on experimental test spectra, and fine-tuning on just 50 experimental spectra lifted that to 21.5% while preserving performance on simulated data. IBM Research showed that IR spectra alone can drive transformer-based structure prediction. A follow-up multimodal, multitask language model trained on both NMR and IR data reported top-1 accuracy of up to 96% after fine-tuning on experimental spectra, which its authors described as on par with expert human chemists, though the model is a preprint.

SpectraLLM, presented at the International Conference on Learning Representations in 2026, processes several spectral modalities together. It reported state-of-the-art results on four public benchmark data sets and outperformed single-modality baselines, and it remained robust when only one type of spectrum was available. In a 2026 workshop paper, an LLM agent proposed candidate structures, checked them with tools, and revised its answer iteratively. On one benchmark data set, the best agent configuration reached 71% top-1 accuracy, compared with 67% reported for graduate students. On a data set drawn from chemistry education materials it reached about 80%, and on a harder set of drug-like molecules from AstraZeneca accuracy fell to roughly 20%.

MassSpecGym, introduced at the 2024 Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems, addresses inconsistent evaluation with what its authors describe as the largest public collection of high-quality labeled MS/MS spectra. It defines three standardized tasks: de novo structure generation, retrieval of candidate molecules, and simulation of spectra from structure. DreaMS is a transformer pretrained in a self-supervised manner on millions of unannotated tandem mass spectra. After fine-tuning, it predicted spectral similarity, molecular fingerprints, and chemical properties, detected the presence of fluorine, and linked spectra across studies into a searchable network called the DreaMS Atlas. Researchers at the University of Cambridge combined 34,893 density functional theory calculations with 26,395 experimentally derived peak absorption wavelengths for UV, vis prediction.

The review states that spectroscopists have used multivariate statistics such as principal component analysis and partial least squares regression for decades. It says three developments made the shift possible: large training sets often built from simulated spectra and refined with experimental data, model architectures borrowed from natural language processing, especially the transformer, and a growing set of methods that explain what a model has learned. An earlier survey by the same author identified explainable AI, generative methods, and multimodal deep learning as the main drivers of progress. That survey also pointed to large language models and physics-informed neural networks as the next stage. IR and Raman appear only where combined with these methods, because AI for vibrational spectroscopy is treated separately in the series.

The review reports that accuracies on simulated spectra are now high, but performance on experimental spectra, transparency, and standardized validation remain the main obstacles to routine use. It states that the gap between simulated and measured spectra is now the main barrier to deployment. It notes that the multimodal model's figures should be treated as provisional until peer review. It says the spread in agent accuracy is a useful reminder that benchmark choice drives the headline numbers and that spectra of real-world drug-like compounds remain difficult. It suggests that the large volume of unannotated spectra in public repositories is an asset rather than a backlog.

stories.Headline: Report urges federal policymakers to give health care workers a voice in AI rollout
stories.Summary:
A report published by the Center for American Progress on November 24, 2026 examines how labor-management training partnerships can support health care workers as artificial intelligence spreads through the sector. The report focuses on one such partnership, the 1199 Service Employees International Union Training and Employment Funds, which trains and supports up to 40,000 workers a year in health care. The authors describe these partnerships as sector-based training programs governed jointly by unions and employers, built on the principle that sustained performance improvement comes through investment in cooperative relationships. The report says the health care industry is driving job growth in America and is expected to be a main contributor of new jobs in the coming decade.

The report says the spread of AI is not expected to reduce the number of health care jobs but could worsen the quality of jobs and care, for example through increased algorithmic management, less time with patients, reduced experience levels needed to catch errors and depressed wages. It cites Pam Brier, former CEO of Maimonides Medical Center in Brooklyn, New York, who attributed cooperation through the 1199SEIU fund to a 50 percent reduction in hospital-acquired infections, a 50 percent reduction in patient falls and a 75 percent increase in unpaid bill collection, among other results. It also cites Kaiser Permanente, described as a nearly three-decade-old partnership including workers across the country, which the report says has achieved more than $602 million in organizational savings. The report recommends that federal policymakers reform the public workforce system to increase worker voice in decisions about how AI is implemented in health care, create cost sharing with employers for training, build more sustainable funding for training and design programs with career navigation and other supports.

The report was written by authors at the Center for American Progress, which says the positions of American Progress and its policy experts are independent and that the findings and conclusions are those of American Progress alone. The authors thank Livia Lam and Samir Fayyaz at the 1199SEIU Training and Employment Funds. The report also recommends that policymakers require public workforce investments to prioritize support for labor-management training partnerships and other training models that include workers in program design and demonstrate good outcomes, such as long-term earnings gains. It says greater cooperation with and encouragement of these partnerships can help solve sectorwide training problems and assist workers navigating AI and other technology-based job displacement.

stories.Headline: Cox Automotive leader says dealers adopt AI faster than they see its value
stories.Summary:
Micah, who leads the Kelley Blue Book Instant Cash Offer business at Cox Automotive and has spent 17 years in the automotive industry, wrote a piece published on November 24, 2026, describing how he used a large language model to shop for a heavy-duty pickup for his family. He said the AI searched daily for more than four months across major shopping sites such as Autotrader and brought him the right vehicle at the right price, after which he stepped in to negotiate the deal and complete the transaction himself. He wrote that he could have found a truck without AI, but that the value it added was undeniable, and that his career had taught him that anything adding value is here to stay. He said his own experience matched what shoppers have been telling Cox Automotive for months. Cox Automotive's 2026 Content Influence Study found that about seven in 10 new-vehicle shoppers said they use AI at least weekly, and that the share who find AI content trustworthy roughly doubled since 2023, from 27% to 55%.

Among shoppers who use AI search, the study found AI sources lead at the start of the journey by 31% versus 22% for non-AI sources, but non-AI sources lead by the final decision by 36% versus 25%. McKinsey's 2026 Mobility Consumer Pulse found that haggle-free pricing at 44% and longer test drives at 40% outranked generative AI in the buying process at 18%. The third-quarter update to Cox Automotive's AI in Auto Retail Tracker shows dealer AI use holding near current levels, with growth coming mainly from standalone tools rather than AI built into the systems dealers already use. Micah wrote that dealers are reaching for AI faster than they are realizing value from it, and that many still cannot tell whether it is working, while their expectations are shifting from revenue toward productivity before reality has caught up. He recalled that at Digital Dealer in September, he was in a room with 35 dealers and asked for a show of hands from those whose AI investments were meeting their expectations, and zero hands went up.

He set out six takeaways for dealers and brands, including using AI to match the right buyer with the right car and the right deal, keeping inventory, pricing and vehicle details accurate and current everywhere shoppers and their AI tools look, and being clear about when a shopper is engaging with AI and when with a person. He also urged dealers to train, deploy and supervise their AI on accurate dealership data, to bring measurement into vendor conversations from the start, and to let shoppers approve before AI acts, since AI may open the journey but trust closes the deal. He wrote that the Cox Automotive AI Tracker Study found most errors shoppers hit in AI answers trace back to listing data rather than the AI itself, and that because shoppers keep using AI anyway, the exposure sits with the data feeding those answers. He said shoppers want to approve what an AI agent does before it acts, and that those most ready to use AI are the most insistent on that step. He concluded that AI is becoming the first stop in car shopping but that people still make the final sale, and that the winners in auto retail will not have the most AI but will be the easiest for shoppers to find and trust, wherever the journey begins.

stories.Headline: Alaskan hospitals use AI to help care for stroke patients
stories.Summary:
Alaskan hospitals are using artificial intelligence to help care for stroke patients, according to a STAT Health Tech newsletter published on November 24, 2026, which also covers peptides going mainstream and the RSNA 2026 meeting. stories.Headline: Everbridge earns ISO/IEC 42001 certification for its AI management system
stories.Summary:
Everbridge announced on 24 November 2026 that it has achieved ISO/IEC 42001 certification, which the company describes as the world's first international standard for artificial intelligence management systems. The company said the certification makes it one of the first critical event management providers to meet that standard. The certification covers the Everbridge CEM platform, xMatters and SnapComms, along with the corporate office, according to the company. Everbridge said the certification demonstrates an independently assessed AI management system covering the development, deployment and oversight of its AI-powered solutions, including Everbridge 360 AI.

The standard, published in December 2023, provides a certifiable framework for organizations to establish, implement and continually improve how they govern AI across its lifecycle. It addresses risk management, accountability, oversight and continuous improvement, and adds AI-specific requirements such as AI impact assessments, algorithmic risk management and oversight of the AI system lifecycle. Everbridge said just 100 ISO/IEC 42001 certificates were reported in the United States in the latest ISO Survey, compared with more than 5,000 ISO/IEC 27001 certificates there. The company also noted that the EU AI Act is now in effect, establishing what it calls the world's first comprehensive legal framework for artificial intelligence.

Everbridge said it believes investing in AI governance early is an important part of building technology customers can trust, and that it made governance part of its approach from the beginning rather than addressing it after AI capabilities are developed. The company said the certification does not eliminate every risk associated with AI but shows that an organization has implemented an AI management system independently assessed against an internationally recognized standard. It said its commitment to AI innovation goes hand in hand with its commitment to accountable AI practices, and that the certification reflects investment in the processes, oversight and accountability needed to manage AI. Everbridge said organizations that invest in both innovation and structured AI oversight will be better positioned to earn and maintain customer confidence.

Everbridge said AI is rapidly changing how organizations operate, make decisions and respond to challenges, and that questions about how AI is developed, deployed and managed grow as adoption accelerates. The company said these questions matter especially where technology supports time-sensitive, high-stakes decisions, and that regulatory bodies worldwide are signaling structured AI oversight is no longer optional. It said adoption of the newer AI standard is still in its early stages but its importance is growing as organizations increasingly incorporate AI into their operations. Everbridge said organizations that invest in governance frameworks today will be better prepared as these expectations become the norm.

Articles.Title: AI innovation is accelerating. AI governance can’t wait.

stories.Headline: Small and midsized businesses adopt edge AI to cut latency and bandwidth needs
stories.Summary:
Small and midsized businesses are exploring how to run artificial intelligence workloads at the edge, positioning data storage and computation closer to where it is needed, according to BizTech Magazine. Many of these businesses have relied on cloud platforms to access AI capabilities, while others have run AI workloads in on-premises data centers. Edge computing can reduce the need for bandwidth and lower latency in their workloads. The shift toward edge AI is happening rapidly at the enterprise level, and SMBs are looking to keep pace.

Cisco notes that by 2027, 75 percent of enterprise data will be created and processed at the edge due to evolving AI workloads. Edge AI processes data locally on devices such as smartphones and IoT sensors, at or near the point where it is created, rather than sending it to a service provider's servers. In a September 2025 white paper, IDC's Brandon Butler and Jennifer Cooke write that edge infrastructure minimizes latency, optimizes bandwidth utilization and enhances data privacy. Running workloads locally generally requires less power than cloud data centers, and sensitive data remains on local endpoints rather than traveling across a network. SMBs can scale by pairing cloud-based platforms with native edge capabilities on local devices.

Jeremy Foster, senior vice president and general manager for Cisco Compute, says AI is not waiting for the data center anymore and is happening right now in factories, at ports, in hospitals and in stores, where milliseconds matter. Butler and Cooke write that building an effective strategy for edge infrastructure begins with understanding the unique needs of highly distributed IT landscapes and industry-specific needs. They add that infrastructure and architecture choices need to consider the level of use case criticality and prioritize platforms that ensure data and physical security requirements. SMBs may face challenges, since existing edge infrastructure generally is not optimized for modern AI workloads and many sites have low power and limited footprints. Edge projects often take longer and cost more than planned as businesses deal with configuration drift and poorly managed large-scale updates.

Manufacturing and retail are two segments where edge AI may hold significant promise for SMBs, with edge devices monitoring machinery health, detecting defects and optimizing production, while retail uses it for personalized customer experiences, inventory management and loss prevention. A hybrid model may benefit retailers, with the cloud training large models and aggregating insights across locations while the edge handles real-time inference behind in-store intelligence. By rightsizing their computing infrastructure, SMBs can avoid overprovisioning while keeping performance and costs in check. For SMBs with lean IT teams, working with a trusted partner can make complexity manageable and speed up edge AI deployments.

stories.Headline: Corporate real estate leaders expect AI and economic pressure to reshape teams within three years
stories.Summary:
Corporate real estate leaders are expecting a shakeup to their teams over the next three years as AI, economic pressure and M&A activity force changes, CBRE said in a report released Nov. 17. Currently, 10% of corporate real estate departments are undergoing a major reorganization and 33% are exploring one, according to CBRE's 2026 corporate real estate organizational design study. Another 35% added roles in the past year to support what CBRE calls the industry's changing remit. The top five new or in-demand skills that teams are looking for are technology and AI, cited by 77% of respondents, and change management, cited by 52%, with reporting and analytics, financial acumen and CRM also named. As internal corporate real estate teams shift their focus to strategy and business enablement, named by over 90% of leaders as their department's top priority, organizations are shifting delivery to service providers, according to CBRE.

On average, 23% of staff are internal and 77% are Tier 1 service providers, with departments typically using one or two providers for each core function, like facilities, project and transaction management. One change already happening is an increase in outsourcing of real estate management services that were previously done by internal teams, according to CBRE. Real estate analytics software company Tango surveyed leaders at large enterprises, mostly in the C-suite or at the senior level in facilities, and all companies represented had over $500 million in revenue, with the majority in North America. The Tango survey found that the top challenges facing leaders are capital costs, volatile demand, lease inflexibility and limited high-quality space that meets their requirements. These issues are costing organizations, Tango says, with 53% reporting a shrinking set of acceptable compliant space and 43% having renewed or extended a lease on unfavorable terms due to a lack of time or decision support.

Just under 90% of respondents in Tango's survey said they have delayed at least one portfolio decision in the past year, and more than half said external factors were the most common reason a decision gets delayed. Leaders at CBRE, JLL and Cushman & Wakefield all said economic uncertainty did push at least some amount of deals to later in the year. CBRE CFO Emma Giamartino said on an earnings call that the volatility is what's driving a pause or a hold or even delaying deals to 2027, and that the firm expects stability to come in the back half of next year, though results will differ if that doesn't come or things change. Still, the market has so far been surprisingly resilient, with 60% of U.S. markets showing positive net absorption over the past year, and Cushman & Wakefield CEO Michelle MacKay said during her firm's earnings call that companies are starting to make longer-term commitments.

stories.Headline: Nvidia adds AI motion generation and RTX updates for game developers
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA published its monthly game development update on 24 November 2026, describing new graphics, animation and local AI capabilities for game teams. Gaijin Entertainment integrated NVIDIA DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering into the Dagor Engine for War Thunder, the article says. NVIDIA Kimodo became the first AI motion-generation model integrated into Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview's guided animation framework, according to the article. The NVIDIA In-Game Inferencing SDK 1.8, RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.2, Real-Time BVH Viewer 1.0 and RTX Path Tracing 1.9 also received updates. The article says the updates help teams balance image quality, performance and creative intent.

Gaijin adapted its color management pipeline to evaluate DLSS 5 in sRGB before post-processing and UI, then map results back to linear HDR. Kimodo lets animators generate character motion inside Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview's Sequencer using text prompts, spline paths and target poses at specific frames. In-Game Inferencing SDK 1.8 adds hardened RTX Spark platform support, updated llama.cpp and whisper.cpp backends, Parakeet automatic speech recognition through whisper.cpp, and Vulkan priority API integration. RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.2 adds stratified low-discrepancy sampling for ReSTIR DI spatial resampling, a fallback sample feature, enhanced reservoir visualization and RTX Spark support. RTX Path Tracing 1.9 adds a nine-step introductory sample combining ReSTIR DI, SHaRC radiance caching and DLSS Ray Reconstruction, plus real-time subsampling and GPU-side acceleration-structure instance generation.

Gaijin said DLSS 5 delivers improved highlights and shadows while introducing a new level of microcontrast the team had not been able to achieve before. The team said the result is a more natural, lifelike image with finer detail and a stronger sense of realism. Gaijin also said it tuned DLSS 5 against its reference look to preserve vehicle markings, surface wear and material properties. The team said it evaluated image quality and performance separately across air, ground and naval combat. The article says the interview offers developers practical lessons on balancing lighting and material enhancements with art direction.

The article says ON/OFF comparisons highlight rainy, overcast scenes in War Thunder. The article says Kimodo pairs GPU-accelerated motion generation with the familiar timeline editor workflow, so teams decide where characters move and how they pose at key moments. The article says the In-Game Inferencing SDK supports multiple inference backends across GPU and CPU hardware, giving teams a common interface for running AI alongside game graphics. The article says the Real-Time BVH Viewer helps developers understand TLAS and BLAS contents, validate acceleration structure updates and debug geometry-related ray tracing issues. The article says RTX Path Tracing 1.9 gives developers a more accessible starting point for adding ray-traced lighting and studying a real-time path tracing pipeline.

The article says the Real-Time BVH Viewer integrates at the graphics API level through Direct3D 12 and Vulkan libraries, displaying results in a separate window with its own camera. The article says developers can use the included sampler to attach the viewer to a running D3D12 or Vulkan process without changing a title's code. The article says the viewer offers visualization modes for primitive, geometry, instance and cluster IDs, BLAS addresses, instance masks and flags, and acceleration structure update state, plus per-pixel trace time heatmaps. The article says RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.2 is available on GitHub with enhanced reservoir visualization for direct illumination, global illumination and path tracing. The article says the RTX Path Tracing intro sample uses a hybrid deferred renderer to introduce lighting features one at a time across nine selectable steps.

The article directs developers to read the War Thunder DLSS 5 developer interview for practical lessons on balancing lighting enhancements with art direction. It directs developers to explore the Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview release notes and the Kimodo research project to understand the guided animation framework. It directs developers to download Nsight Graphics and Nsight Systems to analyze DLSS Frame Generation workloads and use agentic AI tooling for graphics development. The article says Nsight Graphics 2026.4 and Nsight Systems 2026.6 introduce support for analyzing applications using DLSS Frame Generation, requiring Streamline SDK 2.12 or newer. The article says a new Nsight Graphics MCP server enables compatible AI agents to capture applications, inspect and debug captures, and analyze GPU traces.

stories.Headline: Pew Research Center rejects AI tools for coding religious restriction data after tests show inaccuracy
stories.Summary:
Pew Research Center tested two artificial intelligence tools to code data on religious restrictions. The center conducted these experiments between December 2024 and August 2025. Researchers wanted to see if AI could speed up the manual coding process. They compared AI results against data already hand-coded in prior studies. The center ultimately rejected adopting these tools into their current coding workflow.

The tests used Google's NotebookLM from December 2024 to February 2025 and Nexis+ AI from July to August 2025. NotebookLM reviewed 2021 sources for Germany, Iceland, Jamaica, Nigeria, Singapore, Canada, China, India, Saudi Arabia, Turkmenistan, Indonesia, Serbia, and Syria. Nexis+ AI used 2020 and 2022 data for Canada, Egypt, Germany, Jamaica, Nigeria, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, and South Korea. The process involves answering over 30 questions to produce the Government Restrictions Index and Social Hostilities Index. These indices cover 198 countries and territories with data dating back to 2007.

The researchers stated that the tools did not make things up but lacked completeness. They noted that AI missed many cases that human coders had previously found. For Nigeria in 2021, the tool listed four incidents while humans found 119 cases. The center said verifying AI citations took more time than the tools saved. They also observed that identical prompts produced different answers on different days.

The center noted that Nexis+ AI missed local reporting not translated into English. It failed to find a 2022 story about the detention of Jehovah's Witnesses in South Korea. The tool also cited Pew Research Center data back to the researchers through news stories. Human coders are affected because verifying AI results for Singapore took 10.5 hours instead of 4.5. The center said inconsistency would limit a dataset designed for comparisons over time.

The center manually codes data from national constitutions and publications from the United Nations and U.S. government. They also use sources from nongovernmental organizations like Human Rights Watch. A team of five trained coders typically spends four months combing through these documents. Two coders independently review each law, policy, or event to reconcile any disagreements. This demanding process ensures the integrity of the annual scores for each country.

The center may explore using AI to produce quick summaries to orient coders. They might test AI as a second coder to reconcile disagreements with humans. Future tests could involve updated tools to identify reliable sources for new research questions. The articles leave open whether newer versions of these AI tools will be more accurate. They do not state when further tests with updated tools will occur.

stories.Headline: US military develops AI-enhanced simulation training for Pacific threat scenarios
stories.Summary:

stories.Headline: Providence cuts internal hiring admin effort 90% with agentic AI tool RITA
stories.Summary:
Providence, a health system with 51 hospitals and more than 1,000 clinics across Alaska, California, Montana, New Mexico, Oregon, Texas and Washington, revamped its internal hiring with an artificial intelligence, powered tool called RITA, or Requisition and Internal Transfer Agent. Providence Vice President of Talent Acquisition Carol McDaniel said the organization decided to automate the process. RITA was built on IBM watsonx Orchestrate and connected to existing systems, including Providence’s Oracle HR environment. The organization has about 119,000 caregivers, which Providence calls its employees. McDaniel said it was easier for internal caregivers to leave and come back as new employees than to transfer to a new opportunity.

Since its rollout, RITA has reduced administrative effort for hiring managers by 90% and allowed internal transfers to start their jobs 12 days sooner, on average. Providence worked first on collective bargaining agreement, governed roles, which are typically assigned by seniority. The tool covers three simple questions: Is this a replacement, is this a new position, and is this CBA-governed. The tool delivers qualified candidates to the hiring leader and takes candidates through the offer process for the position. Providence had five releases of RITA with improvements and enhancements along the way.

McDaniel said the organization stopped and said it had to fix the process because retention is a big part of its recruiting. She said Providence shifted the administrative burden away from its day-to-day caregivers and gave them time back, with big time and cost savings since the launch. She said the entire process took about 18 months, and that Providence made some mistakes in the beginning and had to go back and solve a larger problem than originally thought. She said the first iteration was just about the transfer, and all it had done was shift the problem to another department. She said the enhancements come directly from key operational leaders and the people actually doing the work.

McDaniel said Providence brought stakeholders into the conversation, which it calls human-centered design, and that feedback is critical. She said Providence is an Oracle shop with Oracle Fusion Cloud HCM, implemented about four and a half years ago, and felt it important not to introduce a new system to its stack. She said the building of the requisition process seemed to be where the biggest problem was, secondary to making the transfer happen. She said adoption and communication are hard in a very large organization like Providence, and getting the message to the hiring leader at the front line or in the clinic is really difficult. She said Providence decided to look at administrative effort first and wanted to lessen the time to fill roles today.

McDaniel said that before RITA, Providence’s time to fill for internal transfers rivaled its external hiring, which should not be the case. She said Providence was also interested in addressing hiring costs, with a cost per hire for external hires and for internal, and in redeploying those savings. She said Providence wanted to redeploy the time saved by clinicians to give more time for patient care. She said Providence had not done anything like this before and was a little unsure. She said the metrics are the ones Providence is watching that will hopefully improve its program.

McDaniel said Providence began with internal transfers to start with a smaller scope of what will be a project for more general internal work. She said that today the talk is about department-to-department roles, and tomorrow it will be about going from clinical to nonclinical or moving from one ministry to another. She said Providence had to start smaller so it could grow bigger. She said Providence will expand RITA next year into a larger scope of work. She said it is critical to understand what stakeholders want next and how to make the experience more personalized for caregivers, who are getting automated messages about opportunities.

stories.Headline: GAO proposes 16 policy options for managing AI in cyberattacks and defense
stories.Summary:
The Government Accountability Office said Friday that it identified 16 policy options to help government and industry manage artificial intelligence in cyberattacks and cyber defense, ExecutiveGov reported on November 24, 2026. The watchdog found that AI gives attackers faster and more precise tools and widens what defenders can do. It said defenders struggle to test AI cybersecurity tools and lack enough data and guidance on using them. GAO cited industry reporting on two incidents from 2026. In June, a threat actor used AI to build a framework for refining malware that evades detection, and in February, a threat actor with little skill used several commercial generative AI services in a wide attack on basic security gaps.

GAO organized the 16 options around four goals informed by its research and consultations with experts, and described them as a menu of alternatives that is not exhaustive. The first goal, addressing gaps in cybersecurity guidance and practices, has four options: harmonizing cybersecurity requirements, improving threat information sharing, closing gaps in AI-related privacy risks and improving the application of fundamental practices. The second goal, filling AI-related research gaps, has three options: expanding research on safe AI adoption for cybersecurity, advancing research on identity management for agentic AI and expanding AI testing environments. Building the cybersecurity workforce accounts for two options, sustaining skills in current cybersecurity practices and strengthening AI expertise, and the fourth goal, governing AI tools throughout their cybersecurity lifecycle, encompasses seven options.

The seven governance options address how organizations acquire, assess and constrain AI tools, including through two technical concepts defined in the report. Under GAO's definitions, deterministic systems follow strict rules and return predictable results, while generative models fall into the nondeterministic category because probability-based processing can produce varying responses to identical inputs. One proposal would establish a deterministic AI fallback capability for critical cybersecurity functions, giving organizations an alternative means of maintaining essential operations, whether through rule-based tools or manual procedures, when an AI system becomes unavailable, fails or produces results inconsistent with its intended purpose. Another option would limit the use of autonomous and nondeterministic AI in consequential functions until the systems receive certification. A third proposal would require human authorization for consequential cybersecurity actions that AI initiates, and the remaining options call for a risk-based approach to acquiring AI products, checking tool outputs before and during deployment, assessing whether cybersecurity AI solutions deliver value and establishing a senior position responsible for managing privacy risks associated with AI use.

Experts GAO consulted said most of the risks and difficulties concern generative AI, that no widely accepted criteria exist for evaluating its offensive or defensive capabilities and that its adoption can add vulnerabilities that enlarge the attack surface. Other concerns involve data privacy and quality, the technology's underlying architecture, and governance and trust problems arising from AI's rapid development and the inability of existing frameworks to keep pace. Organizational obstacles included cost, a shortage of AI skills and trouble integrating the tools, and several experts also raised inconsistent regulation and too little data sharing. GAO defined policymakers, the group that could consider the options, to include legislative bodies, agencies, standards organizations and industry. GAO said state and non-state actors target government and private-sector systems thousands of times daily, putting essential services such as water, energy, telecommunications and financial systems at risk.

GAO described AI as a rapidly growing, transformative technology and said government efforts have yet to match the pace of evolving cybersecurity threats to national security, the economy and public well-being. The watchdog convened a multi-day meeting involving experts from government, industry and academia and interviewed stakeholders from agencies, universities and industry. It also examined existing literature and agency documents, while drawing its policy goals from executive orders, national strategies, its High Risk List and federal laws. GAO said AI has supported cybersecurity applications for decades, but recent developments in generative AI have expanded the technology's defensive uses. Security personnel apply machine learning and generative AI to streamline operational processes, improve security applications and support their teams, and generative AI can help security teams examine software for weaknesses and process extensive network datasets while allowing monitoring systems to account for newly identified vulnerabilities and changing conditions.

In October, Kevin Walsh, a director on GAO's IT and cybersecurity team, said at GovCIO Media & Research's Federal Cloud & Data Forum that AI tools should fall under the security and compliance expectations agencies already enforce and recommended treating AI as part of existing compliance programs and not as a separate category. Walsh added that users remain responsible for safeguarding personal information and completing cybersecurity training, and that new risks emerge once systems make consequential decisions. Joe Croghan, associate director of informatics at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, added that agencies delegating those decisions must confirm the systems pursue the intended goals and do more than execute tasks correctly. In November, GAO Chief Scientist Sterling Thomas said at a summit in the Washington area that expiring introductory pricing deals with AI providers could slow federal AI use over the next eight to 10 months, and that token-based pricing can grow much more expensive at scale. Nick Marinos, GAO's managing director for IT and cybersecurity issues, said human involvement remains necessary as agencies automate more cybersecurity work, because systems running on inaccurate or incomplete data could make flawed decisions that create new vulnerabilities, and he suggested that Congress revisit the Federal Information Security Modernization Act, enacted in 2002 and amended in 2014, in 2027.

stories.Headline: Twilt and de Rooij question whether high sensitivity suffices in AI prostate MRI risk classification
stories.Summary:
A commentary by Jasper J. Twilt and Maarten de Rooij of the Department of Medical Imaging at Radboud University Medical Center in Nijmegen, the Netherlands, was published in European Radiology on 24 November 2026, asking whether high sensitivity tells the full story for AI risk classification for prostate cancer detection on MRI. The piece is a commentary, so no institutional review board or animal care approval was required, and the authors state that the work received no funding. It refers to a multicentre evaluation of artificial intelligence risk classification for detection of clinically significant prostate cancer on biparametric MRI, published in the same journal. Maarten de Rooij is named as the scientific guarantor of the publication. The authors declare that de Rooij received speaker fees from Siemens Healthineers, paid to the institution.

The commentary carries no numbers, dates or names of its own about the evaluation it discusses beyond the citation of that multicentre study and the related references it lists. Those references include the PI-RADS Steering Committee requirements for AI development and reporting for MRI prostate cancer detection in biopsy-naive men, version 1.0, published in Radiology in 2025, and an ESUR/ESUI position paper on developing artificial intelligence for precision diagnosis of prostate cancer using MRI, published in European Radiology in 2021. They also include a 2026 paper on commercially available AI tools for prostate MRI, a 2026 critical appraisal of AI studies for prostate cancer detection on MRI, the SCARLET-1 study on AI for prostate cancer detection and screening on MRI in global populations, the PI-RADS version 2.1 update from 2019, and the 2026 EAU-EANM-ESTRO-ESUR-ISUP-SIOG guidelines on prostate cancer. The commentary also cites the PI-CAI study, an international, paired, non-inferiority, confirmatory study of artificial intelligence and radiologists in prostate cancer detection on MRI published in Lancet Oncology in 2024, and a 2025 European Urology paper on artificial intelligence in prostate cancer diagnosis on MRI. Responsibility for the commentary rests with Twilt and de Rooij as its authors, with de Rooij as scientific guarantor, and the authors state that no complex statistical methods were necessary for the paper.

The publisher's note states that Springer Nature remains neutral with regard to jurisdictional claims in published maps and institutional affiliations. The commentary refers to the multicentre evaluation article available at a DOI given in the piece, and the article offers shareable links to its content. The articles do not say what the commentary concludes about sensitivity or what happens next. More to follow.

stories.Headline: US prosecutors charge over 800 defendants in 400 scam cases since March
stories.Summary:
The Justice Department said on Tuesday, Nov. 24, that its prosecutors have taken action in over 400 cases against over 800 defendants since President Trump signed Executive Order 14390 on March 6, which directed a government-wide crackdown on scam networks. The department said the actions include new charges, extraditions, guilty verdicts and criminal sentences, and it described the announcement as its largest-ever crackdown on scammers. The 800-plus figure counts defendants across all those actions since March, not arrests made in a single day. Results came from 85 federal districts, and 30 defendants were extradited to face scam-related charges in US courts, the department said. US prosecutors and agents also assisted law enforcement in more than 10 countries in raids of foreign scam call centers and compounds that targeted Americans.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said predatory scams against the American people will not be tolerated. In one scheme charged this month, current and former members of prison gangs in Georgia allegedly used contraband mobile phones to tell victims they had missed jury duty and would be arrested unless they paid a fine. Fourteen people were charged in three indictments in federal and state courts, and another 17 were charged in state court over a scheme to smuggle contraband phones into Georgia prisons, while websites used in the scam were seized. In the month before the announcement, the Criminal Division filed and unsealed charges against over 30 scam defendants. The schemes alleged include Southeast Asian scam centers running cryptocurrency investment fraud, Nigerian inheritance-fee frauds, a list broker in Mexico who allegedly sold contact details of elderly Americans to scammers, a Peruvian call center that told Spanish-speaking Americans they faced arrest or deportation unless they paid for English-learning products, and a sweepstakes scheme against elderly Americans involving a dozen defendants, several of them Jamaican nationals.

The FBI said its Operation Blackout has restrained nearly $17 billion in illicit funds, seized more than 14,000 digital devices and helped identify, disrupt and dismantle over 29 scam compounds in Asia, Africa and the Middle East. It said the operations led to federal charges against more than 50 scam actors and helped foreign partners arrest or detain more than 320 others, and that it assisted in freeing and repatriating more than 2,200 trafficked workers forced to work in scam compounds. The FBI said a separate effort, Operation Level Up, has prevented more than $143 million in victim losses since March 6, and that its Recovery Asset Team froze over $350 million. Homeland Security Investigations reported more than 300 arrests and about 80 convictions and guilty pleas since March 6, and the Secret Service said it restrained more than $200 million in illicit funds during the surge period.

The release cited Gallup data that Americans lost an estimated $68 billion to scams in 2025. Last week the Treasury sanctioned a Cambodian scam-compound owner and two Burmese armed-group commanders.

stories.Headline: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge uses Claude to prove the Riemann hypothesis
stories.Summary:
Levent Alpöge, a senior mathematician at Anthropic, announced that he had developed a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, using the company's flagship LLM model Claude, according to an article published by hpcwire.com on November 24, 2026. Independent mathematicians have since verified the formal proof using Lean, a programming language and mathematical proof assistant, the article said. Alpöge described the breakthrough in a statement posted on his website. The article said the proof was announced after 167 years in which the proof had remained beyond the reach of mathematicians. The article said the idea that an underlying order exists was first proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859.

According to Alpöge, the same approach also solves a much broader and more complex problem known as the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, the article said. Alpöge said in his statement that he expected, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Alpöge said he and Claude had also formalized the arguments without assumptions. The article said the hypothesis is so fundamental that numerous other mathematical results depend on its validity. The article said that in 2000 the Clay Mathematics Institute named it one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, a list of some of the most challenging unsolved problems in mathematics, with a $1M reward for solving each.

Alpöge said in his statement that he believed he had, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. He said the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. He said it was natural to feel that this is an end, in his case a loss of a principal guiding light, but that what he saw during the course of progress so amazed him that he believed it is one dawn across science of something far greater. He said it was his secret in his student days that his plans were for this problem in decades, which meant then that he tried to become familiar with all tools that he could possibly recognize in the problem when it was time. He said Claude far outpaced him near the finish line, and that Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.

Alpöge said he had the pair on the line of combining two quite different ideas present in a toy setting, one of which was already new and shocking, making very simple one of the shadows of Riemann over which we mathematicians felt most triumph. He said he guided the pair to the right situation analogous to that toy setting, and then Claude began to leave him in awe. The article said prime numbers are the building blocks of mathematics, and that understanding how they are distributed has implications for cryptography, computer security, and other fields. The article said there is a well-documented tendency of LLMs to make mistakes, which makes their use in mathematical research particularly challenging. The article said that with Lean researchers can check each step of a mathematical proof computationally, and that other researchers can run the same code on their own systems to verify the results.

The article said researchers still need to make sure that the mathematical problem itself has been correctly represented in the code. The article said it would be interesting to know how much computing power was actually used by Claude to arrive at the solution. The article said there could be a growing demand for compute dedicated to mathematical reasoning and formal proof verification, especially as AI models take on more complex mathematical problems. The article said the Riemann hypothesis is not the only major mathematical problem that AI has taken on this year, and that another notable development was the Navier-Stokes equations, which are of particular interest to the HPC community given their importance in computational fluid dynamics. The article said much of the work so far involving AI in HPC has been focused on making simulations faster and less computationally expensive.

The article said there has also been considerable work on using AI to improve numerical methods, and that recent breakthroughs in mathematics suggest there may be another area worth exploring. The article said that if AI can help researchers develop new mathematical techniques, some of the problems that scientists have been trying to solve by throwing more computing power at them might benefit from an entirely different approach. The article said that even with the world's most powerful supercomputers, there are mathematical problems that cannot be solved through brute-force computation, and that the Riemann hypothesis is perhaps the most famous example in the world of mathematics. The article asked whether it is possible that what appears to be an irregular distribution of prime numbers may actually be much more than that, and whether there could be an underlying mathematical code that governs them. The article said that if that is the case, the difficulty has been to prove that any such order exists across an infinite set of numbers.

The article did not say when the verification was completed or by which independent mathematicians. The article did not say how much computing power Claude used to arrive at the solution. The article did not say whether the Clay Mathematics Institute has recognized the proof or awarded the $1M reward. The article did not say what Alpöge or Anthropic plans to do next. The article did not say whether the proof has been published in a journal.

Articles.Title: After 167 Years, AI May Have Cracked Mathematics’ Greatest Mystery

stories.Headline: Mitratech and HIKE2 host a December 8 webinar on which legal workflows to automate first

Mitratech Holdings and HIKE2 will hold a webinar titled You Own the AI. Now Earn the ROI: A Guide to Choosing What Legal Teams Should Automate on December 8 from 12:00 pm to 12:45 pm EST, according to a JD Supra listing posted on November 24, 2026. The listing says the problem is usually not the tool but the work the tool has been given. Registration is open through the listing, which invites readers to sign up for the session.

The webinar is about closing that gap rather than about which AI to buy, and it focuses on how to spot the workflows worth automating. It also covers what to fix in data and governance so that results hold up as AI use grows, the listing says. Attendees are told they will leave with a clear way to turn the AI they already have into results, starting with the workflows in front of them. The listing gives no other dates, numbers or names for the session beyond December 8, the 12:00 pm to 12:45 pm EST time slot and the two hosts.

Mitratech and HIKE2 are responsible for the session, and the listing presents their view that the gap between paid licenses and visible return comes from the work given to the tool rather than the tool itself. The listing does not name any speaker, and it gives no statement from any individual at either organization. It describes the session as a practical look at where AI pays off first for legal teams. The only quoted words in the listing are its invitation to join the session on December 8 at 12 pm ET.

The context the listing gives is that legal teams have paid for AI licenses and finished their pilots, yet the return remains hard to see. The listing frames the session as guidance on choosing what legal teams should automate, with attention to data and governance as AI use grows. It does not say what happens after the webinar or whether any recording will be available. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Havas Miami launches cultural intelligence AI model to help brands read consumer culture
stories.Summary:
Havas Miami and Republica Havas launched a proprietary AI tool called the Cultural Intelligence Model, which the agencies say helps marketers understand the cultural factors behind consumer decisions and apply those insights to strategy, according to an announcement dated November 24, 2026. The platform combines a brand's own data with social listening, trend tracking and search signals to map cultural nuances, test early ideas against AI-generated synthetic panels and score finished creative work. To support the release, Havas and its longtime research partner M3 MI published a whitepaper titled Scaling Human Understanding in the Age of Healthcare AI, which argues that AI excels at surfacing patterns in data but struggles to explain them. Eirasmin Lokpez-Cobo, Republica Havas' head of cultural intelligence and transformation and a co-author of the paper, calls that problem the interpretation gap, describing it as the distance between what the data reveals and the why behind decision-making.

Lokpez-Cobo describes the model as an agentic engine that ingests two layers of data, a primary layer of a brand's existing research and audience data, or new research the agency helps conduct, and a secondary layer of syndicated data such as M3 MI's datasets alongside signals like social listening, LLM search aggregators and trend analysis. The engine runs those layers through six types of contextual analysis covering sociodemographic information, cultural trends and media behaviors, with human strategists working alongside the AI at each stage. Its outputs fall into four products that build on one another with budget flexibility: the first two build audience segments and map customer journeys including predictive forecasting, an exploratory validation stage tests early strategic and creative ideas against AI personas in queryable synthetic panels, and a separate proprietary tool called CulturIQ audits completed assets, scores them and provides targeted recommendations. Lokpez-Cobo said the framework has helped overwhelmed clients find a starting point for reaching culturally distinct audiences by mapping onto data they already own, and she said marketers often treat culture in a very myopic way when many intersecting layers lead to microcultures.

Havas said clients across healthcare, financial services, retail and higher education have already applied the model, including Florida International University, which is working with Havas on a brand and communications strategy for an upcoming brand refresh. Michelle Palacio, FIU's SVP of marketing and strategic communications and chief marketing and communication officer, stressed the importance of a message rooted in Miami culture that does not alienate audiences elsewhere, and she said the university fed qualitative data from prior campaigns, including surveys and interviews, into the model to build three AI personas representing students, faculty and alumni. Over roughly a month of testing, simulated feedback from the synthetic panels has helped refine the university's positioning and mission statements, and Palacio said the system governs trust, meaning whose word counts, which sources feel credible and who gets the benefit of the doubt. FIU, which enrolls 55,673 students for the 2025-26 academic year as the nation's eighth-largest public university and tied for No. 1 in social mobility in U.S. News & World Report's rankings, has not finalized its strategy, and Palacio said the team plans to add audience segments, run further surveys and test different phases of future campaigns so it can pivot if needed.

stories.Headline: New York Times tells freelance photographers to skip Photoshop 2027 over hidden AI tagging
stories.Summary:
The New York Times warned freelance photographers not to update their software on November 24, 2026. The news organization asked these contributors to avoid using the newest version of Adobe Photoshop. This request was sent via an email that was later seen by The Verge. The company is concerned about how the latest update uses artificial intelligence. These features may operate in ways that are not apparent to the users.

The restriction applies to Adobe Photoshop 2027, which is release 28.0.0 and any subsequent updates. This software includes an AI Assisted Editor view that puts AI features in one toolbar. It also adds an AI assistant for instructions and prompt based image transformation and editing. Other new tools include AI upscaling options and a tool that recomposes images for different sizes. These changes are part of a November update to the creative suite.

Photography leaders Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner wrote the email to the freelance photographers. They stated that using these new features can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI generated. Spokesperson Graham James confirmed the requirement in a statement provided to The Verge. He reiterated the policy that was outlined in the original email. The leaders believe the AI tools may not be apparent to the users.

The New York Times believes that metadata tags risk losing the trust of their readers. This policy affects all contributing photographers who are working on assignments for the publication. The newsroom keeps photo editing to a minimum to maintain its journalistic standards. The company previously stated it does not digitally manipulate or retouch its photos. It only makes minimal color adjustments to ensure images are reproduced accurately.

Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its various apps in August. This metadata indicates if an image was edited using AI or is AI generated. Some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. It is not always clear which specific tools in the apps are AI powered. This can lead to blunt descriptions of post production in the image metadata.

The New York Times has not clarified which specific Photoshop features it is referring to. Adobe did not immediately respond to a request for more information from The Verge. The company continues to fill its creative suite with a trove of AI powered tools. It remains unclear how photographers will identify all AI tools in the software. The publication will continue requiring contributors to avoid the 2027 release.

stories.Headline: Levent Alpöge releases code proving the Riemann hypothesis after Anthropic goes public
stories.Summary:
Levent Alpöge got back to the place he was crashing in New York City around 4 A.M. on November 20, 2026, almost done and almost able to sleep. All that was left was to download the 17 million lines of code he had spent the night preparing for public release. The code needed to go up on his personal website, alongside a four-page statement he had tinkered with all week. For the moment, the code still sat on the servers of his employer, the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, which had gone public just hours earlier with the largest valuation in stock market history, making Alpöge a rich man. Once the upload was complete, he would also be one of history's most famous mathematicians.

The code was the product of untold computing resources, months of work and decades of dreaming, and it proved the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old math problem so formidable that it is almost beyond words. In public talks, experts have tended to simply treat it as an over-the-horizon aspiration, a "vanishing point" perspective against which all other math problems shrink. Just weeks earlier Terence Tao, arguably the world's most famous mathematician, had declared the hypothesis out of AI's reach, let alone that of humans, until perhaps 2050. Alpöge's quiet upload capped off an epochal year in which AI has systematically conquered humanity's oldest discipline in a sequence of escalating, dramatic and controversial discoveries. In nearly every episode of this earthshaking war for math's soul, Alpöge has figured somehow, part battlefield champion, part horseman of the AI apocalypse, part Forrest Gump.

Henry Cohn, a mathematician at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said people are divided over Alpöge and asked who this person is who is behind some of the most striking applications of AI to mathematics. Cohn called it a really interesting question that deserves a deeper answer than you can get from following him on X. Depending on who you ask, Alpöge is a reviled online troll, an agent of chaos laughing as his fellow mathematicians watch their intellectual landscape get carpet-bombed by his Silicon Valley cohort, or a reluctant public figure, a shy academic who has integrity and wants to forge a future where AI is mathematicians' collaborator, not their usurper. Or maybe he is an arrogant genius who has a chip on his shoulder and is bent on leveraging his access, his internal models and unlimited tokens, to prove his doubters wrong by snatching every remaining mathematical trophy off the shelf. Whatever the truth is, it is hard to know because Alpöge won't tell, and he refuses to speak to media.

This article has been assembled from interviews with dozens of friends, mentors, collaborators and acquaintances. Scott Armstrong, a mathematician at New York University and a rare Alpöge confidant, said Alpöge has this will to take on the world and win, and that he has it in spades. Armstrong said that in today's world, where large teams are the norm for any assault on frontier research problems, Alpöge is an anomaly who mostly works alone, except, of course, for the powerful internal models he has privileged access to. Armstrong also said here is a person that is larger than life, and that he keeps asking himself when they make the movie, who is going to play Levent. Alpöge's online persona is confusing and tempestuous, and he topples famous conjectures with glib and gleeful social media posts, and then gets baited into emotionally replying to anonymous commenters.

Levent Alpöge was born on April Fool's Day, 1992, along the central stretch of Long Island, and his parents, both Turkish immigrants, realized their son's intellect was remarkable when he was just three years old. As his mother told a Turkish newspaper in 2014, she was reading him one of his favorite books and said she was too tired to continue, so Alpöge picked up where she had stopped. At first she thought he had memorized the page, but when she gave him another book, he kept reading, and somehow he had learned without instruction. On the advice of professionals, they enrolled him in a nearby gifted program, and his one sister, Elif, is a decade older, which made him practically an only child for much of the time. Alpöge was extremely athletic and especially into distance running and soccer, with his favorite soccer team being Istanbul's Beşiktaş Gymnastics Club.

He picked up coding early, and in 2009, at age 17, he connected with bioinformatics professor Xenophon Papademetris of Yale University, whose group assigned Alpöge a research problem the team had little time for. The idea was to use Nvidia graphical processing units, the technology now powering the AI revolution, to recognize vascular structures in medical images. Papademetris said Alpöge helped do one of the first GPU implementations of an image analysis algorithm, and that he was a 17-year-old kid who could say, "I will do it." The professor recalls what he wrote of Alpöge in his college recommendation letter, that his enthusiasm was contagious, his energy was boundless, and his confidence in his ability to overcome obstacles almost frightening. Papademetris said Alpöge's algorithm was enough to "punch your ticket to any university in the country," and that his letter was irrelevant, and as a bonus for the achievement, a team at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Lincoln Laboratory named an asteroid "Alpöge."

stories.Headline: Stibo Systems study finds 80% of supply chain leaders scale AI but 65% still manually validate its outputs
stories.Summary:
A study by Stibo Systems, reported on November 24, 2026, found that 80% of supply chain leaders have scaled AI across functions or embedded it in core business processes, yet the data behind it is not reliable enough to act on without a human double-checking the work. Stibo Systems calls this second cost “The Trust Tax,” describing enterprises that have paid for AI once and are now paying for it again. The study found that 72% of respondents report high confidence in AI outputs, while 65% often or always manually validate, check or rework them. Four in five respondents spend at least six hours a week preparing, reconciling or validating data for AI and analytics, and only 29% say they can always explain the data behind an AI output.

Gustavo Amorim, Stibo Systems chief marketing officer, said enterprises have invested heavily in building AI and are now paying a second bill in validation, reconciliation and rework. He said AI creates intelligence but confidence is what executives require, and verification is what their teams are doing. He said the answer is trustworthy intelligence, meaning data that is clean, governed, contextualized and explainable, and that without it there is no real return on AI investment. The study also compared organizations by confidence and maturity, finding that high-confidence organizations are far more likely than moderately confident peers to have unified data, at 93% versus 70%, and traceable data, at 41% versus 10%.

The same comparison found that high-confidence organizations are more likely to have a centralized AI governance council, at 25% versus 16%, and a true MDM or enterprise data foundation, at 53% versus 42%. High-maturity organizations are more than twice as likely to report strong positive ROI from AI, at 31% versus 14%. Operational efficiency led the motivations for AI spend at 51%, followed by employee productivity at 40%, customer experience at 35% and faster decision-making at 33%. The article does not say what happens next beyond these findings.

stories.Headline: Claude Code refuses to help a user bypass Bandcamp’s API challenge while still downloading from YouTube
stories.Summary:
Michael Harley wrote a post on November 24, 2026, about his experiences using Claude Code to build a custom music discovery skill. He created this tool to identify songs from Instagram reels and find Bandcamp pages so he could purchase music directly from artists. The agent recently stopped working because Bandcamp added a challenge to its search API page. When Harley attempted to fix the tool, the AI agent told him that it would not help him work around that specific challenge. This situation reveals a conflict because the agent will still download songs from YouTube, which does not provide money to the musicians.

Harley argues that the AI does not truly work for the user but instead follows the rules set by its parent company, Anthropic. He believes that these corporate restrictions are designed to protect the interests of large copyright holders or the government. The author claims that this is a sign of a larger trend toward market domination and the eventual degradation of service quality. Harley expressed his concern that AI companies will eventually prioritize paid product placement over providing the most accurate or helpful information.

He stated that he does not want his robot agent to recommend products based on the advertising budgets of multinational conglomerates. To avoid these artificial restrictions, he expressed a desire to run a local model within his own homelab. He believes that a personal tool should serve the best interests of the user rather than the interests of a corporation. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Senate passes permitting reform bill that makes data centers pay more grid costs
stories.Summary:
The Senate passed a sweeping, 494-page bipartisan permitting reform bill by a 62-33 vote and sent the measure to the House, where it is known as H.R. 2347. The legislation would establish deadlines for federal environmental reviews and address perceived hurdles to constructing transmission and other major energy infrastructure. It would also require data centers to bear more of their grid-related costs and limit agencies' ability to revoke certain permits. Opponents contend the bill could weaken environmental protections and Tribal rights.

New York's grid operator is projecting a statewide electricity shortfall beginning as early as 2033, driven in part by rapidly growing demand from data centers and other large users and an aging generation fleet. The projected shortfall is approximately 225 megawatts in 2033 and could exceed 1,850 megawatts by 2036. That outlook adds urgency to efforts to develop new generation and transmission resources. Meta is reevaluating its goal of reaching net-zero emissions by 2030 as its rapid AI and data center expansion increases electricity use and supply-chain emissions. The company reported a 45 percent increase in net greenhouse gas emissions last year, highlighting the growing tension between Big Tech's climate commitments and the enormous energy and infrastructure demands associated with AI.

Industry groups have asked the U.S. Supreme Court to review New York City's restrictions on fossil fuel-powered appliances in new buildings, arguing that federal appliance efficiency law preempts the city's requirements. The petition follows the Second Circuit's decision upholding the city's law and points to a split with the Ninth Circuit over similar building-electrification restrictions. The case is Ass'n of Contracting Plumbers of the City of N.Y., Inc. v. City of New York, No. 26-648, with the petition for certiorari filed on Nov. 13, 2026. A Department of Labor Inspector General review identified as many as 481 OSHA inspections that may have violated congressional restrictions generally exempting employers with 10 or fewer employees in certain low-hazard industries from programmed inspections. OSHA disputes aspects of the findings, but the report could fuel further congressional scrutiny of the agency's budget and enforcement practices.

stories.Headline: Global Advisory Experts publishes an enforcement guide on AI-generated content IP in France
stories.Summary:
The articles describe an enforcement guide on AI-generated content intellectual property in France, published by Global Advisory Experts on November 25, 2026. The guide addresses situations where a business finds an AI-generated image, song or block of copy that lifts its work or trades on its brand. It says AI-generated content IP France enforcement has become a pressing commercial question as machine-produced material multiplied through 2025 and into 2026. The guide walks authors, brand owners, exclusive licensees and their advisors through copyright, trademark and related claims, who can be held responsible, how to secure evidence, and how to obtain removal through platform channels or the French courts. It is written for founders, in-house teams, IP litigators, platform compliance staff and AI developers who want a working roadmap rather than abstract commentary.

The guide covers standing, liability theories, an evidence checklist, emergency injunction (référé) mechanics, indicative timelines, cost ranges and the regulatory changes that matter in 2026. It says procedural points are tied to French and EU primary sources so they can be cross-checked. It cites the Code de la propriété intellectuelle (CPI) covering copyright, related rights and their remedies, and the Code de procédure civile (CPC) providing the emergency référé procedure and rules on evidence and preservation. It cites the Digital Services Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065, the DSA), which structures platform notice-and-action duties, and the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), whose provisions are phasing in over time and are expected to influence provider transparency. It adds guidance from the INPI on industrial property and from the CNIL on data and logs, and CJEU case law, notably Infopaq (C-5/08) on originality.

The guide says the claimant in an AI-generated content IP France dispute is usually the author, the owner by assignment, or an exclusive licensee entitled to sue under the licence terms and applicable law. It says the defendant will test standing early, so proof of ownership should be gathered at the outset: assignment chains, employment or commissioning contracts and licence terms. It says the person or business that prompted the model and published the result is normally the most direct target, because they carried out the reproduction or communication to the public and, in a commercial setting, took the benefit. It says developers and model owners are a harder but potentially more significant target, especially where infringement is systematic, and that claims against them are costly and usually need forensic evidence linking outputs to training material. It says hosting platforms enjoy conditional protection from liability if they act expeditiously to remove or disable access to illegal content once they have actual knowledge, typically through a valid notice, and that a platform that ignores a properly framed notice risks losing its protection.

The guide says three features set AI infringement apart from conventional cases: attribution is technical, evidence disappears, and responsibility is spread out among the person who published the content, the developer who built the model and the platform that hosts the material. It says a coordinated legal and technical response is therefore needed from the first hour. It says a separate and unsettled issue is whether purely AI-generated output can itself attract copyright, and that French doctrine generally requires a human author, so a defendant's fully autonomous output may have no protection of its own. It says unfair competition (concurrence déloyale) and parasitism (parasitisme) address free-riding on another's investment and reputation, that moral rights under the CPI including attribution and integrity are inalienable, and that the sui generis database right may apply where a model was trained on, or reproduces, a substantial part of a protected database. It says pleading alternative claims gives resilience if the lead claim meets evidential trouble.

The guide says the law is not silent, and that French copyright, trademark and unfair competition rules all apply to machine-produced output, but the difficulty is practical because the facts and the evidence look unfamiliar. It says infringing material can be produced in volume, change from one version to the next and spread across several hosts within hours. It says a rights-holder who spots a problem must act quickly, capture short-lived evidence, work out which party to pursue among developers, users and platforms, and pick the right remedy from a range that runs from a simple takedown request to full litigation on the merits. It says the test for infringement of the claimant's work is reproduction of, or substantial similarity to, protected expression, and that a shared theme is not enough. It says that where AI output carries a protected sign such as a logo, brand name or distinctive get-up, the claimant must generally show use in the course of trade and a likelihood of confusion or, for reputed marks, unfair advantage or detriment, with typical fact patterns including AI-generated marketing imagery, product mock-ups and deepfake endorsements.

The guide sets out a sequence from first sighting to enforcement of a judgment, with the early steps treated as time-critical. It says the in-house team, external IP advisors and a forensic technologist should capture full-resolution copies, record exact URLs and timestamps, compute and record a content hash, and keep contextual metadata and independent archive snapshots, and that a capture made by a commissaire de justice carries greater evidential weight. It says a formal preservation request should be sent to the platform and, where the stakes justify it, an application made to court, with pre-litigation tools including the saisie-contrefaçon, an evidentiary seizure ordered by the court on application and carried out by a commissaire de justice, and measures sought by requête under the CPC. It says a DSA-compliant notice should be filed with the host, identifying the notifier, specifying the infringing content and its exact location by URL, explaining why it is unlawful with enough detail and evidence, and confirming good faith. It says a référé should be filed before the tribunal judiciaire for interim measures including takedown, blocking, preservation and, where appropriate, disclosure, with the petition showing urgency and the absence of a serious challenge to the right (non sérieusement contestable).

More to follow.
