stories.Headline: Molecular Devices adds AI assistant and label-free viability analysis to its imaging software
stories.Summary:
Molecular Devices said on November 24, 2026 that it had added two artificial intelligence software features to its ImageXpress line of high-content screening systems, including the recently launched ImageXpress HCS.ai Advanced Duo system, according to the company's press release. The company said the MetaXpress Acquire AI Assistant lets scientists ask natural-language questions about how to use the acquisition software and returns a direct, step-by-step answer in near real time without leaving the platform. According to the release, the assistant stays within the scope of available Molecular Devices documentation and clearly indicates when more guidance is needed. Molecular Devices said the second feature, a new release of its IN Carta Image Analysis Software application, assesses cell viability from transmitted-light images without fluorescent viability markers for supported workflows.

According to the release, the label-free viability application identifies individual cells in transmitted-light images and classifies them as live or dead, removing the need for a fluorescent live/dead marker in validated HeLa, U2OS and HCT116 cell lines. Molecular Devices said it developed and trained the underlying models in advance, so researchers get a ready-to-use analysis instead of having to build and train their own. The company said the MetaXpress Acquire AI Assistant is now available as a free software update for ImageXpress high-content imaging systems, while the label-free viability application is available for purchase through IN Carta Image Analysis Software. The release said the assistant represents an early step in a planned, broader roadmap that Danaher's businesses intend to pursue with Microsoft to advance instruments and software that include agent functionality.

Mary Duseau, President of Molecular Devices, said the company's approach is to apply AI purposefully where it can remove friction from scientific workflows and help researchers reach meaningful answers with greater confidence, according to the release. She said that by embedding AI into tools scientists already rely on, the company can make complex workflows more intuitive and efficient while advancing Danaher's broader vision for using AI to accelerate scientific discovery and improve human health, the release said. Molecular Devices described itself in the release as a Danaher company and a leading provider of high-performance life science solutions. The release said the company is headquartered in Silicon Valley, California, with offices around the globe.

stories.Headline: Zendesk launches Outcome AI Platform with outcome-based pricing and unlimited seats
stories.Summary:
Zendesk announced on November 25, 2026, that it is launching a new concept called the Outcome AI Platform, which it describes as designed for an era in which the way people and organizations engage is changing significantly. The company said the platform comes with a new pricing plan called Zendesk Unlimited, which moves away from the traditional per-seat model and lets customers pay according to the outcomes actually achieved. Alongside it, Zendesk announced the Open Service Directory, which lets personal AI assistants find a company's official support channels, and Zendesk Bridge, which connects the AI tools and agents a company uses to Zendesk's service platform while managing security and privacy and allowing human oversight. The company said the new features are provided with unlimited seats, a shift from the previous pricing model that it presents as a new standard of paying for outcomes. Under the Outcome AI Platform plan, customers can use Zendesk AI with features that depend on their pricing tier, set an outcome budget, and pay for resolved inquiries and completed tasks that are billed, according to the release.

Zendesk said the platform aims to automate more than 80 percent of requests, shorten resolution time from hours to minutes, and improve customer satisfaction, and that it will assess the quality and completeness of each outcome so customers can see which outcomes count against their budget. The Open Service Directory is an open specification and public directory that companies can use even if they do not use Zendesk, and Zendesk said it does not access customers' personal data or carry out support actions. Zendesk said it plans to adopt protocols that complement the directory and called on customer experience platforms, AI agent developers and brands to take part, naming Betterment, ElevenLabs, Flex, TeamSystem, TBA Auctions, Telekom Payment S.A. and Wireless Logic as initial participants. Zendesk Bridge lets companies choose any AI interface and connect it securely to Zendesk's information, workflows and actions, with every action passing through the bridge for identity checks, permission checks, policy enforcement, human approval, visibility and auditing. Tom Eggemeier, Zendesk's chief executive, said customers and employees do not want to think about which channel, system or department to use when contacting a company and simply want help resolving their issue, and he said the platform combines the needed information and ability to act so that any starting point leads quickly to the right outcome.

He said it learns from outcomes and applies the experience when results fall short, and he called this the standard companies focused on loyalty and satisfaction should aim for. Taro Mori, president of Zendesk's Japan entity, said the new pricing strategy links investment to business outcomes through the resolutions Zendesk's AI delivers rather than through seat counts, and he said he is confident the AI features will raise productivity and customer satisfaction in the Japanese market, where companies must balance business results with cost efficiency. The release cites Zendesk's CX Trends Report 2026, which found that 75 percent of Japanese consumers see AI as essential to modern customer service, and that 85 percent of customer experience leaders globally regard AI as part of their workforce or team, compared with 66 percent in Japan. Zendesk said the platform connects every support function to business outcomes, including specialized AI agents that handle complex tasks for customers and employees, and self-improvement features that help teams keep identifying and resolving root causes. The release lists availability notes: Zendesk Bridge is in an early access program, some features are generally available, the Open Service Directory is in a limited early access program, and the availability of each feature differs in Japan, with customers asked to contact the company for details.

stories.Headline: Fujitsu pilots AI-linked transport bookings for medical visits in Kawasaki
stories.Summary:
Fujitsu Limited said on November 24, 2026 that it will run a pilot project in Kawasaki City from December 1, 2026, to January 30, 2027, as part of the COMmmmONS regional transportation DX promotion project led by the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism. The pilot aims to make travel for medical visits smoother by linking appointment times at healthcare facilities with demand-responsive transportation services. Besides booking transport to healthcare facilities, the pilot will use AI to predict when patients will leave after consultations, examinations and payments, a time the release calls the healthcare facility departure time. A patient-facing medical visit application will then coordinate bookings for the return journey. Fujitsu said it will evaluate the effectiveness of mobility support tailored to individual patient needs, aiming to improve access to healthcare by making transport to and from facilities more convenient.

At Kawasaki Municipal Kawasaki Hospital the pilot runs from December 1, 2026, a Tuesday, to January 29, 2027, a Friday, for patients receiving prenatal checkups who consent to take part, using the Knowroute KAWASAKI demand-responsive service. At Nakahara Kosugi Motosumiyoshi Hoshioka Internal Medicine, Gastroenterology and Endoscopy Clinic it runs from December 1, 2026, a Tuesday, to January 30, 2027, a Saturday, for patients scheduled for gastroscopy or colonoscopy who consent, using the Choisoko Kawasaki service. The application differs by facility: HOPE LifeMark-Concierge from Fujitsu Japan Limited at the hospital, and Medical Revolution byGMO from GMO Reserve Plus Co., Ltd. at the clinic. Fujitsu will upgrade the rule-based departure time prediction model used in an initiative at Tokushima Prefectural Central Hospital in Tokushima Prefecture in 2025 to an AI model using machine learning. The application will confirm and change consultation and transport reservations and provide reminder notifications.

Fujitsu said it will be responsible for leading the pilot and building an integration platform connecting healthcare information systems with demand-responsive transportation services. Fujitsu Japan Limited will be responsible for developing the healthcare facility departure time prediction model utilizing machine learning. Fujitsu said that in the future it aims to create new service experiences covering the stages before and after travel by connecting destinations including nursing care and welfare facilities, retail facilities and government services with diverse transportation services such as on-demand transportation, buses, taxis and autonomous driving. Fujitsu said that through Uvance it aims to develop a new approach to healthcare access integrating healthcare and transportation through AI-powered data integration. Fujitsu said it aims to create new value for sustainable local transportation by connecting transportation demand with transportation resources.

Fujitsu said the pilot is part of COMmmmONS, which the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism launched in fiscal 2025 to significantly enhance the added value and productivity of regional transportation by promoting standardization of systems, data, business processes and other elements. Fujitsu said that against the backdrop of an aging population and labor shortages in public transportation, securing local transportation options including those for medical visits has become a challenge. It said that for medical visits the completion times of consultations and examinations vary, making it difficult to secure return transportation in advance, while waiting times and transfers burden patients. It said closer coordination between healthcare and transportation is needed to better match patient transportation needs with available local transportation resources.

The 2025 Tokushima initiative at Tokushima Prefectural Central Hospital verified the feasibility of round-trip transportation reservations based on consultation appointments and predicted hospital departure times by linking an electronic medical record system with an on-demand transportation service. Fujitsu said that through the pilot it will examine mechanisms to support transportation tailored to each patient's circumstances. Fujitsu described Uvance as a business model committed to realizing customer transformation and creating social value in an era where AI is reshaping the world. The articles do not say how many patients will take part, which transport providers operate the two demand-responsive services, or what results Fujitsu expects.

stories.Headline: Green Bay develops a policy on artificial intelligence use in public art
stories.Summary:
Green Bay is developing a policy for the use of artificial intelligence in public art, according to a report published by WSAW on Nov. 25, 2026. The idea for the policy came from staff discussions and from policies adopted by two communities in Idaho, the station reported. The report did not name the two Idaho communities or say which staff took part in the discussions. It also did not give a date for when the policy might be finished or voted on.

The report gives no further details about what the policy would require of artists or how it would treat art made with artificial intelligence. It does not say whether the policy would cover city-funded murals, sculptures or other works, or how it would be enforced. No numbers, dates or names beyond the two Idaho communities are given in the article. The station published the item on the evening of Nov. 25, 2026, and updated it about three hours later.

The report does not say who in Green Bay is responsible for writing the policy or what any official said about it. It attributes the idea only to staff discussions and to the Idaho policies, without naming the staff members involved. No statement from a city official, artist or resident appears in the article. The article also does not say whether the public will have a chance to comment on the policy.

The article offers no context on how other cities regulate artificial intelligence in public art, beyond the mention of the two Idaho communities. It does not say what happens next, whether the policy will go to a committee or the city council, or when the public might see a draft. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Ten large AI data center projects near Philadelphia total nearly 20 million square feet
stories.Summary:
Three hyperscale AI data centers larger than 1 million square feet were under construction near Philadelphia as of mid-November 2026, and seven more of that size or larger had been proposed, according to the Inquirer. The three under construction are the 2.4-million-square-foot DataOne center in Vineland, Cumberland County, the 3.7-million-square-foot Amazon data center in Falls Township, Bucks County, and the 1.5-million-square-foot facility in East Whiteland, Chester County. The DataOne center, already partially operational on the outskirts of Vineland, will power Microsoft's AI tools, and construction was ongoing there in June. The Amazon campus is being developed on a 250-acre site within the Keystone Trade Center in Falls Township, on land formerly occupied by U.S. Steel. Preliminary construction has also begun at the East Whiteland facility, which is being built on the 79-acre Cyprus Foote Mineral Co. property, a Superfund site at the border of East and West Whiteland Townships near the Chester Valley Trail.

The ten projects would add up to nearly 20 million square feet of data centers in the Philly region if all come to fruition, the Inquirer reported. In Limerick Township, MCD 7 LLC is proposing a revised plan known as Project Laurel for eight two-story data center buildings, three substations, and 80,000 square feet of support buildings across 191 acres between the Philadelphia Premium Outlets and the Limerick Clean Energy Center. Also in Limerick Township, Limerick Town Center LLC proposes eight two-story, 65-foot-high buildings with backup generators, water and wastewater treatment facilities, an electrical switchyard and substation on a 191-acre site off Main Street on the Linfield peninsula, the former Publicker Industries property. Penn Hurst Holdings DE LLC proposes a data center on the 124-acre site of the former Pennhurst State School and Hospital in East Vincent Township, with revised plans raising the square footage from 1.3 million to 1.9 million. Brian O'Neill's MLP Ventures proposes a 2-million-square-foot data center at the 66-acre former Cleveland-Cliffs steel mill in Plymouth Township, a 4.6-million-square-foot campus on five sites in Upper Merion Township, and a 1-million-square-foot three-story data center on a vacant 60-acre property along Front Street in West Conshohocken.

Hexa Builders, a Princeton-based real estate developer, wants to build a 1-million-square-foot data center on a wooded, undeveloped property on South Black Horse Pike in Monroe Township, Gloucester County. Amazon has been approved for five environmental air and water discharge permits, including approval last year for 72 diesel-fired emergency engines, and has applied to install 280 natural gas-fired "critical backup generator engines" at 4,287 horsepower each plus three more diesel backup generators, permits the DEP is reviewing. Peco has applied for a 67-megawatt, one-mile-long electrical distribution line that would cross the Schuylkill from Limerick Township to East Coventry Township for the MCD 7 data center. The Limerick Town Center site would use public water and public sewer and a closed loop cooling system fed by on-site wells or from the river, with wastewater treated on site if an open loop system is used. The Penn Hurst plans call for a power generation and battery storage area and a power supply substation, with the data center served by public water and public sewer.

The East Whiteland data center was originally approved by the township as far back as 2018, and in May a Chester County Court of Common Pleas judge denied an appeal challenging the township zoning hearing board's original decision and the board of supervisors' 2024 approval of plans for the site. The East Vincent Township Board of Supervisors voted to deny the Penn Hurst conditional use application in May, and Penn Hurst Holdings filed an appeal in June that is before the Chester County Court of Common Pleas. The Upper Merion Township Board of Supervisors unanimously rejected O'Neill's plans in August, and O'Neill and his team appealed, asking a judge to reverse the denial, grant the proposal preliminary approval, and appoint a third-party "referee" to oversee the rest of the process, while a separate lawsuit seeks unspecified monetary damages. In Plymouth Township, O'Neill's resubmitted plans are being scrutinized in a series of zoning hearing board meetings, and he has filed a legal challenge to the township's zoning ordinance, a move Plymouth Township Council Chair Lynne Viscio equated to "throwing a tantrum," while O'Neill has denied township officials' accusations.

The Monroe Township planning board unanimously denied Hexa's application and banned data centers in the Gloucester County municipality, and Hexa sued township officials for $300 million, saying the ban and rejection violate its constitutional rights, with the case recently moved to federal court. West Conshohocken Borough Manager Doug Borgerson said the Front Street project is in the "early stages" of the review process. Residents have banded together against proposed data center developments in towns nationwide, expressing concerns about pollution, noise, power and water use, and the potential impact on their electric bills and home values. In the midterm elections earlier this month, voters elected many candidates who promised to take tough stances against the facilities and sided against data centers in 40 of 41 local ballot measures, including one in Downe Township, Cumberland County.

In August, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro placed guardrails on data center development in the commonwealth but stopped short of issuing the moratorium for which many activists have been pushing. Residents were outraged in January when the state Game Commission approved Limerick Town Center's proposal to swap land with the state, and on Friday commission spokesperson John Buffone said the state is no longer "moving forward with the exchange." Residents of East Whiteland have questioned how safe it is to build on a site still listed on the National Priorities List for Superfund sites, and in October they notified officials that they planned to sue, arguing there were violations of township ordinances in approving the plan. The Inquirer reported that the map covers hyperscale AI data centers officially proposed or approved as of mid-November and is not an exhaustive list of all data center proposals in the region.

The article noted that older versions of these facilities have operated for decades, some run by telecom companies like Comcast, and that developers are floating plans for new AI data centers all the time. The MCD 7 project would be built over two phases, and the developer proposes to relocate portions of two roads and a gas main. The Amazon project has both local and state approvals for the first of two expected phases of the project's build-out. The article did not say when the remaining proposed projects would be decided or what the outcome of the pending appeals and lawsuits would be.

stories.Headline: Pantheon Electric unveils domestic copper supply plans to help utilities avoid foreign equipment bans
stories.Summary:
Pantheon Electric is unveiling domestic supply plans for utilities and grid equipment makers to increase reliability this month. The company aims to help power providers secure American copper components before the U.S. Department of Energy finalizes security rules between late December and January 2027. These rules follow a national emergency declared by President Donald Trump in August regarding security and economic risks from certain foreign actors. The federal ruling will bar access to grid equipment and critical components made by China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea. This shift comes as artificial intelligence and data centers rapidly increase the demand for copper.

The new requirements align with the Grid SCALED initiative from the Department of Energy, which provides 237 million dollars to bolster domestic energy reliability. Pantheon Electric, which claims to be one of North America's largest copper component manufacturers, processes over 1 million pounds of copper daily across 14 U.S. plants. The company operates facilities in New York, Pennsylvania, Kentucky, South Carolina, and Texas to provide conductors and busbars. Its Pennsylvania facility alone processes more than 100 million pounds of scrap copper every year. These domestic efforts seek to avoid a projected copper shortfall of 10 million metric tons by 2040.

CEO Gregory J. Smith stated that utilities need a supply chain they can count on regardless of the final rules. He explained that the grid cannot afford to depend on materials that fluctuate based on global events and tariffs. Smith believes that sourcing copper made at home gives utilities one less factor outside of their own control. The company is working directly with equipment makers and utilities to close the supply gap during the rule finalization. This strategy aims to reduce reliance on foreign refining while expanding domestic manufacturing options for the power grid.

The current U.S. grid is growing faster than the supply chain can support the expansion. A study from Johns Hopkins University indicates that data center transformers require over four times the copper of conventional ones. Researchers warned that this increased demand could trigger shortages of grid equipment as early as 2027. A single next-generation hyperscale facility can reportedly consume 50,000 tons of the metal. The Department of Energy intends to use these domestic reinvestments to cut costs and keep funds within the United States.

stories.Headline: Yifan Cheng builds an AI trained on Buffalo and Seattle sewer data to predict overflows
stories.Summary:
A University at Buffalo researcher will develop an artificial intelligence model that simulates how water moves through aging sewer systems and predicts when they will send untreated sewage into nearby waterways, the university said. The project is supported by a five-year, $875,000 grant from the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Science. Its recipient is Yifan Cheng, an assistant professor in the university's Department of Earth Sciences. He is one of 67 researchers nationwide the office selected this year for its Early Career Research Program. He will work with the Buffalo Sewer Authority and the King County Wastewater Treatment Division in Washington.

Sewers that date back 100 years or more often carry stormwater and wastewater in one set of pipes, and in these combined systems heavy rain can overwhelm the pipes and spill untreated sewage into rivers and lakes. More than 700 U.S. communities have combined systems that are vulnerable to overflows, according to EPA. Great Lakes cities like Buffalo face especially high stakes, the university said, because pollutants from overflows may end up in Lake Erie and Lake Ontario. Once there, they could threaten drinking water supplies and feed harmful algal blooms that disrupt power plant cooling systems.

Cheng's team will base the AI on EPA's Storm Water Management Model, a computer model that tracks water through sewer pipes during storms and forecasts overflows. Thousands of SWMM simulations of the two cities' sewers will train the AI, which will learn how water moves through pipes, where backups form and when overflows happen. Once trained, it will predict overflow timing without rerunning SWMM's complex calculations for each forecast. Lower computing costs will let the team add the AI and its sewer simulations to urban flood models, including the Energy Department's Energy Exascale Earth System Model. E3SM simulates interactions across Earth's environment, but its urban simulations leave out water flowing through underground sewers.

Once the AI is added, the researchers will check whether E3SM predicts flooding more accurately with sewers included, the university said. They will compare its forecasts with records of major past storms in Buffalo and Seattle, as well as Hurricane Harvey in Houston. The Energy Department-funded research will also test whether adding sewer simulations to a federal Earth system model improves flood forecasts.

stories.Headline: GPT-6.2 Astra becomes first model to beat Googlers' 2015 code golf records on 256-cell benchmark
stories.Summary:
GPT-6.2 Astra is the first model to beat Googlers' code golf records, according to a benchmark posted on bjin.github.io on 2026-11-25T06:00:00Z. The author, who wrote about half the problems under the name @binjin, brought back 32 problems from a code-golf contest played at Google in 2015. Each model gets 30 minutes per problem in each of eight languages to make its solution as short as it can. The leaderboard scores byte counts, not just whether the code works. The author said he wanted to see how frontier models would do against the people he used to golf with eleven years later.

The site supported JavaScript, Python, Go, C++ and Haskell in 2015, and Rust was added after the author left. The benchmark uses 32 problems, and a cell is one problem in one language, giving 256 cells in all. For JavaScript, Python, C++ and Haskell, the archived scoreboards record the shortest solution any Googler submitted, including improvements made during the challenge phase. There are no 2015 human records for Ruby, Raku, Racket and GolfScript, so an oracle run supplied a reference size for each cell. The oracle was GPT-6 Astra, and in 126 of the 256 cells its solution is shorter than every competitor's.

The author said the rule was simple, that the shortest program passing every test case won. He said undefined behavior, compiler quirks, non-standard library features and even hardcoding every test case were all allowed. He said a passing solution is saved only if it is strictly shorter than the model's previous best. He said every response includes the current best known size because without a target it is easy to decide a solution is short enough and stop. He said the sandbox reproduces the 2015 environment for the four original languages, down to the compiler or interpreter version, flags and quirks.

The author said Haskell has human records but they are much weaker than the other three, so the humans' main score, JS/PY/C++, leaves Haskell out. He said only a few regulars golfed in Haskell and suspected that mostly reflects how few Haskell users there were at Google in 2015. He said models have already beaten 31 of the 32 Haskell records. He said counting Haskell in the human score would measure how few of us wrote Haskell, not how good the people who golfed were. He said humans have no Overall score because they have no entries in Ruby, Raku, Racket or GolfScript.

The author said he spent a lot of time on an internal site called go/codegolf in 2015, with one problem a week. He said any Googler could propose a problem by posting a statement and a full test suite, and votes were called LGTMs. He said you could see your own submissions but nobody else's, and only your shortest passing solution in each language counted. He said after seven days the rankings froze and every submission became visible, and a challenge had to be strictly shorter than both the winning solution and every earlier challenge entry. He said the problem's author could compete too.

Match the best known size and you get 100%, a solution 10% longer gets 82.6%, and twice as long gets 25%. Overall averages all 256 cells in all eight languages, and JS/PY/C++ averages the 96 cells in JavaScript, Python and C++. A gold mark on a problem's scoreboard means that solution matches the best known size, a filled mark means no other competitor has matched it, and an outlined mark means a tie. The oracle is unranked and only supplies best-known sizes, and when it beats every competitor in a cell the Problems page shows its byte count as Known Best but never its code. The articles leave open which models other than GPT-6.2 Astra were tested and how each of them scored.

stories.Headline: GitHub user lsernau publishes a machine-checked Lean 4 proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis
stories.Summary:
A repository called grh-lean was published on GitHub on 25 November 2026 by the user lsernau, offering what it describes as a short Lean 4 proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. The repository holds two versions of the same five theorems, a readable edition of about 300,000 lines and a compact edition of about 76,000 lines, each set up as its own Lake project with its own README. The README calls the work a research artifact that is not maintained and not accepting contributions, and it states that the proof has passed machine checks only, as listed in each folder's README. It also states that no mathematician has read the proof through and that no paper accompanies it, so the claim to a proof rests on the machine checks alone.

The README says the proof is based on work by Levent Alpöge, with Claude, and it links to a document at alpo.ge for that basis. The repository lists its axioms as propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, and it points readers of the readable edition to a guide file in the grh folder. The README gives a build time of 85 minutes more if the Mathlib cache is missing, which indicates how long a full check may take. The repository carries an Apache-2.0 license, and at the time of the page it showed 351 stars, 27 forks and 1 watcher, with a single commit in its history. The page describes the project as a short Lean 4 proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis in its About section.

The author is identified only by the GitHub username lsernau, and the README gives no further statement from that person beyond the text of the repository itself. The README does not present the result as settled mathematics, since it says plainly that no mathematician has read it through and that no paper comes with it. It frames the work as a research artifact rather than a maintained project, and it declines contributions, which suggests the author is not offering it as a finished or supported piece of software. The only named collaborator in the README is Claude, credited alongside Alpöge as the basis for the proof, and the only outside link is the document at alpo.ge.

The repository offers no peer review, no accompanying paper and no mathematician's reading, so the status of the claimed proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis remains unestablished by the terms the README itself sets out. What exists is a machine-checked artifact in two sizes, with the compact edition at about 76,000 lines and the readable edition at about 300,000 lines, both containing the same five theorems. Anyone who wants to assess the work would need to build each Lake project, allow for the 85 minutes more if the Mathlib cache is missing, and read the guide in the grh folder. Beyond that the articles say nothing about what happens next.

stories.Headline: Wes Moore leads governors in urging federal oversight of frontier AI while states keep authority over consumer harms
stories.Summary:
On November 22, the National Governors Association published a three-page statement on who should govern artificial intelligence, according to a GitHub post dated November 24, 2026. Maryland Governor Wes Moore helped lead the bipartisan council that wrote it. The NGA announcement names Indiana’s Mike Braun, North Carolina’s Josh Stein and Utah’s Spencer Cox alongside him. The statement asks Washington to oversee frontier models, require independent evaluations and receive reports of serious security incidents. It asks states to retain power over harms people encounter when models are put to work, such as a benefits decision, a job application, a school chatbot or a disputed insurance claim.

The document begins with five general principles and then lists five federal recommendations and fourteen for states. The federal list starts with a risk-based framework for the most advanced general-purpose models and calls for evaluation or audit by independent experts. It also calls for reports of security breaches and significant safety incidents to federal authorities and affected states. Washington would set national approaches to critical infrastructure, chemical, biological and nuclear risks, international cooperation and research. The state list describes consumer remedies, anti-discrimination enforcement, children, workers, consequential decisions, public-sector AI and local cyber defense, and asks states to coordinate definitions and oversight.

The NGA document is a recommendation with no binding force. Moore’s November statement puts his emphasis on workers, consumers and children. Bloomberg Law reported the effort as a bid for federal AI rules without surrendering state protection. The Next Web described the central bargain as Washington handling risks at national scale while states keep room to govern uses affecting their residents. Neither report turns the proposal into enacted law.

The White House has offered a different starting point. Executive Order 14365, signed in December 2025, directs federal agencies to review and challenge state AI laws it considers onerous and asks for a minimally burdensome national framework. The order states that a patchwork raises compliance costs, particularly for startups, and can regulate beyond state borders. It also tells officials not to propose preempting otherwise lawful state laws on child safety, data centers and state procurement. The eventual scope of federal preemption remains a legislative and legal question, not a completed fact established by the order.

A 2024 executive order directed Maryland agencies to examine their own AI use, and the Artificial Intelligence Governance Act requires an inventory and a framework for developing and using systems. Maryland now publishes AI use cases and a list of systems and software, including mundane productivity tools and proposed assistants for state services. The Responsible AI Policy requires agency review and risk management. The governor’s September agenda says high-risk state uses, including benefits, lending and law enforcement, need impact assessment, bias testing, human oversight and periodic audit. A 2025 report from Maryland’s Department of Information Technology recommended keeping the governor’s AI subcabinet as a cross-agency group rather than creating a standalone department.

The May 2026 AI Innovation Lab announcement described a controlled sandbox, vulnerability testing and support for agencies building AI tools, and offered an agent helping state fleet drivers find approved maintenance vendors as an example, forecasting $1 million to $1.5 million in annual savings. Anthropic’s November 2025 announcement described assistance for benefits caseworkers with document verification and policy guidance, and Axios independently reported the planned use across benefits and housing. In February, Maryland’s Department of Labor announced $4 million across three grant programs: $2.5 million for internships and upskilling in selected industries and $1.5 million for supervised cyber training. The state’s later AI principles page says the first group of investments reached nearly 600 Marylanders. The articles leave open how to decide which rule controls when federal and state hands overlap.

stories.Headline: Christmas Market Canceled After AI-Generated Ads That Looked Nothing Like Real Event Led to ‘Scam’ Allegations
stories.Summary:
The Kernow Christmas Market in Cornwall, England, canceled all vendor bookings and refunded stallholders after backlash over AI-generated advertisements that did not match the actual event, according to the BBC. Posters shared to the market's Facebook page, which was seemingly deleted on Wednesday, Nov. 25, showed ornate outdoor stalls with twinkling lights and Christmas decorations. Photos of the actual market showed a setup inside a concrete warehouse-style space, with a few vendors under fluorescent lights and sparse decorations. The market was located inside Pool Market and was organized and operated by Pool Market as an additional event alongside Cornwall Winter Wonderland.

David Rowland of Rowlands Attractions, who reportedly created the AI images, said the controversy was a "lesson learned," the BBC reports. Rowlands Attractions confirmed the cancellation and said it was "gutted" things "didn't go as planned," adding that all current and future bookings would be canceled and fully refunded and that Kernow Christmas Market would take no further bookings for 2026. The company said any traders who wished to continue must book directly with Pool Market. In a video on the Facebook page of Cornwall Winter Wonderland, which is outside Pool Market and not part of the canceled market, Rowland said Rowlands Attractions does not run the inside of Pool Market and that its Christmas stalls outside are its Winter Wonderland.

Rowland said in the video that Pool Market, or Kernow Christmas Market, was advertised by his company and that it regrets using the AI images. He said the bad press and focus on the Winter Wonderland was untrue, and walking around the space he showed festive decor and noted the Winter Wonderland is set to run until Jan. 3. He said that if people think it is canceled or that the market reflects the Winter Wonderland, it will cause problems and the event might have to be pulled down early. He said all traders had been refunded and offered a free space to trade inside the actual Winter Wonderland. PEOPLE reached out to Cornwall Winter Wonderland and Rowland for comment but did not receive an immediate response.

Articles.Title: Christmas Market Canceled After AI-Generated Ads That Looked Nothing Like Real Event Led to ‘Scam’ Allegations

stories.Headline: Mathematician Levent Alpöge and Anthropic's Claude AI claim a proof of the Riemann hypothesis
stories.Summary:
Levent Alpöge and Claude AI claimed to prove the Riemann hypothesis during the week before November 25, 2026. Alpöge is a mathematician who works at the company Anthropic. This event follows a period where large language models struggled with basic arithmetic. The AI now resolves very hard problems with ease. This development marks a shift from mathematical conjecture to a formal proof.

The Riemann hypothesis was proposed by Bernhard Riemann in 1859 and relates to the distribution of prime numbers. The proof addresses a problem that had remained unsolved for nearly 170 years. In October, OpenAI published hundreds of AI generated papers containing proofs to unsolved problems. These proofs were created by tens of thousands of AI agents using millions of dollars of computing power. The process involves using a zeta function to analyze integers greater than 1.

Levent Alpöge said that Claude AI flew, danced, and sparkled towards the conclusion. He stated that the process left him in a state of awe. AI evangelists argue that mathematicians are being precious about the methods used. They claim it does not matter if humans are left behind as knowledge frontiers move. These boosters suggest that autonomous AI models may eventually code their own successors.

Some mathematicians described the sudden arrival of AI proofs as the mathocalypse. Hannah Fry, a Cambridge professor, called one of the OpenAI proofs almost hilariously ugly. Many researchers feel their life's work is being crushed under silicon bulldozers. Others feel a combination of excitement, skepticism, and anger. These professionals worry that machines may generate proofs that humans cannot comprehend.

The Riemann hypothesis had previously held up more than 12 trillion times without being proven. Andrew Wiles previously solved Fermat's Last Theorem by building bridges between different mathematical realms. AI proofs are described as windowless lifts that reach the summit without showing the path. The author compares the current AI boom to the dotcom bubble and the rise of railways. This background suggests a pattern of irrational exuberance followed by economic correction.

Humans must now complete a long process of verification to ensure the machines took no rogue shortcuts. Early indications currently back the AI results. The articles leave open whether the AI investment bubble will burst like previous industrial booms. It remains unclear if the industry will succumb to regulatory constraints or corruption. The final validity of the Riemann hypothesis proof is still awaiting full human verification.

stories.Headline: Google adds Familiar Faces AI detection to Walmart Onn cameras via Home app update
stories.Summary:
Google released a software update for the Google Home app on November 26, 2026. This update allows certain budget cameras sold by Walmart to recognize people using artificial intelligence. The new capability brings the Familiar Faces detection feature to these specific home security devices. Users can now receive alerts when the cameras identify known individuals around their property.

The update adds this support to the Onn Outdoor Camera Plug-In which costs 35 dollars. It also enables the feature for the Onn Floodlight Camera Hardwired which costs 77 dollars. To access these face recognition alerts, users must have a Google Home Premium subscription. Additionally, these two devices and the Nest Cam Outdoor wired second generation now include a remote siren control. This tool lets users start or stop a 30-second security siren through the live video feed.

Google is responsible for these changes to the smart home ecosystem and its app. The company is also rolling out improvements to Gemini Live over the coming weeks. These updates use a new speech-to-speech architecture to provide faster response times for users. Google says that Gemini Live now supports daily actions like turning off lights or setting timers.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Google files a patent for My Channel, an AI system that generates personalized videos starring user avatars
stories.Summary:
Google filed a patent last May for a system called My Channel to create personalized AI video feeds. The company designed this system to generate videos and advertisements based on information it knows about its users. Patentlyze first spotted the patent, which was published last week before it was eventually rejected by officials. This system would use Google servers to generate content tailored to the specific interests of each individual user.

The system requires demographic data, viewing history, IP addresses, GPS locations, and the specific age of the user. It would use these details to create prompts for a large language model to generate various movie genres. My Channel could connect to other streaming services to gain more user information and training data for videos. The system would use photos, videos, and audio clips to create digital avatars of the users themselves. These avatars would then be placed as the protagonist or lead character in the generated AI content.

The patent describes a system that could serve content like Odysseus: The Fall if users watch The Odyssey. Google's proposal suggests that viewers would be entertained simply by seeing themselves onscreen as the main characters. The company intends for the system to use current news, sports scores, and social media for prompts. This approach allows the company to create bespoke content that appeals to the assumed tastes of users. The system is designed to keep people glued to the service by providing an endless supply of content.

Charles Pulliam-Moore says the system is a convoluted way to create AI knockoffs of professionally produced art. He claims the system is an unholy cross between JibJab and the panoptic elements of the company. The author argues that generative models cannot think or feel like directors, writers, and actors can. He suggests that this technology discourages users from using their imaginations to empathize with or relate to characters. This process could lead to a future where the internet is flooded with garbage that nobody wants.

The background provided is that some entertainment companies and studios claim AI will revolutionize the industry for the better. These companies insist that the technology will improve the field, despite claims that AI videos are just slop. Generative models can mimic visual elements of the data they are trained on but lack creative intention. This lack of intention is why some people believe AI cannot create compelling stories like human artists. The system aims to provide entertainment that is deeply at odds with engaging with art in worthwhile ways.

Google might appeal the rejection or resubmit an amended version of the patent to bring it to market. The articles leave open whether the company will successfully strike licensing deals with other streaming services. It remains unclear if the system will eventually be approved after the company makes the necessary changes. The future of whether users will accept artless AI regurgitations of preexisting content is not yet determined. The text does not say if Google will change the core design of the My Channel system.

stories.Headline: Oracle shares fall 70% as debt-funded AI buildout turns free cash flow negative
stories.Summary:
Oracle shares have fallen about 70% since their September 2025 record, when the company was worth more than $900 billion. A debt-funded AI buildout has turned free cash flow negative, and the market now values Oracle near $300 billion. Oracle’s value was estimated at $922 billion after a 36% surge on Sept. 10, 2025. Oracle is at the same level it was in December 2023. Oracle reported free cash flow of negative $23.7 billion for fiscal 2026.

Oracle still reports a $664 billion contracted backlog and expects at least $90 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue. Shareholders and bondholders are supplying capital through $20 billion in new stock and notes. Oracle sold $10 billion of notes on Nov. 4 at coupons of 7% to 8.65%, and sold $10 billion in stock, an SEC filing shows. The first quarter of fiscal 2027 added a $5 billion deficit, filings show. S&P estimates OpenAI accounts for about half of the $638 billion backlog reported then.

S&P Global Ratings cut Oracle to BBB-, one notch above junk, on July 9. Moody’s affirmed Oracle’s Baa2 rating with a negative outlook on Nov. 2. Oracle said on Nov. 20 that its OpenAI contract is fully funded. The company targets positive free cash flow in the second half of fiscal 2028, its Investor Day filing shows. S&P warns an OpenAI payment shortfall could bind Oracle to data center leases that are hard to unwind.

S&P Global Market Intelligence data show Oracle’s five-year credit default swap spread reached 356 basis points, from below 80 a year earlier. Shares fell more than 5% on Oct. 8 after a report raised questions about OpenAI’s revenue. The outcome hinges on OpenAI, whose reported $300 billion contract starts in 2027. Lenders holding data center loans tied to similar projects could face the same question. If payments arrive on schedule, the credit signals may prove overdone.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: US and China build competing global AI cooperation frameworks
stories.Summary:
In November 2026, the United States government introduced new restrictions on remote access to advanced AI semiconductors for Chinese companies. This action followed a controversy involving Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang and his relationship with a businesswoman named Alice Huang. Alice Huang is suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence and is associated with a Singaporean company called Megaspeed. Jensen Huang resigned as the chief executive of Nvidia on 12 November during this period of high controversy. The board of Nvidia reinstated him as the chief executive less than two weeks later on 23 November.

The new restrictions target Chinese companies that use server rental arrangements to access computing facilities in third countries. Megaspeed is under scrutiny for allegedly flouting American export controls to help Chinese companies access restricted Nvidia processors. The Republican administration may use this scandal to tighten AI export restrictions after suffering losses in the midterm elections. President Xi Jinping launched the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, or WAICO, in July 2026 in Shanghai. WAICO members include Russia, Pakistan, Brazil, Indonesia, and various countries across Asia and Africa to create an inclusive framework.

President Xi Jinping stated that AI development should be a symphony of international cooperation rather than a solo performance. He said that the world must guard against the overstretching of national security concerns during the development of AI. The official Chinese narrative in People's Daily claims that the West treats computing power as an exclusive and scarce resource. Beijing claims that the West is moving toward a technological monopoly through technology denial restrictions and export controls. China positions its own approach as a universally beneficial public good that is anchored in serving humanity.

The United States government assesses that computing power will underpin economic growth just as oil and steel did previously. This assessment affects the race to build an AI ecosystem encompassing energy, critical minerals, and advanced models. Pax Silica is a US led initiative that focuses on securing supply chains critical to advanced artificial intelligence. Kazakhstan is the only country that has joined both the Pax Silica and the WAICO cooperation frameworks. Singapore is a Pax Silica participant that is considering an invitation from China to join the WAICO framework.

China established the Digital Silk Road in 2017 as a component of the Belt and Road Initiative. This initiative helps China develop relationships with countries across Asia, Africa, Europe, and Latin America through technological cooperation. Some WAICO members like Pakistan, Russia, and Indonesia had more than 50 recorded projects between 2013 and 2021. Other members including Tajikistan, Lesotho, Nicaragua, and South Africa had fewer than five projects during that same time period. Kenya adopted Chinese surveillance technologies to address security concerns and connected police stations through smart city initiatives.

The US and China are evolving into competing blocs with divergent approaches to AI regulation, safety, and data governance. These competing frameworks may make it difficult for the international community to establish common standards for AI systems. A country's association with either grouping could shape its access to advanced AI systems and related critical resources. The articles leave open whether existing economic relationships fully explain why countries choose to join the WAICO framework. It remains unclear how Singapore will respond to the invitation to join the Chinese led AI organization.

stories.Headline: Researchers unveil AIMS-QA framework to assess corporate modern slavery statements beyond compliance
stories.Summary:
Researchers unveiled an artificial intelligence evaluation framework called AIMS-QA to automate and deepen assessment of corporate modern slavery disclosures across international supply chains, according to a report dated 25 November 2026. The team designed the framework to assess statements beyond basic formal compliance. Modern slavery legislation in the United Kingdom in 2015 and Australia in 2018 legally mandates large corporate entities to submit annual public statements. Those statements detail actions taken to identify, assess and address human exploitation risks within operations and direct supplier relationships. Tens of thousands of statutory reports have accumulated across public registries and corporate portals over the subsequent decade.

Administrative agencies and independent monitors struggle to review more than a modest fraction of those reports. Most institutional evaluations remain restricted to labor-intensive manual inspections that merely verify basic formal compliance against statutory criteria. The substantive depth, practical quality and verification of reported corporate human rights initiatives remain largely unexamined. The researchers synthesized thirteen distinct open-source benchmarking frameworks established by civil society organizations, institutional investors and academic consortia. Across these source methodologies the investigation systematically identified 473 unique evaluative metrics.

The researchers consolidated those metrics into 209 streamlined questions distributed across 115 thematic topics. The analytical structure anchors upon the seven statutory reporting criteria stipulated under Section 16 of the Australian Modern Slavery Act 2018. Those criteria enumerate mandatory requirements including reporting entity identification, operational structure, slavery risk identification, mitigation and remediation activities, effectiveness measurement, consultation with owned subsidiaries and governing body sign-off. The authors adopted this framework as their primary operational benchmark because Australia's statutory design provides an exhaustive list of mandatory content requirements. The researchers introduced an explicit two-tier categorization system across their taxonomic question set.

Every question is labeled as either a statutory baseline obligation or a beyond compliance expectation. Statutory baseline questions mirror precise jurisdictional mandates, such that a negative finding signals probable corporate non-compliance with legal requirements. Beyond compliance questions capture advanced stakeholder benchmarks including supplier monitoring beyond direct tier-one operations, living wage provisions and dedicated worker grievance channels. The authors extracted an operational 37-question priority framework because the comprehensive 209-question taxonomy remains excessively expansive for rapid computational screening. Selection into this core analytical layer required meeting strict convergence or baseline criteria.

The team established a consensus threshold requiring that an indicator appear across at least three independent benchmarking systems, identifying 36 questions exhibiting broad stakeholder alignment. From this group, 35 questions were incorporated after discarding a single time-bound indicator regarding pandemic-era operational risks that lacked long-term cross-cycle relevance. The researchers integrated two non-negotiable statutory baseline questions addressing official board signatures and formal reporting entity identification. AIMS-QA deploys two sequential algorithmic agents, Agent 1 as a sentence-level classification and extraction engine and Agent 2 as a retrieval-augmented generation watchdog. The agents cooperate sequentially to extract verbatim evidence segments directly from unstructured statement files.

Agent 1 splits the text into discrete sentences before passing them to a fine-tuned ModernBERT transformer model. When an affirmative match is identified, an automated evidence retriever extracts the target sentence along with a surrounding contextual buffer of 100 preceding and following tokens. This evidence window is fed into the Gemma 2 27B open-weight large language model, which executes chain-of-thought instructions to generate an explanatory reasoning chain and an initial response. Agent 2 segments the disclosure document into multi-sentence overlapping text chunks of approximately five consecutive sentences using an automated chunk splitter. A fine-tuned SentenceBERT retriever transforms both the text chunks and the specific streamlined question into high-dimensional numerical vectors.

The researchers evaluated the standalone classification accuracy of Agent 1 across the fifty annotated statements comprising the AIMS.au test corpus, recording a macro F1 score of 0.740 across mandatory compliance criteria. The classifier achieved an F1 score of 0.866 for governing body approval and 0.820 for operational structure and supply chains. More nuanced qualitative categories yielded lower scores, such as 0.756 for risk identification, 0.785 for mitigation and remediation, 0.785 for responsible officer signature, 0.722 for consultation with controlled entities, 0.595 for effectiveness assessment and 0.594 for reporting entity identification. End-to-end operational testing was conducted across two successive evaluation phases using ten corporate disclosures drawn from the AIMS.au test repository. During diagnostic testing on five initial statements, researchers identified systemic context truncation when complex mitigation evidence exceeded a strict 2000-word context cap.

The team updated the pipeline to automatically divide oversized evidence spans into sequential chunks for individual inference before consolidating partial answers. The revised framework was validated on a held-out evaluation set of five distinct statements across all 37 priority questions, generating 185 unique statement-question instances assessed by two modern slavery domain experts. Statistical evaluation recorded an overall inter-rater agreement of 0.848 and a Cohen's kappa coefficient of 0.695 across the 185 evaluated instances. Concordance proved higher on the 177 question instances resolved directly by Agent 1, where expert agreement reached 0.858 with a Cohen's kappa of 0.714. The eight ambiguous instances routed to Agent 2 exhibited lower agreement of 0.625 and a Cohen's kappa of 0.000.

When benchmarked against expert human annotations, the complete system attained an overall accuracy of 0.838 against Expert 1 and 0.913 against Expert 2. The system achieved perfect accuracy across well-defined statutory requirements including approval, signature and entity identification. Error analysis revealed the language model occasionally struggled to separate related legal concepts, such as conflating statutory minimum wage compliance with voluntary living wage guarantees. The model also mistook generic internal whistleblowing hotlines for fully realized grievance mechanisms accessible to external supply chain workers. Criterion-level evidence retrieval occasionally caused the model to produce correct binary answers based on partially off-topic narrative evidence.

To preserve governance integrity, the system logs structured audit trails comprising model versioning, prompt scaffolding and cited textual spans, maintaining human interpretive authority. The articles state that ModernBERT was selected following prior comparative benchmarking on the sentence-annotated AIMS.au dataset, where it delivered the strongest classification accuracy across mandatory statutory tasks. The articles state that traditional question answering systems relying solely on general-purpose large language models remain prone to hallucinations. The articles state that conventional retrieval-augmented generation often retrieves misleading or tangentially related passages when confronted with domain-specific legal texts. The articles state that the watchdog operates at question-level granularity rather than Agent 1's broader criterion-level scope.

The articles state that the watchdog acts as a dedicated fallback mechanism for ambiguous or evidence-scarce filings. The articles state that the system triggers Agent 2 should Agent 1 fail to identify pertinent sentences or if the language model concludes the supplied context provides insufficient information. The articles state that the researchers refined compound question phrasing during the update. The articles state that the two modern slavery domain experts independently assessed the 185 instances to evaluate predictive accuracy and inter-annotator concordance. The articles state that the eight ambiguous instances reflected the inherent interpretive difficulty of edge cases that defeat initial classification.

The articles leave open what happens next, giving no deployment date, no adopting agency and no publication venue for the framework. The articles leave open whether administrative bodies will use the screening system and how its two-tier labels would be applied in practice. The articles leave open how the system would handle statements beyond the ten corporate disclosures drawn from the AIMS.au test repository. The articles leave open whether the lower agreement on the eight Agent 2 instances would be addressed in later versions. The articles leave open how the logged audit trails would be reviewed and by whom.

stories.Headline: TSX 60 boards treat AI as a risk but rarely assign oversight, study finds
stories.Summary:
The articles report that an empirical investigation of public regulatory disclosures filed by constituent corporations of Canada's benchmark TSX 60 index found a pronounced institutional disconnect between recognizing artificial intelligence as a material strategic operational risk and formally embedding technological oversight into corporate governance architectures. The articles state that corporate boards of directors have largely treated artificial intelligence through broad, generalized risk declarations while delaying the formal structural integration necessary for effective oversight, despite accelerating deployments of complex generative systems and predictive algorithmic software across primary organizational operations. The articles state that researchers examined approximately two hundred and forty corporate disclosure documents filed on the SEDAR+ repository as of December 2024, covering fiscal periods across 2023 and 2024. The articles state that the empirical corpus encompassed annual information forms, management's discussion and analysis reports, management information circulars, and standalone sustainability or corporate governance publications. The articles state that the analytical evaluation coded corporate practices across six core dimensions: material risk identification, board-level oversight structures, demonstrable director literacy, operational use, active technical development, and structured corporate educational initiatives.

The articles state that forty-five of the sixty index constituent companies, representing seventy-five percent of the TSX 60, explicitly identified artificial intelligence as a material corporate risk factor within their mandatory public filings. The articles state that cybersecurity vulnerabilities appeared as the predominant concern, documented in more than seventy percent of disclosures that acknowledged technological challenges, with companies consistently evaluating artificial intelligence as an operational attack vector or an amplifier of existing network breaches. The articles state that data privacy and regulatory uncertainty formed the second and third most prevalent concerns, reflecting heightened corporate anxiety over compliance with evolving international data protection mandates and undefined domestic statutory standards. The articles state that reputational exposure stemming from potential implementation failures, as well as internal technical governance deficits, also registered across company reports. The articles state that disclosures notably omitted critical risks prominent in contemporary research, such as generative algorithmic misinformation, autonomous decision-making liabilities, and systemic workforce displacement.

The articles state that only slightly more than half of TSX 60 constituent corporations reported having established any designated form of technological oversight at the board level, either through an assigned committee mandate or through the explicit revision of an existing board committee charter. The articles state that only two of the sixty examined companies disclosed the existence of an independent board committee with a defined mandate directed toward artificial intelligence. The articles state that merely ten percent of the firms documented the operational establishment of an executive management committee charged with technical stewardship. The articles state that the absence of specialized governance bodies suggests that while corporate leadership acknowledges escalating exposures, the vast majority of boards maintain unstructured, non-specialized deliberations that leave technical risk supervision distributed across general audit or risk committees. The articles state that demonstrable technological literacy was identified in only five percent of evaluated corporate directors, using a standard that credited any current or historical employment with technological firms, executive roles relevant to automated systems, relevant corporate directorships, accredited professional credentials, or specific technical leadership titles.

The articles state that sectoral evaluations demonstrated that this scarce expertise remains heavily concentrated within dedicated technology corporations, while federally regulated financial institutions and capital market participants lag behind despite managing extensive data-heavy algorithmic networks. The articles state that approximately forty percent of surveyed enterprises explicitly disclosed utilizing artificial intelligence within operational workflows, whereas less than ten percent reported developing proprietary software models. The articles state that researchers noted that formal operational figures likely understate shadow adoption by staff, an informal operational dynamic that heightens unmonitored intellectual property leakage and network security exposures. The articles state that slightly more than half of the TSX 60 corporations documented that their sitting directors had received structured presentations or continuing educational briefings concerning technological transformations and machine learning systems. The articles state that this finding stands in contrast to broader private and public corporate survey benchmarks, where sixty-four percent of surveyed directors reported never having participated in specialized technical education programs.

The articles state that two-thirds of the TSX 60 cohort failed to disclose the formal adoption of comprehensive, company-wide internal policies or binding conduct guidelines regulating algorithmic deployments. The articles state that approximately five percent of evaluated TSX 60 constituent enterprises reported voluntary compliance with the federal Voluntary Code of Conduct on the Responsible Development and Management of Advanced Generative AI Systems promulgated by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada. The articles state that under the Canada Business Corporations Act, as well as provincial commercial statutes in Quebec, corporate directors bear an unyielding fiduciary duty of loyalty to act in good faith with a view to the best interests of the corporate entity as an ongoing legal person. The articles state that decisions rendered by the Supreme Court of Canada in the landmark Peoples and BCE adjudications established that this institutional duty is owed strictly to the corporation itself rather than exclusively to residual equity shareholders. The articles state that this objective authorizes directors to evaluate contextual stakeholder interests, encompassing employees, consumers, creditors, and environmental considerations.

The articles state that corporate directors operate under an objective duty of care requiring the diligence, skill, and prudence that a reasonably competent individual would exercise under comparable operational circumstances. The articles state that Canadian jurisprudence has firmly recognized that this monitoring obligation entails an institutional duty of corporate oversight, compelling boards to maintain robust internal control architectures and operational reporting channels that deliver timely, objective visibility into managerial execution and statutory compliance. The articles state that the formal securities regulatory framework governing Canadian reporting issuers continues to rely upon a disclosure-centric approach anchored in National Policy 58-201 and National Instrument 58-101, established in 2005 by the Canadian Securities Administrators and adopted by provincial regulatory commissions, operating on a flexible comply-or-explain structure. The articles state that the foundational governance guidelines codified within National Policy 58-201 have not undergone substantive revision since their initial promulgation, preserving a static normative standard that entirely omits contemporary computational systems, automated data models, and enterprise digital risks. The articles state that the regulatory body released Staff Notice and Consultation 11-348 in December 2024 to clarify that existing reporting standards govern computational systems in capital markets, and that non-binding staff interpretations afford broad subjective latitude that impedes cross-market consistency and undermines investor evaluation.

The articles state that Glass Lewis updated its formal benchmark voting guidelines for the 2025 proxy season, explicitly establishing expectations that corporate boards implement verifiable oversight architectures, invest in director technical education, and publish comprehensive disclosures detailing board accountability. The articles state that the proxy advisory firm cautioned that identified managerial negligence or unmitigated technological harm could trigger explicit negative voting recommendations against responsible board committee members. The articles state that institutional shareholder organizations, including the Mouvement d'education et de defense des actionnaires in Canada, filed formal corpora, and the articles end there. The articles leave open what the filed formal corpora contain and what response, if any, the sixty TSX 60 companies or Canadian regulators have made to the study's findings. The articles leave open whether National Policy 58-201 will be revised and what the 2025 proxy season outcomes will be. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Doctor West outlines patient opt-out rules for AI use in healthcare
stories.Summary:
Dr. Brittanie West discussed the parameters for artificial intelligence in healthcare in Ghent, West Virginia. She spoke about the progress and usage of this technology in medical settings. The doctor aimed to clear up confusion regarding how AI is used. This discussion occurred around November 25, 2026.

The system requires a framework to protect patients and make the lives of physicians easier. Many health networks and facilities across the nation are creating governance committees. These organizations are also putting together AI taskforces to oversee the usage of the technology. Patients will have the option to opt out of AI usage during appointments. AI is predominantly used for transcription purposes in a generative capacity.

Dr. West is a graduate of the West Virginia School of Osteopathic Medicine. She stated that people cannot run without rules for this technology. She believes that opting out of AI is a valid patient choice. This is similar to refusing a recommended medicine or surgery. It is also like asking for a second opinion from another person.

Some people may be cautious about if or how AI is used in the doctor's room. Patients are the ones affected by these governance rules and the ability to opt out. The physicians' lives are also affected by the implementation of these tools. The framework is designed to balance physician ease with patient protection.

The articles provide background on the progress of artificial intelligence within the healthcare field. AI is now being integrated into various medical settings across the country. This integration has led to the need for oversight and specific rules. The technology is currently being used for generative transcription tasks.

The articles do not state what will happen next for these taskforces. They leave open how specific governance committees will implement their rules. It is unclear which health networks have already finished their frameworks. The text does not say how many patients choose to opt out. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Report says investment firm should answer for client AI assistant trades
stories.Summary:
A Canadian investment executive told researchers their company would answer for mistakes its AI made, even if the software came from a supplier, according to a report released Nov. 24 by FAIR Canada and ParameterInsights. Some investors are already using AI they chose themselves to buy and sell shares. None of the executives interviewed for the report described who would be responsible when a customer's own AI assistant acts on an investment account. The report says the company that gives the assistant access should answer for what it does, just as it would for an employee.

stories.Headline: China urges AI-driven security defence to counter emerging tech risks
stories.Summary:
On Wednesday, November 26, 2026, an official commentary warned that China must strengthen its ability to assess and prevent new and unseen security risks. Fu Xiaoqiang, the president of the China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations, wrote the piece published in Study Times. He argued that technological revolutions and shifting global power balances are creating unprecedented challenges for the nation. These deepening social transformations have made the national security landscape facing China increasingly grim and complex.

The proposed solution requires the construction of a comprehensive framework centered on awareness, prevention, governance, and innovation. This new approach aims to address the security threats emerging from the current era of rapid technological change. The strategy emphasizes the need for an AI-driven security defence to counter these evolving dangers. By integrating these four pillars, the government hopes to better manage the risks associated with modern innovation.

Fu Xiaoqiang is the official responsible for these warnings as the leader of a think tank affiliated with the Ministry of State Security. He stated that the world is currently experiencing momentous changes unseen in a century that shape the modern environment. These shifts have rendered the existing security situation more difficult for the country to navigate. He believes that the nation must adapt its defensive capabilities to survive these new pressures.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Apple gains 30.61% in 2026 as light AI spending shields it from selloff
stories.Summary:
Apple stock gained 30.61% in 2026 while Nvidia lost 21.35%, according to TradingView data, as the AI selloff rewarded the company that spent least on AI infrastructure. Apple shares slid 7.5% between Oct. 23 and Nov. 3, which the article says suggests holders swapped AI spending risk for valuation risk. Apple cut capex by 29% in fiscal 2026, CFO Dive reported, while research and development spending rose 32% to $45.8 billion. Amazon plans $220 billion in capex this year, Microsoft $170 billion, Alphabet targets up to $205 billion and Meta $145 billion. Apple rebuilt Siri on Google's Gemini models through a June partnership and runs heavier AI tasks on Nvidia chips inside its Private Cloud Compute servers, CFO Dive added.

Apple reported September-quarter revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12% from a year earlier. Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh guided to 7% to 10% growth for the holiday quarter and said AI gives customers a reason to upgrade, which ties the new Siri to iPhone demand. Parekh also flagged rising memory costs and warned that gross margin would soften from the September quarter's 47.9%. The Nasdaq 100 sat about 15% below its October record as of Nov. 18, and Apple set an intraday record of $360.83 on Nov. 13. Only Apple and Amazon were beating the S&P 500 fund SPY's 7.4% gain as of Nov. 17.

Apple's 5.31% one-day jump on Nov. 4 was its best session in 1.5 years, and the stock then slipped only 1.5% while the Nasdaq fell 5.52%. Nvidia shares fell 11.3% in premarket trading after Jensen Huang's resignation on Nov. 12, and a 30% rebound on his return faded within a day. The Securities and Exchange Commission has reportedly opened a probe into Nvidia's accounting practices, and TradingView shows Nvidia down 33.01% over three months. The analysis put Apple at about 39 times earnings against 28 for Microsoft, a premium that assumes the holiday guidance holds. Analyst estimates put peer capex above $700 billion this year.

The article says investors long criticised Apple as an AI laggard, and the same lean spending now works as insulation since peers carry the data center bills. It says the case depends on AI spending staying unrewarded, and if that spending starts producing revenue the old criticism of Apple as an AI laggard could return. Siri's reliance on Gemini adds a second exposure, this time to a direct rival, and memory costs add a third. The article says the rally shows investors treating AI capex as a cost until it earns a return. It says Apple's climb has not been without its volatility and that the tech giant has showed remarkable resilience in a market currently under pressure.

More to follow.
